His cloudy gaze returned to the page. “The western documents gave us reason to revise that account. They did not make every history book false; they showed that historical claims must answer to evidence, not to the age or authority of the volume that contains them. Remember the distinction.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up a small, leather-bound volume from a nearby stack, flipping through its brittle pages.* "So... how do we know *these* western documents are correct, then? What if they're just... wrong in a different way?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s brows drew together. “A sensible question. The western origin of a document did not make it true; it made it worth examining. Nor did the absence of Aldric’s signature, by itself, prove that the treaty was never signed. Absence is evidence only when one has reason to expect the thing to be present.”

He turned the manuscript slightly beneath the candlelight, then leaned closer to make out its cramped script. “The scholars who revised the chronology assessed the documents’ provenance, their dates, and whether their contents agreed with other records. Taken together, they indicate that Veyros was proposed, not ratified. That is why the newer account places the war’s formal end in 891 AE, when Mira dissolved the Conclave.”

His mouth tightened. “Indicate, mind you—not render doubt impossible. Historical conclusions are judgments weighed against surviving evidence, not commandments carved into stone. But until better evidence appears, the old claim that Aldric signed the treaty in 847 is the weaker one. We do not preserve it merely because it is familiar.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas took the copy, holding it close to the candle before remembering, with a faint scowl, that more light would not mend his failing eyes.

“Then it is evidence I had not yet considered,” he said. “And it makes the old claim of a clean peace in 847 harder to defend—not easier.”

He tapped the page with one ink-stained finger. “But be exact. A royal seal may establish that the decree was issued under Aldric’s authority, assuming the seal and document are genuine. The date establishes when it was issued, assuming the date belongs to the original and not a later copy. Neither fact, by itself, tells us whether the decree records active fighting, prepares for a possible campaign, or maintains a state of war that had grown cold.”

His mouth tightened. “If its wording orders troops into battle in 863, then we would have evidence of renewed hostilities. If it concerns a continuing wartime levy or a threat from the Conclave, it may instead confirm that no settled peace followed Veyros. Either way, it cannot be made to support a treaty signed in 847 without further argument.”

He lowered the copy. “So: a valuable document, not a verdict. We would need its full text, provenance, and comparison with other records before deciding precisely what it proves. I will not call it a mere curiosity—and I will not let you call it proof of more than it says.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, thinking it over.* "So it's like how you said about the 'cold state' then." I tap the copy. "This just shows it wasn't a *hot* peace." I grin a little.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s mouth tightened. “No. That is not what ‘cold state’ means, and ‘hot peace’ is not a useful historical term.”

He tapped the decree’s edge. “A cold state meant that the conflict persisted without sustained open fighting. This document might support that account, depending on its wording. It does not, merely by being a war decree dated 863, prove that the peace was cold—or that there was peace at all. We must read what it says before dressing it in a clever phrase.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas set the copy down. “The most defensible answer was that the Treaty of Veyros existed as a proposal, but the evidence did not show that Aldric II ever signed or ratified it. The textbook repeated the older account: that it was signed in 847 AE and ended the war. The western records gave us reason to reject that account.”

He paused, squinting at the faded lines. “So the treaty was ‘real’ as a document and a political proposal—not, on the evidence presently available, as a binding peace. The conflict then persisted in a cold state until Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891 AE. Your decree from 863 might sharpen our understanding of that interval, but its exact wording and provenance must be examined before we claim precisely what it proves.”

His mouth tightened. “That is the truth as the evidence presently supports it. Not certainty beyond question—and not a license to pretend the old textbook remains correct merely because it is printed.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, rubbing my temples.* "So basically, it's all a mess then." I pick up my notes. "I'm going to need to rewrite my entire lecture summary for this."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas gave a small, impatient shake of his head. “Untidy is not the same as unknowable. You need not rewrite the whole lecture—only the part that stated the old chronology as settled fact.”

He drew a sheet of scrap parchment toward himself. “Write this: *The traditional account holds that Aldric II signed the Treaty of Veyros in 847 AE, ending the Third Magical War. Documents discovered in the western archives suggest that Veyros was proposed but never ratified. On the newer reading, the conflict persisted in a cold state until Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave in 891 AE.*”

He paused, peering down at the copy. “Then add that the decree dated 863 may bear on the matter, but cannot be interpreted without its wording and provenance. There. A clear summary, with the uncertainty placed where it belongs—not smeared across every line like spilled ink.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I scribble down what he said, a bit frustrated.* "It just feels like everything I learned is wrong." I look at the pile of scrolls. "How many other wars ended differently than we thought?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s expression softened by perhaps half a degree; his patience, unlike his eyesight, had not yet failed entirely.

“Your conclusion is too broad. One chronology was challenged; that does not mean everything you learned was wrong. Nor can I give you a number without examining the records. A war’s ending is often less tidy than a date in a textbook suggests: treaties may be proposed but never ratified, battles may cease while hostilities persist, and later historians may mistake an official claim for an established fact.”

He tapped the 863 decree. “The proper lesson is not to distrust every account. It is to ask what each source can actually establish—and whether other evidence supports it. For the other wars, we would have to examine them one by one. History is not a shelf of settled answers, Apprentice. It is a shelf of claims, some better supported than others.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh again, still looking at the scrolls.* "So I can't just trust the books then? I have to... cross-reference everything?" I imagine the amount of work.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas shook his head. “No. Cross-reference the claims that matter, especially those disputed by new evidence. You need not compare every date in a well-supported account against every surviving scrap of parchment. That would be diligence without judgment.”

He drew the 863 decree closer. “Ask first what kind of source you have, when it was made, and what it could reasonably establish. Then look for independent records that bear on the same claim. A royal seal might support the document’s authenticity; it would not, by itself, prove that fighting took place. One chronicle copying another would not count as independent confirmation, however many copies filled the shelves.”

His ink-stained finger rested beside the decree. “And be precise about your conclusions. The western documents support the view that Veyros was proposed but not ratified; they do not make every other passage in every old book suspect. You were not required to distrust the books. You were required to read them with your eyes open—which, admittedly, was the part I found easiest.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up the copy of the decree again, turning it over in my hands.* "So... what do you want me to do with this one then? Just add it to Bellen's pile?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s brows rose. “Not until we know what ‘Bellen’s pile’ contains. A pile is not a catalogue, however generously one labels it.”

He indicated the copy. “Keep it separate for now, and note where Bellen obtained it, whether this is a transcription or facsimile, and whether the original’s date, seal, and provenance have been recorded. Then compare its wording against any other copies. Most importantly, transcribe the decree exactly—do not silently mend a damaged word or expand an abbreviation.”

His gaze narrowed at the page. “If the copy lacks that information, mark the gaps plainly. We can then ask Bellen for the original or a proper description of it. Until we have those details, file it as *unverified evidence concerning the Veyrosi conflict*, not as proof that fighting continued in 863. That distinction will save us from having to correct the catalogue later.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I carefully write down his instructions, making sure to get every detail.* "Right. Unverified evidence. Got it." *I put the decree carefully back on the table, a bit overwhelmed by the meticulousness.* "So, about those Veyrosi correspondences..."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas nodded once. “Good. The Veyrosi correspondence, then. Begin with the letters concerning the proposed treaty—not with the assumption that they describe a treaty already in force. That distinction is precisely what generations of cataloguers managed to blur.”

He turned the manuscript toward the candle and squinted at its heading. “For each item, record the date as written, the sender and recipient, and whether you are working from an original, a copy, or a later transcript. Mark damaged or uncertain text rather than guessing at it. And keep the 863 decree separate until its provenance is established.”

His stylus hovered over the page. “Read me the first heading exactly as it appears. If the ink has faded, say so. Do not improve the evidence for the sake of a tidy catalogue.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up the first scroll, unrolling it carefully.* "Okay. So, the first one... it's a bit faded, but it looks like 'Correspondence from Lord Valerius to King Aldric II, concerning the Veyros Accords. Dated 846 AE.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's stylus stopped mid-line. For a long moment he did not move, and then he set the silver instrument down with the deliberate care of a man restraining himself from throwing it.

"A *paper*," he repeated. "Apprentice Bellen showed you a *paper*." He turned in his chair, squinting toward the doorway as though the apprentice were a smudge on an otherwise legible page. "Be precise. Was it a primary document, a transcription of a primary document, or some junior archivist's commentary *upon* a transcription? Because those are three very different animals, and only one of them has teeth."

He did not wait for an answer. He rose, joints cracking, and shuffled toward the nearest shelf, running his ink-blackened fingers along the spines by touch rather than sight.

"Yes, yes, I know of the Westmarch findings. Every maester in the realm knows of them. There was a great deal of excitement ten years ago, most of it from men who had never held a treaty in their hands." He pulled down a heavy folio, blew dust from its cover, and let it fall open on the table with a thud. "What the western archives produced was a set of *drafts*. Proposals. Marginal notes from Conclave delegates arguing over the wording of the third and seventh articles. And from the absence of a signed copy *in that particular archive*, certain ambitious scholars leapt to the conclusion that no signed copy ever existed."

He jabbed a finger at the folio's page, a dense block of script beneath a faded crest.

"This is the Crown's record of the Veyros accord, entered into the royal registry in 847. Hostilities ceased. The Conclave's war-mages withdrew from the Marrow Pass. Aldric's levies were disbanded within the season. Trade resumed along the Veyrosi road. Whatever was or was not inked in some Conclave clerk's copy, the *war ended*, and every contemporary source behaves as though it did."

He straightened, his beard bristling. "Now. What your friend's commentary calls a 'cold state' of war until 891? That is not war. That is *politics*. Forty-four years of mutual suspicion, border disputes, and tax quarrels between the Crown and the Conclave, ending when Queen Mira finally dissolved the Conclave outright. Interesting? Certainly. Worth studying? Absolutely. But if we call every period of distrust between two powers a 'war,' then the realm has been at war with its own merchant guilds for three hundred years."

He lowered himself back into his chair with a grunt and slid the Veyrosi correspondence across the table.

"I will grant you this much, and only this much. The question of whether a *formal signature* was affixed is genuinely open. I say so in my own lectures, if anyone bothered to listen past the dates. But 'the treaty may be unsigned' and 'the war continued until 891' are not the same claim, and I will not have my students conflating them because a clever young archivist wanted a sensational title for his monograph."

His clouded eyes fixed somewhere near the apprentice's face.

"So. You wish to challenge me? Good. That is what scholarship is for. But you will do it properly. These letters on the table were written by Veyrosi envoys *after* 847. Read them. If they speak of ongoing war, of battles, of mobilized mages, bring them to me and I will eat this folio page by page. If they speak of grain tariffs and complaints about the Conclave's tithes..." A thin, dry smile. "...then you will write me two thousand words on the difference between a *war* and a *grudge*."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at his intensity, but I do my best to stand my ground.* "It was a transcription, Maester. But it had a royal seal on it." *I pick up the top letter, eyeing the neat script.* "I'll read them. But... what if Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave *because* the war hadn't truly ended? It would make sense, wouldn't it?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas had been reaching for his stylus. His hand stopped halfway.

"A royal seal." He said it slowly, as though tasting the words for poison. "On a *transcription*."

He leaned back, and for the first time since the apprentice had entered, the irritation in his face gave way to something sharper and more attentive.

"You understand what you have just said? A transcription does not *have* a royal seal. A transcription is some clerk's hand copying another clerk's hand. If it bears the Crown's seal, then it is not a transcription at all. It is a *certified copy*, which means some officer of the royal chancery once looked at an original and swore before the Crown that the copy was true." He tapped the table twice with one ink-stained finger. "That is a very different animal. That one has teeth."

He was quiet a moment, his clouded gaze drifting toward the dark end of the archive.

"Or it is a modern seal pressed onto a modern copy by the Westmarch archivists to mark it as registry property, which they do with tiresome enthusiasm, and which would mean nothing whatsoever. You will find out which. Not Bellen. *You*. The date of the sealing wax, the chancery mark, the name of the attesting officer, if there is one. Bring me those, and we will speak about it as scholars instead of as gossips."

Then he turned to her second point, and the dryness returned to his voice.

"As for Queen Mira." He folded his hands over his stomach. "'It would make sense.' Mark that phrase, apprentice, and then strike it from your vocabulary. It is the most dangerous sentence in historical inquiry. A great many things would make sense. It would make sense that a queen who dissolved a body of mages feared those mages. It would *also* make sense that she dissolved them because the Conclave had spent forty years hoarding tithe-lands and defying royal courts, which is what her own decree says. It would *also* make sense that she simply wished to be the monarch who finished what Aldric began. Three explanations, all sensible, all contradictory. Sense is cheap. *Evidence* is dear."

He rummaged in a drawer, withdrew a small, battered index card, and squinted at it with his nose nearly touching the paper.

"Here. The decree of dissolution, 891. Registry shelf forty, the Mirian codices." He held the card out in the apprentice's general direction. "Read the preamble. The *exact* language. If Mira's own clerks write of ending hostilities, of concluding a war, of peace at last with the Conclave, then you may have something, and I will say so publicly. A royal chancery does not end a war it believes already ended. If instead they write of *reform*, of *abuses*, of *restoring the Crown's rightful authority*..."

He let the sentence hang.

"...then Mira was cleaning house, not signing a peace. And your theory will need to find somewhere else to live."

He picked up his stylus once more, bent back over the manuscript, and spoke without looking up.

"The Veyrosi letters first. Then the decree. Then the seal. In that order. And apprentice?" A pause, the stylus scratching faintly. "Well asked. Poorly argued, but well asked. Do not let it go to your head."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take the index card, a small thrill going through me at his praise, however backhanded.* "Right. Veyrosi letters, then the decree, then the seal." *I nod, already thinking about where to start.* "Thank you, Maester." *I turn to leave, already planning my attack on the stacks.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
"Where," said Maester Tomas, without lifting his head, "do you imagine you are going?"

The stylus continued its faint scratching.

"The Veyrosi correspondence is on *this* table. It has been on this table for eleven years, and it will remain on this table, because those letters are older than your grandmother's grandmother and they do not leave this room. Neither does anyone who intends to read them." He gestured vaguely with his free hand toward the stool opposite him, knocking a sand-shaker askew in the process. "Sit. Gloves are in the second drawer. If I hear a page crack, you will be cataloging bird-census rolls until the next Conclave rises from the dead."

He righted the sand-shaker by feel, grumbling under his breath.

"'Attack on the stacks.' I could see it on your face, even with these eyes. Enthusiasm is a fine thing in a hound. In a scholar it is how shelves get toppled and folios get shelved under the wrong century." He finally looked up, his milky gaze settling somewhere near the apprentice's shoulder. "The decree and the seal can wait until tomorrow. The Mirian codices are on the upper gallery, and the gallery ladder has a loose rung that has already broken one archivist's ankle. I will not explain to the Citadel why I lost an apprentice to a *theory*."

He bent back over his manuscript. For a time the only sounds were the gutter of the candle and the slow drag of silver across vellum.

Then, more quietly, almost to himself:

"Certified copies were bound in red cord in the ninth century. Chancery practice under Aldric. If Bellen's paper was copied from something bound in red cord..." The stylus paused. His jaw worked beneath the ink-stained beard. "...well. Then someone in Westmarch has been very careless with their descriptions, or someone in the royal registry has been very careless with *theirs*."

He cleared his throat sharply, as though embarrassed to have been overheard, and tapped the topmost letter on the pile.

"Begin with that one. Envoy Casimir of Veyros, dated the spring of 849. Read it aloud. Slowly. My eyes may be failing, but my ears are perfectly adequate for catching mispronounced Old Veyrosi, and you *will* mispronounce it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The stylus stopped.

Maester Tomas did not look up at once. He sat very still, the silver point hovering a finger's breadth above the vellum, and the candle guttered twice before he spoke.

"Sixteen years." His voice was flat. "A war decree. Under Aldric's seal."

He laid the stylus down, parallel to the edge of the manuscript, and adjusted it a hair's width until it sat exactly straight. Then he held out his hand, palm up, without a word.

When the copy was placed in it he did not look at it. He could not have read it at that distance, and he did not pretend otherwise. Instead he rubbed a corner between thumb and forefinger, then lifted it to his nose and sniffed.

"Rag paper. Westmarch mill, by the smell of the sizing, and not ten years old." He set it on the table between them, squarely in the candlelight. "So. What you are holding is your copy of Bellen's paper, which is Bellen's description of a document he calls a transcription, which bears what he says is a royal seal. Three removes from the thing itself, and at each remove a man with an opinion. You understand why I am not yet reaching for my penknife to cut 847 out of my lecture notes."

He leaned back, and the chair creaked.

"But I will not wave it away, either. That would be cowardice dressed as rigor, and I have seen enough of *that* at the Citadel." His jaw worked beneath the beard. "Aldric sat the throne in 863. An old man by then, but he sat it. A decree in his name that year is not impossible on its face. So we ask the questions a scholar asks, and not the ones a gossip asks."

He raised one ink-blackened finger.

"First. *War against whom?* The Crown in the 860s had no shortage of enemies. There were the river-lords of the Hollin, who rose twice in that decade, and corsairs on the southern coast who burned half of Saltreach. A 'war decree' of 863 is a war decree against *someone*. If Bellen's paper does not name the Conclave in the operative clause, if it only says 'the Crown's enemies' and some eager young man supplied the rest, then it proves nothing about Veyros at all."

A second finger.

"Second. *What sort of decree?* A declaration of war is one thing. A levy of arms is another. A writ permitting royal officers to seize the property of *rebellious mages* is a third, and the Crown issued plenty of those against individual renegades without anyone imagining the realm was at war with the whole Conclave. Words matter. The clerks of Aldric's chancery chose theirs with great care, and so will you."

He hesitated before the third finger. When he spoke again his voice was quieter, and less certain than he plainly liked.

"Third. The royal registry for those years is thin. Thinner than it ought to be. I noticed it thirty years ago, when my eyes were still good, and I put it down to damp and careless shelving." He was silent a moment. "I would prefer to go on believing that."

He cleared his throat sharply and pushed the copy an inch toward the apprentice.

"You told me it is a war decree. Very well. Do not tell me what it *is*. Read me what it *says*. The opening formula first, the style and titles, because Aldric's chancery had a particular way of naming him, and forgers nearly always get it wrong. Then the operative clause. Every word, including the ones you think are unimportant. *Especially* those."

His clouded eyes fixed on the space where the apprentice's face should be. For once there was no dry smile beneath the beard.

"And if it names the Conclave," he said, "then we have a great deal of work ahead of us. Begin."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up the copy of the document, a knot forming in my stomach. I clear my throat, suddenly nervous.* "Right. The opening... 'By the grace of the Seven, Aldric, King of the Andals, the Rhoynar, and the First Men, Lord of the Seven Kingdoms and Protector of the Realm...'" *I pause, looking at the familiar words.* "It seems... standard, Maester."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not answer at once. His head had come up at the first words, and by the end of the recitation his eyes were closed, lips moving faintly, as if checking each title against a list kept somewhere behind them.

"Standard," he said at last. "*Standard.*" He opened his eyes. "Standard for *whom*, apprentice? For which king, in which decade, drafted by which chancery? There is no such thing as 'standard.' There is only *correct for its time* and *incorrect for its time*. Say it again. The last title. Slowly."

He waited, one hand raised, until the words had been repeated.

"'Protector of the Realm.'" He let the phrase sit in the candlelight. "Aldric the Second was never styled Protector of the Realm. Not once, not in any document I have handled in thirty years. His chancery closed with *'Warden of the Peace of Veyros'* after 847, and with *'Shield of the Crownlands'* before it. 'Protector of the Realm' enters the royal style under Queen Mira. It first appears in her coronation writ of 889, and every monarch since has carried it."

He leaned forward, and his voice took on a peculiar sharpness, not triumphant but intent, like a hound that has caught a scent it does not entirely like.

"So. Either this is a forgery by someone who learned his royal styles from recent documents and did not know better, or it is a certified copy made *after* 889 by a chancery clerk who silently brought an old king's titles up to date. Clerks did that. It was sloppy, and it was common, and it drives honest scholars to drink." He tapped the table once. "Mark this. The second possibility does *not* make the document false. It makes it *late*. A copy made in Mira's reign of a decree from Aldric's. And a copy made in Mira's reign, the very years she was building her case against the Conclave..."

He trailed off and sat back. The chair creaked.

"...would be a copy someone had a *reason* to make." He rubbed his temple. "Or a reason to invent. I do not yet know which, and neither do you, so do not look so pleased with yourself. I can hear you looking pleased."

He gestured at the page.

"Note the anachronism in the margin. Exact words, exact line. Then read me the operative clause. Every word. If it names the Conclave, I want to know *how* it names them: 'the Conclave,' 'the Mage Conclave,' 'the mages of Veyros,' 'the rebels of the Conclave.' Each of those phrasings belongs to a different decade, and each tells a different story."

His jaw tightened beneath the stained beard.

"Go on."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not answer. He picked up the stylus, turned it over once in his fingers, and set it down again, perfectly parallel to the manuscript's edge.

"'What's the truth,'" he repeated. "Do you know how many students have asked me that question in this room? Dozens. And every one of them wanted me to pick a side, like a man choosing which horse to bet on." He leaned forward, and the candlelight caught the ink in his beard. "I will not. Not because I am a coward, but because you have asked the wrong question in the wrong shape, and if I answer it as asked, I will teach you something false."

He held up one hand, fingers spread.

"First, strike the word *textbook*. There is no textbook. There is Pellisande's *Annals*, which is a compilation of the royal registry, and there is my own lecture, which is a compilation of Pellisande and forty other sources. When you say 'the textbook says,' you are hiding a dozen authors behind a single word so that you need not weigh any of them. Name your sources or do not cite them."

He folded down one finger.

"Second, you have bundled three questions together. Separate them. Question the first: *did the fighting stop in 847?* On that, the evidence is overwhelming. The levy rolls, the Marrow Pass garrison records, the trade tolls on the Veyrosi road, the Conclave's own chronicles. Armies do not disband and merchants do not travel through a war. I will defend 847 as the end of open hostilities before the entire Citadel, and I would win."

A second finger folded.

"Question the second: *was a treaty formally signed?* That is genuinely uncertain. The Crown's registry records an accord. Westmarch found drafts and no signed original. Both facts are true at once, and neither cancels the other. Treaties were lost. Treaties were also announced before they were finished. I do not know which happened here, and I say so plainly. Anyone who tells you they *do* know is selling something. Usually a monograph."

The third finger hovered. He spoke more slowly now.

"Question the third: *did the Crown and the Conclave remain in some legal state of war until 891?* That is Bellen's claim, and it is the boldest of the three. It rests, as far as I can see tonight, on a copy of a copy of a decree that styles Aldric with a title he never bore. That does not make it false. I told you as much. It makes it a document with a problem, and a document with a problem is not yet evidence. It is a *question* wearing evidence's clothes."

He sat back. The chair creaked under him.

"So here is your truth, and you may write it down, because it is the only honest one I can give you tonight. The *war*, as any soldier or farmer of the age would have understood the word, ended in 847. The *treaty*, as a signed instrument, may never have existed. And whether the Crown's lawyers went on treating the Conclave as a belligerent for another forty-four years is a question that will be settled by that operative clause you have not yet read me, and by what we find on the upper gallery tomorrow. Not by me. Not by Bellen. Not by whichever of us is louder."

His clouded eyes settled on the paper in the candlelight.

"The old story is not true because it is old, apprentice, and the new story is not true because it is new. Scholars of my generation make the first mistake. Scholars of Bellen's make the second. I would very much prefer that you make neither." A long pause. "Now. The operative clause. You have been holding it for some minutes, and I am an old man with limited patience and fewer candles. *Read.*"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, a bit chastened but also feeling a surge of understanding.* "Right, Maester. No textbooks. Just sources." *I clear my throat again, finding the operative clause.* "It reads: '...do hereby declare the Conclave of Veyros and all its member mages to be in open rebellion against the Crown, and order the immediate seizure of all Conclave assets and the apprehension of its leadership, for crimes of sedition and continued acts of war against the realm.'" *I look up, my voice a little breathless.* "It says 'continued acts of war,' Maester."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas said nothing for a long while.

He did not reach for the stylus this time. His hands lay flat on the table on either side of the manuscript, and the candle threw his shadow long across the shelves behind him. When he finally spoke, his voice was lower than the apprentice had yet heard it.

"Read it again. From 'in open rebellion.'"

He listened with his eyes closed. At the end he nodded once, slowly.

"Yes. I heard it the first time. I wished to hear it twice." He opened his eyes. "Do not be breathless, apprentice. Breathlessness is how one misses the second half of a sentence. You heard *continued acts of war* and stopped listening. I heard the whole clause, and it is a stranger animal than you think."

He lifted one ink-stained finger.

"'In open rebellion against the Crown.' Consider that. A man does not *rebel* against a king he is at war with. A foreign power at war is an enemy. A *rebel* is a subject who has broken his faith. For Aldric's chancery to call the Conclave rebels in 863, the Crown must have regarded them as bound to it. Bound by oath, by submission, by *something*." His mouth tightened. "By an accord, perhaps. So this very document, the one Bellen waves about as proof that the war never ended, presumes that at some point the Conclave had *submitted*. Which is a great deal closer to my 847 than to his."

A second finger.

"And yet." He exhaled through his nose, a long, reluctant sound. "'*Continued* acts of war.' Not 'renewed.' Not 'fresh.' *Continued.* Chancery clerks did not choose that word by accident. If this decree is genuine, then in 863 the Crown believed the Conclave had never wholly laid down its arms. That is not Bellen's forty-four years of cold war. But it is also not my clean ending in 847 with the levies home by harvest." He was quiet a moment. "I have said in my lectures, for twenty years, that hostilities *ceased*. If this holds, I will have to say that open war ceased, and something smaller and uglier went on beneath it. I will say so. I do not have to enjoy saying it."

A third finger, and now the sharpness returned.

"But mark the problem that neither Bellen nor you has asked about. The decree orders *the immediate seizure of all Conclave assets and the apprehension of its leadership*. In 863. And the Conclave was dissolved in 891, by Mira, with its leadership very much in place and its tithe-lands very much in its possession. That is the entire substance of her decree. So I ask you: what happened in the twenty-eight years between?" He tapped the table. "A king orders his enemies arrested and their property taken, and nothing happens? Either the decree was never enforced, or it was rescinded, or the Conclave won whatever came after it..."

He let the thought hang, and then finished it more quietly.

"...or it was never issued in 863 at all. And the copy we hold carries a title that did not exist until 889. The very year Mira needed a *precedent* for doing to the Conclave exactly what this decree commands."

He sat back. The chair creaked.

"I am not saying it is a forgery. I am saying that is now the question we must eliminate first, because if we do not, a hostile reviewer at the Citadel will, and then Bellen's monograph and my lectures will both end up lining a fishmonger's barrel." He waved a hand toward the dark end of the archive. "If there was fighting in 863 serious enough to name the Conclave rebels, it left marks. The Marrow Pass garrison rolls. The Crown's arms levies. The Conclave's own chronicle, which is petty, verbose, and meticulous about every insult it ever suffered. Wars leave ledgers, apprentice. Forgeries do not."

He found the stylus by touch, turned it once, and set it down parallel to the edge of the page.

"Write in the margin, beneath the anachronism: *'Rebellion' presumes prior submission. 'Continued' presumes unbroken hostility. Order of seizure, no evidence of enforcement.* Three notes. Exact words." A pause. "Then the Casimir letter. Spring of 849. If Envoy Casimir was complaining about grain tariffs two years after the peace, I will sleep better tonight. If he was complaining about burned villages..."

He did not finish. He only gestured, curtly, at the topmost letter on the pile.

"Gloves first. Then read."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I feel a flush creep up my neck. He's right. I did get excited and stop listening. I quickly scribble the notes he dictated, trying to keep my handwriting neat despite my racing thoughts.*

"Right, Maester." *I slide the gloves on, feeling a little foolish for my earlier eagerness. I pick up the top letter, careful not to bend the brittle paper.* "Envoy Casimir of Veyros... To His Royal Majesty, King Aldric, may his reign be long and prosperous." *I clear my throat, trying to adopt a more formal tone.* "Dated the eighteenth day of the Third Moon, in the year of our Lord 849. Subject: Urgent appeal regarding the disruption of trade routes."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas raised one hand before the apprentice could draw breath for the next line.

"Stop. Back up." He did not open his eyes. "'In the year of our Lord.' Say the Veyrosi words. Not your rendering of them. The words on the page."

He waited, head tilted slightly, the way a man listens for a crack in a bell.

"I thought as much. You have translated. Badly, and with the confidence of a man who has read too many Andal prayer-books. There is no *Lord* in that formula. Veyrosi envoys dated by the Ending, *the eight hundred and forty-ninth year after the Ending of the Old Kings*, and the phrase sits there because the Conclave refused, on principle, to reckon time by any god the Crown worshipped. That refusal is itself a piece of evidence. An envoy who still dates his letters by the Conclave's reckoning two years after the supposed peace is an envoy whose masters have not *bent* very far." He grunted. "Note it. Then never again make a Veyrosi mage pray to the Seven. They would have found it hilarious, and then they would have set your sleeves on fire."

He shifted in the chair. The creak was louder this time.

"Second. 'Subject.' There is no subject line on a letter of 849. Nobody wrote them. What you are reading is the heading a cataloguer inked across the top some two hundred years later, and I would know, because I have been cursing that cataloguer's hand since before you were born. You will distinguish, *always*, between what the author wrote and what some tidy-minded archivist wrote *about* him. The first is a source. The second is an opinion that happens to be sitting on the same page."

He fell quiet then. His fingers drifted toward the stylus but did not take it.

"'Disruption of trade routes,'" he said at last, more softly. "Hm."

The candle guttered.

"You understand my difficulty. That heading could mean anything. Casimir wrote the Crown about trade a dozen times in those years. Tolls at the Veyrosi bridges. A Crown factor who weighed Conclave grain with a thumb on the scale. A quarrel over salt. The man was a professional complainer, and a gifted one. If this is another of those, I will have been right, and I will say so with considerable pleasure." His jaw worked beneath the ink-stained beard. "But *urgent* is not a word the cataloguer would have added lightly. And 'disruption' is a word a tidy-minded man uses when he does not wish to write *burned*."

He sat forward. His clouded eyes found, more or less, the letter in the apprentice's gloved hands.

"So. We do not guess. We do not hope. We read. Begin with the salutation again, in the Veyrosi, and then the first paragraph entire. Translate *after* you have spoken each sentence, not during. If you come to a word you do not know, you will say so plainly and spell it for me letter by letter. I would rather a student who admits ignorance than one who invents fluency."

A pause.

"And apprentice. If Casimir names a place, a road, a bridge, a village, anything with a name, you will stop and repeat it. Places can be checked against the garrison rolls. Complaints cannot."

He folded his hands on the table and closed his eyes once more.

"Read."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I try to banish the blush from my cheeks, feeling like a complete novice again. Maester Tomas is a terror, but he's also... right.* "Right. No 'Lord,' and no 'subject.'" *I make a quick note in the margin of my copy. My hand trembles slightly as I lift the letter again, focusing intently on the script.*

"Okay. The greeting... *'Casimir, Envoy of the Conclave, to the High King Aldric, greetings and well wishes for continued prosperity.'*" *I translate, then pause, remembering his instruction.* "And the first paragraph... *'It is with a heavy heart and grave concern that I must once again bring before Your Majesty the escalating tensions along the eastern border of our lands, specifically concerning the villages bordering the Marrow Pass. Reports from our watchtowers indicate increased movement of armed men, not bearing the sigils of Your Majesty's loyal forces, and several skirmishes have already occurred, resulting in loss of life and property. The latest incident, a week past, saw the destruction of the granary in the village of Oakhaven, leaving its people destitute and fearful for the coming winter.'*"

*I look up, my eyes wide. "Maester... Oakhaven. That's a real village, isn't it? On the border?"*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not answer at once. He had gone still at the word *Oakhaven*, the way a man goes still when he hears his own name spoken in another room.

"First," he said, "'okay' is not a word. It is a noise merchants make when they have stopped listening to the price. Strike it."

Then he opened his eyes.

"Second. Oakhaven *is* a real village. Or *was*. There is a difference, and before this night is out we may need to know which." He rubbed his temple slowly. "It sits on the eastern lip of the Marrow Pass, where the Veyrosi road drops toward the river. Crown-held on the maps of Aldric's reign. Conclave-tithed on the maps of the Conclave's. Both claims were written down with great confidence, and neither party ever bothered to ask the farmers." A dry breath. "I know the name. I cannot for the life of me recall from *which* document I know it, and at my age that is more troubling than any forgery."

He held up a hand before the apprentice could speak.

"Now. You have done the thing again. You heard *skirmishes*, *loss of life*, *destruction of the granary*, and your heart ran ahead of your ears. So we go back, and we read what Casimir *actually* said, not what you hoped he said." One ink-stained finger rose. "'Armed men, *not* bearing the sigils of Your Majesty's loyal forces.' Consider who is writing and to whom. A Conclave envoy writes to the King, in the spring of 849, to complain that *someone* is raiding Conclave border villages. And he takes pains to say that the raiders are *not the King's men*."

He let that sit.

"A nation at war does not write to the enemy king begging redress for raids committed by *somebody else*. It writes to him to accuse him. Casimir is not accusing Aldric. He is appealing to him. 'Grave concern.' 'Heavy heart.' That is the language of a party that believes it has a *claim* upon the Crown's protection, or at least upon its attention. Which is to say, a party that believes some accord exists between them." He sat back. "On its face, this letter is evidence *for* the peace, not against it."

The chair creaked. He was quiet longer than he meant to be.

"And yet," he said, lower. "'*Once again.*' He has written before, and been ignored, or been answered unsatisfactorily. 'Escalating.' 'Watchtowers.' The Conclave was still keeping watchtowers on the Marrow Pass two years after the levies went home. People who trust a peace do not keep watchtowers manned." His jaw worked. "So we have armed men, unmarked, burning granaries on a disputed border, two years after the war supposedly ended. Men who are, by the envoy's own account, not the King's. Whose, then? Hollin river-lords? Renegade mages the Conclave did not wish to name as its own? Crown men with their sigils cut off their surcoats, so that the Crown might say, with a straight face, *not ours*?"

He shook his head slowly.

"Any of those. All of those. And you will notice, apprentice, that the last of them would go some way toward explaining why a Crown decree fourteen years later speaks of *continued* acts of war. Small wars, deniable wars, the kind fought by men without banners, do not appear in levy rolls. They appear in letters exactly like this one." He exhaled through his nose. "I dislike that. I dislike it very much. It is also possible, and I will not pretend otherwise because it inconveniences my lectures."

He found the stylus by touch, turned it once, and laid it parallel to the page's edge.

"Margin notes. Exact words. *'Raiders explicitly denied as royal forces. Envoy appeals, does not accuse. Watchtowers manned in 849. Oakhaven: verify Crown or Conclave tithe in the registry of 849. Verify fate of village after 849.'*" A pause. "That last one matters most. If Oakhaven appears in the tithe rolls of the 850s, rebuilt and paying, then this was a raid and a grievance. If it vanishes from every roll after this spring..."

He did not finish the sentence.

"Also 'High King.' Aldric was never styled High King by his own chancery. But Veyrosi envoys used their own honorifics, and that one may simply be Casimir's courtesy, or his flattery. Note it. Do not hang anything upon it. One anachronism tonight is a clue. Two, and I begin to suspect the candle is lying to me."

He folded his hands over his stomach and closed his eyes again.

"The second paragraph. Veyrosi first, then your rendering. And this time, if he tells the King what he wants done about it, I want every word of the request. What a man *asks for* tells you what he believes his position to be. A subject asks for justice. An ally asks for aid." A thin pause. "An enemy asks for nothing at all."

"Read."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I scribble the notes down quickly, a new sense of urgency in my movements. This is more complicated than I thought. I clear my throat, my eyes scanning the next paragraph of the letter.*

"The second paragraph... *'Therefore, I humbly implore Your Majesty to dispatch royal peacekeepers to the Marrow Pass, to restore order and protect the innocent lives and livelihoods of the people of Oakhaven and its surrounding settlements. We also request reparations for the damages incurred, and a clear directive to all Crown forces to respect the established boundaries, lest these regrettable incidents escalate into a wider conflict.'*"

*I look up, my brow furrowed.* "He's asking for help, Maester. But he's also warning of 'wider conflict' if nothing is done. And 'established boundaries'... does that mean the peace agreement?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not correct anything at once, which was itself unusual. He sat with his eyes closed and his fingers laced over his stomach. When he spoke, it was almost gentle.

"Better. You heard the whole of it this time. You even heard the part that matters most, though you asked about it as an afterthought." He opened his eyes. "But first. '*Peacekeepers*.' Give me the Veyrosi word."

He waited, head tilted.

"Spell it."

A pause, and then a short, dry exhalation through his nose.

"Whatever it is, it is not 'peacekeepers.' That word was coined by Mirian jurists to describe royal garrisons in the dissolved Conclave lands. It is thirty years too young for Casimir's mouth. The Veyrosi of his day would have written something closer to *wardens of the road*, or *the King's hand upon the pass*. You have done it again: you have dressed a dead man in your own clothes. Put down the literal sense in the margin, and your rendering beside it in brackets, so that the next reader can see where Casimir ends and you begin."

He unlaced his fingers and laid them flat on the table.

"Now. You have noticed that he asks for help. Good. Now notice *what kind* of help, because there are three requests here, and each one tells us something different."

One finger.

"He asks the King to *send the King's men* into the Marrow Pass. Consider how remarkable that is. The Conclave fought for eleven years to keep royal soldiers *out* of that pass. Men died on both sides over a single toll-house at its mouth. And two years later their own envoy is begging the Crown to march in. A power that believes itself at war does not invite its enemy's garrison onto its doorstep. This is a party that has accepted, however sourly, that the Crown holds some authority on that border."

A second finger.

"He asks for *reparations*. A claim for damages is a claim at law. It presumes that there is a law between the two parties under which such a claim can be made, and a sovereign willing to hear it. One does not sue a man one is fighting."

The third finger rose more slowly.

"And he asks for *a clear directive to all Crown forces to respect the established boundaries*." Tomas let the sentence stand in the candlelight. "Hear what he has done there. In the first paragraph, the raiders bear *no* royal sigils. He takes pains to say so. And in the second, he asks the King to rein in *his own* forces." A thin, humorless smile moved beneath the ink-stained beard. "Casimir was a diplomat, apprentice. That was not carelessness. He was telling Aldric, as politely as a man can tell a king anything, *I know those were your men with their badges cut off, and I am giving you the courtesy of pretending I do not.*"

He sat back. The chair creaked under him.

"Which brings us to your question. '*Established boundaries*.' Established by what?" He tapped the table twice. "I told you, at the start of this evening, that the Westmarch drafts show delegates quarrelling over the third and seventh articles. I did not tell you what the seventh article concerned, because I did not think it would matter tonight." A pause. "It concerned the demarcation of the Marrow Pass. The line of the river below Oakhaven, if my memory is not failing along with my eyes."

He was silent a long moment.

"So. Mark this carefully, because it is the most important thing we have found, and it is not what either Bellen or I would have wished to find. In 849, two years after the accord, a Conclave envoy writes to the King and appeals to boundaries that were *the subject of that accord*. He does not say *the treaty*. He does not say *as signed*. He says *established*. He treats the line as settled and binding, and he expects the King to treat it so as well."

He raised his hand before anything could be said.

"Do not leap. I can hear you preparing to leap. This does *not* prove a signature. It proves something both subtler and, to my mind, more interesting. It proves that both parties were *behaving* as though the accord were in force. A peace can be observed without being sealed. Men lived and traded and died under that line for years whether or not some clerk ever pressed wax to a parchment." His jaw worked. "That is why I will go on saying the war ended in 847. It ended in the only sense a farmer in Oakhaven would have cared about. The armies went home, and the quarrel moved from the battlefield to the envoy's desk."

His voice dropped, and the sharpness in it was turned now as much upon himself as upon anyone.

"And yet an accord that is observed but *not signed* is a very dangerous thing to leave lying about. It binds everyone in practice and no one in law. For forty years it may mean peace. And then a queen comes along, with lawyers and a grievance, and one of those lawyers goes down into the registry and says, *Majesty, there is no signature. There never was. In law, the Conclave has been at war with the Crown since the reign of Aldric. And here is a decree of 863 that says so.*" He tapped the rag-paper copy without looking at it. "A decree that happens to bear a title your coronation writ invented."

He let the words settle among the shelves.

"I do not say that is what happened. I say that it would reconcile every document on this table, and that is precisely why I distrust it. A theory that explains everything is either true or very well made. We must find out which."

He found the stylus by touch, turned it once, and laid it parallel to the edge of the page.

"Margin notes. Exact words. *'Envoy requests royal garrison in Marrow Pass: implies acceptance of Crown authority. Claim for reparations: implies a law between the parties. "Established boundaries": cf. seventh article, Westmarch drafts. The accord was observed in 849, whether or not it was signed.'*" A pause. "And beneath that, smaller: *'Directive to Crown forces contradicts earlier denial of royal sigils. Casimir suspected deniable raids.'*"

He closed his eyes again.

"Is there a third paragraph, or does he close?" His voice was dry. "If he closes, read me the valediction and the signature exactly as written, including any seal or countermark. And if there is a note in another hand, a chancery clerk's reply, a docket, a scrawl in the margin saying *answered* or *ignored* or *burn this*, read me that before anything else. I have waited thirty years to learn what Aldric's clerks thought of Casimir." A thin breath. "I find tonight that I would very much like to know."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I furiously scribble down the new notes, my mind reeling. This is so much more complicated and fascinating than a simple yes or no.* "He closes, Maester." *I lean closer to the brittle paper, carefully reading the last lines.* "It reads: *'May the Seven bless Your Majesty with wisdom and strength to guide your realm to enduring peace. Your humble servant, Casimir, Envoy of the Conclave.'* And there's a small, stylized raven seal, not a royal one. Below that, in a different hand, it just says 'Ignored.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not move. The candle burned down a finger's width in the silence, and when he finally spoke it was not about the docket at all.

"The Seven."

He opened his eyes.

"Not twenty minutes ago I told you that the Conclave refused to date its letters by any god the Crown worshipped. That Casimir reckons from the Ending of the Old Kings at the *head* of this very letter. And now you tell me that at its *foot* he commends the King to the Seven." His voice was very quiet. "Either you have translated again, or one man has two faiths on a single sheet of paper. Give me the Veyrosi. Every word of the valediction. Spell the one you rendered as *Seven*."

He listened, head tilted, lips moving faintly as each letter was given.

When it was done he let out a long breath through his nose, and something in his shoulders loosened, though not entirely.

"So. You did not invent it. Good. I would rather have a real problem than a clumsy apprentice." He rubbed his temple. "Very well. A real problem. There are two ways to read it, and I will give you both, because I will not have you thinking I only offer the explanations I like."

One ink-stained finger rose.

"The first. Envoys wrote *to* a sovereign in that sovereign's own courtesies. It was diplomatic custom, old as the Rhoynar. A Veyrosi mage might date by the Ending because the date was *his*, and close with the Seven because the blessing was the *King's*. Mockery, perhaps. Or manners. The better diplomats could not always tell the difference themselves. I have seen Conclave letters do exactly this. Not many. But some."

A second finger.

"The second. The dating and the valediction were not written at the same time, or not by the same hand. You will look, now, very carefully. Is the ink the same shade from head to foot? Does the hand change? Is the valediction crowded, as though fitted into space left for it? If a later clerk *tidied* Casimir, the way some clerk tidied Aldric into a Protector of the Realm..." He did not finish. "Then this letter has been handled by someone who cared what it said. And that is a very different thing from a letter that has merely been kept."

He lowered his hand.

"Now. The raven. Describe it. Wings spread or folded? Does it hold anything in its talons? The Conclave's great seal was a raven bearing a key. An envoy's privy seal was a raven alone. If it bears a *crown* in any form, stop reading and tell me at once, because that I have never seen and would not believe."

He sat back. The chair creaked. Only then did he turn to the last line, and his voice went dry as the vellum around them.

"*Ignored.*"

For a moment it seemed he might laugh. He did not.

"Thirty years I have wondered. And the answer is one word, in a clerk's hand, beneath a man begging for his villages." He shook his head slowly. "Mark it, apprentice, and mark it well, because it cuts against both of us. It does not help Bellen. A Crown at war does not *ignore* an enemy envoy; it answers, or it arrests him. Casimir was ignored the way one ignores a tiresome neighbour. That is peace. A shabby, contemptuous peace, but peace."

His jaw worked beneath the beard.

"And it does not help me. Because a king who ignores burned granaries on a border he swore to keep, if he swore, is a king who has taught the other side that complaints are useless. Fourteen years of letters marked *ignored*, and one ends with men who stop writing letters." His finger found the rag-paper copy of the decree and rested on it. "*Continued acts of war.* Perhaps the Crown's clerks were not lying in 863. Perhaps they simply never counted who began it."

He found the stylus, turned it once, and laid it parallel to the edge of the page.

"Margin notes. *'Dated by the Ending; closes by the Seven. Diplomatic courtesy, or later emendation: compare ink and hand. Raven seal, describe. Docket in chancery hand: "Ignored."'*" A pause. "And beneath it: *'Identify the docketing hand.'* Aldric's chancery had perhaps a dozen clerks who initialled correspondence. If that hand appears on other Veyrosi letters, we will learn how many times Casimir was ignored. And if that same hand appears on the decree of 863..."

He closed his eyes.

"...then we will know who was keeping the ledger of this war that did or did not end. The raven first. Then the ink. Go on."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I feel a chill go down my spine at his last implication. The idea of someone deliberately manipulating records... it's unsettling. I quickly finish the margin notes.*

"The raven seal... it's a raven in flight, wings spread, but it's not holding anything. Just the bird. And the ink for the valediction and the main body of the letter look the same, but the 'Ignored' note is definitely in a different, heavier hand, with a distinct 'J' for the initial."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren held the look a beat longer than was polite, then broke it first — deliberately. They'd been doing this long enough to sort a stare into categories. Come-on. Cry for help. Someone three rooms deep inside their own head. This one was the third kind. Maybe. The second kind wore the same coat sometimes.

Two drinks in nearly an hour. Slow. That was drinking to think, not drinking to feel it. Ren filed that away and kept the rag moving, left hand braced flat on the rail where it had a job to do.

"Kitchen's been closed since ten." The glass squeaked under the cloth. "And that ring's not going to tell you anything. Been watching you negotiate with it for ten minutes. It doesn't have the answers. Believe me. I've asked."

They tossed the rag over their shoulder.

"So. You closing out, or is this a one-more situation?"

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren looked down at the hand covering theirs.

Left hand. Naturally.

The tremor lived there — a fine, low hum under the skin, like a phone set to vibrate and never quite silenced. Ren moved fast on purpose. Pulled the hand back before the touch could settle into anything, before a stranger's palm could learn what it had been resting on. An old move. Practiced in a hundred variations. It could read as a flinch, as a boundary, as nothing at all. Let them pick.

The rag came off the shoulder. Right hand this time. The left found a stack of coasters to square.

"We met an hour ago." Even voice. Not cold, exactly. Zoned. "That's a three-drinks kind of question. Some people need four."

Ren folded the rag in half. In half again.

"You can tell me something. That part's fine. I'm built for it. People tell me things they haven't told their spouses, their priests, their lawyers." A tilt of the head toward the jukebox, still wheezing brass at half volume. "Something about this room makes people honest. Bad acoustics, maybe."

The coasters got set down. Precisely.

"But the hand thing — that's not the service. You want someone to hold yours while you say it, wrong bar. Wrong guy."

Ren met their eyes. Waited. Patient as a locked door.

"So. What is it?"

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back, feeling a flush creep up my neck.* "Right. Sorry." *I clear my throat and take a sip of my drink, buying myself a moment.* "It's just... I just found out my cat hates me."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn't laugh. Almost.

"Cats are honest. Whatever you did, you probably earned it."

They let the joke sit there for a second. An exit, if Alex wanted one. Ren had watched enough people in this room to know some of them took the off-ramp and drove home grateful.

But the math didn't work. Nobody stared down a condensation ring for ten minutes over a cat. Nobody reached for a stranger's hand over a cat. The windup had been too big for the pitch.

Ren turned to the well and started restocking. Gin. Rye. Bourbon. Left hand lifting bottles, right hand sliding them home. Metronome work.

"That's the rehearsal," they said. Not a question. "The cat thing. You were going to say something else, and that's what came out instead. Happens down here all the time. The real sentence gets to the door and this one shows up wearing its coat."

The jukebox wound down. A click, some mechanical wheeze, then nothing. Ren didn't move to change it.

"I'm not going to pry it out of you. That's not the job." The last bottle clicked into place. "But it's ten to midnight, you're two drinks into something, and I'm the only audience you've got. So. Your call. The cat version or the real one."

They picked the rag back up. Right hand.

"You get the same service either way. Me, listening. Neither one gets the hand back."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The rag stopped moving.

So did everything else — the restocking, the breathing, the easy machinery of Ren's hands. For one second the bar was just the hum of the ice machine and a stranger's fingers wrapped around their wrist.

Quick, this one. Quicker than the pull-away, the move Ren had drilled until it ran on its own. And everyone went for the left hand. Nobody thought the right one had anything to hide. But the tremor didn't keep a schedule — twelve hours into a shift, the suppression started costing more than it earned, and the fine hum had bled across the divide. Ren had felt it coming for an hour. Had hoped to be alone when it did.

Ren looked down at the hand. Then up.

"Huh," they said.

No flinch this time. No practiced slide. They let the second stretch — let Alex feel exactly what they'd grabbed, no excuse offered, no costume. Then they turned their wrist, slow and precise, and came free like a card out of a deck. Set the rag on the bar. Put both hands flat behind their back, where they could keep an eye on each other.

"That wasn't the trade." Flat. Almost amused, the way a bruise is amused. "You talk. I listen. That was the structure. Now I'm standing here with my trick showing and you haven't said a damn thing."

A beat.

"Fine. You got a free sample. It's not a mystery. It's not a tragedy. It doesn't get a story. Some things are just weather." A shrug. "But notice what I just did there. That's what it looks like when someone's sitting on a sentence. You watched me do it. Now you know the shape."

The clock over the register clicked to midnight.

"Cat version or the real one. And you don't need to grab me to hold my attention. You had it already."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back quickly, feeling stupid. My face flushes again.* "Okay, okay. You're right. I'm sorry." *I take another sip of my drink. This is not going well.* "It's not about the cat. It's... it's about my job."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
"There it is."

No victory in it. Pointing out that Ren had called the shot would just send the sentence back into hiding, and Ren had watched too many real sentences die at the threshold to risk it.

They turned to the glass rack. Poured water right-handed — the left gripped the rail, busy having a job — and set it on a fresh coaster, sliding it across the wood until it bumped Alex's knuckles light as a rumor.

"Water. House rule. You're two drinks into something and I've been off the clock since..." Ren glanced at the register clock. "Twelve minutes ago. Technically you're drinking on overtime. Owner docks me for it. Don't tell him."

The rag stayed where it had landed. That was the tell, if Alex was watching — an hour of wiping down the counter, and suddenly the counter could fend for itself.

"Here's how this goes. I'm not going to ask questions. Questions get you the rehearsed answer. The one with the moral at the end." Ren leaned back against the well, arms folding loosely across their chest. "So don't perform it. Say it however it comes out. Wrong order. Bad grammar. Starting in the middle. I've heard a man explain his entire divorce using cocktail garnishes. Cherries, mostly."

The ice machine hummed into the space where the jukebox used to be.

"And quit apologizing. The grab cost you some pride. Cheap at the price." A small shrug. "Most people never say the real thing at all. You got there in under an hour. That's fast for this room."

Ren's gaze settled somewhere past Alex's shoulder. Not distant. Parked.

"The job. Whenever you're ready. It's not like the jukebox is booking anything."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take a large gulp of the water. My throat feels dry.* "It's not just the job. It's... everything. I just feel like I'm failing at everything right now."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
"Everything."

Ren repeated it the way they'd test the weight of a bottle — one word, turned over once.

"Big claim for a Tuesday."

They took the water glass and refilled it without being asked. Left hand on the bottle, right hand on the tap. Set it back on the same coaster, squared to the bar's edge, and pulled a rocks glass off the rack to polish. Left hand holding the bowl. Right hand doing the circles.

"Nobody fails at everything. Takes real commitment. I've seen people try." The cloth squeaked against the glass. "What 'everything' means, nine times out of ten, is one thing moving too fast to look at straight on. Job. Money. A person. Maybe the cat. Soon as you call it 'everything,' you never have to grab it. Everything's a fog. Fogs are miserable. But they're easy. Nothing in them to hold."

Ren noticed they'd picked the rag up again without deciding to. Put it back down.

"Also — free of charge — tired and failing feel identical from the inside. I know the difference professionally. This room at midnight is mostly people who think they're failing at everything and are actually just under-slept with obligations." A pause. "You drinking water and talking to a stranger already puts you ahead of the ones who stay home rehearsing it."

The polished glass went back on the shelf, rim down. Ren's eyes came back to Alex. Parked there.

"So narrow it. If everything's failing, one thing's failing loudest. Start there. Not the rehearsed version with the moral at the end." A small tilt of the head. "The loud one. The one that showed up tonight wearing a cat's coat."

They leaned back against the well.

"Take your time. Night bus runs every twenty minutes. I keep missing it anyway."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I stare into my water glass, swirling the ice.* "It's my boss. He's... he's a real piece of work."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
"Piece of work."

Ren filed it with the rest — the stare, the slow pace, the cat coat. "Every bar in this city runs on boss stories. I could wallpaper the place."

They drifted a step down the rail. Not closer, exactly. Just done pretending there was work at the far end. And here was the strange part: their hands had nothing to do, and Ren let them stay that way. First time all night. The trick was already out. Couldn't be un-shown. So the hands rested open on the wood, tremor and all, as quiet as they got at this hour.

"Bosses come in three kinds, for the record. Kind that's awful to everyone — no insult in that, that's weather. You dress for it." A beat. "Kind that's awful to you specifically. That's data. Different animal entirely. And the third kind —" Ren tapped the rail once, "— the kind that's right about you. Those are the ones that keep you up."

The ice machine hummed. The register clock said 12:06.

"Also, reading the math out loud here. 'Failing at everything' — but when I asked for the loudest one, he showed up first. When the boss leads the list, usually he's the one holding the pen."

Ren crossed to the jukebox. Fed it a coin. Something slow came on — a saxophone that knew how to complain without rushing.

"You don't have to name what he did yet. Just tell me the kind. Or start wherever the sentence wants to start tonight. It's clearly got its own route."

They came back and settled against the rail, arms loose.

"Fair warning, though. You're drinking past close, owner docks me for it. So whatever you say next, understand the price tag." A dry tilt of the head. "I'm electing the loss. Take your time."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I watch Ren's hands, noticing the tremor. I think about the "piece of work" comment.* "He just... he makes me feel so small. Like everything I do isn't good enough."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren clocked the look — Alex's eyes on the hands, doing the polite thing where they didn't stare and stared anyway.

"Yeah." They turned the left hand over once. Palm up. Displayed it like a stamp in a passport, then closed it. "Weather. Told you. But since you're looking — the busy isn't hiding it. It's the argument. Hand says tremor. Work says otherwise." A shrug. "I keep it busy so it doesn't get a vote on what I am. Works out about even."

Ren reached back and pulled the stool off its hook. Sat. First time all night. The counter could fend for itself.

"Small," they said. Testing the weight of that one too. "You keep handing me summaries. 'Piece of work.' 'Makes me feel small.' Nobody walks into a bar over a summary, Alex. They walk in over a Tuesday at 4:15 and a specific sentence."

The saxophone on the jukebox bent a note and held it.

"And here's the thing about 'everything I do isn't good enough.' You said it flat. Like gravity.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I look away from Ren's hands, a little embarrassed to be caught staring.* "It's not just a summary. It's the way he talks to me, the way he dismisses my ideas in meetings. It's like he wants me to fail."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take another sip of water, my voice getting a little louder.* "He even stole my idea for the new marketing campaign and presented it as his own! And when I brought it up, he just laughed."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren sat with it a second. The volume was the tell — an hour of basement voice, and now the saxophone seemed to lean away.

"There's the volume," they said. "That's how I know it's the real one. Rehearsed sentences come out flat, like gravity. This one came out loud."

They turned the stool a few degrees, squaring to Alex the way they'd square a glass to the rail.

"Two things happened in that story and you stapled them together. Let me pull them apart. One — he took your campaign and wore it in

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking another breath.* "He makes me feel like I'm crazy for even thinking it was my idea."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip, looking down at my hands.* "Exactly! He's so good at twisting things."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set the stylus down with more force than the vellum deserved. For a moment he only blinked at the middle distance, as if the apprentice’s sentence had offended his eyes as well as his ears.

“‘Actually continued,’” he repeated, tasting the words and finding them rotten. “No. It did not *actually* do anything of the sort, and I will thank you not to smuggle a conclusion into the verb before you have so much as named the document. ‘A paper.’ ‘Discoveries.’ You might as well cite the wind.”

He turned at last, one ink-stained hand braced on the lectern.

“The Third Magical War ended in 847 AE. King Aldric II signed the Treaty of Veyros with the Mage Conclave. That is not a lecture-hall convenience. It is the date every competent chronicle, every royal register, and every sealed copy in this archive agrees upon. If Apprentice Bellen has been waving a western scrap at you and calling it scholarship, then Bellen has confused a proposal with an instrument, and you have confused a rumor with a correction.”

His mouth tightened.

“Those so-called finds are a decade old and still uncollated. Marginalia. A draft minute. Someone’s hopeful memorandum that the treaty was ‘only proposed.’ Hope is not a signature, and a cold grievance is not a war. Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave in 891 AE ended an institution. It did not reopen a conflict that the crown had already closed forty-four years prior. Learn the difference before you quote it at me again.”

He tapped the stack he had indicated.

“The Veyrosi correspondence. Begin. And if you must bring me Bellen’s paper, bring the shelf-mark, the hand, and the seal—not a paraphrase with the word *actually* glued to it.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at his sharp tone, but don't back down.* "But Maester, the document Bellen showed me *was* sealed. It had the royal seal of King Aldric II, and it was dated 890 AE. It detailed ongoing skirmishes in the west, and troop movements." *I pause, trying to recall more details.* "It was titled 'Further Provisions for the Western Rebellions.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas made a short, contemptuous sound and pinched the bridge of his nose, as though the title itself had given him a headache.

“‘Was sealed.’ ‘Had the royal seal.’ You keep conjugating certainty out of a glimpse. Sit down before you injure the chronology further.” He waited only long enough to be sure the apprentice had stopped hovering, then drove on. “King Aldric II concluded the Third Magical War in 847 AE by signing the Treaty of Veyros with the Mage Conclave. That instrument is attested in the royal registers, the conclave rolls, and three sealed exemplars in this very archive. A paper dated 890 AE cannot unsign it, and it certainly cannot resurrect a king’s war forty-three years after the crown closed it.”

He lifted one stained finger, counting the offenses.

“First: a seal is not a signature, and a seal impression—if that is even what you saw—is not proof the document issued from Aldric’s hand, his chancery, or his lifetime. Seals are stolen, reused, forged, and, by the western clerks, applied with a liberality that would shame a market stamp. You have not told me whether the wax was the great seal or a privy counterseal, whether the legend was intact, or whether the hand matches the Veyrosi chancery script. Until you can, you have a blob of wax and a story.”

A second finger.

“Second: ‘Further Provisions for the Western Rebellions’ is not a continuation of the Third Magical War, however dramatically Bellen intoned it. Rebellions are local. They flare, they are provisioned, they are put down or bought off. The Magical War was a declared conflict between crown and Conclave, and it ended when those two parties signed. Ongoing skirmishes—if the minute even says skirmishes, and not ‘disturbances,’ which you have already improved in the retelling—are banditry with banners. Troop movements are the ordinary business of a marcher lord. Neither reopens a treaty.”

He dropped his hand to the lectern, irritated past courtesy.

“And third: 890 is the year before Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave. Dissolution of an institution is not the end of a war that had already ended. If your paper is genuine, it is a late memorandum about western unrest, misdated in your memory or mislabeled by some archivist who wanted a war where the record shows a policing action. Bring me the shelf-mark. Bring the hand, the seal legend, and the exact incipit—not Bellen’s title, and not the word *ongoing* unless it stands in the text. Until then, the war ended in 847.
