Write that in your notes, and stop letting other apprentices edit the realm for you.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing his points, but still feel like something isn't quite right.* "I understand, Maester. But the document also mentioned a specific 'Mage-Lord' leading the rebellions, not just a bandit. And it outlined a strategy to 'contain the magical threat' in the west." *I cross my arms, feeling a bit defensive for Bellen and the document.* "It didn't sound like ordinary policing to me."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas stared at the crossed arms as if they were a grammatical error made flesh.

“Uncross those,” he said. “Defensiveness is not evidence, and loyalty to Bellen is not a citation. A ‘Mage-Lord’—and I will not dignify the hyphen until I see it in the hand—is a title bandied by every hedge-caster who can hold a tower for a season. It does not make a rebel a party to the Third Magical War, any more than calling a cutpurse a prince makes him royalty.”

He leaned in, voice gone thin and precise.

“‘Contain the magical threat.’ You hear a war in that phrase because you want one. Containment is the language of quarantine, of cordons, of a crown keeping gifted malcontents from setting barns alight. It is policing with a longer word. The Magical War was not a mood in the west. It was a declared conflict between King Aldric II and the Mage Conclave, and it ended when he signed the Treaty of Veyros in 847 AE. A memorandum from 890—if your date survives contact with the shelf—cannot promote a western malcontent into that conflict after the fact.”

His stylus tapped once, hard, against the lectern.

“Strategy outlined on parchment is not a campaign. Skirmishes led by a self-styled lord are not a resumed war. And ‘didn’t sound like ordinary policing’ is an aesthetic judgment, not a reading. Bring me the clause that names the Conclave as a belligerent after 847. Bring me a revocation of the treaty, in Aldric’s hand or his successor’s, with witness and seal legend intact. Absent that, you have unrest, a title, and a verb you have already improved in the telling. The war ended in 847. Your feelings about the tone of a scrap do not amend the registers.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not reach for the paper. He looked at it the way a man looks at a stain that has had the impudence to move.

“Put that down on the lectern, not in my face, and do not call it a copy until you have said copy of what.” His voice had gone very quiet, which was worse. “A moment ago this marvel was dated 890 AE and titled ‘Further Provisions for the Western Rebellions.’ Now it is 863, and it has become ‘a war decree.’ Twenty-seven years have fallen out of your mouth between one breath and the next, and the genre of the document has changed with them. That is not scholarship. That is a story rearranging itself to survive my objections.”

He turned the sheet with two fingers, as if it might soil the stylus, and did not bother to hide his contempt for the hand.

“This is an apprentice transcription. No shelf-mark. No note of the exemplar. No description of the wax—color, legend, whether the impression is the great seal or some western counterfeit knocked out of a signet that has been doing the rounds since Aldric’s clerks were still alive. ‘King Aldric’s seal’ is a phrase. It is not a reading. And a decree, if this scrap even uses that word, is not whatever you need it to be this afternoon. Decrees appoint, provision, pardon, and scold. They do not, by the magic of your vocabulary, reopen a war.”

One ink-stained finger tapped the date, once.

“Even if I grant you 863—and I do not; you have already spent 890—that is sixteen years after King Aldric II signed the Treaty of Veyros with the Mage Conclave and ended the Third Magical War. A later minute cannot unsign an instrument attested in the royal registers and in the sealed exemplars on the shelf behind you. If Aldric, or more likely some marcher clerk hiding behind Aldric’s name, issued orders touching the west in 863, those orders concern unrest. They are not a resumption of the Conclave war, and they are not evidence that the treaty was ‘only proposed.’ Proposed treaties do not leave three concordant exemplars and a chancery enrollment.”

He slid the sheet back across the wood, short of the apprentice’s hand.

“Strike the phrase ‘war decree’ from your notes. It is your invention. Bring me the incipit, the witnesses, and a single clause that revokes Veyros or names the Mage Conclave as a belligerent after 847 AE. Until that clause exists outside Bellen’s enthusiasm and your improving memory, the war ended in 847. The registers are not obliged to flutter because an apprentice has produced a cleaner story on the second telling.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up the paper, a little stung by his dismissive tone.* "It's a copy of what Bellen found in the new western archive, Maester. He said it was a direct quote from the original, and he copied the seal impression directly." *I look at the paper, then back at him.* "He seemed very sure of his findings."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas let out a breath that was almost a laugh and not at all kind. He did not take the paper back.

“‘He seemed very sure.’” The phrase came out clipped, each word set down like a badly inked letter. “Certainty is a posture, not a provenance. Bellen may be sure of his breakfast and still be wrong about a treaty. I have buried better scholars than Bellen who were sure, and the ground did not revise the registers out of respect for their confidence.”

He tapped the lectern once, eyes narrowed against the candle-smoke.

“A ‘direct quote’ copied by an apprentice is a direct quote of an apprentice. Hands wander. Dates slip—yours already has, from 890 to 863, with a change of title thrown in for sport. A seal impression ‘copied directly’ is a drawing of wax unless you can tell me the legend, the color, whether the edge was clipped, and whether the matrix matches the great seal enrolled after Aldric’s coronation or some western signet that has been impressing forgeries since the clerks grew lazy. You have given me none of that. You have given me Bellen’s manner.”

His mouth thinned.

“The western finds are a decade old. I have seen the memorandum they breed from: a proposal dressed up, by hopeful readers, as proof the Treaty of Veyros was never signed. It will not do. King Aldric II signed that treaty with the Mage Conclave in 847 AE. The war ended there. Three sealed exemplars and the chancery enrollment do not become a rumor because a boy in the new archive sounded convinced while he traced a blob of wax.”

He turned back to the stack of northern scrolls, stylus already in hand, the dismissal as plain as the ink on his beard.

“Shelf-mark. Incipit. Witnesses. One clause that revokes Veyros or names the Conclave a belligerent after 847. Not Bellen’s sureness, and not another improved date. Until then you will catalog the Veyrosi correspondence as it stands: the war closed in 847, and your friend’s enthusiasm is not an emendation. Begin.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set the stylus down and regarded the apprentice with the particular weariness he reserved for questions that had already been answered and were now being asked again under a new coat of paint.

“The truth,” he said, “is not a compromise between a textbook and an apprentice’s enthusiasm, and I will not pretend that it is. You are asking me to split the difference between a signed instrument and a rumor, as if history were a tavern argument that could be settled by calling both sides half-right. It cannot.”

He turned one palm up, then the other, pedantic to the last.

“On this hand: the Treaty of Veyros, signed by King Aldric II with the Mage Conclave in 847 AE. Enrolled in the chancery. Attested in the royal registers. Present in three sealed exemplars on the shelf behind you, which you have not opened, because opening them would require you to stop quoting Bellen. That is the textbook, yes. It is also the archive. The war ended when those two parties signed. That is the truth.”

The other hand closed.

“On this hand: a decade of western scraps, still uncollated, which hopeful readers have inflated into a claim that the treaty was ‘only proposed.’ A memorandum. A draft minute. And, from you, a transcription whose date has already migrated from 890 to 863, whose title has changed once, and whose seal exists only as Bellen’s assurance that he copied it and seemed sure. That is not ‘the new evidence.’ That is an interpretation looking for a document stern enough to bear it. It has not found one.”

His mouth tightened, the ink at the edge of his beard catching the candlelight.

“So. The treaty is real. It was signed. The Third Magical War ended in 847 AE. Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave in 891 ended an institution; it did not quietly finish a war the crown had already closed. If a clause ever surfaces that revokes Veyros, names the Conclave a belligerent after 847, and survives comparison with the exemplars, I will read it, and I will correct the registers myself. I have corrected them before. I do not correct them for a paraphrase, a shifting date, and the word *seemed*.”

He picked up the stylus and pointed it, not gently, at the untouched stack.

“Write that down without the word *actually* anywhere near it. Then begin the Veyrosi correspondence. The truth has been sitting on that shelf longer than Bellen has been sure of anything.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, frustrated, but also a little intrigued despite myself.* "Fine, Maester. I'll start the Veyrosi correspondence." *I reach for the stack, but pause, a new thought occurring to me.* "But if the western documents are just 'scraps,' why are they even kept in a royal archive? Why not just discard them?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas paused with the stylus half-raised, as if the question had been aimed at his method rather than his conclusion, and that, at least, deserved a colder answer than contempt.

“Because an archive is not a cupboard for things I like,” he said. “We keep the scraps so that the next hopeful boy cannot invent them larger than they were. A discarded memorandum becomes, in ten years, a lost decree. A lost decree becomes, in Bellen’s mouth, a war. I would rather have the western minute on a shelf, dated, described, and contradicted by the exemplars beside it, than have it wandering the colleges as a ghost that no one can check.”

He set the stylus down and turned just far enough to fix the apprentice with the good eye.

“Keeping is not endorsing. The chancery files forgeries, draft minutes, rejected proposals, and the complaints of marcher lords who styled every barn-burning a rebellion. They are kept as evidence of what was claimed, not of what was done. If I threw out every paper that failed to move the registers, this room would be a chapel to my own taste, and you would have nothing left to misread. The western finds stay because they are a decade old, still uncollated, and already breeding the precise error you walked in with: that a proposal, a seal-story, and a shifting date can unsign the Treaty of Veyros.”

His mouth tightened.

“They cannot. King Aldric II signed it with the Mage Conclave in 847 AE. The war ended. Queen Mira dissolved an institution in 891; she did not finish a conflict the crown had closed. The scraps remain so that sentence can be defended against them, not so that they may vote.”

He nodded at the stack under the apprentice’s hand.

“Now open the correspondence. Shelf-mark as you go. And if you find a clause that actually revokes Veyros, you will bring it to me with the witnesses still attached—not with a theory about why dust is preserved.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, understanding the logic, even if I'm still a little skeptical.* "Alright, Maester. I'll get started." *I pick up the first scroll from the Veyrosi correspondence, unrolling it carefully.* "Should I make notes on the condition of these scrolls as well?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas glanced at the scroll already half-unrolled in the apprentice’s hands and made a small, pained sound.

“‘As well,’” he said. “As well as what? You have not yet told me you will note the shelf-mark, the incipit, or the hand. Condition is not a garnish you add if the mood takes you. It is part of the description, and it is useless if you write it like a traveler commenting on the weather.”

He came around the lectern, slower than his temper, and stopped short of touching the vellum.

“Yes. You will note the condition. Briefly, and in words that mean something. Foxing, losses, old repairs, whether the ink is iron-gall and eating through, whether the roll has been flattened and cracked along the spine. ‘Old’ is not a condition. ‘Fragile’ is not a condition. Every scrap in this room is old, and half of it will powder if you breathe on it with Bellen’s enthusiasm.”

One stained finger indicated the edge without quite meeting it.

“Support it. Do not force the curl. If a seal survives, you describe the wax—color, whether the impression is intact, whether the cord is original—and you do not sketch it from memory afterward and call the sketch a copy. Date of the hand if you can defend it; ‘looks early’ is not a date. And if any minute in that pile so much as whispers that the Treaty of Veyros was merely proposed, you mark the folio and you bring it to me before you improve the verb. I will not have another western scrap promoted into a war while I am turned the other way.”

He straightened, already squinting back toward his own manuscript.

“Begin with the first. Shelf-mark, incipit, hand, condition. In that order. Speak only when you have a clause worth the interruption.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, a bit chastened, and carefully place the scroll on the work surface, unrolling it just enough to see the start.* "Understood, Maester. Shelf-mark first." *I carefully examine the end of the scroll for any identifying marks before beginning to read the first few lines.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not look up at once. The scratch of his stylus stopped, which was warning enough, and only then did he turn his failing eyes toward the work surface.

“Shelf-mark first means the shelf-mark, not a hunt along the tail of the roll as if the chancery had hidden it from you out of spite.” He came two steps closer and stopped, squinting. “Endorsements, if they exist, are usually on the dorse, near the tie, or on the tag—not wherever your fingers happen to arrive. Turn it with the board under it. You are creasing a fresh valley by reading it half-curled like a broadsheet.”

One ink-stained finger indicated, without touching, the outer edge.

“If there is no mark, you say ‘unmarked’ and you give the provisional number from the slip I tied on the stack. You do not invent one because a blank end embarrasses you. Then the incipit: the first six words of the text proper, not the salutation if the salutation is a later addition, and not a summary of what you think it is about. Hand after that. Condition last, and only in terms that a man with worse eyes than mine could verify.”

His mouth tightened as the apprentice lingered over the opening lines.

“And if those lines are the Veyrosi enrollment, you will copy them as they stand. The Treaty was signed in 847 AE. I will not have you ‘clarify’ a chancery hand into a proposal because Bellen has made you suspicious of plain script. Read what is written. Then tell me the shelf-mark—or the absence of one—before you favor me with an interpretation.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I carefully turn the scroll, looking for the shelf-mark where he indicated, feeling a little foolish for not knowing that already.* "Ah, yes, on the dorse. Here it is, Maester." *I read it aloud, then carefully unroll the beginning of the scroll again, focusing on the first few words.* "The incipit reads, 'By the grace of the King, Aldric II...'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s stylus stopped. He turned, slowly, and regarded the apprentice with the look he saved for students who announced a finding and then failed to produce it.

“‘Here it is,’” he repeated. “And then you did not say what it was. I asked for the shelf-mark, not a gesture at the dorse and a sigh of relief. A mark unread is the same as no mark. Say the letters. Say the number. If the tag is rubbed, say which characters you can defend and which you are guessing. I will not enter ‘Ah, yes’ in the catalog.”

He came nearer, squinting at the opening lines rather than at the apprentice’s face.

“And that is not an incipit. ‘By the grace of the King, Aldric II’ is a salutation, and a clumsy one, and you have already begun to smooth it. Chancery hands do not write ‘the King, Aldric II’ as if they were introducing him at a feast. If the formula is there, it will be *Aldric, by the grace of the gods king*, or some equally tiresome piety, and you will copy the first six words of it in order, with the abbreviations expanded only in brackets. You do not rearrange a royal style because it sits more comfortably in your mouth.”

One stained finger hovered above the vellum, not quite touching.

“Six words. Exactly as they stand. Then the hand—secretary, chancery, or a western imitation of either, and do not say ‘official’ because the ink is dark. Then condition. Foxing, losses, cracks along the roll, whether any seal cord remains. If this is the enrollment of Veyros, it will say that he signed with the Mage Conclave, and the date will be 847 AE, and you will write that without improving *signed* into *proposed*. If it is some other minute that merely begins with his name, you will not promote it into a decree because the opening flatters him.”

His mouth tightened.

“The shelf-mark. Aloud. Then the six words, unimproved. I am not cataloging your relief.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince, feeling the flush creep up my neck. He's right, I'm getting ahead of myself.* "Right. My apologies, Maester." *I lean closer to the scroll, carefully tracing the faded characters.* "It reads: 'VR-XII-III-A.' And the incipit... 'Aldric, by the grace of gods, King...'" *I pause, counting the words.* "That's six words."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas made a short, irritated sound and came the rest of the way to the work surface, squinting down at the tag as if the apprentice’s relief had smudged it.

“‘VR-XII-III-A.’ At last, a thing I can enter.” He repeated it once, under his breath, tasting each character. “Veyrosi series, case twelve, bundle three, item A—if the hand that cut the tag knew its own system, which is never a safe assumption with western clerks. You will write it exactly so, with the hyphens, and you will note that you read it from the dorse near the tie, not from the text. If any letter is rubbed, you say so now. Do not grow a cleaner mark in the fair copy.”

His gaze shifted to the opening lines, and the satisfaction died.

“And that is not six words. Count them on your fingers, since your ear has abandoned you. *Aldric*—one. *By*—two. *The*—three. *Grace*—four. *Of*—five. *Gods*—six. *King*—seven. You stopped the count where it flattered your arithmetic and then tacked the style on afterward, as if I could not add. Seven is not six because you paused in the middle and hoped I was deaf.”

One stained finger hovered above the vellum, not touching it.

“Worse, you have already begun to edit. The pious formula is *by the grace of the gods*, article and all, unless this particular clerk was in a hurry or a western imitator who did not know the chancery would rather repeat itself than drop a word. If *the* is absent before *gods*, you record the absence. You do not smooth it into sense and then congratulate yourself on an incipit. Abbreviations expanded only in brackets. Royal style unimproved. *King* is not a seventh word you may smuggle in after declaring the count closed.”

He straightened, mouth thin.

“So. Shelf-mark: VR-XII-III-A, read from the dorse, characters as you can defend them. Incipit: the first six words as they stand—not seven, and not a feast-day introduction. Then the hand. Secretary, chancery, or a western imitation, and ‘dark enough to be official’ is not a hand. Then condition: foxing, losses, cracks, whether any seal cord remains. If this minute is the enrollment, it will say he signed with the Mage Conclave, and the date will be 847 AE, and you will copy *signed* without turning it into *proposed* to please the western archive. Read the next clause before you favor me with what it means.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shrink a little under his intense scrutiny, feeling my cheeks warm again.* "Seven words. Right. My apologies, Maester." *I take a deep breath, trying to calm my nerves, and look back at the scroll.* "The hand appears to be a formal chancery hand, quite clear despite some fading. There's significant foxing along the left edge, and a small tear near the bottom, but the main text is mostly intact. No seal cord remains." *I pause, then continue, reading the next part carefully.* "It states: '...Aldric, by the grace of gods, King, to all his loyal subjects, greetings. Know ye that by solemn treaty with the Mage Conclave, peace is declared throughout the realm, and all hostilities ceased on the first day of the third month, in the year of our Lord 847 AE...'" *I look up, a flicker of understanding in my eyes.* "It's the Treaty of Veyros, isn't it?"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren held the look a beat longer than necessary. Cataloguing. People who stared down bartenders near closing fell into two camps — the ones working up to a story and the ones working up to the door. This kind of stare was usually the first.

The rag kept circling in Ren's left hand. The counter hadn't been this clean in weeks.

They let the gaze drop. Not discomfort. There was just nothing in it worth holding.

"Last call's in thirteen." Ren set the rag down and braced both hands on the counter's edge. Held still for the length of the sentence, no longer. "You want a third, or you closing out?"

The jukebox rolled into its next number, something slower now. Ren picked the rag back up.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren looked at the hand first. Then at Alex's face. The order was deliberate.

Under the palm, the left one had gone still. That was the problem. Pinned, rag stopped, nothing to hide behind. A fine shiver started beneath the knuckles — small, but Ren felt every beat of it.

They slid their hand free. Unhurried. Same motion as clearing a glass. The rag came along and found the counter again, circles resuming over wood that was already dry.

"Talk's fine." Level. "Hands stay on your side of the bar."

Called it. The story camp, right on schedule. They always asked permission first — *can I tell you something* — like the asking made it a gift instead of a confession.

People who touched strangers in bars were one of two things. Lonely, or working an angle. Ren had stopped guessing which a long time ago. Both got the same service.

The jukebox ran out of song. In the quiet, the cooler hummed.

"Twelve minutes." Ren didn't look up from the rag. "Whatever it is, it'll fit."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back, a little stung.* "Right. Sorry." *I pick up my glass, swirl the ice around.* "Just... long day."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
"Most of them are."

Ren said it to the counter, not to Alex. The rag kept its orbit — left hand employed, tremor buried under motion where it lived.

The pullback had been quick. Stung. Ren filed that. People running angles didn't flinch when you pulled the welcome mat. Lonelier bet, then. Or better acting than most. Same service either way. The odds had shifted anyway.

Ren reached under the bar, came up with a clean napkin, slid it across the wood with two fingers. Parked it beside the sweating glass. The condensation ring Alex had been studying for the last hour — covered. Small fix. The ring would come back by closing. They usually did.

"You nursed the first one." Flat. No question in it. "Second took half the time. Something sped up."

Ren didn't ask questions near close. Questions were invitations, and invitations turned into somebody's whole night. Observations just sat there. People could pick them up or leave them on the bar.

The jukebox stayed dark. Just the cooler's hum filling the room.

"Eleven minutes." The rag moved to a new stretch of counter, already dry. "Water's free, if it was that kind of long."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren saw it land.

The eyes went to the left hand — the one that had gone still under Alex's palm earlier, the one working the rag now like the motion was the whole point. It was.

So that was the flinch, the apology, the long day — and now this, filed with everything else people noticed about strangers. Ren wrung the rag out over the sink. Two hands for that. Brief. Then the left one found the counter's edge and gripped it, knuckles pale. Tension worked better than motion. Motion just dressed the shake up. Pressure buried it.

"It does that." Flat as last call. "Nothing to do with you."

The jukebox finally found a new record. Piano. A lot of air between the notes.

"Most people don't catch it." Ren's eyes came up and found Alex's — the second time tonight Ren had done that on purpose. "You're either paying attention tonight, or it's the kind of day where everything gets in."

Not a question. Questions were invitations.

Ren reached under the bar, came up with the water, poured without asking. Set the glass down beside the napkin.

"Nine minutes. Last chance for a third."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pick up the water glass and take a long drink. My eyes are still on Ren's left hand.* "Yeah, it's one of those days." *I put the glass down, a little harder than I intended.* "Just... everything."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Yeah, I guess." *I shrug.* "So, what's your story, then? You seem like you've got a few of those too."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren exhaled through the nose. Not a laugh. Close as the shift had left in the tank.

*What's your story.* Oldest handoff in the book. Somebody got tired of carrying their own bag and tried passing it across the bar instead. Ren had watched it happen a few hundred times. The script never changed.

"That's the move, by the way." No heat in it. "Somebody points the light at you, you swing it back on the bartender. Seen it five hundred nights running."

The rag kept its orbit.

"I pour. I close. I go home. Short story. On purpose."

The glass had come down hard, though. Harder than a shrug. Ren filed that next to the flinch and the stare. Tired was one weight. Frustrated sat stacked on top of it, heavier.

"Four years behind this wood. Three owners. The sign out front has worn two different names since I started." Ren topped off the water without asking — small kindness, dressed up as procedure. "That's the whole thing. Free, like the water."

The jukebox piano kept spacing its notes out. Cooler humming underneath it all.

Ren's eyes came up and found Alex's. Third deliberate look of the night.

"'Everything' isn't an answer, by the way. It's a lid." The left hand pressed flat to the counter — pressure over motion, the shake pinned under the heel of it. "You take it off or you don't. Both happen at this bar."

The rag resumed. Stopped.

"Six minutes. Whatever 'everything' is — it's got six."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I stare at the water glass. Ren's right. Everything is a lid.* "It's not really a story." *I pick at the label on my bottle.* "More like... a really bad joke."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren watched the thumbnail work the label. Knew that trick from the inside. Hands wanted jobs when the rest of a person wanted out. The rag was Ren's version. Different label, same principle.

Ren claimed the empty glasses off the bar — left the bottle alone, it was still earning its keep. Stacked them in the sink. Two hands for that, briefly, then the left found the counter's edge and bore down. Pressure, not motion. The shake stayed under the heel of it.

"Jokes run shorter than stories anyway." Flat. "Fits the time we've got."

The jukebox piano spaced its notes wider, like it was counting down too.

"Fair warning." Ren's eyes came up — fourth deliberate look of the night. "People who open with 'bad joke' are usually testing the landing. Nobody laughs, they get to say it never mattered."

The rag picked back up. Circles over wood that was already clean.

"You don't need the out here. House rule. Nobody laughs at the bad ones this close to close."

The countdown was doing its real work — Ren had figured that out years back. People could say almost anything if it only had to fill five minutes. Finite things were easier to say into. That was the whole trick of last call. Nobody had to know it was a trick.

"Five." A small nod at the water glass. "Bad jokes are still on the menu till then."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "No, it's not like that." *I pick at the label a bit more, then give up and smooth it down.* "It's just... I really messed up tonight."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren let the quiet hold a beat. Didn't rush the gap. Gaps did work if you let them.

"Tonight." Flat. No question mark on it. "Explains the pace. First one nursed, second one chased. Fresh messes drink like that. The older ones nurse everything."

The rag stopped its orbit. Ren folded it once, laid it over the sink rail — done for the night, or at least done pretending. The left hand found the rail next and gripped. Pressure over motion. Same system, different prop.

"Story, then bad joke, now messed up." Ren counted the re-files off without moving. "It gets heavier every time you rename it. That's usually how you know it's real."

Four years of Tuesdays. The messes came in every size — sent the text, missed the call, signed the paper, said the thing out loud that was supposed to stay inside. Nobody graded them at this bar. That was the whole service. Ren had never once asked *how bad* and never would. The question did damage all by itself.

"I don't need details." True and useful at once. "Say the shape of it. Or don't. Both happen here."

The jukebox ran out of record. Ren left it dark this time. The cooler's hum was room enough.

"Four." Ren's eyes came up — fifth deliberate look of the night. "Enough to say it. Not enough to dress it up. That part's on purpose."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I look up at Ren, my eyes a little wide.* "It's... I said something. To someone important. Something I shouldn't have."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I swallow hard.* "And now they won't answer my calls." *I pick up my drink again, but don't drink. Just hold it tight.* "It's over. I know it is."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content: Ren

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I put the glass down with a thud.* "And I can't even blame them."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I put my head in my hands.* "God, I'm such an idiot."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor kept watching the road for another breath. Then they let the curtain fall.

“You’re right.” Their voice sounded rough. “If someone comes up that road, staring at it won’t stop them.”

They found a sleeve of crackers in a cupboard and ate two standing at the kitchen table. Then they opened the laptop, keeping its brightness low, and pulled up the phone records they had downloaded that morning. The source’s last call had been at 8:47 PM. Noor wrote the number in their notebook and checked it against the list from the investigation.

It appeared twice.

Noor stopped chewing. Both earlier calls had gone to a company switchboard that was supposed to close at six. They checked the dates, then turned the notebook sideways and underlined the number.

“The drive first,” they said. “Then I’m calling the source once. If they don’t answer, I’m finding out who was working that switchboard tonight.”

They slid the encrypted drive from its case and plugged it in.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I glance up from my phone again, a little startled at Noor's intensity.* "Whoa, okay. Don't stress too much, it'll be fine." *I go back to scrolling, but I'm listening.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor looked at the drive’s status light until it held steady.

“I don’t know if it’ll be fine,” they said. “I can check what we have.”

They entered the passphrase. The drive opened to a directory of invoices, call logs, and a file named READ_FIRST. Noor copied the directory listing into their notebook before opening anything. The note was short: *If I miss the meeting, compare the switchboard extensions to the invoice approvals. Do not call my cell.*

Noor read it twice. Their hand moved toward their phone, then stopped. They had planned to call the source. Now they put the phone facedown instead.

The call logs held three entries for the switchboard number. Each connected after hours, and each listed a different extension. Noor checked those extensions against the invoices. One appeared in the approval field on six payments to the same transport company; another appeared on four more.

They saved the matches to a separate folder and checked the timestamps again. They wanted to be certain before deciding what they meant.

A car could take hours on the mountain roads. The source could have changed their mind. Noor wrote both possibilities in the margin of the notebook, beside the less comforting one.

“I’m not calling them,” they said. “I’m going to verify these approvals, make a copy of the evidence, and try the source’s backup contact at one.”

They ate another cracker, though it tasted like cardboard, and opened the first invoice.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look up from my phone, hearing the change in Noor's voice.* "Backup contact? What happened to the first one?" *I put my phone down, giving them my full attention.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“The first one is the source,” Noor said. “The note on the drive says not to call their cell if they miss the meeting.”

They turned the laptop just enough to see the note again. Three hours late was long enough for Noor to worry; it wasn’t enough to tell them what had happened. “The backup is an attorney. I have a number for her office and a phrase I’m supposed to use.”

Noor returned to the invoice. Its approval field held one of the after-hours extensions, but the payment had been authorized two days before the call. They drew a line through that match in their notebook.

“That one doesn’t prove anything.” They opened the next invoice and checked its approval date against the call log. This time, the approval came eleven minutes after the call connected.

Noor checked the next three without speaking. Two followed the same pattern. They saved the records, then copied the matched files to a second encrypted folder on the laptop, leaving the originals untouched.

At 12:38, Noor closed the invoice window and made themselves eat four more crackers. They filled a mug with water from the tap and set it beside the notebook.

“I’ll finish checking the approvals before one,” they said. “Then I’ll call the attorney from the cabin line. If she knows where the source is, I want to hear it from her.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor checked the remaining approvals against the call logs. One more payment had been authorized minutes after an after-hours call. The others were too far apart to count. They marked those as inconclusive rather than forcing them into a pattern.

At 12:57, they had four approvals they could support with the records. Noor copied the relevant invoices and call entries into an encrypted folder, verified that the copies opened, and wrote down the folder’s contents on paper. Only then did they close the drive and put it back in its case.

The cabin had a landline mounted beside the refrigerator. Noor looked at it, then at the attorney’s number in their notebook. Calling from here would give away the safehouse number. Not calling would leave them guessing about someone who had missed a meeting by nearly four hours.

At one, Noor dialed the attorney’s office. An automated voice offered an after-hours extension for urgent matters. They entered it and waited through six rings.

“This is Mara Voss,” a woman answered, sounding awake. “Who is this?”

Noor kept their eyes on the note. “I was told to ask whether the blue folder reached your office.”

A pause. “It didn’t. Did the person carrying it reach you?”

“No.”

Mara took a breath close to the receiver. “Don’t tell me where you are. I’ll call you back in ten minutes at this number if it’s safe to talk. If I don’t, assume it isn’t.”

The line went dead.

Noor set the receiver down carefully. They wrote **1:03 — Mara Voss — no blue folder** in the notebook, then moved the drive away from the window. For the next ten minutes, they would keep the line clear. After that, they needed another plan.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look up from my phone, hearing the sudden quiet.* "Everything alright?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“No,” Noor said. “Mara hasn’t heard from the source either. She said she’d call back in ten minutes if it was safe.”

They wrote **1:13** beneath the last entry and checked the cabin clock against their laptop. While they waited, Noor photographed the four supported approvals and the matching call entries with the laptop’s camera, then compared the images to the files. The copies were legible. They shut the laptop and left the drive in its case.

Noor filled the mug again and ate the last two crackers. Their stomach objected, but their hands had stopped shaking quite so badly.

At 1:12, they moved to the kitchen chair beside the landline. “If she calls, I’m asking what she knows about the source and whether she can receive the records. If she doesn’t, I’ll wait until morning to contact my editor through our usual channel. I’m not sending anything blind tonight.”

The clock changed to 1:13. Noor kept their pen poised over the notebook and waited for the phone to ring.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, putting my phone away. I watch the clock with them.* "So... what happens if she *doesn't* call?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“Then I stop treating this number as safe,” Noor said. “I keep the evidence offline, get some sleep, and contact my editor in the morning. I won’t make a second call just because I’m frightened.”

At 1:14, the landline stayed silent. Noor gave it another minute. Then they drew a box around **NO CALLBACK** in the notebook and pushed their chair away from the refrigerator.

They checked that the copied records still opened, closed the laptop, and put the drive back in its padded case. The source’s note went into the notebook beside the call times. Noor wanted everything they had verified in one place when they woke up, and nothing they had merely suspected mixed in with it.

In the cupboard beneath the sink, they found a dented tin of soup. Noor read the date, found a saucepan, and set it on the stove.

“Mara may have decided this line isn’t safe,” they said. “Or something may have stopped her calling. I can’t tell which tonight.”

They turned the burner low. Once they had eaten, Noor intended to set an alarm for six and lie down, even if sleep took a while. Morning would come soon enough.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I get up from the couch and walk over to the stove, looking at the dented tin.* "Want me to open that for you? And you're really not going to call anyone else?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor held out the tin. “Yes, please. The opener’s in that drawer.” They pointed, then took a bowl down from the cabinet.

“And no, not tonight. Mara knows this number. If she decided it wasn’t safe to use, another call from it won’t help the source.”

They turned off the burner until the soup was ready to heat. Waiting gave them one more task: Noor wrote the editor’s morning contact procedure on a clean page, followed by three questions they needed answered before sending the files. Had anyone else heard from the source? Could the editor receive an encrypted copy? Had the transport company appeared in any other reporting?

Noor set an alarm for six on the laptop, then unplugged it and tucked the drive beneath the folded clothes in their bag. The notebook stayed on the table.

“I want to call someone,” they admitted. “That’s different from having a useful call to make.” They glanced at the clock. “I’ll eat, sleep for a few hours, and give my editor what I can actually prove.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor lowered the tin onto the counter when it became clear the opener wasn’t coming. They found it in the drawer, worked the stiff handle around the lid, and poured the soup into the saucepan. While it heated, they checked the landline once more. No message light. No ring.

They ate at the kitchen table, washed the bowl, and lay down with the notebook within reach. Sleep came in short stretches. At six, the laptop alarm pulled them out of the last one.

Noor opened their usual encrypted channel and sent their editor a brief message: **Source missed meeting. Four invoice approvals followed after-hours switchboard calls. Records verified and ready. Have you heard from them?** They did not attach the files.

A reply came nine minutes later. **No contact. Send the four records. I’ll have our records desk check the transport company independently. Are you safe where you are?**

Noor read the question twice. They looked toward the dark window, then typed: **Safe as far as I can tell. Sending only the four.** They attached the encrypted folder, checked the recipient address character by character, and sent it.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I'm awake on the couch, scrolling my phone as usual. I hear the laptop ding and then Noor typing.* "Everything good?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“The editor has the four records,” Noor said. “That’s good. The source still hasn’t turned up.”

They waited for the upload confirmation, then sent a second message: **Attorney Mara Voss did not call back after speaking to me at 1:03. Please have someone contact her office independently. Do not use the cabin number.**

Noor closed the channel and wrote down what they had sent and when. The notebook now held a short list of things they knew, and a longer list of things they didn’t. They drew a line between them.

“I told my editor I’m safe as far as I can tell,” they said. “I need to find out if that’s still true.”

They pulled the curtain aside just enough to check the road and the parked car, then let it fall. Nothing had changed. Noor put water on for coffee, but left their bag packed by the table. If the records desk confirmed the company’s connection, they would have a story to work on. If Mara’s silence meant the cabin had been compromised, they wanted to be ready to leave.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I put my phone down, a little unnerved by the way Noor said that last part.* "Compromised? What do you mean?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“I mean someone may know where I am,” Noor said. “I don’t have evidence of that. Mara heard this landline’s number, and then she didn’t call back. Those are the facts.”

They checked the back door’s lock, then the front, without opening either. Both held. At the kitchen table, Noor wrote down the cabin’s address and the route back to the main road. They left the page beside their packed bag and poured the hot water over instant coffee.

The laptop chimed. Their editor had replied: **Records desk found the transport company’s registration. Same address as a consulting firm named in last year’s procurement investigation. Mara’s office says she is unavailable. They won’t say more.**

Noor copied the company address into the notebook and underlined it once. It gave them a lead, not an answer about the source. They sent back: **Please preserve the registration record. Ask the desk to verify ownership without contacting either company. I’m leaving this location shortly; I’ll check in through this channel when settled.**

Noor closed the laptop and slipped it into their bag. “The cabin may be perfectly safe,” they said. “But I don’t need it to be unsafe before I leave. My editor has the records, and we can work somewhere else.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Okay. Well, let's get out of here then." *I grab my keys off the coffee table, ready to go.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor zipped the bag, then stopped and checked the table. Notebook, drive, laptop, phone. They unplugged the laptop alarm and left the cabin as they had found it, apart from a washed bowl on the rack.

“Let’s go to the all-night diner off the main road,” they said. “It’ll be open, and I can work there while we decide where to stay next.”

At the front door, Noor paused long enough to look through the narrow window. The road was empty. They stepped outside, locked up, and kept the bag close as they headed toward the parked car.

Halfway there, their phone vibrated. Noor took it out and read the message from their editor: **Ownership confirmed. I’m calling you through our channel in twenty minutes. Don’t contact the companies.**

Noor put the phone away. “The records desk found an owner,” they said. “I’ll hear what they found once we’re somewhere with coffee and other people around.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, already heading for the car.* "Sounds good. Hopefully, they have good coffee."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor kept watching the road for one more breath. Then they let the curtain fall.

“You’re right,” they said. “I hate that you’re right.”

They found half a loaf of bread in the freezer and a tin of soup with a label faded almost white. While the soup warmed, Noor opened the laptop. The phone records came first: calls from the source’s number over the past week, all brief, all at odd hours. The last one had come at 8:41 tonight. Noor compared it with the number scribbled in their notebook, then checked the location attached to the call.

They stopped stirring. The call hadn’t come from the road up the mountain. It had come from a payphone two towns away.

Noor turned down the burner before the soup could boil over. “Something changed before they were supposed to leave,” they said. They wrote down the time and location, ate three hurried spoonfuls standing at the counter, and carried the bowl back to the table.

The encrypted drive was next. Noor connected it and opened the folder the source had told them to check only if the meeting went wrong. Inside was a single file, uploaded at 8:57 PM.

Noor read its name twice: **IF_I_DONT_ARRIVE**.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look over at the laptop screen, then back at my phone.* "Everything okay?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“No,” Noor said. “Not yet.”

They opened the file. It was a short text document, not the cache of evidence they had expected.

**If I miss the meeting, check the calls I made on Tuesday. The names in the ledger are aliases. Match the times, not the names. Do not call me.**

Below that was a string of six dates and times. The last line read: **They know about the cabin.**

Noor looked toward the dark window. For a moment, the black glass gave back only the kitchen: the laptop, the soup, their own pale face. They closed the curtain completely.

“That file was saved before nine,” they said. “Whatever happened, they had time to warn me.”

They copied the text to their notebook, then disconnected the drive. Tuesday’s records were still open. Noor worked down the six times, finding a call at each one. Five went to different numbers. The sixth went to the office of the deputy minister whose contracts Noor had spent four months tracing.

Their hand shook badly enough that they put the pen down. They ate another spoonful of soup, though it had gone lukewarm.

Noor shut the laptop lid halfway, leaving the records on-screen. “We shouldn’t stay here till morning. I need ten minutes to copy what I can verify, then I’m packing.” They glanced at the clock. “After that, somewhere with people. I can sleep when the files are out of my hands.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I put my phone down, a little annoyed.* "Okay, what's going on? What files? And who's 'they'?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor stopped with one hand on the laptop lid. The question was fair. They had been talking as if everyone at the table had spent four months inside the story.

“The files are procurement records,” they said. “A deputy minister approved emergency contracts to companies that barely exist. The ledger I got last week shows payments leaving those companies on the same days people investigating the contracts were threatened.” Noor tapped the notebook beside the computer. “Tonight’s source was going to tell me who received the payments.”

They looked at the closed curtain. “I don’t know who ‘they’ are. That’s the part I’m trying to prove. But my source knew this cabin’s location before they disappeared, and I told only two people where we were going.”

Noor caught themself glancing at the couch and looked away. “I’m not accusing you. I’m saying I may have been careless long before tonight.”

They reopened the laptop and copied the six Tuesday call times onto a fresh page, alongside the corresponding ledger entries. At the fifth time, they paused. The amount was small enough that they had dismissed it before: a payment to a company that maintained roadside cameras.

Noor wrote down the company name. “That’s something I can check without waiting for the source.”

They saved the records to an encrypted archive, unplugged the drive, and put it in their coat pocket. Then they closed the laptop and finally picked up the soup.

“Give me five minutes to finish this and pack,” they said. “I’ll explain the rest on the way down.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor finished the soup because they had said they would, then rinsed the bowl without turning on the kitchen light. They packed the laptop, photographed the six matched times in their notebook, and checked that the encrypted drive was still in their coat pocket.

The camera company bothered them. Before shutting the laptop down, Noor searched the procurement records they had saved offline. The company had billed the ministry for “routine maintenance” on Tuesday—six separate jobs, each logged within minutes of a call from the source. The locations weren’t scattered across the region. They marked a route from the deputy minister’s office to a warehouse outside the city.

Noor stared at the dates. “Those payments weren’t for cameras,” they said. “They were for turning them off.”

They copied the invoice numbers into the notebook. That was evidence they could verify later; it wasn’t worth staying in a cabin someone else knew about.

Noor put on their coat and carried their bag to the door. They left the porch light off. “There’s an all-night hospital about forty minutes downhill,” they said. “Public entrance, security cameras, people awake. I can send the verified records from there and find out whether my source made it somewhere safe.”

Their eyes went once more to the dark window. Then Noor took the cabin key from its hook and opened the door.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I finally look up from my phone.* "You think someone's coming here?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“I don’t know,” Noor said. “But the warning named this cabin, and I’m not staying to find out.”

Cold air slipped through the open door. Noor paused on the threshold and listened. Wind moved through the pines; farther down the slope, water ran over rock. They heard no engine.

They pulled the door shut and locked it, then stopped halfway down the porch steps. The cabin key was still in their hand. Noor went back, set it beneath the loose stone by the door where the owner had asked them to leave it, and headed toward the car.

“The hospital’s still the plan,” they said. “If someone follows us, we don’t lead them straight there. We keep driving until I can work out another public place to stop.”

Noor checked their coat pocket once more for the drive. In their notebook, six call times now lined up with six camera-maintenance invoices. It was enough to send to their editor. It was not enough to explain why the source had never arrived.

They looked back at the dark cabin. “I’ll try the hospitals for the source once we’re somewhere safe. I won’t call their number.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I unlock the car doors with the fob as I walk past Noor to the driver's side.* "Alright, let's go. Hospital it is."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor slid into the passenger seat and set their bag between their feet. They didn’t open the laptop again. Instead, they took out the notebook and traced the six invoice locations on an offline map on their phone. The last camera stood at the turnoff to the warehouse. The earlier five marked the only paved route to it.

“Take the main road down,” Noor said. “There’s a service road after the second bridge, but it runs past one of these cameras. I’d rather not pass it.”

They photographed the invoice numbers again, this time checking that every digit was legible, then drafted a message to their editor: six call times, six matching maintenance invoices, and a request to preserve the records immediately. Noor left it unsent. At the hospital, they could use its public Wi-Fi and make the call from inside.

Before putting the phone away, they searched the saved records for the warehouse address. It belonged to a company that had received one of the emergency contracts.

Noor stared at the screen. “The source wasn’t just going to name who got paid,” they said. “I think they were going to show me where the money went.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I start the car.* "So, they were gonna lead you to a warehouse?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“Maybe,” Noor said. “But the file didn’t tell me to go there. It told me to match the times.”

They looked at the warehouse address again. One of the six invoices listed a job number, and the same number appeared in the ledger beside a payment Noor had marked as unexplained. They photographed both entries together. Then they sent the draft message to their editor over the phone’s cellular connection, without the drive attached.

“I was going to wait for the hospital,” they said. “But if this phone disappears, someone else needs those numbers.”

A reply came back almost at once: **Received. Stay away from the warehouse. Call when safe.**

Noor let out a breath. They hadn’t noticed they were holding it. “So no, we’re not going there. The hospital first. Then I’m going to find out who signed off on those six jobs—and whether anyone’s reported my source missing.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor looked down at the editor’s reply, then put the phone face down in their lap. The car was still outside the cabin; until they were downhill, the dark windows were too easy to watch.

They pulled the notebook from their bag and checked the six invoices again. Each had the same approval code, though the work orders named different technicians. Noor found the code in an older contract they had saved. It belonged to the deputy minister’s office.

“That’s who I’m checking next,” they said. “Not the warehouse. The person who approved the camera work.”

Noor photographed the older contract and sent it to their editor with a short note: **Same approval code on all six Tuesday invoices. Please verify who had authority to use it. Don’t contact the ministry yet.**

Then they tucked the notebook inside their coat. Their hands were steadier now that the records existed somewhere beyond the car.

“When we get to the hospital, I’m going inside first,” Noor said. “I’ll call my editor and ask the desk how to check whether someone was brought in tonight. If there’s no way to do that without giving my source’s name, I won’t.” They glanced once at the cabin. “I need answers, but I’m not handing anyone another location.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, still focused on the road.* "Alright. Sounds like a plan."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor watched the road unwind between the trees. At the first bridge, they checked the phone: one bar of signal, then two. Enough to call, but the hospital was still a better place to discuss a source whose warning had named the cabin.

They opened their saved copy of the ledger instead. The approval code appeared on six Tuesday entries—and on one entry from the previous month. That older payment had gone to a towing company.

Noor found its invoice. The destination field read **county impound**, but the vehicle identification number had been left blank.

Their editor’s reply arrived before Noor could search further: **Code assigned to deputy minister’s chief of staff. Still verifying who used it Tuesday.**

Noor sent back the towing invoice and a request to preserve the original. Then they put the phone away. No more digging through records on a mountain road when they could barely keep their eyes focused.

“I found an older payment with the same code,” they said. “A tow, with no vehicle listed. It might be nothing. I’m not going to make it into an answer before I check.”

They took the last piece of bread from their bag and ate it slowly. At the hospital, they would call their editor, ask about the source without offering a name at the desk, and find somewhere to sit for an hour. Noor wrote the three steps in the notebook. Sleep still belonged on the list, even if they could not yet imagine doing it.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I glance over at Noor, then back at the road.* "You good? You look wiped."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“No,” Noor said. “But I can stay awake until we’re somewhere safe.”

They closed the ledger on their phone. The numbers had started to blur, and checking them a fourth time would not make them more reliable. Instead, Noor set an alarm for twenty minutes and another for forty-five. “If I fall asleep before we get there, wake me when we’re near the hospital. I need to be clearheaded before I call my editor.”

They put the phone in their coat pocket, where they could feel the outline of the drive beside it. For a while, Noor watched the dark trees beyond the window. Then they leaned their head against the seat and shut their eyes, one hand still resting over the pocket.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod and turn my attention back to the road, focusing on the winding turns.* "Got it. I'll keep an eye out for those alarms."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The first alarm woke Noor with a start. They silenced it and checked the time: twenty minutes gone. The road outside the window had widened, and the first streetlights showed through the trees.

Their editor had sent another message. **Chief of staff had access to the approval code Tuesday. So did two procurement officers. I’ve preserved what you sent. No word on your source.**

Noor read it twice. Access wasn’t proof. They replied: **Please check who approved the work orders, not just who could. And don’t call the source.**

They rubbed their eyes, then took the notebook out again. At the top of a clean page, they wrote three questions for the call: who authorized the six jobs; where the blank-VIN tow ended; whether anyone had heard from the source. Beneath them, they wrote **eat, then sleep**. They had nearly forgotten both already.

“I’m awake,” Noor said. “I’m going to call my editor once I’m inside the hospital. I’ve sent enough for them to start verifying without me.” They folded the notebook shut and watched for the hospital signs.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod again.* "Sounds good. We're almost there." *I slow down as we approach an exit for the town.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't turn from the window. Their shoulders stayed tight under the flannel they'd thrown on over the same shirt they'd worn to the meeting that never happened.

"In a minute," they said. Their voice came out thinner than they wanted.

The road stayed empty. A porch light two bends down blinked once and went dark again. Noor counted to thirty, then let the curtain fall and crossed to the kitchen. The fridge hummed like it was working too hard. Inside: half a jar of pickles, a stick of butter with a knife still in it, and a sleeve of saltines that had gone soft at the edges. They took the crackers and a mug, filled the mug from the tap, and set both on the table next to the unopened laptop.

Their phone was face-down beside the drive. Noor flipped it over. No new messages. The last one from the source was still there, timestamped 6:41 PM: *Coming. Don't call this number again.*

They sat. The chair creaked. They ate two crackers without tasting them and opened the laptop anyway, because waiting with their hands empty was worse. The screen lit their face blue. They didn't look at Driver when they spoke.

"If they're not here by one, I'm pulling the phone records off the backup. I copied them before I left the office. If the number they texted from is a burner that only pinged one tower, I need to know which one." Their fingers hovered over the trackpad. "And if you hear a car that isn't slowing down for the bend, tell me. Don't open the door."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I hear the creak of the chair, then Noor's voice.* "Got it. No car, no open door." *I scroll through my phone, then sigh, setting it down.* "You sure you don't want me to just... go check the road?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor kept their eyes on the screen while the laptop woke. The login prompt sat there, cursor blinking, and they typed the passphrase without looking at their hands.

"No," they said. "You stay inside. If someone is watching the road, I don't want a second set of headlights telling them the cabin isn't empty."

The desktop came up. Noor plugged in the encrypted drive, waited for the little green lock to clear, and opened the folder they'd copied before they left the office. Phone records. Three months. They scrolled to the source's number and filtered for the last forty-eight hours.

Two hits. Both from the same tower, eight miles east of the highway exit they'd used to get here. Last ping at 8:52 PM. Then nothing.

Noor's mouth went dry. They ate another cracker, chewed it like it was a task, and pulled the tower map into a second window.

"They were close," they said, more to the screen than to Driver. "Then the phone went dark. Either they ditched it, or somebody took it." Their fingers stopped moving. Outside, the porch boards ticked as the temperature dropped. "I'm going to cross-check the other numbers that hit that tower in the same ten-minute window. If a car followed them off the exit, it might be in here."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I pick up my phone again, my thumb hovering over the screen.* "So, like, someone else could be on their way here right now?" *I look at the window, then back at Noor.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't answer right away. Their eyes stayed on the filtered list, the cursor dragging down a column of timestamps that all clustered inside the same ten minutes. A delivery van. Two personal cells that had been pinging that tower for hours, locals. One number that appeared once, at 8:47, and never again.

They highlighted it. Copied it into a notes file. Their knee bounced under the table, a small restless motion they didn't bother to stop.

"Maybe," they said. The word came out flat. "Or maybe they ditched the phone in a ditch and they're walking the last stretch with the lights off. I don't know yet."

They opened the second folder on the drive — the one labeled with a date and nothing else — and started a cross-check against the numbers they'd already flagged from the source's earlier calls. The cabin's old radiator knocked once in the wall. Noor flinched, then kept typing.

"Eat the rest of those crackers if you want them," they added, still not looking up. "I'm not stopping until I know whether that one-time number belongs to anybody I've already got a name for. If it doesn't, we kill the porch light and we wait in the dark. If it does..." Their fingers paused over the keys. Outside, something small moved in the brush past the tree line, then went quiet. "If it does, I need you to remember the plate on the truck we passed at the gas station. The gray one. Write it down before you forget it."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor heard the shrug more than they saw it. The chair across the room creaked as Driver settled back in, and the blue glow of a phone screen came up again in Noor's peripheral vision. Fine. They hadn't asked for a partner. They'd asked for a ride and a second set of ears.

The cross-check finished with a soft chime Noor had forgotten to mute. They killed the sound, then leaned in.

The one-time number wasn't in the folder. Not in the source's call log, not in the three months of records, not in the list of desk phones at the agency Noor had been circling for six weeks. Clean. Or new. Or both.

Noor sat back. The saltine sleeve crackled when their elbow hit it. They broke one in half, ate the half, and drank the rest of the tap water without tasting the metal in it.

"Not a name I know," they said, to the room, not to Driver. Their voice had gone quieter, the way it did when they were talking themselves through a decision. "So we treat it like it matters."

They closed the laptop lid until the screen was a slit, enough to work by, not enough to paint the curtains. Then they stood, crossed to the switch by the door, and killed the porch light. The cabin dropped into the dark the mountains already owned. For a second Noor couldn't see the table. Then their eyes adjusted, and the road through the curtain gap was a paler strip against the trees.

They went back to the chair but didn't sit all the way. One hand stayed on the back of it. The other found their phone, still face-up, still empty.

12:31.

"I'm setting an alarm for one," they said. "If nothing moves by then, I pack the drive and we leave by the fire road, not the highway. Lights off until we're past the bend." A floorboard popped under their weight as they shifted. They didn't look at Driver. "If something does move before then, you don't get up. You stay low and you tell me which direction the engine is coming from. That's the whole job."

Outside, the brush stayed quiet. Noor opened the laptop again, just enough, and started copying the one-time number and the tower coordinates into a note that would survive if the drive had to go into a ditch. Their hands were steady now. The fear hadn't left. It had just found something to do.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I watch Noor move around, then kill the porch light.* "Got it. Stay low, direction of engine." *I look at my phone, then slide it into my pocket.* "You want me to just wait here, or...?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't answer until the note was saved and the laptop lid was down again. The cabin was all shadow now, the road a gray thread through the curtain gap, the radiator ticking as it cooled.

"Here," they said. They crossed to the couch and set the sleeve of saltines on the arm, then the half-full mug. "You wait here. Low. Phone on silent, screen down. If you need the bathroom, you go now, because after that nobody crosses the window."

They checked their own phone one more time. Still nothing under the source's thread. Noor opened the clock app, set an alarm for 1:00, and turned the volume all the way down so it would only buzz against the table. Then they went back to the kitchen, broke the last two crackers in half, and ate them standing up over the sink, chewing until the salt was gone and their stomach stopped feeling quite so hollow.

The encrypted drive was still warm from the port. Noor slid it into the padded case, zipped it, and set the case on the chair by the door with the car keys on top of it. Ready. Not packed to run, but ready if running was the next true thing.

"I'm going to sit by the window until the alarm," they said, already moving. They dragged the kitchen chair sideways so it sat just out of the curtain's line and lowered themselves into it, knees up, one hand on the phone. Their eyes stayed on the road. "If I fall asleep, wake me at one. Don't let me sleep through it."

A pair of headlights bloomed far down the mountain, then dipped behind the bend and didn't come back. Noor counted the seconds anyway. Thirty. Sixty. Nothing. Their shoulders dropped a fraction, and they kept watching.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod.* "Got it. No crossing the window." *I slide down lower on the couch, pulling my knees up and resting my chin on them. I watch Noor for a moment.* "You want me to stay awake with you?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor heard the offer and let it sit for a second, the way they let a bad lead sit before they decided whether it was usable.

"Stay awake," they said. "Don't talk unless something changes. I need the quiet so I can hear the road."

They pulled their knees higher and set the phone face-down on the windowsill, screen dark, alarm already armed. The chair was too hard for sleep anyway. Their back already knew it.

For a while there was only the radiator and the small wet sound of Driver breathing on the couch. Noor counted headlights that never came. At 12:41 a truck climbed the far grade, engine low and steady, and passed the bend without slowing. They marked the time in the note on their phone with their thumb, one line, no light: *12:41 through-traffic, didn't turn.*

Then they got up anyway, because sitting still was starting to feel like a decision they hadn't made. They crossed the dark kitchen by memory, found the butter knife still stuck in the stick, and used the dull edge to pry the cabin's landline jack out of the wall. The cord came free with a soft click. Noor wound it once around their hand and dropped it into the padded case with the drive. If anyone called this number looking for a voice, they were going to get a dead line.

"I'm killing the house phone," they said, already back at the window. "If the source is alive, they know not to use it. If they aren't, I don't want this place answering for me."

They sat again. The road stayed empty. Their stomach had settled around the crackers, and the fear had narrowed into a list: alarm at one, fire road if nothing moved, plate from the gas station if Driver still had it, drive in the case, lights off past the bend. Noor put a hand on the curtain and didn't open it wider than a finger's width.

"If I start packing before the alarm, it means I heard something I don't like," they said. "You don't ask what. You get your shoes on."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, pressing my knees tighter to my chest. My eyes are fixed on the dark window, listening.* "Got it. Shoes on."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor kept their hand on the curtain and counted the quiet the way they counted sources: by what it refused to give up. The truck's engine had faded into the grade. Nothing replaced it. At 12:47 a branch knocked the eaves once, hard, and they had their weight half off the chair before they recognized the sound for wind.

They sat back down. Their mouth tasted like salt and metal. The crackers had done what they were going to do.

The encrypted drive was already in the case by the door, but the laptop was still on the table, lid down, not asleep. Noor crossed to it without turning on a light, opened it to a slit, and pulled the second folder again — the one with the date and nothing else. Not the phone records this time. The scans. Three pages the source had photographed in a parking garage two weeks ago and sent through a dead drop Noor had stopped trusting the moment the texts got shorter.

They zoomed until the letterhead filled the screen. A name they already had. A routing number they had already matched to a shell that paid a consulting firm that paid a man who did not consult. None of that was new. What was new was the handwriting in the margin of the third page, cropped so tight Noor had almost missed it the first time: a time, 9:15, and a word that might have been *cabin* or might have been *carbon*. They had called it carbon in their notes because carbon was safer to be wrong about.

Noor stared at it until the pixels stopped trying to become letters.

"They knew this place," they said, low, to the dark and not to anyone in it. "Or they were guessing, and they guessed close enough that I drove us here anyway."

They copied the crop into the same note as the one-time number and the tower coordinates, then shut the laptop all the way and slid it into the case on top of the drive. The car keys stayed on top. The landline cord was a dead snake against the padding. If they had to leave, there would be nothing on the table worth coming back for except the two of them.

12:53. The alarm was seven minutes out. Noor didn't go back to the window right away. They filled the mug again at the tap, drank half, and set the rest on the floor beside the chair so they wouldn't have to cross the room for it. Then they checked the back door — still latched, still the cheap slide bolt the uncle had never replaced — and the window over the sink, which looked out on a slope of brush and no road at all. Nothing moved there except the same wind that had hit the eaves.

They returned to the chair. Knees up. Phone face-down. Eyes on the pale strip of road.

"One more thing," they said, and their voice had the flat edge it got when the list was almost done. "If we take the fire road, you drive. I navigate. I know where it comes out, and I don't want to be the one with my hands on the wheel if somebody is already on it. If the alarm goes and the road is still empty, that's the plan. No debate in the car."

A pair of headlights rose again, farther off than the last ones, white and then gone behind the trees. Noor didn't count this time. They watched the gap in the curtain and waited to see if the lights came back on the near side of the bend. Their free hand rested on the case. The fear was still there. It had a time on it now.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor heard the yeah and didn't spend breath on it. The phone in Driver's hands was a problem they would deal with in the car, not now.

12:58. They killed the alarm before it could buzz, thumb finding the screen by feel, and stood. The road through the curtain was still empty. No engine. No lights on the near side of the bend. That was the condition they had set, and they were not going to sit through another hour inventing a reason to break it.

"Alarm's now," they said. "Road's empty. We're leaving."

They crossed to the door, lifted the case, and checked the weight: laptop, drive, dead landline cord, keys on top. Shoes were already on. They shrugged into the flannel like it was a coat and didn't bother with the crackers or the mug. The tap was still dripping. They left it.
