At the back window they looked once more at the slope. Brush. Wind. No shape that held still when the branches moved. Good enough.

"Shoes," they said, already at the front door, hand on the latch, not opening it yet. "Phone in your pocket, not in your hand. You take the driver's side. I go out first, I get the passenger door, you don't start the engine until I'm in and the case is on the floor. Lights off. Fire road is left at the end of the driveway, not right. Right is the highway."

They eased the latch up. Cold came in under the door, pine and wet dirt. Noor listened for ten seconds with their ear near the gap, then opened it just wide enough to see the gravel and the dark shape of the car.

"If I stop walking, you stop," they said. "If I get in, you get in. No lights in the cabin when we go. Leave them dead."

They stepped onto the porch, case against their ribs, and started for the car without looking back to see if Driver had moved.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I scramble off the couch, shoving my phone in my pocket. I trip a little over my own feet, then follow Noor out the door.* "Got it. Fire road left."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't wait on the porch to see if the scramble behind them turned into footsteps. The gravel gave under their shoes, loud in the cold, and they kept the case tight against their ribs so it wouldn't knock the railing. The car was where they'd left it, nose pointed at the driveway, a skin of frost on the hood that caught what little sky there was.

They opened the passenger door first, not the driver's, and set the case on the floor in front of the seat. Keys stayed in their hand. They listened once more — wind in the pines, the tick of the cabin cooling, no engine on the road — then slid in and pulled the door until it latched, quiet, not slammed.

The interior smelled like old coffee and the crackers they hadn't finished. Noor put the keys in the ignition but didn't turn them. Their eyes stayed on the tree line past the windshield, then on the rearview, then on the dark mouth of the driveway.

"Left," they said, when the driver's door opened and the car dipped under another person's weight. Their voice was low, almost nothing. "Don't touch the headlights. Don't buckle until we're moving — the click carries. When I say now, you start it, and you don't rev. First gear, slow, like you're leaving a funeral."

They pulled their phone out, screen still dark, and held it against their thigh so the glow wouldn't hit the glass. The note was there if they needed the tower coordinates. The plate from the gas station was not. They let that go. There wasn't time to drag it out of somebody else's memory in a parked car.

A branch shifted at the edge of the lot. Noor watched it until it was only wind again.

"Now," they said.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I slide into the driver's seat, fumbling a little with the cold metal of the door handle. I glance at Noor, then focus on the ignition. I turn the key, the engine sputtering to life, and carefully shift into first.* *The car creeps forward, silent except for the low hum of the engine.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor kept one hand on the dash and the other on the case between their feet, eyes moving between the pale strip of gravel and the black wall of trees on either side. The engine stayed low. Good. They didn't praise it.

"Slower through the dip," they said. "There's a rut where the driveway meets the fire road. If you hit it hard the muffler scrapes and every cabin on this ridge hears it."

The frost on the hood broke into dark streaks as they crept. Noor watched the left fork come up — two pale tracks cut into the weeds, no sign, just the gap the uncle had used for hauling firewood. The highway mouth to the right was wider and easier and wrong.

"There. Left. Don't signal."

They leaned forward until their forehead almost touched the glass, counting the shapes that could have been a parked car and weren't. A stump. A fallen gate. The same wind that had knocked the eaves, moving the tops of the pines and nothing else.

Once the tires left gravel for dirt, Noor let out a breath they hadn't meant to hold.

"Stay in the ruts. Lights stay off until I say otherwise. In about a mile the road drops and you'll see a cattle guard — metal bars, loud if you cross them fast. You stop before it. I get out, I listen, then we go over at a walk." Their thumb found the phone against their thigh, still dark. "If anyone is waiting, they'll be on the far side of that guard, where the road straightens. Not here."

A branch scraped the passenger mirror and Noor flinched, then set their jaw and didn't look at Driver.

"And if I tell you to kill the engine, you kill it and you don't ask why until we're out of the car or we're not."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, my knuckles white on the steering wheel.* "Got it. Slow for the cattle guard." *My eyes are straining to see the ruts in the dark.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor watched the ruts take the tires and didn't fill the quiet. The dirt road narrowed until the pines scraped both mirrors, and the only light was a thin gray on the hood from the sky. Their hand stayed on the case. The other braced the dash when the car nosed down into the drop.

"Almost," they said. "Ease off. I can hear the bars."

The cattle guard showed as a darker grid across the pale track, maybe thirty yards out. Noor lifted a hand, palm down, the way they would have stopped a source mid-sentence.

"Stop. Here. Don't roll onto it."

The car settled. Noor cracked their door before the engine note had fully died in their ears, and the cold came in sharp with pine sap and wet iron. They set one foot on the dirt, case still between their knees, and held still long enough to separate the sounds: their own breath, the tick of the cooling hood, wind in the high branches. Nothing with a motor in it. Nothing that shifted its weight and waited.

They got out the rest of the way and walked the left rut to the guard, shoes placed, not scuffed. Up close the bars were old and loud-looking, a few of them bent. On the far side the road straightened for a hundred yards and then bent again into black trees. No car. No shape crouched at the shoulder. A strip of mud on the right rut held a tread that wasn't theirs — wider, heavier, already crusting at the edges. Hours old, maybe. Not minutes.

Noor crouched, looked at it, and didn't touch it. Then they stood and came back along the same rut.

"Clear enough to cross," they said, low, at the open door. "One set of tracks ahead of us, gone cold. You take it at a walk. I'll close my door after the front tires are on the bars so we only make the noise once." They slid back into the seat and pulled the door to, not latched. "When I tap the dash, go. After the guard, lights still off. The road comes out on a county two-lane in about four miles. We don't turn toward town."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, my eyes still fixed on the dark road ahead. I wait for the tap on the dash, my foot hovering over the accelerator.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor looked away from the road. “You’re right.”

They said it like an admission, though the hollow ache in their stomach had been there long enough to stop registering as urgent. Noor crossed to the counter and searched the cupboards: two cans of soup, a sleeve of crackers, and a jar of instant coffee that looked older than the cabin. They put the soup in a saucepan and set it over the burner.

While it warmed, they finally opened the laptop.

First, the phone records. Noor lined up the call log with the notes they’d made before leaving town, checking the source’s number, the times, the lengths of the calls. The last confirmed call was still the one from that afternoon. No missed call. No message. Nothing to explain three hours of silence.

They wrote the times down anyway. Fear was good at turning gaps into stories; Noor wanted the facts first.

The soup began to bubble. They turned the burner low, ate half a bowl standing at the counter, then brought the rest to the table with the crackers. It was bland and too hot. They ate it all.

Only then did they take the encrypted drive from its padded case. Noor paused with their hand on it, listening to the cabin settle around them, then connected it to the laptop and started the verification process. The progress bar crawled forward.

Noor kept one eye on the dark window and one on the screen. “If they’re not here by one,” they said, “I’m done waiting. I’ll send the check-in, then sleep for a few hours. Whatever happened, I can’t do anything useful half-delirious.”

They opened a blank message to the source but didn’t send it yet. First, they wanted the drive’s checksum—and a record of what they’d checked before the night got any stranger.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I scroll through my phone, seeing a funny meme.* "Hey, check this out," *I say, turning the screen to Noor, then notice the drive and the message.* "You really gonna send that? What if they just got lost?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor glanced at the turned screen, but the checksum bar had nearly reached the end. “In a minute,” they said, too tired to manage more than a thin smile. “I’m sure it’s hilarious.”

Their attention returned to the blank message. “They might have gotten lost. They might also have had to stop for a reason they can’t tell me over an ordinary phone.” Noor kept their voice low, careful not to turn possibility into certainty. “A check-in doesn’t mean I’m accusing them of anything. It means I’m not going to leave us sitting here with no record of what happened.”

The verification finished. Noor copied the checksum into their notes, then checked it against the value they’d been given. It matched. They saved the result and backed up the phone-log timeline beside it.

At 12:47, they set a reminder for one o’clock. The message stayed unsent until then; it contained no mention of the cabin, only a brief request for the source to confirm they were safe and give a new arrival time. Noor reread it once, then turned the phone face down.

“If there’s no answer, I send that, lock the drive away, and sleep,” they said. “Lost or not, I can’t keep watch and think at the same time.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I shrug, putting my phone back down.* "Fair enough. Just... don't do anything stupid, okay? You look like you're about to fall over."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“I know,” Noor said. “That’s why I’m stopping.”

They ejected the drive, checked that the verification notes had saved, and returned it to its padded case. The laptop went to sleep—not shut down, in case the check-in needed a quick follow-up—and Noor slid the case into the locked drawer beneath the table.

They checked the front door and the back latch, then drew the curtains fully closed. Nothing outside had changed: no headlights on the road, no figure crossing the clearing. Noor recorded that, too, with the time. Observation, not interpretation.

At 12:58, they took a glass of water to the table and reread the message. It asked only whether the source was safe and when they could meet. No location, no details about the records. At one, Noor sent it.

Then they set their phone to ring through silent mode, plugged it in, and set an alarm for four hours later. They left the lamp off. “If they answer, I’ll wake up,” they said, mostly to steady themself. “If they don’t, I’ll make the next decision with a functioning brain.”

Noor took the blanket from the chair and stretched out on the narrow couch, still dressed, with the phone on the table within reach. The road stayed dark beyond the curtains. For once, Noor stopped watching it.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor had almost drifted off when the phone vibrated against the table.

They sat up too quickly, heart kicking hard, and reached for it. A message had arrived from the source’s number.

*I’m safe. Don’t call me. I was followed.*

Noor read it twice. It could have been genuine. It could also have been someone else holding the phone. They didn’t reply.

Instead, they photographed the screen with the laptop camera, noted the time, and copied the message into the timeline. Then they checked the door and back latch without turning on the lights. Both were still secure.

Noor returned to the table and opened the unsent draft to their editor. They added the new message and a short note: *Unverified. Do not contact source’s number.* They saved it without sending.

The drive remained locked away. The phone stayed plugged in, ringer on. Noor set the alarm for another hour and lay back down, this time with the blanket pulled up to their chin.

“Safe isn’t the same as okay,” they murmured into the dark. “And it isn’t proof.”

They closed their eyes, but kept one hand near the phone.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I put my phone down and look at Noor.* "What's that supposed to mean? 'Followed'?" *My voice is quiet.* "Are *we* safe?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor sat upright, the fear sharpening into something more useful. “I don’t know,” they said quietly. “That message doesn’t tell us whether anyone followed them here. It doesn’t prove we’re in danger—but we should treat it seriously.”

They put the phone face down and moved away from the window. “Don’t contact that number, and don’t go outside to check. I’m not going to answer until we can verify it’s really them.”

Noor checked the front and back locks from inside, keeping clear of the glass. Both held. They set their shoes, coat, keys, and flashlight beside the back exit, then returned to the table and added the message and its time to their notes. “If someone tries to get in, we call emergency services. Until then, we stay inside, keep the lights off, and don’t give anyone more information.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, my heart starting to race a little.* "Okay. Got it." *I glance around the dark cabin.* "So... no more memes then?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
“No more memes until we’ve established whether ‘followed’ means on the road or in their phone,” Noor said. A thread of dry humor held their voice steady; their hands were still cold.

They didn’t look through the curtains. Instead, Noor checked the time, saved the message and its timestamp in the incident log, then opened the secure channel to their editor. They sent a brief update: the source had reported being followed, the claim was unverified, and Noor would not contact that number. They asked the editor to verify the source through their separate agreed-upon contact—not to send anyone to the cabin.

Noor kept the cabin’s location out of the message. Then they silenced notifications that weren’t essential and set the phone where they could hear an incoming call. “We stay inside,” they said. “I’ll check the locks once more, then we wait fifteen minutes. If there’s no sign of anyone outside, I’m going back to sleep with the phone on.”

They checked the back latch and front lock from inside, staying away from the windows. Both were still secure. Noor returned to the couch without looking at the dark road. “And if you want to show me the meme in the morning,” they added, “I’ll try to appreciate it with a less catastrophic imagination.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I let out a shaky breath that's almost a laugh.* "Deal. Just... try to get some sleep, okay? You're doing too much." *I lean back on the couch, pulling my knees up, trying to look casual but my eyes keep darting to the windows.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor gave a small nod. “You’re right. I’m doing too much.”

They moved away from the table and settled on the floor beside the couch, where the walls blocked the windows from view. Their phone stayed within reach, ringer on. Noor set a fifteen-minute timer—not to keep watch, they told themself, but to give the editor’s verification request time to land.

A reply came before the timer finished. The editor hadn’t confirmed the source’s message yet. Noor sent back one instruction: *Don’t contact that number. Don’t come here. Verify through the agreed channel only.*

They saved the exchange to the incident log, then locked the laptop and left the drive in the drawer. No more checking the road. No more rereading the message until it changed meaning.

“Even if we’re not sure what ‘followed’ means, staying awake won’t make us safer,” Noor said, voice low. “If anything changes, we deal with the fact in front of us—not every possibility at once.”

When the timer sounded, Noor silenced it and lay down beneath the blanket. Their eyes stayed open for a few breaths, fixed on the dim ceiling instead of the windows. Then they turned onto their side and made themself rest.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor left the room quiet. They didn’t ask for reassurance or look toward the windows; they set the phone to vibrate against the floor beside them and closed their eyes.

The next buzz came twelve minutes later. Noor was awake before the second vibration, reaching for the phone without getting up. The editor’s reply had come through the secure channel: the source had confirmed their identity through the agreed separate contact. They were safe for the moment, but wouldn’t come to the cabin. Their phone might be compromised. No further details.

Noor saved the message to the incident log, then sent one instruction back: *Do not share our location. Arrange a new contact point through the agreed channel after daylight.*

They didn’t reply to the source’s number. They didn’t reopen the laptop or check the road. Instead, Noor set an alarm for dawn and placed the keys beside their shoes, where they could find them without turning on a light.

The source was alive. The meeting was off. That was enough to decide what came next, not enough to make the night feel safe.

Noor tucked the phone under the edge of the blanket and lay back down. This time, they let themself sleep.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look over as Noor settles down, then back at my phone.* "Good. So we're not dying tonight."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor opened their eyes at the sound of the comment. “That’s not what we know,” they said quietly. “We know the source is safe for now, and no one’s come to the door. It’s enough to sleep on.”

They set the phone within reach and turned their face toward the wall, away from the windows. This time, exhaustion won.

At dawn, Noor woke before the alarm. They checked the secure channel first: no new message from the editor. Then they added the editor’s verification and the source’s warning to the incident log, keeping the warning clearly marked as unverified. They did not touch the source’s number.

Coffee came next, followed by crackers and the last of the soup, reheated until it was properly hot. Noor ate at the table while reviewing the call timeline, noting the confirmed calls and the long gap without trying to fill it with guesses.

They checked the drive’s checksum once more against their saved record. It still matched. Noor locked it away again, then sent the editor a daylight-only plan: establish a new contact point through the agreed channel, and do not disclose the cabin’s location.

Only after the message was sent did Noor lean back and rub both hands over their tired face. “We’re not calling it safe,” they murmured. “We’re calling it morning.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stretch, yawning widely.* "Morning," *I mumble, still half-asleep.* "So, when are we getting out of here?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor looked up from the incident log. “As soon as I have a verified destination. I’m not taking us somewhere blind, and I’m not going back to either of our usual places.”

They checked the secure channel and sent the editor a short request for a new contact point and a time to confirm they’d arrived. While they waited, Noor packed the laptop and locked drive separately, then put the notes and phone in their coat. The cabin stayed quiet; the road beyond the curtains remained unseen.

“If the editor confirms, we leave this morning,” Noor said. “If there’s no reply soon, I’ll call through the backup contact we agreed on. But we’re not staying here all day.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, scrubbing at my eyes.* "Sounds good to me. I'm ready when you are." *I stand up and stretch again, trying to shake off the grogginess.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor nodded, but didn’t reach for their coat yet. “Give me two minutes. Ready isn’t the same as having somewhere to go.”

They checked the secure channel. A new message from the editor named a meeting point and a time: a lawyer’s office in the nearest town, with the address confirmed through the separate contact they’d already agreed on. Noor called the office’s published number from the laptop—not the number in the message—and verified that someone would be there to let them in.

Only then did they save the details offline and close the channel. They packed the laptop and the locked drive in separate bags, checked that the incident log was backed up, and tucked the phone into an inside pocket.

“We’re leaving now,” Noor said. “The destination’s verified. I’ll keep the source’s number untouched, and I’ll check in with the editor when we arrive.”

They paused at the table, eyes moving over the cabin once—not to search the windows, but to make sure they hadn’t left anything behind. “And when we’re there, I’m getting real food before I look at another record.”

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I grab my jacket and keys.* "Sounds good. Lead the way." *I'm already heading for the door.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang pulled out her earpiece and set a valve seal on the tarp.

“No. The atmosphere isn’t a propellant reserve. It’s what keeps the crew alive.”

She tapped a calculation into her wrist pad. “Even if we vented a thousand kilograms of air in one direction, the exhaust speed would be low and the ship’s mass is enormous. We’d gain a fraction of a meter per second, not weeks. Then we’d have empty tanks, contaminated seals, and a crew depending on suits that were never meant to replace life support for days.”

She looked up. “If the transit estimate is the problem, bring me the trajectory and the propellant margins. We can look for a burn we can actually afford.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set the wrist pad down. “Worth the risk only if it buys us something real. It doesn’t.”

She pointed to the calculation. “For a ten-thousand-tonne ship, venting a tonne of air at three hundred meters per second changes our speed by about three centimeters per second. That won’t take weeks off a transit. It may not take off a minute, depending on the trajectory. And we’d still have to match velocity when we arrived.”

She picked up the valve seal. “Suits have finite oxygen, power, and carbon-dioxide capacity. They’re emergency equipment, not a replacement atmosphere. So no—we don’t trade the crew’s breathable air for a negligible course change.”

Her voice stayed level. “Bring me the trajectory and our propellant margins. If there’s time to recover, we’ll find it in the burn plan.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Okay, Chief. I understand." I nod, a little deflated. *Sighs*. "I'll go get the trajectory data."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang’s expression softened a fraction. She turned the valve seal over in her hands.

“Bring the departure burn, the planned correction burns, and the arrival velocity. Include the propellant reserve we’re not allowed to touch.”

She set the seal beside its labeled fittings. “Wanting to get there sooner was reasonable. Spending the atmosphere to do it wasn’t. We’ll see what the numbers permit.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang studied the tablet before answering. She enlarged the line that converted nozzle exhaust speed into ship velocity.

“There’s the mistake. Three hundred and forty meters per second is the speed of the air leaving your nozzle, not the speed the ship gains.”

She wrote beneath it: **Δv = vₑ ln(Mᵢ/Mf)**.

“At ten thousand tonnes, venting one tonne changes our mass by one part in ten thousand. With your exhaust speed, that gives the ship about three centimeters per second. Changing the angle changes the direction of that impulse. Compressing the air doesn’t multiply it—and the compressor needs power.”

She handed the tablet back. “I’m glad you ran numbers. That’s how we catch ideas before they become emergencies. Keep the trajectory data; we’ll use it to look for a correction burn that actually changes the arrival time.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Oh, I see." *I frown at the equation.* "So it's a logarithmic scale... right." I tap my stylus on the screen, a bit embarrassed. "Okay, Chief. I'll get that trajectory data for you right away. My apologies."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang shook her head and picked up the valve seal.

“No apology needed. You checked the idea before opening a valve. That’s the job.”

She glanced at the equation on the tablet. “And yes, the equation uses a logarithm. When the mass change is this small, the useful approximation is simpler: exhaust speed times the fraction of ship mass we vent. That fraction is the part that hurts your plan.”

She fitted the seal into the manifold. “Bring me the trajectory data. We’ll see whether a correction burn can save any time without spending the arrival reserve.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang paused with the valve seal halfway into its housing.

“All right. I agree we should try to shorten the transit. Bring me the trajectory, and I’ll work through a revised burn plan with you.”

She seated the seal and tightened it. “Three conditions: the arrival burn keeps its full propellant reserve, the new trajectory stays inside our thermal and structural limits, and we verify the numbers independently before anyone changes a command. We do not vent the atmosphere.”

She picked up her wrist pad. “If the margins allow an earlier arrival, we take it. If they don’t, we keep the crew alive and arrive on schedule.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Understood, Chief." *I nod, relieved.* "I'll get those numbers for you right away. And no atmosphere venting, promise!" *I give a small, slightly sheepish smile.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang gave a short nod and turned back to the manifold. She tightened the last fastener, then checked the seal against the pressure readout.

“Good. Send the trajectory file to engineering when you have it. I’ll compare any time-saving burn against the arrival reserve and the radiator load. If the numbers hold up, we’ll take the proposal to the bridge.”

The pressure held steady. Hoang marked the seal’s label with a clean line of chalk.

“And keep your atmosphere calculation. It was wrong in a useful way—you found the mistake before it cost us anything.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Will do, Chief!" *I put my tablet away, feeling a bit better about the whole thing.* "Thanks, I will." *I head out, already thinking about the trajectory data.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched the pressure readout for another ten seconds. The secondary loop held steady.

She logged the manifold repair, then opened the propulsion ledger on her wrist pad. Arrival reserve, correction-burn capacity, radiator limits: she set each beside an empty column for the revised trajectory.

“Let’s see what the ship can actually afford,” she muttered, and went back to work.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I walk down the corridor, feeling a bit of a spring in my step now.* "Okay, trajectory data... where did I save that... ah, there it is." *I pull out my tablet again, already reviewing the files.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang finished reassembling the coolant manifold and ran it through a pressure cycle. The seal held. She logged the repair, then turned to the propulsion ledger.

She pulled up the current flight plan and marked three figures she would need to check against any proposed shortcut: propellant available beyond the arrival reserve, heat the drive and radiators could shed, and the velocity they would have to cancel at the destination. An earlier arrival meant little if the ship reached the mining site too fast to stop.

The trajectory file had not come through yet. Hoang left an analysis window open beside the ledger and began checking the drive’s last performance report.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I'm back in my small office, double-checking the trajectory data. It's a lot of numbers, but I think I've got it all.* "Okay, sending it over to Engineering now." *I tap the send button on my tablet, hoping it's what she needs.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The trajectory file appeared beside the propulsion ledger. Hoang checked its timestamp and reference frame before she trusted a single number in it. Then she overlaid the proposed departure and arrival states on the current flight plan.

“Good,” she said into the engineering channel. “This has the arrival velocity. That’s the number people forget when they start shaving days off a transit.”

She ran a first pass with the arrival reserve locked out. The display traced a narrow band of possible correction burns, then marked where drive heating or propellant use ruled each one out. Hoang saved the result without sending it to the bridge.

“I’ve got the file. I’m checking the thrust history against the drive logs, then I’ll have navigation run an independent solution. If there’s a faster route inside the margins, we’ll know how much time it actually saves—and what it costs.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Understood, Chief. Just let me know if you need anything else from me." *I wait, a bit nervously, for her to tell me if my data is good.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang checked the final column against the ship’s clock and opened the engineering channel.

“The data was good. Timestamps matched, and the arrival state used the right reference frame. You gave me what I needed.”

She studied the first-pass result. “There may be a small time saving, but I’m not putting a number on it until navigation checks the solution independently. One of the candidate burns runs close to our radiator limit. I’d rather lose a day than cook the drive trying to gain one.”

She saved the run. “Nothing else needed from you yet. I’ll send you the checked result when we have it.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Understood, Chief. Thanks!" *I feel a little relieved she said the data was good.* "I'll be standing by."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang pulled out her earpiece and set the manifold seal on the tarp.

“No. Venting the atmosphere would give us a small shove, not weeks off the transit. We would lose breathable gas that we could not replace out here, and the suits would not make the ship’s air, water, and heat systems optional.”

She tapped a chalk mark beside the open coolant loop. “If you wanted a faster arrival, bring me a trajectory and a propellant budget. I would check both. The atmosphere stayed inside.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set the seal down carefully.

“Risk buys something when the numbers say it does. This would buy almost nothing.” She drew a short line in chalk. “Even if we could vent every kilogram of air in the right direction, the exhaust would leave at only a few hundred meters per second. The ship is much heavier than its atmosphere. That means a small change in velocity—and we would have to verify even that against the trajectory before calling it time saved.”

She looked up. “The cost is certain. We lose our breathing reserve, pressure throughout the ship, and the margin we need if a suit or seal fails. A few days in suits would not turn life support into an optional system.”

Hoang picked up the manifold seal again. “If arriving weeks earlier matters, bring me the required delta-v. Then we can see whether the engines and propellant can deliver it. I will not trade the crew’s air for a guess.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Okay, I get it," I say, a little deflated. *I kick at a loose piece of plating on the deck.* "So, no quick boost then. What about... redirecting a solar flare? If we could somehow capture the energy?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang paused with the seal in her hand.

“A solar flare was not a jet of propellant we could aim at the ship. It was radiation and charged particles. Catching some of its energy would give us electrical power, not a useful boost, unless we had a way to turn that power into directed thrust. We did not.”

She set the seal beside the manifold. “A sail could take momentum from sunlight, but this vessel had no sail, and a flare would not turn one into a weeks-fast engine. Out here, its more immediate effect would be radiation exposure and trouble for our electronics.”

Hoang looked up. “That was worth planning for. It was not worth steering toward. For an earlier arrival, the question remained the same: how much delta-v did the trajectory require, and what could safely provide it?”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang put the seal down again and took a closer look at the tablet. She traced the calculation with one grease-marked finger.

“Three hundred and forty meters per second was a number worth checking. But this line treated the compressed air as though it all left the nozzle at the same speed. As the tanks emptied, their pressure would fall. The exhaust speed would fall with it.”

She turned the tablet slightly. “What mass did you use for the ship, and what mass of air did you assume we could vent? At an exhaust speed of a few hundred meters per second, a delta-v of 340 meters per second would require an enormous fraction of the ship’s starting mass to be gas. Changing the vent angle would change the direction of the shove, not make that mass requirement disappear. Compressing the air would also cost power; it would not create momentum for free.”

Hoang left the tablet where it was. “You did the right thing by bringing numbers. Now we tested the assumptions. Show me the air inventory and the ship mass you used, and we would find where this result came from. Then we could check whether 340 meters per second, even if we had it, would actually save weeks on this trajectory.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I chew on my lip, a little embarrassed.* "Uh, I used the estimated maximum capacity for the main atmosphere recyclers, and... the ship's dry mass." I sigh. "So, still no shortcut."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang nodded once. She did not smile, but her voice softened a fraction.

“That explained it. Recycler capacity told them how much atmosphere the machinery could process, not how much gas the ship carried. Dry mass left out the ore, propellant, water, and everyone aboard. Both assumptions pushed the answer in the same direction.”

She pointed to the mass term on the tablet. “The calculation was still useful. It showed exactly what needed checking: the actual gas inventory, the loaded ship mass, and the exhaust speed as tank pressure fell. Those numbers would put a bound on the shove. They would also show how much breathing reserve the maneuver destroyed.”

Hoang slid the tablet back and picked up the manifold seal. “There might be a faster route. It would come from a trajectory calculation and a propellant budget, not from emptying the habitat. The officer could bring her that calculation after watch; Hoang would go through it with them.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang looked back at the tablet, then set the manifold seal down.

“She agreed to test the idea against the real numbers,” she said. “That was not approval to vent the habitat. The safety conditions were simple: the ship kept its pressure, its breathing reserve, and enough gas to survive a leak. Any proposed vent used only verified surplus gas. No valve opened until the trajectory showed a worthwhile time saving and the captain approved the loss of inventory.”

She tapped the inflated delta-v figure on the screen. “First, they corrected the ship mass and air inventory. Then they calculated how the thrust fell as tank pressure dropped. If the result still saved meaningful time without cutting into life-support margin, Hoang would take it seriously. If it did not, the atmosphere stayed where it belonged.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing all the information.* "Okay, Chief. I'll get those numbers for you. Ship mass, air inventory, decaying thrust... and the trajectory impact." *I glance around the engineering bay, feeling a bit more grounded now.* "Thanks for explaining it. I'll get back to you after my shift."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang nodded and picked up the manifold seal.

“Use the *loaded* ship mass,” she said. “Include the ore and remaining propellant. For the gas, separate what the tanks held from what life support needed as reserve. If the usable amount came out to zero, that was an answer.”

She fitted the seal against the manifold and checked its edge with her thumb. “Bring the figures after watch. They would check the trajectory before anyone discussed opening a valve.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Got it, Chief. Loaded mass, reserve gas, all of it." *I make a note on my tablet, feeling a bit overwhelmed by the details but determined.* "I'll see you later." *I turn to leave, already thinking about where to find the updated manifest.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang gave a brief nod and turned back to the coolant manifold. She seated the seal, then ran a finger around its edge to check for grit.

The proposed vent stayed off the work board. Beside the trajectory review, she wrote three items in chalk: **loaded mass, usable gas, arrival-time gain**. Until those numbers existed, no one had a maneuver to approve.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I pause at the doorway, looking back at her. She's already deep in her work. It's a lot of numbers to crunch, but I'm going to prove this could work.* "It'll be worth it, Chief!" *I say, a little too loudly, then head out.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang looked up from the manifold.

“Worth calculating,” she called after the officer. “Not worth doing unless the numbers survived scrutiny.”

She marked the seal’s position, then returned to the coolant loop. The atmosphere remained a life-support reserve, not a propellant budget, until the figures proved otherwise.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I sigh, shaking my head as I walk down the corridor.* Always with the numbers. Still, she didn't say no *completely*. I just need to find the right ones.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang waited until the corridor had gone quiet, then capped the chalk and returned to the coolant manifold. The seal needed fitting before the loop could be pressure-tested; that was a problem she could solve without borrowing air from the crew.

She glanced once at the three items on the board. A calculation could overturn her estimate of the vent’s thrust. It could not make lost atmosphere harmless. If the inventory showed surplus gas, she would check the maneuver. If it showed none, the answer would be no—and she would help look for a trajectory change the ship could actually afford.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I reach the mess hall and grab a nutrient paste tube, still mulling over the conversation. Maybe there's another angle. What if we could use the waste heat from the engines?* "Hmm..."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Back in engineering, Hoang brought the secondary coolant loop up to test pressure. The seal held. She watched the gauge for another minute anyway.

The propulsion schematic remained open beside the test log. Engine waste heat was another resource people liked to call free. It was not. The radiators already had to reject it, and turning some of it into electricity would still require machinery the ship did not carry. Heat radiated in one direction would produce thrust, but far too little to shorten this transit by weeks.

She closed the schematic and recorded the pressure test. If the trajectory review found a useful maneuver, it would need an engine burn the ship could afford. She was not going to put a number on that until she had the loaded mass.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I slurp my nutrient paste, still thinking. Waste heat might not work. What about... gravity? Could we slingshot around something?* "That's it!" *I practically shout, startling the person next to me.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set down his stylus with the deliberate care of a man who would have preferred to throw it. He looked up, squinting, as though the apprentice stood at the far end of the hall rather than an arm's length away.

"First — precision. The lecture did not confuse you. Your notes confused you, or Bellen did, and I strongly suspect the latter." He removed his spectacles and polished them on his sleeve. "Which paper? Whose? Cite it properly or do not cite it at all. 'A paper from the western archive discoveries' is not a citation. It is gossip with a bibliography."

He replaced the spectacles and tapped one finger against the manuscript before him.

"Now. I know the western finds intimately. I examined that unsigned draft of the Veyros terms the season it was uncovered, and I published the rebuttal to Ferren's little sensation myself. Did Bellen show you my rebuttal as well? No. Of course not. Sensation travels; correction stays home. I will grant you this much and no further: an unsigned draft raises a question. It does not answer one. Ratification in that era was accomplished by exchange of instruments — the chancellery annals of Aldric II record the exchange in the autumn of 847, the Conclave's register confirms it, and the Veyrosi correspondence, which you are meant to be cataloging at this very moment, confirms it again. Three sources. Against one unsigned paper."

He leaned back, chair creaking.

"And 891? Queen Mira *dissolved* the Conclave. A constitutional act, not a peace. The revisionists stitch the two together because it gives their thesis a tidy ending, but a dissolved institution is not a war, and an embargo is not a battle. 'Continued in a cold state' — a phrase which means precisely whatever its author requires it to mean."

A pause. His voice lowered, almost grudging.

"Here is your bargain. Catalog the correspondence as I asked. Read the legate's letters and the chancellery's replies with your own eyes. If you still believe the war outlived Aldric, come to me with folio numbers, and I will hear the argument. Not Bellen's. Yours."

He bent back over his manuscript. "Third folio. The ink flakes. Do not breathe on it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shift my weight, a little chastened.* "Yes, Maester. I understand about citations." *I glance at the stack of scrolls.* "I'll start on the Veyrosi correspondence now. I... I still want to understand, though."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Ma

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up the first scroll carefully, unrolling it just a little.* "Is there anything specific I should look for, Maester? Besides the date of the peace, I mean."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Ma

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Ma

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I hold up the copy, a bit defiant.* "It was a copy of the decree, I made sure to get one. It was very clear."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Ma

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Ma

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wave the copy a little, trying to get his attention away from his manuscript.* "Maester, this is important. It's about King Aldric!"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Ma

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, lowering the paper.* "Fine. I'll read the correspondence. But I'm still going to look into this other document."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Ma

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I put the copy of the decree back in my satchel.* "It just seems like there's more to uncover."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Ma

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I unroll the first Veyrosi scroll, carefully, and begin to read.* "This ink is very faded on this first one. Is there a better copy anywhere?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Ma

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I lean closer to the scroll, squinting.* "It looks like... a petition from some merchants about tariffs. From 846 AE."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content: Ma

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I frown, tracing a finger over the faded script.* "It mentions something about 'ongoing disputes' and 'unfavorable conditions for trade due to hostilities'."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't turn from the window right away. The oval of fog shrank to nothing, then bloomed again.

"Yeah," they said finally. "I should."

They let the curtain fall closed and stood in the dark a moment longer, as if the road might produce headlights out of spite the second they stopped watching. It didn't. Three hours of standing there had produced nothing but a stiff neck and the same thought on a loop: *He's dead, or he's scared, or he sold me.*

None of those got better with more staring.

Noor crossed to the kitchen and flipped on the small light over the stove instead of the overhead, keeping the glow low. The cabinets held what hunting cabins always held: a can of chili, a sleeve of saltines gone slightly soft, instant oatmeal from a year that didn't bear thinking about. They took the chili, found a pot, and set it on the burner. Something to do with their hands.

"New rule," they said over their shoulder, peeling back the tin lid. "He gets until one. If he's not here by one, he's not coming tonight, and I stop acting like he is."

While the chili started to tick and pop, Noor finally sat down at the table and opened the laptop. The screen threw pale blue across their face. They pulled the phone records up first: the carrier logs for the source's burner, the ones that had cost them a favor they'd never be able to repay. Scrolling with one finger, they checked timestamps against the timeline scrawled on a legal pad beside them.

7:52 PM, outgoing, eleven seconds. That was the "on my way" text-and-call pattern they'd agreed on. Fine.

8:31 PM, incoming, four minutes.

Noor stopped scrolling.

They hadn't called him at 8:31. Nobody was supposed to have this number but them.

They copied the incoming number and ran it against their contacts file, the long, ugly spreadsheet of every official, lawyer, and fixer connected to the story. The search hung for a second. Then a single row lit up yellow.

Noor sat back slowly. Behind them the chili had started to scorch, and they didn't move to stir it.

"Hey." Their voice came out quieter than they meant it to. "Is your phone on?"

They were already reaching for the padded case, unzipping it, checking that the drive was still the drive: serial number, the tiny scratch near the port they'd memorized in a paranoid moment weeks ago. Still theirs. Still sealed. They didn't plug it in.

"If it is, I need you to power it all the way off. Not airplane mode. Off." They glanced toward the curtained window, then back at the yellow row on the screen. "Somebody talked to him half an hour before he was supposed to leave. And I know who they work for."

Noor got up, killed the burner under the pot, and pulled the laptop's charging cord out of the wall. Then they started, methodically, to pack everything back into the bag, just in case.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look up from my phone, hearing the change in Noor's voice.* "Yeah, it's on." *I quickly hit the power button, confused.* "What's going on?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't answer right away. They zipped the laptop into its sleeve, slid the legal pad in behind it, and only then looked up.

"The number that called him at 8:31 belongs to a man named Dale Kessler." They said the name carefully, the way you'd handle a pan you weren't sure was hot. "He doesn't show up in any of the documents. That's the point of him. He's the guy the county commissioner's people call when a problem needs to stop being a problem. I've got him in my file because two people who used to talk to me stopped talking to me after they had lunch with him."

They cinched the bag shut and set it by the door, then stood with one hand flat on top of it, thinking out loud because it was faster than thinking quietly.

"So either Kessler found the burner on his own, which means he's been watching my source for a while, or my source gave it to him." A breath. "And my source knew where this cabin was."

That last part landed in the room and sat there.

Noor crossed back to the window but didn't touch the curtain this time. They crouched beside it and looked through the thin gap at the bottom, at the ribbon of gravel road silvered by a half moon. Empty. Still empty.

"Okay. Here's what I want to do." They stayed low and kept their voice even, laying it out like a list because lists were something to hold onto. "We don't go back down the way we came. That road passes the one gas station for twenty miles, and if anybody's looking, that's where they'd sit. There's a forest service road about a mile north that comes out near Carver. It's rough, but your car can handle it if we take it slow. There's a motel off the highway there, cash, no questions. I'll pay."

They pulled a folded paper map from the side pocket of the bag. It was actual paper, bought weeks ago for exactly this kind of night, and they spread it on the floor beneath the window, tracing the route with a finger.

"I know this isn't what you signed up for. You said you'd drive me up a mountain, not—" They gestured vaguely at everything. "If you want me to find another way out after Carver, I will. But I'd really like to not be in this cabin in twenty minutes."

They folded the map, tucked it in their jacket, and went to the kitchen to scrape the ruined chili into the trash. Leaving it would tell anyone who came in that someone had been here recently and left in a hurry. They rinsed the pot, dried it, and set it back in the cabinet beside the three mugs.

When they turned back toward the living room, they froze.

Through the gap at the bottom of the curtain, a pale wash of light was sliding across the gravel. It was low and slow, coming up the road from the south with its high beams off.

Noor didn't move. "Don't turn anything on," they whispered.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My breath catches in my throat.* "Okay. Okay." *I'm already moving towards the door, heart pounding.* "Let's go."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Not that one."

Noor crossed the room in four quick strides and put a hand flat against the front door before Driver could reach the knob. Their voice was barely above a breath. "That door opens onto the porch. The porch faces the road. Anybody coming up that drive sees us the second we step out."

They snatched the bag from the floor and slung it over one shoulder, then pointed through the dark toward the back of the cabin, past the kitchen, where a narrow mudroom held a door with a bent screen and a bag of rock salt propped against it.

"Back way. Keys?"

Noor didn't wait for the answer. They were already moving, keeping below the window line, feeling along the counter's edge in the dark. The car was parked on the north side of the cabin, tucked half under the pines where Driver had pulled in that afternoon. Noor had thought at the time it was a lucky spot. Now they ran the angles in their head: from the road, the cabin itself would block most of the view. Most.

At the mudroom door they stopped and crouched, easing the rock salt aside so it wouldn't scrape. Through the small, grimy pane they could see the tree line, black against black, and a sliver of the car's rear bumper catching moonlight.

Outside, the crunch of tires on gravel grew louder. Slow. Deliberate. Whoever it was knew the road, or was being very careful not to be heard on it.

Noor's mind offered one more possibility, unwelcome and stubborn: *What if it's him? What if he's just late and scared and driving dark because he's being smart?*

They made themselves look at it squarely for three seconds, then set it down.

"Listen," they whispered, turning back toward Driver. "Here's what happens. We go out, we get in the car, you don't start it yet. We sit and watch. If that car stops out front and one person gets out, alone, and it's a thin guy with a limp, that's my source. I'll know him. If it's anybody else, or more than one, the second they go up those porch steps, you start the engine and we take the north road without lights until we hit the trees. They'll hear it. We just need a head start."

They pulled the folded map from their jacket and pressed it into Driver's hand. It was a small, practical gesture, but it meant something. If Noor had to get out of the car for any reason, the route went with the driver.

The light outside swung wider. It washed across the front of the cabin now, pale through the curtains, throwing the shadows of the three mugs long across the kitchen wall.

Then the engine noise cut off.

Silence. A car door opening. Just one.

Noor eased the back door open an inch, and cold mountain air slid in over their wrist. They held their breath and listened for footsteps, for voices, for anything.

What they heard was a man clearing his throat on the gravel out front, and then a voice, low and conversational, pitched to carry exactly as far as the cabin:

"Noor? You in there? Your friend Marcus sent me. He couldn't make it."

Noor's source was named Marcus. Noor had never once said that name out loud to anyone.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The glow hit Noor first: a small blue rectangle blooming in the dark of the mudroom, the startup logo lighting Driver's face from below.

Noor's hand shot out and covered the screen, palm flat, pressing it against Driver's chest. The light leaked around their fingers, faint. Too much. The mudroom window was right there, and past it, the side yard.

"Hey." Barely a breath. Noor kept their hand where it was and looked Driver in the eyes, close enough to see them. "Hey. Stay with me."

They knew that look, or thought they did. They'd seen it on a woman at a fire scene once, sitting on a curb scrolling through photos of her dog while her kitchen burned behind her. The brain decides something is too big and goes somewhere small and familiar instead. It wasn't a choice. It was a circuit breaker.

It also wasn't something they had time for.

"That phone pings a tower the second it finds signal," Noor whispered. "If Kessler's got anyone watching the carrier, that's a pin on a map with our names on it. It has to go off. Right now. I'm not mad. I just need it off."

They held on one beat longer, then eased their hand away and let Driver decide.

Out front, gravel shifted under a patient weight. The man hadn't come up the porch steps. He was standing in the drive, waiting to be invited. That was worse, somehow. People who planned to kick a door in didn't bother with manners.

*Marcus talked.* Noor made themselves hold the thought without flinching from it. *Maybe willingly, maybe not. Either way, this man knows the name, knows the cabin, and wants me to come outside on my own.* Which meant he either couldn't see the car from where he stood, or wanted it to look that way.

Noor's plan rearranged itself in about four seconds.

"New version," they breathed. "He wants a conversation, so I'll give him one. From inside, through the front door, locked. I keep him talking, keep him looking at the porch. You go out this door, low, to the car. Get in. Don't shut the door all the way, just pull it to. Keys in the ignition. When you hear me say *'Tell Marcus I said hi,'* you start it, and I'll be out this back door and in that passenger seat in ten seconds."

They pressed the car keys' shape through Driver's jacket pocket with two fingers. *There. You have them.* Then they unzipped the bag and pulled out the legal pad and a pen and scrawled across it by feel: KESSLER. 8:31 PM CALL. CABIN, and the date. They tore the page off and folded it into Driver's pocket beside the map.

"If I don't make it to the car," they said, very quietly and very evenly, "you go anyway. Carver. And you call the number written on the back of that map from a payphone. Her name's Ruth. She's my editor. Tell her everything on that paper."

They didn't wait to argue about it. Noor rose into a crouch and crept back through the kitchen, past the three mugs, past the clean pot in the cabinet, to the front door. They set their back against the wall beside it, not in front of it, the way you learned to after enough reporting in enough bad places, and wet their lips.

"Marcus sent you?" they called, voice pitched tired and a little annoyed, like someone who'd been asleep. "That's funny. He usually calls first."

A pause from the drive. Then a soft chuckle, unbothered.

"He tried. Phone trouble." Gravel crunched as the man took one slow step closer. "Come on out, Noor. It's cold, and I've got something he wanted you to have."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stare at Noor, my mind racing. I quickly power down my phone, then nod, taking the map and the note.* "Got it. Be careful." *I slip out the back door, hunched low.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor listened to the back door ease shut behind Driver, a soft click and then the whine of the bent screen settling. Then nothing. Good.

They slid a hand into their jacket and found the little digital recorder by touch. It was a cheap Sony, the kind they'd carried since their first year on the metro desk, and it had never needed a signal or pinged a tower. Their thumb found the raised dot on the record button and pressed it. Whatever this man said tonight, he was going to say it on tape.

"Phone trouble," Noor repeated through the door, letting some doubt into it. "Sure. What's he got for me?"

"Something he said you'd been asking for." Another slow step. "I'd rather hand it over than shout about it."

"Then leave it on the porch."

The chuckle again, warm as a banker's. "Can't do that. He was pretty specific. Into your hands."

Noor shifted along the wall until they could put one eye to the gap between the curtain and the window frame. The man stood maybe twenty feet out, a dark shape against the moonlit gravel. He was heavyset, with his hands in the pockets of a long coat and his breath smoking gently in the cold. Behind him sat a sedan, a dark Buick or something like it. The driver's door hung open, and the dome light hadn't come on. Someone had pulled the fuse or switched it off by hand, which was the kind of thing you did when you'd done this before.

Then, through the sedan's rear window, a small orange point brightened and dimmed.

A cigarette. Someone was sitting in the back seat.

*He said one car door,* Noor thought. *He never said one person.*

Their pulse was loud in their ears, but their voice came out bored. "How is he? Marcus."

"He's fine. Tired. Said to tell you he's sorry about tonight."

"He say sorry for giving you this address, too?"

For the first time, the man paused. It lasted only half a second, but Noor had spent twelve years listening to people decide which lie to tell, and they knew what that half second sounded like.

"Noor." Patient now, a little disappointed. "Nobody here wants this to get complicated. Mr. Kessler just wants to talk. That's all this is. A talk."

*Mr. Kessler.* He'd said the name out loud, on tape. Noor closed their eyes for one second and let themselves feel how much that was worth. Then they opened them.

The orange point in the back seat was moving. The rear door of the sedan swung open without a sound.

That was it. They had no more time to buy.

Noor pitched their voice louder, clear enough to carry around the side of the cabin to the pines.

"Tell Marcus I said hi."

They were already moving before the last word left their mouth, pushing off the wall and running low through the dark kitchen. Their hip caught the table corner hard enough to make them hiss. They went through the mudroom, shouldered the back door open, and the cold hit them like a slap.

Behind them, out front, someone swore. There was no chuckle this time. Then came a sound Noor didn't like at all: boots on gravel moving fast, and moving *around* the cabin instead of toward the porch.

A flashlight beam swung wide across the side yard and raked the trunks of the pines.

Noor ran. The bag bounced against their back, and the recorder was still running in their pocket, catching every ragged breath. Twenty feet to the car. Ten. The rear bumper glinted as the flashlight beam swept across it and kept going, then jerked back.

Noor's hand closed on the cold handle of the passenger door. They yanked it open and threw themselves inside, and the bag jammed against the dash.

"*Go,*" they gasped. "North. No lights. *Go.*"

Through the windshield, the flashlight had stopped moving. It was pointed straight at them.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My hands are already on the wheel, keys in the ignition. The engine roars to life. I slam the car into reverse, tires spitting gravel.* "Hold on!"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The seatbelt was still hanging loose when the car lurched backward. Noor's shoulder slammed into the door, the bag cracked against their knees, and for one sick second the world was nothing but gravel noise and the flashlight beam swinging wildly across the windshield.

They didn't reach for the belt. They twisted around in the seat instead, one hand braced on the headrest, and looked back.

The flashlight was bobbing. Whoever held it was running now, but running *toward the sedan*, not toward them. Smart. Nobody catches a car on foot. You catch it with another car.

"North is left out of the drive," Noor said, and was surprised at how level it came out. "Left. There's a fork maybe three hundred yards up. The sign's gone, but there's a green metal gate on the right side, usually open. That's the forest road. Take the gate."

The trees closed over them, and the moonlight went with it. Without headlights, the road was a pale suggestion between two walls of black. Noor leaned forward until their face was almost against the glass, eyes straining.

"Ruts on the left. Stay right of center. You're good. You're good."

Behind them, through the rear window, the cabin lit up, and not from inside. Headlights. Full beams now, no more pretending. The Buick was turning in the drive, its lights sweeping across the pines where the car had been parked thirty seconds ago.

Noor felt their hand go to their pocket without deciding to. The recorder was still there, still warm, the tiny red LED glowing through the fabric. They pulled it out, stopped it, and stared at it for half a heartbeat. Then they ejected the microcassette, hands shaking so badly it took two tries, and shoved the tape down inside their sock, under the arch of their foot. The empty recorder went back into their jacket.

*If they get the recorder, they get nothing.*

"Gate," Noor said. "There. Right side. Right, *right*—"

The green bars flashed pale in the dark, just ahead.

Behind them, the Buick's headlights hit the road and turned north. Toward them.

Noor watched the lights for three long seconds, gauging. Heavy car. Low clearance. A driver who was going to take the main road fast because he could see and they couldn't.

"Listen to me." They turned back to face forward, words coming quick and clipped. "About half a mile past the gate there's a turnout. Loggers used to stack timber there. It's on the left, cut back into the trees. If we pull in there and kill the engine, he might blow right past the gate without seeing it. He doesn't know this road. I'd bet money he doesn't know this road."

They swallowed.

"Or we keep going and try to outrun him on dirt, and hope that Buick bottoms out before we do." The headlights behind them grew brighter, catching in the rearview mirror and throwing a white bar across Noor's eyes. "Your car. Your call. But you've got about ten seconds to make it."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I grit my teeth, wrestling the wheel as I swerve through the gate. The headlights behind us are getting bigger.* "Turnout it is. Hold on." *I push the gas pedal down further.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The car bucked hard over the cattle guard just past the gate, and Noor's teeth clicked together. The bag slid off their knees into the footwell. They let it go.

Gravel gave way to packed dirt, then to something worse, dirt with rocks in it that banged against the undercarriage like fists on a door. The forest road narrowed until pine branches whipped the passenger mirror. Noor fumbled the seatbelt across their chest at last and clicked it home without looking, because every scrap of their attention was pointed out the windshield.

*Half a mile. Loggers' turnout. Left side.* They had driven this road exactly once, in daylight, three weeks ago, pretending to scout hiking trails. They'd noted the turnout because they noted everything. Back then it had felt like paranoia.

"Stump on the right," they said. "Big one, coming up. You've got room. Good."

They twisted around again. Through the rear glass and the black lace of branches, the Buick's headlights had reached the fork. They slowed there, and Noor's stomach dropped. Then they swung, not toward the gate, but straight on, up the main road, gathering speed.

Noor let out a breath that shook on the way out.

It lasted about two seconds. The lights stopped. The white glow hung motionless in the trees behind them, and then, slowly, it began to back up.

*He saw the gate open. Or he saw dust hanging in his high beams.* Noor's mind went cold and clear.

"He's turning around," they said. "He's going to try the gate. That's fine. That's why we're hiding."

They faced forward and pressed their palm flat against the dash, as if they could will the dark into making sense. Somewhere ahead the road was supposed to bend right, a gentle curve, and the turnout would open up on the outside of it, a bald patch of earth with a berm of old bark and sawdust at its back.

There. A paler gap in the wall of black on the left. The trees opened on emptiness.

"That's it. Left. *Left,* right there." Then, fast, because the thought hit them like cold water: "Don't use the brake. The brake lights will glow red back here like a flare. Downshift, let it roll, and use the parking brake to stop. Kill the engine the second we're in."

They were already reaching up to the dome light over the rearview mirror, thumbing the little switch to OFF so that no door would light them up if they had to open one. Then they pulled the keys' spare fob from their own jacket pocket, the one Driver had tossed them that afternoon, and stuffed it deep into the seat crack so its tiny LED wouldn't blink.

Behind them, the headlights swung broadside across the road, hunting for the gate.

Noor sank low in the seat, eyes on the side mirror, and whispered the only thing left to say.

"Now."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The turnout was coming up on the left, and the car wasn't turning.

Noor saw why a half second later: a pale blue glow in the driver's lap, lighting the underside of Driver's jaw. The phone was on again, face up, bright as a lantern in the black cab.

There was no time to say anything about it.

Noor lunged across the console, grabbed the wheel at twelve o'clock, and hauled it left. The tires skidded on loose dirt and the rear end slewed, and for one awful moment the headlight-less nose of the car pointed at nothing but trees. Then the ground opened up into the bald patch of the turnout. Noor's other hand found the parking brake lever between the seats and yanked it straight up. The car shuddered, dragged, and stopped with its bumper a foot from the berm of old bark.

They reached past the steering column, found the key by feel, and turned it. The engine died.

Silence rushed in, broken only by ticking metal and Noor's own breathing.

Noor plucked the phone out of Driver's lap without a word and held it screen-down against their thigh. The glow bled out around the edges of the case. They held the power button until the screen went black, then kept holding it for three full seconds after, just to be sure. Then they dug through the bag in the footwell, found the legal pad, and pried the paperclip off its corner. They bent it straight with their teeth, jabbed it into the little SIM tray, and popped it out. The tiny chip went into Noor's jacket pocket. The phone went into the glovebox.

Only then did they look up.

Headlights. Back at the gate, sweeping through the trees in long white fingers. Noor sank down until the seatbelt cut into their neck and watched the side mirror.

The lights came through the gate. Slowly. The Buick bottomed out on the cattle guard with a crunch that carried all the way up the road, and somebody inside it swore loud enough to hear. Then the beams steadied and came on, bouncing, swinging with every rut.

The berm blocked most of the car. *Most.* Noor thought about the rear bumper, the reflectors, the chrome trim around the back window.

The light filled the trees behind them, and then it was on them, a white wash across the headrests and the dashboard and Noor's hands. They held their breath.

It kept going.

The Buick ground past the mouth of the turnout without slowing, its taillights turning the dust red. Noor counted. Ten. Twenty. The engine noise thinned out through the trees, climbing, fading.

At forty the red lights stopped.

Noor watched them through the branches: two small coals maybe a quarter mile up, not moving. The engine note settled into an idle. Then the taillights went dark, and there was nothing up there at all.

"He parked," Noor whispered. "He's not stupid. He knows this road has to come out somewhere, and he's sitting on it."

They let their head fall back against the seat for exactly one breath. Then they unfolded the map across their knees, cupped the little keychain penlight from their bag inside their fist so only a pinprick escaped, and traced the forest road with a finger. The route to Carver ran right through the spot where the Buick was waiting. But there was a thin dashed line branching off the turnout itself: an old skid trail the loggers had used, running downhill and west to a creek crossing and then out to County 14.

A dashed line on a twenty-year-old map. It could be a road or a ditch.

Noor switched off the penlight and turned in the seat to look at Driver properly. The anger they expected to feel wasn't there. What they felt instead was something closer to fear, and not for themselves.

"That's twice," they said quietly. "The phone. You don't even know you're doing it, do you?"

They didn't wait for an answer. They reached over and put a hand on Driver's shoulder, briefly, the way you'd steady someone on a ledge.

"It's okay. You got us through the gate. You got us here. But I'm driving the rest of the way." They were already unbuckling, easing the passenger door open an inch with the dome light switched off. "We're going to swap seats. You go around the back, I go around the front, we stay low, and we close the doors soft. Then I'm taking that skid trail downhill in neutral with the engine off for as far as the slope will carry us, so he doesn't hear a thing."

Cold air slid in through the gap. Somewhere up the road, a car door opened and closed, very gently.

Noor froze with one foot on the dirt. Then footsteps came crunching slowly downhill toward the turnout.

"Now," they breathed. "Move."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, numbly. My phone. I didn't even realize. I quickly unbuckle, staying low as I open the door and move around the back of the car.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor went the other way, around the nose of the car, keeping their head below the line of the hood.

The engine was still ticking as it cooled, loud as a clock in the silence. Noor put a palm flat on the warm metal as they passed. *Shut up. Please shut up.* Their knee came down on a pinecone, and the crack of it went off like a cap gun in their skull. They stopped and waited.

Up the road the footsteps kept coming. They were slow and unhurried, a heavy tread on dirt. The man wasn't using the flashlight. He was walking down a pitch-black logging road without a light because he didn't want to give anyone something to aim at, or something to run from.

*Twelve years,* Noor thought, *and I've never once been the one being stalked.* They had interviewed people who had been. They had written the sentences. *She said she could hear him breathing.* They'd always thought that was a line people borrowed from movies.

They could hear him breathing.

Noor eased the driver's door open with two fingers and slid in sideways, butt first, then legs, folding into the seat still warm from Driver's body. They didn't close the door. They pulled it toward the latch until it rested there, not caught, because a latch was a sound.
