Their hand found the key. They turned it one click, to accessory and not to start, just far enough that the steering wouldn't lock when they needed to turn it. The dash stayed dark. Noor had checked that three weeks ago, too, sitting in a grocery store parking lot running through every switch in this car while Driver was inside buying snacks. Another thing that had felt like paranoia at the time.

They reached across the console and pushed the passenger door open wider from the inside, just a hand's width, and held it there.

"In," they breathed into the dark. "Door to the latch. Don't close it."

Footsteps. Closer. The man had to be near the bend now, a hundred feet off, maybe less. Noor could picture him without seeing him: the long coat, hands out of the pockets now, head cocked, listening the same way they were.

Then his voice came, soft, almost kind, pitched to reach exactly as far as the turnout.

"Noor. I know you pulled off somewhere. I heard the engine quit." A pause. Gravel shifted. "Marcus said you were smart. He also said you had a friend with you who doesn't have anything to do with any of this. You want to think about that friend."

Noor's jaw locked tight. It was the oldest move there was: find the thing someone would feel guilty about and press on it. They had watched cops do it in interview rooms. They had done it themselves, God help them, to a city clerk who'd cried afterward.

It still worked. Knowing that didn't make it work any less.

They made themselves breathe through their nose, slowly. Their left hand went to the gearshift and eased it into neutral, feeling each gate click home through their palm. Their right hand closed around the parking brake lever, thumb resting on the release button, not pressing it. The car sat nose-down on the slope toward the mouth of the skid trail, and Noor could feel the weight of it straining gently against the brake like a dog on a leash.

*Let go of this and gravity does the rest. No engine. No lights. Just rolling.*

Unless the dashed line on the map was a ditch.

Up the road, a flashlight clicked on.

The beam wasn't pointed at them yet. It was aimed down at the dirt, sweeping side to side, reading the road. Reading the tire tracks. Noor watched it through the windshield, a white oval sliding over ruts and stones, and understood with total clarity that in about thirty seconds it would follow the fresh skid marks straight into the turnout.

Their thumb pressed down on the brake release. They didn't lift the lever yet.

"When you're in," they whispered, not taking their eyes off the light, "hold on to something. I don't know what's at the bottom of this."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I scramble in, pulling the door almost shut.* "Got it!" *I grab the door handle, knuckles white.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The whisper was louder than Driver meant it to be. Noor heard it land in the dark like a dropped plate.

Up the road, the flashlight beam stopped sweeping. It rose off the dirt slowly, deliberately, and swung toward the turnout.

Noor let go of the brake.

For one terrible second nothing happened. The car sat there on the slope, and Noor thought, *wrong angle, not steep enough, we're going to sit here like a stone until he walks up and taps on the glass.* Then the weight shifted. The tires crept. Pine needles crackled under the treads, and the car began to roll, nose first, off the bald earth of the turnout and down into the black gap where the skid trail was supposed to be.

The flashlight hit the rear window.

It filled the cab with white, threw Noor's shadow across the dashboard, and lit the dust hanging in the air like snow. Behind them a man shouted a word Noor didn't catch. Then feet pounded on dirt, fast now, no more patience in them.

"Head down," Noor said, not whispering anymore. There was no point. "Get your head down."

The trail tipped steeper and the car picked up speed. Branches closed in on both sides and dragged along the doors with a long fingernail shriek. Noor hauled on the wheel and felt how heavy it was. With the engine off there was no power steering, just their own arms against a ton and a half of metal. Their shoulders burned. The trail bent left, and they wrestled the car around it by feel, following the faint pale seam of old ruts between the trunks.

The flashlight behind them bobbed, shrank, and fell away. The man couldn't run downhill in the dark as fast as gravity could. Nobody could.

Then a sharp flat crack echoed off the trees.

Noor's whole body went cold. It wasn't a branch. They knew the difference; they'd stood in enough courtrooms listening to people describe the difference. Something smacked into the dirt somewhere to the right, or the trunk of a tree, or nothing at all. There wasn't a second shot. The light was gone around the bend.

*He fired at a car he couldn't see,* Noor thought, very distantly. *Write that down later. That's attempted murder with a witness in the passenger seat.*

The car was going too fast now. The trees came out of the dark only a few yards before they would have hit them. Noor tapped the brake pedal once, carefully, and felt it answer firm. Vacuum reserve. They'd get two good presses, maybe three, before the pedal turned to stone and they'd be standing on it with both feet for nothing. They'd read that somewhere at two in the morning weeks ago, reading about cars and engines and everything else that could go wrong on a mountain. *Paranoia,* they'd called it.

They saved the second press and pulled up on the parking brake instead, gently, feeling the rear tires bite and slip and bite again. The car slowed. Held. Rolled on.

Noor heard the creek before they saw it. It was a low rushing under the rattle of the suspension, getting louder. Then the trees opened, and moonlight fell through the gap onto moving water, black and silver, maybe twenty feet across. The trail ran straight down into it and came up the far bank as a pale scar in the brush.

How deep was it? The map hadn't said. Maps never did.

"Hold on," Noor said.

The front tires hit the water with a slap that sprayed the windshield. The car lurched, dipped, and lost speed all at once, and Noor was thrown forward against the belt. Cold water hissed against the undercarriage. The nose kept going, then the rear, the current shoving sideways at the doors. Halfway across, the car slowed to a crawl. Then it stopped.

Water murmured around them. Nothing else.

Noor sat with both hands on the wheel, breathing hard, and listened back up the slope. They heard wind in the pines and the creek. Far off, maybe, an engine starting, the Buick, or their imagination. They couldn't tell.

*He can't bring that car down here. He'll go back around. He'll try to guess where this comes out.*

"Okay," they said, mostly to themselves. Their voice shook, and they let it. "Okay. Now we find out if your car likes me."

They pushed in the clutch and turned the key.

The starter ground once, twice. It caught on the third turn and coughed. Water rushing over the tailpipe gurgled and spat, and the engine settled into a rough, living idle. Noor let out a sound that was almost a laugh and put it in first. The tires spun, found gravel under the silt, and dragged the car up out of the creek onto the far bank in a long streaming rush of water.

They didn't turn on the headlights. Not yet.

Twenty yards up the far side, where the brush screened them from the water, Noor stopped the car, left it running, and reached into their jacket pocket. They took out the little SIM chip and turned it once in their fingers. Then they cracked the window and flicked it into the dark, toward the sound of the creek.

"You'll need a new number," they said. "I'll pay for that, too."

Then they checked the things that mattered, one by one, the way they'd check facts on a draft at deadline. The bag was in the passenger footwell. They leaned over and felt through the side for the padded case, and the drive was still there. They reached down to their ankle and pressed a fingertip against the hard little rectangle of the microcassette under the arch of their foot. Still there, too.

A man saying *Mr. Kessler* on tape, and a gunshot in the dark behind it.

Noor sat back and finally, carefully, looked over at Driver in the faint dashboard glow.

"County 14 is maybe two miles on," they said. "Then Carver. There's a payphone outside the Shell by the motel. I'm calling Ruth before I do anything else, before we check in, before I even take my shoes off." A pause. "And then I'm going to sit you down with something hot to eat, and you're going to tell me what's going on with you tonight. Because I'm scared, too. But you've been somewhere else since the cabin, and I need to know where."

They put the car in gear, rolled it to the edge of the brush, and looked left and right down a thin ribbon of dirt road silvered by the moon.

Empty. For now.

Noor switched on the headlights.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stare blankly ahead, the cold seeping into my bones. My phone. The phone. I didn't even...* "I think... I think I just froze." *My voice is barely a whisper, a little shaky.* "Like, I just... stopped."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't answer right away. The road needed both hands and all of their eyes: washboard dirt, the headlights finally carving it out of the dark, a deer's eyes flashing green in the brush and gone.

They reached over and cranked the heater to full. It blew cold for a second, then warm, smelling faintly of creek water and burnt dust.

"Yeah," Noor said at last. "You did."

They let that sit, because pretending otherwise would have been a kind of lie, and Driver deserved better than a lie tonight.

"You know what I did when I ejected that tape back there? It took me two tries. My hands wouldn't work." They flexed their fingers on the wheel, and even now there was a tremor in them. "And in the cabin, when I heard him say Marcus's name, there was a second where I couldn't think of a single thing. Not one. I just stood there. It only looked like I had a plan because I'd written it down weeks ago and my body remembered it before my brain did."

The dirt road bent, dipped, and spat them out onto blacktop. County 14. Noor stopped at the edge of it with the engine running and looked both ways for a long time. There was no Buick and no taillights, only a yellow center line running off into the dark in both directions and a green reflective sign: CARVER 6.

They turned right.

"Freezing isn't a character flaw," Noor went on, quieter. "It's wiring. Some people's bodies run, some fight, some just shut the doors and wait for it to be over. Yours reached for the most normal thing in the world, which was a phone. That's all it was." A glance sideways, brief. "I'm not mad. I was scared *for* you, back in that turnout. That's different."

The asphalt hummed under the tires. Noor kept the speed exactly at the limit, which was its own kind of hiding.

Carver arrived the way small mountain towns do: a closed feed store, a church, a single blinking yellow light, and then the Shell glowing like an aquarium on the far corner, open all night, with the Pine Rest Motel's dead neon sign squatting behind it. The payphone stood at the edge of the lot under a flickering bulb, a relic someone had forgotten to rip out.

Noor pulled around the side of the station, out of view from the road, and killed the engine.

"Stay in the car. Doors locked. If anyone pulls in that isn't a pickup full of hunters, honk twice." They dug in the bag's side pocket and came up with a roll of quarters, taped, bought for exactly this. "Two minutes."

The cold outside bit hard after the heater. Noor fed the phone, dialed Ruth's home number from memory, and turned so their back was to the wall and their eyes were on the road.

It rang four times. Then came a thick, sleep-wrecked voice: "*If this is who I think it is, you'd better be alive.*"

"I'm alive." Noor closed their eyes for one second. "Ruth, listen. Kessler's people came to the cabin. Two men, one armed. He fired a shot at the car. I have one of them on tape saying 'Mr. Kessler wants to talk.' The call logs show Kessler's number hit Marcus's burner at 8:31. I'm in Carver. My friend's with me. We're both okay."

The silence on the line lasted long enough that Noor checked to see whether the quarters had run out.

"Okay," Ruth said, fully awake now, her voice gone flat and precise the way it did on election nights. "Okay. Here's what happens. You don't go to local police, not in that county. I'm calling Abrams, and she'll have someone from the state AG's office on the phone with you by morning. You get a room, you don't use your names, and you don't open that drive on anything connected to anything." A breath. "Noor. There's something else."

Noor's grip tightened on the cold receiver.

"Marcus called the tip line. 11:40 tonight. Night desk flagged it and forwarded the audio to me an hour ago, and I've been trying to reach you since." Ruth's voice dropped. "He's alive, or he was then. He said he's sorry. He said, and I'm quoting, '*They have my sister. Tell Noor the second copy's where we said.*'"

Noor stood very still under the buzzing bulb.

*The second copy.* They'd made that arrangement once, half-joking, over bad coffee in a laundromat in March. *If anything ever happens, you leave one somewhere only I'd look.* They'd never thought he'd listened.

"I know where it is," Noor said slowly.

"Of course you do." Ruth sighed, and it sounded like a prayer. "Don't you dare go get it tonight. Sleep. Call me at seven."

The line clicked dead.

Noor hung up and walked back to the car. They didn't get in right away. They stood by the driver's window, looking through the glass at Driver's pale face in the station light, and then they opened the door and leaned down.

"Marcus is alive. They've got his sister. That's how they got him to talk." They said it plainly, because it was a fact and facts were easier to carry than feelings. "And he left me something. Tomorrow's problem."

They straightened up and nodded toward the bright glass front of the Shell, where a teenager behind the counter was reading a paperback beside a rotating hot dog roller and a coffee pot that looked like it had been on since Tuesday.

"But tonight's problem is you. Come on. I'm buying the worst gas-station food in the state, and you're going to eat it with me, and then we're going to get you warm." A pause, and something almost like a smile. "Deal?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look at Noor, my eyes wide. Marcus. The sister. It's a lot to take in. I manage a small, shaky nod.* "Deal."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang’s humming stopped. She pulled the earpiece free and set it beside the labeled manifold.

“No,” she said. “That wasn’t an emergency boost. It was throwing away the crew’s air for a poor exhaust velocity.”

She pushed herself up from the deck, careful not to disturb the parts on the tarp. The ship’s pumps kept humming around them.

“The atmosphere is life support, not a propellant reserve. Even if we could route it through a proper nozzle—and we can’t—the impulse would be small compared with what a weeks-long reduction in transit time would require. You’d also need a trajectory that could use that extra delta-v. Vents alone don’t make a useful engine.”

Hoang wiped her hands on a rag and looked back toward the manifold. “Bring me the proposed burn profile and the mass budget. I’ll check whether there’s a safe way to shorten the transit. The air stays where it is.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang’s expression stayed level. “Time mattered. So did arriving with a functioning crew.”

She tapped the manifold with the rag. “The question isn’t whether the risk is worth *some* time. It’s whether the thrust we could actually get is worth the air we’d lose. Without a pressure vessel, a controlled feed, and a nozzle, venting the cabin would mostly be an uncontrolled leak. Even with those things, the available gas would give us a finite, calculable impulse—not weeks off the trip by declaration.”

She folded the rag once. “And suits don’t replace life support. They’re emergency equipment with limited consumables, maintenance requirements, and failure points. Keeping everyone suited for days would add risk while making repairs and routine work harder.”

Hoang glanced toward the propulsion readouts. “Show me the ship’s mass, the atmosphere inventory, and the trajectory. I’ll calculate the best case. If the numbers justify a controlled propellant burn, we’ll discuss it. Until then, the air stays in the ship.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Right." I deflate a little, looking down at my boots. "I just thought it was a clever idea." I kick at a loose bit of plating. "So, no venting the atmosphere then."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang’s gaze softened by a fraction. “It was a useful question. You checked whether the ship had an obvious reserve we weren’t using. It doesn’t.”

She set the rag down and turned back to the manifold. “So, no venting the atmosphere. But if you want to save time, bring me the burn profile. A clever idea is one that survives the mass budget.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang took the tablet and read the calculation without comment. Her finger stopped at the line marked **340 m/s**.

“Show me the exhaust velocity you used, the mass of gas expelled, and the ship’s mass before and after the burn.”

She looked up. “And where did the compressor’s energy come from? Compression ratio isn’t free delta-v. If the compressor used ship power, that energy belongs in the budget too.”

Hoang tapped the trajectory diagram. “The angle changes the direction of the burn, not the amount of delta-v. Only the component aligned with the useful part of the trajectory helps us.”

She returned her attention to the numbers. “The rocket equation has to use the actual exhaust velocity and mass ratio. If 340 came from treating cabin pressure or compression ratio as a magic multiplier, it’s not a valid result. Give me the assumptions and I’ll check it properly. Until then, it’s a promising number—not a burn plan.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I take my tablet back, a little sheepish.* "The compression ratio just makes it *feel* like more thrust, right? Like a garden hose." I chew my lip. "Okay, so the power... I figured we could just use, like, auxiliary power. It's only for a bit."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang gave the tablet back without letting go of it immediately.

“A garden hose feels stronger because the water is being pushed through a smaller opening. That can change the thrust at the nozzle, but it doesn’t create energy. The compressor has to put work into the gas; when the gas expands, you get some of that work back, minus losses. We’d have to count the compressor, the plumbing, and the nozzle as one system.”

She released the tablet and wiped a streak of coolant from her thumb.

“And auxiliary power isn’t spare just because it has that label. It’s feeding pumps, controls, and reserves the ship may need when something fails. A short draw can still trip a bus or eat the margin we rely on for life support.”

Hoang’s voice remained matter-of-fact. “Bring me the compressor’s power draw, efficiency, gas mass, nozzle area, and the ship’s mass. I’ll check the best-case impulse against the actual trajectory. Until those numbers close, 340 meters per second is an assumption wearing a decimal point—not permission to vent the cabin.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang studied the figures once more, then gave a short nod.

“All right. I’ll approve the plan for a controlled trial, subject to hard limits. Not a direct dump of the cabin atmosphere.”

She set the tablet beside the manifold. “The gas has to be metered into a pressure vessel rated for the job, then expelled through a proper nozzle. The habitat stays sealed, and we keep enough oxygen and total pressure in reserve to support the crew through the burn and any credible failure. No one spends days in suits to make the arithmetic look better.”

Her finger tapped the power budget. “The compressor gets a dedicated power limit. It does not draw from the life-support margin, and it trips off before it can endanger the pumps. We verify the pressure vessel, valves, and nozzle; model the actual exhaust velocity and mass ratio; and check that the burn helps the trajectory rather than merely changing our velocity in the wrong direction.”

Hoang’s expression remained practical. “We start with a small instrumented test. If the measured impulse, power draw, or pressure behavior disagrees with the model, the system shuts down. The 340 meters per second stays a target until the test and the mass budget support it.”

She picked up the rag again. “So yes, the idea gets a review and a safe test. It does not get permission to spend the crew’s air on faith.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Okay, understood!" *I beam, already feeling better.* "So, a test. And no messing with the main atmosphere. Got it." *I tap my tablet, already thinking about the next steps.* "I'll get those specs to you right away, Chief."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang gave a short nod. She said the test would wait until she had the specifications and had checked the system as a whole.

She listed what she needed: the pressure vessel’s rating and inspection history, compressor draw and efficiency, the proposed gas source and mass, the nozzle data, and the burn profile with the ship’s mass and trajectory. She also wanted the shutdown thresholds and confirmation that the compressor had an isolated power limit.

“The trial stays small and unmanned until the hardware and model agree,” she added. “And the habitat remains sealed. A promising calculation is not a safety case.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Right, right. All of it." *I nod quickly, making a mental note to get everything she asked for.* "I'll get it all to you. Thanks, Chief!" *I head out, already pulling up the schematics on my tablet.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang waited for the hatch to seal, then turned back to the coolant manifold. She replaced the earpiece but did not restart the music.

Before the trial, she would check the power bus margins herself. A dedicated limit was only useful if the wiring, breakers, and shutdown logic all behaved as specified.

She picked up a chalk stub and added a note to the parts list: **verify isolation under load**. Then she resumed work on the loop. The ship had no shortage of clever proposals. What it needed was proof they could fail safely.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I'm back in my quarters, staring at the schematics.* This is more complicated than I thought. *I sigh, rubbing my temples.* "Isolation under load," she said. What does that even *mean* for this system?

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang added a clarification to the trial checklist and sent it over the maintenance channel.

“By *isolation under load*, she meant electrical isolation—not shutting down life support to prove a point. The compressor had to run at its expected draw while the normal pumps and controls were operating. They would verify that it didn’t pull the life-support bus voltage down, feed power backward through a cross-tie, or interfere with pump controls.”

She specified that the compressor’s breaker and shutdown logic also had to be tested: if the circuit tripped, the compressor had to stop cleanly without disrupting essential loads. The first check would use a dummy load, before any gas was routed into the pressure vessel.

Her final note was brief: **Keep the life-support bus live. Test the compressor’s separation from it.**

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I read the message, nodding slowly.* "Okay, that makes sense. Electrical isolation." *I start cross-referencing power schematics, muttering to myself.* "So, a dedicated breaker, and make sure it doesn't brown out the rest of the system." *This is a lot of detail.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang sent one more note over the maintenance channel.

“A dedicated breaker was necessary, but it wasn’t proof of isolation by itself,” she wrote. “The schematics had to show where the compressor circuit tied into the bus, including any cross-ties and control wiring. During the dummy-load test, they’d monitor bus voltage and pump behavior at startup, steady draw, and shutdown. The compressor had to trip without taking an essential load with it.”

She added a final line: “If the diagrams don’t make the isolation path clear, don’t guess at the panel. Flag the section and bring it to me.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I slump a bit in my chair.* "Don't guess at the panel..." *I sigh, running a hand through my hair.* This is way more complicated than just doing the math. I'll have to go through *everything*.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang read the message, then replied over the maintenance channel.

“You don’t have to audit the whole ship,” she wrote. “Trace this circuit from its source to the compressor, including any cross-ties and control feeds. Mark anything the drawings don’t explain. That’s enough for the first review.”

A second message followed.

“And don’t open a live panel or change a connection to make the diagram clearer. The dummy-load test comes after we’ve reviewed the path together. The point is to find uncertainty on paper before it becomes a fault in the bus.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I read the new messages, feeling a little relieved.* "Okay, just this circuit. That I can do." *I start tracing the lines on the schematics, a bit more confident now.* "And no touching anything live. Got it."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set down his stylus with the deliberate care of a man restraining his temper. He pushed his spectacles up his nose and, for the first time, properly looked at the apprentice.

"Bellen showed you 'a paper,'" he said. "The western archive yielded four documents and two fragments, apprentice. Not 'a paper.' Precision. This library runs on it, even if nothing else in this citadel does."

He rose from his stool and paced to the window, ink-stained fingers laced behind his back.

"First: I did not say the war *ended* in 847. I said the Treaty of Veyros was concluded in 847, which is what every chronicle in this citadel repeats, because every chronicle in this citadel copies the same three sources — two of which were written by Aldric's own chancery. That is not history. That is a family legend with a seal pressed into it.

"Second: you were not *confused* by my lecture. Confusion is what the inattentive suffer. You were underinformed, which is curable. Now attend.

"The 'treaty' preserved in the western material is a *draft*. Mark the word. It is headed *Articles Proposed for the Consideration of the Conclave*. It bears no Great Seal. And it carries a marginal instruction to the king's envoys — 'obtain their mark, or failing that, their silence' — which is not the language of concluded peace. It is the language of a man hoping to end a war he could not win. And where is the Conclave's counterpart instrument? Nowhere. What the Conclave records *do* preserve is Queen Mira's dissolution writ of 891, which ends — read it closely — 'the long and lingering war.' Lingering. A genuine peace signed four decades prior does not *linger*, apprentice.

"So. Hostilities ceased in 847. The legal state of war persisted until Mira dissolved the Conclave and ended the pretense. The books conflate the two because the conflation flattered a dead king. I teach 847 in the hall because the curriculum is fixed and the convocation examines on it. But do not stand in my archive and tell me the discoveries say the war 'actually continued' as though Bellen *found* the idea. I have been arguing this before the convocation for nine years and been called a madman by men who have never touched the documents."

He tapped the manuscript before him once, sharply.

"Now. Third shelf. Iron-banded box — the transcriptions. My eyes will not resolve the fair hand anymore. Bring it here, open it to the endorsement page, and read me the marginal note in full. Every word.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, slightly deflated but also intrigued.* "So the books are wrong, but we still have to learn them as if they're right for exams?" *I shake my head, then turn towards the shelves.* "Alright, Maester Tomas. Third shelf, iron-banded box." I start scanning the shelves, muttering the shelf number to myself.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I trace my fingers along the spines of the books, searching for the iron banding.* "It seems... inefficient, to teach something you know isn't entirely true." I finally spot the box, heavier than I expected. "Found it!"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not turn from the window.

"You have found it where it has sat for eleven years. Reserve your triumphs for things that were lost, apprentice."

He crossed back to the worktable and swept stylus shavings and spilled sand from its center with the side of his hand, clearing a space.

"And I will thank you not to say the books are *wrong*. Wrongness requires a falsehood, and the chronicles contain none. They record, truthfully, that the fighting ceased in 847. Their fault is that they stop there and name the stopping a peace. That is a conflation, not a lie. As for 'inefficient' — no. Inefficiency is doing badly a thing that might be done well. The convocation does a false thing *deliberately*, which is not inefficiency. It is policy. It is also why two of their three sources were drafted in Aldric's own chancery. Propaganda is seldom wrong, apprentice. That is precisely what makes it dangerous."

He held out one ink-stained hand, palm up, waiting.

"And you will not learn the chronicles 'as if they are right.' You will learn what they *say*, because the convocation examines on what is written — and you are capable of holding two ideas in your skull at once. I have managed it for half a century, and with considerably worse light. First you master the received account. Then, and only then, are you fit to weigh evidence against it. One does not hand a first-year a chisel and point him at the cathedral."

He lowered himself back onto his stool and rubbed the bridge of his nose where the spectacles had pinched.

"Now. Set the box down. The buckle's tongue sticks — lift it before you pry, unless you fancy mending leather on top of cataloging. The transcriptions are in Orderon's fair hand. The endorsement page is the fourth leaf, ribbon-marked. Take it to the window, where the light is kinder than my eyes. Read the marginal note aloud, exactly as it stands — no paraphrase, no improvements. If your eye fails on a word, say 'unread' and continue on. Do not guess."

He folded his hands upon the table.

"Guessing, apprentice, is how the chronicles got to be the way they are."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I hold out the folded paper, a bit crumpled from being in my pocket.* "See? He called for more levies."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I tap the paper.* "And if the war was truly over, why would he be calling for more soldiers?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I look at the paper in my hand, then at the Maester, genuinely confused.* "So it was a war, but not *the* war? How many wars did they have?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, feeling a headache coming on.* "This is... much more complicated than the lectures made it sound."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I put the paper back in my pocket.* "So, when does a war officially end, if not with a treaty?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, trying to process this.* "So, essentially, it ends when no one is fighting anymore, even if the paperwork isn't done."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas closed his eyes as though the words had struck him somewhere behind the spectacles, and for a long moment he said nothing at all. When he opened them again, there was something very nearly like grief in his face.

"No," he said quietly. "No, apprentice. You have taken nine years of my argument and inverted it in a single sentence — and you have done it using the chancery's own logic. Sit down.

"'It ends when no one is fighting anymore.' That is Aldric's account. That is the received account. That is *the whole error*. The chronicles say: the swords stopped in 847, therefore peace. You have merely swapped 'therefore peace' for 'therefore the war is over,' which is the same mistake in different clothing. By your formulation the war ended in 847 — and you would be standing shoulder to shoulder with every scribe I have spent a decade arguing against."

He raised one ink-stained finger, then a second, then a third.

"Three events, kept distinct. *First*, the cessation of arms: the day the killing stops. *Second*, the settlement: the executed, sealed instrument by which the parties conclude the war. *Third*, the termination of the legal state itself. In a well-made peace these fall together, or near it. In this one they fell forty-four years apart. The swords stopped in 847. No settlement was ever executed — the draft was never sealed, and its Conclave counterpart does not exist. The legal state endured until Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891, and *that* act — not the silence of armies — ended the war. Her writ calls it 'the long and lingering war,' and the word doing all the work in that sentence is *long*."

He leaned forward, knuckles on the table.

"A tower abandoned is not a tower demolished. A debt is not discharged because the creditor tires of collection; it dies by instrument, or by statute, or by death, and not one day sooner. Wars are states of law, apprentice. Men do the dying; the law does the persisting. The paperwork is not an ornament hung upon a finished war. Once the killing stops, the paperwork *is* the war. And here the paperwork was never finished — which is precisely my point, and precisely why the war ran to 891."

He straightened, rubbed the pinched bridge of his nose, and nodded at the iron-banded box.

"Now. You have brandished that crumpled decree twice this afternoon, and both times it carried you away from the leaf I actually asked for. Your 863 levies sit comfortably enough in the account I have

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing the distinction. My earlier frustration melts into a deeper understanding.* "So the decree isn't wrong, it just... fits into a different part of the story." *I finally pick up the iron-banded box and bring it over to the table, carefully lifting the buckle's tongue.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I try 8-4-7-0-0-1... 8-4-7-0-0-2...* "Anything yet?" I whisper, mostly to myself. This is taking too long.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: The hum of the servers is really getting to me. No sticky notes, nothing. "Ugh, this is useless." I pull a small device from my pocket. "Time for the old faithful." *I plug it into the keypad's data port.*

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Damn it!" *I glare at the keypad, then back at the timer.* "This thing better work fast."

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I watch the device intently, hoping for a green light or a beep.* "Come on, come on..."

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I glance at the timer again. This is getting tight.* "Any progress at all?" I mutter, tapping my foot impatiently.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Seriously? Still nothing?" *I pull out the device and stare at it, then at the keypad.* "This isn't good."

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I start checking the keypad itself for any smudges or wear patterns.* There has to be a clue here somewhere.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I lean in close to the keypad, angling my head to catch the light.* Maybe some of the buttons are cleaner than others?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**1:20**

The display rejected **847000**, then **847001**, then **847002**. Each response took several seconds; the keypad would not accept another entry until its red light went dark.

After the third rejection, the screen changed:

**TOO MANY ATTEMPTS — RETRY IN 05:00**

The countdown began. The safe would accept no more codes until **6:20**. Above it, the ceiling strips kept pulsing every four seconds. The guard’s rotation would end at **15:00**.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**7:50**

Until **6:20**, every keypress met the same message: **RETRY IN 05:00**, its numbers steadily falling. The lockpick kit offered no shortcut; the safe had no visible keyway.

When the keypad finally cleared, it rejected **847003**, **847004**, and **847005**. Testing the three took ninety seconds. After the last rejection, the screen changed again:

**TOO MANY ATTEMPTS — RETRY IN 05:00**

It would unlock at **12:50**. Six of the thousand possible endings had been ruled out. The guard was due back at **15:00**.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Damn it! This is taking too long." I look around the vault, frustrated. "There has to be another way in."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**8:25**

A sweep of the vault revealed no keyway and no exposed hinges. The safe’s power cable disappeared into the wall; cutting it looked more likely to leave the bolts locked than release them.

Beside the nearest server rack, a maintenance clipboard hung from a hook. Its top sheet read **VAULT EQUIPMENT — SERVICE CALL LOG**. Several entries were folded beneath it, and a small sealed envelope marked **SAFE: EMERGENCY PROCEDURE** was clipped to the back.

The keypad’s countdown showed **04:25**. The guard would return in **6:35**.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**9:45**

A careful search turned up no sticky note or notebook. The racks had inventory labels, but none carried a six-digit number.

The maintenance clipboard was more promising. On the visible service log, an entry dated that morning read: **Safe keypad fault — emergency procedure filed with equipment log.** The sealed envelope marked **SAFE: EMERGENCY PROCEDURE** was still clipped to its back.

The keypad displayed **03:05** until it would accept another code. The guard was due in **5:15**.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I grab the clipboard, tearing the envelope free.* "Finally, some luck!" I rip open the envelope, looking for a code.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**10:03**

Inside the envelope was a single service slip. Beneath a warning that the code was temporary, someone had written:

**SAFE ACCESS — 847392**

The first three digits matched the inside source. Whether the slip was still current remained an open question.

Across the vault, the keypad glowed red: **RETRY IN 02:47**. It would accept the code at **12:50**. The guard would return at **15:00**.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**10:03**

The keypad’s red display still read **RETRY IN 02:47**. It would accept another code at **12:50**. The guard was due back at **15:00**—**4 minutes, 57 seconds** remained.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Okay, 8-4-7-3-9-2. Got it." I watch the keypad, drumming my fingers impatiently. "Come on, come on."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**12:50**

The red digits counted down through the server racks’ steady hum. At zero, the warning vanished. The keypad’s light turned green, and its display read **ENTER CODE**.

The safe remained shut. The guard was due back at **15:00**—two minutes and ten seconds away.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I quickly punch in the code: 8-4-7-3-9-2.* "Please work, please work!"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**13:02**

The keypad accepted **847392**. Its green light held steady while the bolts withdrew with three heavy clicks. The safe door eased open a fraction.

Inside sat a foam-lined case containing a single encrypted drive, its label bearing the same asset number as the maintenance log. A paper inventory sheet lay beneath it.

Beyond the vault door, the building remained quiet. The guard was due back at **15:00**—**1 minute, 58 seconds** remained.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I grab the drive and the inventory sheet.* "Got it!" I close the safe door and try to quickly re-lock it. "Time to go."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**13:24**

The safe door settled into its frame. For one uneasy second, nothing happened. Then the bolts drove home, and the keypad displayed **SECURED**.

The drive and inventory sheet were out. At the vault entrance, a green **PUSH TO EXIT** bar glowed beneath the door’s hydraulic housing. Beyond it lay the hall the guard would reach at **15:00**.

**1 minute, 36 seconds remained.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I push the exit bar.* "See ya, wouldn't wanna be ya." I need to get out of here before he shows.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**13:31**

The exit bar yielded. Hydraulics drew the vault door open just wide enough to expose the hall, where the lights had dimmed to their overnight setting. The guard was not in sight.

A service stairwell stood twenty paces to the left. To the right, the corridor ran toward the security desk; a camera above it swept slowly across the floor. The vault door began to close behind the opening.

The guard’s rotation would end at **15:00**. **One minute, 29 seconds remained.**

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I dart out of the vault, heading for the service stairwell.* "Almost there!"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**13:41**

Twenty paces passed beneath the dim hall lights. The camera over the security desk continued its sweep to the right; its lens did not turn toward the service stairwell.

The stairwell door had a push bar. Through its narrow window, concrete steps descended into darkness. A small sign beside the frame read **ALARM SOUNDS IF OPENED**.

Farther down the hall, a latch clicked. The guard was due back at **15:00**—**1 minute, 19 seconds** remained.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Crap!" *I hesitate, glancing back at the security desk camera. No time for that.* "Guess I'm taking the stairs!" *I push the bar, bracing for the alarm.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang listened to the whole pitch without moving. Then she pulled the earpiece out, set it carefully on the tarp beside a chalk-marked gasket, and wiped her hands on a rag that was dirtier than her hands.

"Sit," she said, nodding at an overturned parts crate. "Let's do the math. Out loud. It's good for you."

She picked up a stylus and started writing on the deck plating, since that was what was closest.

"Pressurized volume on this boat, ring plus spine, is about six thousand cubic meters. Air's roughly one point two kilos per cubic meter. So we're carrying maybe seven tonnes of atmosphere." She wrote *7 t* and circled it. "Loaded, this ship masses around twenty thousand tonnes. Now, what's our exhaust velocity if we dump cold air through a hatch? It's not a rocket nozzle. It's a hole. Call it four hundred meters per second, and that's generous."

She scrawled the rocket equation underneath and worked it in her head faster than she wrote it.

"Four hundred times the natural log of twenty thousand over nineteen thousand nine hundred ninety-three." She tapped the result. "Point one four meters per second."

She let that sit for a moment.

"We're doing a transit of several hundred million kilometers. You'd be shaving off," she squinted, "a few hours. Maybe. And that assumes we thrust in a straight line, which we won't."

She held up a finger for each problem.

"One. Our vents are on the ring. The ring rotates. Dump air out of a spinning structure and you don't get thrust, you get a wobble. Now I'm burning RCS propellant to stop us precessing, and we come out *behind* where we started.

"Two. Going faster means you have to slow down harder at the other end. Every meter per second you gain, you pay back at the brake. The drive budget was planned around that. You don't just get to arrive early. You arrive fast, and then you're a very expensive meteor.

"Three. Air isn't just for breathing. It carries heat. Half the electronics in this ship are cooled by convection. Vacuum them out and they cook within hours. Some of them are the ones keeping your suit charged.

"Four. Suits for 'a few days.' Our suits are rated for eight-hour EVAs. Twelve if you push it. Scrubber cartridges, water, waste handling, pressure sores. Forty people doing days in suits means someone gets hurt, and nobody can get to them because the medbay is also in vacuum.

"Five. Then we have to put the air *back*. From reserves. Nitrogen's the stuff we can't make out here, and we only have enough reserve to recover from one bad breach. You'd be spending our entire safety margin on purpose, to buy three hours."

She put the stylus down.

"Now. Here's the part I don't want you to lose." Her voice lost some of the lecture edge. "You thought about mass as reaction mass. Anything you throw off the back of the ship pushes you forward. That's the right instinct. The problem is that air's terrible reaction mass, and we already have a drive that throws hydrogen out the back at thirty kilometers a second. It's about seventy-five times better at this than a hatch."

She picked up a coupling from the tarp, inspected it, and set it back in its chalk outline.

"If you want to get us there faster, the answer is boring. Better burn efficiency. Trimming dry mass. Going over the trajectory with nav to see if there's a gravity assist somebody missed." She raised an eyebrow again. "That's real work, and I'd look at anything you bring me. Just bring it with numbers next time. Deal?"

Without waiting, she slid back under the coolant loop and reached for a torque wrench.

"And hand me the three-eighths while you're thinking about it."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The torque wrench stopped turning.

Hoang lay still under the coolant loop for a moment. Then she slid back out on the creeper, sat up, and rested her forearms on her knees. She didn't look annoyed. She looked like someone deciding which tool to use.

"What time?"

She let the question hang, then tapped the stylus against the numbers still chalked on the deck.

"Point one four meters per second. I told you a few hours, and I was being generous because I was working fast. Let's do it properly." She wrote beneath the first calculation, slower this time. "Cruise is about twenty kilometers a second. Point one four out of twenty thousand is seven parts in a million. Transit's roughly a hundred and seventy days, call it fifteen million seconds. Seven millionths of that is..." She underlined the result twice. "A hundred and five seconds."

She set the stylus down.

"Less than two minutes. Before we spend propellant stopping the wobble, and before we pay it back at the brake. Net, it's probably negative. You'd arrive *later*."

She pulled the rag from her pocket again, found a slightly cleaner corner, and wiped chalk off her fingers.

"So no, it isn't worth the risk. But I'm going to answer the question you actually asked, because you'll ask it again someday about something that isn't this stupid." Her tone was flat but not unkind. "'Worth the risk' is a sum. What you gain, times how likely you are to get it, against what you lose, times how likely *that* is. You don't get to feel your way through it. You write both sides down. Here, one side is two minutes. The other side is our whole nitrogen reserve, a cooked avionics bay, and some fraction of forty people dying in suits. You can't make that sum come out in your favor. The gain isn't big enough to be worth even one person."

She was quiet for a second, studying the junior officer's face.

"You said 'weeks.' That number came from your gut, not from a calculation. Out here the gut is wrong about orbital mechanics nearly every time, mine included. That's why I work the math on the floor instead of trusting how it feels." A faint, dry smile. "Twenty-some years, and I still do it with chalk."

Then the smile faded, and she asked the next thing more carefully.

"Now, you're pushing hard. Harder than a bad idea usually earns. Is there a reason you need us there sooner? Somebody sick? Something at the other end that can't wait?" She held up a hand before any answer could come. "You don't have to tell me. But if there is, that's a different problem, and it might have a real answer. Comms windows, a medical consult relayed ahead, a priority slot at the station. None of that needs us to breathe vacuum."

She lay back down on the creeper and pushed herself halfway under the loop, then stopped with only her boots and knees showing.

"Either way, I still need the three-eighths."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I blush a little, feeling foolish.* "No, Chief, no one's sick." *I grab the wrench from the toolbox.* "Just eager to get there, that's all." *I hand it to her.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
A hand came out from under the coolant loop, palm up. Hoang took the wrench without looking, weighed it once in her grip the way she did every tool, and fitted it to a fitting somewhere above her face.

"Eager's fine," she said to the underside of the manifold. The wrench clicked. "Eager's what gets people out here in the first place. Nobody signs up for a hundred and seventy days in a tin can because they're patient."

Click. Click. A pause while she checked the torque against a figure written in chalk on the pipe itself.

"And don't do that thing where you go red and decide you're an idiot. You're not. You had a bad idea, you defended it, I showed you the numbers, and now you know. That's the job. The ones I worry about are the ones who never say anything out loud, so nobody ever gets to check their math." The wrench stopped. "You'd be surprised how many engineers go their whole careers without learning that air makes lousy reaction mass. You learned it on a Tuesday, sitting on a crate."

She slid out partway, far enough to look up at the junior officer from the creeper. There was a smear of coolant residue across one cheekbone that she either didn't know about or didn't care about.

"Here's the thing about transit, though. The ship doesn't get there any faster, so you have to stop *waiting* to get there. First long haul I did, I counted days. Had a little chart. By day sixty I was chewing on bulkheads." She shrugged against the deck plating. "Second one, I decided the transit *was* the work. Went a lot better."

She nodded at the tarp, at the rows of components in their chalk outlines.

"Which brings me to that. Secondary loop's been running two degrees warm for a week. Probably scale in the manifold, maybe a bad seal. I've got it apart, and now every piece has to be cleaned, inspected, measured, and logged before it goes back together. It's boring and it's slow, and if it's done wrong, the aft electronics bay cooks." She held out the wrench, handle first. "Better use of your eagerness than venting the atmosphere."

She tipped her head toward a battered case at the edge of the tarp.

"Calipers are in there. Start with the gaskets, left to right. Thickness at four points each, write it next to the chalk mark. Anything under two point eight millimeters, you set aside and tell me." A beat. "And if you see something weird, say it out loud. Even if you think it's stupid."

She lay back down and pushed herself under the loop again, reaching up toward the next fitting by feel.

"*Especially* if you think it's stupid."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang slid out from under the loop, sat up, and held out a hand for the tablet. She didn't sigh. If anything, she looked pleased.

"Now we're talking."

She wiped her fingers on her coveralls before taking it, a courtesy she didn't extend to her own tools, and scrolled through the work slowly, lips moving slightly. The engineering bay hummed around them. Somewhere aft, a pump cycled.

"Okay. Your exhaust velocity." She tapped a line. "You've got the air compressed and expanded through a nozzle instead of dumped through a hatch. Seven hundred ninety meters per second." She tilted her head. "That's actually good. Ideal expansion of room-temperature air tops out somewhere around seven-sixty, seven-seventy, so you're a little optimistic, but you're in the right neighborhood. Better than my four hundred. I was being lazy and you weren't. Credit where it's due."

She scrolled down one more line and stopped.

"And here's where it goes sideways."

She turned the tablet around and put her fingertip under a single number.

"Initial mass. Twenty thousand." She looked up. "Twenty thousand what?"

She waited, then answered it herself, gently.

"You typed kilos. The ship's twenty thousand *tonnes*. You're off by a factor of a thousand, and it's the one number in the equation that matters most. Your version has us venting a third of the ship's mass as air. That's why it looks so good. You didn't build a better thruster. You built a lighter ship."

She picked up the chalk and wrote next to her earlier sums, keeping his numbers this time.

"Seven ninety times the log of twenty million kilos over twenty million minus seven thousand." The chalk scratched. "Log of that is about three point five times ten to the minus four. Times seven ninety..." She circled it. "Point two eight meters per second."

She sat back.

"Twice my number. Because your nozzle's better than my hole. Still less than four minutes off the transit, before cosine losses on that angle you picked, before the ring wobble, before the braking burn pays it back." She tapped the tablet's diagram, where a vent angled off the hull. "And the angle only hurts you. Any thrust not pointed straight along the velocity vector is thrust you're wasting."

She handed the tablet back but didn't let go right away.

"One more thing, because you'll want to know. To actually get three hundred forty meters per second out of air at that exhaust velocity, you'd have to vent about eleven thousand tonnes of it. We carry seven." A dry pause. "We'd need about sixteen hundred ships' worth of atmosphere."

She let go of the tablet.

"And even then, three forty out of a twenty-kilometer-a-second cruise is under two percent. That's about three days off a hundred and seventy. Not weeks. So even the version where the math was right wasn't the version you pitched me first. Check that, too, next time. Does the answer match the claim?"

She reached over, picked up a gasket from the tarp, and turned it in the light.

"Now, here's what I want you to take away. Your physics was fine. Your nozzle work was better than mine. You lost it on units. Out here that's what kills people. Nobody gets the rocket equation wrong. They get the kilos wrong. There was a probe back home, before either of us was born, lost because one team used pound-seconds and the other used newton-seconds." She set the gasket back in its outline. "Hundreds of millions of dollars. One column header."

She tapped the tablet in his hands.

"Write the units next to every number. Every time. Even when it feels stupid. *Especially* when it feels stupid." A faint, crooked smile. "Seems to be a theme today."

She nodded toward the calipers case.

"Gaskets. Left to right. Millimeters." She lay back down on the creeper. "And write the *millimeters*."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking it all in, feeling my face flush again.* "Okay, Chief. Millimeters." *I grab the calipers and open the case, pulling out the first gasket.* "And no more 'weeks,' just numbers."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
"Good," Hoang said from under the loop. "Numbers don't care how anybody feels, which makes them excellent company."

The wrench clicked twice more. Then it stopped.

There was a long pause, the kind that had nothing to do with a stuck fitting. The creeper rolled out slowly, and Hoang sat up with a frown aimed not at the junior officer but at her own chalk on the deck plating.

"Hang on."

She picked up the stylus and wrote beneath everything else, small and fast.

"Three forty over seven ninety. Point four three. E to the point four three is about one point five four." Scratch, scratch. "So final mass is twenty thousand tonnes over one point five four. Thirteen thousand. Which means you vent..." She stopped and tapped the stylus against the deck. "Seven thousand tonnes. Not eleven."

She looked at it for a second, then drew a clean line through her earlier figure and wrote the new one beside it, with *t* after it.

"I told you eleven thousand tonnes and sixteen hundred ships' worth of air. Wrong. It's seven thousand tonnes, a thousand ships' worth." She said it the way she'd report a pressure reading, without embarrassment or ceremony. "Conclusion doesn't change. We carry seven tonnes, not seven thousand. But the number I gave you was wrong, and I said it like I was sure. I did it in my head, on the fly, right after lecturing you about checking whether the answer matches the claim."

She set the stylus down and gave the junior officer a long, level look.

"That's the lesson, by the way. It isn't *juniors make mistakes*. Everybody makes mistakes. The Chief makes them while holding a torque wrench upside down. The difference is whether somebody checks. So when I give you a number, you're allowed to check it. You're *supposed* to. Rank doesn't make arithmetic right."

A faint, crooked smile returned.

"Put that in your log if you like. 'Day forty-one. Chief was wrong about air.' I won't mind."

She nodded at the calipers in the junior officer's hands and got practical again.

"Before you measure anything, close the jaws and zero them. Every time you pick them up, not just the first time. Measure at the twelve, three, six, and nine positions around the ring. Don't squeeze. Let the jaws touch and stop. If you press, you'll compress the gasket and read it thin, and then I'll throw out a good part because of your thumb." She tapped the tarp beside the first chalk outline. "Write all four readings, not the average. If one side's thinner than the others, that tells me the flange is warping, and that's a bigger problem than a worn gasket."

She lay back on the creeper, then paused with one hand on the manifold above her.

"Read me the first one out loud when you have it. With units."

The creeper rolled back under the loop. The wrench found its fitting again.

"And if I get it wrong," her voice echoed slightly off the pipes, "tell me."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang didn't answer right away. The wrench kept clicking, slow and even, and the pause stretched long enough that it was clear she was thinking rather than working.

Then the creeper rolled out. She sat up, looked at the chalk on the deck for a long moment, and tapped the stylus against her knee.

"All right. You get a yes."

She held up a finger before the word could land too hard.

"Not to venting the atmosphere. That's dead, and it stays dead. But you're right about one thing, and I've been sitting under that loop annoyed about it." She pointed the stylus aft, toward the spine. "We already throw gas overboard. Every day. The Sabatier reactor scrubs our CO2, turns it into water and methane, and we keep the water and dump the methane. Forty people, call it fourteen, fifteen kilos of methane a day, out a side port on the spine. Nobody aimed it. It just goes wherever the plumbing happened to point."

She wrote it out beneath the struck-through numbers, adding units without looking up.

"Methane's light. Cold-gas exhaust velocity's somewhere around eleven hundred meters per second through a decent nozzle, so it's better than air. Two and a half tonnes over the whole transit. Eleven hundred times two point five over twenty thousand." She circled it. "Point one four meters per second, total. Time saved is seconds." She looked up. "But it's free. We're dumping it anyway. And a vent pointed the wrong way puts a small torque on the ship that RCS quietly corrects for months. Point it straight aft, on the spin axis, and we stop paying for that too. The honest benefit is that we stop wasting propellant fighting our own garbage. The thrust is the bonus."

She set the stylus down and started counting on her fingers, the way she had the first time.

"Conditions. Non-negotiable.

"One. It's the waste stream only. The line gets physically isolated from the habitable volume. There's no valve anywhere that connects that nozzle to the air we breathe. If the only thing stopping it is a valve being closed, the design fails.

"Two. Spine, aft-facing, on the spin axis. Nothing touches the ring.

"Three. Two check valves in series and a burst disc. If line pressure goes outside the band, it isolates itself without anybody deciding to do it.

"Four. Methane burns. That line doesn't route through any occupied compartment, and every joint gets a leak check with the sniffer before it's pressurized. You find a leak, you tell me. You don't tighten it and hope.

"Five. Bench test first. We build the nozzle, mount it on a load cell in the machine shop, and run a bottle through it. You predicted seven ninety for air, so predict methane before we measure, and we'll see how close you get.

"Six. Nav models the torque change and the captain signs off. I don't modify a hull penetration on my own say-so, and neither do you."

She lowered her hand.

"Seven. You write the procedure. Every number gets a unit. I check it. Then you check my check, because we both know how today's gone."

The crooked smile came back, briefly.

"It's small, it's boring, and it'll take you about three weeks of evenings to do properly. Which, if you think about it, is a pretty good use of the transit."

She lay back on the creeper and pushed herself under the loop, then stopped with only her boots showing.

"Gaskets first, though. I'm still waiting on that first reading."

*(OOC: I kept her from agreeing to vent the main atmosphere, since she's written to refuse plans that could kill the crew and the physics doesn't pay off. Instead she agreed to a real, smaller version of the idea with strict conditions. If you meant a different plan, tell me and I'll adjust.)*

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Okay, Chief. This is... great!" *I say, a big grin spreading across my face.* "I'll get started on those gaskets right away, and then I'll look into the methane system." *I glance at the stack of gaskets.* "First one reads... 2.92 millimeters." *I say, remembering to add the units.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
"Two point nine two millimeters," Hoang repeated from under the loop. The wrench paused. "Good. Units and everything. I'll make an engineer of you yet."

Then, after a beat: "Which position?"

She let the question sit, and the wrench started clicking again, unhurried.

"That's one number. I asked for four. Twelve, three, six, nine." The fitting above her gave a small metallic complaint, and she muttered something at it in Vietnamese before continuing. "Two point nine two at twelve o'clock and two point nine two at six means a healthy gasket. Two point nine two at twelve and two point seven at six means the flange is pulling crooked, and I've got a warped mating surface somewhere up here that I haven't found yet. Same first number, completely different problem. One reading can't tell those apart."

The creeper rolled out a few centimeters, just far enough for her to tilt her head and look at the gasket in the junior officer's hand. She squinted at it.

"And tell me you zeroed the jaws before you measured."

She didn't wait long for an answer. She reached over, took a scrap of chalk from the tarp, and wrote *G1* on the deck plating beside the first outline, then drew a small circle with four tick marks around it, like a clock face with only the cardinal hours.

"There. Write each reading next to its tick. Clockwise from the top, starting wherever the part number's stamped. That's your twelve. If you pick the twelve at random, the next person to measure this gasket can't compare against yours, and the whole log's worthless." She set the chalk down. "The methane system's going to be exactly like this, by the way. Most of the work isn't clever. It's writing things down in a way that somebody else can check six months from now, when you're asleep and they're the one holding the part."

She pushed herself back under the loop and found the next fitting by feel.

"Three more for that one. Then gasket two." A pause, and when her voice came back it was a little drier. "And don't let the grin make you rush. Two point nine two is a good number. I'd hate to find out it was your thumb."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My grin falters a little.* "Right. Four readings. And zero the calipers." *I quickly pull the gasket back, zero the calipers, and re-measure, this time carefully checking all four points.* "Okay, Gasket one, twelve o'clock, 2.92. Three o'clock, 2.91. Six o'clock, 2.93. Nine o'clock, 2.90. All millimeters." *I write it down next to the chalk mark she made.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The wrench went quiet. From under the loop came a short hum, the kind Hoang made when a number arrived where she expected it.

"Two point nine zero to two point nine three." The creeper rolled out halfway, and she craned her neck to read the chalk upside down. "Spread of three hundredths of a millimeter. Those calipers are good to about two hundredths on a good day, so most of that is the tool, not the part. Flange is pulling flat. Gasket's healthy." She nodded once. "Keep it."

She studied the four numbers a moment longer, then looked up at the junior officer. Her expression wasn't quite a smile, but it was close.

"That's a clean reading. Zeroed, four points, units, written where it belongs. It took you about a minute longer than the first try, and now it's worth something. The first one was a guess that happened to be right." She tapped the chalk clock face with a knuckle. "Don't lose the grin, by the way. I just want it pointed at the right things. This is one of them."

She lay back down and slid under the loop, but this time she didn't reach for the wrench. There was a scraping sound, then a longer silence.

"Huh."

When she spoke again, her voice was muffled and interested.

"Well, there's my two degrees." A hand came out from under the manifold, holding a small inspection mirror. On the back of it was a smear of pale, chalky crust, flaky and faintly green. "Scale. Calcium and copper carbonate, looks like, built up on the inlet side of the third branch. It's not much, maybe a millimeter, but it's right at the narrowest point. Narrows the bore, drops the flow, and the aft bay runs warm." She turned the mirror in the work light, frowning at it with something like affection. "Which means the water chemistry on this loop drifted somewhere upstream, and scale was only the symptom. I'll want the conductivity logs from the last three months."

She set the mirror carefully on the tarp, outside every chalk outline, and wrote *SCALE: BR3 INLET, ~1 mm* beside it. Then, after a second's thought, she added *est.*

"Estimated," she said, mostly to herself. "I haven't measured it yet. I'm not going to write down a number like it's measured when it isn't. Not today."

The creeper squeaked as she settled back under.

"Gasket two. Same drill. Find the stamp, that's your twelve." A pause. "And when you get to gasket four, it's the one off branch three. Measure it extra carefully. If the scale's been sitting against it, it may have chewed up one side, and I'd like to know before I go looking for a warped flange that doesn't exist."

The wrench found its fitting again and started clicking, slow and patient.

"Out loud, with units. You know the rest."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, focusing on the task.* "Understood, Chief." *I pick up the next gasket, find the stamp, and start carefully measuring.* "Gasket two, twelve o'clock, 2.93. Three o'clock, 2.92. Six o'clock, 2.93. Nine o'clock, 2.91. All millimeters." *I write it down on the deck.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
"Two point nine one to two point nine three millimeters," Hoang said. The wrench kept its rhythm. "Healthy. Keep it."

Then the clicking slowed, and stopped.

"Read me the nine o'clock on both of them again."

She didn't wait for it. The creeper rolled out, and she propped herself on one elbow to squint at the two chalk clock faces side by side. Her finger hovered over each nine o'clock tick in turn. *2.90. 2.91.*

"Both thinnest at nine," she said. "Both."

She was quiet for a moment, chewing the inside of her cheek.

"Now. That's one hundredth of a millimeter, and the calipers are good to two. So it's inside the noise. By itself it means nothing, and if I pulled this whole manifold apart because of it I'd be an idiot." She tapped the deck between the two gaskets. "But two out of two is a pattern, even if it's a quiet one. If gaskets three and four also come in thin at nine, then it's probably not the tool, and something is pushing on that side of the whole assembly. The mounting bracket, maybe. Thermal stress from the scale running the pipe hot on one side."

She picked up the chalk and wrote beneath the two clocks, small and neat: *G1, G2 min @ 9 o'clock. Within tool tol. Watch.*

"That's how you write down a hunch," she said. "You say what you saw, you say why it might be nothing, and you say what would change your mind. Then you keep working instead of falling in love with it." She glanced up. "Half of good engineering is noticing things. The other half is not believing them too early."

She rolled back under the loop, reached up, and felt along the manifold's underside with her fingertips, slowly, the way someone reads braille.

"Bracket feels fine from here," she reported. "Which doesn't prove anything either."

The wrench came back into her hand.

"Gasket three. Same drill. Measure it the same way you did the first two. Don't go looking for thin at nine. If you expect it, your thumb will find it for you." A pause. "Then four, off branch three. That's the one I care about."

Somewhere aft, the pump cycled again. Hoang hummed a few bars of whatever had been on her earpiece, still off-key.

"Out loud when you've got it."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, understanding the subtlety.* "Got it, Chief. Noticing things, not believing them too early." *I pick up gasket three and begin my measurements, taking my time to be precise.* "Gasket three. Twelve o'clock, 2.94. Three o'clock, 2.92. Six o'clock, 2.93. Nine o'clock, 2.91. All millimeters." *I write it down, noting the 2.91 at nine o'clock again.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang didn't say anything for a few seconds. The wrench didn't move.

"Two point nine one at nine," she said finally. "Three for three."

The creeper rolled out, and this time she sat all the way up, pulling her knees in and looking at the three chalk clocks in a row. She didn't reach for the chalk yet.

"Okay. Here's the trap." She held up a finger. "You're thinking, three in a row, that's a one-in-sixty-four coincidence. It isn't. I didn't pick nine o'clock ahead of time. I picked it *after* I saw the first two. So only gasket three counts as a test, and any given gasket has about a one-in-four chance of being thinnest at nine just by luck. One in four isn't evidence. It's a coin that came up heads twice."

She lowered the finger.

"But it didn't come up tails, either. So we check the thing nobody ever suspects." She nodded at the calipers. "Us."

She leaned over and tapped the tarp near the junior officer's hand.

"You measure clockwise. By the time you're at nine o'clock, where's your wrist? Twisted. Awkward angle, jaws a little cocked, a bit more pressure from the thumb because you're fighting your own arm. That could shave a hundredth off every time, and it'd look exactly like a warped bracket." She almost smiled. "I've chased a *measurer* before. Took me two days. It was me.

"So. Pick up gasket one again. Rotate it half a turn in your hand so the stamp is at the bottom. Then measure the same four points on the *part*, twelve through nine by the stamp, but your hand will be in different positions. If the thin spot follows the stamp, it's the gasket, and I go look at the bracket. If the thin spot stays wherever your wrist is awkward, it's you, and we just learned something about how you hold calipers." She shrugged. "Either answer is useful. Only one of them costs me a morning upside down under this manifold."

She picked up the chalk and added one line beneath her earlier note, *G3 min @ 9. Test: rotate G1, re-measure. Operator vs. part.*

Then she lay back on the creeper but didn't slide under. She stayed where she could see the tarp.
