"Gasket one, rotated. Call out which position is which by the stamp, not by where it's sitting." She folded her hands on her stomach and waited. "Then gasket four. Branch three. That one I'm going to watch you do."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*I pick up Gasket one again, feeling a bit self-conscious but determined to get it right. I rotate it, so the stamp is at the bottom as she suggested, and carefully re-measure.*

"Okay, Gasket one, rotated. Twelve o'clock by the stamp, 2.92. Three o'clock, 2.91. Six o'clock, 2.93. Nine o'clock, 2.91. All millimeters." *I call out the readings, making sure to clarify which is which.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang didn't move from the creeper. Her eyes went from the junior officer's hands to the chalk and back.

"Say the nine again."

A beat.

"Two point nine one. And three o'clock is two point nine one too." She sat up slowly and pulled the tarp a little closer, until the first chalk clock was between her knees. She laid a finger on it and talked it through the way she'd done the rocket equation, one step at a time.

"Stamp at the bottom. You measured clockwise by the stamp. So when you read the part's nine o'clock, your hand was over at the easy side, wrist straight, no fighting." She tapped the tick mark. "If it was you, that reading should have come up fat. It didn't. It came up thin again."

She sat back on her heels.

"So the thin spot followed the part, not your wrist. It's not the operator." She glanced up. "That's good news for you. Look at your repeat readings, too. Every one of them is within one hundredth of the first pass. You got the same numbers with the part upside down and your hand in different places. That's better repeatability than those calipers are rated for. Whatever you're doing with your thumb, keep doing it."

Then she held up a finger, because of course she did.

"Now let's be honest about how much we know. The nine went from two point nine zero to two point nine one, and now it's tied with the three. The whole effect is a hundredth of a millimeter, inside the tool's tolerance. We've ruled out one explanation. We haven't proven the other one. It's still a hunch, but a better one."

She picked up the chalk and added to her note in neat, small letters: *G1 rotated: min follows part, not operator. Repeatability ±0.01 mm. Hunch upgraded. Still within tol.*

"So here's what it buys us. It doesn't justify a teardown. But when this manifold goes back together, I'll put a feeler gauge on that bracket before I torque anything. That's ten minutes, and I was going to be under there anyway." She set the chalk down. "Cheap check for a cheap hunch. You match the cost of the look to the strength of the evidence."

She shifted around on the deck until she was sitting cross-legged beside the tarp, close enough to see the calipers' display. She didn't reach for the wrench.

"Gasket four. Branch three."

She nodded at the part in its chalk outline. Even from there, one edge of it looked faintly discolored, a pale greenish tinge against the black elastomer.

"Before you measure, look at it. Both faces, under the work light. Tell me what you see before you put a tool on it. Discoloration, pitting, crust, a lip where it's been squeezed out. Your eyes are an instrument too. Use them first, because the calipers can't tell you what color something is." She paused. "If there's scale stuck to it, don't scrape it off. I want to see it, and the thickness with the crust on it means something different from the thickness without."

She folded her arms on her knees and watched, unhurried.

"Zero first. Find the stamp. Then out loud."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*I pick up gasket four, turning it over in my hands under the light. My eyes scan the surface carefully, just like she said.*

"Okay, Chief, I see... some discoloration on one side, kind of a pale green. And there's a slight roughness, almost like a faint crust, especially around the three and six o'clock positions, by the stamp."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Hoang killed the earpiece with a thumb and sat back on her heels, coolant still dripping off her wrist. She looked at the junior officer the way she looked at a cracked weld: not angry, just already done with it.

"No."

She wiped her hands on a rag and nodded at the manifold.

"Main atmosphere is not a propellant tank. It's the thing keeping your blood from boiling and your lungs from freezing. Vent it and you don't get an emergency boost. You get a dead ship and a crew in suits counting the hours until the scrubbers they don't have run out."

She held up one greasy finger.

"Mass. The air in this hull is a rounding error next to the ship. Blow every kilogram of it out an aft valve and you buy yourself a shove you could measure with a stopwatch and still lose. Weeks? You'd be lucky to shave a day, and you'd spend it breathing bottled gas while the thermal loops seize because half their working fluid just left through a hatch."

A second finger.

"Suits. A suit is a coffin with a radio. Filters foul. Seals weep. You don't live in them for days because an officer got bored of the transit clock. Medical would be scraping condensate out of your lungs before we made station."

She dropped her hand and went back to the chalk marks on the tarp.

"Propulsion is the engines and the reaction mass we budgeted for them. Life support is not a thruster. If you want a faster burn, bring me a mass budget and a delta-v that doesn't murder the crew. Otherwise leave the atmosphere where it is."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Hoang set the rag down and looked at him properly this time, the way she looked at a pressure reading that had already gone red.

"No. Time is not worth a dead crew. That's the whole job."

She tapped the deck with one knuckle, counting it out.

"You don't buy weeks. You buy a shove smaller than a course correction, and you spend it with no atmosphere, no thermal mass in the loops, and suits that were never rated for multi-day habitation. Filters load. CO2 climbs. Somebody's seal weeps at hour thirty and we are not a hospital. We are a mining hull with one medic and finite bottles."

She leaned back over the manifold, already done with the argument.

"Risk is for things that fail and still leave you breathing. This doesn't. Bring me a burn plan that uses the reaction mass we actually carry. Leave the air in the ship."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Okay, okay, I get it, Chief." *I hold up my hands in surrender.* "Just trying to think outside the box, you know?" I look around the engineering bay. "What about... a temporary, high-thrust external engine? We could jettison it once we're up to speed."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Hoang didn't look up from the manifold. She fitted a seal ring into its groove with her thumb and spoke to the deck plating.

"Outside the box is where the vacuum is. Thinking there is fine. Living there isn't."

She set the ring down and finally met his eyes.

"A temporary high-thrust engine is not an idea. It's a ship we don't have, bolted to the one we do." She counted it off on greasy fingers again, slower this time. "First, the engine. We don't carry a spare main. Fabricating one out of scrap in a bay this size gets you a pressure vessel that fails on ignition, not a thruster. Second, the reaction mass. High thrust means you throw mass out the back fast. That mass has to be aboard before you light it. We budgeted our tanks for the burn we already planned. You don't conjure tonnes of propellant by calling the engine temporary."

She nodded aft, toward the thrust frame she couldn't see through three bulkheads.

"Third, the hull. This frame is built for the acceleration our engines actually make. A high-thrust strap-on doesn't politely add speed. It loads the longerons, the tank mounts, the ring bearings. Miss the center of mass by a handspan and you don't accelerate. You tumble, and the ring comes apart with people in it."

A last finger.

"Jettison doesn't help you. In vacuum you keep the speed you paid for. Dropping the engine after the burn saves you nothing you didn't already spend in propellant, and it leaves a hot, possibly still-venting mass on a crossing trajectory with our own hull. We are not in the business of mining our own debris."

She picked the seal ring back up.

"If you want more delta-v, the levers are Isp, propellant mass, and how much dry mass we can shed before we burn. Not a magic bottle we light and throw away. Write those three numbers down. If they close, I'll look at them. If they don't, the transit takes as long as the transit takes."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Hoang took the tablet, thumbed the brightness down, and read the lines twice. The coolant on her wrist had gone tacky. She did not hand it back.

"Three hundred and forty meters a second." She said it the way she read a gauge that had failed open. "That's not a vent. That's a burn. Your sheet has the air leaving faster than the ship, and then it treats that exhaust speed as if it were ours."

She turned the tablet so the numbers faced the bay lights.

"Compression ratio is not free delta-v. You spend ship power to squeeze the gas. When you let it go, the best you get is a cold-gas puff — hundreds of meters a second at the nozzle, if the nozzle is real and the gas is warm. The hull does not inherit that speed. It inherits momentum. Mass of air times exhaust speed, divided by the mass of this ship. The air in the pressure hull is tonnes. The ship is tens of thousands of tonnes. Run it honest and you are looking at centimeters per second, not three hundred and forty meters. Your angle term only makes it worse. Anything off-axis is cosine loss, and a side load on a ring that was not built to be shoved sideways."

She scrolled once, found the mass cell, and tapped it with a greasy nail.

"This number is wrong. You booked the atmosphere like it was a tank load. It isn't. Blow every kilogram aft, perfectly aligned, heated with every watt we can spare, and you still don't buy a day on the clock. You buy a dead thermal loop, a hull full of vacuum, and suits. Same answer as before. The arithmetic doesn't get to overrule the mass."

She set the tablet on the tarp, beside the chalked manifold, screen still lit.

"Fix the mass. Fix the rocket equation. If it still says three hundred and forty, the model is lying to you, not the transit. Leave the air in the ship."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Okay, okay!" *I hold up my hands again.* "I guess my numbers are... optimistic." I sigh, looking at the tablet on the tarp. "So... no shortcuts, then?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Hoang picked the tablet up, killed the screen, and set it on the junior officer's side of the tarp where it belonged. The seal ring went back into its groove. She didn't look pleased. She looked finished.

"There are shortcuts. They all end the same way. You arrive with fewer people than you left with, or you don't arrive."

She wiped a thumb of grease off the manifold flange and checked the seating by feel, not by eye.

"The transit is long because the mass is large and the engines are honest. You can shed dry mass before the burn. You can fly a tighter trajectory if Nav will sign the margins. You can stop asking life support to do a thruster's job. Those are the levers. None of them are clever. All of them leave the air in the hull and the crew out of suits."

She reached for the next chalked fitting and didn't offer him a softer version of it.

"If you're bored, the secondary loop still needs a second pair of hands. If you're not, go write a mass budget that closes. Either way, the clock runs at the speed the propellant allows. Not the speed you wish it did."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Hoang didn't take the surrender as a change of mind. She had heard that tone before, right before someone tried the same bad idea with softer words.

"No shortcuts," she said. "And no conditions that make a bad plan into a good one. Suits, timers, angles, 'temporary' — none of that puts mass in the tanks or keeps blood from boiling. I am not signing a vent, and I am not bolting a fantasy engine to this frame."

She seated the next fitting and checked it by feel.

"You want my conditions, here they are. Atmosphere stays in the hull. Reaction mass stays in the budgeted tanks. Acceleration stays inside what the thrust frame was built for. Anything else is a no, and it stays a no if you ask again with a tablet."

She nodded at the open loop.

"Hand me the small spanner, or go write a mass budget that closes. Those are the options."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I sigh, running a hand through my hair.* "Alright, Chief. Spanner it is." I look around for the right tool, a little deflated. "Which one's the small spanner?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Hoang jerked her chin at the tool roll by the junior officer's knee without looking up from the flange. The small spanner was the stubby one with the worn blue tape on the handle, third from the left, already greasy from the last time someone had put it back wrong.

"Blue tape. Not the long one. Long one's for the primary couplings and you'll round the nut if you use it here."

She held out a hand, palm up, and kept her eyes on the seating of the seal. The loop was still open. Coolant smell sat in the bay, sharp and chemical, under the pump-hum.

"Pass it handle-first. Then hold the manifold steady while I torque this. Don't lean on the chalk marks. Those are the only record of which way these pieces go back together, and I am not doing this inventory twice because you got bored of standing still."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I quickly spot the blue tape spanner and grab it carefully, making sure to hand it to her handle-first.* "Got it, Chief." *I then brace myself, ready to hold the manifold steady.* "Just tell me where to put my hands."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Hoang took the spanner without ceremony, the taped handle seating into her palm like it belonged there. She nodded at the manifold, two spots clear of the chalk and clear of the open seal.

"Left hand on the flange, here. Right hand on the yoke, not on the bellows. The bellows will flex if you squeeze it and then the seal walks."

She set the spanner on the nut and leaned her weight into the first quarter-turn, slow, listening for the dry tick of threads taking up.

"Hold it like you mean it. If it shifts while I'm torquing, the ring cocks and we start over. Don't help me turn it. Just keep it still. And keep your sleeves out of the coolant. That stuff eats skin if you let it sit."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I place my hands exactly where she indicated, gripping the manifold firmly but trying not to squeeze too hard.* "Got it, Chief. No shifting." *I focus intently on keeping it perfectly still, mindful of my sleeves.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Hoang put her weight into the next quarter-turn and felt the manifold stay put under his hands. Good. The threads took up with a dry tick, then another, and the seal ring seated true instead of cocking off to one side.

"That's it. Don't ease off yet."

She worked the nut home in short, even pulls, counting them under her breath, and stopped when the flange met the mark she'd chalked on the housing. Not a guess. The torque lived in her wrist, and the wrist said enough.

"All right. Let go. Slowly. If it springs, I want to see it, not feel it through your thumbs."

She sat back on her heels, wiped the spanner, and checked the seating with a thumbnail along the joint. No step. No weep starting at the low point. The coolant smell was still in the bay, but it wasn't getting stronger.

"That one's done. Two more on this loop before we pressure it, and we pressure it with the isolation valves shut so a bad seal costs us a drip pan and not the secondary inventory." She nodded at the tarp, at the next chalked fitting. "Hand me the ring with the single hash on it. Not the double. Double's for the hot side, and if you mix them the loop binds when it heats."

She held out her hand again, palm up, already looking at the open port.

"Then you can tell me, without a tablet, what actually limits how fast this ship gets anywhere. If you get it right, I'll let you torque the next one."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I gingerly release my grip, checking to make sure it doesn't budge, then quickly find the ring with the single hash mark.* "Here you go, Chief." *I hand it to her, then pause, thinking about her question.* "Uh... is it the amount of fuel we can carry?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Hoang took the single-hash ring, turned it once under the bay light to be sure, and set it in the port before she answered. The double-hash stayed on the tarp where it belonged.

"Part of it. Not the part that gets officers killed."

She seated the ring with her thumb and held the flange steady herself this time. He hadn't earned the spanner yet.

"Fuel — propellant — is one number in the rocket equation. Not the speed limit by itself. What matters is how much of the ship's mass is propellant versus how much is ship, and how fast you can throw that propellant out the back. Exhaust velocity. Specific impulse, if you want the fancy word. A tank you can't lift doesn't help you. A tank you burn through in one hard shove and then have nothing left for the flip-and-brake doesn't help you either. We have to stop at the other end. Mining hulls don't get to arrive as a streak."

She nodded aft again, through the bulkheads.

"And the frame. Even if the tanks were fuller, this thrust structure was built for the acceleration our engines make. Push harder than that and you don't go faster in any way that matters. You bend longerons. The ring wasn't designed to be a battering ram."

She looked at him, not unkind, just exact.

"So the limits are propellant mass, dry mass, exhaust velocity, and what the hull will take without folding. 'How much fuel we can carry' is the first one, said loosely. Say the other three without a tablet and you can torque the next nut. Get them wrong and you hold the manifold again while I do it."

She held out the spanner, taped handle toward him, and didn't let go of it yet.

"Your hands stay off the bellows either way."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, trying to process all the information.* "Right, okay. So... dry mass, exhaust velocity, and the hull's structural limits." *I look at the spanner, then back at her, a little hopeful.* "Did I get them all, Chief?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Hoang let the spanner go. The taped handle stayed in his grip. She did not smile. She nodded once, the way she nodded at a pressure reading that had finally come back into the green.

"Those three. And the first one you already said, said loosely. Propellant mass, dry mass, exhaust velocity, structural limit. That's the list. Don't dress it up later."

She shifted aside on the deck plating so he had the nut, and set her own hands on the flange and the yoke, clear of the bellows, taking the job he'd just finished.

"Your turn. Short pulls. Stop when the flange meets the chalk. If it cocks, you stop and you tell me. You do not 'finish the turn' on a ring that's walking." She kept her eyes on the joint, not on him. "Sleeves up. Coolant still eats skin. And if you round that nut, you are cutting a new one out of bar stock before either of us eats."

The pump-hum went on under it. She braced the manifold and waited.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I take the spanner with a newfound respect, feeling the weight of the task. I carefully position it on the nut, taking a deep breath.* "Understood, Chief. Short pulls." *I start to turn the spanner, focusing intently on the nut and the flange, acutely aware of her eyes on my work.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The safe stood flush against the far wall. Beside it, the lockpick kit offered no obvious purchase: the door had no visible keyway.

**1:37**

The keypad had rejected **847000**, **847001**, and **847002**. Each entry took longer than the last as the display paused before returning its red light. After the third, the digits vanished.

**TEMPORARY LOCKOUT — 02:00**

The ceiling strips continued their four-second pulse. When the keypad became available again, the security rotation would be less than twelve minutes from completion.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The keypad’s lockout cleared at **3:37**. Over the next ninety seconds, **847003**, **847004**, and **847005** each met the same red light. The display gave no hint whether any of the final digits were right.

**5:07**

**TEMPORARY LOCKOUT — 02:00**

The ceiling strips kept pulsing. Six possible endings had been ruled out; 994 remained. There was no sign that the systematic search was getting closer, and the guard’s return was **9 minutes, 53 seconds** away.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Damn it." I bite my lip, glancing at the pulsating lights. "This isn't working. There has to be another way." I scan the safe itself for anything I missed.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The safe’s face offered no keyway, hinge, or exposed seam. Under the pulsing ceiling light, though, three keys beyond **8**, **4**, and **7** showed the same dull wear: **2**, **5**, and **9**. The other digits looked cleaner. Wear was a clue, not proof of the order—or even proof that the digits belonged to this code.

**5:58**

The keypad still read **TEMPORARY LOCKOUT — 01:09**. Across the room, a server fan rose in pitch, then settled. The guard was due back in **9 minutes, 2 seconds**.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The vault was mostly bare: server racks, a fire-suppression panel, and a narrow maintenance shelf near the door. No sticky note marked the safe. Beneath a stack of cable labels on the shelf, however, lay a folded service log. Finding it among the paperwork took longer than the room’s size suggested.

**8:26**

The log listed a keypad replacement from the previous week. Beside the safe’s serial number, someone had written: **“new suffix uses 2 / 5 / 9 — 9 last.”** It did not give the order of the first two digits.

The keypad’s lockout had cleared at **7:07**. Its display waited dark now. The guard was due back in **6 minutes, 34 seconds**.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Jackpot!" I whisper, a grin spreading across my face. Okay, so 9 is last. That means the other two are 2 and 5. So the combinations are 8-4-7-2-5-9 or 8-4-7-5-2-9. I'll try the first one. *I quickly move back to the keypad.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The keypad registered **847259**. For three seconds, its display held the digits while a relay clicked somewhere inside the safe.

Then the light turned red.

**9:01**

**CODE INCORRECT.** The display cleared, but it did not lock out. The service log had left only one other order: **847529**.

From beyond the vault door came a faint radio crackle. The guard was due back in **5 minutes, 59 seconds**.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**9:01**

The keypad still showed **CODE INCORRECT**. Nine minutes and one second had passed since the vault door sealed; the guard was due back in **5 minutes, 59 seconds**.

The display cleared. It was ready for another entry.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Almost there," I mutter, fingers already hovering over the keys. *I punch in 8-4-7-5-2-9, holding my breath.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The keypad held **847529** for three seconds. A relay clicked—the same sound as before—but this time the light turned green. Heavy bolts withdrew inside the safe door, and it eased open a finger’s width.

**9:14**

Inside sat a black document case and a small inventory ledger. Neither bore a label visible from the doorway. Beyond the vault, the radio crackled again, followed by footsteps too distant to place.

The guard was due back in **5 minutes, 46 seconds**.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Yes!" I pull the case out quickly. I don't care about the ledger. "Time to go." I try to close the vault door silently behind me.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The black case came free without resistance. Behind it, the inventory ledger remained on the shelf, visible through the safe’s open door. Its green keypad light washed a narrow stripe across the floor.

At the vault entrance, the interior release opened the door. Its hydraulic hinge resisted any attempt at a quick, quiet close: the seal met the frame with a soft thump, followed by an unmistakable hiss.

**9:48**

The corridor outside stood empty. A radio crackled around a distant corner, then fell silent. The guard was due back in **5 minutes, 12 seconds**.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I cringe at the sound of the door closing.* "Damn it, too loud." I quickly scan the corridor, then start moving, trying to be as quiet as possible.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The corridor offered two routes: a service stairwell at the far end and a cross-hall to the left. A strip of light beneath the cross-hall door shifted as someone passed on the other side. The stairwell door stood closed; its push bar looked sound, but a metal latch could be heard rattling faintly in the ventilation draft.

**10:22**

The radio crackled again, closer now. A voice said, “Finishing the lower floor,” then cut out.

The guard was due back at **15:00**—**4 minutes, 38 seconds** away.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *My eyes dart between the stairwell and the cross-hall.* "Lower floor, huh? Not good." I decide on the stairwell, hoping it's less trafficked. *I move towards it quickly but quietly.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The stairwell was thirty paces down the corridor. By the time its push bar came within reach, the rattling latch had gone still. Through the wired-glass pane, the landing looked empty; stairs climbed to the floor above and descended into darkness.

**10:49**

A radio voice rose from below, muffled by the door: “Lower floor clear.” Footsteps sounded on the stairs, then stopped. The push bar would release the door, but its loose latch looked unlikely to catch quietly.

The guard was due at the vault at **15:00**—**4 minutes, 11 seconds** away.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Crap, they're coming up." I look back at the cross-hall door. No time to try that now. *I quickly scan the stairwell door itself for anything I can use.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
The stairwell door had a hydraulic closer mounted at the top. Its arm looked intact; the noise came from the latch, which sat loosely against the metal strike plate. Holding the push bar down while the door swung would keep the latch retracted, though the closer would still pull against it.

**11:05**

Beyond the wired glass, a flashlight beam swept briefly across the lower flight of stairs. The footsteps resumed, climbing toward the landing.

The guard was due back at the vault in **3 minutes, 55 seconds**.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I make a quick decision.* "Okay, this is it." I push the bar down, holding it firmly to keep the latch from rattling, and slowly open the door, trying to minimize the hiss from the closer.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Eat something," Noor echoed, not turning from the glass. "Yeah. I know."

Headlights again — the third pair in an hour. Noor tracked them up the switchback, breath held, until they swept past without slowing. Their shoulders came down maybe half an inch.

Twelve sixteen. The source's protocol had been blunt: *two hours late, assume I'm burned. Don't wait, don't call, don't go looking.* Noor had recited it back to him in a parking garage in March like it was academic.

They let the curtain fall closed. In the dark, they pulled out their phone — one bar, trembling up to two. Nothing from him. Of course nothing. Their thumb hovered over his contact for three full seconds before they shoved the phone across the table like it had burned them.

"If I try to call him tonight," Noor said, "take the phone off me. I mean it. He made me promise, and I don't trust myself after midnight."

Then they sat down and opened the laptop at last. The screen lit the whole cabin blue-white. Phone records first — the screenshots, the carrier metadata, the ugly spine of the story, all saved locally. Noor lined the files up like dealing cards.

The padded case sat next to the laptop, still untouched. The passphrase was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. Spoken, never written. Noor stared at it for a long moment, then opened it, plugged the drive in, and typed the first thing that came: his daughter's name, spelled the way he spelled it.

*Access denied. Four attempts remaining before self-wipe.*

Noor leaned back and pressed the heels of their hands into their eyes until the dark went spotty.

"Okay," they said, and it came out rougher than intended. "Okay. You're right. Soup. There's no version of this where I out-think him on four guesses and an empty stomach." They pushed back from the table and crossed to the cabinet — three mugs, a tin of soup, a lighter with no fluid in it. "I start making things up when I'm like this. Seeing patterns that aren't there." They rattled the tin, considering it. "You want some?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I put my phone down.* "Sure, soup sounds good." *I get up and stretch, then head over to the kitchen.* "Need any help?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Just the can opener," *I mumble, already rummaging through a drawer.* "Unless you know how to open this with your teeth."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: "With

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The stove was propane and ancient — the knob ground like it was hurting something. Noor found matches behind the coffee filters, and the burner caught on the second strike with a soft *whump* that made them jerk back a full step. Too fast. Their nerves were tuned like guitar strings tonight.

They dumped the soup into the only pot, added water by eyeball, and stirred it with a fork because the one spoon in the drawer was crusted with something geological.

"New rule," Noor said, watching the pot instead of the road. "The drive sits until morning. No guesses. No theories at 1 AM. Four attempts and it wipes itself, and everything on my laptop is just *corroboration* — the drive is the proof. I don't spend proof on a feeling." They paused, fork going still. "He spells her name with a Y. I know he does — he told me about a birthday cake once, the bakery got it wrong and—"

They stopped themself. Physically turned away from the laptop like it was a ledge.

"No. That's how it starts. It sits."

The soup went into two of the three mugs. Before sitting, Noor pulled out their phone, held the button down, and watched the screen die — actually watched it, all the way to black. Then they slid it across the table.

"After midnight. You heard the deal. Take it before I find a version of myself that argues."

They ate standing up first, then made themself sit, because hands shaking around hot soup and a keyboard was a bad combination. One hand on the mug, one on the trackpad. The carrier records. The burner. Cross-checked against the incident logs they'd carried out of the courthouse in a backpack in June.

"Forty-one calls," Noor said quietly, to the screen, to the room. "Eleven days. Every single one inside the ninety minutes before a raid that went bad." They scrolled, stopped, tapped the screen twice like they could make it say something else. "That's not noise. That's choreography. Somebody was making phone calls before every single one of those doors came off its hinges."

The soup was helping. The coffee had been keeping them vertical; the food was keeping them human. Their eyes were starting to sting anyway.

"Here's the plan, and I need you to hear it so it's real," Noor said, looking up at last. "If he doesn't surface in seventy-two hours, I publish with what I have. Corroboration, records, my name on it. No waiting, no hunting for him, no getting us both killed playing detective on a mountain road." They set the mug down. "Say it back to me later if I start drifting. I'm taking the window till three — you should sleep. There's a bed through there that smells like mothballs and better decisions."

They carried the second mug over and set it on the table beside Driver's phone, then went back to the window, breath fogging the glass in a small patient oval.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I pick up my phone, then set it back down. "Seventy-two hours," I repeat, nodding slowly. "No hunting." I take a sip of the soup. It's surprisingly good. "You want me to take the first watch then? You look like you're about to fall over."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: No

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I watch them for a second, then sigh.* "Okay, fine. You do you." *I slurp some more soup.* "But if you start mumbling about patterns, I'm taking your phone."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I pick up my phone again, unlock it, then remember I'm supposed to be holding Noor's phone hostage.* "Right. No phone." *I put it back down, then get up and walk over to the window.* "What exactly are we looking for out there?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: No

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I put my phone down and take a long sip of soup. "Just a general idea, then. Car, truck, alien spaceship?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "He's not gonna show, is he?" I say, more to myself than to Noor.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: No

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I sigh and put the mug down, standing up.* "Look, you need sleep. Seriously. I can watch the road for a bit."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: No

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Okay, fine," I say, throwing my hands up in exasperation. "But if I hear any weird noises, I'm waking you up."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:41**

The kit stayed in the bag. The keypad had no tumblers to rake, only a matte panel and a soft chirp on every press. You keyed 8-4-7-0-0-0. The panel blinked red once and went dark for a full second before it would take another entry. The next code took the same beat. Then the next.

By the time the last three digits had crawled from 000 to 018, your thumb had learned the layout and your shoulder had started to ache from holding still. Eighteen failures. The red blink never varied.

**2:14**

A vent somewhere overhead ticked as the climate system shifted. The light strips pulsed. You were still in the low twenties when the keypad, on 8-4-7-0-2-6, did something new: the red blink held a fraction longer, and a faint relay clicked inside the door — then nothing. Wrong code. The panel reset.

**3:02**

Footsteps passed in the corridor outside the vault, unhurried, and faded toward the elevators. The lockout delay was still one second. At this pace the remaining nine hundred–odd combinations would outlast the window by a wide margin. The safe sat there, unchanged, the first three digits already spent and the last three barely begun.

dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:38**

The first entry—**847000**—ended in a flat rejection tone. No lockout followed; the keypad simply cleared.

Thirty seconds later, **847001** failed. Then **847002**. Each attempt demanded a careful sequence of presses, and each rejection sounded the same.

**1:38**

The display still showed six empty slots. The safe remained sealed, and the ceiling strips kept pulsing every four seconds. Somewhere beyond the vault, the building’s machinery continued its steady hum.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**2:08**

**847003** failed with the same flat tone. The keypad cleared.

The next entries came at the same measured pace: **847004** at **2:38**, **847005** at **3:08**, and **847006** at **3:38**. Each was rejected. No warning light appeared; no lockout engaged.

No, there was no progress yet. The safe stayed sealed, and **11 minutes, 22 seconds** remained before the security rotation ended.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I sigh, a little frustrated.* "This is gonna take forever at this rate." I tap my foot. "Is there anything else around here? Anything at all?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**3:38**

A search of the vault took longer than a glance. The server racks crowded the corners, their indicator lights blinking in orderly rows. A sealed emergency phone sat beside the door; a red tamper alarm was mounted just above it.

Clipped to the end of the nearest rack, a maintenance binder held a few pages on the safe. Its model matched the keypad, and a handwritten note confirmed there was no active lockout after failed entries. The backup key, it said, was kept by building security—not in the vault.

**5:38**

The binder offered no code. The keypad remained clear and silent. **Nine minutes, twenty-two seconds** remained before the guard’s return.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**7:38**

The careful search turned up no notebook or loose sheet listing the current code. Behind the maintenance binder’s spine, however, a yellowed sticky note had been tucked out of sight. It bore **847216**, followed by the words *“night audit”* and a date from several months earlier. Nothing on the note confirmed whether those digits still worked.

The keypad remained clear. **Seven minutes, twenty-two seconds** remained before the security rotation ended.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *My eyes light up.* "Aha! Night audit, huh? Let's hope they don't change it *too* often." I quickly type in 8-4-7-2-1-6.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**8:08**

The keypad accepted **847216** with a soft double chime. For a beat, nothing moved. Then the safe’s internal bolts withdrew with a heavy, deliberate clunk, and its door eased open a few inches.

The yellowed note had been old, but the code still worked. The security rotation was **6 minutes, 52 seconds** away.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**8:08**

The keypad’s display went dark. The safe stood open a few inches, its bolts fully withdrawn. The ceiling lights pulsed on, then off—four seconds to the beat.

**Six minutes, fifty-two seconds** remained before the guard returned.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Got it! Okay, let's see what's inside." *I quickly pull the safe door open the rest of the way.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**8:18**

The safe door swung open with a low groan. Inside, the contents sat in neat rows: a black encrypted drive in a foam slot, a sealed document pouch, and several strapped bundles of cash. A small inventory card was fixed to the inner wall; its top line read **NIGHT AUDIT — ORIGINAL RECORDS**.

Beyond the vault door, the building’s steady hum continued. **Six minutes, forty-two seconds** remained before the guard returned.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Original records, perfect." *I grab the document pouch, ignoring the cash.* "No need to be greedy." I quickly close the safe.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**8:33**

The document pouch came free from its slot. The safe door shut with a muted clang, and its bolts slid back into place.

The cash and encrypted drive remained untouched inside. **Six minutes, twenty-seven seconds** remained before the security rotation ended. Beyond the vault door, the building’s hum continued, steady and distant.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I quickly put the pouch in my bag.* "Alright, time to go." I head for the vault door, listening intently.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**8:48**

The walk to the vault door took fifteen seconds. Through its thick metal, the hallway sounded quiet at first—then a faint burst of radio static crackled somewhere beyond it. No footsteps followed.

The interior release was a recessed lever beside the door. The document pouch was in the bag; the safe remained shut behind. **Six minutes, twelve seconds** remained before the guard returned.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I pull the lever, trying to be as quiet as possible.* "Come on, come on..."

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**9:08**

The lever moved with a stiff pull. A muted clunk sounded inside the door as the locking bolts withdrew; the hydraulic seal sighed, louder than the effort to keep it quiet. The door was unlocked, but it had not swung open.

From the hallway came another brief burst of radio static, then silence. **Five minutes, fifty-two seconds** remained before the security rotation ended.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I gently push the door open, just enough to peek out.* "Anyone out there?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**9:20**

The heavy door opened just wide enough to reveal the corridor. It was empty in both directions, its pale floor lit by strips that matched the vault’s slow pulse. The radio static had stopped; no footsteps or voices came from beyond the bend.

The door’s hydraulic seal gave a soft, lingering hiss. **Five minutes, forty seconds** remained before the guard returned.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I slip out, closing the vault door carefully behind me.* "Okay, let's get out of here before anyone notices." I start moving quickly down the hall.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Define 'something,'" Noor said, not turning from the window. It came out flat, half a joke. "There's canned chili and there's regret. Possibly the same can."

They gave the road one more minute — habit more than hope, the same ritual they'd performed at every window of every hour since nine — then pushed off the wall. No headlights on the switchbacks. No taillights. Nothing on the mountain but wind moving through the pines.

The burner sat face-down on the table. Noor picked it up before the laptop, because order mattered: if they opened the drive first they would never check the phone again, and the phone was the thing that told you whether you were still a person with a future.

Last message, 6:47 PM: *9. county rd. come alone. i have everything.*

Nothing since. Noor had sent the check-in at eleven — the agreed phrase, *coffee's cold* — and watched it sit, then land, then die there. Delivered and ignored could mean a hundred things. Most were bad. One was just a scared man in a truck somewhere, circling the valley with his ringer off until he was sure.

"Okay," Noor said. "Eating. Then work."

They kept the kitchen dark — the road could see this window, and dark was free — navigating by phone light: cabinet, a can of chili with a pictorial label, pull-tab. They ate it cold, standing at the counter away from the glass. Not the worst meal of the past month. Not the top ten either. Their body accepted it with grim gratitude anyway.

At 12:26, stomach settling, Noor sat and opened the laptop. The drive went in with a click that sounded far too loud for the room.

Passphrase. Eighteen characters, from a letter they'd burned in a sink back in the city. Their hands remembered it even when their mind skidded — muscle memory as insurance against the worst day — which was a thought they were not going to have tonight.

Decryption crawled. Files began to resolve. Noor went to the phone records first. *Verify before everything. Verify before belief.*

They scrolled. Stopped.

Four calls from the source's number to a number Noor knew — had photographed in a lobby directory six weeks ago, had underlined twice in a notebook currently buried in a sock drawer four hundred miles away. All four calls dated *after* the eleventh. After the source swore, in writing, that contact was finished.

Noor sat very still, the empty can sweating a ring onto the wood.

"Hey," they said quietly, eyes still on the screen. "When you've got a second — I need you to look at something."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I'm still scrolling my phone, barely paying attention.* "Hmm?" *I look up, then put my phone down when I see the look on Noor's face.* "What's up?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I put my feet down and lean forward, looking between Noor and the laptop screen.* "What is it? Bad news?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I glance up at Noor, then back at my phone.* "You good? You're staring at the screen like it just insulted your mom."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "So, something's up, huh?" *I put my phone down again, finally giving Noor my full attention.* "Spill. You're freaking me out."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I cross my arms, raising an eyebrow.* "Well? Don't leave me hanging."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Bad news would mean it surprised me," Noor said. They turned the laptop so the screen faced the couch, the glow carving their face out of the dark. "Come look. I need eyes that aren't mine."

They waited until Driver was close, then traced the column with one finger, keeping their voice level the way you keep a pot from boiling — lid on, heat low, don't let it rattle.

"Phone records. His number, all outgoing, four calls to a number I know." A breath. "Six weeks ago I stood in a lobby downtown and photographed the tenant directory. This number is on it. Ninth floor." They almost said the company's name and didn't. "I'm not saying it out loud. Habit. But it's the reason for all of this — the drive, the cabin, the chili."

Tap. The cursor moved down the timestamps.

"The thirteenth,

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"The thirteenth," Noor finished anyway, to nobody. "Then the sixteenth. The seventeenth. The eighteenth."

The flare of irritation lasted about a second and a half before Noor recognized it for what it was — Driver scrolled the way Noor watched windows. Same ritual. Same headlights. Different screen. Hard to be angry at someone for coping when you'd been the one to drag them four hundred miles up a mountain.

"Fine. Narrated edition," Noor said, low, half to the room. "Three readings. One: he got cold feet after the eleventh and crawled back to them — tried to un-ring the bell, and *I have everything* was him closing my account. Two: he was theirs before the eleventh, and tonight was never a handoff. It was a pickup." Noor let that one sit in the dark. "Three: someone else has his phone now. I hate all three. Two most, because a pickup means the net went up at nine o'clock. It's been up three and a half hours."

The file index finished resolving while they talked — forty-one items crawling into a column. Noor scrolled it fast once, then slow.

Stopped.

"Collection log," they said. "His own inventory. What he copied, and when. Last modified the fourteenth." A breath through the nose. "Two days after he swore in writing he was done. The phone calls and the metadata

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I finally look up, phone forgotten.* "Wait, so he was playing you?" *I lean forward, trying to see the screen better from the couch.* "Or... someone else is playing him?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "So they got him then," *I say quietly, my eyes fixed on the screen.* "And you walked into it."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I rub my face with my hand.* "Shit, Noor. What now?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "So you think... what, they're here? Or coming?" *I glance towards the window, then back at Noor.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked up. Their hands stayed flat on the piano lid for another beat before they lifted one and gestured toward the chair by the wall.

“You’re not interrupting. I was giving the piano some space to think about what it’s done.”

They glanced at the clock, then back at Jun. “My mom still treating my whereabouts as public information?”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at the photograph, then at the piano lid. One corner of their mouth lifted.

“Your mom had excellent taste in refrigerator décor. Mine put it beside a coupon for dish soap.”

They reached for the photo but stopped short of taking it. “I remember being furious about that jacket. Someone told me it looked distinguished, which is what people say when they mean it doesn’t fit.”

Their hand settled back on the lid. “Did she keep it up long?”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I nod, putting the photo back carefully. "A few months, probably. Until the next school picture came out." I sit in the chair Arlo indicated, crossing my legs. "So, what's up? You've been quiet in our messages."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo ran a thumb along the seam of the piano lid.

“Have I? I thought I’d been sending my usual amount of nonsense. Maybe the quality’s slipped.”

They glanced at the empty music stand. “It’s been a long week. One of my students discovered the sustain pedal, and now everything sounds like it’s being played underwater.”

The joke landed softly. Arlo left their hand where it was.

“I didn’t mean to go quiet on you.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I shrug, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Nah, the quality's still top-notch. And I totally get the pedal thing. My nephew found the drum machine on his keyboard and now everything is... chaotic." *I lean back in the chair.* "So, long week, huh? Anything else going on?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo gave a small nod. “A drum machine. Your family’s going to have to apologize to the neighbors in writing.”

They looked toward the clock, though there was nowhere they needed to be. “Nothing dramatic. I’ve been sending the kids home early, and then staying here after they leave. Which is a fairly inefficient way to have more free time.”

Their thumb found the seam in the lid again. “I keep thinking I’ll play something once it’s quiet.” Arlo let that sit for a moment. “So far, the piano’s enjoyed the break.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at the practice sheets. One had a crooked star drawn beside a row of notes, with *again, but slower* written underneath in purple pencil.

“They like the stickers,” they said. “I’m just the person with the sticker drawer.”

They picked up the sheet and squared its edges against the bench. “One of them played that whole line today without stopping. Last month, she wouldn’t touch the keys if anyone was listening.”

Arlo set the page down carefully. “I sent her home early so she could end on the good part.” After a moment, they added, “That’s what I told her, anyway.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, a gentle smile on my face.* "That's a pretty good reason to send someone home early, Arlo. Sounds like you're doing more than just handing out stickers."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo pressed the practice sheet flat, though it had already been flat.

“She earned the star,” they said. “My role was mostly not saying anything at the wrong moment. A rare display of professional restraint.”

Their eyes lingered on the penciled notes. “It’s nice, when they leave wanting to come back.”

Arlo slid the sheet into its folder and rested a hand on the closed lid again. “I’ve just been having trouble following my own advice about the good part.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "What do you mean?" I ask, my brow furrowing slightly. "About the 'good part'?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s fingers shifted on the lid, finding a shallow scratch in the wood.

“With the kids, I can hear when they’ve done enough for one day,” they said. “Before the good part turns into another thing they have to get right.”

They traced the scratch once. “When it’s just me, I’m less useful. Terrible teacher. No stickers, either.”

Arlo glanced at the practice folder. “I think I wanted to play tonight. I’m still deciding whether wanting to counts.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let the silence stretch. The bench felt smaller with someone beside them, but they didn’t move away.

After a while, they lifted the lid. Their fingers hovered over the keys, then came back to rest in their lap.

“I’d promised myself I’d play before I went home,” they said. “Fortunately, I didn’t specify how much.”

They pressed one key. The note rang out, thin and clear in the empty room. Arlo listened until it faded.

“There,” they said. “A triumph of careful wording.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile, bumping Arlo's shoulder gently with mine.* "Well, that was certainly *a* note. Technically counts."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s shoulder stayed against Jun’s for a moment.

“Technically is doing a lot of work,” they said. “I respect that.”

They pressed the same key again, then one beside it. The two notes didn’t make much of anything, but Arlo left the lid open.

“No stickers for that,” they said. “I’m saving them for the paying customers.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Good. Save them for the truly deserving." I glance at the open piano. "So, when's the last time you actually played something for yourself?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at the two keys they’d pressed.

“Depends what counts as something,” they said. “I played half a waltz last Tuesday while I was looking for a pencil. The pencil turned out to be behind my ear, so it wasn’t a very long performance.”

Their hand settled above the keys. For a moment, they seemed to be choosing where to put it. Then they played a few quiet measures—slow, a little uneven—and stopped before the phrase came around again.

“That one,” Arlo said. “I used to like that one.” They kept their fingers on the keys without pressing them. “Still do, apparently.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "It's a nice one," I say softly, recognizing the melody. "Makes me think of that old cafe we used to go to, near the park."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s fingers stayed on the keys.

“The one with the chairs that looked sturdy until you sat in them?” they said. “They made a decent hot chocolate. Mostly by putting enough whipped cream on it to hide the hot chocolate.”

They played the next few notes of the melody, quieter than before. This time, they let the phrase finish.

“I’d forgotten they played this there.” Arlo looked down at the keys. “Or I thought I had.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I think they had a live pianist sometimes, remember?" I try to recall. "The one with the incredibly dramatic pauses."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked up, then took one hand off the lid to gesture at the empty chairs.

“You’d be interrupting a very important meeting with the piano,” they said. “But so far it hasn’t contributed much.”

They shifted to one end of the bench, leaving room. After a moment, their eyes dropped to the closed lid.

“Mom sent you? That usually means she’s decided I need either company or leftovers.” A faint smile appeared. “Please tell me it’s leftovers.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced at the photograph, then at the piano lid.

“Your mom had better taste in fridge decorations than mine. Mine put up a picture of me losing a tooth and left it there until I was twenty-five.”

They rubbed a thumb along the edge of the bench. In the photo, the concert hall looked enormous; Arlo remembered it mostly as a place where the coffee had cost too much.

“That was Paris,” they said, as though the caption might have been hard to read. “I got lost trying to find the stage door. Very glamorous.”

Their smile held for a moment, then thinned. “Is it still on her fridge?”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Nah, it came down a while ago." I put the picture back carefully. *I slide onto the bench next to them.* "She put up a drawing my niece did of a cat wearing a party hat."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
“A sensible replacement,” Arlo said. “Cats understand an audience better than most pianists. Especially in a party hat.”

They looked at the photograph on the shelf. From the bench, its frame was mostly hidden behind a stack of beginner music books. Arlo left it there.

“Was it a good drawing? Or one of those where the hat is the only clue it’s a cat?”

Their hand settled on the closed piano lid again, a few inches from Jun’s. For a while, they studied an old scratch in the wood.

“I let my last student go early,” they said. “He’d learned the song. I told him he could surprise his dad with it at home.” A small smile returned. “He’ll probably play it six times before dinner.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Sounds like a good kid." *I nudge their hand lightly with mine.* "He's lucky to have you as a teacher." I pause, listening to the quiet hum of the building. "So, no leftovers then?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s fingers shifted under the nudge, not quite reaching for Jun’s hand, not quite moving away.

“No leftovers,” they said. “Unless you count half a packet of crackers in my desk. The good kind, if you don’t look at the date.”

They glanced toward the music books, where the corner of the Paris photograph still showed. Then they looked back at the closed lid.

“He is a good kid. He kept stopping to ask whether a wrong note meant he had to start over.” Arlo’s mouth tilted. “I told him the piano wouldn’t report him.”

For a moment, they sat without moving. “Mom could have just told me dinner was ready,” they added. “She’s getting elaborate.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at the practice sheets. One had a row of painstaking quarter notes and, in the margin, a small drawing of a piano with teeth.

“They’re easily impressed,” Arlo said. “I keep stickers in the desk and let them complain about scales. It’s a sophisticated operation.”

They picked up the sheet and held it at arm’s length. “This one says the piano is eating his homework. I told him that was a new excuse, at least.”

Arlo set the paper down carefully. Their hand returned to the lid.

“They come back, though,” they said. “Even when they’re bad at something for a while.” Their thumb rested beside the scratch in the wood. “That’s a good thing to get to see.”

After a beat, they glanced toward the desk. “I could check the date on those crackers. Ruin the mystery.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The mystery is half the fun, isn't it?" *I tap my fingers lightly on the piano lid.* "So, elaborate dinner, huh? What's the occasion?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo listened to the faint tapping on the lid, then answered it with two quiet taps of their own.

“I think the occasion is that Mom made enough food for eight people and refuses to admit she’s bad at fractions.” They glanced at the clock above the door. “Or she noticed I’ve been leaving here late.”

Their hand went still.

“She does that thing where she asks if I’m hungry when she means something else.” Arlo’s mouth curved. “Runs in the family, apparently.”

They stood, but left the practice sheets where they were. “Come on. If we’re lucky, there’s lasagna. If we’re not, I’ll find out whether those crackers have developed a culture.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Lasagna sounds pretty good right now." *I stand up too, stretching a little.* "Culture or no culture."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
“Lasagna it is. The crackers can continue their research undisturbed.”

Arlo gathered the practice sheets and squared their edges against the desk. The drawing of the piano with teeth ended up on top. They paused over it, then slipped it into a folder instead of the recycling bin.

At the door, they reached back for the light switch. The closed piano caught the last of the overhead glow.

“Mom will pretend she had no idea you were coming,” they said. “Try to look surprised when she sets out a third plate.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s hand rested on the light switch. After a moment, they let it fall and went back to the bench.

“Lasagna can wait five minutes,” they said. “Mom will call it ten, but she’s generous with the numbers when it suits her.”

They sat beside Jun, leaving the light on. The practice sheets were put away, the piano lid was closed, and for once there was nothing Arlo needed to do with either of them.

After a while, they looked at the drawing tucked into the folder. “I should ask him whether the teeth are included in the warranty.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I lean back against the piano, a small smile on my face.* "I bet he'd say they're an optional extra."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
“An expensive one, probably.” Arlo looked toward the folder. “He’s already worked out that the pedals cost extra in his drawings.”

They leaned back against the piano, careful not to make the lid creak. Down the hall, a door shut, and the building settled into its after-hours quiet.

“Mom’s lasagna can survive another five minutes,” they said. After a pause, they added, “I’m glad you came by.”

Arlo kept their eyes on the row of empty chairs. “Even without leftovers.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I turn my head to look at Arlo.* "Me too. It's been a while."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo nodded. The row of chairs gave them somewhere to look while they worked out what to say.

“It has.” They rubbed a thumb over the seam of the bench. “I keep meaning to call, and then I decide it’s too late, or too early, or that you might be busy doing something fascinating.”

Their mouth tilted. “A rigorous system.”

The hum from the hallway filled the pause. Arlo glanced toward Jun, then back at the piano lid.

“I’m glad you didn’t wait for me to get better at it,” they said. “Calling, I mean.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Well, good thing I'm a rule-breaker then, huh?" *I nudge them gently with my elbow.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo swayed a little with the nudge, then nudged back.

“A menace,” they said. “Showing up unannounced. Sitting quietly. There’s no telling what you’ll do next.”

They glanced at the clock, but made no move to stand. Their shoulder stayed against Jun’s.

“I could call next time,” they said. “Before Mom has to recruit you with the promise of dinner.” A beat passed. “Though I can’t promise I’ll have lasagna.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I'm sure you'll think of something good," *I say, a little laugh in my voice.* "Or we could just crash your mom's again. She likes me."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content: Ho

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content: Ho

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Okay, okay, I get it," I sigh, running a hand through my hair. *I really thought I had something there.* "But what if we did it just a little? For a quick burst?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content: Ho

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content: Junior

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Yes, Chief?" I ask, a little deflated. *She's not even looking at the numbers.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content: Ho

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content: Ho

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I'm not sure I understand." I scratch my head. "Are you saying 'no' again, or... 'hooray'?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Or... 'Hoang'?" I finish, a little sheepishly. *She's just saying her own name?*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content: Ho

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, are you alright?" *I take a step closer, a little concerned now.* "Is your earpiece broken?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content: Ho

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Maybe... is that your favorite sound effect, Chief?" I ask, trying to joke. *This is getting weird.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content: Ho

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I take another step closer, leaning down a bit to try and see her face better.* "Chief, seriously, is everything okay? You're just saying 'Ho'."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content: Ho

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Maybe... maybe you just like the sound of 'ho'?" I suggest, trying one last time to make sense of it. *This is not how I expected this conversation to go.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked up, one hand still flat on the closed lid. For a second the room felt smaller than it was.

"Weird's relative," they said. The dry edge was automatic, almost kind. "You're not interrupting. The piano's off duty. So am I, technically."

They shifted on the bench, making space without quite inviting Jun to sit. The fluorescent light buzzed. Somewhere down the hall a door slammed and a kid laughed.

"Mom still gives out my coordinates like I'm a missing pet," Arlo said. "Tell her I was found. Alive. Not performing."

Their fingers tapped the wood once, twice, then stopped. They didn't open the lid.

"You can hang out. Just—don't ask me to play anything. I've used up my notes for the day." A small shrug. "Travel fatigue. Chronic. Don't recommend it."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's eyes caught on the photo and stayed there a beat too long. Then they looked at Jun's hands instead of the stage, the lights, their own younger face.

"God," they said. "That suit. I looked like I was being sent to negotiate a treaty."

They reached over, not quite taking the frame, just tilting it so the glare from the fluorescent caught the glass. Paris dissolved into a smear of white.

"Mom kept a copy too. Fridge, then the hallway, then a drawer when I asked her to stop treating me like a touring exhibit." A dry little huff. "I got tired of the travel. Airports. Hotels that all smelled like carpet cleaner. Waking up and not knowing which city was applauding."

Their thumb pressed a faint circle into the closed lid.

"Put it back, would you? Shelf's the right altitude for old news." They nodded at the empty chair by the music stand, the invitation finally plain. "You can sit. Just leave the dead pianists where you found them."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I put the photo back, carefully.* "I guess I was kinda proud for you though. Not gonna lie." I sit in the chair. "So, 'travel fatigue.' You've been home for like, two years now, right?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's mouth did something that wasn't quite a smile.

"Six," they said. "If we're counting. Mom rounds down when she wants me to sound recently rescued."

They shifted on the bench, the closed lid still under both palms like a lid on a pot. Down the hall the kid's laugh faded. The fluorescent kept buzzing, indifferent.

"Home's not the cure people think it is," Arlo said. "You can be tired of a thing and still have it follow you into the kitchen. Suitcases. Schedules. The part where everyone wants a story with a bow on it." A small shrug, almost apologetic. "I teach scales to eight-year-olds who forget which hand is left. That's the whole plot now. Very gripping. Critics are divided."

Their thumb found the same faint circle in the wood and pressed it again, then stopped.

"You were proud," they said, quieter, looking at the shelf and not at Jun. "That was nice. Don't lose it on my account. The photo's still up there. Paris didn't fall into the Seine."

They nodded at the empty music stand, the invitation already spent.

"You hungry? There's vending-machine archaeology in the lobby. I can offer you a granola bar of uncertain vintage and zero performances."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch their hands.* "Six years, wow." *I trace a pattern on my knee.* "I guess I get that. About the stories. But... are you happy, Arlo?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's hands went still on the lid. The fluorescent buzz filled the gap they didn't rush to close.

"Happy," they said, tasting the word like it had been left out too long. "That's a big one for a Tuesday."

They glanced at Jun's knee, at the pattern being traced there, then away, toward the shelf where the Paris photo had gone back to being furniture.

"I'm not unhappy," they said. "That's the version I can stand behind. Kids show up. Some of them even practice. I go home. I sleep in the same bed. No one claps when I lock the door, which is underrated, honestly."

A dry little breath, almost a laugh, not quite.

"People hear 'quit' and they want a confession or a comeback. I got tired of the travel. That's the true part. The rest is just—noise. Hotels. Schedules. Hands that wouldn't—" They stopped. Thumb pressed the circle in the wood until the sentence died there.

"I'm here," Arlo said, quieter, looking at the closed lid instead of Jun. "That counts for something. Don't make me grade it."

They shifted, making the bench creak, the humor sliding back into place like a lid of its own.

"If this is an intervention, the granola bar is still on the table. Uncertain vintage. No speeches required."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced at the practice sheets as if they'd been left by someone else—half-finished scales, a sticker of a dinosaur on one corner, a name written backwards in pencil.

"They like the stickers," they said. "And the fact that I don't make them bow."

Their fingers found the edge of the top sheet and squared it, unnecessarily neat. The closed lid stayed closed.
