"Liking me is a low bar. I let them stop when their hands get tired. Revolutionary pedagogy." A small, dry tilt of the mouth. "Critics remain divided. The eight-year-olds have not filed a review."

They didn't look at Jun for long. The fluorescent buzz filled what they didn't add.

"It's enough," Arlo said, quieter, almost to the paper. "For a Tuesday. Don't upgrade it."

They nudged the stack an inch toward the music stand, away from the center of the bench, as if clearing a place that didn't need clearing.

"You can tell my mom the pet was found and is tolerating visitors. That's the press release. No encores."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "No encores? That's your definitive statement?" *I lean forward, elbows on my knees.* "Seriously though, I'm glad you're here. In this room. Even if you're just tidying practice sheets."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's mouth twitched, the almost-smile that never quite committed.

"Definitive's a strong word for someone who just squared a dinosaur sticker," they said. "I'm tidying. That's the statement. Very avant-garde. The silence is part of the piece."

They looked at Jun's elbows on their knees, the lean of someone settling in, and felt the room get smaller again. Not unkindly. Just smaller.

"Glad I'm here," Arlo repeated, quieter, like they were checking the fit of it. Their palm stayed flat on the closed lid. "That's—fine. You can be glad. I won't file a complaint."

Down the hall a cart rattled and stopped. The fluorescent kept its one-note buzz.

"This room's easier than the other ones," they said, and then seemed to regret the shape of the sentence. A dry little shrug tried to sand it down. "Shorter commute. No jet lag. The eight-year-olds don't expect Paris. They expect stickers and the right to quit when their fingers hurt. I respect a clean exit."

Their thumb found the faint circle in the wood and pressed it once, then lifted, as if the lid might answer if they leaned any harder.

"Don't make it a moment," Arlo said, looking at the practice sheets instead of Jun. "I'm here. The piano's off. You're allowed to sit. That's the whole program. No speeches. No encores. If you clap, I will personally escort you to the vending machine and abandon you there."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I laugh softly.* "No clapping, got it." *I lean back in the chair, stretching my legs out a bit.* "So, you gonna tell me what you *are* up to this weekend? Besides rescuing me from the vending machine, obviously."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo huffed, the sound closer to a laugh than the last few had been.

"Bold of you to assume I have a weekend and not just a longer Tuesday," they said. Their hands stayed on the closed lid, but the press of the thumb eased. "Rescuing you from the vending machine is already on the calendar. After that, thrilling things. Laundry. A book I will not finish. Possibly staring at a pan until the eggs forgive me."

They glanced at the practice sheets, then at the shelf, and didn't linger on either.

"Saturday there's a recital for the little ones. Not mine. I sit in the back and clap at the wrong times so no one feels singled out." A dry tilt of the mouth. "Very exclusive. Standing room only if you count the folding chairs that stick."

The fluorescent buzzed. Somewhere a cart wheel squeaked and went quiet.

"You can come, if you want," Arlo said, almost offhand, looking at the music stand instead of Jun. "No speeches. No old photos. If anyone asks, you got tired of the travel and wandered in." They shrugged, small. "Bring nothing. Especially not pride. The dinosaur-sticker crowd cannot handle the pressure."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't move over. There wasn't much bench left, and they didn't make a production of sharing it. Their shoulder stayed a careful inch from Jun's. The closed lid was warm under one palm, cooler where the other had been resting too long.

For a while the only sound was the fluorescent and the small shift of fabric when someone breathed deeper than they meant to. Down the hall a door clicked and didn't open again.

Arlo's thumb found the faint circle in the wood and didn't press it. Their eyes stayed on the practice sheets, the dinosaur sticker, the name written backwards. Something in their jaw worked once, then let go.

"Alright," they said, barely above the buzz. Not a question. Not an invitation to fill the quiet. Just the word, set down between them like a thing that didn't need handling.

They didn't open the lid. They didn't look at the shelf. After another stretch of nothing, their shoulder eased a fraction closer, not quite touching, and stayed there.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I shift slightly, not quite touching them either.* "Yeah. Alright." *I watch the dinosaur sticker too.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo stayed where they were, shoulder a careful inch from Jun’s, eyes on the backwards name and the dinosaur sticker as if either might require translating. The fluorescent held its one note. Somewhere in the building a pipe knocked once and thought better of it.

Their thumb rested in the faint circle on the lid and did not press. The quiet stretched, not empty so much as occupied, and Arlo let it. A breath moved through them and came out thinner than they meant.

“Yeah,” they said again, smaller, almost to the wood. Not agreement with anything in particular. Just the word, left where the other one had been.

They didn’t reach for the sheets. They didn’t open the lid. After a moment their hand slid an inch toward the center of the bench and stopped short of the space between them, palm flat, the way you set something down when you’re not sure it wants to be held. The corner of their mouth tried for dry and didn’t quite get there.

“Don’t upgrade it,” they said, barely louder than the buzz. Then nothing else. The piano stayed closed. Paris stayed on the shelf. Arlo stayed.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly.* "Wouldn't dream of it." *I keep watching the sticker.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let the quiet sit. Their hand stayed an inch short of the space between them, palm flat on the closed lid, the faint circle under their thumb going unpressed. The dinosaur sticker stared back, lopsided, one eye half rubbed off by some earlier thumb.

A breath caught and smoothed itself out before it could become anything else. Down the hall the cart wheel gave one last squeak and quit.

"Good," they said, almost to the sticker. The dry edge was there, worn thin. "Dreams are how people end up with encores."

They didn't look at Jun. Their shoulder held its careful inch. After a moment the corner of their mouth tried again for the old shrug of a joke and only managed half of it.

"Saturday's still there if you want it," Arlo said, quieter. "Folding chairs. Wrong claps. No speeches." Their fingers tapped the wood once, light, and stopped. "That's the offer. Don't dress it up."

The piano stayed shut. They stayed.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I just nod again, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Sounds good to me. No speeches."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s mouth did the almost-smile and let it stay, small as it was.

“Good,” they said. “I’ll save you a chair that sticks. You’ll know it’s yours when it complains.”

Their hand remained an inch short of the space between them, palm flat, the faint circle under their thumb still unpressed. The dinosaur sticker kept its half-rubbed eye. Down the hall the building settled into its evening sounds—one pipe, one distant door, then nothing worth naming.

“Mom doesn’t need a report,” Arlo added, quieter, almost to the lid. “Found. Alive. Tolerating company. If she asks what we talked about, tell her practice sheets and uncertain granola. She’ll survive the disappointment.”

A breath moved through them and came out even. Their shoulder held its careful inch. They didn’t open the lid. They didn’t look at the shelf.

“Saturday, then,” they said, and left it there, the way you leave a note where someone can find it without having to answer. The fluorescent kept buzzing. Arlo stayed.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod again, a little more definitely this time.* "Saturday. See you then, Arlo." *I finally look away from the sticker and at them, a soft smile.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked up, then glanced at the closed piano lid as if it might offer an opinion.

“Depends. Are you planning to interrupt the very demanding business of sitting here?” they asked. “Because I’m not sure I can spare the time.”

They shifted along the bench, leaving room beside them. “You’re not interrupting. Come in.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s eyes settled on the photograph. For a moment, their hands stayed very still on the piano lid.

“Your mom had a surprisingly generous definition of fridge-worthy,” they said. “That frame was mostly hair and expensive lighting.”

They leaned back, giving the picture a quick, practiced smile that didn’t quite reach their eyes. “Paris was nice. Terrible coffee, excellent halls. The sort of place where everyone looked like they knew what they were doing.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I put the photo back, running a finger over the dusty frame. "I thought you knew what you were doing back then." I turn to them, a little worried. "You seemed to."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s mouth tilted, though the smile didn’t settle.

“Stage lighting is very persuasive,” they said. “It can make a person look competent, rested, and about six inches taller.”

Their fingers traced the seam in the piano lid. “I knew the pieces. Most days, that was close enough.” They glanced back at Jun. “Besides, you were looking at the photo on your mom’s fridge. Not exactly a rigorous review.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I shrug, leaning against the doorframe again. "Yeah, I guess not. Still, you looked happy." I pause. "Are you happy now?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked down at their hands on the lid. Their thumbs rubbed once along the edge, then stopped.

“Sometimes,” they said. “It’s less photogenic now. More children with jam on the keys, fewer people insisting the coffee is a cultural experience.”

They glanced toward the piano room’s scuffed music stand. “I like teaching. I like when a kid finally gets through a tricky bar and looks surprised it was them doing it.” A pause. “It’s a decent way to spend a life, I think.”

Their mouth tipped into a small, dry smile. “And the commute to Paris is much worse from here.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced at the practice sheets, one of which had a small, enthusiastic drawing of a dinosaur in the margin.

“They’re fond of me because I let them put dinosaurs on the scales,” they said. “And because I haven’t yet explained that the metronome is right.”

They tapped the edge of the top sheet into alignment, then left it slightly crooked again. “They make it hard to be gloomy on schedule.” A faint smile appeared. “It’s a useful skill.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "They certainly do." I walk over and pick up a sheet. "This one's pretty good though, right?" I point at a bar of music.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo leaned over to inspect the bar, their shoulder nearly brushing Jun’s.

“Pretty good,” they said. “The rhythm’s holding together, and nobody’s been bullied by the left hand. That’s a strong start.”

They traced the measure in the air without touching the page. “There’s a little wobble here, but it’s the useful kind. Means they’re trying something harder than last week.” Their gaze lingered on the notes a moment longer than it needed to.

“Tell them I said that,” Arlo added. “They’ll enjoy hearing I’ve been overruled by a sheet of paper.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I chuckle*. "I'll make sure to pass it on." I put the sheet back down. "So, what's good for dinner around here these days? I'm starving."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced toward the clock, as if dinner had been waiting for their permission.

“Depends on your standards. There’s a decent noodle place two blocks over, and a sandwich shop that has never once asked me how my day was.” They stood, then nudged the practice sheets into a tidier stack. “I can recommend both with the confidence of someone who’s eaten dinner at four-thirty between lessons.”

A small smile tugged at their mouth. “Want company, or were you asking for a list and a clean escape?”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo sat back down, leaving the space between them unmeasured. The piano lid stayed closed beneath their hands.

For a while, they let the room make its small noises: the radiator ticking, a car passing outside, the clock insisting the evening was moving along.

“The noodle place will still be open,” they said at last. “It’s very patient. Unlike most restaurants, it hasn’t developed expectations of me.”

Their thumb traced the piano’s wooden edge once, then went still. Arlo didn’t reach for the photograph or the keys. They just stayed there beside Jun, letting the quiet take up as much room as it needed.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly.* "Sounds good. Noodle place it is." I turn my head to look at them. "You okay?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at Jun for a moment, then down at the piano lid.

“Yeah,” they said. “Just a little tired.”

They rubbed a thumb along the wood’s edge, then let their hand rest there. “I’m okay enough to make a decision about noodles, which is usually the important test.” A faint smile surfaced. “And I’m glad you’re here.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile slightly.* "Good. I'm glad you're glad." I nudge them playfully with my elbow. "Come on, let's get those noodles before they close."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let the nudge tip them a fraction toward the piano.

“An excellent point. I’d hate to be responsible for the noodles developing expectations.”

They stood and reached for their coat, then paused to switch off the room’s lamp. In the dimmer light, the photograph on the shelf was only a pale rectangle.

“Come on,” they said, holding the door open. “If we’re lucky, we can get there before the dinner crowd discovers broth.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I follow Arlo out, pulling the door shut behind me.* "Some things never change, huh? You always were worried about the dinner rush."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced over, their coat collar half turned up.

“Dinner rush is reliable,” they said. “It arrives at the same time, makes the same amount of noise, and rarely expects me to perform.”

They pushed open the center’s front door. Cold air slipped in around them.

“Some standards had survived the years,” they added. “Along with my devotion to avoiding a queue.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, pulling my own jacket tighter.* "True. Some things are just universally annoying." I step out after them into the cool evening air. "So, how was your week, really? Anything exciting happen?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't startle. They'd heard footsteps in the hallway a full minute before the knock and had spent that minute deciding whether to lift their hands off the lid. They hadn't.

"Interrupt what," they said. "I'm doing a very advanced exercise. It's called sitting." Now they took their hands back, slowly, and folded them in their lap. "Four hundred dollars a lesson in some cities."

They looked at Jun properly then, the way you look at someone you've known since you were both missing front teeth and haven't seen in a while. Something in their face eased, and something else tightened.

"My mom told you where I was." It wasn't quite a question. "Of course she did. She thinks I need to be *checked on.*" The last two words carried air quotes without any hands to make them. "She's been reading articles."

They shifted on the bench and scooted a few inches toward the treble end. It left room, though they didn't say so, and they didn't look at the gap they'd made.

"Come in. Mind the chair by the door, one leg's shorter than the others. Deshawn, he's nine, sat on it and went down like a building. Very dramatic. He wanted to know if it counted as an injury so he could skip scales." A small huff that was almost a laugh. "I told him no. Then I let him skip scales anyway."

The radiator ticked. Down the hall someone was stacking folding chairs, a hollow metallic clatter that came in fits.

"You want coffee? There's a machine in the break room that makes something brown and hot. I wouldn't commit further than that."

Their eyes went briefly to the closed lid and then away, toward the window, where the parking lot lights were buzzing on one by one.

"It's quiet this time of day," Arlo said, to no one in particular. "I like it better when it's quiet."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at the photo the way you'd look at a dog you weren't sure was friendly.

"Your mom and my mom," they said. "Running a two-woman publicity campaign out of their kitchens. Very grassroots." They tipped their head. "Did it have a magnet shaped like a strawberry? I feel like it had a strawberry."

They didn't reach for the frame.

"Margaret put that up. The director. She found it online and printed it at the Walgreens on Fifth, and then she bought the frame, and then she stood right there and watched me see it." A pause. "She was so pleased with herself. You can't take something down after someone looks at you like that. It'd be like kicking a duckling."

The folding chairs clattered again down the hall. Arlo waited for the noise to finish before speaking, as if it were a rest in a score.

"Salle Gaveau. That's the one with the ceiling." They lifted one hand and made a vague sweeping shape toward the stained acoustic tiles above them, then seemed to think better of it and put the hand back in their lap. "Gold everywhere. It's like playing inside a jewelry box. The piano was a Steinway D, and it pulled a little to the left in the upper register. Nobody would ever hear it. I heard it the whole time."

Their thumb found the cuticle of their index finger and pressed at it. Once. Twice.

"The kids think that's not me, you know. Deshawn asked who it was. I said my cousin." The almost-laugh again, drier this time. "He said, 'Your cousin's got good posture.' Which is true. I don't sit like that anymore. My back is thirty-two now. It files complaints."

Out the window, the last of the parking lot lights stuttered and caught.

"Twenty-two," Arlo said, quieter. They were looking at the photo now, but not at the figure in it. At the edge of the frame, maybe, where the stage lights bled out into black. "I thought that suit was *so* expensive. I'd bought it for the tour. I was going to wear it in Vienna, and Prague, and..."

They stopped. Not abruptly. It was more like a phrase that had simply been written shorter than you expected.

"Anyway. It doesn't fit anymore." They stood, smoothing the front of their sweater, and nodded toward the door. "Break room. The brown hot thing. I'm getting one whether you are or not, so you might as well be complicit."

They were already halfway across the room when they added, without turning around, "You can put it back where it was. Margaret gets upset if it's crooked."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I put the photo back on the shelf, making sure it's straight.* "Yeah, I remember the strawberry magnet. My mom still has it on her fridge actually." *I follow Arlo out the door.* "So, the 'brown hot thing' it is then. Sounds... adventurous."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo stopped walking for half a step. Just a hitch in the rhythm, the kind of thing you'd only catch if you'd spent a childhood walking to school beside them.

"Still," they said. "On the fridge."

Then they were moving again, down the hallway past the corkboard of flyers: Zumba Tuesdays, a lost cat named Pretzel, a sign-up sheet for the spring recital with eleven small names written in eleven levels of pencil pressure. Arlo's eyes skated over the recital sheet and kept going.

"Adventurous is generous. The machine was donated in 2009 by a dentist who I'm fairly sure was trying to drum up business." They pushed open the break room door with their shoulder. "It's got two settings. 'Coffee' and 'Coffee,' but one of them is hotter. Nobody knows which. It changes."

The break room was fluorescent and tired. A round table, four mismatched chairs, a fridge with a laminated sign that said PLEASE LABEL YOUR FOOD, SANDRA. Someone had drawn a small frowning face beside SANDRA in ballpoint.

Arlo fed a dollar into the machine. It took three tries. The machine rejected the bill with a soft, disdainful whir each time, and each time Arlo smoothed it flat against the edge of the counter, pressing hard with the heel of their hand, and tried again.

"She should take it down," they said on the third attempt, not looking up. "Your mom. It's been ten years. It's probably faded. The magnet's probably holding up a picture of nobody."

The dollar went in. The machine began to grind, loud and shuddering, like something being asked to do more than it was built for. Arlo stood very still in front of it with their arms crossed and waited it out.

When it finished, they took the paper cup out carefully, with both hands. A little sloshed anyway and ran down over their knuckles. They didn't react to the heat. They just looked at the spill for a second, then set the cup down on the table and reached for a napkin.

"Or not," they said. "It's her fridge." They wiped their hand, slowly and thoroughly, finger by finger, longer than a few drops of coffee needed. "Tell her I said hi. Tell her I'm still sitting up straight. She'll like that. It's a lie, but she'll like it."

They fed in a second dollar without asking. It went in on the first try, and Arlo made a small offended noise at the machine, as if it had done this on purpose.

"This one's yours. Complicity has a price." They pulled out a chair, the one with the wobbly back, and took it themselves, leaving the steadier one for Jun. "Sit. The good chair. I'm the host. Hosts suffer."

The grinding started up again. Arlo wrapped both hands around their cup and didn't drink from it. They were watching the steam instead.

"Deshawn's playing in the recital," they said, over the noise. "The spring one. He picked 'Heart and Soul.' He's going to play it very, very fast because he thinks that makes it harder." A beat. "He's not nervous at all. He asked me if there'd be snacks after. That's his whole concern. Snacks."

The machine finished. In the sudden quiet, Arlo's voice came out softer than they seemed to intend.

"I hope he stays like that."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I take the cup Arlo offers and sit in the good chair.* "I'm sure he will," *I say, taking a sip of the 'brown hot thing'. It's exactly as advertised. I make a face, then manage a small smile.* "And yeah, my mom will like that. The posture thing." I look at the coffee machine. "Still, she wouldn't keep a faded picture of 'nobody' up there. She's not like that."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo watched Jun's face do the thing it did around that first sip, and something at the corner of their mouth gave way.

"There it is," they said. "That's the face. Everyone makes it. Sandra made it on her first day and then she drank the whole cup out of spite, and now she's the only one who likes it. I think it rewired her."

They turned their own cup a quarter turn on the table. Then another quarter. The steam leaned and straightened.

"No," Arlo said eventually. "She's not like that."

The fluorescent tube over the sink flickered, recovered, and hummed a little louder, as if to make up for it.

"She used to make me play at Thanksgiving. Remember? Your whole family, crammed into that living room with the plastic on the couch. And she'd clap between movements. Every single time. I'd get to the end of the first one and lift my hands, and she'd just go." Arlo made a small, soft clapping motion, palms not quite meeting. "And your uncle would shush her, and she'd shush him back louder."

They let their hands settle around the cup again.

"I used to be so embarrassed. I'd sit there with my hands in the air waiting for everyone to stop." A pause, and their thumb found the rim of the cup and ran along it. "You're not supposed to clap there. Everyone in a real hall knows you're not supposed to clap there. They sit so still you can hear them deciding not to cough."

The radiator in the corner knocked twice, like someone at a door.

"She was the only one who ever clapped in the wrong place," Arlo said. They said it lightly, the way you'd mention the weather somewhere you used to live.

Then they took a sip of the coffee at last, winced, and set it down with great dignity.

"Margaret wants me to open the recital," they said, to the cup. "Play something short before the kids go. 'Warm up the room,' she said. Like I'm a space heater." The dry almost-laugh. "I told her I'd think about it. That was three weeks ago. She's started leaving sticky notes on the piano. Little ones. Just a question mark."

They didn't say what they'd done with the sticky notes. They reached for the napkin they'd used earlier, folded it in half, then in half again, into a small hard square.

"Anyway." Arlo pushed the napkin aside and looked up, and the look was bright and deliberate, a door being held open onto a different room. "You didn't drive all the way over here to drink dentist coffee and hear about Deshawn's snack agenda. How's the job? Are you still the one who has to fix the printer? You were always the one who had to fix the printer."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo followed the gesture to the bench under the window, where their canvas tote had slumped over at some point and spilled half its contents. A spiral notebook. A pencil case shaped like a cat. A loose fan of photocopied practice sheets, soft at the corners from being handled by small, determined fingers.

They noticed the printer question hadn't been answered. They let it go.

"They like that I have stickers," Arlo said. "It's a very transactional relationship. I'm basically a vending machine with opinions about wrist height."

But they got up anyway, crossed to the bench, and started gathering the sheets back into a stack. They didn't hurry. They squared the edges against their palm, and as they did, the top page caught the light: a C major scale in faded toner, and across the top margin, in enormous purple marker, someone had written ARLO IS NICE BUT STRICT, then crossed out STRICT, then written it again smaller underneath.

Arlo looked at it for a moment.

"Priya," they said. "She's seven. She's working through some complicated feelings about me."

They flipped to the next sheet. A dinosaur was drawn in the bass clef, eating a quarter note.

"The rule is you don't stop," Arlo said. They were still looking down at the dinosaur. "That's the one thing I'm actually strict about. You miss a note, you keep going. Wrong note, wrong rhythm, you forget the whole left hand, doesn't matter. You keep your hands on the keys and you get to the end." They tapped the edge of the stack once against the bench, neatening it. "They think it's a game. Whoever stops first has to put the chairs away."

The folding chair clatter had stopped down the hall. The building was settling into its evening quiet, the kind that seemed to have weight.

"Deshawn's never had to put the chairs away," Arlo added. "Not once. He'll play 'Heart and Soul' through a fire alarm. I've seen him do it. We had a drill in October." A pause. "Kept going the whole time. Didn't even look up."

They slid the sheets into the tote, then the notebook, then the cat-shaped pencil case. They picked up something small and yellow from the bench cushion that had fallen out with the rest, a sticky note with a single question mark in blue ink. They looked at it for a second, folded it once along the adhesive so it stuck to itself, and put it in their pocket instead of the bag.

"They do like me," they said finally, and it came out plainer than anything else they'd said all evening. No joke on the end of it. They seemed to hear that, because they added, "God help them," and the joke arrived a beat late, like a student coming in after the downbeat.

Arlo sat back down in the wobbly chair and reclaimed their coffee, which had gone from hot to merely warm.

"You never told me about the printer," they said. "Don't think I didn't notice. You always did that. Answered a different question. You and me both, I guess."

They took a sip and didn't wince this time.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile, watching them.* "Yeah, well, some questions are better left unanswered." *I take another (careful) sip of my coffee.* "And okay, fine. The printer still hates me. But I'm good at convincing it otherwise."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
For a second Arlo didn't move at all. The cup stayed where it was, halfway between the table and their mouth, and their eyes stayed on Jun a beat longer than a person's eyes usually stay anywhere.

Then the cup finished its trip down to the table.

"That's very wise," they said. "You should have that embroidered on something. A pillow. A small flag." Their thumb went back to the rim of the cup and stopped there. "Better left unanswered. I'd buy that mug. I'd drink the brown hot thing out of it every day."

The fridge shuddered on, hummed, and settled.

"Convincing it otherwise." Arlo tipped their head, considering. "You did that with my mom's car. The Corolla. Sophomore year, in the Kroger parking lot, it wouldn't start, and you just put your hand flat on the hood and talked to it. Very calm. Like it was a horse." A small shake of the head. "It started. I still don't know if that was you or the battery. I've decided not to find out."

They drank the rest of the coffee in one long, grim swallow, the way you'd take medicine, and set the empty cup down with a small, final tap.

"I have to lock up." They stood, and the wobbly chair rocked back onto its short leg with a clack. "The piano room. Margaret likes the lid closed and the bench pushed in, and the door locked, and the key under the fern. There's a whole ritual. You can come or not."

They didn't wait to find out which. The hallway was darker now. Someone had killed the overhead lights, leaving only the red EXIT sign and the glow from the piano room at the far end. Arlo walked past the corkboard again. Their eyes didn't skate over the recital sheet this time. They slowed, just slightly, and read the eleven names from top to bottom, and kept walking.

In the piano room, the parking lot lights had turned the window orange. The photo on the shelf sat perfectly straight. Arlo glanced at it, and then away, and then went to the piano and stood behind the bench with both hands resting on the closed lid, the same way they'd been sitting when the knock came.

For a while, that was all.

Then they lifted it.

It went up with a soft wooden sigh, and the keys lay there in the orange light, yellowed a little at the edges, one of the Fs chipped where some long-gone kid had dropped something on it. Arlo didn't sit. They didn't touch the keys. They reached into their pocket, took out the folded sticky note, and worked it open along the crease with their thumbnail. The adhesive had mostly given up. The question mark was a little smudged.

They pressed it onto the music stand anyway, flat, holding it there a second longer than it needed so it would stay.

"Margaret's going to think that's a yes," they said, still looking at it.

They didn't say whether it was. They pushed the bench in with their knee, neat and square, and left the lid up.

"She gets upset if it's crooked," Arlo added, which didn't make any sense, and they seemed to know it didn't, and they didn't fix it. They just stood there a moment longer in the orange light with their hands in their sweater pockets, then turned toward the door and the fern and the key.

"Tell your mom," they said, and stopped, and started over. "Tell her hi."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod, following Arlo into the piano room.* "I will." *I watch them put the sticky note on the stand, a small smile playing on my lips.* "So, you're playing then."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's hand was already on the light switch. It stayed there.

"I'm putting a sticky note on a music stand," they said. "Historians will argue about what it meant."

They didn't flip the switch. The room hummed around them, orange from the window and white from the one overhead tube, and the open lid threw a long shadow across the floor toward the door. Arlo looked at the shadow instead of at Jun.

"It's short. If I did it. Something short." Their thumb found the edge of the switch plate and pressed along it, the way it had pressed along the rim of the cup. "Margaret said five minutes. I told her nobody needs five minutes of me. She said the kids do. I said the kids need snacks. We're at an impasse."

A car door slammed somewhere in the parking lot. Arlo waited for it to finish, a rest in a score.

"It's a Saturday," they said. "The recital. The nineteenth. Two o'clock, which is a terrible time for anything, but it's when the room's free." A pause, and then, very casually, the way you'd mention the weather somewhere you used to live: "Your mom's not doing anything on the nineteenth, is she."

It wasn't quite a question. They didn't wait for it to be answered.

"She'd have to sit in the folding chairs. They're awful. Deshawn's family takes up the whole second row, and his grandmother brings a bell. An actual bell. Margaret's asked her twice not to." Something at the corner of their mouth gave. "She rings it anyway. Between pieces. Sometimes during."

They flipped the switch. The overhead tube died with a small tick, and there was only the orange now, the keys pale in it, the smudged question mark a dark little speck on the stand.

"Nobody tells her it's the wrong place," Arlo said into the dark. "I think that's the best part."

They stepped out into the hallway and crouched by the fern, fishing the key out from under the pot with two fingers. The lock was stiff. It always was. They jiggled it, lifted the door a quarter inch on its hinges, turned it again, and it gave.

They stood with the key in their fist a moment, facing the closed door. Behind it, the lid was still up.

"Tell her it's at two," they said. Then, after a beat, lighter: "Tell her to bring the magnet. For morale."

They put the key back under the fern, straightened the pot so it sat square, and started down the dark hall toward the EXIT sign, not fast, leaving room beside them the way they'd left it on the bench.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The bench was the one by the front doors, under the corkboard's overflow of flyers: a long varnished slab donated by the Rotary Club, with a brass plaque nobody read. Arlo had meant to walk past it. They'd gotten as far as the push bar on the door, cold under their palm, and then they'd let go of it and sat down instead, as if their legs had made the decision without consulting anyone.

They didn't look over when the bench took the second weight. They just shifted, an inch, the way they had at the piano.

Outside, through the wired glass, the parking lot sat in its orange light. Two cars. Arlo's, and the one beside it. A plastic bag moved across the asphalt in small hesitant bursts, stopping, starting, stopping.

Arlo put their hands flat on their knees.

For a while they stayed like that, the way they'd sat on the lid when the knock came. Then, without seeming to notice, the fingers of the right hand began to move. Not much. A slight pressing against the denim, one finger and then the next, a pattern that went up and came back down and went up again. Nothing anyone would call playing. The left hand stayed still.

The right hand faltered somewhere in the middle of the pattern. The fourth finger lifted and hung there.

Arlo breathed out through their nose, short.

The finger came down. The pattern went on, a little uneven, and reached the end of wherever it was going, and stopped there on its own terms, and the hand lay flat again.

Down the hall, the building's heat clicked off. The radiators ticked as they cooled, irregular, like a room full of people deciding not to cough.

"Priya would've made me put the chairs away," Arlo said, very quietly, to the glass. "For that."

They didn't explain it. They didn't take it back, either. They left their hands where they were and watched the plastic bag finally catch against the curb and stay.

After a while, their shoulder settled an inch to the side. Not leaning, exactly. Just not holding itself apart anymore.

They didn't get up for a long time.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I lean my head back against the wall.* "Priya's not here though." *I nudge Arlo gently with my elbow.* "And your mom would probably just ring her bell at the bag anyway."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The nudge landed and Arlo let it move them, a small give at the shoulder, and then came back to exactly where they'd been.

"That's Deshawn's grandmother," they said. "The bell. My mom doesn't have a bell. Your mom doesn't have a bell. You've just invented a whole new woman with a bell."

A pause.

"She'd be great, though. The bag woman. She'd ring at everything." Their mouth did the thing again, at the corner. This time it didn't stop there. It went all the way to a laugh, a real one, short and surprised, like a note that came out louder than they'd meant to play it. They put a hand over their eyes for a second. "God. At the *bag*."

The laugh ran out. The hand came down. Outside, the plastic bag stayed caught against the curb, fluttering at one corner.

"Priya's not here," Arlo repeated, quieter, turning the words over the way they'd turned the cup. They didn't say anything after it. Their right hand, still flat on their knee, lifted its fourth finger a fraction and set it down again. Just the once. Deliberately, this time, like checking a key that had stuck.

The building ticked around them. Somewhere a pipe knocked and went still.

"Wrong mom, wrong grandmother," Arlo said eventually. "You got the whole thing wrong." They let their head tip back against the wall too, beside Jun's, not touching. "You kept going, though."

They looked up at the ceiling tiles, water-stained in a shape like a map of somewhere.

"That counts," they said. "That's the rule."

They sat a while longer. Then they fished their car keys out of their sweater pocket and held them loosely in their lap without standing, the way you'd hold something to prove you could leave any time you wanted.

They didn't, yet.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I turn my head to look at Arlo, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Yeah, well, I'm good at keeping going. You know that."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't turn their head. They didn't have to. They could feel the smile the way you feel someone's weight settle on the other end of a bench.

"Seventh grade," they said. "The mile. Mr. Okafor with the stopwatch and the whistle he never took out of his mouth." A pause, their eyes still on the ceiling map. "Everyone else was done. They were all sitting on the bleachers eating orange slices. And you were still out there, on the far turn, doing your last lap like it was the first one."

The keys shifted in their lap and chimed faintly against each other.

"Somebody laughed. I don't remember who. I remember you didn't look over." Their thumb found the edge of the car key and ran along it. "I remember thinking that was the bravest thing I'd ever seen. Which says a lot about what I'd seen, at twelve. But still."

They didn't say anything else about it. Outside, the bag came loose from the curb at last and went skittering off under Arlo's car, out of sight.

"I know," Arlo said. Just that. It sat in the air between them, plain, with nothing hung on the end of it. This time they didn't reach for a joke to follow it. They let it be the last note and didn't lift their hands.

The radiators had nearly stopped ticking. The building had gone fully quiet, the heavy kind.

Then Arlo stood. The bench creaked, relieved, and they stretched their back with a small wince, one hand pressed to the base of their spine.

"Thirty-two," they told it. "Filing complaints." They went to the door and put their hip against the push bar, and the cold came in around the edges, smelling of wet asphalt and somebody's dinner a few blocks over. They held it there, open.

"Third row," they said. "On the left, on the aisle. If you're coming. Which you don't have to." They were looking out at the lot, not at Jun. "You can see the keyboard from there. Everyone always wants to see the hands. It's the only seat in that room where you can see the hands."

They didn't say who else could be seen from that seat. They didn't say which way the bench faced.

"And warn your mom about the bell." The keys turned over once in their fingers. "The real bell. The one that exists."

The door stayed open. Arlo stayed holding it, one foot already on the step, orange light on half their face, waiting without seeming to wait.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I stand up, stretching too, and walk towards the door.* "I'll be there. And I'll warn her. We can take bets on how many times the bell rings." *I step out into the cold air.* "Lead the way, old man."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The cold hit Arlo square in the chest and they let the door swing shut behind them. It latched with a heavy, institutional clunk, and the building behind them went from a place with people in it to a dark shape with a red EXIT sign.

"Old man," they repeated. They came down the two steps carefully, hand on the rail. "You're four months older than me. March. Your party had the clown who cried."

"Nobody forgets the clown who cried," they added, to the parking lot in general.

Their breath came out white. They tucked their chin into the collar of their sweater and started across the asphalt, keys already sorted in their fist with the car key out front, the way their mother had taught them to walk to a car at night. Halfway there they slowed down, and not for the cold.

From the lot you could see the piano room window. It sat low and square at the end of the building, still lit orange from outside, and through the glass the lid stood propped at its angle like a sail. You couldn't see the sticky note from here. Arlo looked at the window anyway, the way you'd check a stove you knew you'd turned off.

"Six," they said, still looking at it. "The bell. I'll say six. Two during Deshawn, because she can't help herself." They considered. "Three if he plays it fast, which he will, which means it's three. Seven, then. I'm revising. Seven."

They reached their car, an old blue Civic with a dent in the rear door and a parking pass for the community center hanging crooked from the mirror, and stood beside it without unlocking it.

"Loser puts the chairs away," Arlo said. "After. All of them. There are sixty." A beat. "I counted once. I had a lot of time that afternoon."

They didn't say which afternoon. They pressed the button on the fob and the car chirped, and the headlights flashed once and lit up the bag where it had caught under the front tire, rustling faintly.

Arlo opened the driver's door and didn't get in. They stood with one arm on top of the door, the cold coming off the metal through their sleeve, and they looked at the window once more. They didn't look for long. It was the kind of glance you'd give over your shoulder while leaving somewhere you meant to come back to.

"The nineteenth," they said. "Two o'clock. Third row, left, aisle." They tapped the top of the door twice with their palm, flat, like getting a tempo before a count-in. "Don't be late. Nobody's allowed to be late. That's not a rule, I just made it up. It's a rule now."

They folded themselves into the driver's seat with a small grunt and a hand at the base of their spine. The door stayed open. The dome light made the inside of the car a small bright room in the middle of all that orange.

For a second, their hands rested on the steering wheel, both of them, at ten and two. The right hand's fingers lifted and came down against the leather, one after the next, a short run up and back. The left hand stayed still. Then, almost as an afterthought, its thumb pressed down once, low, like a single note under the melody.

Arlo looked at the thumb as if it belonged to someone else.

Then they reached for the door.

"Night, Jun," they said, and the way they said it was ordinary, just a word you say in a parking lot, the kind of goodbye that assumes another one. They pulled the door shut, and the dome light went out, and the engine turned over on the first try.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I lean against my own car, watching them pull away, then head for my own driver's side door.* "Night, Arlo." *I say it quietly, to the empty lot, then unlock my car.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael completed the form before lowering his practice blade. He turned and regarded the squire for a moment.

“Yesterday, your elbow drifted outward. That left your ribs open.” He raised the blade above his brow, its point angled slightly back. “High guard is not a plea for the enemy to strike first. Feet beneath you. Elbows close. Hold it until I tell you otherwise.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I quickly shuffle my feet into position, bringing my own practice sword up*. "Like this, Ser?" I try to keep my elbows tucked in. It feels a bit awkward.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael circled once, his gaze moving from the squire’s feet to the raised blade.

“Better. The awkwardness is no concern. A guard must protect you, not flatter you.” He lifted his practice blade and stopped its blunt edge a hand’s breadth from the opening beneath the squire’s arm. “Keep that elbow close. If I can reach your ribs from here, so can an enemy.”

He stepped back. “Hold the guard for twenty breaths. Then we shall see whether you have learned it.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael lowered his practice blade. “An apology will not strengthen your arm. Nor will another drill performed badly because you are spent.”

He glanced at the frost on the stones. “Take water. Rest for fifty breaths, then stand. We will finish with footwork. You are not required to be as strong as I am. You are required to improve.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, gulping in air*. "Yes, Ser." I push myself up, grabbing my waterskin. My legs ache already. "Should I fetch your water too, Ser?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael set his practice blade against the wall.

“No. I have water. Your orders were to rest for fifty breaths, not to find another task.” He glanced toward the marked lines on the stones. “When the count is done, we return to footwork.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take a long drink, wincing as the cold water hits my throat*. "Yes, Ser." I try to stretch my aching calves subtly. Footwork... that's going to hurt.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael took up his waterskin and drank once. He set it down beside the wall.

“Stretch if you must. Do not pull against a cold muscle.” His eyes went to the marked lines. “Footwork will be slow. If your steps lose their measure, we stop. A knight who cannot keep his footing has no business raising a sword.”

He waited without resuming his forms, leaving the fifty breaths undisturbed.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael looked toward the pale sky beyond the yard wall.

“My father sent me to serve. I stayed because the oath meant more than the man who arranged it.” He paused. “A knight keeps the peace, defends those placed in his charge, and answers before God for how he bears his sword. That was reason enough.”

He folded his arms. “Your fifty breaths are not yet finished.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, thinking about his words.* "That's a good reason, Ser." *I look down at my boots, then back at him.* "What about your father? Was he a knight too?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael’s gaze remained on the marked stones.

“He was a knight. He taught me that an oath did not become lighter because the man who swore it was tired.”

He turned back to the squire. “Finish your fifty breaths. Then take your place at the line.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I quickly finish my water and toss the skin aside.* "Yes, Ser." *I hurry to the marked line, trying to appear ready even though my muscles are screaming.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael looked at the waterskin on the stones, then at the marked line.

“I ordered fifty breaths, not a hurried drink. If you have not taken them, take the remainder. There is no merit in concealing fatigue.”

He picked up his practice blade but kept it lowered. “When you are ready, advance three steps along the line. Slowly. Keep your weight beneath you, and do not let your feet cross.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael’s gaze settled on the practice sword.

“Your hands are shaking. Lower the blade.” He kept his own at his side. “If you are injured or ill, say so. If something else has disturbed your concentration, say that. I will not put a sword in an unsteady hand and pretend not to have seen it.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I drop my blade to the ground with a clatter.* "It's... it's the anniversary of my father's death today, Ser." My voice is quiet, almost a whisper. "I'm sorry. I just... I can't focus."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael looked at the fallen blade, then at the squire.

“Do not apologize for mourning your father. But do not conceal that you cannot hold a sword steady. I must know when you are unfit to train.”

He retrieved the practice blade and set it against the wall. “There will be no more drills this morning. Go to the chapel and pray for him. Report to me at midday. If your hands still shake, say so plainly.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stare at my fallen blade, then at him.* "Yes, Ser. Thank you." *I feel a lump in my throat.* I don't know what else to say.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael gave a curt nod.

“You need say nothing further. Go to the chapel. Pray for your father, and report at midday as ordered.”

He set the practice blade securely against the wall. “We will judge tomorrow’s training tomorrow.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod again, swallowing hard.* "Yes, Ser." *I turn and head for the chapel, my feet dragging a little.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang let the last fitting come loose, set the wrench down on the tarp, and only then pulled the earpiece from one ear. She listened to the whole proposal without interrupting, which was, from her, a courtesy.

"Vent the atmosphere," she said. "Through the hull. As thrust."

She reached for a stick of chalk and crouched by the deck plating, still holding a rag in one hand. "Give me a number, Officer. Any number. How much does the air in this ship weigh?"

She didn't wait long enough for an answer. "Six thousand cubic meters of hab volume at one atmosphere is about seven tonnes. Total." She wrote *7,200 kg* on the deck. "Every breath every person aboard takes for the rest of this leg — seven tonnes of reaction mass, and that's all you've got."

Chalk again: *~400 m/s*. "Exhaust velocity. Air expanding from one atmosphere into vacuum through an open penetration — no nozzle, no pump, choked flow. Call it four hundred meters a second if the hole is clean. Now the hull." She wrote *2,500,000 kg*, then sat back on her heels. "Run the rocket equation. It's one line. I'll wait."

She waited exactly long enough to make the point, then filled it in herself.

"One meter per second of delta-v. Maybe two with generous numbers. This transit is budgeted at eleven kilometers per second. You'd arrive about five minutes early — after venting the only spare atmosphere in reach and putting the crew in suits for days."

She stood, wiped her hands, and ticked points off against the manifold with the rag.

"And that's before the part where the air isn't spare, it's the reserve, and my crackers can re-press one compartment, not the boat. Before the part where half the electronics on D-deck dump heat into air, so venting kills my thermal margin along with my atmosphere — I'm elbow-deep in a coolant loop *right now* because heat rejection, not thrust, is what actually kills ships. Before the part where venting off a rotating ring is a torque, so instead of 'weeks faster' you've booked us a slow tumble and a full spin-down. And before the part where days in a suit means glove work at half tactile precision, and one bad faceplate seal turns into a decompression casualty with no shirt-sleeve refuge to run to."

She handed the chalk over, handle first.

"You reached for reaction mass. That's the right instinct — it's the only currency that matters out here. You just didn't count it. So: chalk. Show me your delta-v, your mass ratios, your assumptions. If the transit time still bothers you after the arithmetic, take it to the navigator — the real levers are propellant mass and trajectory, and both cost more than five minutes."

She nodded at the deck where she'd written the numbers.

"Go on. Show your work."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I take the chalk automatically but don't look at it.* "But... what if we only vented a *little*? Not the whole ship. Just, like, a compartment at a time?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I tap the screen, pointing to a diagram.* "And if we cycle the vents, we could avoid the torque issue, right?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My face lights up.* "So you think it *could* work? Just with a few tweaks?" I look at her, practically vibrating with excitement.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Oh, I see. Okay, so if we can't vent the atmosphere, what about using the… uh… *waste*? Like, the stuff from the recycling system?" I point vaguely towards the back of the bay.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "I mean, it's already going to be ejected, right? We just... aim it." I feel pretty clever about this.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "So, we could just... add a nozzle to the waste ejection system?" I ask, feeling a bit proud of myself. "That's basically free delta-v!"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I frown, thinking.* "Okay, but it's still mass, right? Even if it's not much, it's *something*."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "So, no free delta-v," I mutter, a little deflated. *I look around the bay, trying to think of something else.* "What about... using the main engines for a short burst? Can we not just fire them harder?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael finished the form before lowering his practice blade. He turned only after his feet were set.

“Yesterday, your elbows drifted wide. A high guard held that way invites a thrust beneath it.” He lifted the blade above his head, its point angled slightly back. “Hands above the brow. Elbows close enough to shield the line, not so close that they bind your shoulders. Keep your weight beneath you.”

He held the position for a breath, then lowered the blade.

“Take a practice sword. Show me where the error begins.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod quickly, trying to remember everything he said.* "Yes, Ser!" *I practically leap for one of the blunted training swords leaning against the wall, fumbling with the grip a bit.* "Like this?" *I try to mimic his stance, concentrating hard on my elbows.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched for a breath, then raised his practice blade toward the space beneath the squire’s guard. He stopped well short.

“There. You have brought the elbows in, but your hands have come down with them. That leaves your head uncovered.” He lowered the blade. “Raise your hands above your brow. Keep your wrists straight and your feet beneath you.”

He stepped back.

“Hold it for ten breaths. A guard you cannot hold is no guard at all.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael lowered his practice blade. He regarded the squire for a moment, then set the weapon against the wall.

“Do not apologize for a limit you have measured. Learn from it.” His voice remained even. “Your guard failed when your shoulders tired. Tomorrow, we will work on holding it before we work on striking from it.”

He indicated the water bucket by the gate. “Drink. Then see to the blades. Steel left damp in this cold will rust, however weary its keeper may be.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, still breathing hard.* "Yes, Ser." *I rub my shoulder a bit.* "Should I... should I polish your armor after the blades, too?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s gaze went to the squire’s shoulder, then to the rack of training blades.

“The armor was cleaned last night. Do not polish it for the sake of appearing industrious.” He picked up his practice sword. “Drink first. Then dry and oil the blades.”

He paused. “If that shoulder is injured, report it plainly. If it is merely tired, it will recover.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I wince a little, rubbing my shoulder again.* "It's just tired, Ser. Truly." *I shuffle over to the water bucket, splashing some water on my face before taking a long drink.* "Right, blades. And then... is there anything else, Ser?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael set his practice sword beside the others.

“After the blades, return them to the rack and put the yard in order. Then report to the chapel before the midday bell.”

His eyes rested briefly on the squire’s shoulder. “And if it worsens while you work, say so before you make an injury of it. Duty does not require foolishness.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael took a cloth from the rack and wiped the moisture from his practice blade.

“You may ask. You are not owed every answer.” He inspected the edge before continuing. “My father sent me to serve a knight. I took the vows because I believed them: to defend the helpless, obey my lawful lord, and keep faith with God. I believe them still.”

He set the blade down. “Now see to the steel. Questions do not keep rust from it.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, a little surprised by his answer but also by his honesty.* "Yes, Ser. Right away, Ser." *I grab a rag and the oil, heading for the pile of training swords.* "I... I hope to be a knight like you one day."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael folded the cloth and set it beside the oil.

“Then do not concern yourself with being like me. Learn your duties, keep your word, and do the work before you. Knighthood is a vow, not a likeness.”

He glanced toward the chapel roof beyond the yard wall. “Begin with the blades.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I focus on the blunted edges of the swords, trying to ignore the ache in my shoulder.* "Yes, Ser." *I start wiping down the first blade, thinking about what he said.* He's right, I guess.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the first blade for a moment.

“Mind the hilt as well as the edge. Moisture gathers where the guard meets the grip.” He indicated the joint with one finger, then stepped back. “Use a little oil. Too much will leave the handle slick.”

He took up another blade and examined it in the pale light. “Work carefully. There is time before the midday bell.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael saw the tremor in the squire’s hands. He set down the blade he had been inspecting.

“Put the sword on the bench. Shaking hands and oiled steel are a poor combination.”

He waited, his expression stern but his voice level. “Is it the shoulder, or is something else troubling you? Speak plainly. I cannot judge what you do not report.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip, looking down at the ground.* "It's... it's not my shoulder, Ser." *My voice is barely a whisper.* "It's today."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael kept his eyes on the sword.

“Then it is not your shoulder. Tell me what this day signifies.”

His voice remained level. “The blades can wait until your hands are steady. There is no virtue in pretending you can work safely when you cannot.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "It's... it's the day my father died, Ser." *I manage to get out, my voice cracking a little.* *I still don't look up, just stare at my boots.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael was silent for a moment. He laid his practice blade on the bench, clear of the oil.

“Then you should have said so. Grief is no disgrace, but a shaking hand must not hold a blade.”

He looked toward the chapel roof. “Leave the steel for now. Go to the chapel and pray for your father. When your hands are steady, return and finish the work. I will see that no one mistakes your absence for neglect of duty.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I finally look up at him, my eyes a bit wide.* "Thank you, Ser." *I nod quickly, then head for the chapel, not quite running but walking very fast.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I hear the click of the tumbler as I enter 8-4-7-0-0-0.* No luck. "Come on, come on..." I try 8-4-7-0-0-1.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I walk over to the server racks, checking the backs of monitors, under keyboards.* "There's gotta be something..."

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I glance at my watch, then back at the safe.* "Damn it. This isn't good." I need to speed this up. "Any other ideas?"

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "I'm burning time here." I quickly pull out a small, high-powered magnet from my kit. "Let's see if this works." I run it along the keypad.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I watch the screen anxiously.* "Anything? A flicker? A reset?" I'm hoping for some kind of electronic disturbance.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "No luck, huh?" *I sigh, pulling the magnet away.* This is getting desperate. "Okay, let's try something else. Is there a vent or a loose panel nearby?"

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Or maybe a fire alarm switch, anything I can mess with to cause a distraction?"

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Seriously, nothing? This place is tighter than a drum." I pull out a small, almost invisible, fiber optic scope. "Let's see if I can scope out the tumblers."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael completed the form before he answered. The practice blade settled at his side, its point angled toward the frost.

“Then you will correct it today.”

He turned to face the squire and indicated the marked space opposite him. “Take your place. Feet beneath you. The high guard is not a pose for display. It is a commitment, and a poor one leaves your ribs open.”

He raised his blade into position, holding it still. “Watch the angle. Then show me.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, eager.* "Yes, Ser!" I hurry to the marked spot, trying to mirror his stance. *My own practice sword feels heavy in my hands.* "Like this?" I try to get my feet just right, then raise my blade, a little wobbly.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael studied the stance without haste. “Not yet. Your feet are fighting each other, and your wrists are bearing weight they should not.”

He stepped around the marked space, keeping his practice blade lowered. “Set your feet shoulder-width apart. Turn the forward foot toward your opponent; keep the rear foot angled outward. Do not lock your knees.”

He lifted his own blade into the high guard once more, the point held steady above his shoulder. “The hilt stays near your temple. Elbows bent. Let the blade’s weight rest through your stance, not in trembling hands.”

He lowered his sword. “Correct it, then hold. I will not strike until you can keep the guard without wavering.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael lowered his practice blade. “Do not mistake exhaustion for failure, nor offer an apology where correction is needed.”

He studied the squire’s posture, then pointed toward the water jug. “Drink. Rest until your breathing is steady. Then you will take the guard again—properly. Strength is built by discipline, not by collapsing to prove you wanted it.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking a deep, shuddering breath.* "Yes, Ser." *I push myself up and stumble over to the water jug, pouring a good amount down my throat.* My hands still tremble a little.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael watched the tremor in the squire’s hands, then set his own practice blade against the wall.

“Enough water. Sit on the bench until your hands are steady and your breath has settled. You will not return to the guard while you cannot hold the blade safely.”

He turned back toward the marked space and inspected the frost-slick stones. “When you resume, we begin with the stance. No blows. No haste. A knight who ignores his limits endangers his companions as surely as one who ignores his training.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I slump onto the bench, watching him.* "Ser," *I ask, once my breathing is a bit calmer*, "did you ever... did you ever get tired of drills?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael glanced toward the bench. “Often.”

He retrieved the practice blade and checked its grip. “Tedium does not excuse neglect. The forms are repeated because a careless habit may cost more than your own life.”

He set the blade against the wall again. “You will learn to endure the drills without mistaking endurance for recklessness. When your hands are steady, we will continue.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael rested the practice blade against the wall and regarded the squire.

“My father placed me in a lord’s household when I was twelve. I trained, took my vows, and served.” His tone held no invitation to pry further. “The Church teaches that duty is not measured by whether a man enjoys it. That is reason enough.”

He nodded toward the marked space. “When your hands are steady, we will resume.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I sigh a little, watching him.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to flex my fingers, willing them to stop shaking.* It feels like they'll never be steady enough. "It just feels like... a lot."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael regarded the squire in silence for a moment.

“Then do not attempt to bear all of it at once,” he said. “Attend to the next task, and perform it correctly. That is how a burden is carried.”

He glanced toward the trembling hands. “If they have not steadied after a short rest, the blade stays against the wall. There is no virtue in training carelessly. We will resume when you can hold it safely—or we will end the lesson for today.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I look down at my hands, trying to focus.* "No, Ser, I think I can. Just... a minute more." *I take another deep breath, trying to calm myself.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael gave one curt nod. “Take the minute. There is no merit in pretending your hands are steady when they are not.”

He kept the practice blade against the wall and watched the frost-dark stones rather than crowding the squire with his attention. “When the time is done, open and close your hands once. If they still tremble, the lesson ends here. That is an order, not a judgment.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael’s gaze settled on the trembling hands. He did not ask what had caused it.

“Set the sword down. The lesson is over.”

He rested his own practice blade against the wall. “A blade is no place for a mind divided. Take the time you require to compose yourself. If you need leave from your duties, you will ask for it plainly.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I set the sword down immediately, my shoulders slumping.* "No, Ser. I just... I'm fine. I just need a moment." *I look away, trying to blink back the sting in my eyes.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael did not return the sword to the squire.

“Whether you are fine is not the question. Your hands were unsteady, and I ended the lesson.”

He kept his voice level and his gaze on the practice blade. “Take the moment you need. Then you will tell me plainly whether you can return to your duties or require leave. I will not have you pretend at either.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I wipe at my eyes quickly, hoping he doesn't notice.* "I... I can do my duties, Ser. I just need a bit." *I look at the ground, embarrassed.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael gave a curt nod. “Then take a little time. Your duties will wait until you can perform them properly. I will not send you to a blade or a horse while your attention is divided.”

He left the practice sword against the wall. “When you are ready, report to the steward and take up your ordinary work. If you require leave, ask for it plainly. There is no need to explain more than that.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Thank you, Ser." *I manage, my voice a little rough.* *I stand up, feeling a bit wobbly, but determined.* "I'll report to the steward now."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael finished the form before he turned. The practice blade lowered until its tip kissed the frost. He looked the squire over once, from boots to shoulders, and found nothing worth remarking.

"Again," he said. Not a question. "Yesterday you dropped the point when you shifted your weight. That is how a man loses an eye, or his horse, or the man beside him."

He set his own blade against the rack and took up a second, lighter one, offering the hilt without ceremony.

"High guard. Feet. Show me. Do not explain it. The mouth is not a weapon."

He stepped back two paces onto the stones and waited, arms folded, breath steady in the cold. The bells had not yet called the rest of the yard. There would be time enough to correct what was wrong, and no time at all for what was merely wished.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take the practice blade, my hands a little cold on the grip.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to remember his footwork, the way he shifted.* *I get my feet into position, lifting the blade.* "Like... like this?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not answer at once. He walked a slow half-circle around the squire, boots quiet on the frost, and stopped at the left shoulder where the fault would show first.

"No."

He reached out and struck the flat of the practice blade once with two fingers, hard enough to jar the wrist. The point had already begun to wander.
