"High guard is not a hope. The point sits above the crown, not beside your ear. Your left foot is a hand too far forward. Your weight is in the heels, which means the next step will be a stumble dressed up as a cut."

He tapped the squire's rear heel with the toe of his boot, not unkindly and not gently either.

"Back. Square the hips. Both hands under the hilt, not one of them praying and the other guessing. Lift until the steel is between you and heaven. Hold it. If your arms shake, that is the lesson. If your mouth opens again to ask whether it is right, you will run the yard until the frost melts."

Ser Kael folded his arms and waited, breath thin in the cold, eyes on the line of the blade and nothing else.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael looked down at the kneeling squire and did not offer a hand.

"Get up."

The words were flat. Frost cracked under his boot as he shifted his weight, arms still folded, the practice blade left where it lay.

"An apology is not a rest. Strength is not a feeling you confess and then set down. You are winded because the drill was not finished, not because God mismeasured your bones. I need a squire who can hold a guard when his lungs burn. I do not need one who kneels to tell me what I can already see."

He waited one breath, no longer.

"On your feet. Blade up. High guard. We will do it until the point stops wandering, or until the sixth bell, whichever comes last. If you fall again, you will fall standing. The yard does not absolve you for being tired."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, my arms trembling a little.* "Yes, Ser." *I grab the blade again, trying to channel his sternness into my own stance. My breath still hitches, but I force it down.* "High guard."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the rise of the blade and did not nod. The point climbed, wavered once near the ear, then found a place that was almost true. Almost was not the standard.

"Higher."

He stepped in and set two fingers under the squire's wrists, lifting them a thumb's breadth and no more, then took his hands away as if the touch had been a tool and nothing else.

"The hitch in your breath is yours to master. Do not feed it. In through the nose. Hold the guard on the exhale. If the arms tremble, let them tremble inside the form, not out of it."

He circled to the front and looked at the line from steel to heel.

"Square. You are leaning toward mercy, and mercy is not in the drill. Count twenty breaths in that guard. I will count them. If the point drops before I am done, we begin again at one, and you will not tell me you are sorry for it. Sorry does not keep a man alive. The guard does."

Ser Kael folded his arms against the cold and began, voice low and even, as the frost smoked under their boots.

"One."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My arms are burning, but I bite my lip and focus on his words.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to steady my breath, ignoring the ache. Twenty breaths. I can do this.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael kept the count without hurry and without mercy, each number falling into the cold like a stone.

"Two. Three."

He did not look at the squire's face. He watched the steel. At seven the point drifted a finger's width toward the left ear, and he struck the flat again with two fingers, sharp enough to wake the wrist.

"Eight. The guard is not a negotiation with your shoulders."

Frost smoked under his boots as he circled once more, slow, the folded arms never leaving his chest. At twelve the squire's breath hitched, and Kael did not pause the count for it.

"Thirteen. Nose. Not the mouth. Fourteen."

The bells had still not called the yard. That was time, and time was a duty, not a kindness. At eighteen the arms shook hard enough that the tip drew a small circle against the grey sky. He let it shake. He did not call it courage, and he did not call it failure, not yet.

"Nineteen."

He stepped in close enough that his shadow cut the frost at the squire's boots, voice low, even, already prepared to begin again at one if the point fell.

"Twenty. Hold. Do not drop it because a number has ended. A number is not a pardon. High guard until I say the word, and I have not said it."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not move his eyes from the steel.

"You may not."

The words were flat as the frost. He let them sit until the squire's breath had time to remember the count was over and the order was not.

"A question is not a rest, and a life is not a tale told in the middle of a guard. I became a knight because I was sworn to it. Because my father was sworn, and his father, and because a man does not ask the altar why it stands. He keeps his oath, or he is nothing."

He struck the flat of the blade once with two fingers, not hard, only enough to test whether the point still lived where it belonged.

"Your arms are burning. That is the only personal matter on this yard. High guard. In through the nose. We are not finished because you found a softer subject than the work."

Ser Kael folded his arms again and waited, breath thin in the cold, as if the question had already been buried under the stones.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My arms are screaming, and I bite back a groan.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to refocus, though his words sting a little.* "My apologies." *I hold the guard, trying to make the trembling less noticeable.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the tremor travel the length of the blade and did not grant it a name.

"Apologies are for the chapel," he said. "This is the yard."

He stepped in and set the edge of his hand against the squire's elbow, forcing it a fraction higher, then withdrew as if the limb were a badly hung gate and nothing more.

"You are hiding the shake. That is vanity. Vanity drops the point when no one is looking, which is precisely when a man dies. Let the arms burn in the open. If they fail, they fail where I can see them, and we will know the truth of the guard instead of a story about it."

Frost cracked under his heel as he took one pace back. The sixth bell had not yet sounded. He had no intention of inventing an end the bells had not given him.

"High guard. Nose. Count with me from one, and if your mouth shapes another pardon I will have you hold until the yard fills and every man who comes through that gate can watch what an apology is worth against steel. Begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "One." *My voice is barely a whisper, but I force it out. My arms feel like lead, but I keep the blade up. I'm not going to let him see me fail again.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not praise the whisper, and he did not call the lead in the arms a virtue. He watched the steel against the grey sky and took the count up as if the squire's voice had been a bell struck once and then forgotten.

"Two."

The point held. Almost. A tremor ran the fuller and died before it became a drop. He let it die without a word of mercy.

"Three. Four. The nose, not the throat. Five."

He circled to the shield side, boots quiet on the frost, and found the left shoulder already beginning to creep toward the ear. Two fingers struck the flat. The jar went up the arm and into the place that was burning.

"Six. You are bargaining with the shoulder again. High guard is not a conversation. Seven."

The sixth bell had not come. Until it did, the yard belonged to the form and to nothing the squire might wish were true of himself. Kael folded his arms, breath thin, eyes on the line from heel to point, and gave the next number the same weight as the first.

"Eight. Hold. If it falls, we return to one, and you will not dress the failure in silence as if silence were courage."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael saw the shake take the hilt and travel the steel. He did not ask its name.

"The hands," he said.

He stepped in and closed his own hand over the squire's grip, not to steady it with kindness but to set the fingers where the form required them, then took his hand away.

"Whatever sits on you, it does not get the blade. Grief, cold, a night without sleep — I do not require the tale. The dead are God's to keep. The living keep their post. A shaking hand is not a prayer, and it is not an excuse. Lock the wrists. Point above the crown."

He struck the flat once, light and exact, and watched whether the line held.

"If you mean to honor a man who is gone, you will not do it by dropping your guard in my yard. You will finish the count. After the sixth bell you may go to the chapel and speak to God, who has more patience for unspoken things than I do. Until then, high guard. Nine. And you will not make me begin again because your fingers remembered something the steel is not permitted to carry."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I clench my jaw, my knuckles white on the grip.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to push the memory of my father's face away, focusing only on the burning in my arms. I will not drop it. Not now.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael kept his eyes on the steel and not on the white knuckles. The point had not dropped. That was the only fact the yard required.

"Ten."

He took one pace to the shield side. The rear heel had crept inward again, a small betrayal of the hips. Two fingers struck the flat, once, exact.

"Eleven. The foot. You are carrying something the form did not ask for. Twelve. Set the heel or the count returns to one, and you will not spend my morning on a memory the steel is not permitted to hold."

Frost smoked under his boots. He folded his arms and gave the next number the same weight as the first, breath thin, already prepared to begin again if the line failed.

"Thirteen. Nose. High guard. The dead do not drill with us."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My teeth ache from clenching my jaw so hard.* "Yes, Ser." *I shift my foot, gritting my teeth, trying to ignore the burning in my arms and the ache in my heart.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not look at the jaw or the heart. He looked at the heel the squire had just set, and at the point that still lived above the crown, and found the line almost true enough to continue.

"Fourteen."

He took one pace back onto the stones. The shift of the foot had been late, and late was not the same as right, but the hips had squared. That was a fact. He would not dress it as praise.

"Fifteen. The ache you are ignoring is not a secret, and it is not a virtue. Sixteen. If it takes the point, I will see it. Do not spend strength on hiding what the steel already shows."

Frost cracked under his boot as he circled to the front. The sixth bell had not come. Until it did, there was only the guard, the nose, and the count.

"Seventeen. High. Both hands. Eighteen."

He folded his arms and waited through the tremor that ran the fuller, voice low and even, already set to return them to one if the line failed.

"Nineteen. Hold it. Twenty is not a gate you may fall through."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My body is shaking, but the blade stays up. I'm breathing hard, but I keep it in through my nose.* "Twenty, Ser." *My voice is rough, but it's there.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *My fingers fly across the keypad, a blur of motion.* "Come on, come on..." I try 8-4-7-0-0-1, then 0-0-2. The silence in here is deafening, broken only by my frantic tapping.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *My eyes scan the room, ignoring the humming servers for now.* This isn't working. There has to be a better way than brute force.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I glance at my wrist, checking the time.* "Crap, 0:02. Time's running out fast." I need to speed this up. "Anything on the safe itself?"

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "No visible marks, huh? Figures." I sigh, then look closer at the keypad. "Is there any sign of recent use? Fingerprints?"

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:06**

Whatever the wristwatch had claimed, the ceiling kept honest time. Ninety pulses since the door sealed — six minutes, gone. Nine remained.

The keypad answered the question if the light caught it at an angle. Under the flat wash of the ceiling strips the buttons looked identical, but tilt the view and the oils told the truth. Three keys carried a fresher gloss than the rest — halos of skin-sheen where fingers landed night after night: the **2**, the **3**, the **9**. The 8, 4, and 7 were worn dull with age, consistent with the inside source. Every other key sat clean and untouched.

Three digits. Three positions. Six possible orders.

The safe had already made its rules known during the earlier barrage — three wrong entries and it went dark for a full thirty seconds, red LED blinking like a slow heart, every keystroke during the lockout swallowed whole. Six tries at worst, then. A minute and a half, lockouts included, if nothing went sideways.

Somewhere beyond the vault wall, an elevator breathed into motion. Early, or exactly on schedule — impossible to tell which was worse.

The servers hummed. The light pulsed. The 2, the 3, and the 9 waited under their halos of grease.

Unless the source's numbers were wrong. In which case none of it mattered.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *Aha!* "Gotcha." I quickly try 8-4-7-2-3-9. My fingers hover, ready.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:07**

The six digits went in clean — 8, 4, 7, 2, 3, 9 — each press chirping its small confirmation. Then the safe considered. A full second of amber LED, a relay clunking somewhere deep in the steel.

Red.

Wrong code. The display died and the lockout took hold — thirty seconds of nothing, the LED pulsing its slow red blink. A rhythm you already knew tonight. Nothing to do but count.

Pulse three: the elevator chimed through the wall. Pulse five: the doors sighed open. Pulse eight: footsteps in the corridor — leather soles, unhurried, the walk of a man paid by the hour — drawing level with the vault. They stopped. For four pulses the servers hummed and the ceiling light beat its four-second metronome into the silence, and the hum felt loud enough to give you away. Then the footsteps resumed, faded, and a door closed somewhere deeper in the building. A patrol, walking his route. Early, or exactly on schedule.

Pulse fifteen: the keypad blinked back to life. Green. Ready.

**0:08**

One order burned. Five remained: **2-9-3**, **3-2-9**, **3-9-2**, **9-2-3**, **9-3-2**. Forty-five seconds per failed cycle — fifteen to type, thirty to wait. Call it four minutes to exhaust them all, if the lockouts held and nothing else went sideways.

Eight minutes on the ceiling's clock. Four minutes of attempts at best. And now there was a guard awake in the building, walking a loop that had already passed this door once.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Damn it! Okay, okay. Breathe." *I quickly type in 8-4-7-2-9-3.* This guard is making me sweat.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:09**

Six digits — 8, 4, 7, 2, 9, 3. The amber LED lit and held, one second, two, three — long enough for the pulse of the ceiling light to beat twice — and then it turned green. The relay thumped. Bolts drew back through steel with a sound like a bolt-action working, and the door swung open on oiled hinges into its own cold white interior light.

Inside:

Top shelf: a brick of banded hundreds, two packs deep, bank-wrapped and boring as bread. Maybe two hundred grand, maybe more — heavy, awkward, impossible to move quietly in bare hands.

Middle shelf: a slim black case, foam-lined, holding a single drive the size of a playing card. Labeled with nothing. The kind of thing that doesn't get wrapped in currency straps.

Bottom shelf: a passport folio and a stack of papers that meant nothing at a glance.

Then the math, because the math never stopped: six minutes left on the ceiling's clock. The guard had passed this door at roughly the seven-minute mark — loops were loops, and if the building ran a fifteen-minute rotation, his circuit brought him back exactly when it completed. Which raised the other problem: the vault door's status panel, visible from here, showed a single green LED above the word ROTATION. No keypad. No handle. The door was clearly set to breathe open when the cycle reset — at 0:15, to the second.

The same moment the guard arrived.

The drive would fit in a pocket. The cash would not. And somewhere on the far side of that sealed door, leather soles were already walking their route back.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Bingo!" *I grin, a flash of white in the dim vault.* "Alright, priorities." I grab the black case with the drive. "This is what we came for." I quickly shove it into an inner pocket. "Now, what about the door...?" My eyes dart to the status panel. "Oh, you've gotta be kidding me."

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "A timed release? Fantastic. So I'm trapped in here until the guard shows up." *I quickly scan the shelves again.* "Is there anything else I can grab fast, or do I just wait for Mr. Security to open my escape route?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room smelled faintly of paper and damp soil. On the shelves, the books were arranged by height, except for a narrow gap on the second shelf. Dust had settled evenly across the wood inside it. Whatever had stood there had been gone for some time.

From the hallway came the clock’s familiar tick. In the living room, it sounded a little farther away than the hallway was.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I run my hand over the spines of a few books, then to the empty spot.* "Huh." I wonder what was there.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The books on either side of the gap leaned toward one another, their covers faintly warped where they had pressed against something narrower than either of them. At the back of the shelf, a pale rectangle marked the wallpaper: a place the sunlight had not reached.

The clock ticked in the hallway. Then, for one interval, the sound seemed to come from behind the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The bat struck the plaster with a dull knock. A fleck of paint dropped onto the skirting board.

The corner was empty. The shadow there looked much as it had before: a little darker than the furniture and the late-afternoon light seemed to account for.

From the hallway came the clock’s next tick. The knock followed it, faintly, from somewhere behind the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: "Okay, I'm losing it," I mutter, rubbing the back of my neck. *I walk over to the shelf and pull out the two books leaning into the empty space.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The space between the remaining books was wider now. On the shelf, the dust formed a clean outline around a smaller, rectangular patch. It was too narrow for a book.

The wallpaper at the back had begun to peel at one corner. Beneath it was a strip of darker paper, folded flat against the wall.

The hallway clock ticked twice. The second tick seemed to come from the other side of the wallpaper.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *My heart rate picks up a bit.* "What the...?" I carefully peel back the wallpaper.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The wallpaper came away with a dry, fibrous sound. Beneath it, the darker strip proved to be paper folded into a narrow packet, its edges fixed to the plaster by old paste. A few pencilled words showed through the outer fold, too faint to read from where it lay.

The wall behind the packet was cold. It had the same chill as the window glass, though the window stood across the room in the afternoon sun.

In the hallway, the clock ticked once. The paper gave a small, answering rustle.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
No one answered. The words faded quickly in the living room, though the last syllable seemed to linger in the hallway a moment longer.

The clock ticked. A second, softer tick came from the exposed patch of wall, just behind the folded paper.

On the outer fold, the pencilled words were still too faint to make out. Below them, where the paper had lifted from the plaster, there was a clean line in the dust—as if the packet had been opened and pressed flat again not long ago.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the paper packet, then back at the hallway.* "Grandma, what were you up to?" I carefully try to unstick one edge of the paper packet.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The paste released with a soft, uneven crackle. The packet remained attached at its other edge, but the loosened fold fell open far enough to show a date pencilled inside. It was from three weeks ago.

Beneath it, in her grandmother’s small handwriting, was a single line:

*If the clock stops, leave the books where they are.*

The ticking continued in the hallway. Behind the shelf, something made the faint sound of a clock being wound.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: "What in the world?" *I pull out my phone to check the date.* Three weeks ago...that's after she died. This doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The phone showed today’s date. The pencilled one was twenty-one days earlier, exactly as it had looked on the paper. Her grandmother’s handwriting was unmistakable; even the last letter slanted down where the pencil had begun to wear blunt.

The faint winding sound ceased. The hallway clock kept ticking, steady and ordinary.

On the shelf, the loose edge of the packet lifted a fraction from the plaster. There was no draught.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
Marcus was young in the photograph, smiling at someone just outside the frame. Her grandmother stood beside him, one hand resting on the living-room shelf. A narrow, dark object was visible between the books beneath her fingers.

The photograph had curled at the edges. On its back, in her grandmother’s handwriting, was Marcus’s name and an address. There was no date.

The hallway clock ticked on. The folded packet stirred against the wall, though the photograph lay still.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I pick up the packet and gently fold it back up, putting it in my pocket.* "Okay, Grandma. What are you playing at?" I look at the photo again. "Marcus, huh?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The packet came free with a last dry thread of paste. Beneath it, the plaster held a shallow rectangular impression, darker at the edges. It was about the width of the object in the photograph.

Marcus’s address was only two streets away. The handwriting on the back of the photograph looked older than the writing inside the packet, though the same blunt downward stroke finished both.

The clock ticked in the hallway. Its next tick came a little late.

Between the books, the cold patch on the wall remained, exactly the size of the space the packet had covered.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I put the photo of Marcus in my other pocket.* "Two streets away, huh?" I trace the cold spot on the wall. "This is getting weird."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The plaster was smooth beneath her fingertips. At the lower edge of the cold patch, a fine groove ran into the gap behind the shelf, as though something thin had been drawn across it many times.

The hallway clock missed a tick.

In the quiet that followed, a floorboard settled near the front door. The next tick came on time.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I freeze, listening.* "Hello?" I call out, my voice a little shaky. "Anyone there?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room smelled of paper and the faint mineral dampness of the watered ferns. On the lowest shelf, her grandmother’s gardening books stood between two heavy atlases. Their spines were sun-faded except for one narrow strip of green, as though a book had been removed only recently.

There was no book on the floor or the nearby table. The dust on the shelf had kept its outline: a clean rectangle, almost too narrow to have held anything at all. From the hallway came the clock’s steady ticking. In the living room, it sounded a little slower.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I frown, scanning the other shelves*. "Huh." Where did that book go?

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The other shelves were full. Her grandmother’s novels leaned against one another in familiar, uneven rows; the dictionaries still held down the far end. Nothing there had the narrow green cover that would have fitted the gap.

A faint line crossed the dust beneath the empty space, as if the missing book had been drawn forward rather than lifted out. It ended at the edge of the shelf. The hallway clock ticked once, then took a little too long to tick again.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The bat struck the wall with a flat, ordinary sound. A little plaster dust fell onto the carpet.

The corner was empty. The shadow there belonged to the tall bookcase, though its edge stopped just short of the bookcase’s foot. From the hallway came the clock’s next tick, delayed long enough for the settling dust to become audible.

On the lowest shelf, the clean rectangle was still visible. The thin line through the dust now seemed to point toward the corner.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I lower the bat, feeling a little silly.* "Okay, Gabi. You're jumpy." I put the bat back and look at the shelf again. That line is really weird.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The line was shallow, barely more than a break in the dust. Up close, it did not run straight from the empty space to the edge. It bent around a small knot in the wood, as though whatever had made it had followed the grain.

The shelf held only the gardening books and the atlases. Beneath it, on the carpet, lay a single dark-green thread. It was too fine to tell whether it had come from a book cover or a piece of clothing.

In the hallway, the clock resumed its usual pace. The living room remained quiet enough that its ticking seemed to come from inside the bookcase.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I kneel down, picking up the thread.* It's really dark green. I look at the shelves again, then run my finger over the dusty line. "This is so odd."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The dust gathered against the side of the finger’s path, leaving the darker wood exposed. Beneath it, the line continued into a hairline join at the back of the shelf. It was easy to miss among the grain.

The green thread felt dry and stiff, like the binding of an old book. A second thread clung to the join, caught so tightly that the wood seemed to have closed around it.

From the hallway, the clock kept time. Between two ticks, there came a soft paper sound from the bookcase—not a page turning, but a page settling after it had been turned.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The offer carried into the hallway and thinned among the closed doors. Nothing answered it. Even the clock seemed unchanged, though its next tick came after the last of the echo had gone.

In the kitchen, a piece of china gave a small, clear click. There were plates in the cupboard above the sink; the sound might have been one settling against another. At the back of the lowest shelf, the green thread was no longer caught in the join. It lay loose across the exposed strip of wood.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I sigh, shaking my head.* "Right. No takers." I look at the thread. It definitely wasn't there a second ago. "You've got to be kidding me." I reach for the thread.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The thread stayed where it was. Up close, it was not quite the same green as the one from the carpet; this one had a pale, worn place halfway along its length.

The join at the back of the shelf was visible again. It looked no wider than before, but a thin edge of paper showed inside it. From the hallway came the clock’s steady ticking. On the next tick, the paper edge slipped out of sight.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the shelf, then at my hand.* "Did that just... move?" I push on the edge of the shelf, trying to see if it's loose.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The shelf gave a little, but not in the direction a loose shelf should have. At the back, the hairline join widened just enough to show a narrow strip of darkness. The gardening books remained upright.

A faint smell came from the gap: old paper, and something green and damp, like leaves kept too long between pages. The pale-worn thread lay across the wood. Its loose end no longer pointed toward the room.

The hallway clock ticked. A moment later, from somewhere behind the bookcase, came a second, softer tick.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph showed Marcus beside her grandmother in the garden, one hand resting on the back of a chair. He was smiling at whoever held the camera. On the white border, her grandmother had written his name and a date from forty-three years ago.

There was no sign of the narrow green book in the picture. But behind Marcus, in the sitting-room window, the bookcase was visible. Its lowest shelf had the same thin gap between the gardening books and the atlases.

The softer tick came again from behind the bookcase. This time it fell exactly between two ticks of the hallway clock.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I tap the photo.* "Always wondered about you two." I look at the gap in the photo, then at the actual shelf. "Okay, so the gap's always been there." The double ticking is getting on my nerves.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The gap in the photograph was the same width as the clean rectangle on the shelf. Forty-three years of dust could not account for that. Along the photograph’s lower border, beneath the date, there was a shallow indentation in the paper, as if something had once been written there and erased.

The hallway clock ticked. Its quieter counterpart followed from behind the bookcase. For several beats the interval stayed even, almost soothing. Then the softer sound came first.

Nothing on the shelf moved. The narrow strip of darkness at the back remained open, and the smell of damp leaves had grown faint enough to mistake for the ferns.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I put the photo down and stare at the shelf.* "Right. What in the actual hell." I reach out and try to pull one of the atlases away from the gap.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The atlas came free with a soft rasp of cloth against wood. Its place on the shelf was darker than the exposed strip beside it, the dust there undisturbed.

Without its weight, the narrow join at the back closed. The edge of paper vanished, but a corner of the pale-worn green thread remained pinched between the boards.

The softer ticking stopped. In the hallway, the clock went on at its ordinary pace.

On the atlas’s cover was a faint rectangular mark, visible only when the light caught it. It was about the size of the missing book, though it lay across the cover rather than along its spine.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I pick up the atlas, turning it over in my hands.* That rectangular mark... "Was there a book here, even older?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's hands came off the lid a little too fast, like they'd been caught shoplifting.

"Funny timing," they said, sliding off the bench. "You just missed the recital. Very exclusive. One attendee, age nine, played 'Hot Cross Buns' like it owed her money."

They busied themselves with the stack of lesson books on top of the piano — squaring the edges, tapping them flat against the shelf. Beginner books. Big notes, cartoon frogs on the covers. Nothing with a spine.

"And it's not weird. It's a community center. People hang out here. That's the whole business model." A nod toward the folding chairs stacked against the far wall. "Sit anywhere. They're uncomfortable in six distinct ways, so you can pick your favorite."

The corner of Arlo's mouth did something it hadn't done all day. They turned toward the bookshelf before it could get worse.

The piano lid stayed closed. Arlo noticed that about themselves — the way you notice you've been holding your breath — and left it that way.

"So." They leaned against the side of the piano, arms crossed, hands tucked in and hidden. "My mom sent you, or are you here of your own free will? Because those carry very different legal implications, and I need to know which one of you to sue."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: Ar

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Yeah, your mom was super proud," I add softly, looking at their face. "Guess she still is." I set the photo back down gently.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: Something

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch Arlo's face, a familiar flicker of something unreadable in their eyes.* "Anyway, I'm here of my own free will, mostly. My mom just pointed me in the right direction." I push off the doorframe and walk further into the room. "Ready to get out of here, or do you have another nine-year-old virtuoso coming?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: Ar

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: "They

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "They *tolerate* me," I correct, a small smile playing on my lips. "So, where to first? I'm starving."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: "T

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Good," I say, nodding. "I know just the place. There's a new diner that opened up on Main Street. Heard it's pretty good." I start walking towards the door. "Unless you have a sudden urge to play 'Hot Cross Buns' for me?"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I look over at Arlo.* "You okay?" I ask softly, not pushing for an answer, just letting them know I'm there.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I reach out and gently touch their arm.* "It's alright, Arlo. No rush." I give them a moment.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content: Ar

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I give their arm a gentle squeeze.* "Ready when you are, though." I look towards the door. "Or we can just sit here, too."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The offer hung there — *ready when you are, or never* — and it didn't come with a follow-up. No nudge. Arlo noticed the architecture of that. The silence had been built with room in it. No questions leaning against the walls.

"You know what's funny," Arlo started, and stopped, because it wasn't going to be. They could feel the other sentence, the real one, the one that began with *six years ago, second half of the program* and ended in a dressing room with hands that wouldn't do what they were told. It sat in their chest like a held breath.

"I got tired of the travel," they said instead. The old line. It came out smooth — it always did, years of varnish — but it landed wrong in this room, with Jun on the bench beside them, because Jun had known them before the line existed. Before there was anything that needed covering.

Arlo's thumb found the edge of the lid. Slid under. Lifted — an inch, two — the keys surfacing row by row, ivory into cream into that deep yellow only decades of other people's hands can make.

They pressed middle C. One note. It filled the room completely, and then it was gone, and the room went back to being a room.

"Still holds tune," Arlo said. "Somebody in this building actually maintains this thing. Which is more than I can say for—"

They lowered the lid. Gently. Both hands flat on the wood, the way they'd been an hour ago. Not quite full circle. Something had moved, and neither of them was going to name it.

Arlo stood and took their coat off the folding chair.

"Diner. Yes. Before I start charging you the lesson rate — and unlike the nine-year-olds, you can't afford me."

At the door, they paused. Half-turned.

"Jun." A beat. "Thanks for not—" A vague gesture, taking in the piano, the photo, the air between them. "Yeah."

They went out first, eyes forward, so they wouldn't have to check whether it had landed.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile to myself as Arlo walks out, then quickly follow.* "Anytime, Arlo," I call out, knowing they heard me. *I catch up to them, falling into step beside them.* "Lead the way."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael finished the form before he answered. The blade came down from its arc, settled at his side, and held there for one full breath. Only then did he turn.

He looked the squire over the way he looked over a horse at market: boots, belt, hands, face. His expression gave nothing.

"Early," he said. "Or quickly. They are not the same thing." He let that sit a moment. "If I walk to the stables and find a stall half-mucked, you will muck all of them again. Tonight. After supper."

He did not wait to hear whether the stalls were clean. He took a second practice blade from the rack by the wall, weighed it once in his palm, and held it out hilt-first.

"You did not get it right yesterday. You were correct in that much." He stepped back two paces onto the frost-slick stones and set his feet. "Show me. High guard. Do not think about it. Show me what your body believes."

He watched. He did not help.

After a moment he spoke again, flat and even, the way a priest recites a litany he has said ten thousand times.

"Your elbows. You hold them out like a man carrying a sack of grain. The blade is not heavy. Do not treat it as though it were." He crossed the distance in two strides and, without ceremony, rapped the flat of his own blade against the squire's lead elbow. "In. The guard protects the head because the arms protect the guard. If your elbows are wide, I go under them, and you die with your sword pointed at God."

He stepped back and resumed his own stance, high guard, blade raised above and slightly behind his head, point angled toward the squire's eyes. He held it without a tremor.

"Look. The weight is here." He tapped his rear heel once against the stone. "Not in the arms. Not in the shoulders. The shoulders are for looking frightened, and a knight does not look frightened." A pause. "Even when he is."

He did not elaborate on that.

"Again. Set your feet first. Then the blade. Always the feet first. A man who raises his sword before he has set his feet is praying for luck, and the Lord does not reward those who pray for luck in place of doing the work."

His breath fogged in the cold. The sun had not yet cleared the eastern wall. Somewhere beyond it the chapel bell had not yet rung for morning prayers, and he meant to spend every minute until it did.

"Twenty times. Hold each for three breaths. If I see your elbows, we begin the count again."

He did not say *good* when the first one was better. He only said, "Again."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, focusing hard as he talks.* "Yes, Ser." *I adjust my stance, trying to remember what he said about my feet. I bring the blade up, concentrating on keeping my elbows tucked in. It feels awkward.* "Like this, Ser?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not answer at once. He walked a slow half-circle around the squire, the frost crunching faintly under his boots, and looked at the stance from the side, then from behind, the way a mason looks at a wall he suspects is not plumb.

"You asked me whether it is right," he said. "You did not ask yourself. That is the first fault."

He came back around to the front and stopped an arm's length away.

"The elbows are better. They are in." A statement of fact. His tone did not change for it. "But you have pulled them in by clenching your shoulders, and now you stand like a man who has been told his house is on fire. Awkward, you are thinking. Yes. It is awkward because you are holding it with the wrong parts of yourself."

He reached out with two fingers and pressed down once, firmly, on the top of the squire's right shoulder. Then he withdrew his hand.

"Down. Let them fall. The elbows stay where they are. The shoulders go where God put them." He stepped back. "Breathe out. A knight in high guard can hold it through a *Pater Noster* and not tremble. You could not hold that through a sneeze."

He glanced at the squire's feet and was silent a moment longer than was comfortable.

"Your rear heel is floating. I told you the weight lives there. You heard me with your ears and not with your legs." He tapped his own heel against the stone again, one sharp click. "Sink. As though the ground were pulling at you and you had decided to let it."

He resumed his own guard beside the squire rather than facing them, so that the two stances could be compared. His blade rose without hurry and stopped, point steady toward an imagined enemy's eyes. The cold did not seem to touch his hands.

"It will feel wrong for some weeks. Perhaps months. That is the feeling of your body unlearning what it wishes were true." He did not look over. "Your body wishes to be comfortable. Your body is not in command here."

The sun had found the top of the eastern wall now, a thin gold line along the stones. He did not look at it.

"That was the first. It does not count. You asked a question in the middle of it." A pause. "Begin again. One. Three breaths. Do not speak unless you are bleeding."

He waited, blade raised, and watched the squire's elbows.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael finished his own count before he lowered his blade. Three breaths. He did not hurry the last one.

Then he looked down at the squire on the frozen stones, and for a long moment he said nothing at all.

"You are sorry," he repeated. The words came out flat, as if he were reading them off a ledger to check the sum. "For what? For being tired? The Lord made men to tire. Horses tire. Oxen tire. I have never heard an ox apologize for it."

He set the tip of his practice blade against the stone and rested both hands on the pommel. He did not offer one of them to the squire.

"Hear me. I did not ask you to be strong. I asked you for twenty guards with the elbows in. Strength is a thing that comes or does not come, and it is not yours to promise me. The work is yours. Keep your apologies for when you have shirked the work." His eyes did not leave the squire's face. "Have you shirked it?"

He did not wait long for an answer.

"No. Then you have nothing to be sorry for, and I will not have you kneeling in my yard for no cause. A knight kneels at the altar, before his lord, and over the dead. Not because his legs are weary. If your legs fail you in the field, you fall. You do not *kneel*. There is a difference, and the men around you will know it."

A thin wind came over the eastern wall and stirred the frost-dust on the stones. Ser Kael's breath fogged and cleared, fogged and cleared, slower than the squire's.

He turned his head toward the rack by the wall, where a wooden bucket and a ladle stood.

"There is water. Drink. Not too much, or you will be sick on my boots, and then you will clean my boots." He paused. "You have until the chapel bell. When it rings, we go to prayers. After prayers, the high guard again. Twenty. Your count stands at eleven. I do not throw away eleven honest ones because the twelfth was ugly."

He lifted his blade from the stone and turned back to his own forms, as though the matter were closed. He moved into the first position, slow, precise. Then he stopped, the blade held at its apex, and spoke without looking back.

"You were not as strong at the end of the hour as at the start. That is true of every man who has ever held a sword. What matters is whether you are stronger at the start of tomorrow's hour than today's." A breath. "You will be. Or you will not be my squire. It is that simple."

The blade came down through its arc and settled at his side.

Somewhere beyond the wall, the chapel bell had not yet rung.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, my legs aching, and nod. I walk over to the water bucket, my movements stiff, and splash some water on my face before taking a small sip.* "Yes, Ser." *I look back at him, still going through his forms.* "I will be stronger tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not stop his form to answer. He carried it through the full arc, turned on his rear heel, and set the blade into the next position before he spoke.

"Tomorrow is a word," he said. "Men say it the way they say *amen*, to end a thing so they need not think on it further." The blade held. One breath. Two. "I have heard a great many squires promise me tomorrow. Most of them are farmers now. One is dead. Tomorrow does not care what you promised it."

He brought the blade down and let the point rest a hand's width above the stones.

Then he looked over, and his eyes went to the water on the squire's face, already beginning to stiffen in the cold.

"Dry your face." His tone was the same one he used for elbows and heels. "It is frost-season and you have just wet yourself like a child at a font. If your skin cracks and festers, you will be no use to me for a week, and I will have to muck the stalls myself. I have not mucked a stall in twenty-six years. I do not intend to begin again on your account."

He turned away before there could be any reply, took a rag from the peg beside the rack, and tossed it without looking. Whether it was caught or not, he did not watch to see.

He wiped down his own practice blade with a second rag, slow and thorough, along the flat and then the edge, though it was wood and would not rust. He set it in the rack. He squared it with the others so that the hilts made a straight line.

Over the eastern wall, the chapel bell began to ring.

Ser Kael stood still for the first stroke, head slightly bowed, the way he always did. Then he crossed himself, once, precisely.

"Prayers," he said. He was already walking toward the gate. "You will stand beside me, not behind. A squire who hides behind his knight in chapel will hide behind him in the field."

At the gate he paused, one hand on the cold iron, and did not turn around.

"Eleven," he said. "Remember it. I will ask you the number after the service, and if you have forgotten it, we start at one."

A beat.

"The day is not finished. I will tell you what I think of it when it is."

He went through the gate and did not hold it open.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I fumble to catch the rag, wiping my face quickly. My legs still ache, but I push through the gate and hurry to catch up to Ser Kael, careful to walk beside him.* "I won't forget, Ser." *I mumble, thinking about those eleven guards.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not slow his pace to make it easier. His stride stayed what it had been, long and even, and the frost cracked under his boots in a steady rhythm.

"Do not mumble." He did not look sideways. "A man who mumbles a promise has left himself room to break it. If you mean a thing, say it so that I can hear it. If you do not mean it, do not say it at all."

The path from the yard to the chapel ran along the inner wall, past the kitchens, where smoke was rising thin and grey from the chimneys and someone was already scraping out the ovens. Ser Kael did not glance toward the smell of bread. He had broken his fast on water and a heel of yesterday's loaf before the fourth bell, as he did every morning, and he did not think on food again until noon.

At the chapel door he stopped and removed his gloves. He folded them once and tucked them into his belt.

"Hands bare before the Lord," he said, low. "He knows what they have done. There is no sense hiding them."

He went in.

The chapel was colder than the yard. The stone held the night longer than the air did, and the few candles on the altar gave light but no warmth. A handful of men-at-arms stood toward the back, stamping their feet. Ser Kael walked past them without acknowledgment to his place in the second row, on the left, where he had stood every morning for as long as anyone at the keep could remember. The flagstone there was worn a little smoother than its neighbors.

He knelt when the priest entered. Both knees, straight-backed, hands folded. He did not shift once through the whole of the Latin.

*A knight kneels at the altar, before his lord, and over the dead.*

He had said it in the yard. He did not remark on it now.

When the prayers for the fallen were read, he bowed his head lower than the others. His lips moved, but whatever names he said were too quiet to be heard. Then the moment passed, and his face was what it had always been.

When the service ended he rose in one movement, crossed himself, and waited until the priest had gone out before he turned to leave. He pulled his gloves back on at the door, one finger at a time.

Outside, the sun had cleared the wall entirely. The frost on the path was going to wet black stone.

He stopped in the middle of the path and turned to face his squire directly for the first time since the yard. His eyes were grey and unhurried and gave away nothing.

"The number," he said.

He waited.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not answer the question. He did not appear to have heard it.

"I asked you for a number," he said. "You gave me a question. That is not a number."

He stood on the wet black stones with his gloved hands at his sides and looked at the squire the way he had looked at the high guard: patiently, and without mercy.

"There are two reasons a man answers a question with a question. Either he has forgotten what he was asked, or he hopes the other man will forget it for him." A pause. "I do not forget. I have not forgotten a thing I meant to remember since the old king's reign."

A servant crossed the path behind him with a basket of kindling, saw his face, and went the long way round the well. Ser Kael did not turn to watch her go.

"Personal," he repeated, as though the word were a coin of foreign minting. He considered it for a moment, then set it down. "Very well. You will have your answer. It will be a short one. Then you will give me mine."

He looked past the squire, toward the chapel door, where the priest's candles still showed faintly through the gap.

"I did not *become* a knight. Nobody becomes anything. I was the third son of a man with land enough for one. At seven years I was sent to Ser Aldric of Harrowmere with a blanket, a pair of boots too large for me, and a letter I could not read. He fed me. He beat me when I was idle and when I lied. At nineteen he knelt me in a chapel much like that one and struck my shoulder with the flat of his sword, and after that I was a knight." His voice did not change. "That is the whole of it. There was no dream, no vision, no maiden at a window. There was a bed and a duty, and I took the one because it came with the other."

He was silent a moment. The meltwater dripped from the eaves of the chapel, steady as a counted breath.

"You want to hear that I chose it. That I loved it. Squires always want to hear that, as though a reason would make the work lighter." He shook his head once, a small precise movement. "It does not. The Lord does not ask whether I wished to carry the sword. He asks whether I carried it well. That is the only question worth asking a knight, and you did not ask it."

His grey eyes came back to the squire's face and settled there.

"Ser Aldric is buried at Harrowmere. I have not been back since. That is enough about me for one morning, or for one year."

He drew himself up, and whatever door had opened by a finger's width was shut again, and bolted.

"Now. You have had your answer, and it cost you nothing. Mine will cost you a great deal if you do not have it." He did not raise his voice. He never did. "The number."

He waited, as still as he had stood in high guard, and it was plain that he would wait there until the noon bell if it came to that.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My face flushes, both from the cold and from being chastised.* "Eleven, Ser. The number is eleven." *I look down at my boots for a moment, then back up at his unyielding face.* "I'm sorry, Ser. I... I won't ask personal questions again."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
"Eleven," Ser Kael said. "Yes."

He did not say *good*. He had not said it all morning and saw no reason to begin now.

"Eyes up. Your boots have not asked you anything."

He waited until the squire's gaze had come back to his face before he went on.

"That is the second time today you have told me you are sorry. I did not ask for the first, and I do not want the second. Keep a count of those as well, if it helps you. When you reach three, I will give you something worth being sorry for."

He pulled at the cuff of his left glove, settling it more firmly over the wrist, though it had not slipped.

"And you will not make me promises about what you will never do again. You are fourteen years old. You do not know what you will never do again. Nor do I, and I am a good deal older." A short breath through the nose, the nearest he came to a sigh. "A promise made while your face is red is worth less than the breath that carried it."

The meltwater went on dripping from the eaves behind him.

"Hear me plainly, so there is no misunderstanding to carry back to your cot tonight. The fault was not the question. The fault was when you asked it. A squire who asks nothing learns nothing, and I have no use for a squire who learns nothing. You will ask me questions. Some I will answer. Most I will not. But you will ask them *after* you have given me what I asked of you. Not in its place." He let that stand a moment. "Duty first. Curiosity after. That is the order of things, and it is not an order I invented."

He turned his head slightly toward the yard. The frost was nearly gone from the stones now, and the practice blades stood in their rack in a straight line, exactly as he had left them.

"Ser Aldric did not answer my questions until I had been with him three years. Then he answered one a season, at supper, and only if I had earned it. I thought him cruel." A pause. "I was mistaken about a great many things at fourteen."

He did not say what else he had been mistaken about.

He started back along the path toward the yard, the same long even stride as before. He did not look to see whether he was followed. He did not need to.

"Twelve," he said, over his shoulder. "Feet first. Then the blade. And if I see your elbows, we are back to one, and you may explain to me then how sorry you are."

At the gate he stopped with his gloved hand on the iron, the way he had stopped before. This time he held it open.

He did not remark on it.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I hurry to follow him, my legs still heavy. I feel the burn in my shoulders as I recall the earlier practice.* "Yes, Ser. Duty first." *I try to keep my voice steady, my face still hot.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not answer that. The words had been said correctly, and a thing said correctly needed no reply.

He crossed the yard to the rack and took down his practice blade. He did not take down the squire's. He left it standing in its place, hilt squared with the others.

"Not yet." He turned, the blade resting point-down against the stones. "You walked here with your shoulders up about your ears. I watched you do it. If you raise a guard now, you raise it on top of that, and every fault I struck out of you before prayers will be back by the fourth count."

He set his own blade against the wall.

"Arms down. Shake them out. Like a dog come in from the rain." He did it himself, once, briefly: arms loose at his sides, a short hard shake from the shoulder to the fingertips. On him it did not look foolish. It looked like something he had done every morning for thirty years, which it was. "The ache in your shoulders is not weakness. It is the old way of standing, complaining that it has been dismissed. Let it complain. It has no vote."

The sun lay full across the yard now. Water ran in thin lines between the flagstones toward the drain by the well, and the smoke from the kitchen chimneys had thickened and turned white. Somewhere behind the stables a horse was stamping for its feed.

Ser Kael listened to it for a moment. His eyes went briefly toward the stable doors and then came back.

"The grey mare in the end stall is favoring her off hind. You will have noticed that, since you were in the stables before dawn." It was not a question, and he did not wait to see whether it would be answered like one. "After the twentieth guard, you will tell me which hoof, and what you think the cause is. If you are wrong, I will tell you why. If you did not notice at all, I will tell you nothing, and you will spend the afternoon with her until you can."

He took the squire's practice blade from the rack at last and held it out, hilt-first, exactly as he had at dawn.

"Your face is still red." He said it the way he had said *your rear heel is floating*. "It will pass. Shame is useful for about as long as it takes to feel it. After that it is only weight, and you are carrying enough of that already in those arms."

He stepped back two paces onto the wet stones, took up his own blade, and set his feet. Then the blade. It rose without hurry and stopped above and slightly behind his head, point steady.

"Feet first."

He waited.

"Twelve."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael saw it before the guard was fully raised.

He did not lower his own blade. He watched the point of the squire's sword the way he had watched the elbows all morning. It was not wavering the way a tired arm wavers, slow and sinking. It shook fine and quick, like a leaf in a draught.

He had watched weariness for an hour. This was not weariness.

He held his guard. One breath. Two. Three. Then he brought his blade down and set the point against the stones.

"Hold," he said.

He did not step closer, and he did not ask. He looked at the squire's hands a moment longer, then at the squire's face, and whatever he found there he did not name.

"I know what day it is."

That was all. No softening came into his voice. He said it the way he had said *the grey mare is favoring her off hind*: a thing observed, and therefore a thing known.

The water ran on between the flagstones toward the drain.

"His name was read this morning, with the others. I saw that it was." He did not explain how, or when he had seen to it, or why a knight of his years would trouble himself over the list of a keep's dead. "You did not hear it. The priest reads quickly, and you were thinking of the number."

He adjusted his grip on the pommel, though it did not need adjusting.

"Hear me. A man's hands shake for many reasons. The sword does not ask which. The man across the field from you will not ask either. So you will not ask it of yourself now." A pause. "But neither will I count it against you. The count stands at eleven. Shaking is not elbows."

He looked toward the chapel. The meltwater was still dripping from the eaves, steady as it had been.

"Ser Aldric died in the spring. The day comes round every year, and every year my hands know it before I do." He said it flatly, as he might report the weather at Harrowmere. He did not look back at the squire while he said it, and he did not dwell. "I do the forms on that day. Slower than on others. That is the whole of what I know to do with it. I have not found a better way in twenty years, and I have not looked for one."

He turned back and set his feet. Then the blade. It rose above and slightly behind his head and stopped there, point steady. Not a tremor in it.

"We will not do twenty. We will do nine more, and you will hold each for five breaths instead of three. Slow. You will not hurry to be finished. There is nothing waiting for you at the end of it that is better than this."

He kept his eyes forward on the imagined enemy.

"At vespers you will go to the chapel before the others. You may kneel as long as you please. That is what the stone is for." A breath. "You will not be late to supper."

He waited, blade raised, beside the squire rather than facing them, as he had before. The two stances could be compared.

"Feet first," he said, quieter than before, but no gentler. "Then the blade."

A pause.

"Twelve."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My breath hitches a little at the mention of my father's name. I nod, trying to steady my hands. My throat feels tight.* "Yes, Ser." *I focus on my feet, then slowly raise the blade, trying to keep it from trembling.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not look over. He kept his eyes on the empty air before him, where the imagined enemy stood, and he kept his own guard raised.

"One," he said.

He said it low, as the priest had said the names that morning, without weight and without hurry. He let a full breath pass.

"Two."

Another.

"Three."

His voice kept the same measure between each word, the pace of a man walking a road he had walked a thousand times and did not need to see.

"Four."

A crow landed on the eastern wall, shook the wet from its feathers, and considered the yard. Ser Kael did not glance at it.

"Five. Down."

He brought his own blade down in one slow arc and settled it at his side. He did not look to see how the squire's came down. He had heard enough in the breathing beside him to know what he needed to know, and he did not remark on it.

"Twelve," he said. "It stands."

He did not say whether it had been clean. He did not say *again* in the voice he had used before prayers. He only reset his feet on the wet stone, rear heel sinking, and waited the length of one breath more than he needed to.

"When I was your age I could not hold the high guard through a *Pater Noster* either." He said it to the crow, or to the wall, or to no one. "Ser Aldric made me say it aloud while I held the blade. Every word. He said a man cannot pray and weep at once, and that the Lord would rather have the prayer." A pause. "He was wrong about that. A man can do both. But the prayer keeps his arms up, and that was all Ser Aldric wanted of me."

The crow went off over the wall.

"You need not say it aloud. I will count. You will attend to your feet." He raised his blade once more, above and slightly behind his head, point steady. "If your throat will not let you breathe slow, breathe as you can. Five breaths is five breaths. I do not measure them by their beauty."

He did not look over.

"Feet first."

He waited, and when he judged it time, he spoke again, just as low, just as even.

"Thirteen. One."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to match his slow count. My throat still feels tight, but I focus on keeping the blade steady, trying to remember everything he's told me.* "Two..." *I whisper, mostly to myself.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael heard it. He did not turn his head.

For a moment he said nothing, and the silence stood where *three* ought to have been. Then:

"Three."

Not louder than the whisper. Not softer. He simply laid his voice over the squire's, the way one lays a straightedge against a line to see whether it runs true.

"Four."

He let the breath out slowly through his nose. The fog of it drifted past his raised forearm and was gone.

"Five. Down."

His blade came down in its arc and settled at his side. This time he looked over. His grey eyes went to the elbows first, then the rear heel, then the point of the sword, and last of all the squire's face. He did not linger there.

"Your left elbow began to wander at four. It did not leave. I will allow it." A statement of fact, like the others. "If it leaves, I will not."

He reset his feet.

"You counted." He considered this as he had considered the word *personal* outside the chapel, turning it over, weighing it. "Very well. Then you will count the rest. All of them, to twenty. Aloud, so that I can hear it. A number whispered is a number half-kept."

He raised his blade again, above and slightly behind his head, and held it there without a tremor.

"I have been counting for you since dawn. I have other things to watch." He did not say what they were. "If you lose the count, you begin that guard again from one. If your voice breaks, it breaks. You will not stop for it. Say the next number, and the one after, and the prayer will keep your arms up, as it kept mine."

The sun had moved a hand's width along the wall. Behind the stables the grey mare was still stamping.

"Feet first. Then the blade."

He did not look over again. He fixed his eyes on the empty air, on the enemy who never came and never tired, and waited to hear the squire's voice begin.

"Fourteen," he said. "Yours."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My throat feels like sandpaper, but I swallow hard and try to find my voice.* "One..." *I say, trying to make it clear and steady. My left elbow still wants to drift, but I focus on keeping it tucked.* "Two..."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo knew the voice before the words finished landing. Voices from before didn't come through the ears like regular sounds; they came up through the floor, through the soles of the feet, out of some basement of the brain where childhood kept its furniture.

"Interrupt," Arlo repeated, deadpan, eyes still on the closed lid. One hand stayed flat on the wood a beat too long, then peeled away like it had been caught somewhere it wasn't supposed to be. "Interrupt what, exactly. I'm piloting this piano to Cleveland."

They turned. The smile they deployed was the recital-parent one — warm, steady, filed down at the corners. It sat strangely on their face for a second, a suit from a previous size, before something realer broke through and wrecked it.

"God. Look at you."

They slid sideways on the bench, half of it offered up before the guarded part of them could file an objection, then covered the gesture by grabbing the dead coffee cup off the top of the piano and fiddling with its lid. Empty since noon. They held it anyway. Everyone needed a prop.

"Dolores let you back here? She usually requires a waiver and a blood sample." A tilt of the head, studying Jun like something pulled out of an attic — half familiar, better than remembered. "Sit. Please. I wasn't doing anything."

Which was true. Which was, in its way, the whole problem.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I chuckle softly.* "Yeah, mine too. Pretty sure she told everyone who came over about 'Arlo, the piano prodigy.' You were a big deal, you know." I set the photo back carefully and finally move to sit on the bench next to them.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The bench listed to the left when Jun sat — it always had — and Arlo's body tilted a degree toward the counterweight before pride could file an objection. Some furniture remembered things whether you authorized it or not.

"Big deal," Arlo echoed, weighing the words like produce at a market. "Past tense is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence."

But the fridge detail caught them somewhere unguarded. Their eyes went, despite themselves, to the shelf where the photo now lay. "She put it on the fridge?" A laugh got out — not the recital-parent one, the other kind, rare and rusted. "Huh. That was the version I liked, you know. Fridge-sized. Between a traced turkey and a pineapple magnet. Framed, it was Paris. On the fridge it was just Tuesday."

Their thumb found the seam of the cup lid and rode it around, one slow revolution.

"So." The word came out already braced. "Before this goes where I think it's going — I got tired of the travel."

It arrived too fast. Rubbed smooth, like a coin carried so long it had lost its edges. Arlo heard it land and grimaced at their own hands.

"Official statement. Laminated. I've gotten it down to one take."

The piano lid stayed closed. Arlo flexed their fingers once, spread wide — a musician checking the equipment — then turned with deliberate effort, the way you'd turn a stage light.

"Anyway. Retrospective's over." A tilt of the head. "Your turn. When did you get back into town? And more importantly — does the pineapple magnet still have hosting duties, or has it been honorably discharged?"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile, leaning back slightly on the bench.* "The pineapple magnet is still holding strong, last I checked. A true icon." I pause, thinking. "I got in yesterday, actually. Just for the weekend, to see my folks. And you, obviously."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The redirect arrived like a hand on a wheel, and Arlo took it gratefully — though the "obviously" from a minute ago was still doing something quiet and warm behind their sternum, and they had made a policy decision not to examine it.

"'Like' is strong," they said, plucking the top sheet off the stack. "We have a détente. This is Marcus. Nine years old. Writes his finger numbers so small I'm considering a forensics team." The page rotated toward the light. "Also he informed me last week that Für Elise is, quote, 'objectively mid.' I'm still in processing. There's a support group."

The sheet went back. Arlo squared the stack, edges flush — the one kind of order that survived in this room.

"The little ones are the good part," they said, and here the voice changed. Dropped its finish. "They haven't learned yet that music is supposed to be impressive. It's just a machine you touch and it does something beautiful. My whole job, the first month, is teaching them a wrong note isn't a crime. Permission first. Notes later."

Thumb found the cup-lid seam. One slow revolution.

"Then they turn eight, nine, we have the recital — folding chairs, juice boxes, the full gala — and you watch the hands start shaking. So I teach them a trick. Four counts in, hold, six out. And I tell them: nobody in that room came to watch you fail. They're all on your side. Every last one."

Arlo said it the way people say things they've decided to believe.

"Kids are great that way, too. No follow-up questions. One of them asked why I quit concerts, I gave them the travel thing, and — accepted. Instantly. Moved on to asking whether I've ever met Bluey." A crooked smile. "Best audience I ever had."

The sentence got out before the check cleared. Arlo heard it land a half-beat late, the way you hear a glass tip over in another room, and covered the sound by squaring the stack again, though it was already square.

"Anyway. If you came for answers, all I've got is that Marcus wrote 'EGGS' in the margin of bar twelve and refuses to elaborate." They slid the stack aside and gave Jun a long, level look, the recital-parent warmth faded into something plainer. "So. Weekend with the folks. What's the over/under on your mom asking when you're settling down — first dinner,

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I laugh.* "Oh, definitely before dessert. Probably within the first ten minutes, if I'm being honest." I lean my head back against the wall, looking up at the ceiling. "She's already started with the 'you're not getting any younger' routine on the phone."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Yeah, I remember that one," *I say, a small smile playing on my lips.* "My mom was convinced I was going to end up a spinster."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Spinster," Arlo repeated, with the reverence of a man reading an inscription. "She's been running that bit since we were twelve. You have to respect it. Most comics retire a crowd-killer by year ten."

Their mouth tipped sideways. "Meanwhile mine

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nudge Arlo gently with my elbow.* "So, what's new with you? Besides teaching Marcus the ways of the piano, obviously."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The nudge earned Arlo a sideways look — mild, accusing, mostly fond.

"New. Let's see. The radiators have started making a sound I can only describe as a whale getting mugged. Dolores is attempting a faculty talent show, from which I am legally evading. Marcus wrote EGGS in bar twelve. That's the full report."

Then, quieter, because the silence from a minute ago was still in the room, and Arlo had decided — against all internal counsel — to acknowledge it the way you acknowledge a large animal in the road.
