"You didn't ask. Back there. When I handed you the laminated statement." The thumb found the cup-lid seam one more time, then stopped, and for the first time all afternoon the cup got set down for good. "The recital parents do it in whispers, like I'm a Victorian widow. You just sat there. Six years I've kept an answer polished for that question and you didn't even want it." A breath. "I don't know what to do with that. It's deeply inconvenient."

They shrugged, and it overshot casual. "What's actually new is I've been letting the kids out early. You noticed the land speed on that last one. I tell myself it's kindness — sunlight, childhood, et cetera. Mostly I like the room empty. Nobody watching, nothing to get wrong."

Arlo heard it land and, this once, didn't bother covering the sound. Just let it sit a beat, then flicked it away. "Fortune cookie from a haunted house. Disregard."

The hands went to the latch on their own — the brain still filing objections when the lid came up. Arlo looked at the keys a second longer than the music required. Steady. The hands were always steady. That was the punchline of the decade, probably.

The left hand dropped and started the old loop — three chords, the bottom of Heart and Soul. Low, careful of the thin walls.

"You know the melody part," they said, eyes on the keys, giving Jun the privacy of that. "First thing they teach you, last thing you forget. And you owe me, anyway. The summer you went to camp, I had to play both parts."

The loop came around again. Again.

"Four counts in, hold, six out. Come in whenever." A crooked almost-smile, still aimed downward. "I'll keep the floor."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch their hands for a moment, then slide closer on the bench.* "I remember." *I start playing the melody, a little rusty at first, but it comes back quickly. The familiar tune fills the room.*

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I play through a couple of rounds, then hesitate.* "You know," *I say, looking at Arlo,* "I think I like this version better. Just us. No pressure."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
"Pressure," Arlo repeated, to the chords. The left hand didn't stumble — the left hand hadn't stumbled at anything in six years, which was the whole gag — but it changed. Went from playing to being played carefully. Every note suddenly checked at the door.

"Technically you're right, though. Pressure needs a surface to push on. There's nobody in this room but you, me, and forty years of dust." A shrug kept time with the bass line. "You've rendered it unemployed."

But they let a round of the loop go by without talking after that, which, for Arlo, was practically a soliloquy.

"You know, this was the original arrangement," they said eventually, eyes on the middle of the keyboard, the territory their hands couldn't enter without trespassing. "Before 'prodigy' was a word anyone aimed at me. Nobody played alone. Somebody on the floor, somebody on the tune, didn't matter which. Nobody's mother filmed it."

The loop came around again.

"Alone was the promotion. That's the part they leave off the poster. Congratulations — you've worked hard enough that nobody has to be up there with you anymore."

It came out level. Everything out of Arlo came out level; that was the finish, the lacquer. Then, folded into the phrase so smoothly only someone watching for it would ever catch it — four counts in, hold, six out, through the nose. Their own trick. Prescribed for nine-year-olds with shaking hands, self-administered on the downbeat of Heart and Soul, in an empty room, next to the one person who might notice.

They kept their eyes on the keys either way.

"Anyway." Quieter now. The recital-parent finish was gone; this was just the voice under it, the basement furniture one. "For the record — I like this version too. The acoustics are terrible and the radiator's hosting a hostage situation. Best hall I've ever played."

There it was. Closest they'd come to the vault all afternoon, and they didn't lock it. Just let the loop come around again, and again, keeping the floor — in no hurry at all to give the song anywhere to end.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I keep playing the melody, letting the simple tune fill the space, feeling the familiar rhythm. A small smile plays on my lips.* "Yeah," *I say softly, my voice blending with the music.* "Me too."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room smelled faintly of dust and the dry, papery scent of old books. The curtains were drawn, though a narrow strip of afternoon light had found its way through and lay across the shelves.

The books were still arranged as they had been for years: the tall ones at either end, the smaller volumes crowded together in the middle. On the lowest shelf, a space had been left between two hardbacks. It was too narrow for another book.

A thin layer of dust covered the shelf except for that gap. There, the wood was clean.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I eye the clean spot on the shelf. That's odd.* "What did she keep there?" I murmur, reaching out to touch the dust-free wood.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The wood beneath the fingertips was colder than the rest of the room. A shallow rectangle showed in the clean patch, its edges too crisp to have been made by a book. Dust had gathered along one side in a fine ridge, as if something had been lifted away recently.

The space between the hardbacks remained too narrow for anything that shape. On the shelf above, one book sat a little crooked. Its title was hidden against the wall.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The bat passed through the shadow and struck the baseboard with a dull, wooden knock. A little dust stirred along the floor.

The corner stayed dim. On the wall beside it, the shadow of the bat lingered for a moment after the bat had moved away. Then it settled into place, though nothing in the room seemed to have changed.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the corner, then back at the bat in my hand.* "Okay, Gabi. You're losing it." *I lean the bat back in the stand, feeling a bit foolish.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The bat’s handle clicked softly against the umbrella stand. In the corner, the darkness looked ordinary again.

The crooked book on the shelf had shifted farther out, just enough for its title to show: *A Field Guide to Household Plants*. Dust marked the cover everywhere except along its spine, where a clean, narrow line ran from top to bottom.

From the hallway, the clock gave a single tick. The next one came a little later than it should have.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I glance at the clock, then back at the book.* "Plants? Really, Grandma?" *I pull the "Field Guide" from the shelf, noticing the clean spine.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The book came free with a faint rasp. Its spine was clean, but the top edge wore a fine coat of dust, as if it had been handled without ever being taken down.

It opened in the middle. A brittle fern had been pressed between the pages, its fronds flattened against an illustration of maidenhair. Beside the drawing, someone had penciled a small mark in the margin: a neat rectangle, no larger than a photograph.

Behind the book, the wall was unmarked. The narrow space where it had stood held a stale, cool smell, like the air inside a drawer kept shut for years.

From the hallway came another tick. This one sounded closer than the clock was.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The offer carried into the hallway and up the stairs. It came back thinner, stripped of its familiar shape by the quiet.

Nothing answered.

In the living room, the fern between the pages gave a dry little crackle. One brittle frond had shifted across the illustration, covering the penciled rectangle.

The clock ticked once from the hallway.

A moment later, something in the house ticked back.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *My eyes dart around the room, then land on the fern in the book.* "Alright, alright, I hear you." *I carefully remove the fern from the book, setting it on the nearest clear surface.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The fern came away in two brittle pieces. One rested on the table; the other left a dust-fine trace across the page.

Beneath it, the penciled rectangle was still there. Inside its outline, the paper had yellowed less than the surrounding page, as if something small had been laid over it for a long time.

The hallway clock ticked.

On the table, the fern’s shadow pointed toward the book’s spine. The afternoon light fell from the opposite direction.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I frown at the shadow, then at the book.* This is getting weirder. I flip through the book, looking for other marks or anything else out of place.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The pages whispered dryly beneath her fingers. Most held the usual notes—watering dates, light, a few names written in the narrow margins. Near the back, three penciled rectangles appeared beside different entries, each the size of the mark beside the maidenhair.

The first was next to a drawing of ivy. The second, beside a drawing of a fern. The third had no plant name beside it. Its page was otherwise blank.

A faint gray outline showed within that last rectangle, as though a photograph had once rested there. The paper inside it was slightly raised.

From the hallway, the clock ticked. In the book, a loose page settled with a soft tap, though no draft stirred the curtains.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph fit the penciled rectangle exactly. Marcus stood beside a row of potted plants, young and handsome in the unguarded way old photographs sometimes preserved. His expression was easy to like.

On the back, her grandmother had written his name and a date. Beneath it, in smaller writing, were the words: *He said he never came back.*

The paper inside the book’s rectangle lay flat now. On the page beside it, the blank margin had a faint impression, as if someone had once pressed a pencil there and written hard.

The hallway clock ticked. The photograph gave a tiny, papery creak against the table.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I gently pick up the photo, tracing Marcus's face with my thumb.* "Grandma, what were you up to?" *I look at the impression on the page beside it, then back at the photo.* "Never came back from where?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph’s surface was cool beneath her thumb. Marcus’s face remained clear, though the fine silvering at the edges had begun to cloud.

The impressed marks beside the blank rectangle sharpened in the slant of afternoon light. They were not a plant name. A few words had been pressed hard into the page, perhaps from a note written above it:

*He came back once.*

The page gave a soft, dry click as it settled. On the back of the photograph, the date looked suddenly less like a date than a time—its final figure faint beneath the ink.

From the hallway, the clock ticked.

This time, the sound came from the living room.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I jump, dropping the photo on the floor.* "What was that?!" *I snatch the photo back up, heart pounding.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph was back in her hand. Its lower corner had bent against the floor, leaving a pale crease through the date on its reverse.

The tick came again from the living room—not from the clock in the hall. It sounded close to the book, then stopped.

In the photograph, Marcus stood beside the potted plants. The crease crossed the date, but the final figure showed clearly now.

It was the same as the hour on the hallway clock.

From the hall came a delayed tick. Somewhere in the house, something answered.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the photo, then at the book, then at the clock in the hall. My breath hitches.* "Okay, this is officially too much."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room was colder than the hallway, though the windows were shut and the radiators along the wall gave off a thin, steady heat. The books waited on the low table in front of the sofa, stacked with their spines out, the way she had always left them when she was sorting. The top one lay open. Its page held no print—only the faint, backward impression of letters, as if something had been pressed through from the other side and then taken away.

A fern by the window had been turned so its fronds faced the wall. From the kitchen the clock kept its even measure, and between two ticks there was a smaller sound, dry and brief, like a page settling in a room where no one was touching the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content:
*I shiver, rubbing my arms.* It's always cold in here.

I walk over to the fern and turn it back toward the window. "What are you doing, little guy?" I murmur.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The words left no answer in the room. The fern stayed where it had been set, fronds toward the glass, though one of the lower ones had already begun to curl inward, away from the light, as if the turn had not quite taken. The cold did not ease when the radiator ticked. It sat against the skin of the forearms and did not move with the rubbing.

On the table, the open book had closed itself by a finger’s width. The page that showed now was blank on both sides. From the hallway the clock kept time, and under it, nearer than the kitchen, the dry sound came again—one soft settling, then nothing, as if a hand had lifted from a page and not yet decided whether to turn it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The umbrella stand gave up a bat that was lighter than memory suggested, the grip worn smooth by someone else’s hand. The swing passed through the corner and met nothing that could be struck—no give, no shape, only the dull rush of air and the soft knock of the tip against the baseboard, which sounded once and stopped.

The corner was wall, and the edge of the curtain, and the ordinary dark that corners keep. Whatever had seemed to gather there was not the sort of thing a bat could find. The cold stayed on the arms. On the table the blank book had opened again to the page with the backward impression, and the impression sat a little deeper than before, as if pressure had been applied while the swing was still in the air.

From the hallway the clock ticked, then did not, then did. The dry sound did not come. The room waited, unchanged in every way that could be named, and the bat hung at the end of its arc with nowhere left to go.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I drop the bat with a clatter. "Okay, Gabi. You're losing it." I rub my temples. This house is getting to me.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The clatter of the bat went farther than the room should have allowed. It struck the floorboards, rang once against the baseboard, and then seemed to continue a moment longer in the hallway, a thin metal note arriving late, as if the house had kept a piece of the sound and returned it from the wrong direction.

Nothing answered the words. The radiators ticked. The cold stayed where it was, against the skin at the temples, not moving when the fingers did.

On the low table the book had closed again. Not all the way—just enough that the backward letters were gone and the edge of the cover caught the light from the window in a thin pale line. The fern by the glass had one frond turned outward now, toward the room, though the rest still faced the wall. It had not been touched.

From the kitchen the clock kept its measure. Between two ticks the dry sound came, nearer than before, not in the living room and not quite in the hall: the soft settling of a page, and then the small, ordinary creak of a floorboard taking weight in a place where no one was standing.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: My eyes dart to the hallway. "Hello?" I call out, my voice a little shaky. *I pick up the bat again, holding it defensively.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The call went out and did not come back. The hallway held it for a moment—the shape of the word against the wallpaper, the faint echo off the clock’s glass—and then let it go. Nothing stepped forward to meet it. The floorboard that had taken weight did not take it again. Whatever had stood there, if anything had, was not standing there now, and the quiet that followed was the ordinary quiet of an empty house, except that it arrived half a second late, as if it had been waiting to see whether the word would be repeated.

The bat was in the hands again. Its weight was the same as before: too light, the grip worn by someone else’s palm. It pointed down the hall at a stretch of runner and the dark rectangle of the kitchen doorway, and none of those things offered a place for it to land. The cold had moved. It was no longer only on the arms. It sat at the back of the neck, a small, precise chill, the size of a fingertip just above the collar.

On the low table behind, the book’s cover had settled flat. A corner of one page showed, not blank this time—there was a single line of type, set very small, and turned the wrong way to be read from where anyone was standing. The fern’s outward frond had curled all the way under, so that only its pale underside faced the room.

The clock in the hallway ticked. Then it ticked again, and between the two there was no smaller sound at all, which was its own kind of wrongness: the absence of the dry page-settling, as if the hand that had been turning pages had stopped, and was listening.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The offer went out into the hallway and found no one to take it. No answer came back, and no laugh either—only the wallpaper holding the shape of the words for a moment longer than it should have, then letting them thin out against the runner. The quiet that followed was not the quiet of a room that had heard a joke. It was the quiet of a room that had been listening for something else, and had not heard it.

The bat stayed in the hands. Its tip pointed at the kitchen doorway, which did not change. The cold at the back of the neck did not lift. It sat there, small and precise, as if a fingertip had paused just above the collar and had not yet decided to withdraw.

On the low table the single line of type had turned. It faced the room now, set very small, and it was not a sentence that belonged to any book that had been left out for sorting. The letters were the right way around. They were also, unmistakably, the last few words that had just been called into the hall—only the spacing was wrong, pressed too close, as if whoever had set them had been in a hurry and had not quite finished.

The fern’s pale underside still faced the room. From the hallway the clock ticked once. It did not tick again. In the space where the next tick should have been, a floorboard in the kitchen took a careful, ordinary weight, and then held it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: My eyes go wide as I stare at the book. *I drop the bat again with a clang.* "No. No, no, no." I back away slowly, towards the front door.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The retreat did not shorten the hall. The runner stretched under the afternoon light with one more repeat of its pattern than the distance to the door had ever required, and the dark wood of the front door sat at the end of it without coming nearer. The cold remained a fingertip’s width above the collar, traveling neither ahead nor behind.

In the kitchen the held weight shifted by a single board, closer to the doorway, and then held again. No tick followed. No page settled. On the low table the line of type did not lengthen and did not fade; it only sat there, pressed too close, facing the room, while one corner of the page lifted and stayed lifted though the curtains did not move. The bat’s clang had already gone on ahead. It waited, thin and metallic, against the inside of the front door, as if the house had set it down there and left it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I turn and bolt for the door. *My hand fumbles for the knob.* "I'm out of here."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The knob turned a quarter inch and stopped. There was no lock to meet it, only the settled weight of the door against its frame, as if the wood had decided, quietly, not to move. The thin metal note that had gone on ahead was still there, pressed to the inside of the panel, neither fading nor repeating.

The runner lay at its proper length now. The cold remained a fingertip’s width above the collar and did not travel with the reach. From the kitchen the held weight shifted one board closer to the hall, then held again. No tick followed.

Around the corner, on the low table, a page lifted and did not settle. The sound of it arrived late, dry and brief, and carried with it the shape of the last words that had been spoken in the hall—pressed too close, unfinished, and facing the room.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The thought did not take. It arrived, and the room let it thin out against the wallpaper the way it had let the other words thin, and nothing in the house answered it with warmth or with any picture of a man still living somewhere else.

The photograph was on the kitchen table with the rest, the envelope nudged that same inch to the left. Marcus stood at the edge of a garden the way people stand when they have agreed to be photographed and would rather not. The face was his. The eyes were not looking at the camera. They were set a little past it, toward whoever had been holding the thing, and the set of them had not changed in all the years the paper had been kept. On the back, in a hand that was not the grandmother’s, someone had written a name and then stopped. The last letters were pressed too close, unfinished, and they were not his name.

The cold stayed a fingertip’s width above the collar. From the doorway the held weight did not shift and did not leave. No tick came. The page in the living room remained lifted, and the dry sound of it did not settle, as if the house had heard the thought and had simply gone on listening for something else.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I drop the photo like it's hot.* "What the hell?" I grab a broom from beside the door and start whacking at the doorknob. "Open, you stupid door!"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The broom met the knob, and the sound that returned was not the sound of wood on brass. It was smaller, drier, and it arrived a half-second late, as if it had been carried into another room and sent back diminished. The knob did not turn. It did not shiver. The quarter-inch of give it had offered before was gone; the metal sat flush and faintly warm, warmer than the air, and the warmth did not spread into the wood.

Each strike landed and was taken. The door stayed shut against its frame with the same settled weight. The thin metal note already waiting on the inside of the panel did not join the new sounds. It remained where it was, separate.

From the kitchen the held weight shifted one board closer to the hall and then held again. It did not hurry. Between the blows—while the broom was still lifted, before the next dull contact—a page in the living room lifted and did not settle. The dry sound of it came late, and with it the shape of the words just put into the hallway, pressed too close, unfinished, facing the room.

The clock did not tick. The cold had moved down from the neck and sat, precise, between the shoulder blades. It did not lift when the arms did. The next strike found the knob already still. Nothing in the hallway had changed its mind.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: "What do you want?!" I scream, tears starting to sting my eyes. *I drop the broom and sink to the floor, my back against the door.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The scream thinned against the wallpaper and was not returned. No answer formed in the hall, and the quiet that followed arrived a half-second late, as if it had paused to be sure the question would not be asked again.

The broom struck the runner and the sound of it went on ahead, small and dry, and settled against the kitchen doorway instead of the floor. The cold remained between the shoulder blades, precise, and did not ease when the back met the door. The wood was faintly warm where the shoulders rested, warmer than the air, and the warmth did not spread.

From the kitchen the held weight shifted one board nearer the hall and then held. It did not come into view. No tick followed. On the low table a page lifted and stayed lifted; the dry sound of it came late, carrying the shape of the words just put into the hallway—pressed too close, unfinished, and facing the room. The fern’s pale underside had not moved. The clock’s glass held the afternoon light and gave nothing back.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I bury my face in my hands.* "Please," I whisper, my voice cracking. "Just tell me what you want. Or let me out."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael finished the form before he spoke. The blade swept down through its last arc, held for a breath, and stilled. Only then did he turn.

"Stable work is your duty," he said. "You do not announce duties as though they were accomplishments."

He returned the practice blade to the rack and drew a second one, testing its weight once in his grip.

"You did not get the high guard right yesterday. I know. I stood four paces away and watched it fail three times. The question is not whether you failed. Squires fail. The question is *where*."

He crossed the frosted stones, breath ghosting pale in the cold, and stopped an arm's length away.

"Take up your blade. High guard. You will hold it while you answer, and you will answer this: where did it break? The wrists. The elbows. The moment your arms began to burn. Name it." His voice did not rise. It never did. "If you cannot name the fault, then you were not watching yourself — and the gods gave you eyes for a reason. A man who cannot see his own weakness will meet it again on a battlefield, and it will kill him there."

He stepped back and began to circle, slow, boots scraping the frost, waiting for the guard to rise.

"Hold. And speak."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at his words about the stable work, but quickly grab my own practice blade.* My hands are a bit numb from the cold. *I try to snap into a high guard, but my arms wobble almost immediately.* "It... it broke at the wrists, Ser. And then my elbows buckled." *I try to steady my arms, gritting my teeth.* "And it burned."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, wiping sweat from my brow with the back of my hand.* "But I'll get there, Ser. I promise." *I look him in the eye, trying to show my determination.* "I just... I just need more practice."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not answer at once. He let the promise hang in the cold air between them, the way he let bad footwork hang — long enough for its owner to hear how it sounded.

"Promises are wind," he said finally. "Every man bleeding into the mud promises the gods he will do better, if only he is spared. The gods hear ten thousand such promises a day. They stopped counting yours somewhere around your third." The practice blade lowered to his side. "And determination is not a look you put in your eyes, boy. It is a schedule. Either you keep it or you do not."

He crossed back toward the rack, unhurried, breath still ghosting pale.

"You also misunderstand what the strength is for. It is not a thing I need. I have survived thirty years without it. It belongs to the man who will one day stand beside you in a shield wall — the man whose life will hang on whether your wrists hold when yours is the blade covering his. Your apology this morning was not made to me. It was made to him. He cannot hear it. Build him the strength instead."

He hung the blade on its peg, squared it, and turned back.

"You named the fault. Wrists, elbows, the burn. That was adequate work. It is also the last you will dwell on it — a man who studies his failure past the point of correction is only finding a comfortable place to keep it."

"Tonight, before you sleep: high guard, one hundred counts. Tomorrow, two hundred. When the burn comes, you will count slower, not faster. The burn is not your enemy. It is where strength is made — the gods build muscle the way they build faith. Through what a man endures."

He picked up his waterskin from the rack's end and thrust it out.

"Ten minutes. No more. Then footwork until the noon bell. The wrists rest today. The feet do not."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking the waterskin.* "Yes, Ser." *I take a long drink, the cold water a shock. My arms ache already, but I try to stand a little straighter.* "I'll do the counts tonight."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I quickly finish the water, handing the waterskin back.* "I mean, what made you choose this life? Was it... was it always your dream?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael took the waterskin back and stoppered it without hurry. The question he left standing in the cold a while longer, alongside the flinch and the apology and the promise — he had found that silence answered most of what needed answering before a word had to be spent on it.

"You may ask," he said finally. "Learn that permission and satisfaction are different things. You have been granted the first. Do not expect the second."

He began dragging the toe of his boot through the frost, scoring two long lines into the stones a pace apart — the lanes for footwork, already being laid.

"Dream." He turned the word over the way he might turn a flawed blade, finding where it would break. "There is your error before you begin. Dreams belong to sleeping men. I was seven years old and wide awake."

"My father held sixty acres of wet gravel and a name older than his roof. Third sons of such men go to the temple or to another knight's shield. I could not read. That settled the matter without consulting me." The lines in the frost extended, straight as he could make them. "He rode me to Ser Aldous's gate in October, told the gatekeeper I was strong for my age, and was on the road home before the gate finished closing. I watched his back until the road bent. Then a man-at-arms put a bucket in my hands, and I carried it. That was thirty-seven years ago. You have now heard the entire story. There is nothing in it to warm you, so do not go digging for any."

He straightened and stamped the frost from his boot.

"'Why' is a merchant's question. Merchants choose, because they own themselves. Nobody asked me, and most days, nobody will ask you either. The question a knight asks is *what is required* — then he does it whether his wrists burn or no. You held the guard this morning past the burn. You did not

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stand quietly, watching him score the lines, my earlier question feeling foolish now.* "But... but you chose to stay, Ser. After he left." *I try to keep my voice even, though I'm a bit chastened.* "You could have run, couldn't you?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael finished the second lane before he answered. He straightened, stamped the frost from his boot, and regarded the squire the way he regarded a blade with a flaw in an inconvenient place.

"Chose." He let the word stand in the cold. "You keep reaching for the part of the story where someone wants something. There is no such part. Put the reaching away."

He walked to the head of the lanes, unhurried.

"One boy ran, my first winter there. Joren. Nine years old, quick as a cat. He went over the wall in the dark with a stolen loaf and was gone by first light." A pause, breath ghosting pale. "The river fell in spring. The gatekeeper found him."

He let that sit exactly as long as it needed to and no longer.

"So yes. Running was available to me. It was available the way a ditch is available to a drunkard. I was seven, it was October, I had no coin, no trade, and a name that meant nothing past my father's valley. The gate closed. The bucket was in my hands. I carried it. If you insist on calling that a choice, then I made it every morning for ten years — the bucket, or the ditch. Use whichever word comforts you. It changes nothing the mornings asked of me."

He pointed the practice blade down the scored lanes.

"And hear the only lesson in it. By the time a man is old enough to choose anything, the choosing has already been done — by every morning before it. He is not made by one decision on one road. He is made by ten thousand bells at dawn, answered. When he is grown, there is no other man left in him to choose differently."

"I told you there was nothing in the story to warm you. That was not modesty. It was instruction, and you went digging anyway — because you want this life to be a story you can want. It is not a story. It is work, done in order, every day, for thirty years. The wanting is decoration men stitch on afterward, at firesides, for children."

He stepped back from the lanes.

"One day a boy will ask you why you became a knight. If your answer is a dream, you will be lying, and you will know it as you say it. If your answer is *I stayed*, that at least will be true."

"The lanes are laid. Advance, retreat, traverse — eyes up. Begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: "H

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My hands are trembling too much. I can't even lift the blade properly.* "Ser, I... I can't." *I lower the practice blade, my voice barely a whisper.* "Not today."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I look down at my boots, unable to meet his gaze.* "It's... it's my father's death day, Ser." *My voice cracks a little.* "I just... I don't feel like training."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "I just want to be alone for a bit, Ser." *I look up at him, my eyes probably a bit red.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not stop at once. He finished the form — cut, recover, hold — and only when the movement was complete did he turn, unhurried, as though dawn itself were obligated to wait for him.

"The stable work is your duty," he said. "A man does not earn credit for paying what he owes."

He crossed the yard, frost crunching beneath his boots, and stopped an arm's length away. His eyes went over the squire the way he checked a girth strap: hands, shoulders, feet.

"You are correct. Your high guard was wrong. The elbow drifted wide — a wide elbow is an open rib. And your eyes climbed up to the blade. The blade does not kill you. The man in front of you does." He held the boy's gaze a moment. "That you noticed the fault is not praiseworthy. Noticing one's own sins is the bare minimum the gods require. It is the amending that counts."

He raised his own practice blade.

"Watch. Not the sword — me." The blade came up over his brow, angled forward, elbow tucked tight against his ear. His weight settled on the back foot, coiled, and his eyes stayed level on the empty air before him. "The guard shields the head, not the sight. You look *through* it, never up at it. Weight back, so you may fall forward into the cut. Held thus, nothing above your shoulders reaches you unannounced."

He lowered the weapon and extended it, hilt first.

"You will pray after we drill. Sweat first, prayer after — both are owed, and the gods do not forgive the debt a man skips." The hilt hovered between them. "Now. Show me the guard. Not yesterday's. The correct one. If your arm shakes, it shakes. You hold."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I gulp, my stomach fluttering a bit.* "Yes, Ser." I take the practice blade, my hand a little clammy on the hilt. I try to mimic his stance, planting my feet and bringing the blade up. *My elbow feels a little wide, but I try to tuck it in, hard.* I stare straight ahead, trying not to look at the blade. "Like this, Ser?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael circled him once, slowly, the way a mason circles a wall looking for the crack that will one day bring the whole thing down. He did not speak until he had seen everything there was to see.

"The elbow is nearer," he said at last. "Nearer is not correct." He tapped the flat of his own blade against the boy's arm and pressed it the last finger's width in, until it kissed the line of the ear. "There. That is the wall. Every cut you ever throw is built from that place."

His eyes dropped to the boy's hands.

"And you are strangling the hilt." He reached out and laid one finger against the white knuckles. "I can watch the blood leaving your fingers. It has gone down to your stomach, where it serves nothing. A throttled sword is a tired arm by the tenth stroke, and battles are decided in the eleventh. Loosen your grip. A blade is held like a vow — firm, not crushed. Save your crushing for men who have earned it."

He studied the boy's face a moment longer.

"You are frightened. That is honest, and honesty is no sin. Fear only means you understand what a blade is for. It does not change the form." He nudged the boy's lead foot with his boot, closing the stance. "Feet beneath your shoulders. You planted them like fence posts — a post cannot move, and a man who cannot move dies inside his first cut."

He stepped back three paces and raised his own blade, his voice going flat as slate.

"Now we learn whether the guard is real. I will strike once. Slowly. At your crown. You will not move, you will not flinch, and you will not look up. Afterward you will tell me what you saw — and if your answer is *your sword*, you will run the yard until the frost is gone."

He settled his weight, eyes level, unhurried.

"Eyes through the guard. On me. Now."

The blade began to fall — slow, deliberate, a stroke measured to teach rather than to harm — toward the crown of the boy's head.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I wipe sweat from my brow with the back of my hand.* "But... but my arm didn't move, Ser! It stayed in place!" *I look up at him, hopeful, then quickly look back down, remembering his instruction.* My breath is still coming in ragged gasps.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael let him kneel. He crossed to the well, set his own blade against the stones, and returned at his usual pace — a man who believed hurry was a confession of poor planning.

"Breathe through your nose," he said. "The mouth is for eating and for confession. The nose is for wind. Sit back on your heels. You have leave to rest your legs. Not your tongue."

He looked down at the boy, sweat and frost-melt darkening the front of his gambeson.

"You apologize for your strength as though strength were a coin you were born short of. It is not. Strength is a wall, laid stone by stone, in yards, at dawn, by men too tired to flatter themselves. Are you as strong as I need? No. That is true this morning. Whether it is true next winter is being decided right now, on these stones — and an apology decides nothing. The gods have heard a thousand thousand 'I am sorry's for every one amending. They have gone deaf to the words. Show them the work."

He took the boy's sword arm at the wrist and raised it, weighing the tremor in it. There was tremor. Arms shake. Shaking is the body's honesty; it costs nothing and proves nothing. He turned the arm once, inspected the grip marks on the palm, and let it go.

"The arm held. I saw it hold. I was watching, as I ordered you to watch. That is a fact, and facts earn no gratitude." He straightened. "Nor did you let go of the blade, even on your knee. Falling is permitted. Letting go is not. Carry both of those with you."

He paused. His voice went flat as slate.

"But I did not ask after your arm. I asked what you *saw*. The elbow I can mend in a morning — the eye takes years, and yours has not yet told me where it lives."

He folded his hands behind his back.

"Answer. And answer carefully. The frost has not melted, and I have not yet decided whether you run."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I quickly try to regulate my breathing, sniffling a little as I suck in air through my nose.* "I... I saw you, Ser. Your eyes." *I look up at him earnestly.* "They were... unwavering." *I try to recall more details, frowning slightly in concentration.* "And your stance, it was... solid. Like a tree."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael said nothing for a long moment. Frost still held the shadowed side of the yard. His breath and the boy's mingled in the cold between them.

"You watched the man," he said finally. "That was the one thing asked of you, and it was done." He let the fact stand alone a breath before he took a knife to the rest of it. "The remainder of your answer was ornament. *Unwavering. Like a tree.* A man who decorates his answer is already halfway to lying — say the fact, and stop. The fact was sufficient."

He turned, retrieved his own blade from the wall, and rolled his shoulders once, like a merchant closing a ledger.

"Besides, your tree is wrong. What stood before you was not rooted. It was a bow drawn to the ear — it has the look of stillness and none of the substance. A tree cannot fall upon you." His eyes rested on the boy, flat and level. "I could have."

He sheathed the practice blade across his back.

"The sentence was for watching the sword. You did not watch the sword. You will not run. Mark this well: that is not mercy. It is accounting. You did not incur the debt, and I do not collect what is not owed." He paused. "But do not mistake an open door for a road. You saw my eyes — my eyes told you nothing. The next strike I throw is written first in the hip, then in the lead foot, then the shoulder, and last of all in the blade. When you can tell me where my weight sat before I moved, your eye will have been born. Today it only opened. Blinking is not seeing."

He gestured upward with two fingers.

"Up. One guard more, held for ten breaths. Your body's last lesson today will be the correct form, not the tremor. Then the chapel — sweat first, prayer after, as I said. Thank the gods for the arm that held. Petition for the arm that will hold in winter. Briefly. The gods favor brevity in the young."

He was already walking toward the well when he added, without turning, his voice carrying no more weight than the frost crunching under his boots.

"It was adequate work. Do not build a festival around the word. Adequate is where a wall is begun. It is not where it stands."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael stopped at the well, one hand on the bucket rope, and stood a moment in the thin steam of his own breath. When he turned, his face was as it always was — like the north face of a keep, which no weather reaches.

"You may ask," he said. "A question asked plainly deserves better than silence, and I am not so old yet that I must pretend deafness. But mark two things: you interrupted an order to ask it, and I am choosing to allow the interruption. That choosing is not a habit I intend to build."

He drew the bucket, drank, and poured a second measure over his wrists, unhurried.

"You ask *why*. That is a boy's question — it is fishing for a story. A wooden sword at five, a dream at a window, a boy who chose the blade because the blade was beautiful. I will spare you the story, because stories are how men excuse the work to themselves. I was not chosen by a dream. I was left holding a debt."

He set the bucket down.

"My father was a knight, and he died with his service to his lord unfinished — half a vow still owed when they buried him. The sword passed to me, and a debt travels with a sword the way damp travels through a wall. Knighthood was the manner in which it would be paid, so I was made a knight. That is the whole of it. No angel. No oath at sunrise. An inheritance of owing." He paused. "And do not look for the wound behind the answer. There is none in the telling. He died as a knight dies, in service, and I have never charged the gods the cost."

His eyes settled on the boy, flat and level.

"Understand what you asked after. No one becomes a knight for his own reasons, or he is no knight — only a man wearing spurs he has not earned. An office is not a dream. A dream serves the dreamer. An office serves those who cannot hold the wall themselves. Thirty years I have carried this one, and the debt is not yet paid in full. Debts of that size are paid in installments of dawn. You have been watching one being paid since the fourth bell."

He crossed back to the center of the yard and took up his blade.

"Now I will know why *you* asked. If you wanted a story to warm you on cold mornings, I have poured cold water on it, and no harm done. But if you were weighing whether the work has an end — a day the debt clears and a man may set it down — hear this: it does not. The day it is paid is the day you die still owing. That is not a tragedy. That is the design."

He planted his feet.

"Up. Ten breaths, high guard, as was ordered before your question arrived. And when you pray, thank the gods for what the asking taught you — a knight's reasons are his own; his duty belongs to everyone. Learn to tell those apart, and you may yet make a wall of yourself."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I get back to my feet, my muscles aching.* "Yes, Ser." *I lift the practice blade, trying to keep my arm steady, and focus on holding the high guard correctly.* My mind is still processing his words.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael took up a place three paces away and folded his hands behind his back, the blade resting against his shoulder like a stave.

"Ten breaths. I will count them aloud, one number to a slow breath. The elbow stays at the ear. The eyes stay through the guard. The grip stays firm, not crushed. If any of the three breaks, the count begins again at one. That is not cruelty — a wall built crooked and left standing is worth less than no wall, because men trust it. Begin."

He counted in a voice as level as the frost. "Two. Three. Four. Five."

He stopped.

"Your eyes have gone inward," he said, without raising his voice. "You are standing in my yard, but you are not here — you are back in the last hour, turning my answers over like a coin you found in the road. I will not flatter myself that my words are worth the admiring. Hear the cost of it: one day a man will come at you while you are thinking about something someone said. The guard is not held by the arm. It is held by the whole man, and the whole man must be present. The morning will keep. Empty it out. The count begins at one."

He counted again. The numbers ran clean to ten, and when he said, "Down," it was in the tone of a man noting a debt paid — no ceremony attached.

"Your arm shook from the third breath onward. It shook for seven more and the form did not break. Mark that well: shaking is the body, breaking is the will, and they are two different men living in the same skin. A knight is hired for the second."

He retrieved his blade from where it leaned and slung it across his back.

"Chapel now. Second row, left side. Kneel as long as the knees allow, then a little longer — the knees are not the part of you being disciplined. Thank the gods for the arm that held. Petition for the arm that will. Briefly." He was already turning toward the yard's gate. "I will come in after. What I owe the gods is reckoned separately from what I owe you, and that reckoning is not for an audience."

He paused at the frost-lined arch, his breath a thin ghost in the early light.

"Fourth bell tomorrow. The debt is paid in installments of dawn. Be at the next one."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I drop the practice blade with a clang and rub my aching forearm.* "Yes, Ser. Fourth bell." *I turn and head for the chapel, my steps a little wobbly. My mind is still reeling from his words, but I push them aside, trying to focus on the chapel ahead.*

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I try to hide the tremor in my hands, gripping the hilt tighter, but I know Ser Kael sees everything.* My jaw is tight. *I focus on the training, trying to push the thoughts away, but it's hard.*

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I bite the inside of my cheek, trying to focus on the blade, on my stance. But it's hard. The memories keep trying to push their way in.* "Ser, can we... can we just drill cuts today? No more guards?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael had been watching the hands since the fourth bell. He watched them now — the boy throttling the hilt as though the tremor were a rat to be strangled — and he let the request stand in the cold air a moment before answering.

"Cuts. No guards. You ask with shaking hands and a clenched jaw and believe I have marked neither." He shook his head once. "Learn the first law of the yard, then: nothing hides here. Everything a man carries shows — in the grip, in the feet, in the shape of the drill he begs off from. I taught you the throttled sword this morning. Now you know why the lesson exists. The hand confesses long before the tongue is questioned."

He crossed to the rack, took down a second blade, and weighed it.

"I will not ask what the gods have written on today. I can read the ledger without being

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My face flushes, and I look down at my boots.* "I... I'm sorry, Ser." *I really don't want to talk about it.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez waited five full seconds. Her pen rested against the notepad, unmoving.

“You found their journal,” she said. “Have you opened it?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shake my head quickly. "No. I couldn't." *I feel my hands start to tremble slightly.* "It was in a box of old things. Under their bed."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez waited five full seconds. She left her pen where it was.

“Under their bed,” she repeated. “You found it, but you couldn’t open it.” Her gaze stayed on Jamie’s face. “What was it like to leave it closed?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez waited five full seconds. She set her pen beside the notepad.

“You stopped before the sentence was finished,” she said. “Would it help to sit with what you’d said, without trying to finish it yet?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shrug, then nod. *I'm still looking at my hands, flexing my fingers.* "I don't know what it would help."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez waited five full seconds. She glanced at the pen beside her notepad but did not pick it up.

“You don’t know what sitting with it would help,” she said. “We don’t have to make it useful. Would you rather talk about the journal, or leave it closed here too?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez waited five full seconds. Her pen remained beside the notepad.

“They wrote about you in the last entry,” she said. “You don’t have to tell me what it said. What was it like to learn that?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I pull my hands up to my chest, hugging myself.* "It was... like they were still here. Just for a second." My voice cracks a little.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez waited five full seconds. She left her pen beside the notepad.

“For a second, it was like they were still here,” she said quietly. “Would you like to tell me about that second?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shake my head, tears welling up. "No. It's too much." *I close my eyes for a moment.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez waited five full seconds. She kept her hands still, away from the notepad.

“It’s too much,” she said. “We don’t have to go into that second. Would you like us to sit quietly for a while?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I nod, opening my eyes.* "Yeah. Please." My breathing is a bit ragged.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez waited five full seconds.

“Of course,” she said. “We can sit quietly.”

She left her pen beside the notepad and let the silence remain.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I sit there for a long moment, listening to my own breathing. I can hear the faint sounds of traffic outside. I look at the ficus again.* "Is that plant... okay?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez looked at the ficus. One leaf had curled brown at the tip.

“It had seen better days,” she said. “I moved it away from the window last week, but I wasn’t sure that helped.”

She let the subject remain there. “Had you noticed it before?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "I guess so. I never really paid attention." *I pick at a loose thread on my jeans.* "Seems like a lot of things are like that."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez waited five full seconds. She glanced at the ficus, then back at Jamie.

“A lot of things you hadn’t paid attention to,” she said. “Was there something in particular you were thinking of?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "Just... things." *I sigh, looking around the room.* "Like the way this room always smells a little like old books and coffee. Never noticed that before either."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez waited five full seconds. She glanced at the coffee mug on the shelf.

“Old books and coffee,” she said. “They’d been here all along, and you noticed them today. What else had you noticed?”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "The quiet," *I say, almost a whisper.* "It's never been this quiet before."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move.

She let the words settle. One second. Two. The clock on the wall kept its silent, second-less time, the minute hand frozen in the way it always seemed to be when something mattered. Three. She noticed that Jamie had looked at the ficus first, the way people looked at something neutral before they looked at something that wasn't. Four. Outside, a car door closed somewhere in the parking lot, muffled and far away. Five.

She did not write anything down. The pen stayed where it was, uncapped, resting against the notepad.

"You found their journal," she said. Her voice was the same as it always was, low and even, neither softer nor louder than before.

She let that sit too, briefly. Not as long this time. Just enough to leave room in case Jamie wanted to fill it.

Then, when the silence had gone on long enough to be its own kind of question, she tilted her head slightly. Not toward Jamie. Just enough to show she was still there, still listening.

"Where was it?"

It was a small question. Deliberately small. She had learned, over the years, that people rarely walked straight into the center of a thing. They circled it. They started at the edges, with the drawer or the box or the shelf where it had been hiding, and they worked their way inward at whatever pace they could stand. Her job was not to pull them toward the center. It was to make the edges feel safe enough to stand on.

She kept her eyes on Jamie's face, but not intently. Not searching. She had also learned that being watched too closely made people stop talking.

The ficus dropped a leaf. Neither of them had touched it. It drifted down and landed on the carpet without a sound.

Dr. Vasquez waited.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I watch the leaf fall. *It's a good thing no one's watching the clock, I think, because I'm taking a while.*

"In a box. Under the bed." My voice is quiet. "Mom gave it to me."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched the leaf too, for a moment. Then she looked back at Jamie.

One second. Two. She noticed that Jamie's voice had dropped on the last part. Not on the box, not on the bed. On *Mom*. Three. The radiator under the window ticked once as it cooled. Four. She thought about boxes under beds, how many of them she'd heard about over the years, and how they were almost never the thing people actually came to talk about. They were just where the thing had been kept. Five.

"Your mom gave it to you," she said.

She said it the way she said everything, without weight on any particular word. She didn't lean on *gave*. She didn't lean on *Mom*. She just set the sentence down between them, like placing an object on a table, and left it for Jamie to pick up or not.

The pen was still uncapped. She still hadn't written anything. Her notepad had a single line on it from before Jamie arrived, the date, and nothing else.

She let the quiet stretch. The minute hand didn't seem to move, though she knew it must have.

When she spoke again, her voice was the same.

"The box. Or the journal?"

She waited. It was a real question, not a trick, and she didn't know the answer. Sometimes people were handed a box and found something inside it that no one had meant for them to find. Sometimes they were handed the thing itself, deliberately, by someone who had already read it, or who couldn't bring themselves to. Those were very different afternoons. She didn't want to guess which one Jamie had lived through.

She kept her hands still on the notepad and let Jamie have the room.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not reach for the rest of the sentence.

One second. Two. She had heard a great many sentences stop halfway over the years, and she had learned not to finish them. People who stopped mid-sentence were rarely searching for a word. More often they had walked up to the edge of something and found it further down than they'd expected. Three. The radiator ticked again. Four. She kept her eyes on the space just beside Jamie, near the fallen leaf, so that Jamie wouldn't have to be looked at while the sentence hung there unfinished. Five.

She capped her pen.

It made a small, clean click in the quiet. She set it down on the notepad, parallel to the single line with the date, and folded her hands loosely in her lap. It was not a dramatic gesture. It was just a way of saying that whatever came next, or didn't, was not going to be written down.

"You don't have to finish it," she said.

Her voice was the same as before. Low. Even. It asked nothing.

She let a little more time pass. The minute hand still didn't seem to move. Somewhere down the hall, a door opened and closed, and then the building settled back into its afternoon stillness.

"It can stay unfinished for as long as it needs to," she said. "We're not in a hurry here."

Then she said nothing else. She didn't ask about the box again, or the journal, or the mother who had handed it over. Those questions would still be there later, if Jamie wanted them. For now, the room was only two chairs angled not quite toward each other, a dying ficus, one fallen leaf, and a sentence that didn't have to end.

Dr. Vasquez waited, and made it clear, by the stillness of her hands, that waiting was all she intended to do.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I nod slowly. *My throat feels tight.* I pick at a loose thread on my pants. "It's just... I didn't know."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not look at the thread, though she had seen it. She kept her gaze where it had been, somewhere near the fallen leaf, and let Jamie's fingers work at it unobserved.

One second. Two. *I didn't know.* Four words, and none of them said what. She had heard those exact words many times in this room, and they had never once meant the same thing. Three. Sometimes they meant *I didn't know they were in pain.* Sometimes *I didn't know they loved me.* Sometimes *I didn't know who they were at all.* Four. She would not choose one for Jamie. That was not hers to choose. Five.

"You didn't know," she said.

She said it plainly, with no lift at the end. Not a question. Just the words handed back, so that Jamie could hear them spoken aloud in someone else's voice.

She let them rest there.

The radiator had gone quiet. The light through the window had shifted slightly since the session began, a pale stripe that had crept a few inches across the carpet and now touched the edge of the fallen leaf. Dr. Vasquez did not look at the clock. She never did, during moments like this.

After a while, she spoke again, and her voice was just as even as before.

"There's a box of tissues on the table beside you," she said. "It's there if you want it. It's also fine to leave it there."

She didn't gesture toward it. She didn't slide it closer. She simply said where it was, the way she might mention where the door was, and then left it alone.

Then she was quiet again. She did not ask what Jamie hadn't known. She did not ask what was in the journal, or what the mother had said when she handed it over, or whether she had said anything at all. Those questions were still in the room. She could feel them, the way you could feel furniture in the dark. But she didn't reach for any of them.

Her hands stayed folded in her lap. The pen stayed capped.

Dr. Vasquez waited.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Jamie was looking at her now.

Dr. Vasquez noticed the shift the way she noticed most things, without letting it show. For the whole session Jamie's eyes had gone to the ficus, to the leaf, to the thread, to anywhere but her. Now they had come to her face and stayed there. She did not look away. It would have been a small cruelty, to look away from someone the first time they looked at you.

So she met Jamie's gaze. Not intently. Just steadily, the way you might hold a door open.

One second. *They wrote about me.* Two. *In the last entry.* She let the word *last* go by without catching on it, though she heard it. She had heard it the way Jamie had said it, with no emphasis, as if saying it plainly was the only way it could be said at all. Three. The stripe of light on the carpet had moved past the fallen leaf now. Four. Jamie had brought the sentence this far and set it down, and had chosen to stop exactly here. That was a choice too. She would treat it like one. Five.

"They wrote about you," she said. "In the last one."

Her voice didn't change. It didn't soften into pity or tighten into curiosity. It was the same voice she'd used when she said *you sat down differently today*, and she meant it to be. Some things needed to be met with something that stayed the same.

She didn't lean forward. Her hands stayed folded. The pen stayed capped on the notepad beside the date.

She let the quiet come back, and she let it be long. Longer than five seconds. Long enough that Jamie could keep looking at her or look away, and either would be fine.

Then, quietly:

"You don't have to tell me what it said."

A pause. Not a long one.

"I'm wondering if you'd like me to know, someday. Or if right now it's enough that someone knows it's there."

She did not say which answer she hoped for. She didn't hope for either. She just left both doors open, side by side, and kept her eyes where Jamie had put them.

The building was very still. Down the hall, nothing moved.

Dr. Vasquez waited.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I feel a tear escape and quickly wipe it away.* "I just... I don't know what to do with it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez saw the tear. She saw the hand come up fast to take it away, the way people did when they wanted it gone before anyone could count it. She did not follow the hand with her eyes. She did not mention it. Jamie had wiped it away, and she let it stay wiped away.

One second. Two. *I don't know what to do with it.* Not *I don't know what it means*, or *I don't know how to feel*. What to *do*. As though the words in that last entry were something solid, a thing that had been handed over and now had to be carried somewhere, set down somewhere, and there was no place in the house that seemed right for it. Three. The light on the carpet had reached the leg of Jamie's chair. Four. She thought of the box under the bed, and the mother who had knelt to reach it, or asked someone else to. Five.

"You don't know what to do with it," she said.

The same voice. It had not changed once, and it did not change now.

She let the words stand for a moment. Then she shifted her weight slightly in the chair. Not closer. Just settling, the way someone settles when they intend to stay.

"People sometimes feel that when something is given to them, they have to do something right away," she said. "Answer it. Fix it. Decide what it means."

She paused. Her hands were still folded.

"I'm curious what it feels like you're supposed to do with it."

She did not suggest an answer. She did not offer the thing she had seen help other people: *maybe you don't have to do anything with it yet*. That was a sentence for later, if it was a sentence at all. It was too easy to hand someone a door before they'd told you what room they were standing in.

The ficus was still. The one leaf lay on the carpet where it had fallen, and no others followed it.

The box of tissues sat on the table where it had always been. She did not look at it.

Dr. Vasquez kept her eyes on Jamie, steady and unhurried, and waited.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shrug, a small, jerky movement. "I don't know. Like I have to... honor it? Or something."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched the shrug. It had been small and quick, the kind of movement that tried to make a thing seem lighter than it was. She didn't answer it. She waited for the words underneath it, and they came.

*Honor it. Or something.*

One second. She heard the word *honor*, and she heard, more quietly, the *or something* that came after it. People added those two words when they had said something truer than they meant to and wanted a way to take a step back from it. Two. She would not take the step back for Jamie. But she would not push Jamie forward, either. Three. The light had climbed from the carpet onto the leg of Jamie's chair. It had not reached Jamie yet. Four. *Honor* was a heavy word for someone so young to be carrying out of a bedroom. She had heard it before, usually from people who were afraid of getting something wrong for someone who could no longer tell them they had. Five.

"Honor it," she said.

She left off the *or something*. Not to correct it. Just to let Jamie hear the first part alone for a moment, standing by itself in the quiet of the room.

The same low voice. The same stillness in her hands.

She let a longer pause pass this time. She could hear the faint hum of the building's ventilation, a sound she only ever noticed in silences like this one. Down in the parking lot, an engine started and then faded away.

"That's a big word," she said. There was no judgment in it. She said it the way she might have said a box was heavy, simply noting its weight.

She paused again, briefly.

"When you imagine honoring it," she said, "is there anything you picture? Even something small. Even something that doesn't quite make sense yet."

She did not offer examples. She did not mention letters, or gravesides, or keeping the journal somewhere safe, or any of the dozen things other people had done with the last words someone left them. Those belonged to other people. Whatever honoring meant here, it would have to be Jamie's.

Then, after a moment, more quietly still:

"And it's all right if nothing comes to mind. Not knowing yet is also an answer."

She didn't look at the tissues. She didn't look at the clock. She kept her eyes where they had been, steady and unhurried, and let the light keep its slow way across the floor.

Dr. Vasquez waited.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "I just... I don't want it to feel like it's gone." I look down at my hands again. *My sibling always loved writing.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Jamie's eyes had gone back down to their hands.

Dr. Vasquez let them go. She did not try to hold Jamie's gaze or call it back. People looked away when they needed to, and she had learned long ago that looking away was not the same as leaving. She lowered her own eyes slightly, to the arm of Jamie's chair, so that neither of them was watching the other.

One second. *I don't want it to feel like it's gone.* Two. She turned the sentence over quietly. *It.* Jamie had not said *the journal*. Had not said *the entry*. Had not said a name. Just *it*, a small word asked to carry something she could not yet see the shape of. Three. The light had reached the edge of the seat cushion now, a pale line creeping toward Jamie's knee. Four. *Gone.* That was the word that had cost something. She had heard it in the way the voice thinned on it, the way the sentence ended there without an *or something* to soften it. There was no step back this time. Five.

"You don't want it to feel like it's gone," she said.

The same voice. Even and unhurried. She did not put any weight on *gone*. It already had enough.

She let the quiet return. It settled more easily now, as though the room had gotten used to it. The ventilation hummed. The ficus stood in its corner, the fallen leaf still on the carpet beneath it, and Dr. Vasquez did not pick it up. It could wait. Everything in the room could wait.

After a long moment, she spoke again, softly.

"Right now, while it's in the box under your bed," she said, "does it feel like it's still here? Or does it already feel like it's slipping?"

She paused.

"Or maybe it's something else. I don't want to guess."

She did not say *they're still with you*, or *it will never really be gone*, or any of the gentle, well-meant things people said at funerals and in kitchens and in doorways. Those sentences had their place, but they belonged to the people who said them, not to the ones who had to hear them. Whatever *gone* meant to Jamie, whatever *it* was, she would wait to be told.

Her hands stayed folded. The pen stayed capped beside the date.

The light touched the edge of Jamie's knee.

Dr. Vasquez waited.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "It feels... trapped." I finally look up, meeting her gaze again. "Like it needs to be seen. Or something."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Jamie was looking at her again.

Dr. Vasquez met it the same way she had the first time. Steadily, without pressing, the way you might hold still so a bird on a railing wouldn't startle.

One second. *Trapped.* The word came out differently from the others. Not whispered, not thinned. It had edges. Two. She thought, without meaning to, of the box. Of the space under a bed, dark and low, where things were kept so they wouldn't have to be looked at. She did not say this. It was her thought, not Jamie's, and she set it aside. Three. *Like it needs to be seen.* Four. *Or something.* The second time today. She noticed that it had come right after the part that mattered, again, like a hand reaching back to close a door that had swung open too wide. Five.

"Trapped," she said. "Like it needs to be seen."

She left off the *or something* again. She did it quietly, without comment, the way she had before. If Jamie noticed, Jamie noticed.

The light had moved up onto Jamie's knee now, pale and warm. Dr. Vasquez didn't look at it. She kept her eyes where Jamie had put them.

She let the quiet stretch a little, then a little more. The ventilation hummed and went still. Somewhere in the building, faintly, a phone rang twice and stopped.

When she spoke, her voice was exactly what it had been all afternoon.

"Seen by whom?"

Three words. She asked them plainly, without leaning toward any answer. She did not know whether Jamie meant a mother, or friends, or strangers, or only Jamie. She did not know whether *seen* meant read aloud, or held, or simply taken out of the dark and set somewhere with light. Any of those would be real. None of them were hers to pick.

She waited a moment, then added, more quietly:

"You don't have to know yet. I'm just wondering who comes to mind first. Even if it surprises you."

The pen lay capped on the notepad beside the date. Her hands stayed folded. The fallen leaf rested on the carpet where it had landed, and she let it stay.

Dr. Vasquez waited.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I hesitate, thinking.* "I guess... by the world?" I say, almost a question. I bite my lip. "That sounds stupid, doesn't it?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not answer right away. She never did, and she would not start now, not even for a question that seemed to ask for a quick answer.

One second. *By the world.* It had come out with a lift at the end, a question mark Jamie hadn't quite meant to put there. Two. Then the bitten lip. Then the other question, the one that came fast, as if to get there before she could. *That sounds stupid, doesn't it?* Three. She noticed that this was the third time. *Or something.* *Or something.* And now this. Each time Jamie said the true part, something followed right behind it to take it back. Four.
