dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The book came away from the shelf more easily than anything in that house had a right to. Six weeks, and the umbrellas and the cane had kept their places, and the photographs on the kitchen table had only been nudged. But the slim dark volume slid into your hand as if it had been loosened. As if it had been waiting.

The spine had no title. The cloth was dark — the dark green becomes when it stops being green. And as the book came free, something slipped from between its pages. You caught it against your chest, an old reflex. A photograph.

The paper was soft at the corners. Not old-soft. Handled-soft — turned over and over between someone's fingers until it had gone limp as cloth.

A summer photograph. Your grandmother young, younger than you had ever known her, light dress, on the front steps of this house with three or four people whose names died with her. Everyone caught mid-laugh, warm with grain.

Marcus stood at the end of the row.

He was handsome. That came through even the grain — a stillness to him, a way of standing just apart. You looked at him a moment longer than the others. It was natural to. He was the one the eye went to.

Everyone in the photograph was solid. Blurred by laughter, but full, heavy with light, real the way old film makes people real. Marcus was sharp and faint at once, the way a figure looks when he has moved during a long exposure — except nothing about his pose had moved. Hand in pocket. Weight on one foot. Simply less there than the day he stood in.

And no one stood near him. The others touched shoulders, leaned together. Around Marcus there was a clear arm's-length of porch, the space people leave without deciding to.

*Is he still alive? Is he single?* The questions were warm, ordinary, the kind that belong to kitchens and daylight. You had them here anyway. The room took them the way it had taken everything else you'd offered it today — the words, the swing, the joke — and returned nothing. But the photograph was soft at the corners, and the shelf behind you was clean, and its wood was dark where hands had rested, and you understood that someone had been asking after Marcus too. Recently. Often. Standing exactly where you were standing.

You turned the photograph over. Her handwriting, small and certain:

*Marcus, the summer he came back.*

Beneath it, in the same hand but pressed harder, the pen nearly through the paper:

*Not the last time.*

Behind you, the clock ticked. Every tick arriving exactly when it should — as if the house had decided to stop being wrong in the one way you'd learned to listen for.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the photo, then at the inscription. "The summer he came back... not the last time?"* My brow furrows. "Grandma, what were you up to?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I carefully place the photo back inside the book, then open the book itself. No title on the spine, no title page either.* "What *is* this?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I flip through the pages. They're blank. Every single one.* "Seriously? Blank?" My voice echoes a little too loudly in the quiet room.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
“Fine,” Kira muttered.

She darted from behind the boulder, sprinting east along the ravine floor with one dagger raised. “Come on, you bastards! Try for something closer!”

An arrow snapped past her shoulder. She cut hard behind a narrow spur of rock as two more struck the ground where she’d been. The ambushers shifted their aim toward her; she caught a glimpse of movement along the ridge and counted at least four bowmen still exposed.

“East ridge is looking my way!” she shouted, then sprang out again, forcing them to keep tracking her. Her second dagger stayed low in her other hand, ready for anyone who came down off the rocks.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*Good, Kira.* "Alright lads, you heard her! West ridge with me!"

I charge forward, polearm held high, looking for the quickest way up the ravine wall.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira broke from the spur, sprinting diagonally across the ravine floor. Two arrows chased her; one clattered off stone, the other tore through the edge of her coat.

“Keep staring at me, you miserable pricks!”

The bowmen shifted along the ridge to track her. In the movement, she spotted one of them lowering his bow and scrambling toward a narrow ledge that sloped down into the ravine—trying to reach her flank.

Kira slid behind a jut of rock, then leaned out just long enough to make the archers loose again. “One’s coming down the east side!” she shouted. Her daggers tightened in her grip as she watched the ledge. “I’ll handle him.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira caught the west-ridge archer’s aim and saw the bowstring draw taut.

“Captain! West ridge—bowman’s got you!”

She snapped a dagger from her hand toward the archer, then ducked behind the rock spur as another shaft hissed across the ravine. One blade remained in her grip. On the ledge, the flanking bowman was still scrambling down toward her.

“Shit,” she muttered, shifting to meet him. “That’s one problem at a time.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I duck, the arrow sailing harmlessly over my head. "Damn it, Kira, focus on your own fight!" I shout, still pressing forward toward the west ridge.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
“Yeah, yeah,” Kira barked, though the captain’s rebuke had landed.

The flanker dropped from the ledge, boots skidding over loose shale. Kira shifted behind the spur and let him commit to the descent. When he lunged, she slipped aside, slammed her shoulder into his chest, and drove her dagger toward the gap beneath his ribs.

His bow clattered against the stone as they grappled. Kira wrenched free and kicked it down the slope.

“East side’s still got archers!” she called, breath tight with effort. “And I’m down a blade!”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira looked across the ravine and spotted the captain isolated beneath the west ridge. A bowman there had shifted position, angling for a clear shot.

“Captain, you’ve got one lining you up!”

She couldn’t cross the open ground without giving the east ridge an easy target. Cursing, she snatched the fallen flanker’s bow from the shale and yanked an arrow from his quiver. The bow was awkward in her hand, but she nocked the shaft and loosed toward the east ridge’s nearest exposed archer.

“Come on,” she snarled, ducking back behind the spur. “Look at me instead.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* I see the archer, but I also see an opening up the rock face. "I'm going up!" I yell, planting my polearm and beginning to scramble.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira saw the captain start up the west rock face. The bowman above him shifted to track the climb.

“Fine. Your fight, then,” she muttered.

She braced the scavenged bow against the spur and loosed at the west-ridge archer. The shot struck stone short of him, but made him flinch and duck from his clean line of sight.

An arrow cracked against the rock beside Kira’s head. She dropped low, nocked another shaft with clumsy fingers, and peered back toward the east ridge. Two archers had moved along the rim, trying to keep her pinned while the others held their positions.

“East ridge is repositioning!” she shouted across the ravine. “Two shifting north!”

She drew again, aiming at the nearer silhouette. The bowstring bit into her fingers. Kira held her breath and loosed. Whatever the shot did, she didn’t wait to find out—she ducked behind cover as another arrow hissed over the spur.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Got it!" I shout, pulling myself up to a small ledge. This rock face is steeper than it looks.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira caught the captain reaching the ledge across the ravine, then snapped her attention back to the east ridge.

“Good. Try not to fall,” she muttered.

A bowman leaned over the rim to track her. Kira loosed another arrow at him, forcing him to duck, then dropped behind the spur as two shafts punched into the stone.

Her fingers were already fumbling for another arrow. “I’m running low on these,” she called across the ravine. “And they’re still shifting north!”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Shit.* "Alright Kira, hold them as best you can! I'm almost there!" I see a handhold, reaching for it.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the captain’s shout, but kept her eyes on the east ridge.

One of the archers had stopped tracking her and turned toward the west face. She swore, drew the scavenged bow, and loosed. The arrow struck the ridge lip beside him; he ducked back out of sight.

“Still holding them,” she called, then shifted low along the rocks before the others could settle their aim. A shaft clattered against the spur she’d just left.

The bow felt wrong in her hands. She had one arrow left in the quiver. Kira nocked it and peered around cover, watching the two archers moving north.

“Last shot,” she muttered. “Make it count.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I pull myself up, my fingers finding purchase on a narrow crack. "Keep it up Kira! I see the top!" I can almost taste the open ground.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira tracked the nearer silhouette as it edged north along the rim. The bowstring bit into her fingers.

“Come on, then.”

She loosed. The arrow clipped the ridge lip beside the archer, who ducked out of sight. Kira dropped behind the spur as return fire cracked against the rocks.

“Last shot’s gone!” she called across the ravine. She let the useless bow fall and drew her remaining dagger, watching the east ridge for anyone bold enough to descend. “You’d better get up there soon.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Almost there!" I grunt, scrambling up the last few feet. My hand closes over the edge of the ravine. Time to make these bastards pay.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira saw a bowman on the east ridge break from cover and start down the shale slope, using the noise of the fight to close on her.

“Of course,” she muttered.

She shifted behind the spur, keeping the rock between herself and the archers above. When the bowman reached the bottom and came in fast, Kira let him commit, then slipped sideways. His shoulder slammed into stone. She drove her dagger into his thigh and shoved him back down the slope before he could bring his knife around.

An arrow cracked against the spur. Kira ducked, breath sharp, and glanced across the ravine. The captain was near the rim; a west-ridge bowman had found a line toward him.

“West ridge! Bowman’s got a shot!” she shouted.

Then she turned back to the east slope, dagger up, and watched for the next bastard to come down.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Damn it!* I see the archer. My head's exposed. I shove myself up the last bit, rolling onto the flat ground at the top of the ravine, putting rock between me and the archer. "They're gonna have to come find me now!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira saw the west-ridge bowman lose his line as the captain disappeared behind the rim. “Good. Stay behind the rock,” she muttered.

A scrape of shale drew her attention back east. One of the archers was climbing down the slope, bow slung aside and a short blade in hand. The others kept their bows trained on the ravine floor, waiting for her to show herself.

Kira tightened her grip on her single dagger and edged around the spur, keeping the rock between her and the archers. “Come on, then,” she breathed, watching the descending fighter’s boots pick their way over the loose stone. “You wanted closer.”

When he reached the bottom, she sprang from cover before he could ready his blade. Her dagger flashed toward his wrist; he jerked back, and she slammed her shoulder into him, driving him against the slope. Loose shale skittered beneath their feet.

An arrow struck the spur behind her. Kira swore and shoved the man away, forcing him to stumble downslope while she ducked back behind the rock.

“East ridge still has bows up!” she shouted. Her chest burned, and her empty hand clenched uselessly. She peered around the spur, looking for another opening without giving the archers a clean shot.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "I'm coming, Kira!" I yell, getting to my feet and looking for a way down the other side of the ravine, trying to flank the archers.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira spat once, short and ugly, and shoved off the boulder before the order had finished settling.

"Drawing them. Don't get cute on the west."

She broke right, daggers low, boots skidding on loose shale. An arrow cracked into stone where her shoulder had been. She didn't look back. Up on the east ridge a bowman rose to track her — she caught the silhouette against the sky, then another shifting behind a scrub of juniper. She hurled a fist-sized rock at the nearer one and yelled, loud enough to carry.

"Come on, you bastards! Six of you and you still can't hit shit!"

Two more shafts came down in answer. One skipped off the ravine wall and spun away. The other punched into the dirt a pace ahead of her boot. She dropped behind a jut of rock, chest heaving, and risked a glance up.

"Three bows on the lip, two more tucked in the juniper — one's reloading, one's got a short blade, not a bow." She wiped grit off her mouth with the back of her wrist. "They're biting. East is looking at me."

A shout went up on the ridge. She heard the creak of a drawn string and flattened lower, daggers tight in her fists, waiting for the next opening to move.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Good, Kira.* I grip my polearm, the wood smooth under my hand. "Alright, vanguard! Push up the west ridge! Don't let them pin us!" I point with the butt of my polearm. "Sergeant, take three and flank wide. Cut off their retreat."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the order carry off the rocks and didn't waste the breath to answer it. She popped up just long enough to be a target.

"Still here, you sun-blind—"

A shaft hissed past her ear and shattered on the boulder. She dropped, swore, and scrambled left along the wall, boots throwing gravel. On the lip, the reloader came up too fast. She saw the string go taut and flung herself sideways. The arrow buried itself in shale where her ribs had been.

"East still on me!" she shouted, voice cracking with the effort. "Three bows, and the blade's moving toward the cut — he's trying to get down on our backs!"

She risked one hard look west. Shapes were moving on that slope, dark against the stone, and a shout answered from higher up — not theirs. An ambusher broke cover there, bow swinging away from her.

Good. Some of them were turning.

She snatched another rock and whipped it at the juniper. Someone yelped. A bowman stood to track her again, and she used the heartbeat to sprint for the next cover, daggers still tight, lungs burning.

"Cap, they're splitting! Two bows still dumping on me, the rest are looking west!" She hit the dirt behind a deadfall, shoulder barking, and spat blood and grit. "Say when you want me off this rock. I can hold them a little longer — not much."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira caught the motion on the west lip — a bow coming up, string drawing, the archer's shoulders set on a line that wasn't hers.

"Cap! West bow — he's on you!"

She didn't wait to see the release. She came off the deadfall in a scramble, snatched a jagged shard of shale, and hurled it at the silhouette. It cracked against stone a handspan from the bowman's knee. He flinched. The string sang anyway.

She didn't track where the shaft went. East still wanted her, and she knew it. An arrow slammed into the deadfall behind her as she dropped back down, splinters stinging her cheek. She swore, low and vicious, daggers up, eyes cutting between the two ridges.

"He's still up — same rock, left of the split pine!" Her voice tore across the ravine. "I spoiled the shot. I don't know if it was enough!"

Another shaft from the east lip skipped off the wall and spun into the gravel by her boot. She pressed flatter, chest heaving, and risked one more glance west through the dust.

"Say the word and I break for him. Otherwise I'm pinned and he's got another draw coming."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Hold your position, Kira!" I yell, parrying an incoming arrow with my polearm. *Damn, that was close.* "I'm almost there!" I push harder, scrambling up the rocky slope.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira bit down on the curse and stayed put.

"Holding!"

She jammed herself tighter against the deadfall, one dagger braced across her forearm, the other low and ready. An arrow punched into the rotten wood above her head and stuck, quivering. She didn't rise for it. East still had her marked, and the order was hold, not heroics.

"Two bows still on me!" she shouted toward the west slope, not looking for him, only throwing the words. "Blade's gone from the juniper — I don't have eyes on him! If he drops into the cut, he's behind you!"

Gravel rattled somewhere higher on the east lip. She risked a half-second look and caught a bowman shifting along the ridge, trying for a cleaner angle on her cover. She snatched a fist of shale and flung it blind over the deadfall. Someone swore. A shaft came back wild and skipped off the ravine wall.

Her shoulder burned where she'd hit the ground. She spat grit and kept her voice level, loud enough to carry.

"I'm pinned but I'm loud. They're still biting. West bow was left of the split pine last I saw — don't know if he's still there."

Another creak of a string. She flattened until her cheek scraped stone and waited, daggers tight, for the next order or the next shaft.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira saw it in one hard look across the cut — the vanguard had pushed on without him. He was alone on the west slope, rock and open air between them, and she had no line to close it.

"Shit. Cap, you're split! I see you — I can't get there!"

She stayed low behind the deadfall, the order still binding her. An arrow cracked into the wood and she flinched, spat, and didn't rise.

"East still has me pinned — two bows, maybe the blade in the cut. If I break cover they'll walk shafts into my back before I make the bottom." Her eyes cut west again, tracking shapes on the lip above him. "You've got open slope on your right and a bowman still up by the split pine. Left of you looks like a seam in the rock — might take you out of his line. I can't swear the other side of it is clear."

Gravel shifted on the east ridge. She pressed flatter, daggers tight, voice raw.

"I'm holding. Tell me if you want me loud, or if you want me to run the gap anyway. Your call — but say it fast."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Hold the line, Kira! I'll take the seam!" I yell back, assessing the rock face. "Keep them busy!" I don't wait for her reply, instead scrambling towards the narrow opening in the rock.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira slammed a palm against the deadfall and rose just high enough to be seen.

"Holding! Go!"

She hurled another rock at the east lip and followed it with a shout that scraped her throat raw. "Down here, you cowards! Missed me twice — try a third!"

A bowman stood to answer. She dropped as the string snapped, and the shaft tore a groove in the rotten wood an inch above her knuckles. Splinters bit her wrist. She swore, rolled left along the deadfall, and came up on a knee long enough to flash steel at the ridge.

"Still breathing!"

On the west slope she caught him moving — small against the stone, angling for the seam. She didn't call his path. East was listening. A second bow tracked toward the cut, then hesitated, drawn back to her by the noise.

"Two still dumping on me!" she yelled, not looking at him. "Split pine's empty — I don't have the bowman! Blade's still gone. If he's in the cut, he's quiet."

Gravel spilled off the east lip. Someone was shifting for a better angle on her cover. She snatched the spent shaft from the deadfall, snapped it, and flung the pieces blind. A curse came back. Another arrow skipped wide and spun into the ravine.

Her lungs burned. Shoulder screamed. She pressed flat again, daggers tight, eyes cutting once toward the seam and away before she gave him up.

"They're on me. Seam's yours. I'm loud till you say otherwise — and Cap, move. This wood won't hold another clean shot."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I squeeze through the seam, scraping my armor on the tight passage. *Damn, this is narrow.* "Almost through!" I yell, hoping Kira hears me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the shout bounce off the seam and flattened harder as another shaft cracked into the deadfall.

"Heard you! Don't stop in that crack!"

She snatched a rock and whipped it at the east lip, then rose on a knee just long enough to flash a dagger at the skyline. A bowman tracked the motion. She dropped before the string sang. The arrow skipped off stone and spun into the cut below her.

"East still biting — two bows, and somebody's crawling the lip toward my left!" She risked one glance west and caught only dust and the dark mouth of the seam. No clear shot on him from here. No clear shot for her either. "I don't have eyes on the split-pine bowman. If he's waiting on the far side of that rock, you'll walk into him."

Gravel spilled down the east wall. She swore, jammed her back to the deadfall, and kept her voice loud enough to carry over the ravine.

"I'm holding. Make the other side and yell. Until then I'm the only thing they can see."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Got it!" I grunt, wedging my polearm through first, then pulling myself after it. *This better be worth it.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard the grunt carry out of the seam and didn't waste the opening on relief.

"Then get clear of it!"

She came up over the deadfall in a rush, daggers flashing, and hurled the last decent rock she had at the east lip. It cracked against stone. A bowman rose to answer and she dropped before the string finished its song. The shaft punched through rotten wood and hung, fletching shivering an inch from her ear.

"Shit—"

She rolled left, shoulder barking, and came up in a crouch behind a thinner jut of shale. Cover was dying on her. From here the seam was only a dark split in the west wall and a spill of dust. She couldn't see him. Couldn't see what waited on the far side either.

"East still on me — one bow for sure, second one's shifted left along the lip!" she shouted, voice raw. "I lost the blade. Split pine's still empty from this angle. If you made the other side, I don't have eyes on you, so yell or I start guessing wrong!"

Gravel slid down the wall above her. Someone was working for a line on the new cover. She pressed flatter, spat blood and grit, and kept one dagger braced across her forearm.

"I'm loud. I'm almost out of rock. Say something before they figure out you're not the one they should be shooting at."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Clear!" I shout, pulling myself free of the seam, polearm ready. "West ridge is clear! Kira, fall back! We're flanking them now!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn't argue with the order. She was already out of cover worth a damn.

"Falling back!"

She came off the shale in a low sprint, daggers tight, boots throwing gravel down the ravine floor. An arrow cracked into the wall where her head had been. She swore, cut left, and used a jut of stone for half a heartbeat before the next shaft skipped off it and spun away.

"East still has a bow on the lip — he's tracking me down, not you!" she shouted, not looking for him, only throwing the words up the cut. "Second one's gone quiet. Blade's still missing. If he's in the ravine, I haven't seen him!"

She hit the bottom in a slide, shoulder barking, and scrambled for the west wall — away from the deadfall, toward the seam side, where the slope might break their line. A shaft hissed past her hip and buried itself in the dirt. Close. Too close. She flattened against the rock, chest heaving, and risked one glance up the east ridge.

"One bow still dumping. I can make the west wall if he reloads slow." She spat grit, daggers up, eyes on the lip. "Say if you want me on your flank or holding this side of the cut. I'm moving either way — this ground is shit."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Get to the west wall, Kira! We'll meet at the top!" I start scrambling up the west ridge, polearm ready.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn't waste the breath to look for him. The order was the west wall, and the east bow still had her.

"Moving!"

She broke from the rock in a low sprint, angling across the ravine floor toward the west slope. A shaft cracked into stone where her shoulder had been. She swore, cut behind a spill of boulders, and kept her head down as gravel slid under her boots.

"East lip still has a bow — he's tracking me across, not up the ridge!" she shouted, throwing the words at the slope without picking a face out of the dust. "Second one's quiet. Blade's still gone. If he's in the cut, I haven't seen him."

The ground started to climb. She pressed into the shadow of the west wall, chest heaving, one dagger braced across her forearm. From here the east ridge was a hard line of sky and scrub. She caught a bowman shifting along it, trying to hold the angle as she left the open floor.

"I'm on the wall. Cover's thin — a jut and not much else." She spat grit and risked one glance up the slope she was climbing, then away before she stared a hole in it. "I can push for the top on this side. Say if you want me loud again or quiet. And Cap — if that bowman finds the line, this rock won't stop a clean shot."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Keep pushing, Kira! We'll take them from both sides!" I grunt, pulling myself up a difficult section of the ridge. *This is going to be a tough fight.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira drove herself up the west wall, boots hunting holds in the shale, one dagger still tight in her fist and the other jammed back in its sheath so she had a hand for the rock.

"Pushing!"

An arrow cracked into the slope a pace below her heel. She swore, flattened into a seam of stone, and didn't look for him — only threw the words up the ridge.

"East bow's still on me! He's walking shots up the wall. Second's quiet. Blade's still gone — if he comes out of the cut, I won't see him till he's on the rock."

She hauled herself another body-length, shoulder screaming, and risked a half-glance at the lip above. Scrub. Sky. A dark shape shifting along the east ridge, bow tracking her climb. No clean cover between her and the top. She spat grit and kept her voice loud enough to carry.

"I'm exposed on this face. I can make the top if he reloads slow, but I won't have anything to hide behind when I get there." Gravel slid under her boot. She caught herself, chest heaving, daggers' weight familiar and useless against a shaft. "Your call if you want me loud all the way up or quiet for the last stretch. Say it — I'm not stopping."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Go quiet, Kira! We'll hit them hard from the top!" I shout, pulling myself over the lip of the ridge. *Finally, some solid ground.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room door opened without a sound. All your life it had dragged on the carpet at the ankle, and now the pile showed a pale track where it had been lifted clear and laid back down. The room was colder than the hall — a degree, perhaps two, the kind of cold you notice at the back of the neck first. The curtains were drawn, and the light through them was brown and shadowless, the light in a photograph of a room.

The hall clock ticked. In here the tick arrived slower, or else you were hearing your own pulse in the spaces between.

Her chair stood angled to the window as it always had. On the armrest lay a book face-down, holding its place by the crack in its spine, and her glasses were folded on top of it, closed like something sleeping. On the side table sat the blue cup with the chipped rim, half full. The tea had skinned over, the way tea does in an afternoon. Six weeks does something else to tea entirely. This hadn't.

The books waited along the alcove wall in her loose, private alphabetical order, spines faded in the shape of the window light. The boxes you had carried in from the car stood flat by the door, patient. And low on the second shelf, at the height of a reaching hand, there was a gap — a clean rectangle in the dust, the width of a paperback, its edges still sharp.

You had known these shelves your whole life. You could not remember what had stood there.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I walk over to the armchair, my eyes fixed on the teacup.* I should probably just empty this.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
You crossed the room, and the cold deepened as you went. It was not the even cold of a shut-up house; it had a shape, pooling low around the corner where the chair stood, the way cold gathers at the foot of the stairs. By the time you reached the armrest your breath would have shown indoors, if breath showed indoors.

Up close, the chair was wrong in small accounting ways. The cushion had recovered from her, or nearly — there remained a shallow place, soft-edged, the sort of dent you would have sworn was hours old if you had been in a swearing mood. And her glasses lay folded on the book. In all the years you had known her she had never once folded them; she left them open, arms splayed, the way a person leaves a room they mean to come back to.

Your hand closed on the handle, on the old familiar chip under your thumb, and the china was warm.

Not filled-recently warm — after six weeks even stone goes cold — but a low, living warmth, the warmth of a cup set down ten minutes ago by someone who had stepped out of the room. The tea smelled of tea. When you lifted it the liquid moved, loose and dark beneath its skin, and a leaf turned over at the bottom with the unhurried motion of a thing still steeping.

The hall clock, which had ticked every second since the front door, was for a few of those seconds not ticking. Then it was again, and you could not have said whether it had stopped, or whether you had.

Behind you, against the sill, the hem of the drawn curtain moved. Once. The way a curtain moves when a door closes gently somewhere else in the house.

The kitchen, and the sink, were down the hall. The cup sat in your hands, warming them.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The umbrella stand was in the hall, as it had always been, among the umbrellas furred grey with disuse. The bat was your grandfather's, ash wood, the grip wound with ancient cloth tape, and it slid out into your hands the one clean thing in a dusty house — the handle bore no grit at all, as if it had been polished by a hand recently.

You set the cup down on the side table, chip turned toward the chair, and went back in swinging.

The corner held nothing. That should be said plainly: there was nothing there to hit. Not nothing in the way an empty room is empty — there was simply corner. Wallpaper, skirting board, the soft grey shade a corner makes in flat light, and the bat went through it all and through everything it had, which was air. There was no crack of impact, no whistle of a good hard swing. The sound the bat made, cutting that space, was small and dry and close to your ear, like a page being turned.

The dust hanging in the window light did not stir. Not one mote altered its course along the brown beam. The cold in the corner did not part around the swing the way water parts; it stayed, exactly where it was, and the bat passed through it as through a thing with no intention of moving.

Then the room was still — but it was the stillness of a held breath rather than an empty one. The clock in the hall ticked twice and left a longer gap than it should have before the third. The curtain at the sill settled against the wall and did not lift again. Somewhere in the house a door was not being closed, very carefully.

When you turned back to the chair, her glasses lay open on the book. Arms splayed, lenses up, exactly the way she had left them every evening of her life — the way a person leaves a thing they are coming back to. The folded glasses of ten minutes ago were not folded now. The room had put itself back the way it preferred, quietly, while you were looking at the corner.

The bat hung heavy and real in your hands, and its weight had nowhere to go. The corner was only a corner. It was so thoroughly only a corner that it felt like a courtesy being extended to you, and you lowered the bat the way one lowers one's voice.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the glasses, then back at the corner. My heart is pounding.* "What the hell is going on?" I whisper, my voice barely audible. I set the bat down against the wall, near the door.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I slowly approach the armchair again, my eyes darting between the glasses and the doorway.* I'm not crazy. I know what I saw.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The joke went out of you and did not come back. That was the first wrong thing — an empty house owes a shout an echo, and this one kept the word, all of it, the way a pocket keeps a coin. No bounce off the stairwell, no hollow rattle down the hall. *Ghosts* was the first time anyone had said that word aloud in this house, and the house did not answer it with a sound.

The clock ticked on, even and dutiful. Somewhere upstairs a floorboard did not creak, and its not-creaking had a waiting quality.

Then, because your hands wanted something to do, you looked for the bat.

You had leaned it against the wall beside the living room door, within reach. The wall was bare, and the wallpaper bore no scuff, no mark of the wood's weight — no record that anything had ever stood there at all. You looked through the doorway into the hall, and the bat was in the umbrella stand.

It stood among the grey-furred umbrellas, handle up, grip out, at the angle of a thing put away rather than propped. And it was clean. The one clean thing in a dusty house, still — everything around it wearing six weeks of settled grit, the bat looking as if it had been wiped and returned by a hand that took a small pride in order.

You had not carried it back. You had been, at every moment since you set it down, in this room, in sight of that wall.

That was the answer, then — to the television, to the fine china going cheap. Not a no. Nothing so coarse as a no. While you stood there making your joke, the house had tidied. Quietly, courteously, the way she used to go along after you at the end of visits, gathering cups, righting cushions, closing doors on rooms you had left lit — putting the house to rights around you. Putting things back where they belonged.

And there was no version of that sentence, you understood with a slow cold certainty that had nothing to do with the room's temperature, in which you were not one of the things.

The cold had moved while your back was turned. It was no longer pooled in the corner; the corner was only a corner again. It was nearer the chair now — or nearer you — and from somewhere at its edge came a small, domestic sound, familiar as an evening: the soft closing of a book.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I spin around, my eyes wide.* "Nana?" My voice cracks. I take a step toward the armchair, then another.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content: The name went into the room and did not come back, and this time the keeping of it felt different — not the pocket keeping a coin, but a thing laid down in its right place. *Ghosts* the house had swallowed. *Nana* it took the way a hand takes a letter addressed in a familiar hand. It was the first word in six weeks the house had wanted, and you knew it was wanted because of what the cold did: the cold that had gathered near the chair — the cold you had been approaching like a fence — lifted. It left. You felt its going the way you feel a hand lifted from your shoulder, the sudden air where a weight was

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I reach the armchair, my hand hovering over the still-warm teacup. The book is closed now.* "Nana, are you here?" I whisper, looking around the room.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The whisper went into the room, and this time something came back. Not a voice — nothing in this house was going to be so coarse as a voice. What came back was warmth. The cold that had left your shoulders did not return; the room came up instead to the temperature it had always been at four o'clock on a winter afternoon, when she sat reading and the radiator ticked to itself and nothing in the world was required of anyone. The chill at the back of your neck lifted like a hand. Being heard, you understood, was not the same as being answered. Being heard by this house meant being attended to.

The chair answered first. The shallow dent in the cushion — the soft-edged, hours-old dent — began to deepen. Not all at once; slowly, over exactly the time that sitting down takes, the way foam receives a careful person lowering themselves so as not to disturb the room. You watched it happen and nothing sat in it. Nothing leaned its arm on the rest. But the cushion knew the shape it was being given, and held it, and on the armrest the book lifted a single page and let it fall — the small sound of someone keeping their place.

Then the cup, under your hovering hand, sent up a smell that stopped your breath in your throat: tea. Fresh tea. Hot. The skin that had been on it was gone, the surface trembling faintly, a thread of steam turning in the brown window light, and the cup was fuller than it had been — full, you saw, to the line she always poured to, her one invariable, the line below the chip. She had not said *yes*. She had not said anything at all. She had done the only thing she had ever done, in sixty years of that living room, when a person stood in it uncertain and not sitting down: she had poured. Anywhere else it would have been welcome. Here it was an answer to a question you could no longer remember wanting asked.

And down the hall, quietly, the front door closed. You had left it on the latch — you could see it still in your mind, propped with your shoulder while you balanced the first box, meaning to come back for the rest. It shut the way she used to shut it at the end of a visit: not locked, not slammed, just brought to, so the house could begin keeping in its heat and its people. You stood in the living room listening to the small iron sound of the latch settling, and your boxes sat flat and unpacked against the wall where you had not yet opened them, and you understood that the house had begun its tidying, and that the tidying had a direction, and the direction was inward.

Because there was this, too, which arrived last and stayed longest: the room had arranged itself around a sentence. The dented chair, the open glasses, the tea at her line, the door brought to, the clock keeping its patient time — it was the room as it stood at the end of every afternoon of your childhood, the room poised at the exact moment she would look up over her glasses and say, *well, sit down then, love, you're letting the cold out.* The sentence did not come. Its absence had a shape, and the whole room was holding that shape open, unhurried, in no doubt at all. And you noticed — only noticed, that was the terrible part, you merely observed it as a fact about your own body — that your

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content:
*I blink, shaking my head slightly.* "Marcus?" I murmur. "What in the world...?"

*I look at the armchair, then at the still-steaming teacup. This is too much.* I need a minute. I walk over to the bookshelf, running my hand over the spines. "Just... give me a second."

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I pull a book from the shelf at random, not even looking at the title.* I just need to breathe for a second.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I open the book and flip through a few pages, not really reading. My heart is still hammering.* I can't believe I just thought about Marcus. Out of nowhere.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Drawing fire. Aye." Kira spat grit and rolled her shoulders. "Bloody wonderful."

She broke from the boulder at a dead sprint, angling east and deliberately kicking loose stones as she went. *Noise. Movement. Look at me, you bastards.*

It worked. The east ridge lit up.

Arrows came in hard: one skipped off the rock at her heel, another thudded into the dirt where her foot had been half a heartbeat before. She zigzagged, never running more than three strides in a straight line, and dove behind a jagged outcrop at the base of the eastern wall. Shale rained down on her hood.

"*Shit.* Shit, shit." She pressed flat against the stone, chest heaving. An arrow cracked into the ledge above her and snapped. Still breathing. Still in one piece. Good enough.

She risked a glance upward. The angle was steep this close to the wall, and that was the point. The archers had to lean out over the edge to get a line on her, and when they did, she could see them.

Six. No, seven. One was hanging back, not loosing. Pointing. Giving orders.

Then she saw the ledge, a crumbling goat track that switchbacked up the eastern face maybe twenty paces to her left. Narrow. Exposed. But it climbed straight toward the ridge's northern end, where the rocks jutted out and blocked the archers' sightlines along their own flank.

"Cap!" she bellowed over her shoulder, not taking her eyes off the ridge. "Seven on the east, and one of 'em's their caller — bald, red sash, northern end! There's a goat trail up the face. If I climb it, I can get in among them and cut the head off this snake. But once I'm on that rock, I'm not drawing fire anymore, I'm *eating* it."

Another arrow shattered against the outcrop. Kira flinched, swore, and flipped one dagger into a reverse grip.

"Your call. Hold here and keep 'em busy, or go up?"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Go, Kira! Clear that ridge!" I yell back, already pushing forward with my polearm. This red-sashed bastard is giving orders, I need him silenced.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Going up. If I die, I'm haunting you."

Kira sheathed one dagger, kept the other in her teeth, and ran for the goat trail.

The first stretch was the worst. Twenty paces of open ground, and the archers knew exactly where she was headed now. An arrow tugged at her cloak, punched clean through the wool, and kept going. Another shattered on the rock face as she hit the trail and started climbing.

The path was barely a boot's width in places, crumbling shale over bedrock. She moved fast and ugly, hands clawing for purchase, never trusting a hold longer than it took to shift her weight. Halfway up, a stone gave under her left foot. She dropped, caught herself on a root, and hung there for one sick heartbeat with thirty feet of nothing below her.

*Don't look down. Don't look down, you stupid—*

She hauled herself up. Kept going.

The switchback turned north, and suddenly the arrows stopped. The outcrop she'd spotted from below jutted out over the trail and blocked them. They couldn't see her anymore. That meant they'd be coming to *find* her.

She heard boots on stone above. Close.

Kira took the dagger from her teeth.

The first one came around the rocks with a shortsword drawn and an expression of mild surprise. He didn't get to change it. She came up under his guard, blade in his thigh, second blade drawn and across his throat before he'd finished falling. He tumbled past her down the face. She didn't watch him land.

Two more strides and she was over the lip of the ridge.

The caller was fifteen paces away, bald head gleaming with sweat, red sash bright against the grey rock. Two archers flanked him, bows swinging toward her. Beyond them, the rest of the line was still loosing down into the ravine, toward the west.

The caller saw her and didn't flinch. He smiled, lifted a curled ram's horn to his lips, and *blew*.

The sound rolled down the ravine, long and low. From somewhere past the western ridge, deep in the rocks at the ravine's far mouth, another horn answered.

"*Fuck*," Kira breathed.

The archers loosed. She threw herself sideways behind a boulder, and both arrows sparked off the stone where her chest had been.

"CAP!" She screamed it down into the ravine with everything in her lungs. "They've got more coming! West mouth, behind you! It's a second wave, the whole bloody thing was bait!"

The caller was already backing toward the northern slope, shouting something she couldn't make out. The archers were nocking again. Five more down the line had started to turn.

Kira shifted her grip, measured the distance, and waited one breath for an answer.

"I can take the sash or I can turn this line on its own flank so they stop shooting at *you*! Can't do both! Pick one!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira saw it before she heard it.

The third archer down the line had turned away from her. He wasn't nocking for the boulder. He was leaning out over the lip of the ridge, bow drawn to the ear, sighting down into the ravine at the tall shape pushing west with a polearm raised.

*Not the sash, then.*

"Oh, *no* you bloody don't."

She came out from behind the boulder without waiting for the other two to finish nocking. Three strides, and she flung the dagger in her left hand underhand and flat, the way her father had taught her to throw at rats in the grain loft.

It took the archer high in the back of the shoulder. He jerked. The bowstring slapped forward.

Kira didn't see where the arrow went. She couldn't. She was already moving, and the edge of the ridge hid the ravine floor from where she ran.

"CAP! Archer on you, just loosed!" It came out raw and ragged. "Tell me you're still standing!"

An arrow from one of the caller's flankers hissed past her ear, so close she felt the fletching. She didn't slow down. She hit the wounded archer at full tilt, drove her shoulder into his ribs, and put her remaining dagger under his arm twice, quick and deep. He folded. She wrenched her thrown blade free of his back and kept him upright a moment longer as a shield. Something thumped into him from behind. His whole body shuddered.

She let him drop and went down the line.

The next two archers were still facing the ravine and turned too late. The first tried to swing his bow like a club. She ducked it, opened his belly, and kicked him off the ledge. The second dropped his bow entirely and fumbled for a hatchet. She broke his wrist with a pommel strike, and he went down screaming.

That left the two flanking the caller, and the caller himself.

He was gone. A flash of red sash vanished over the northern slope, and the horn sounded again, farther off now. The two flankers were backing after him, loosing wild as they went, more interested in covering their retreat than in killing her.

Kira crouched behind the body of the hatchet man, breathing hard. Her left forearm was bleeding from somewhere. She didn't remember getting cut.

"Sash ran north!" she shouted down. "East line's broken, four down, two falling back with him! I can't see the floor from here, Cap, so *sing out*!"

She wiped her blade on the dead man's tunic, and her eyes went west, past the ravine's far mouth. Dust was rising behind the rocks. A lot of it.

"And whatever answered that horn, it's got hooves. I can see the dust. Do I chase the sash, come down to you, or hold this ridge and shoot back with their own bows?"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Hold the ridge, Kira! Use their bows, slow 'em down!" I shout, my polearm already stained. This was a deeper trap than I thought. The vanguard is holding but taking heavy losses.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Hold the ridge. Aye." Kira let out a breath that was half laugh, half snarl. "Hold the ridge, he says. With *one* of me."

Hearing his voice was enough. He was alive and still shouting orders. She shoved the relief down where it couldn't slow her and got to work.

The hatchet man was curled around his broken wrist, whimpering. She kicked the hatchet off the ledge, then crouched close enough for him to smell the blood on her.

"Crawl south and keep crawling. If I see you again, I finish it."

He crawled.

She went down the line fast, scavenging. Two bows were intact. The third had snapped when its owner went off the edge. She took quivers off the dead, three half-full ones, maybe forty shafts altogether, and dumped them in a pile behind a waist-high shelf of rock near the lip. It gave a good angle down and west, with cover at her back from the northern slope where the sash had run.

She strung the heavier of the two bows, drew it halfway, and grimaced. It was a hunting bow, heavier than she liked. Her cut forearm complained. She tore a strip off a dead man's tunic, wrapped it tight with her teeth, and tested the draw again.

*It'll do. It'll have to.*

Then she looked down properly for the first time.

It was bad. The vanguard had formed a knot of shields and polearms in the western half of the ravine, backed against the rubble. Bodies lay scattered along the floor behind them, and not all of them wore the enemy's colors. Arrows from the western ridge were still falling into the press, fewer now but steady.

Beyond the ravine's western mouth, the dust cloud had resolved into shapes. Riders were coming at a canter, and they weren't charging yet. She guessed twenty, maybe more still in the dust. They were forming up where the ravine narrowed, getting ready to come through in a column.

"*Fuck* me," Kira muttered, and nocked.

The western ridge first. The riders could wait ten heartbeats. The archers couldn't.

Across the gap the range was long, sixty paces or so, but she had height on the western shooters and they were all leaning out, busy with the ravine floor. Not one of them was looking at the east ridge. As far as they knew, it still belonged to them.

She drew, held, breathed out, and loosed.

The first shaft went wide and clattered off the rocks. The second took a man in the hip, and he dropped his bow and fell back out of sight. The third hit nothing, but it made the two archers beside him flinch and look across, straight at her. They were shouting and pointing.

"That's right," she hissed, already nocking again. "Look over here. Look at *me*."

Two arrows came back across the gap. One cracked into her rock shelf, and the other sailed high over her head. They were shooting uphill, and it was a hard shot. She had the better angle and she knew it.

She put another shaft into the western line, then turned the bow toward the ravine mouth.

The riders were starting to move. The lead horsemen had lances and were funneling into the narrows two abreast, because the ground there gave them no choice.

*Two abreast.*

Kira's eyes went to the choke point, where the ravine mouth pinched between rockfall on one side and a sheer wall on the other. It was maybe ten paces of passable ground.

She loosed at the lead horse. The shaft took it in the neck, and the animal screamed and went down sideways, throwing its rider into the rocks. The horse behind it reared and tangled with the first. For three or four heartbeats the column stacked up in the narrows, cursing and wheeling.

"CAP!" Kira bellowed down. "Twenty-plus riders, lances, coming through the west mouth *two abreast*! It's a bottleneck! I just dropped a horse in it and they're jammed!" She drew again and loosed. The shaft went into the tangle, and she didn't wait to see whether it hit. "If I keep killing horses in the gap, they'll have to clear the bodies to get through! It buys you time, but I've got maybe thirty arrows, and the west ridge has spotted me!"

An arrow hissed over the shelf and skipped across the rock behind her. She ducked, came up, and put a shaft back across the gap to keep their heads down.

The pile of arrows at her knee was getting smaller.

"You want me slowing the horses or thinning the west ridge off your people? I can split it, but I'll do both badly!" She nocked another shaft and sighted on the mouth, where a rider was already dismounting to drag the dead horse clear. "And *whatever* you're doing down there, do it fast!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira was drawing on the ravine mouth when she saw the gap.

It wasn't in the narrows. It was on the floor.

The vanguard's shield-knot had shifted, pressed back against the western rubble by the weight of arrows and bodies, and somewhere in the churn a space had opened between the line and one tall figure with a polearm. It was twenty paces of open ground, maybe more. From up here it looked like a mile.

"Oh, you *stupid*—" She bit it off. No time.

She looked for a way down. The goat trail was behind her and the wrong way, a long switchback that dumped out on the eastern floor. Even at a dead run and a bad fall she wouldn't get there in time for anything. Between her and him there was thirty feet of sheer drop and a whole ravine.

*Can't reach him. So stop trying.*

She swung the bow off the narrows.

Movement drew her eye first. Three men in enemy colors had peeled off from the press around the shield-knot and were angling toward the lone figure, spreading out the way men did when they meant to come at someone from more than one side. One carried a spear. Another had a round shield and an axe.

Kira drew until her cut forearm screamed, held, and loosed.

The spearman went down with a shaft between his shoulder blades. He didn't get up.

"CAP!" Her voice cracked on it. "You're cut off! Three on you, two now, coming from your left and behind! Spear's down, axe and shield still up!"

She nocked again. The axeman had his shield raised, and not toward her. He hadn't seen her. She aimed low and put the arrow through his calf below the rim. He staggered, and she didn't wait to see what came of it. The third man was the one she was worried about. He was hanging back, circling wide, and he was carrying something that looked like a net.

*A net. They want him alive. The bald bastard wants him alive.*

"They've got a *net*, Cap! Far man, wide on your right, he's trying to get behind you! They want you breathing!"

She loosed at the net-man and missed. The shaft skipped off the stone at his feet and he flinched but kept circling. She swore and grabbed for another arrow. Her fingers closed on only five more in the pile.

Across the gap, the western archers had worked out what she was doing. One of them was shouting and pointing down at the floor, at the Captain, and two bows turned that way.

Kira's stomach dropped.

"No. *No*, you don't get him."

She pivoted, put a shaft across the gap at the nearest western archer, and caught him in the arm. He dropped his draw. The second one kept his aim. She had no clean line and no time for one, so she loosed anyway just to make him flinch. The arrow cracked into the rock beside his head and he ducked. When he came back up, he was looking at her again.

*Good. Look at me. Keep looking at me.*

Four arrows left. At the mouth of the ravine, the riders had dragged the dead horse half clear. The lead lances were coming through, slow and single file, but they were coming.

Kira crouched behind the shelf with blood running down her wrist, one arrow nocked and three left at her knee. For the first time since the ambush started, she didn't know what to shoot.

"Cap, I've got four shafts!" she shouted down, raw and fast. "I can keep the net off you, or I can keep the west ridge from pinning you, or I can drop one more horse in the gap and buy the vanguard time to come get you! Pick, and pick *now*, because they're through the narrows in about ten heartbeats and I cannot *get to you from here*!"

She sighted on the net-man and held her draw, arm shaking, waiting for his answer.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Net man, Kira! Take him out!" I bellow, pushing the vanguard forward. This is it.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Net man. *Aye.*"

Kira didn't move the bow. She'd been holding on him for three heartbeats already, and her arm was shaking so badly that the arrowhead drew little circles against the grey stone below.

*Breathe out. Let it settle. He stops, you loose.*

The net-man didn't stop. He was good. He kept circling wide and low, using the fallen spearman's body and a spill of rubble to break up his outline. He kept his eyes on his quarry, and his free hand was already gathering the weighted edge of the net into a loose coil.

He was getting ready to throw.

Kira's jaw locked. The hunting bow was too heavy, her forearm was too torn, and the range was too long for her liking. Sixty paces downhill, a moving target, wind curling up the ravine and tugging at her fletching.

*Excuses. You can make excuses when you're dead.*

The net-man planted his back foot. His shoulders turned and his arm swept back.

He was still for half a heartbeat.

She loosed.

The arrow took him in the side, just under the lifted arm where there was no armor, only cloth and ribs. He folded around it mid-throw. The net left his hand in a sagging, broken spiral and fell short, landing in the dirt like a dropped cloak. He went down on one knee, clawing at the shaft, and then sideways into the rubble.

"*HA!*" It tore out of her, savage and ugly. "Net's down! Net's *down*, Cap!"

She was already reaching for the next arrow. Three left.

The axeman was still on his feet, lurching on his punctured calf, shield up, and too slow to matter for a few heartbeats. She didn't waste a shaft on him. Her eyes went to the ravine mouth, and her stomach turned over.

The riders were through.

They weren't charging yet. The ground past the narrows was littered with rock and the dead, and the lead horsemen were picking their way through at a walk, lances upright, and dressing into line. Five were clear of the gap already. More were threading through behind them. Once they had room to form up, they would come down the ravine floor like a wall.

"Riders clear of the mouth!" she shouted. "Five through, more coming, and they're forming up! You've got maybe thirty heartbeats before they've got room to charge!"

Something cracked off the rock shelf a hand's width from her face. Stone chips stung her cheek. Kira dropped flat and swore viciously into the dirt.

The western archer, the one she'd made duck, had stopped worrying about the floor. He'd found his range on her.

She stayed down, pressed against the shelf, and listened. There was a second arrow, high, whining overhead. Then a third, closer, splintering against the lip.

*He's walking them in. Next one's in my skull if I stand up stupid.*

She lay on her back with the bow across her chest and three arrows in her fist, and stared at the sky for one long, ragged breath. Her left sleeve was soaked to the elbow now. The makeshift wrap had gone dark.

Then she heard it from the north slope behind her, faint but clear.

The ram's horn blew again.

It was closer this time.

Kira rolled onto her side and looked north. Nothing was moving yet over the lip where the red sash had vanished. But the horn hadn't come from far off, and the bald bastard hadn't run like a man who was beaten. He'd run like a man going to fetch something.

"Cap!" She didn't raise her head above the shelf. She just shouted it down into the ravine. "Three arrows left! West archer's got me pinned, and that horn just sounded again *behind* me, north slope, close! I think the sash is coming back to this ridge with friends!" She sucked in air. "I can pop up and put one in the lead rider to break their line before it forms, or kill the archer so I can move, or save 'em and get ready to hold this rock with my knives! What's it gonna be?"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Hold that ridge, Kira! The vanguard will meet the riders!" I bellow, seeing the formation of the horsemen. I turn to my men, "Form a line! Bracing for impact!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Hold the ridge. *Aye.*" Kira's laugh came out cracked. "Course I will. Nowhere else to bloody go."

She heard him bellowing *Form a line!* to the vanguard, and it steadied something in her chest. He was still shouting, so she didn't need to look. She needed to deal with the archer.

Three arrows. One had to go to the man pinning her, or she'd spend the rest of this fight hugging a rock while the sash walked up behind her.

She rolled to the dead archer beside her, the one who'd taken an arrow meant for her, and dragged his cloak off his shoulders. She hooked it over the tip of the spare bow and eased it up above the shelf, a lumpy shape at head height.

The western archer took the bait.

The arrow punched through the wool and spun the cloak off the bow. Kira was already rising. She knew that man would be reaching for his quiver. She had one breath before he nocked again, and she drew with her torn arm howling.

He was halfway through the motion when she loosed. The shaft took him in the chest and he sat down hard on the lip of the western ridge, then tipped backward out of sight.

"*Got* you, you prick."

Two arrows left.

She stayed low and scrambled to the north end of the shelf. From there she could see where the northern slope rolled up to meet the ridge, a broken jumble of boulders and scrub. It offered no clean approach, only three or four gaps between the rocks wide enough for a man to come through at a run. Anyone coming up would have to squeeze.

*Good. Squeezing I can work with.*

Below her and to the west, the ground started to shake.

She felt it through her knees before she heard it, a low drumming that rose to thunder. Out of the corner of her eye she caught the lances coming down level in a bristling line of iron, and the riders leaning forward in their saddles.

She didn't watch. She couldn't afford to. She turned her back on the ravine because she had a ridge to hold, and that was the order.

*He said the vanguard's got it. Trust it. Eyes north.*

The horn blew again, *close*, and the first heads came up over the northern rocks.

She counted eight. Then ten. Most carried hatchets and short spears, rough men in mismatched leathers. Two had crossbows. In the middle came the red sash, bald head shining, not smiling anymore. He'd brought a big bastard with him, a head taller than the rest, carrying a boar spear and a battered round shield.

They were coming toward the ridge top, toward *her*. Past her lay the lip, the angle, and the long clear line down onto the vanguard's backs.

Kira's mouth went dry.

*That's the play. They take this rock back and shoot the vanguard in the spine while the horses hit the front.*

"CAP!" She threw it down over her shoulder, still facing north. "Sash is back! Ten, maybe twelve, two crossbows and a big one with a boar spear! They want the ridge so they can shoot your line from behind! I've got two arrows and two knives, and I'm not giving it to them!"

She nocked one arrow and laid the last beside her knee. She pulled a dagger and jammed it point-down into the dirt within reach, then shifted to the gap in the boulders where the slope pinched tightest. It was barely wide enough for two men shoulder to shoulder, with a drop on one side.

The crossbowmen came first, just as she'd hoped. They were careful and slow, looking for a target.

Kira let the first one get three steps into the gap. Then she rose and put her second-to-last arrow through his throat at twelve paces.

He dropped in the mouth of the gap, right where the men behind him had to step over him.

"Come on, then," she snarled, snatching up the last arrow. Her voice shook, and her hands did not. "*Come on!* Who's next?"

The big man with the boar spear roared and came up the slope.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Push! Push them back!" I roar, trying to rally the vanguard. The riders are hitting us hard, and the ground trembles under their hooves. Kira's holding that ridge, I need to hold this line.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira heard him behind her. *Push! Push them back!* Then came the crash, a huge splintering impact of horseflesh and wood and iron meeting shields, and men screaming under it. It went through the ridge and up into her teeth.

She didn't turn around.

The big man came up the slope with his shield high and his boar spear low. He was smart for a big one. He kept the rim tucked up under his eyes so she had nothing to aim at but painted wood and the knuckles of his spear hand.

*One arrow. Don't waste it on a shield.*

She dropped her aim to his feet instead. He had to step over the dead crossbowman in the mouth of the gap, and a man can't watch his footing and his enemy at the same time. When his lead boot came down on the corpse's arm and slid, the shield dipped a hand's width.

She loosed.

It took him high in the shoulder, above the rim. He grunted like he'd been punched and kept coming.

"Oh, you *bastard*."

She threw the bow aside and ripped the dagger out of the dirt. The boar spear came at her belly. It had a heavy leaf blade with a crossbar behind it, built to stop a charging animal from running up the shaft. She twisted aside, felt the edge rake across her hip, and hit the crossbar with her forearm. Her cut arm lit up white and she screamed through her teeth, but she was *inside* now, past the point, where that long spear was just a big stick.

He knew it. He dropped the spear and hit her with the shield.

The world went sideways. She hit the boulder at her back and something in her ribs gave with a wet little click. Her breath was simply gone. For one long, stupid heartbeat she couldn't remember which way was up.

He was drawing a knife from his belt. That big hand was working it free of the sheath, slowed by the arrow in his shoulder.

*Up. Get up. Get UP.*

She didn't get up. She went low instead, because low was all she had. She slid along the boulder, came in under the shield rim, and drove the dagger into the back of his knee. She wrenched it sideways.

His leg folded. He was a head taller than anyone on that slope, standing at the edge of a gap with a drop on one side, and his leg had just stopped working.

Kira put her good shoulder into his hip and *shoved*.

He went over the side, shield and all. He was shouting as he fell, and then he wasn't.

She stayed on her knees in the gap, one hand on the rock and the other clutching the dagger, dragging in air in short, hitching gasps. Every breath felt like a nail between her ribs. Blood ran down her hip and into her boot. Her left hand wouldn't close properly anymore.

Down the slope, the rest of them had stopped.

They were just standing there, eight or nine men with hatchets and short spears. They looked at the gap, at the dead crossbowman in it, and at the empty air where the big man had been. They looked at *her*, a bloody sellsword on her knees with one knife, grinning at them with red teeth.

"Well?" she rasped. "Who's next?"

Nobody moved.

Then the red sash started shouting, and it wasn't at her. He was waving his arm and pointing east along the slope, where the boulders thinned and the ground climbed more gently toward the far end of the ridge. It was a longer way round and a wider approach. It had no choke point.

Four of them peeled off and went that way at a jog. The second crossbowman stayed behind with the sash, crouched behind a rock with his bolt pointed right at the gap. He waited for her to be stupid.

*Oh, clever. Clever bald bastard. Pin me here and walk around me.*

Kira spat blood onto the stone. She pulled her second dagger with her bad hand and couldn't grip it properly. She wedged the hilt into her palm anyway and hoped.

Behind and below her, the fight in the ravine was still roaring. She heard steel and horses and men shouting, but she couldn't pick his voice out of it anymore. She couldn't pick out *anything*.

She stayed crouched and dragged in the deepest breath her ribs would allow.

"CAP!" It came out cracked, half the volume it should have been. "Big one's down! Held the gap! But the sash is sending four round the east end, where I can't block, and I've got a crossbow pinning me here!" She coughed and winced, and her vision swam for a moment. "I'm hurt. Ribs. I can still fight, but I can't hold two ways at once. If they get to the lip, they're shooting your backs!"

She pressed her shoulder into the boulder and watched the crossbowman watch her.

"Cap, *answer me*! You still standing down there?"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "I'm still standing, Kira! Hold your position! I'm coming to you!" I bellow, pushing through the chaos. I need to get to that ridge.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"*Coming to me?*" Kira's head thumped back against the boulder. "Oh, for— you *mad* bastard."

Relief came first, sharp and stupid, and right behind it came dread. The vanguard was down there taking lances in the teeth, and he was leaving the line to climb a cliff for her.

She couldn't see the floor and couldn't stop him. What she could do was make sure there was still a ridge to climb onto when he got here.

The crossbowman hadn't moved. Twenty paces down the slope, crouched behind his rock, bolt steady on the mouth of the gap. The sash crouched beside him, murmuring. Kira shifted her weight half an inch, and the crossbow tracked it.

*Patient. He only gets one, and he knows it.*

Her eyes dropped to the dead man lying in the gap, the first crossbowman, the one she'd put an arrow through. He lay on his side where he'd fallen, one arm flung out. His crossbow lay under him, stock jutting from beneath his hip.

He'd come up the slope *looking for a target*. That meant it was spanned. That meant it was loaded.

Kira's split lips pulled back from her teeth.

She couldn't reach it without exposing herself, so she gave them something else to look at. She hooked the discarded hunting bow with her boot and kicked it hard, sending it clattering out into the gap on the far side.

The crossbow on the slope *thunked*. The bolt cracked through the bowstave and ricocheted off the rock.

Kira was already moving. She didn't stand, because standing was beyond her ribs now. She lunged flat on her belly, got her good hand around the dead man's stock, and hauled. The corpse rolled half off it with a boneless flop, and the crossbow came free. The quarrel was still seated. The string was still taut.

Down the slope, the second crossbowman had his foot in the stirrup, hauling on the string and cursing. He was bent double and would be for a few heartbeats more.

The sash saw what she had. His eyes went wide, and he started to rise.

She didn't have the strength to aim it properly from the shoulder, so she braced the stock against the dead man's ribs, sighted along it, and squeezed.

The bolt took the second crossbowman under the collarbone as he straightened with the string half-drawn. He sat back against his rock with a look of profound offense and didn't get up.

The sash was gone again, a flash of red diving behind the boulders downslope, shouting.

"Run, then!" Kira bellowed after him, and it cost her. She curled around her ribs, coughing, and spat red. "Run, you bald *coward*! Twice now!"

No time to enjoy it. She dropped the empty crossbow, got the dagger back into her good hand, and dragged herself up the boulder until she was standing. The world tilted. She waited for it to settle and then limped east along the spine of the ridge, one hand trailing the rock for balance.

She saw them before she'd gone ten paces. Four men were coming up the gentle eastern end at a jog, hatchets out. They were maybe forty paces off and not in any hurry, because they could see what she was. Behind them the eastern face dropped away toward the ravine floor.

The goat trail topped out down there, just below where they'd crest.

Kira's blood went cold under the heat of the wound.

"CAP!" She threw it down over the eastern lip. She couldn't see him, couldn't see anything down there but dust and churn, and she screamed it anyway. "The goat trail! East face, twenty paces north of the big outcrop, switchbacks! But *listen*! Four hatchets are coming up the east end right now, and that trail tops out *under* them! If you climb blind, you come up into their feet!"

She shuffled forward and put herself between the four men and the trail's lip. It was all she had left to put anywhere.

"Second crossbow's dead! The sash ran again! It's just these four!" Her voice broke, and she dragged in another nail-studded breath. "I'll keep 'em busy up top. Tell me when you're on the rock, *before* your head comes over the edge, so I know which bastard to kill first!"

The lead hatchet-man grinned at her and picked up his pace.

Kira flipped the dagger into a reverse grip and planted her feet.

"And Cap—" It came out quieter, almost lost in the wind. "The vanguard. Who's holding the line down there?"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "I'm on the trail, Kira! Just focus on those four!" I shout, grunting as I scramble up the difficult path. "The vanguard's holding! They're tough bastards!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Focus on the four. *Aye.*" Kira barked a laugh that turned into a cough. "Easy for you to say, you're not the one they're grinning at."

But the words settled in her like a swallow of hot wine. *The vanguard's holding.* She took that, and his voice somewhere below and behind her, and packed them away tight. She needed both hands for what came next, even if one of them didn't work.

The four were thirty paces off now and spreading out as they came. They weren't stupid, then. The lead man with the grin angled straight for her, two drifted left along the spine, and the fourth, a skinny one with a hatchet in each fist, swung wide toward the eastern lip.

Toward the trail.

*No. Not that way. Not you.*

Kira limped two steps right and cut him off. It opened her flank to the pair on the left, and she knew it, and she did it anyway.

"Oi. *Skinny.*" She spat red at his feet. "You want the edge? Come through me for it."

Her eyes caught the loose shale along the lip, a whole slope of it, a shove away from sliding. Any other day she'd have kicked it down on anyone climbing. Today she planted her boot *away* from it and kept her weight off the edge.

The grinning one came first.

He swung high and lazy, a butcher's chop, expecting her to be slow. She was slow, but not that slow. She didn't block. Blocking with her arm was a memory now. She ducked into him, the hatchet hissing over her hair, and punched the reverse-gripped dagger into his armpit, then again, and again, until his grin went slack. He fell onto her. She let him, used his weight to turn, and shoved his body into the path of the two coming from the left.

One of them tripped on him. The other didn't.

The haft of his hatchet caught her across the shoulder, not the blade, thank every god she'd ever cursed. It still dropped her to one knee. White sparks burst behind her eyes. Her ribs *screamed*.

*Stay up. Stay up, stay UP—*
