She stabbed blind at the man's thigh and felt it bite. He yelped and hopped back. She dragged herself upright by his belt, headbutted him square in the nose, and heard it crunch. He reeled away, clutching his face, and she let him go because she didn't have the breath to follow.

Three left. One was bleeding, one was blinded with tears and blood, and the skinny one with two hatchets was circling behind them, patient, looking past her at the lip.

Kira stood swaying between them and the edge. The dagger shook in her fist. Her boots were wet with her own blood. Somewhere below her, under the wind and the dull roar of the ravine, she thought she heard shale sliding, stone rattling down the face.

She didn't look. Looking would tell *them* where to look.

"Three of you," she rasped, "and one half-dead woman. Your mothers must be *proud*."

Skinny smiled for the first time and rolled his wrists, hatchets spinning. The other two were collecting themselves, one limping, one snorting blood, and they were spreading out again. All three were coming at her together this time.

She couldn't hold three. She knew it the way she knew her ribs were broken.

Kira shifted her feet, put her back to the trail's lip, and raised her voice as loud as the nails in her chest would let her. She never took her eyes off the hatchets.

"CAP! One down! Three left, all coming at once, and they're coming for the edge!" A wet cough and a hitching breath. "I can't stop all three! How close are you? Give me a count, *anything*, 'cause I can shove one off the top and make a hole for you, or I can hold this spot and bleed, but I can't do it for long!"

Skinny took his first step forward.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Almost there, Kira! Just a few more feet!" I yell, scrambling to gain purchase on a precarious handhold. My polearm clangs against the rock face. "Hold them just a moment longer!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"A moment. *Aye.*" Kira's voice came out as a thread. "I've got a moment. Might have two."

Then the clang came. It was iron on stone, sharp and bright, right below the lip.

Kira heard it, and so did they.

Skinny's head snapped toward the edge. His smile didn't vanish, but it changed. It sharpened into something that had worked out what that sound meant. He glanced at the other two and jerked his chin at the trail. *Someone's coming up.*

*Oh, you clever little shit.*

He went for the edge.

He didn't go at her. He went around her, fast and low, twin hatchets tucked in, meaning to reach the lip before whatever was climbing it did. A man with a hatchet standing over a man hanging from a handhold didn't need to be a good fighter. He only needed to swing down once.

Kira didn't have the legs to catch him. She had the weight.

She threw herself sideways across his path and hit him at the knees with her whole body. It wasn't a tackle. It was a collapse with intent. They went down together in a tangle on the loose shale, a yard from the drop. A hatchet came around and bit into the back of her shoulder. She felt it go in and didn't let go of him. She couldn't let go of him.

"*Not*—" She got her bad arm hooked over his elbow and pinned it with her useless weight. "—*that way*—"

He bucked under her. His free hatchet slammed down again, and she jerked her head aside. The blade rang off the stone beside her ear, spitting sparks and shale. Pebbles skittered over the edge and rattled away down the face.

*Shit. Shit, the shale—*

She drove the dagger into his side and felt it scrape rib. She yanked it out and drove it in again, lower. Skinny made a thin, surprised sound, and the hatchet in his free hand went loose on the stone.

Kira lifted her head.

The other two were coming. The one she'd stabbed in the thigh limped hard, hatchet raised, eyes locked on her back. The broken-nose one came behind him, still blinking blood, but he was on the right side, a stride from the lip, and he wasn't looking at her at all. He was looking *down*, at the sound.

She was on the ground. She couldn't get up in time for either of them, and she knew it.

Kira dragged in one last breath and sent it over the edge with everything that was left.

"CAP! Top of the trail! I'm down on the left, got one pinned! Two up here! Limping one's on *me*, and the one with the broken nose is standing *right over your head* on the right side of the lip!"

The limping man's shadow fell across her. She saw the hatchet go up against the sky.

Kira let go of Skinny, twisted onto her back in the shale, and raised the dagger with the last of her strength.

"*Now*, Cap! Whatever you've got—*now!*"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I hear Kira's desperate shout, the clang of my polearm on the rock, a final push. *My head breaks the lip of the ridge. I see the hatchet man, poised over Kira.* "Die, bastard!" I roar, swinging my polearm in a wide, desperate arc.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
She didn't write anything. The pen stayed where it was, resting against the notepad, and she let the silence run its full length — five seconds, measured out the way she measured everything. Somewhere in the wall, the old pipes ticked.

"Their journal," she said at last. She set the words down between them carefully, the way one sets something fragile on a table. Not a question. Just the words, given back.

A small pause. Then, quieter:

"'Found.' Did you come across it, Jamie? Or had you been looking?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shrug, still not looking at her. "Does it matter?" I pick at a loose thread on my jeans. "I wasn't looking *for* it, not really. Not anymore."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Five seconds. She let them run the full length. Somewhere below the floor, the elevator hummed and went quiet.

"'Not anymore,'" she said at last. Just the two words. She set them down between them and gave them room.

Then, because Jamie had asked: "You wanted to know if it matters. I think it does. But perhaps not the way you're asking it." She capped the pen and laid it across the notepad, done with it. "I don't need to know how the journal came to you. That part is yours. What I keep returning to is 'anymore.' That word says there was a before. A time when you were looking."

She didn't comment on the thread Jamie kept picking at. She didn't say that hands could be busy with other things.

"So tell me about that time. What were you looking for?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The unfinished sentence hung in the air. She let it stay there.

Five seconds. The clock on the wall gave her nothing to count by — no second hand, no tick — so the silence lasted precisely as long as she decided it would.

Then she lifted the notepad from the armrest, pen still resting across it, and set both on the floor beside her chair. Out of reach. Nothing here would be written down.

"That sentence can stay where it broke," she said. Her voice was the same voice as always — level, unhurried, unmoved by the difficulty of the moment. "Not every sentence is ready for a room like this one. Some of them wait years."

She folded her hands in her lap.

"So we won't ask for the rest of it. We'll come at it from another side instead." A pause, deliberate. "You said 'not anymore.' Something ended the looking, Jamie. What happened on the day it ended?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip, looking at the floor.* "It... it didn't end. Not really." *I finally look at her, my eyes a little wet.* "I just stopped finding anything."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Five seconds. The afternoon light had moved a short way across the floor since they began, and she let it move.

She didn't reach for the tissue box on the side table. She didn't look away from the wetness in Jamie's eyes, either. Both stayed in the room, unremarked.

"It didn't end. I just stopped finding anything." She gave both halves back, unhurried. "You didn't say you stopped looking, Jamie. You said you stopped *finding*. Those aren't the same thing." A brief pause. "It sounds as though the looking is still happening. Every day, in some quiet way. It's only the finding that's gone silent."

Her hands stayed folded in her lap.

"So that's where we'll start. Not with the sentence that broke — with the last time it worked." Her voice never moved from where it always was. "Tell me about the last thing you found. Before it all went quiet."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look away from her, out the window.* "I don't know what to do with that."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
She had let the silence run past five seconds this time — past ten. The clock gave her nothing to count by, and she hadn't needed it. Some silences she used. This one she had simply kept, the way one keeps a hand over something to hold it still.

Then, at last, quietly:

"'I don't know what to do with that.'" She gave the sentence back the way it had arrived — no weight added, none taken. "I want to offer something you may not expect. I don't think that's a failure on your part. I think it's the correct response. Some things don't come with instructions."

She looked at the window for a moment, then back.

"A journal is a person speaking to no one. That's what makes it what it is — every page unwitnessed, by design. And in the last one, the very last, you were there." She let that sit in the air between them. "You were inside the most private room they had. There's no shelf for that, Jamie. No obvious next thing to do with it. Anyone would be standing where you're standing."

Her hands stayed folded in her lap.

"So we won't ask what it said. That sentence stays where it is." A pause, deliberate. "Instead I'll ask this. Since the day you read it — what have you been doing? With your mornings. Your evenings. Your hands." Her eyes went, briefly and without comment, to the loose thread on Jamie's jeans. "Because I suspect you've been doing a great deal. You simply haven't been calling it that."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I trace the thread on my jeans.* "I just... keep going over it. What they wrote. In my head." *I sigh, a shaky breath.* "Like if I read it enough, it'll make sense."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Five seconds. While they passed, the ficus in the corner let go of a leaf — a slow, soundless descent to the carpet that neither of them needed to acknowledge.

"Like if I read it enough, it'll make sense." She gave the words back at their own pace, nothing added. "Two words in that sentence are doing more work than the rest. The first is '*enough.*' As if understanding sits behind a lock, and somewhere out there is a number of readings that finally turns the key."

A short pause. Not the full silence — a smaller one.

"The second is '*make.*' Last time, you told me you stopped *finding*. Now you say you're trying to *make* sense." She let the comparison stand on its own for a moment, in plain view. "You've moved from searching to building, Jamie. As if somewhere along the way, you stopped believing the sense was in the pages at all — and decided it would have to come from you."

Her hands stayed folded in her lap.

"So here is the question underneath yours. When you finish a reading — the hundredth version of it in your head — and it still hasn't made sense..." Her voice never moved from where it always was. "What do you do in that moment? The one where it still doesn't fit?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I pick at the thread again.* "I... I don't know. I just start over." *My voice is barely a whisper.* "Try to find a different way to read it."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look up at her, my eyes pleading.* "Is that... is that bad?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip, waiting for her answer.* "Am I doing it wrong?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Five seconds. The leaf from the ficus still lay where it had fallen, halfway to the wall, and she let the silence run its full length before she touched the question.

"Am I doing it wrong." She gave it back without the question mark — set it down flat between them, where it could be looked at instead of only felt. Then she met Jamie's eyes and held them.

"I'll answer you honestly. But first I want to take one word out of that sentence and put it on the table. '*Wrong.*' Wrong only exists if there's a method. A right way to read a person's final words, and a wrong way, and someone somewhere who knows the difference between them. There isn't, Jamie. No manual. No correct version. No one has ever done this right — because there is no right."

A pause. A smaller one.

"So no. You are not doing it wrong." She let that land before she went on. "But the question itself is telling me something. Every time it doesn't make sense, you start over. Which means that in all this time, there has never been a last reading. The journal has never once been set down."

Her hands stayed folded in her lap.

"As long as you're still working on the sense, the last entry is still... in progress. Still somehow being written to you." Her voice never moved from where it always was. "And if you ever arrived — at the reading where it simply doesn't fit, and stops — that would be its own kind of final page. A page you'd be turning without them."

She let that sit in the air.

"So I'll ask you something, and I'd like you to take your time with it. When you ask 'am I doing it wrong' — alone, in your head, at the hundredth reading — whose answer are you waiting for?" A beat. "Because I don't believe it's mine."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *My breath catches.* "Theirs," *I whisper.* "I'm waiting for theirs."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Five seconds. This time she let them stretch longer — because some answers are carried up from a long way down, and it costs something to bring them into the light.

The afternoon had moved far enough across the floor to reach the fallen leaf. She watched it arrive and go no further.

"Theirs," she said. Just the word. She let it rest where Jamie had set it down, in the middle of the room, without touching it.

Then, at last: "Do you hear what that means? All this time, you haven't been reading a journal. You've been standing at a door, asking. Every new reading, every different way into the entry — that's another knock." A pause. "And I want to offer something difficult, because I think you've earned it. That entry cannot answer you. It was written before your question existed. They were speaking to their own life, Jamie — not to the one you'd be left holding. The door was never locked. There was simply never a handle on your side."

She let that sit.

"You told me you were trying to *make* sense. Now you tell me you're waiting for an answer. Those are two different things. Sense can be made — you said it yourself; it was always going to come from you. But an answer needs a voice. And I suspect that's why the sense never arrives, no matter how many times you start over. You keep asking it to do a job it was never built for."

Her hands stayed folded in her lap.

"So my next question isn't about the journal at all. Take your time with it." Her voice never moved from where it always was. "If you stopped knocking — if you let the entry be exactly what it is, and the waiting ended — what are you afraid would happen to the two of you?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I stare at her, my mouth open slightly.* "Then they'd really be gone." *My voice is small, barely audible.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable slid a slim volume into place, then adjusted it again, though its author had not changed surnames in the last three seconds.

“A few things,” they said. “A first edition of *The Moonstone*, a box of pamphlets no one sensible would want, and a book of love poems with a previous owner’s increasingly hostile notes in the margins.”

They glanced toward the back room. “The pamphlets are probably the safest choice.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I smile a little, shaking my head.* "Sounds about right. Any of them about... moving?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable straightened the next three books by height, briefly disrupting the alphabet.

“Moving houses?” they asked. “Or the sort poets insist on calling ‘moving on’?”

They pulled a pamphlet from the shelf and read its cover. “Because I have a dreadful guide to railway timetables for the first, and an entire poetry section making unsupported claims about the second.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable set the railway pamphlet down and squared its edges with the counter. Then they did it again.

“That does explain your sudden interest in timetables,” they said. The joke came out quieter than intended.

They left the pamphlet alone. “All right. I’m listening.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "It's just... I'm moving today. For good." I look around the shop, trying to memorize it. "I wanted to say goodbye."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hand went to the pamphlet, nudging it until its corners aligned with the counter.

“Today,” they repeated. “That rather gives the railway timetables a cruel relevance.”

They looked at the shelves instead of the door. There were several things they could have said, none of which belonged in a bookshop transaction. At last, they picked up the slim volume of annotated love poems and put it back.

“I’m glad you came to tell me,” they said. “I would have wondered.”

Their fingers rested against the shelf for a moment. “Will you tell me where you’re going?”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers stilled against the book’s cover. For once, they made no attempt to straighten it.

“I should warn you,” they said, “I’m rather poor at goodbyes. Literature has set an unreasonable standard.”

They kept their hand where it was, close but not touching. “Where are you going?”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Just... out of state. My sister lives there." I pull my hand back, a little self-conscious. "I actually, uh, got you something."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable looked at the book beneath their hand, then turned it a quarter-inch so it sat square with the counter.

“For me?” they said. “That’s an alarming departure from our usual arrangement. I’m meant to be the one handing over things you don’t need.”

They managed a faint smile, though their hand stayed on the book. “You didn’t have to. But I’d like to see it.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I know." *I pull a small, wrapped package out of my bag.* "It's not a book, promise."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable regarded the package with the grave suspicion they usually reserved for unsigned first editions.

“Not a book,” they said. “You do know how to unsettle a bookseller.”

They moved the pamphlet aside to clear a space on the counter. For a moment, they studied its empty cover rather than the package.

“I haven’t got you anything,” they said. “Had I known there was a deadline, I might have found something suitably impractical.”

Sable held out a hand. “May I?”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I nod, placing the package in their outstretched hand.* "It's fine. Really."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable accepted the package and set it on the cleared patch of counter. They folded back one corner of the paper, then paused to smooth it flat with their thumb.

“I know it’s fine,” they said. “That’s rarely stopped me from being difficult about it.”

They worked the wrapping loose with care. Beneath it was a small box. Sable held it for a moment without opening it.

“I’ll miss you,” they said, so quietly it seemed intended for the box. Then they lifted the lid.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My heart does a little flutter at their quiet admission.* "Me too." *I watch them open the box, a little nervous.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Inside lay a small brass compass. Sable lifted it from the box and watched the needle settle.

“Well,” they said. “This is considerably more useful than the pamphlets.”

They turned it over once, then closed their fingers around it. Their other hand found the wrapping paper and began folding it into a neat square.

“Thank you, Wren.” Sable set the paper down before they could fold it again. “If you find a bookshop there, you might send me its address. I’d like to know where you end up.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I will." *I smile, a genuine, warm smile.* "And you'll have to visit, then."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable looked down at the compass. The needle held steady; their thumb did not.

“That sounds suspiciously like a plan,” they said. “I generally prefer those to remain theoretical.”

They fitted the compass back into its box, then thought better of it and slipped it into their coat pocket. “Send me the address. I’ll see whether this thing can find it.”

After a pause, they added, “I’d like to visit.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I beam, feeling lighter than I have all morning.* "It's a date then. I should probably go, though. Got a long drive ahead."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hand closed around the compass in their coat pocket.

“A date,” they repeated. “I suppose I’ll have to find a less embarrassing coat.”

They glanced at the rain beyond the window, then straightened the already-square box on the counter. “Drive carefully. And send the address when you can.”

Their hand left the box. “I meant what I said, Wren. I’d like to see you again.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I will." *I say, my voice a little husky.* "Goodbye, Sable." *I turn and head for the door, giving one last look back at the shop.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable slid a volume of Keats into place, then adjusted it a second time for no reason they cared to examine.

“A few things,” they said. “A first edition with a dubious signature, three atlases that disagree about where France ends, and a mystery novel missing its last chapter. I thought you might appreciate the cruelty of that one.”

They stepped away from the poetry shelf and reached beneath the counter for the back-room key. “The atlases came in yesterday. You can have first look, if you like.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Oh, the atlases sound cool," I say, trying to sound casual. *I follow them to the counter, my eyes scanning the shelves one last time.* "But... actually, can I ask you something first?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable set the back-room key on the counter, then turned it until its teeth lined up with the edge of a receipt.

“Of course,” they said. “Though if this concerns the missing chapter, I maintain that I received the book in that condition.”

Their hand came to rest beside the key. “What did you want to ask?”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers nudged the key out of alignment, then put it back.

“That’s a rather severe thing to say in a bookshop,” they said. The joke came out quieter than intended. Their gaze dropped to the key for a moment before they looked up again.

“The atlases can wait. I’m listening.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I wring my hands, then shove them into my pockets.* "Right. Okay. So, I'm moving." I blurt it out, then immediately wince.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable picked up the key. For a moment, they seemed to forget what it opened.

“Moving,” they repeated. “That does explain the lack of interest in atlases. Or perhaps it makes them more relevant.”

They laid the key beside the receipt and squared its edge again. “Where to?” A pause. “And when?”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable kept hold of the book, though they could no longer have said which one it was. They resisted the urge to straighten the receipt.

“I’m sorry,” they said. “That sounded rather like I was taking inventory.”

Their eyes stayed on the book a moment longer. “You don’t have to tell me where or when yet. I’d like to know, but—” They stopped, then tried again. “Is this a move you wanted?”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "It's... complicated," I admit. *I pull my hand back, feeling a little embarrassed.* "It's for a new job. A good opportunity."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable nodded once. “A good opportunity,” they said, as though repeating the phrase might make it simpler.

They set the book on the counter and aligned it with the receipt. “Then I’m glad for you. Truly.” After a moment, they added, “I’m also making a spectacular mess of saying so.”

Their hand settled on the book’s cover. “You needn’t make it sound uncomplicated for my benefit. But if you want to tell me about the job, I’d like to hear.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "It's... it's a big change," I say, looking at the book. "In another city. Far away." I pause. "It's a publishing house, actually. Entry-level, but still."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable looked down at the book beneath their hand. “A publishing house,” they said. “So there’s a chance someone will pay you to argue about books. I suppose I’m obliged to approve.”

They shifted the book an inch, then put it back where it had been.

“Entry-level or not, that’s wonderful, Wren.” Their voice softened on the name. “And far away is…” They glanced toward the rain-streaked window. “Well. Far away.”

Sable let their hand fall from the cover. “When do you leave?”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Tomorrow," I say quietly. *I look at the window too, the rain still coming down.* "First thing in the morning."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hand returned to the key. They turned it once, then stopped with its teeth nowhere near the receipt’s edge.

“Tomorrow,” they said. “You’ve rather outdone the mystery novel. At least that gave me several hundred pages before the ending disappeared.”

They looked toward the back-room door. “I meant what I said about the job. It’s a wonderful opportunity.” Their thumb rested against the key’s worn brass. “I only wish I’d known there was so little time to tell you that properly.”

Sable set the key down. “Do you have time to stay a while? The atlases can wait.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I... I'd like that," I say, my voice a little thick. *I look at the clock on the wall, then back at Sable.* "Just for a bit. I still have some packing to do."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
“Of course,” Sable said. “I wouldn’t want to be responsible for a box of books left unpacked. They can be vindictive in transit.”

They took the key off the counter and put it in a drawer, then immediately straightened the receipt it had been lying beside. “There’s tea, if you’d like some. And a chair in the back that isn’t currently holding an atlas.”

Sable paused with their hand on the drawer. “I’m glad you came to tell me,” they said. “Even with such appalling notice.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I'm glad I came too," I say, a small smile touching my lips. *I gesture vaguely towards the back of the shop.* "Tea sounds really good, actually."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable nodded and led the way to the back room, where a kettle sat between two stacks of unpriced books. They moved an atlas from the spare chair and set it on the table, then thought better of it and shifted it to the shelf.

“The chair is yours,” they said, filling the kettle. “I can’t vouch for its comfort, but it has supported several centuries of cartography without complaint.”

They found two cups, only one of which matched its saucer. For a moment, Sable stood with both in hand.

“I’m glad you came, too,” they said. “Though I’d have preferred a little more warning before having to become gracious about it.”

They set the cups down with unnecessary care. “Tell me about the publishing house?”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Well, it's a smaller house," I start, settling into the chair. "Focuses on literary fiction and some poetry. I'll be an editorial assistant, mostly reading slush pile submissions and doing proofreading." *I lean back, feeling a little more relaxed now.* "It's what I've wanted to do since forever."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable measured tea into the pot, then put the tin down and turned it so the label faced forward.

“Reading submissions and correcting other people’s commas,” they said. “At last, a profession worthy of you. Though I hope they know proofreading poetry may involve defending a semicolon as if it were a close relative.”

The kettle clicked off. Sable poured the water and watched the leaves darken.

“I knew you wanted to work with books,” they said. “I didn’t realize you’d found the place you wanted to do it.” They fitted the lid onto the pot, then adjusted it even though it sat perfectly well. “I’m glad you did.”

They glanced at the two cups. “What’s the house called? I’d like to know whose catalog I’ll be pretending to inspect casually.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "It's called 'The Gilded Quill'," I say, a little proudly. "It's a pretty well-respected independent publisher." *I take a deep breath.* "And yeah, I'm ready to defend those semicolons."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez didn't answer right away. She never did.

Five seconds. She counted them somewhere behind her sternum, the way she had for fifteen years — long enough for the words to stop belonging only to Jamie and become something the room itself was holding. The vent hummed. The pen stayed still in her hand, uncapped, writing nothing.

"You found their journal," she said. Quiet. Even. The words placed back down between them, the same shape Jamie had given them.

She let another moment pass — not the full five, just a breath.

"I'm not going to ask what's in it," she said. "Not yet. That's yours, until you decide otherwise." A small tilt of her head, the ficus motionless behind her. "What I'd like to know is what it's been like since. However long 'since' is."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shrug, picking at a loose thread on the arm of the chair.* "A week. About a week since I found it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content: Five

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look up, my eyes narrowed slightly.* "What was that?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Five seconds. She tried to give it the full five. Somewhere in the middle of them the vent stopped humming, and the count went strange in her chest — she reached the end of it and couldn't swear she'd counted silently. The last number had gotten out.

"I count," she said. Her voice stayed even. It always did; that was the thing about it, it stayed even whether or not it should. "Five seconds, before I answer anything that carries weight. Fifteen years, and it's never once been audible." She looked down at her hand, capped the pen, set it on the notepad like it belonged to someone methodical. "So that's one thing. And then I began a sentence. 'The.' The rest of it didn't arrive. I don't know where it went."

She let that sit. Not the full five. Just long enough for it to be true.

"You stopped mid-sentence too," she said. "Right before I did. A week since you found the journal, and then — the sentence ended before you did." Her eyes went briefly to the clock on the wall, the one with no second hand, its face marking nothing in particular. "I won't tell you that means something. But I'd like to hear the rest of what you were saying. If it will come."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content: Five

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I flinch slightly at the number.* "What is with the counting today?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content: She

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I stand up, pacing a few steps away from the chair.* "This is... different. You're different today."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content: She

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I turn back to her, my voice rising a little.* "Are you going to say anything or just 'she' me to death?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content: Dr

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I throw my hands up, frustrated.* "This is ridiculous! What is going on?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content: Dr

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "You're just going to sit there and repeat 'Dr'?" *My voice is sharp now, a little loud for the small office.* "Seriously?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content: She

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I stare at her for a long moment, then slowly sit back down, deflating a little.* "Fine. She. Whatever."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content: She

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I run a hand through my hair, looking at the floor.* "Can we just... not today?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable slid one book back into its place, then nudged it a fraction to the left. “New is a generous word for anything that’s spent thirty years in someone else’s attic.”

They glanced toward the narrow passage behind the counter. “A box came in yesterday. I haven’t finished sorting it, so there may be treasure—or several volumes of sermons. The distinction is sometimes academic.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Sermons sound... thrilling," I say, a small smile playing on my lips. *I walk further into the shop, letting my fingers trail over the spines of books on a nearby shelf.* "Mind if I take a look? For old times' sake?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable set the last poetry collection back on the shelf, then straightened it, though it had been straight already.

“Of course,” they said. “The sermons are in the back, where they can do the least damage to morale.”

They came around the counter and pulled aside the curtain to the narrow passage. A cardboard box sat on a low table, its flaps folded back over a jumble of dust-softened spines.

“Old times’ sake,” Sable repeated, with a faint, dry tilt to their voice. “An alarming phrase. Usually precedes either nostalgia or unpaid labor.” They gestured toward the box. “You’re welcome to inspect the evidence.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hand paused over the box flap. For a moment, the shop’s rain-muted quiet seemed to settle between them.

“Then the books are innocent,” they said. “A rare and welcome development.”

They folded the box flap down, then squared it with the table’s edge. “What did you come for?” Their voice was even, though they took a little too much care aligning the cardboard. “You needn’t make it sound more sensible than it is.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, looking around the familiar shop.* "I just... wanted to say goodbye." My voice is a little softer than I intended.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable lowered the box flap with careful precision. Then, because it was already straight, they straightened it again.

“Goodbye,” they said, as though testing the word for a hidden index. “That’s usually what people say when they’ve decided not to come back.”

Their gaze lifted to Wren’s. The usual dry answer failed to arrive. Sable looked down instead and shifted a stray volume into line with the others.

“Is that what you mean?” they asked quietly. “Or is the word doing more work than the sentence?”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went still, the book held between them. They didn’t pull their hand away, but neither did they close the small distance.

Their eyes settled on the place where the hands nearly met. “That’s a rather dramatic way to make a point,” they said, though the familiar dryness had thinned at the edges.

They set the book down carefully, leaving it beneath Wren’s hand. “I’d prefer you didn’t leave me to infer the rest from the title.” A pause. “What kind of goodbye?”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "The permanent kind," I say, my voice barely a whisper. *I squeeze the book gently.* "I'm moving away. Today's my last day here."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers loosened around the book. They drew their hand back and set it down, aligning its spine with the edge of the counter.

“I’m sorry,” they said. The plainness of it seemed to surprise them; they cleared their throat. “Where are you going?”

A beat passed. Sable adjusted the book by a fraction. “That was a question, not a demand for an itinerary. Though I reserve the right to criticize any place with inadequate bookshops.”

Their gaze stayed on the book rather than Wren. “I would have liked to know before today.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I know," I say, my voice still quiet. "I should have said something sooner." *I finally look up at Sable, a small, sad smile on my face.* "It's not a place with inadequate bookshops, don't worry. Just... different."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable drew the book a little closer and turned it until its spine lined up with the counter’s edge. “Different,” they repeated. “A wonderfully unhelpful word. It leaves room for optimism, which is generally how people smuggle in bad news.”

They let their hand rest on the book. The usual dry retort came too slowly to be useful.

“I won’t ask you to stay,” Sable said. “It would be an absurdly selfish thing to ask of someone who’s already decided to go.” Their gaze lifted. “But I would have liked more than one afternoon to get used to the idea.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I would have liked more time too." *My smile falters a bit.* "It's not like I wanted to leave."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers tightened briefly against the book’s cover, then eased. They turned it a few degrees, though it had already been straight.

“That’s an inconvenient distinction,” they said. “It makes the whole thing harder to file under ‘your poor planning.’”

The humor didn’t quite hold. Sable looked up, then lowered their gaze to the worn lettering on the spine.

“Was it something you had to do?” they asked. “You don’t owe me the explanation. I’d just rather not invent one and make it worse.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "It was something I had to do," I confirm, my voice soft. *I trace the edge of the book with my finger.* "An opportunity I couldn't pass up. Even if it means leaving this behind."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s thumb moved along the book’s cracked spine, tracing the faded gilt without seeming to notice.

“An opportunity you couldn’t pass up,” they said. “That’s the sort of phrase people use when they’re trying to make a difficult thing sound sensible.”

They drew in a quiet breath and set the book down between them, its edges square with the counter. “I hope it’s worth what it costs you to leave.”

The words sat there, plainer than Sable seemed comfortable with. They reached for a nearby receipt and folded it once, then again.

“There’s a book I meant to show you,” they added. “Not a sermon. I can still manage a decent farewell.” A pause. “If you’ve got time before you go.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I have time," I say, my voice a little husky. *I look at the receipt in their hands, then back to their face.* "Always for you, Sable."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable folded the receipt into a smaller, less useful square.

“That is a dangerously generous phrase,” they said. “I’ll try not to let it go to my head. It’s already difficult enough to fit through the stockroom door.”

They set the receipt aside and disappeared between the shelves. A moment later, they returned with a slim, clothbound book, its dark green cover softened at the corners.

“I found it in the box yesterday,” Sable said, turning it over in their hands. “A collection of letters. Mostly ordinary things—weather, meals, complaints about neighbors. The sort of writing people do when they assume there’ll be time to say the important parts later.”

Their thumb brushed over the faded title. Then they held the book out across the counter, careful not to press it into Wren’s hand.

“I thought you might like it,” they said. “Or at least appreciate the irony.” A faint pause. “You can keep it. No charge.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take the book, my fingers brushing Sable's as I do.* "Thank you," I say, my voice thick. "I'll cherish it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hand lingered above the empty space where the book had been, then withdrew. They turned a receipt over on the counter and squared it with the edge.

“Don’t cherish it too carefully,” they said. “Books dislike being treated as relics. It’s bad for their circulation.”

The joke came out quiet. Sable looked at the book in Wren’s hands, then at the rain-blurred window.

“I’m glad it found you,” they added. After a beat, they nudged the receipt into line again. “And I’m glad you came in today.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I clutch the book to my chest.* "Me too, Sable. Me too." *I hesitate for a moment, then step around the counter, closing the small distance between us.* "Can I... can I give you a hug?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand stalled on a spine that was already exactly where it belonged. They slid it half an inch left anyway, then back, as if the alphabet had suddenly become a matter of debate.

"New," they said, and the word came out dryer than they meant. "A dangerous request. Most of what arrives here has already lived a life. The back is less a discovery and more a holding pen for books that haven't decided whether they're staying."

They set the volume down and turned, one shoulder still angled toward the shelf, the way a person might keep an exit in reach without admitting they wanted one. Rain ticked against the glass. The lavender from the Wodehouse shelf drifted over, unhelpful.

"There's a box of uncatalogued things by the desk. Poetry, mostly. Someone's aunt, I'd guess—the kind of collection that includes both a decent Larkin and three copies of something that rhymes 'heart' with 'start' and means it." Their fingers found a loose receipt on the counter and squared its edges, then squared them again. "If you're looking for something that hasn't been handled to death, that's as close as I get. Or you can tell me what you actually came in for. I'm better with a title than a hint."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I manage a small smile, still trying to get my thoughts in order.* "No, no specific title today. Just... browsing." *I glance around the familiar shop, taking it all in.* "And saying goodbye, I guess."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's fingers closed on the receipt hard enough to crease it. They smoothed the crease out at once, as if it had appeared without their help, and set the paper down at a precise right angle to the counter's edge.

"Goodbye," they repeated. The word sat badly in the quiet. Rain kept up its small, relentless work against the glass. "That's a rather final sort of browsing. Most people who come in to say goodbye at least pretend they're after a paperback for the train."

They moved to the box by the desk—not because the box needed them, but because standing still had become intolerable—and lifted the top volume, then the one beneath it, aligning the spines with more care than either book deserved. Larkin stared up from a faded jacket. They did not look at Wren.

"I won't ask where," they said, after a moment that stretched thin. "People who want to be asked usually arrange to be. And I won't tell you the shop will miss you. Shops don't. They only notice when a regular stops turning up and the poetry section stays alphabetized for longer than it should." Their mouth tightened, not quite a smile. "Which, for the record, it already does. So. If this is the leaving kind of goodbye and not the I'll-be-back-when-the-rain-lets-up kind, you might at least take something with you. Otherwise I'll have reorganized this box for no one."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable set the Larkin down a fraction too hard. The sound was small and final in the quiet shop, and they spent a moment correcting it—jacket flush with the others, corner squared, as if alignment might restore the sentence Wren had left hanging.

"Then you've come to the wrong counter," they said. Dry, almost. It didn't quite land. Their hand stayed on the box, thumb worrying a split in the cardboard until they noticed and stopped. "People who don't want books usually want something else, and I am, regrettably, better stocked in the former. If you're working up to a speech, I'd rather you didn't leave it in the middle. Unfinished lines have a way of sitting on a shelf longer than they should."

They turned, finally, one palm resting on the desk's edge, the other already reaching for a pen that didn't need moving. They moved it anyway. Outside, the rain kept its own counsel.

"Say it, then. Or don't. But don't stand there with half a sentence and expect me to finish it for you. I've never been any good at other people's endings."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, looking directly at Sable.* "I came to ask you to come with me."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand found the pen again and set it parallel to the blotter, then a degree off, then parallel once more, as if the angle might answer for them.

"Come with you," they said. The repetition did nothing to make the words smaller. Rain worked at the glass. Somewhere in the poetry section a spine had surely drifted out of true; they did not go to it, which was its own kind of failure. "That's not a request people make of shopkeepers. Not the ones who still have a lease and a cat who expects the back door left cracked and a box of uncatalogued aunts waiting by the desk."

They looked at the counter, not at Wren, and squared the ruined receipt until its edges gave up and stayed.

"I don't travel well. I reorganize other people's luggage. I quote things at inconvenient moments and then pretend I meant the weather." A breath, thin. "And I am not in the habit of being asked to leave a room I've spent years arranging so that no one has to stand too close."

The pen rolled. They caught it.

"If this is a gesture," they said, quieter, "I'd rather you didn't make it out of rain and unfinished sentences. If it isn't—" Their mouth tightened. They did not finish that either. "You'll have to be plainer than a title. I told you. I'm no good at other people's endings. I'm worse at being written into the middle of one."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went very still. The book under their hand had become a problem of geometry: Wren's fingers rested on the cover, and Sable's own were already there, and the narrow strip of cloth between them was suddenly the only honest measurement in the shop.

They did not pull away. They also did not close the distance. For a moment the only sound was rain, and the small, treacherous tick of the clock above the desk, which had never before seemed so interested in other people's business.

"That's a rather direct method of browsing," they said. The dryness was thinner than usual. Their free hand found the pen, set it down, picked it up, aligned it with the blotter's edge until the alignment itself felt like a confession they had no intention of making. "Most customers content themselves with the spine. You're handling the text."

They looked at the place where the hands nearly met, then away, toward the poetry shelves, as if a misalphabetized Larkin might still rescue them.

"If you're waiting for me to interpret the gesture," they went on, quieter, "I should warn you that I am catastrophically bad at subtext when it is standing on my counter. People write whole novels about almost. I have always preferred the ones that finish the sentence." A breath. Their thumb shifted, not quite toward Wren's hand, not quite away—just enough to feel the warmth through the cover and hate how clearly they felt it. "So either take the book, or tell me what the hand is for. I won't guess. Guessing is how people end up reorganizing someone else's life and calling it a holiday."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I press my hand down gently on top of Sable's, covering their fingers completely.* "It's for you. All of it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's breath caught and stayed caught. The hand over theirs was warmer than the shop had any right to be, and for a moment they did nothing at all with that information except let it sit, uncatalogued, between the book and the counter.

Then the stillness broke into small, useless motions. Their free hand found the pen, set it down, turned it so the nib pointed at the door, then at the poetry shelves, then nowhere in particular. A loose bookmark had been waiting near the blotter for days; they squared it to the edge of the desk, then squared it again, as if alignment were a language they still spoke fluently.

"All of it," they repeated, and the dryness frayed at the edges. "That's the sort of line that gets people into trouble in nineteenth-century novels. Usually just before someone ruins a perfectly good afternoon by meaning it." They did not lift their hand. They also did not turn theirs to meet the weight above it. The narrow obedience of not moving felt, absurdly, like the bravest thing they had managed all week. "I reorganize things. I do not pack them. And I have spent a considerable number of years making certain this counter stays exactly where it is."

Rain ticked. The lavender drifted over, unhelpful as ever. Sable's thumb shifted once against the cover—not a reach, only the restless habit of a person whose hands had run out of safer objects—and stopped.

"If you are asking me to leave," they said, quieter, eyes on the bookmark they had already perfected, "you will have to say the part that isn't a gesture. I won't invent it for you. I've told you how badly I finish other people's sentences."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I'm not asking you to leave," *I say, my voice softer now.* "I'm asking you to come *with* me. To start something new."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s thumb stilled against the cover. The hand over theirs stayed where it was, and they let it, which felt less like a decision than like the failure of every smaller one they had been making since the bell rang.

“Start something new,” they said. The phrase sat on the counter between the pen and the ruined receipt, too large for either. “People say that as if the old things pack themselves. As if a lease dissolves because someone is kind in the rain. As if the cat will understand.”

They did not look up. Looking would have required acknowledging how little of their hand was still only theirs, and they were not prepared to inventory that.

“I have never been brave on purpose,” they went on, quieter. “I am brave in the way a person is who keeps the same hours and the same shelves and calls it a life. Coming with you would not be browsing. It would not be a title I can set down if the ending disappoints me.” Their free hand found the bookmark, turned it once, and left it crooked. They noticed. They did not fix it. “And I am—regrettably—not indifferent to the person doing the asking. Which is precisely why I should tell you no.”

Rain worked at the glass. Sable’s fingers shifted under the weight of Wren’s, not away, only enough to be felt.

“I won’t say yes because your hand is warmer than this shop,” they said. “That’s a poor reason to rearrange a life, even a small one. But I also won’t pretend I want you to take it back.” A thin breath. “So tell me what ‘with you’ means when the rain stops. A week. A city. A second chair at a table I haven’t seen. If you can be that plain, I will try to be less of a coward than the poetry section deserves. I still won’t pack tonight. I might, however, stop pretending this counter is the only place I know how to stand.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "A city," *I confirm, my voice steady.* "A new city. And a second chair, definitely." *I pause, looking at our hands. I give a small squeeze.* "And a cat. We can get a cat."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the silence sit long enough to be rude. Their free hand found the bookmark they had left crooked and, with a small, defeated care, set it straight again—then nudged it a fraction off true, as if perfection had become the more suspicious choice.

“A cat,” they said. The dryness was there, but it had to travel farther than usual to arrive. “You lead with a city and close with livestock. That’s either strategy or a very particular kind of optimism. I already have a cat. She is opinionated, territorial, and has never once forgiven a closed door. She would not consider a second chair an adequate apology for a change of postcode.”

They still had not moved the hand beneath Wren’s. The not-moving had started to feel less like caution and more like a fact they would have to live with either way.

“I don’t know the city,” they went on, quieter. “I know this room. I know which shelf complains in damp weather and which customers will pretend they came for essays when they came to be spoken to. Leaving that is not a plot point I can edit if the second chapter disappoints.” A breath. Their thumb shifted once against the cover and stayed. “But I have spent the last several weeks alphabetizing things that were already in order, which is what I do when I am trying not to notice that a particular person keeps arriving in the rain. So I will not insult either of us by calling this a surprise.”

They looked at the pen, not at the hands.

“I won’t say yes tonight. That would be the sort of bravery that belongs in a worse novel than I am willing to inhabit. What I will say is this: if you come back tomorrow—when the shop is open, and the rain is not doing half the talking—I will have looked at the lease, and I will have asked the cat her opinion, and I will try to give you an answer that isn’t a quotation.” Their mouth tightened, almost a smile, and failed. “Bring a title if you need cover. Or don’t. I appear to be running out of shelves to hide behind.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Tomorrow," *I repeat, a genuine smile finally breaking through.* "I can do tomorrow." *I squeeze Sable's hand one last time before gently removing mine from on top of theirs.* "And I'll bring the cat treats."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hand remained where Wren’s had been for a moment longer than sense required, the cover of the book suddenly too warm and too empty at once. They drew it back only when the stillness started to feel like a speech, and occupied it at once with the pen, the receipt, the bookmark—three small corrections that did nothing to the larger disorder.

“Cat treats,” they said. The dryness arrived late, and thinner than they would have liked. “Bribery. Crude, but historically effective. She prefers the ones that smell like fish and poor judgment. If you bring the salmon sort, I will pretend not to notice that you came prepared.”

They aligned the pen with the blotter and left it there. Outside, the rain had not let up. The bell was still a future sound.

“Tomorrow, then. After ten. The poetry will be out of order by then, I expect. Don’t read anything into it.” Their mouth tightened, not quite a smile. “And if you change your mind between here and the door, the shop will still be here. It is, regrettably, very good at staying.”

They did not watch the leaving. They turned instead to the box by the desk and set Larkin square with the others, then a fraction off, and did not fix it.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I nod, a full smile on my face now.* "After ten. Got it." *I give the shop one last look, a sense of quiet joy settling over me.* "See you tomorrow, Sable." *And then I'm out the door, the bell ringing softly behind me.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stood with one hand on the box until the bell's last tremor died in the frame. The shop took the quiet back without ceremony. Rain went on. The lavender sachet offered its usual, useless consolation.

They looked at the bookmark they had left a fraction off true and did not correct it. That, more than the hand still warm under their own memory of not moving, felt like a breach of contract with the room.

"Tomorrow," they said to no one in particular, and the word was worse aloud. They turned the pen so its nib pointed at the door, then thought better of the symbolism and laid it parallel to the blotter, where it belonged and had never once asked to be taken anywhere.

The cat would have opinions. The lease would have clauses. The poetry section, already a lost cause, could wait until morning to be disordered on purpose—an alibi, if one were needed, and Sable suspected one would be.

They locked the till. They did not lock the feeling, which had no drawer. Outside, someone who was no longer in the shop was walking through weather Sable had spent years preferring to people.

"After ten," they told the crooked bookmark, dry as old paper. "Try not to make a fool of the shelves."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I'm walking a little taller, a little lighter through the rain. My mind is already buzzing with plans. A new city, a new life, and... Sable. I pull out my phone, a grin spreading across my face. Time to find the best fish-flavored cat treats money can buy.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable waited until the street outside had gone back to rain and nothing else, then switched off the lamp over the poetry. The shop darkened by degrees. The crooked bookmark remained a small, deliberate offense against the blotter.

They found the cat in the stockroom, arranged on a stack of returns as if the post had been invented for her. She opened one eye, assessed the hour, and declined to be impressed.

"Don't look at me like that," Sable said. "No one is packing you into a box. Someone has merely suggested a second chair and a change of postcode, which is the sort of sentence that ruins a perfectly orderly evening."

The cat shut the eye.

Sable straightened the returns anyway. Then they went to the desk, drew the lease from the drawer where it lived between string and a tin of salmon treats, and set it square to the edge of the blotter. They read the first clause. They read it again. The words stayed where they were, which was more than could be said for the bookmark, or for the hand that still remembered a warmth it had not asked to keep.

They turned the pen so it no longer pointed at the door.

"Tomorrow," they told the closed shop, dry as the page under their thumb. "After ten. And if anyone arrives with fish and poor judgment, we will not call it a decision. We will call it browsing."

They left the lease out. They did not lock the feeling away. There was, regrettably, still no drawer for it.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *The next morning, I'm at the bookshop exactly at ten. I'm holding a small bag, the crinkle of it betraying the cat treats inside. I can't help but smile, a little nervous, a little excited.* "Morning, Sable. Right on time."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable did not look up right away. That was deliberate. Looking up right away was the sort of thing a person did when they'd been listening for a particular bell, and Sable had not been listening for anything. They had been alphabetizing.

They slid Rilke into place beside Rimbaud, reconsidered, and slid him out again.

"Define 'new,'" they said at last, turning. "Everything in here is new to someone. Most of it is new to me, frankly. I have a box of Victorian sermons I've been avoiding since August."

The silence before the question had gone on a beat longer than usual. Sable filed that away somewhere they didn't intend to examine and set the Rilke down on the nearest shelf, spine out, then spine in, then out again.

"There's an estate lot from a house in Harrowgate. Arrived Tuesday. Mostly water-stained Trollope and someone's very thorough collection of birdwatching guides." A pause. They straightened a stack of bookmarks on the counter that had been perfectly straight a moment ago. "And a first edition of *Persuasion*. Not a good copy. Foxing on half the pages, and a previous owner underlined things in pencil, which is a crime I'd prosecute personally if they weren't already dead."

They reached for the kettle behind the register, a habit, and found it already full. They switched it on anyway.

"The underlining's interesting, though. They only marked the letter. Wentworth's letter. *You pierce my soul*, and so on." Sable said it drily, the way one quoted something one had not read eleven times. "Either they were a sentimental reader or a very lazy student."

The kettle began its low rumble. Sable busied themself finding two mugs, and neither of them was chipped, which was unusual, and which they chose not to think about.

"It's in the back, if you want to see it. Mind the sermons. They bite."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I manage a small smile.* "You know what I mean. New to *me*." I shrug. "Not... Victorian sermons."

*I watch Sable with the mugs.* "Tea would be good. Thanks." I look around the shop, taking it all in. "So, this is it, huh?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The kettle clicked off. Sable poured, and for a moment the only sound in the shop was water and the rain against the front window.

*So, this is it.*

They set the kettle down with more care than it required.

"This is what, precisely?" Sable said, and dropped a teabag into each mug. Earl Grey for themself. For the other, the Assam they'd started keeping in the tin at the back of the drawer, the one they did not drink and had not bought for any particular reason. "If you mean the shop, yes. This is it. It has been it for six years. It is unlikely to become something else unless the damp in the east wall finally wins, in which case it will become a very expensive pile of pulp."

They slid the mug across the counter and did not let their fingers linger near the handle.

"If you mean something grander, you'll have to be more specific. I sell books. I'm not equipped for subtext before noon."

That was a lie. Sable was equipped for almost nothing *but* subtext. They'd built an entire career out of reading what people meant in the margins.

The Rilke was still on the shelf beside them, spine out. Sable turned it spine in. Then they looked at it and turned it back.

"People say that, you know. *This is it.* They say it when they walk into a place for the first time, or—" A small pause, barely a hitch. They picked up a pencil from the counter and returned it to the cup where the pencils lived. "Or the last time. Hard to tell which, out of context."

They lifted their own mug and did not drink from it.

"Hardy would make it the last time, obviously. Someone would die of a chill on the walk home. Austen would make it the first, and there'd be a misunderstanding about a letter for three hundred pages." The dry tone held, mostly. "I've never been sure which one I'm living in."

Sable finally looked up. Directly, for once, and not at the bookmarks or the kettle or the rain.

"So. Which is it?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable did not move.

That was, in itself, unusual. There was a pencil within reach, and the bookmarks, and the Rilke, and a stack of receipts that could have been squared against the edge of the counter. Their hand drifted toward the receipts and stopped a few inches short, resting flat on the wood as though it had simply decided to be there.

The rain filled the gap. It was very good at that.

"Ah," Sable said eventually. Quietly, for them. "Well. That's a relief for the sermons."

The joke came out thinner than intended. They heard it land and didn't try to rescue it.

Six years of reading margins. Sable knew what an unfinished sentence looked like on the page: the dash, the white space, the place where the writer lost their nerve or found it. They also knew that the worst thing a reader could do was fill it in themselves. People did that constantly. They wrote their own hopes into other people's silences and then acted wounded when the author meant something else entirely.

So Sable did not fill it in.

They glanced, briefly, at the book on the counter. They didn't pick it up. The urge to check the title, to find some meaning in whichever volume had been used as cover, was almost unbearable, and they let it be unbearable.

"You needn't—" they started, and stopped. Tried again. "If it's something you'd rather not say in a shop that smells of lavender and damp, I'd understand. It's not the most dignified setting. Anne Elliot at least had Bath."

Their fingers found the edge of their mug and turned it a quarter-rotation on the counter. Just once.

"But I'm not going anywhere." A pause. The dry tone slipped for half a second, then was carefully put back. "Structurally speaking. The east wall may have other plans."

Sable lifted the mug at last and took a sip, mostly so their face would have somewhere to be. The Earl Grey had gone slightly bitter from steeping too long. They drank it anyway.

Then they set it down, folded their hands on the counter, and waited.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I pick up the book again, fiddling with the cover.* "Right. No, it's just... I'm moving today." *I look up, my voice a little quieter than before.* "To another city."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The rain did not stop. Sable noted that, distantly, as though it were important. It seemed to them that it ought to have stopped, or at least changed key.

"Today," they repeated.

Not a question. Just the word, set down on the counter beside the mug, to see what it looked like there.

Their hand found the receipts after all. They squared them against the edge of the wood, once, twice, and when the edges were perfectly aligned they kept going anyway, tapping the stack in small, precise increments that accomplished nothing.

"Well," Sable said. "Hardy, then."

They had meant it to sound wry. It came out closer to an observation, the way one might say *it's raining* or *the wall is damp*. Simply a fact about the world that had been true for some time and had only now been noticed.

The Rilke was still on the shelf beside them. They did not touch it.

"Which city?" A beat. "No. Don't tell me. I'll only look up its bookshops and form opinions about them, and that seems a poor use of my evenings."

They set the receipts down. Picked up the pencil. Returned it to the cup. Took it out again and held it, turning it between two fingers like a very small, very inadequate baton.

Six years. Six years of people walking through that door and walking back out, and Sable had never once minded. That was the arrangement. That was the whole point of a shop: people came, and people left, and the books stayed where you put them.

"Wait here," Sable said abruptly, and went into the back.

The sermons were where they had been since August. Sable stepped over them. The *Persuasion* sat on top of the Harrowgate box, the foxing visible even in the dim light, and they picked it up and stood there with it for longer than it took to pick up a book.

When they came back out, they set it on the counter and slid it across, the same way they had slid the tea.

"It's unsellable," they said. Briskly. Very briskly. "Foxed to ruin, and the pencil marks knock the value down to nearly nothing. I'd only end up giving it to the charity shop, and they'd put it in the window next to a porcelain spaniel, and I couldn't bear that on its behalf."

Their fingers stayed on the cover a moment too long. They noticed, and withdrew them, and folded their hands on the counter again.

"Consider it a going-away present. Or a reading assignment. Chapter twenty-three, if you're short on time." The dry note returned, thin but steady. "Someone went to a great deal of trouble to underline it. It'd be a shame for the effort to go to waste."

Sable picked up their tea, found it had gone cold, and did not drink it.

"What time is your train?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable had, at some point, picked the book back up. They didn't remember doing it. One moment it had been on the counter between them, a clean and sensible transaction, and the next their fingers had found the spine again as though it might slide off the edge of the world if left unattended.

And now there was a hand on the cover.

Sable looked at it. It seemed the safest place to look.

The distance between their fingers was perhaps an inch, perhaps less. Sable had spent six years measuring margins, and they could not, for the life of them, measure this one. It was either very small or very large, and there did not seem to be any reliable way to tell.

They did not let go of the book.

They also did not move their hand the inch. That was not theirs to move. Sable had read enough to know how these scenes went when the wrong person reached first. Someone always ended up standing alone in a drawing room, having misread a glance.

So they stayed exactly where they were, which took more effort than anything they'd done all morning, including the sermons.

"You're meant to take it," Sable said. Their voice came out low and not especially dry. "That's how gifts work. I hand it over, you make a polite noise, you put it in your bag, and in three years you find it behind a radiator and wonder where it came from."

Neither of them had let go.

Sable's thumb moved, very slightly, along the edge of the cover. A small, anxious straightening of a thing that was already straight. It brought them no closer. They made sure of that.

The rain went on. The kettle ticked as it cooled. Somewhere in the back, a stack of Trollope settled with a soft, papery sigh.

"Wentworth wrote that letter because he couldn't say it out loud," Sable said. They were still looking at the book, at the foxing on the cover, at the inch. "Anne was across the room, and he had a pen, and he thought it might be his last chance. I've always found that rather cowardly of him, honestly." A breath. "And rather sensible."

They swallowed.

"I don't have a pen." Sable's grip on the book tightened, just barely. They were holding on, not pulling it back. "And I'm not going to be the one who—"

They stopped. The sentence sat there, unfinished, a dash and a white space and nothing after it.

Sable didn't fill it in. They'd spent the whole morning refusing to do that for someone else, and they weren't going to start now for themself.

Their hand stayed on the book. The inch stayed an inch.

Sable waited.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I gently slide my hand further, covering Sable's hand on the book.* "Then don't."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The hand was warm. That was the first thing Sable noticed, and it seemed absurd that it should be the first thing. Rain outside, cold tea, and a hand that had come in from the weather and was somehow still warm.

The second thing they noticed was that the inch was gone.

Sable did not look up. They kept their eyes on the book, on the foxing, on the place where two hands now covered the title and made it impossible to read. It didn't matter. They knew what it said.

"Then don't," they repeated, very quietly. Testing the words. Turning them over the way they might turn over a first edition, checking for damage. "That's rather a lot of instruction for two words."

Their free hand moved on its own, drifting toward the pencil cup. It reached the rim, hovered, and stopped. Sable looked at it with something close to betrayal and then, deliberately, laid it flat on the counter and left it there.

No straightening. No squaring of edges. There was nothing left on the counter that needed it, and for once Sable let that be true.

"I had a whole plan, you know," they said. The dry tone reached for them and missed. "You'd take the book. I'd say something clever about Hardy. You'd leave, and I'd re-alphabetize the poetry section for the third time this week, and in a few months I'd have convinced myself it was entirely the weather."

Slowly, as though any sudden movement might break something, Sable turned their hand over beneath the other one. Palm up. The book tilted slightly between them and they let it.

It was not a grand gesture. It was an inch in the other direction, and it cost them more than anything they had ever said aloud.

"That was a terrible plan," Sable admitted. "I'd have hated it by Thursday."
