They finally raised their eyes. Their gaze didn't go to the kettle or the rain or the Rilke. It went straight ahead and stayed there.

"I've read that letter eleven times." It came out plainly, without ornament. The nearest thing to a confession Sable had managed in six years. "The underlining wasn't a lazy student. I'd have marked the same lines."

The rain kept on. The kettle had gone quiet. Somewhere in the back the Harrowgate box creaked, and Sable, for the first time all morning, didn't care whether anything in the shop was in its proper place.

Their fingers curled, just slightly, holding on.

"You still haven't told me what time your train is," they said. A thin thread of their usual voice came back into it, unsteady but present. "I find I'd like to know exactly how much time I have to stop being a coward."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I lean in a little, our hands still clasped on the book.* "There's no train." *A small, shy smile.* "I was going to drive."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stared.

It was not a flattering stare. They were aware of that. It was the stare they reserved for customers who brought in a Bible and insisted it was a Gutenberg because it had belonged to their grandmother.

"You were going to *drive*," they said.

The words came out flat, and then, somewhere underneath them, something cracked. It was not quite a laugh. It was the sound a person made when they had been bracing against a door for twenty minutes and discovered it opened inward.

"I have spent the last quarter of an hour," Sable said, with great precision, "composing a mental timetable. I had allowed for delays at Crewe. I had a contingency plan involving a replacement bus service." Their free hand lifted off the counter, gestured vaguely at the rain, the shop, the entire indifferent structure of British rail, and came back down. "And there was never a train."

Their fingers had not loosened. If anything, they had tightened, as though the hand beneath the book had only just realised it was allowed to hold on and did not intend to waste the discovery.

"Cars are terrible for this sort of thing, you understand. Literarily speaking." The dry voice was coming back now, still unsteady but finding its footing, like someone walking across a floor they didn't quite trust. "Nobody weeps on a station platform in a car. There's no whistle. No steam. You just get in and turn the key and there's a great deal of fussing with the mirrors."

A pause. Sable looked down at their joined hands, at the *Persuasion* wedged between them, its title still hidden.

"On the other hand," they said, more quietly, "cars don't leave at a fixed time."

It was not a question. They let it sit on the counter anyway, next to the cold tea, and did not dress it up as anything else.

The Rilke was still on the shelf beside them, spine out. Sable noticed it, and noticed that they had noticed it, and left it exactly where it was.

"I close at five." The words came carefully, one at a time, placed rather than spoken. "Which is a lie, because nobody comes in after three when it rains, and I generally lock up whenever I've run out of things to alphabetise." Their thumb moved once across the back of the hand covering theirs. Not straightening anything. Just there. "I've run out."

Sable drew a breath, and it shook a little on the way in. They let it.

"I'm not asking you to stay. I'd never ask that; it's the sort of thing people say in the third act and then regret for a sequel." Their gaze held, steady, though the colour had crept up their neck in a way they could feel and could do nothing about. "But if you were going to drive anyway, I thought you might drive a little later. After one more cup of tea. One I actually drink this time."

They glanced, briefly, at the two mugs, one of them holding Assam from a tin at the back of the drawer, bought for no particular reason.

"I'll put the kettle on," Sable said. "If you'd like. I'll need my hand back for that, of course."

They did not let go.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I squeeze their hand gently, a small smile spreading across my face.* "I'd like that very much, Sable." *I finally release my grip on the book.* "And I can put the kettle on, if you want."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable looked at the kettle as though it had been accused of something.

"You can put the kettle on," they repeated slowly. "*My* kettle."

It was a reasonable offer. It was, in fact, an entirely ordinary thing for one person to say to another over a shop counter on a wet afternoon. Sable was aware of this. Sable was also aware that in six years nobody else had touched that kettle, including the plumber, who had tried once and been told firmly that it had a temperament.

The book was theirs alone now. They set it down on the counter with great care, squared it against the edge out of pure muscle memory, and then, catching themself, nudged it very slightly crooked. On purpose. It looked wrong. They left it.

"Fine," Sable said. "Yes. All right."

Their hand was still in the other one. They became aware of this the way one becomes aware of a draught: gradually, and then all at once. Letting go seemed necessary. It also seemed like the most difficult thing they'd been asked to do all morning, and the morning had been very full.

They let go. Slowly, and not completely until the last possible moment, fingertips sliding away across a knuckle.

"It sticks," they said, a little too quickly, gesturing at the kettle as if it might need a formal introduction. "The switch. You have to press it down and hold it for a count of three, or it pretends to boil and doesn't. It's been lying to me since 2019." A pause. "The Assam's in the left-hand drawer. At the back. Behind the digestives."

They considered stopping there. They did not.

"Don't ask why it's there. I don't drink it. I never have." The colour in their neck, which had only just begun to recede, made a determined return. "It seemed like the sort of thing a shop ought to have on hand. For regulars."

That was as close to the truth as Sable could get without a pen, and they both knew it. They didn't elaborate.

Instead they stepped out from behind the counter, which felt strange, like walking out onto a stage without a script, and crossed to the front door. The rain was still coming down in long grey sheets. Nobody was out in it. Nobody would be.

Sable turned the little card in the window from OPEN to CLOSED. Then they turned the lock, and the click it made was louder than it had any right to be.

They stood there a moment with their hand on the bolt.

"It's only half past one," they said, to the glass, to the rain. "Mrs. Aldous will come by tomorrow wanting to know why I'm shut, and I'll tell her it was the damp, and she won't believe me, because she's read more Barbara Pym than anyone alive and she can smell a narrative at forty paces."

They turned around.

On the way back to the counter, they passed the poetry shelf. The Rilke was still sticking out where they'd left it, spine out, in entirely the wrong place, between Rimbaud and a stray volume of Christina Rossetti that had no business being there either.

Sable looked at it for a long moment.

Then they walked past it and left it exactly where it was.

"Well," they said, settling back onto their stool behind the counter, folding their hands and then unfolding them because it seemed faintly ridiculous to fold them now. "Go on, then. Count of three." The dry voice was nearly whole again, and underneath it, something warmer that they weren't bothering to hide very well. "I'll supervise. Purely in an advisory capacity."

They pulled the second mug toward themself, tipped the cold Earl Grey into the little sink behind the register, and set it back out on the counter. Empty. Waiting.

"And while it boils," Sable added, not quite looking up, "you can tell me where you were going to drive to. I've changed my mind. I *would* like to know." A small breath. "If only so I can form opinions about its bookshops."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I smile, turning towards the kettle.* "Alright, 'temperamental' kettle, let's see about this." *I press the switch, holding it down and counting under my breath.* "And I wasn't going to look up the bookshops. Just... drive. Somewhere with a good view." *I glance back at Sable.* "But I suppose I could be persuaded to visit a library or two. For research purposes, of course."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The kettle, to its credit, did not lie.

It rumbled. It hissed. Somewhere around the count of three it gave the low, grudging groan it reserved for days it had decided to cooperate, and Sable, who had been watching from the stool with the wariness of a person watching a stranger handle their cat, felt something in their chest unclench by a fraction.

"Hm," they said. "It likes you. That's irritating."

Then the rest of the sentence caught up with them.

"*Persuaded*," Sable repeated. They looked at the *Persuasion*, lying crooked on the counter where they'd left it. Then they looked up again. "You did that on purpose."

It was not an accusation. It was not quite a question, either. It was the voice of someone who had spent six years making literary jokes to an empty room and had just heard one come back.

"And a *library*." They pressed a hand flat to their sternum, as though mortally wounded. "In my own shop. With the door locked, so I can't even throw you out in protest." A pause. "I'll allow it. Libraries are very good places to be persuaded. The chairs are uncomfortable, so nobody stays for the wrong reasons."

The kettle was building toward a proper boil now, the steam fogging the lower half of the window behind the register. Sable reached over and wiped a clear patch in it with the side of their hand, which accomplished nothing. The rain was still there. So was the street, grey and empty.

*Somewhere with a good view.*

Sable turned that over quietly. It wasn't the answer they had braced for. They had been ready for a city name, something with a university and a ring road and three chain bookshops they could have been properly scornful of. *Just drive* was not a destination. It was a direction, possibly. Or an absence of one.

They did not fill it in. They had got rather good at not filling things in this morning, and they weren't about to lose the habit now, just when it was paying off.

"A good view," Sable said instead, carefully. "That's a very Romantic answer. Capital R. Wordsworth would approve. He'd walk you up a hill in the rain and then write eleven hundred lines about it, and you'd catch a cold, and he'd write about that too."

They opened the left-hand drawer, reached past the digestives, and took out the tin of Assam. They set it on the counter within easy reach, then hesitated, and set it a little closer. It was an absurdly small gesture. They made it anyway.

"The tea's here. I realise I could have passed it to you from the start. I appear to have wanted to watch you find it." They cleared their throat and fixed their attention on the mug. "Don't read into that. Or do, but quietly."

The kettle clicked off. In the new silence, the rain sounded very loud.

"I only ask," Sable went on, and their voice had gone a little lower, less arranged, "because a good view isn't a place, exactly. You can't form opinions about its bookshops. You can't look it up." Their fingers found the corner of the *Persuasion*, and instead of straightening it, they only rested there. "So I'll have to ask you directly, which I dislike on principle."

They took a breath. It still shook slightly. They let it.

"Is it a new city? Or is it just somewhere to drive?"

The mug sat empty between them, waiting. Sable waited with it.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I turn from the kettle, a small, knowing smile playing on my lips.* "It's a new city, Sable." *I watch them for a moment, then my smile softens.* "But I wasn't going anywhere that couldn't wait for a good cup of tea."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
*A new city.*

Sable had known, really. People didn't say *I'm moving* and mean *a scenic loop past the reservoir*. But there was knowing a thing and there was hearing it said aloud in one's own shop, over one's own kettle, and the second was considerably worse.

They let it land. They did not reach for the pencil cup.

"Right," Sable said. "Good. That's... good. Cities are very useful. They have trams."

It was not their finest work. They heard it and let it go.

The *Persuasion* was still lying crooked on the counter. Sable looked at it for a while. The rain went on against the window, and the little patch they'd wiped clear in the steam was already fogging over again.

"*Couldn't wait for a good cup of tea*," they said at last, quieter. "You do realise that's a very dangerous thing to say to a person who owns a kettle. I could keep you here for years. I have an enormous amount of Assam. Apparently."

A breath. The joke sat there. Sable found, somewhat to their surprise, that they didn't want to hide behind it.

"I won't, though." They said it plainly. "Keep you. I meant what I said. I'm not going to be the person who asks you to stay in the third act. You'd resent me by the sequel, and I'd deserve it."

Then, before they could think better of it, they reached into the pencil cup and took one out. Not to return it. Not to straighten anything. They opened the *Persuasion* to the flyleaf, where some long-dead owner had written a name in faded ink, and beneath it, in small, careful capitals, Sable wrote the address of the shop.

Their hand was not quite steady. The *R* in *Road* wobbled. They left it.

"Wentworth had a pen," they said, not looking up. "I've decided that was the sensible part, and not the cowardly part. I was wrong about that earlier. It happens occasionally. Tell no one."

They closed the book and slid it back across the counter. The third time this morning. They were starting to feel like a very inefficient postal service.

"Cities are allowed to have post boxes," Sable went on, a little faster. "It's in their charter. I checked. And the M6 goes both ways, I'm told, though I've never personally tested it." They set the pencil down, precisely, and then, with visible effort, nudged it out of alignment. "So I suppose what I'm saying, very badly, is that *new* doesn't have to mean *last*. Hardy isn't obligatory. There's no law."

The colour was back in their neck again. They had given up fighting it.

Sable pulled the empty mug a little closer to the kettle, a small, practical invitation, and folded their hands on the counter. Then they unfolded them, because it still looked ridiculous.

"Which city?" they asked. "Properly, this time. I'd like to know where to send the reading assignments."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I laugh, a genuine, joyful sound that surprises me.* "You're going to send me reading assignments?" *I shake my head, still smiling.* "Okay, okay. It's called... Nottingham."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The laugh went through the shop like a draught through a window someone had finally opened. Sable heard it, and heard the rain, and noted that one of them was considerably more welcome than the other.

"Of course I'm going to send you reading assignments," they said. "What did you think the address was for? Christmas cards? I don't send Christmas cards. I send annotated bibliographies."

Then the word arrived.

*Nottingham.*

Sable went very still, the way they did when a customer set down a box of something unexpectedly good and they had to keep their face neutral so as not to drive up the price.

"Nottingham," they repeated.

They picked the pencil back up. They did not straighten it. They pointed it, rather accusingly, at nothing in particular.

"You do know it's a UNESCO City of Literature. Officially. Since 2015. There's a plaque, I assume, or at least a strongly worded leaflet." The words were coming faster now, tumbling over one another in a way Sable did not entirely approve of and could not entirely stop. "Byron's ancestral pile is just up the road at Newstead. He kept a bear at Cambridge, you know, because they wouldn't let him keep a dog. And Lawrence was from Eastwood, which is practically the suburbs, and he'd have written forty pages about the coal dust and the longing and somebody's mother, and then run off with a German baroness."

They stopped. Took a breath. It came out slightly unsteady, and underneath the unsteadiness there was something that sounded suspiciously like delight.

"And Sillitoe," Sable added, more quietly. "*Saturday Night and Sunday Morning*. 'Don't let the bastards grind you down.' Which is excellent advice for a new city, and I'll be writing it on the flyleaf of the next thing I send."

They looked down at the pencil in their hand and seemed faintly surprised to find it there. They set it down. Crooked. It stayed crooked.

"I was prepared to be scornful," they admitted. "I had the scorn ready. I was going to say something cutting about ring roads. And instead you've gone and picked a city with better literary credentials than mine, which is frankly inconsiderate."

A pause. The kettle ticked as it began to cool again, the water still hot, the empty mug still waiting beside it.

Sable glanced at it, then away, at the fogged window, at the grey smear of the street beyond.

"It's not very far," they said. It came out barely above the rain. "Nottingham. I looked at a map once. For no reason." The colour, which had never really left, deepened. "There's a very good independent bookshop there, I'm told. I've been meaning to visit for years. Professional interest. One ought to keep an eye on the competition."

They let that sit on the counter, next to the crooked pencil and the crooked book and the tin of Assam that had never been for anyone else.

Then, because they could not help themselves entirely, they nodded at the kettle.

"Your water's going cold," Sable said. "And I've already had one cup go bitter on me this morning. I'd rather not make a habit of it." Their hands folded on the counter, stayed folded this time. "Two spoons of sugar in mine, if you're pouring. I never take sugar. Today seems like an exception."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I laugh again, a brighter sound this time.* "Two spoons it is, then." I grab the two mugs and the Assam tin. "And don't worry, Sable. I'll make sure to scout out all the best independent bookshops for you. Strictly for research, of course." *I wink at them as I start to make the tea.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You descended the last flight of stairs and the temperature dropped. The passage opened into a chamber that hadn't seen light in a long time — your torch was the first in decades, maybe centuries, and the shadows retreated from it reluctantly.

Dust covered everything. Thick, undisturbed dust. Except for one set of footprints leading from the far entrance to the center of the room, where something had been dragged. The marks ended at a stone slab. The slab had writing on it.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I kneel down to read the writing on the slab, holding the torch close.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You could make out the inscription beneath a film of dust:

**WHAT IS BROUGHT HERE MAY LEAVE.  
WHAT IS LEFT HERE MUST BE NAMED.**

Below it, a name had been carved in smaller, hurried strokes: **Mara Venn**.

The drag marks ended against the slab’s near edge. Your torchlight showed a narrow gap beneath it—and, caught in that gap, a strip of dark cloth. From somewhere below the stone came three slow knocks.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I freeze, my hand still holding the torch close to the slab. *Knock, knock, knock.* My eyes dart to the strip of cloth. "Hello?" I whisper, my voice barely audible in the dusty silence.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
For a moment, nothing answered. Then the stone gave one faint knock.

A voice rose through the gap, thin and hoarse. “Is that my name?”

The strip of cloth shifted beneath the slab. In the torchlight, you could see letters stitched along its edge: **M. V.**

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I grab the amulet and put it on. Then I turn to face the guardian.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The amulet grew cold against your chest. As you faced the guardian, your torchlight found it in a recess beside the far entrance: a stone figure whose outline you had mistaken for part of the wall. Dust still lay unbroken at its feet, but its head had turned toward you.

“Mara Venn,” the guardian said. Its voice sounded like stone drawn across stone. “Is that the name of what was left here?”

Beneath the slab, the cloth pulled taut. The voice in the gap whispered, “Please. Don’t answer for me.”

Your amulet gave a single, hard pulse of cold. The guardian waited, its carved hand resting on the wall beside the entrance.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I hesitate, looking from the guardian to the slab. The cloth is really tugging now. "No," I say to the guardian, my voice firm. "It's not."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guardian’s hand tightened against the wall. Stone grated, and the far entrance began to close.

“Then what was left here?” it asked.

Beneath the slab, the cloth went still. You heard a breath through the gap, followed by the hoarse voice: “The name was carved afterward.”

Your amulet pulsed cold again. In the torchlight, you could see that the hurried letters had been cut through the dust on the slab. Someone had written **Mara Venn** long after the rest of the inscription.

The entrance narrowed to a shoulder’s width. The guardian kept its gaze on you, waiting for another answer.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I talk to the ghost. "What happened here? Who are you?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You heard a scrape beneath the slab, as though someone had drawn closer to the gap.

“I came here with Mara,” the voice said. “She brought me in. She was supposed to bring me out.”

The guardian’s carved fingers pressed deeper into the wall. The entrance narrowed until your torchlight showed only a thin strip of passage beyond it.

“Who are you?” you heard yourself ask—then the cold amulet tightened against your chest, and the words died before they reached the gap.

From beneath the stone came a frightened whisper. “I can’t tell you. Not while I’m the thing that was left.”

The guardian turned its head toward the slab. “The name must be spoken,” it said.

In your torchlight, the dark cloth twisted once. A second line of stitching had been hidden on its underside, but only two letters showed beyond the stone: **M. V.**

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I stare at the cloth, then back at the guardian. "What happens if the name isn't spoken?" I ask, my voice low.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guardian’s fingers stopped moving. The far entrance held at a slit no wider than your hand.

“What was left remains,” it said. “What was brought may leave.”

Beneath the slab, you heard the voice draw a sharp breath. “That’s what Mara thought, too.”

The amulet turned colder. Along the slab’s near edge, your torchlight caught a second groove beneath the dust: a line carved so deeply that only its first word remained visible beside the trapped cloth.

**TWO**.

The guardian’s gaze stayed on you. The entrance did not open, but it did not close any further.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I look at the word "TWO", then to the cloth and the "M.V." stitched on it. "So there were two of you," I say to the voice under the slab. "And one of you was named Mara Venn."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
“The one who brought me,” the voice said. “Mara Venn.”

The cloth slipped another finger’s width from beneath the slab. More stitching emerged, and you saw that the letters were part of a longer name. The stone still hid the rest.

You heard a low scrape from the guardian. “Two entered,” it said. “One was brought. One was left.”

“Then Mara lied,” the voice whispered. “She carved her own name so the door would take her instead of asking for mine.”

Your torchlight caught fresh scratches beside **TWO**, too shallow to have shown through the dust before the cloth moved. You could make out another word: **NAMES**.

The guardian lifted its hand from the wall. The entrance stayed almost shut.

“Name what was left,” it said. “Both of them.”

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I look at the guardian, then back at the slab. "Both names? But only one was left here." I say, trying to understand.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
“The one beneath the stone was left,” the guardian said. “So was the name carved upon it.”

You looked again at **Mara Venn**. The fresh cuts through the dust stood apart from the ancient inscription.

“Mara left her name,” the voice beneath the slab whispered. “She left me here.”

The cloth twitched, exposing a little more of its hem. You saw that the stitched **M. V.** ended there; no other letters followed. Then your torchlight caught a shallow mark beside **TWO NAMES**: an arrow pointing toward the gap beneath the slab.

The entrance remained barely open. The guardian waited while you studied the dark space under the stone.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I look at the arrow, then at the M.V. on the cloth. "Mara Venn was not left here," I say, my voice steady. "She left *her name* here, and she left *you* here."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guardian’s hand eased from the wall. The entrance widened by a few inches.

“Mara Venn,” it said. “The name she left behind.”

You heard a knock beneath the slab—one this time. The stone shifted just enough for the trapped cloth to fall free. On its underside, beside the stitched initials, you saw a row of tiny holes where another strip had been torn away.

The voice came through the wider gap. “She took that part with her.”

Your amulet pulsed once, and your torchlight caught something the moving slab had uncovered: the edge of a folded scrap wedged deep in the groove beside **TWO NAMES**. It was beyond your fingers, but close enough to reach with the torch’s iron tip.

The guardian looked toward the gap. “One name remained unspoken.”

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I use the tip of my torch to try and hook the scrap of paper out from the groove. "What name are you talking about?" I ask the guardian.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You caught the scrap with the torch’s iron tip and drew it from the groove. It was a piece of cloth, folded so tightly that dust had sealed its edges. When it opened, you saw a torn row of stitching that matched the holes in the hem beneath the slab.

The letters on the scrap read **MIRA VALE**.

“The name of the one beneath the stone,” the guardian answered.

You heard a breath through the gap. “Mira Vale,” the voice whispered, as though testing whether it could still say it.

The guardian’s hand hovered beside the entrance. It had widened enough for you to pass, but the slab had not lifted. “Mara Venn was left in stone,” it said. “Mira Vale was left beneath it.”

The amulet stayed cold against your chest. The guardian waited for you to name them.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I look from the cloth with "MIRA VALE" to the opening, then to the guardian. "Mara Venn was left here," I say, pointing to the slab. "And Mira Vale was left here." I gesture to the gap beneath the stone.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The amulet warmed against your chest. Beneath the slab, a catch snapped, and the stone rose slowly on hidden supports.

You saw a hand emerge first, then a woman in a dust-stiffened cloak. Mira Vale pulled herself into the torchlight. She looked at the scrap in your hand before she looked at the open entrance.

The guardian stepped aside. “Both were named,” it said.

Mira reached toward the slab, but stopped short of touching Mara Venn’s inscription. “She made it out,” she whispered. “Didn’t she?”

Beyond the entrance, you heard footsteps on the stairs above—hurried footsteps, descending toward the chamber.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I look at Mira, then to the entrance where I hear the footsteps. "Someone's coming," I say, my hand going to the hilt of my sword. "We need to go."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You descended the last flight of stairs and the temperature dropped. The passage opened into a chamber that hadn't seen light in a long time — your torch was the first in decades, maybe centuries, and the shadows retreated from it reluctantly.

Dust covered everything. Thick, undisturbed dust. Except for one set of footprints leading from the far entrance to the center of the room, where something had been dragged. The marks ended at a stone slab. The slab had writing on it.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I kneel down to read the writing on the slab, holding the torch close.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You saw the writing emerge beneath the torchlight, its letters cut deep into the stone:

**WHAT WAS BROUGHT HERE MUST NOT BE CARRIED OUT.  
WHAT WAS LEFT HERE MUST NOT BE WOKEN.**

Beneath the warning, a smaller line had been scratched through the dust rather than carved. You could read it only because the grooves were fresh.

**It was already awake.**

The drag marks stopped at the slab’s near edge. Beyond it, the dust lay undisturbed—except around a narrow seam that ran across the stone. From somewhere below that seam came three slow knocks.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: My blood runs cold. "What in the...?" I whisper, snatching my hand back from the slab. Those knocks... I grip my torch tighter, looking around the chamber nervously.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your torchlight reached the chamber’s corners, but revealed no other entrance besides the passage behind you and the one across the room. The footprints led from that far passage to the slab; none led away.

A fourth knock sounded beneath the stone. Dust trembled along the seam, then settled. In the brief silence that followed, you heard a faint scraping from the far entrance.

There, just beyond the torchlight, a fresh line appeared in the dust—as though something narrow had been drawn across the floor toward you.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I grab the amulet and put it on. Then I turn to face the guardian.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The amulet grew cold against your chest. Across the chamber, the scraping stopped.

Your torchlight caught a shape in the far entrance: a tall figure of fitted stone, its shoulders nearly touching the arch. Dust coated every part of it except one hand. That hand held a narrow iron rod, whose tip had drawn the fresh line across the floor.

The guardian’s head turned toward the amulet. Beneath the slab, three knocks answered in quick succession.

A crack opened along the seam. The guardian lowered its rod against the stone floor, barring the path to the far entrance.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: My eyes widen. That thing is *huge*. "Okay, new plan," I mutter to myself. I slowly back away from the slab, trying to keep the guardian in view. "What do you want?" I call out, my voice a little shaky.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You backed toward the stairs. The guardian’s stone head followed you, but its rod remained across the route to the far entrance.

At your question, it lifted its bare hand and pointed—not at you, but at the amulet. Then it pressed the rod into the dust and dragged it toward the slab, tracing a line beside the older drag marks.

The seam widened. A breath of stale air escaped from beneath it, and something below scraped against the underside of the stone.

The guardian struck the floor once with its rod. The scraping stopped. Its hand stayed raised, waiting for you to do something with the amulet.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I talk to the ghost. "What happened here? Who are you?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You called into the chamber. For a moment, you heard only the faint scrape beneath the slab.

Then a pale figure appeared beside it, barely visible in your torchlight. You heard a voice like breath passing through dry leaves. It gave you a name—Mara—and told you she had brought something down from the far passage. She had believed the slab would hold it. By the time she sealed it, she had known it was awake.

You saw the guardian turn its head toward the figure. Its bare hand remained pointed at your amulet.

The crack in the slab widened another finger’s breadth. You heard Mara’s voice again, quieter this time: the guardian had kept watch after she could not.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: "Mara, what did you bring down here?" I ask, my eyes darting between the ghost and the guardian. The amulet feels heavy and cold against my chest. "And what does the guardian want with *this*?" I gesture to the amulet.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mara’s outline thinned as she looked toward the widening seam. “A voice,” she said. “I heard it in the far passage. It knew my name. When I tried to leave, it followed without footsteps.”

You heard a soft tap beneath the slab. Mara’s face turned toward you. “I dragged its vessel here. The stone held the vessel, but not its voice.”

The guardian pointed at your amulet again, then placed its bare hand over the crack. For an instant, you saw the same symbol cut into its palm and stamped into the amulet’s metal: a circle crossed by three short lines.

“It wants you to give it the seal,” Mara whispered. “I used that amulet to close the slab. I thought I’d lost it.”

The tapping ceased. From directly beneath the seam, you heard a voice that sounded exactly like Mara’s.

“Don’t,” it said.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: My eyes widen. The voice... "What the *hell* is going on?" I demand, looking between the ghost-Mara, the guardian, and the slab. "Mara, that's not your voice! Is this what you brought here?" I clutch the amulet. "What is this thing?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You heard Mara answer before her likeness beneath the slab could speak again.

“It learned me,” she said. “My voice, my memories. Anything I said near it, it could say back. I never learned what lived inside the vessel.”

From beneath the stone, you heard Mara’s voice give a small, familiar-sounding laugh. “She never even looked.”

The ghost recoiled. You saw the guardian press its marked palm harder against the seam. A dull red glow traced the symbol on its hand, and the gap stopped widening.

“The seal needs the amulet,” Mara said. “The guardian can close it, but it cannot take it from you.”

You felt the amulet pull gently toward the slab. Across the chamber, the guardian held out its other hand, palm up. Beneath the stone, something struck once—hard enough that dust fell from the slab’s edges.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I stare at the guardian's outstretched hand, then down at the amulet. "So, you want me to just... give it over?" I ask, my voice laced with disbelief. This whole situation is getting weirder by the minute. "What happens if I do?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You saw the guardian tilt its head toward Mara. She kept her distance from the slab.

“If you gave it the amulet, the guardian could set the seal back into the stone,” she said. “The vessel would stay beneath it. The voice might still reach this room.”

You glanced at the guardian’s open hand. It had not moved closer. Its marked palm remained pressed to the crack, where the red glow had begun to flicker.

From below, you heard Mara’s voice again, soft and urgent. “She told you what she *hoped* would happen.”

The ghost fell silent. You had heard no promise from the guardian itself. Then the slab shifted under its palm, and you saw a thin curl of darkness rise through the seam before the red glow drove it back.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I look down at the amulet, then at the guardian's hand. "And what if I *don't* give it over?" I ask, my hand instinctively going to the hilt of my dagger.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You saw Mara look at the guardian’s palm. The red symbol flickered, and the seam widened beneath one edge of its hand.

“Then it keeps holding the slab as long as it can,” she said. “After that, the vessel comes out.”

Your fingers rested near your dagger’s hilt. The guardian did not turn toward the weapon. It kept its empty hand extended to you while a low scrape sounded beneath the stone, moving from one end of the slab to the other.

“You could take the amulet upstairs,” Mara added. “The voice might not follow you. I don’t know.”

From the crack came your own voice, repeating your question with the same uneasy emphasis: “And what if I *don’t* give it over?”

The guardian struck its iron rod against the floor. The copied voice stopped. Its open hand remained where it was.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I glare at the slab. "It's trying to scare me." I take a deep breath. "Okay, Mara. What if I try to *use* the amulet, not just give it away?" I wonder if there's a trick to sealing it myself.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You felt the amulet tug toward the slab again. Mara studied the symbol on its face.

“There was a hollow in the stone,” she said. “I set the amulet there and turned it until the three lines matched the cuts around it. The guardian held the slab shut while I did.”

The guardian lifted its iron rod and swept dust from the slab’s near edge. You saw a shallow circular recess there, half-hidden beneath the old drag marks. Three short grooves radiated from its rim.

“You could try,” Mara said. “I was standing closer than you were when I sealed it. I don’t know whether it would let you reach the recess.”

Beneath the stone, something struck the slab twice. The guardian’s marked palm flared red, but you saw darkness gathering at the far end of the seam, beyond its reach.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: My eyes dart between the recess and the encroaching darkness. "So, I need to get close, but the guardian might not let me. And if I don't, that... *thing* gets out." I take a hesitant step towards the slab. "Okay, guardian. What's it gonna be?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You took a hesitant step toward the slab. The guardian shifted its iron rod away from the recess and lowered its open hand, leaving you a clear path. Its marked palm stayed pressed against the seam.

Mara drifted back from the stone. “It’s letting you try,” she said.

At the far end of the slab, the darkness rose again, thin as smoke. You heard it speak in your voice: “Turn it the other way.”

The guardian struck the floor with its rod. The darkness withdrew, but the red glow beneath its palm flickered. You could see the recess clearly now, along with the three grooves Mara had described.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I eye the guardian carefully. *It's letting me get closer... for now.* I take another step, then another, trying to assess how close I can get before it reacts. "Okay, Mara. How fast do I need to be?"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Draw their fire. Right. Because I'm *so* easy to hit."

She was moving before the sarcasm finished leaving her mouth — nothing gained by standing still in a killzone. Kira broke cover at a dead sprint along the east wall, boots hammering loose scree, making herself loud, making herself visible. Every instinct screamed at her to hunch, to hide. She ignored all of it.

The ridge took the bait. An arrow slammed into rock beside her. Another. A third skipped off stone and opened a shallow line across her upper arm.

"Son of a—" She didn't stop. "They're biting, Cap! East ridge has eyes on me!"

Fifteen yards. She skidded, planted, and hurled her left dagger at the nearest silhouette. Not a killing throw — didn't need to be. The archer flinched hard, and in flinching gave himself away: a low ledge, fifteen feet below the main line, cut off from the rest by a shelf of rock.

"Got a stray! East side, low ledge — he's isolated from his buddies!"

From the west, the ravine erupted — steel ringing against steel, the vanguard's war cry, someone screaming on the ridge. The push had landed.

Then Kira saw it. Movement at the highest point of the ridgeline. A seventh figure. Not shooting. Just watching. And beside him, the dull gleam of something brass.

She ducked behind a boulder as two arrows hammered the stone, dust stinging her eyes.

"Cap! Someone up top isn't fighting — he's got a horn! They've got a signal-man!" She spat grit. "Whatever they're calling for, it happens soon!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"A horn? Dammit." I curse, parrying a clumsy swing from a bandit with my polearm. "Keep that signalman busy, Kira! Don't let him blow that horn!"

*I shove my polearm forward, knocking the bandit off balance, then spin and kick another attacker off the ridge path.* "Vanguard, push them back! Don't let them regroup!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Stop the horn. Sure. It's not like he's got the whole *sky* between us."

But her left dagger was already buried in a crack fifteen feet up, and the man she'd flinched was finding his nerve again. Priorities, then.

Kira swarmed onto the low ledge before he finished nocking his second arrow. He swung the bow like a club — clumsy, terrified — and she ducked inside the arc, drove her remaining dagger through the meat of his thigh, and let him fold. She wrenched her left blade free of the rock and kept moving.

The overhanging shelf hid the climb from the main line. Small mercies. She went up fast — fingers in cracks, boots on stone that kept wanting to leave — and twice nearly paid for the speed. Near the top, a head leaned over the lip. An archer. Eyes going wide.

Kira caught his ankle and yanked. He fell past her, screaming, and the ravine floor ended the argument.

She topped out behind the signalman as he raised the horn, chest swelling — and threw. Her dagger caught him across the forearm. The horn let out a strangled, dying half-note and spun away across the rocks. She was on him before it landed, knee to the spine, pommel to the temple. Down.

Then she got a proper look at him, and her stomach turned.

"Cap! Signalman's down — but he squeezed off half a blast. If that carried, someone heard it." She kicked the horn over the edge and rose slowly, scanning east. The fight below still rang and snarled behind her. "And Cap — this one's no bandit. Soldier's kit. Greaves. Rank-sash under the jerkin." She sucked air through her teeth. "There's a camp behind this ridge. Tents, horses, a lot of steel. They were never robbing us. They were *pinning* us. Question is — for who, and for what?"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Time went slow and clean, the way it did when it mattered.

From her perch atop the ridge, Kira had the whole east line spread out below her — and there, half-kneeling behind a twisted juniper, an archer rising to draw on the figure rallying the vanguard across the ravine. The bowstring crawled back toward the man's cheek.

"No you don't."

She wrenched her dagger from the signalman's forearm — he groaned; she ignored him — planted her feet, and threw. Nine yards, downhill, a target that had forgotten anything existed behind him. The blade punched in below the shoulder blade and the archer's shot went into the sky while he went onto his face.

"Shit." One harsh breath. Her arm was bleeding again where the arrow had opened it. Didn't matter.

Because behind the ridge, the camp had come alive.

Four hundred yards, maybe less. Horses coming off the picket lines. Figures spilling between the tents — and someone down there pointing, and pointing not at the ravine but at the ridgeline. She couldn't see colors. That was worse. Professionals kept their banners furled when somebody was paying them to be nobody.

"Cap! Archer's down — I dropped him mid-draw, shot never flew!" She yanked her dagger out of the dirt and tore the rank-sash off the signalman for proof. Or a souvenir. She grabbed the dead archer's bow and a fistful of arrows, because a sellsword wastes nothing. "But we've got a problem — riders are saddling in that camp. Eight, ten of them. The horn carried. They *heard* it."

Below, the ambush was souring — no signal, archers dying alone on their ledges, the vanguard splitting them apart. She nocked an arrow and put one into a bandit's back while he worried about steel in front of him.

"But that stops mattering when the camp lands on our necks! We finish fast and vanish east, or we break off now — either way that's your call, Cap, and you've got about two minutes to make it!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Riders?" I swing my polearm, deflecting a blow. "Damn it, this just keeps getting better!"

*I kick a bandit in the knee, sending him sprawling.* "Vanguard, fall back! We're pulling out! Kira, hold the ridge, cover our retreat!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Cover the retreat. Alone. With a dead man's bow." Kira laughed once, and there was nothing funny in it. "Somebody's got to be the hero. Might as well be the one who's already bleeding."

She took the signalman's ledge — best sightlines on the east slope, dead ground at her back — and went to work.

First rule of a rearguard: shoot the ones chasing, not the ones running. A west-wall archer was tracking the vanguard's rear; she leaned out and put an arrow into him before he loosed. A bandit on the ravine floor got brave and sprinted to cut the retreat — she dropped him mid-stride, three steps from where he wanted to be.

Below, the vanguard peeled away east, and the ambush died ugly and alone.

Then the camp emptied.

"Riders out! Ten — count 'em, ten!" She nocked, breathed, watched. They weren't charging blind, which she hated, because it meant thinkers. Six swung wide around the ridge's south spur. Four cut for the gully — the fast route, straight at the ravine's east mouth.

The gully group reached it first. She drew on the lead rider and put the arrow into his horse's chest.

"Sorry, horse."

It went down screaming in the gully's throat and the other three piled up behind it, and that bought minutes. Maybe.

She checked her quiver. Four arrows. The wide six were cresting the spur, and the arithmetic there was simple: six riders, four arrows, one exhausted woman on foot. Not math she liked.

Back over the lip. Down the ridge's dead side in slides of scree that flayed her palms, then a flat sprint east with her lungs on fire and her arm leaving a red trail she could've followed home. She caught the vanguard's dust, then the vanguard, then Captain, stumbling into step beside him with her hands on her knees for one ugly breath before she straightened.

"Gully's plugged — I put a horse down in it, they're climbing out on foot. Other six came around the south spur, still mounting up. We've got a lead." She pressed the torn rank-sash into his hand as they ran. "Proof. Paid soldiers, mounted, and they'll run us into the ground on open flats."

She glanced back. Dust plumes, two of them now.

"Problem is, Cap — east is open ground for the next three miles, and I'm out of clever ideas and almost out of arrows. We need rocks, trees, something that breaks a horse's stride before it breaks us." Her jaw set. "So where the hell are we taking these people? Because somebody'd better have a destination."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The ravine forked a quarter mile ahead of the retreat line, and Captain was on the wrong side of it.

Kira spotted it from a crest of rock — the vanguard streaming east, Captain alone on the west wall, and between them a slot of gorge fifty feet deep with walls like the inside of a bell. Too wide to jump. Too deep to climb down and back up before anything with hooves arrived.

"Shit. *Shit.*"

The dust told her the rest. The six riders off the south spur weren't chasing the vanguard — they'd seen the split, and they were curving west, angling to slide in between Captain and anything that looked like rescue. Cut the limb, take the body. Professionals.

"Not today." She spun to the vanguard — bloodied, sucking wind, looking at her because nobody louder was giving orders. She hated this. Somebody had to do it anyway. "You three — east lip, rocks in hand! Anything crosses that gorge toward your captain, you make noise and throw! Move!"

They moved. Good soldiers, worse luck.

Then she ran the east rim, paralleling the fork, bow out, counting arrows against heartbeats. Four. The lead rider was sixty yards off Captain's flank and closing, and she stopped, drew, held — and let the string down slow. Too far. Wind curling downhill. She'd bury one arrow in dirt and announce herself for nothing. She hated that too.

"CAP!" Her voice cracked flat across the gorge. "The fork pinches half a mile north — rockslide crosses the floor, you can climb it! I'll be on the east side of it with four very persuasive arrows!" A raw breath. "Or cut south and we raise hell on this rim and pull them to us — either way, PICK ONE AND MOVE, because those are soldiers, not bandits, and soldiers don't ride that hard for pocket change!"

Behind her, the vanguard started hammering stone and bellowing like an army. Below, the gully three had finally cleared the dead horse and were sprinting to join the chase, which meant every second got more expensive.

She nocked an arrow, shoulder tight to a boulder, eyes on the shrinking gap between the riders and him.

"C'mon, Cap. Pick fast." Her arm was bleeding through the wrap again. She ignored it. "I'm running out of everything except bad options."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "North it is!" I bellow back, already moving. *I scramble up the ravine wall, using my polearm to brace myself, cursing under my breath.* "Keep 'em busy, Kira!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I glance back at Kira, a grim nod.* "Don't let them get past you!" *The climb is steep, but I've faced worse. The polearm helps, digging into cracks for purchase.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"North. Because of course the answer involves more climbing."

No time to argue. Arguing was for people with more than four arrows.

Kira slashed a hand at the three vanguard soldiers. "Spread along the lip — move between the rocks, bang stone, sound like twenty! Go!" They fanned out, hammering pommels against boulders, and the east rim started making noise like a small army. Cheap trick. Cheap tricks kept people breathing.

The six riders came around the spur in a crescent — she'd seen that formation before, in companies that paid better. Two of them carried bows. *Wonderful.*

The lead rider kicked into a gallop, cutting for the west wall where Captain clung like a stubborn speck, polearm flashing with every reach. Fifty yards. She led him, breathed out, loosed.

The arrow took his horse in the shoulder. Rider went over the front, hit the slope, rolled.

"Nothing personal!"

Three arrows. And the crescent didn't scatter — that scared her worse than anything. It *split.* The two bowmen reined up and started working the east rim, pinning her to her boulder, arrowheads bursting stone a hand's width from her face. The other four pushed for Captain's climb.

Never shoot twice from the same rock. She rolled left through the scree, came up in a new notch, and caught a bowman bracketing his shot — her arrow hit him square in the chest at eighty yards, half skill, half wind, all luck.

Two.

Then one of the four dismounted and started up the west wall itself. Shield slung on his back. Climbing after Captain like it was a stairs.

"No, no, *no*—"

She couldn't shoot him. Not with Captain directly above him. She put a shaft in a wall and screamed instead: "CAP! CLIMBER ON YOUR HEELS — LEFT HAND, THERE'S A LEDGE!" Whether he heard over his own cursing, the gods only knew.

She ran the rim north, parallel, lungs full of knives, and saw the ugly truth from the high ground: the remaining three riders weren't chasing anymore. They were racing for the rockslide. The crossing. The place Captain *had* to come down.

They weren't hunting him. They were setting the table.

Kira hit the slide first — massive tumbled shelves of stone bridging the gorge floor, the only ladder across — and turned at bay on the east lip. The vanguard three caught up, panting, armed with rocks and fear. The three riders pulled up a hundred yards out and just... waited. Watching her. Watching the wall.

The climber was still on it, moving. So close to the top of the slide. So far.

She nocked her last arrow.

"CAP!" Her voice tore raw across the gorge. "Three riders hold the crossing — you come down the wrong side of this rock and they take you apart! Get up the wall and get to me, and this becomes a siege *they* regret!" She held the draw, arm shaking, sight steady on the nearest rider's chest. "But you got about a minute, so WHATEVER you're doing up there — do it FASTER!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I hear Kira's shouts, the urgency in her voice cutting through the din of my own exertion.* "Got it!"

*I dig my polearm in, finding a small crevice, and pull myself up with a grunt, eyes already scanning for that ledge.* This climb is a pain, but being pincered by these riders would be worse.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I scramble, finding the ledge Kira shouted about. It's barely enough for my boots, but it's a start.* This is going to be close. "Almost there, Kira!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I pull myself onto the ledge, my boots scraping for purchase. I can see the top of the wall now, and the rockslide beyond.* "Just a little further!" *I grunt, pushing off the ledge and reaching for another handhold.*

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *My hand finds purchase on a sturdy root, and I haul myself over the lip of the ravine.* My chest heaves, but I'm out. "Made it!" I yell, spotting Kira and the three riders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Made it!" I yell, spotting Kira and the three riders. *I pull my polearm free of the rock and level it at the riders.* "Now what?"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Draw their fire. Right." Kira spat into the dust. "Daggers against bows. Bloody brilliant."

She broke from the boulder anyway.

An arrow skipped off the stone where she'd been crouching a heartbeat earlier. She didn't run straight — never straight — cutting hard left, then right, boots skidding on loose shale, making herself the loudest thing in the ravine.

"OI! Up top!" Her voice cracked up the wall. "Six of you and you can't tag one woman on open ground? My grandmother shoots better, and she's dead!"

Two bows answered. She heard the strings sing, dropped her shoulder, let one hiss past her ear. The second tore through her cloak's hem and buried itself in the dirt ahead — she ran straight over it.

Somewhere west, steel and shouting rose. The push was moving.

She caught the east ridge in flashes between cover: four archers tracking her — but two figures breaking right, nocking fresh arrows, shifting along the ridgeline toward the western slope.

"Captain! Two bowmen repositioning toward your flank — they're setting up on your line!" she bellowed across the ravine. "Four still on me, and they're shooting slow. Rattled or green, but they're *watching me*!"

Another arrow kissed her forearm — a hot, shallow line of pain. "Shit—" She hissed through her teeth and kept moving, angling for the rockfall at the base of the east wall. If they wanted to shoot her, they'd have to keep their eyes down here.

*Keep looking at me,* she thought, and started up the scree.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Heard you, Kira! Hold them!"

My polearm swept wide, deflecting an arrow that whistled past. We were pushing hard up the western slope, the vanguard a shield wall of steel and grunts. I saw the two archers Kira mentioned, scrambling for a better vantage.

"Spears up! Drive them back!" I yelled, pointing with my polearm.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The scree fought her for every foot. Stone rolled and slid under her boots — two steps gained, one lost — and the archers above had just enough sense to shoot at the slope itself, spitting chips of rock up by her hands, trying to spark a slide.

"That it? Throwing *dirt* at me?" A chip split her knuckle open. She swore, dragged herself onto a shelf, and kept climbing. The graze on her forearm had gone from hot to numb. Small mercies.

The angle was doing her work now. The closer she got, the harder it was for them to draw on her — too steep, too close. One archer leaned out over the edge to track her, bow half-lowered, all his weight forward on loose stone.

Kira didn't give him time to learn from his mistake.

She surged up the last stretch, caught the ridgeline lip, and came over it low and fast. The man staggered back, fumbling his bow up like a club. Her left dagger punched through his thigh, her right opened his bow arm to the bone — the bow dropped, then he did, screaming into the dirt.

One down. Three left. And his screaming didn't help the others' aim any.

She rolled behind a squat boulder as an arrow hammered the far side of it. Below, the western push rolled on — steel on steel, the shield wall grinding up the far slope. But she caught something else up here. One of the remaining archers wasn't shooting at her at all. Black hood, brass whistle at his throat — turned west, arm raised, calling adjustments to the two repositioned bowmen.

He was the one running this ambush.

*Break the head,* she thought, *the body follows.*

"Captain!" she bellowed down the slope. "Black hood, top of the east ridge — he's the one directing their archers! One down up here, two on me, and I'd wager the rest fold if he drops!" Another arrow skipped off her boulder. "And some bloody cover fire wouldn't hurt while I get to him!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content: No

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I grit my teeth.* "I'm a little busy right now, Kira! Take him yourself!"

I parry the incoming arrow with my polearm, the shaft splintering. This fight is getting too close.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I grunt, pushing forward.* "Damn it, Kira! Just hold them!" 

My polearm comes up, sweeping aside another incoming arrow. I need to reconnect with the vanguard.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Separated. Of course he was.

Kira caught him across the ravine in flashes between cover — a lone figure below the shield wall's grind, the vanguard too far above him, nothing in between but open slope and arrow arcs. Going down to him meant giving back the ridge and dying on the scree for the privilege.

But the man with the whistle could reach him. That was the whole problem.

*So kill it at the source.*

The two archers left on her were still shooting slow — draw, hold, release, like they were scared of their own strings. She waited out the next shaft, counted half a breath, and moved on the release, the first man's screaming covering her footfalls.

The nearer archer never got his second arrow nocked. Four strides put her inside his draw before the string came taut. Left dagger across his wrist, right up under the ribs, twist. He folded quiet. Quiet was new for this lot.

The last one broke — fired wild, didn't even make her flinch, then bolted down the far end of the ridgeline, boots skidding past his screaming friend. She let him run. He wasn't killing anybody today.

The black hood was. He hadn't turned to run. He'd turned *west* — and the brass whistle at his throat shrilled two sharp notes.

Across the ravine, on the western slope, both repositioned bowmen pivoted. Drew. Aimed down at the lone figure beneath the shield wall.

"No you don't—" Kira threw on the run. Her left dagger spun once and took him high in the shoulder instead of the throat — *angle, gods damn it* — spinning him sideways, the third whistle note dying in a snarl.

She closed with her last blade bare. He came up with a curved sword, longer than anything she wanted any part of, blood soaking his black sleeve dark.

"Captain!" she roared across the ravine, circling, weight low. "Two bows just turned onto you — keep your head down!"

The hood lunged. She slipped inside the arc.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I hear Kira's warning, but it's almost too late.* An arrow grazes my helmet, ringing in my ears. "Damn it all!" I yell, ducking behind a large rock.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: The mercenary vanguard is still pushing ahead, but I'm pinned. I can't reach them, and I'm a sitting duck here. I need to move.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The sword hissed over her head as she ducked inside the arc. Too close for him now — a curved blade needed room, and she was standing in his lap.

Her dagger raked his ribs. He grunted, twisted, and the guard came around and caught her over the ear — stars, the world tilting, boots skidding on shale. She rolled with it and came up spitting blood from a bitten cheek.

He pressed her, short whipping arcs, her own dagger still buried in his shoulder swinging with every step like a flag. He was good. Bleeding from two places and still good.

But every cut pulled at that wound. She could see it — the hitch, half a beat late on the backhand.

She let him come. Took the next cut on her bracer, pain flaring through the numb graze, stepped *through* it — and her left hand closed on the hilt sticking out of his shoulder. She rammed it deeper. He screamed, the whistle at his throat rattling, and his sword hand found her collar. Her right dagger punched through his sword-arm forearm. The curved blade dropped into the dirt.

Then he did. She put her boot on his chest and finished it clean.

Silence up top — just the wounded man whimpering somewhere behind her and the grind of steel from the west.

She yanked her dagger free and looked across the ravine. The two repositioned bowmen had nocked again, bows trained on the rock the Captain was pinned behind. Waiting for him to move.

*Oh no you don't.*

The dead archer still had his bow. She snatched it up, arrows spilling from the quiver.

"My grandmother shoots better," she muttered, nocking, "and she's dead."

The shot went wide — kicked dirt ten feet off the nearer bowman. Didn't matter. Both heads snapped up toward the ridge, both bows swinging off the Captain to find her.

"CAPTAIN!" she roared. "Handler's dead, and I've got both their eyes on me — they're *off* you! Whatever move you're making, make it now — get up to that shield wall before they remember you exist!"

She nocked again. Her arms burned. The second arrow, at least, made them duck.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I hear Kira's shout, her voice strained but clear.* "That's my girl!" 

I see the archers' attention shift. This is my chance. I break from cover, polearm held ready, and sprint for the vanguard.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content: She

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I reach the vanguard, sliding in just as a spearman falters.* "On me! Push them back!" 

I take his place, polearm sweeping, and we gain ground inch by inch.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content: He

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
He was safe. Good.

She threw the bow down. "Now for the rest of you bastards," she muttered, grabbing her daggers.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I look across the ravine, seeing Kira standing victorious over the ambush leader.* "Kira! The ravine mouth! We're pinned here if they bring up more!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You descended the last flight of stairs and the temperature dropped. The passage opened into a chamber that hadn't seen light in a long time — your torch was the first in decades, maybe centuries, and the shadows retreated from it reluctantly.

Dust covered everything. Thick, undisturbed dust. Except for one set of footprints leading from the far entrance to the center of the room, where something had been dragged. The marks ended at a stone slab. The slab had writing on it.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I kneel down to read the writing on the slab, holding the torch close.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You knelt, and the cold of the stone floor seeped through your knees almost at once. When you brought the torch close, the flame guttered, though there was no draft you could feel.

The dust on the slab's surface had been disturbed. Someone had wiped it clean, recently, in long, careless strokes. Their fingermarks were still visible at the edges where the grime had piled up.

The writing beneath was carved deep, the letters old and angular. Some were worn nearly smooth, but most of it was still legible if you held the light at a low angle and let the shadows fill the grooves:

*HERE LIES THE KEEPER OF THE LOWER DOOR*
*WHO WAS SEALED BENEATH BY HIS OWN CONSENT*
*THAT WHAT HE GUARDED WOULD NOT RISE*
*LET NO HAND LIFT THIS STONE*
*LET NO VOICE SPEAK HIS NAME*

Below that was a name. Or there had been one. It had been chiseled out long ago, leaving only a rough, deliberate scar in the rock.

But that wasn't what held your attention. Along the seam where the slab met the floor, the dust had been scraped away in a thin, even line all the way around. And at the near corner, close enough that your torchlight fell right across it, a fresh gouge marked the stone. It was pale and sharp-edged, the kind of mark a pry bar left.

The drag marks you had followed ended here. Whatever had been hauled across the chamber had been set down right beside the slab. A faint rectangular impression remained in the dust, roughly the size of a small chest or a heavy sack.

The impression was empty now. And there were no footprints leading away.

Somewhere far behind you, back up the stairs you had descended, a single pebble clicked down the steps, one at a time, and came to rest.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I jump, startled by the sound of the pebble.* I quickly glance over my shoulder, my hand instinctively going to the hilt of my sword. "Hello?" I call out, my voice echoing a little too loudly in the silence. I then turn back to the slab, my eyes narrowing. Someone was here. Recently.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You spun on your heel, and the torch swung with you, throwing your shadow long and crooked across the chamber wall. Your fingers found the hilt of your sword before you had even decided to reach for it.

"Hello?"

The word left you too loud. It struck the far walls and came back smaller, then smaller again, until the chamber swallowed it. Nothing answered. The mouth of the stairwell was a black arch beyond the reach of your light. You watched it for a long moment and saw nothing move there. The pebble had stopped. No second one followed.

When you turned back to the slab, the silence felt different. It no longer seemed empty. It seemed to be waiting.

*Recently.* The word sat heavy in your mind as you looked the stone over again. Close up, the signs were impossible to ignore. The gouge at the corner was so fresh that a fine powder of stone dust still clung in the crack. It hadn't settled yet. Along the scraped seam, when you brought the torch low, you saw that the slab didn't sit quite flush with the floor. On the far side a hairline gap showed, no wider than a blade's edge, where the stone had been lifted and let down again slightly out of true.

The torch flame leaned toward that gap. Only slightly, but it held there, bending steadily. Cold air was seeping up from beneath the slab. It carried a faint smell, old and mineral, like wet iron and something sweeter underneath it that you couldn't name.

Then your eyes went back to the empty impression in the dust. Now that you were looking for it, you could see what you had missed before. Leading away from the rectangle was a short smear, as though the object had been tipped or slid rather than lifted. It ran straight to the edge of the slab and stopped at the seam.

The footprints led in. Nothing led out.

Beneath your knees, through the cold stone, you felt it. It was too faint to be sure of, and you might have imagined it. A single slow vibration passed through the floor, the way a door far below might shudder as it swung shut.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I grab the amulet and put it on. Then I turn to face the guardian.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your hand had found it before your mind caught up. A thin chain lay in the hairline gap on the far side of the slab. You had half-seen it without really seeing it, a thread of dull metal pinched between stone and floor, trailing out as though someone had dropped it in their hurry and the slab had come down on it.

You worked it free. It came loose with a dry scrape. At the end of the chain hung a disc of dark metal no wider than your palm, cold enough to ache. It was stamped with the same angular script as the slab. In its center, where a stone might have been set, there was only a shallow hollow in the shape of an eye.

You slipped the chain over your head. The disc settled against your chest, and for a heartbeat the cold of it spread outward through your ribs like water filling a cup. Then it was gone, and the metal was warm. It was as warm as your own skin, as if it had always been there.

The torch flame straightened. It no longer leaned toward the gap. It stood perfectly upright, perfectly still, burning without a flicker.

You turned.

It stood at the edge of your light, where the drag marks began. You had not heard it come. There were still no footprints but yours in the dust. It was tall, taller than a man, and wrapped in something that might once have been a burial shroud and was now little more than grey threads held together by habit. Beneath it you could make out the suggestion of armor, dark with age and fused in places to whatever wore it. Its head was bowed. Where its face should have been, the shroud hung in a smooth, unbroken fall, except for a single place at its center. There the cloth had rotted away, and something beneath caught your torchlight and gave it back, pale and wet.

It didn't move toward you. It didn't raise the long, notched blade that hung from one gauntleted hand, its tip resting in the dust.

It was looking at the amulet.

Slowly, with a sound like old leather flexing, the figure lifted its head. The thing behind the shroud fixed on the disc at your chest, on the empty eye-shaped hollow in its center. Its free hand rose, palm open, fingers spread. It could have been a warning, or a plea, or a demand.

A voice came, though nothing about the figure moved to make it. It was low and cracked, as if it had not been used since the name on the slab was chiseled away.

"*That… is not yours to wear.*"

Beneath the floor, the slow vibration came again. It was stronger this time, and unmistakable.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I clutch the amulet with one hand, my eyes darting from the figure to the slab.* "It was on the floor! Someone left it here, *with* the stone pried open." My gaze flickers back to the shrouded figure. "What did you guard, and what did they take?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The words tumbled out of you and struck the walls, and this time the chamber did not swallow them. They hung in the still air between you and the figure, and the torch flame, upright and unmoving, did not so much as tremble.

The guardian did not answer at once. Its open hand stayed raised. The pale, wet thing behind the rotted cloth shifted its attention from the amulet to the slab, then back to you. When it moved at last, it was only its fingers. They closed slowly, one by one, with the creak of dry leather, until the hand became a loose fist and sank back to its side.

"*On the floor,*" it repeated. The voice came from nowhere and everywhere, low in the stone itself. "*Yes. They would have dropped it. It does not suffer thieves. It burns them, when they try to take it past the threshold.*"

The notched blade dragged a shallow line in the dust as the figure turned its head toward the chiseled scar where the name had been.

"*I was the door,*" it said. "*Not the keeper of it. The door. They laid me beneath the stone so that what lay below would have to pass through me to rise, and I would not let it. That was the bargain. Centuries I held it.*" A pause, and something in the cracked voice slipped, like a foot finding loose scree. "*And then a hand lifted the stone.*"

Beneath you the floor shuddered a third time. It was no longer faint. Dust sifted down from the ceiling in thin grey curtains that caught the torchlight, and somewhere below, far below, you heard a sound. It was long and grinding, like a great weight turning on a hinge that had rusted shut.

"*You ask what they took.*" The guardian's head tilted toward the empty rectangle in the dust, toward the smear leading into the seam. "*They took nothing. They brought something. Down. Past me, while I slept in the dark and did not wake in time.*" The shroud stirred, though there was no wind. "*An offering, or a key. I do not know which. I know only that the lower door is open, and that it has not been open since before your tongue was spoken.*"

It lifted its gaze to the amulet one final time. You felt the disc warm against your chest, warmer than skin now, almost feverish, as though it were answering the look.

"*The eye that belongs in that hollow,*" the guardian said, "*was mine. They cut it from me when they sealed me here, so that I could see only downward, only toward what I guarded. Without it I am blind to them. To the ones who came. I cannot follow.*"

The grinding below stopped. The silence that followed was worse.

"*But you can.*"

The figure did not step toward you. It simply waited, blade tip in the dust, the wet pale thing behind its shroud fixed on your face. From the hairline gap beneath the slab, faint and unmistakable, came the smell again, wet iron and something sweeter. With it, drifting up out of the dark, came the slow, deliberate sound of footsteps climbing.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I talk to the ghost. "What happened here? Who are you?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
"What happened here?" you asked, and the words came out hoarse. "Who *are* you?"

The guardian was silent for a long moment. Below, the footsteps kept climbing. They were slow and patient, and not yet close, but closer than before.

"*Ghost,*" it said at last, as though tasting the word you hadn't spoken aloud. Perhaps the amulet had carried the thought to it. "*No. A ghost is what remains when something ends. I was not permitted to end.*"

Its head turned toward the scar in the slab, the rough, deliberate wound where the name had been.

"*Who I am, they took. That was the price. A name is a door of its own, and anything below that learned mine could call me aside. So they cut it from the stone, and from the records, and from the mouths of everyone who knew it. And then they cut it from me.*" The gauntleted fingers twitched at its side. "*I remember that I had a wife. I remember the colour of the sky over the city that stood above us. I do not remember her face, or the city's name, or my own.*"

The floor trembled, softer this time, and a thin stream of grit hissed down from the ceiling behind you.

"*What happened,*" the guardian went on, and its cracked voice quickened. "*Three nights ago, by the count of the stone, a lantern came down those stairs. Not a torch. A lantern, hooded, so the light fell only where they wished it. Two of them. One carried the burden you saw dragged. The other carried the bar.*"

The pale, wet thing behind the shroud tilted toward the fresh gouge at the corner of the slab.

"*I was sleeping the long sleep. I felt the stone lift the way you would feel a blade slide between your ribs. By the time I rose, they had already gone down past me, into the stair beneath. One of them spoke as she went. She did not say my name. She could not know it.*" A pause. "*She said another. The name of the thing below. She said it gently, the way you would call a dog home.*"

The footsteps stopped.

In the silence you could hear your own breathing, too fast, and the faint tick of the amulet's chain settling against your collar. The disc was hot now, almost painful through your shirt. The hollow at its center pulsed faintly against your skin, like a second heartbeat out of time with your own.

Then, from the hairline gap beneath the slab, came a new sound. It was not footsteps. Something was scratching at the underside of the stone, softly and methodically, testing the seam from below.

The guardian's blade lifted from the dust for the first time. It did not point at you. It pointed at the slab.

"*One of them is coming back,*" it said, very quietly. "*Or something is wearing her.*"

The scratching paused. Then, muffled through a foot of solid rock, a woman's voice called up, pleasant and warm and horribly patient:

"*Hello? Is someone up there? I heard you. I heard you call.*"

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *My hand goes to the hilt of my sword again.* "Heard me call?" I mutter, my eyes wide as saucers. My gaze snaps to the guardian. "What... what was the name she called?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your fingers closed around the hilt, and the leather wrapping creaked in your grip. The sound seemed enormous.
