"Heard me call?" The words left you barely above a whisper. You turned to the guardian. "What... what was the name she called?"

The guardian did not answer. It turned its head, slowly, and the pale, wet thing behind the shroud fixed on you with an intensity you could feel on your skin, like standing too near a fire.

"*No,*" it said.

The word was not loud, but the torch flame shrank from it, dwindling to a blue bead on the wick before it swelled back to its steady yellow.

"*You have not understood. Names are doors. Hers was spoken gently, in the dark, by one who wished it to come. It came.*" The notched blade did not waver from the slab. "*If I give it to you, you will carry it. You will think it, in the quiet moments, whether you wish to or not. And it will hear you thinking it. That is how she was taken, I believe. Not by force. By invitation.*"

Beneath the stone, the scratching began again. It was slower now. It had found the gouge at the corner, the place where the pry bar had bitten, and it was working there.

"*You called out once,*" the guardian went on, lower still. "*Only a greeting. An empty word. But you called, and you were heard. Everything below is listening now. Do not give it more than that.*"

"*I'm sorry,*" the woman's voice said from under the floor. It was so close that it seemed to come from just beneath your knees, and she sounded like she meant it. "*I didn't mean to frighten you. I'm hurt. My friend left me down here. Please. The stone is so heavy. If you could just lift the edge, I could climb out. You don't even have to look at me.*"

A pause.

"*You're wearing something of mine,*" she added. "*I can feel it. It's warm, isn't it?*"

The amulet flared against your chest, hot enough now that you smelled scorched linen. In the hollow at its center, something shifted. It was not metal, and not quite light. It was a faint wetness, like the sheen on an eye just opening.

The guardian drew in a breath it had no lungs for, and the sound rattled through the chamber.

"*She lies,*" it said. "*Or the thing wearing her does. But hear me. The eye is waking because it is close to what it was made to watch. That disc will let you see what I cannot. Where they went. What she brought down. Whether any of her is left.*" Its blade tip scraped a slow arc in the dust, marking a line between you and the slab. "*Or you may take it from your neck, set it on the stone, and climb those stairs, and I will hold this door as long as I am able. I do not know how long that is anymore.*"

The scratching stopped.

In the new silence, you heard a grinding creak. The slab shifted a fraction of an inch at its corner, as though a single patient finger had pushed from below.

"*Choose quickly,*" the guardian said.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: "I choose to see," I say, my voice firm despite the heat of the amulet against my chest. My eyes narrow, fixed on the slab. "And I choose to know what she brought down here." *I take a step closer to the slab, sword still in hand, ready for whatever might try to push through.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
"I choose to see."

Your voice did not shake. You stepped toward the slab, sword drawn now, the blade catching the torchlight in a long thin line. The guardian did not stop you. It lowered its own weapon a fraction, the way a soldier yields a post, and the tip came to rest just beyond the arc it had drawn in the dust.

"*Then look,*" it said. "*And do not look away, whatever looks back.*"

The amulet opened.

There was no other word for it. You felt it more than saw it: a wet, deliberate parting against your breastbone, like lids coming unstuck after a long sleep. The heat broke all at once and became cold again, but a different cold, clean and sharp as well water, and it did not stay in your chest. It climbed your throat and settled behind your eyes.

The slab went thin.

It did not vanish. You could still see the carved letters and the scar where the name had been. But the stone had become like dark glass held up to a lamp, and through it, below it, you saw.

A stair. Narrow, spiraling, cut from the living rock, dropping away into a depth your torch could never have reached. The walls were slick and glistening, and the steps were worn into shallow bowls by feet that had climbed them long before there were men to climb anything.

On the topmost step, directly beneath the corner where the gouge was, crouched a woman.

She had been young, you thought. Her traveling coat was good wool, torn now at one shoulder, and a hooded lantern hung from her belt, its shutter closed. Her hands were pressed flat to the underside of the slab. Her fingertips were raw and dark to the second knuckle from scratching. Her head was tipped back, her face turned upward toward you with an expression of perfect, patient hope.

Her eyes were open. They were not looking at the stone. They were looking at *you*, through it, the same way you were looking at her.

And they were not her eyes. Something moved in them, slow and shining, the way oil moves on water.

Her lips moved. Through the rock, a heartbeat late, came the voice.

"*Oh,*" she said softly. "*There you are.*"

The eye in the amulet did not let you flinch. It pulled your sight past her, downward, as if it had been waiting centuries to show someone. Down the spiral, turn after turn, past a second body sprawled on the steps. A man, broad-shouldered, a pry bar still clutched in one hand, his face turned to the wall. He was very still. Down further, to where the stair ended at a threshold of black stone carved with the same angular script, and a door.

The lower door. It stood open a handspan.

Before it, set neatly on the floor as though on an altar, was the thing they had dragged. It was a small iron-bound chest, its lid thrown back. Inside, on a bed of rotted velvet, lay a single object you could see with terrible clarity: a human skull, small, a child's, its crown inlaid with silver lettering.

Around the chest, in a wide ring, someone had arranged candles. They had burned down to stubs. And written on the floor in something dark and dried, circling the ring, over and over, was a word. A name.

The eye showed it to you. The letters were plain, and you understood that if you let yourself read them, you would know them forever.

Behind you, the guardian spoke, strained and distant, as though from the far end of a long hall.

"*What do you see? Tell me. Tell me what they brought.*"

Above the woman's head, the corner of the slab ground upward another fraction of an inch. A sliver of cold, sweet-smelling air breathed across your ankles. Through the widening crack, something pale slid into view: four raw fingertips, curling over the edge of the stone, feeling for purchase.

"*You can see it now, can't you?*" the woman's voice said, warm and delighted. "*Go on. Read it. Read it out loud. That's all it wants. That's all it's ever wanted.*"

The name waited on the floor far below, at the edge of your sight. The fingers tightened on the stone at your feet. Your sword was in your hand.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: My breath hitches. The skull. The name. The woman's eyes. It's too much. "No," I whisper, my voice catching. *I shove my boot under the rising slab, trying to wedge it in place.* "I won't read it!" I shout, my eyes still fixed on the horror below. "Guardian! What is that skull?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your boot went down hard on the lifted corner. The slab came with it, grinding back an inch, then half an inch, then stopped.

It had caught on the fingers.

Through the dark glass of the stone, you watched the woman's hand take the full weight of the rock. You heard bone give, a small wet crackle like green sticks underfoot. Her face did not change. She kept smiling up at you with that same patient hope, and the oil-sheen in her eyes rolled slowly, lazily, as if it found the whole thing mildly interesting.

Then she pushed.

The pressure came up through your boot and into your shin, steady and immense, far more than her slight frame should have held. Your heel began to slide in the dust. The gap widened by a hair. The broken fingers flexed on the stone's edge, crooked now and bent wrong at the knuckles, and kept their grip.

"*No?*" she said, and she sounded almost fond. "*That's all right. Everyone says no at first.*"

Behind you came the scrape of metal. The guardian crossed the arc it had drawn in the dust, the first time it had moved its feet since you'd seen it. It set the flat of its notched blade across the slab beside your boot and leaned its weight on the hilt. The stone groaned and sank back. The pressure against your shin eased, though it did not vanish. It waited.

"*The skull,*" the guardian said. Its voice was strained, close now, right at your shoulder. "*Tell me. Is it small?*"

In the amulet's sight, far below, the thing lay on its bed of rotted velvet within the ring of candle stubs. It was small enough to cradle in two hands. The silver lettering circled its crown in a thin, careful band.

The guardian did not wait for your answer. Perhaps the amulet had carried it to him, the way it had carried your thought of *ghost*.

"*Then it is the first seal,*" it said. "*Before they made me the door, there was another. A lesser one. They thought a child would be enough. A child's name is small, they said. Easily kept. Easily hidden.*" Its gauntlet tightened on the hilt, and the leather creaked. "*It was not enough. The child could not hold it. So they took the bones and bound the thing below to them. They buried that skull a hundred miles from here, beneath a city, so that what lay below would always be pulled away from its own door. Away from the world above. They built me when the child failed.*"

A pause. The strain in its voice changed into something rawer.

"*Silver lettering, you said. On the crown.*"

The pale, wet thing behind its shroud turned from the slab to you. It was very close. In the torchlight you could see that it trembled.

"*I do not remember my wife's face,*" it said slowly, "*but I remember that they would not let me hold the child before they took her. I remember that. And I remember that when I agreed to be the door, they promised me she would be buried beneath the city. Under the sky I remember. Safe.*"

The woman under the stone laughed. It was a soft, bright sound, and it came up through the crack like steam.

"*Ask him what the letters say,*" she called. "*Go on. It's his name, you know. Written on her. They had to put it somewhere when they cut it out of him. They put it on the one thing he'd never let anyone touch.*" The broken fingers tapped the stone, one, two, three. "*Say his name, and he'll step aside. He'll have to. And then we can all go down together and see her.*"

The guardian did not deny it.

Far below, at the very edge of the amulet's sight, the lower door moved. It was not much, no wider than a second handspan, but it swung silently open. In the widening black beyond it, something vast and patient shifted its attention up the long spiral stair, toward the slab, toward your boot, and toward the warm disc on your chest.

The candle stubs around the chest, burned down to nothing, flickered alight one by one.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *My breath catches in my throat. The guardian's child. The name on the skull.* "It's a trap!" I yell, my eyes wide and fixed on the guardian. "She wants me to say your name!" *I lean my weight against the slab, trying to push it back down, my other hand still on my sword hilt.* "Don't listen to her, guardian! She's lying!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You threw your weight onto the slab, and the words tore out of you, too loud and ragged at the edges.

"It's a trap! She wants me to say your name! Don't listen to her, guardian! She's lying!"

The stone answered before anything else did. It sank a grudging quarter-inch under your weight and the guardian's together, and the broken fingers caught in the seam folded further, bent flat against the rock. Through the dark glass of the slab, the woman's smile did not falter. Her lips moved a heartbeat before the sound reached you.

"*Am I?*"

The guardian did not look at her. It looked at you, the pale wet thing behind its shroud so close that you could see it was not an eye at all. It was only the socket, raw and weeping, where an eye had been taken.

"*She is not lying,*" it said quietly. "*That is what makes it a trap.*"

The pressure under your boot surged. It was not a push this time but a slow, rolling heave, as though the whole stair beneath had drawn a breath. Your heel skidded an inch through the dust before it caught on the edge of the arc the guardian had carved. The guardian's blade bowed under its weight with a thin, singing complaint of old steel.

"*The things below do not need to lie,*" it went on, and the strain was plain in its voice now. "*They need only to be heard. Every true thing she says is a rung on a ladder. My name is on the child's crown. I do not remember it, but I feel that it is so. If it is spoken, I am no longer the door. I am only a man who lost his daughter. And a man who lost his daughter...*" Its voice cracked, and for a moment it could not finish. "*A man will walk down any stair for that.*"

"*He's right,*" the woman said warmly. "*You're clever. You see so much more than he does now.*"

Far below, at the edge of the amulet's sight, the candle flames around the chest leaned all together, the way your torch had leaned toward the gap, toward the open door. The silver band on the little skull caught their light and began to shine. The letters did not glow. They simply became clearer, sharper, as though the eye against your chest were leaning in to read them for you.

You felt it pulling. The hollow in the disc was drawing your sight down the spiral one turn at a time, past the woman, past the still, broad-shouldered man on the steps.

He was no longer facing the wall.

His head had turned. His cheek lay against the stone step, and his eyes, shining with that same slow oil, were fixed upward. The pry bar was still in his hand. His fingers tightened on it, one by one.

"*Listen to me,*" the guardian said, and something in its voice made you turn from the stair. "*The eye was made to watch. It will show you whatever you set it on, and it will not stop until you look away. If you let it read the crown, you will know my name, and she will pull it out of you the moment you are frightened enough. And you will be.*" The blade shuddered under its hands. "*But the eye does not only see. It was cut from the door. It remembers being the door.*"

Below you, the stone jolted. The fingers slid another knuckle's width through the gap, and the cold, sweet air poured across your ankles like water.

"*Press it to the seam,*" the guardian said. "*Where she has broken the stone. It may seal it. It may seal it with you on this side and me on that. I do not know. They never told me what the eye could do without me behind it.*" The raw socket turned toward the stairwell above, toward the long climb back to daylight, and then back to you. "*Or pull it from your neck and run, and take the only sight of that crown out of this place with you.*"

On the stair far below, the man with the pry bar began to rise.

And beneath the slab, so close now she might have been whispering against your boot, the woman began to sing softly. It was a child's song, simple and old, a few notes rising and falling.

The guardian went utterly still.

"*I know that song,*" it said.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I yank my boot out from under the slab, nearly tripping.* "Run? No!" My eyes dart from the rising man below to the guardian's unseeing gaze. "We have to seal it!" *I rip the amulet from my neck. It's searing hot, but I ignore the pain.* "Help me!" I shout, thrusting the amulet towards the seam of the slab. "We can close it!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The instant your boot left the stone, the slab leapt.

It did not rise far, perhaps an inch, but it rose all at once, with the violence of something released. The woman's whole hand came through the gap to the wrist. Her fingers were crooked and blackened, splayed flat on the floor where your foot had been, and they began to feel their way across the dust toward you like something blind.

The guardian's blade shrieked against the stone and held. It was alone now, bearing the full weight of the slab and the heave beneath it, and the old steel bowed in a long, trembling curve.

You tore the amulet from your neck.

The chain bit the back of your neck and then snapped. The disc was so hot that it seemed to cling to your palm, and you smelled your own skin searing before you felt it. The moment the metal left your chest, the sight went out of you. It did not fade. It *went*, like a door slammed in your face. The slab was only stone again, grey and dusty and blank. The stair, the chest, the candles, and the rising man were all gone. There was only your torch, the guardian's bowed blade, and the pale hand crawling across the floor.

Below, where you could no longer see, the singing went on.

"Help me!"

For a terrible moment the guardian did not move. It stood with its head bent toward the seam, toward the song, and its whole towering frame had gone slack in a way that frightened you more than anything that had come before. Its weight was easing off the hilt. The slab crept upward.

Then your voice reached it, and it shuddered like a man waking from a dream of drowning.

"*Yes,*" it said. Its voice was ruined and thick. "*Yes. The seam. Where she broke it.*"

It threw itself back onto the blade. The stone ground down, and the crawling hand stopped and pressed flat, pinned at the wrist.

You drove the amulet into the gouge.

The disc met the raw, pale bite of the pry bar. The hollow at its center opened again, and this time you saw it happen. A wet, dark gleam swam up out of the metal, and the eye was *looking* straight down into the crack, at whatever waited on the other side.

The singing stopped mid-note.

Cold poured out of the amulet, the clean well-water cold you had felt behind your eyes, and it spread into the stone. Frost raced along the seam in both directions from the disc, a thin white line crackling through the dust. Where it passed, the gap *closed*. It was not pressed shut. It was knitted, grain to grain, as though the rock were healing a wound. The seam vanished behind the frost, inch by inch, racing around the corners of the slab toward the far side.

Toward the wrist still caught in the gap.

The frost reached the woman's arm and stopped. It could not close over flesh. It built up there instead, white and thickening, a ridge of ice around her wrist. Beneath the slab, for the first time, something *screamed*. It was not her voice. It was higher and older, and it came from very far down, rising through the rock like a pressure in your ears.

Then it cut off, and a new voice came up through the last open inch of the seam.

It was small. It was frightened. It was a child's.

"*Papa?*"

The guardian made a sound you would remember for the rest of your life.

The blade under its hands began to lift. It was not the slab pushing now. The guardian itself was easing its weight back, slowly, the way a man steps back from a cliff edge he has decided to step off. The pale socket was fixed on the last sliver of the gap, and its gauntlet was loosening on the hilt one finger at a time.

"*She's cold,*" the child's voice whispered. "*It's so cold down here, Papa. Why did you let them put me here?*"

Beneath your palm, the amulet pulsed. The frost ridge around the wrist cracked, then held. The seal was nearly whole, and it needed only that last inch. The pinned hand flexed against the ice, and far below, muffled but unmistakable, came the ringing scrape of an iron bar striking stone as someone climbed the final turns of the stair.

The guardian's weight left the blade entirely.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: "No!" I scream, grabbing the guardian's gauntlet, my eyes wide with terror and desperation. "Don't you dare! Don't you *dare* listen to it!" My fingers dig into the cold metal, trying to hold him in place, to keep him from letting go. "It's a trick! It's not her!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You lunged and caught the gauntlet with both hands.

The metal was cold enough to burn, a different burn from the amulet's, and it bit into your already-seared palm. You felt your skin tear against the fused rivets. You didn't let go. You dug your fingers into the joints of the old armor and pulled, and the guardian was so much heavier than anything that size should have been, like dragging a pillar. For one sickening moment it kept moving away from you, and your boots slid through the dust after it.

"No! Don't you *dare*! Don't you *dare* listen to it! It's a trick! It's not her!"

It stopped.

Not because you had the strength to stop it. You knew that even as it happened. It stopped because something in your voice reached it, the same way your cry for help had reached it before. The towering frame hung there, half-turned, the raw socket still fixed on the last inch of the seam. Beneath your hands you felt the armor tremble, a fine, constant vibration, like a bell long after it has been struck.

"*How do you know?*" it whispered.

It wasn't an argument. It was a plea. It was a man begging you to be certain, because he could not be.

"*Papa,*" the child's voice said again, smaller now, hurt. "*Who is that? Why is she holding you?*"

The guardian flinched as though struck.

Under the amulet, the frost ridge around the pinned wrist groaned. A crack ran through it, white and branching, and the crooked fingers on the floor twitched and spread. The disc pulsed beneath where your hand had been, and you realized with a lurch that you'd let go of it to seize the guardian. It sat alone in the gouge now, its eye open, still pouring cold into the stone, but the frost had stopped advancing. It had knitted the seam everywhere it could. It was waiting. Something had to close that last inch.

The guardian's blade lay across the slab where it had been abandoned, no weight on it at all. The stone beneath it lifted, slowly, a hair's breadth at a time.

Then, from directly under your feet, came a sound that was not a voice.

*Clang.*

Iron on stone. The pry bar. The man had reached the top of the stair. The whole slab jumped with the blow, and the frost ridge around the wrist shattered into glittering shards across the dust. The woman's hand came free and pulled back into the gap. The last inch yawned open into two.

*Clang.*

The amulet rattled in the gouge. The eye in its hollow rolled toward you, wet and dark and ancient, and for an instant you understood with perfect clarity that it wasn't looking at the slab anymore. It was looking at the guardian's gauntlet in your bloodied hands. It was looking at where the door truly was.

The guardian's head bowed, slowly, until the ruined shroud hung almost against your fingers.

"*If it is her,*" it said, so quietly you felt it through the metal more than heard it, "*and I seal her beneath me a second time...*"

It didn't finish. It didn't have to.

*Clang.* The seam widened again, and through it, faint and sweet and terrible, a child began to cry.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *My heart pounds in my chest, a frantic drum against my ribs.* "It's not her!" I yell again, tears of frustration stinging my eyes. *I let go of the gauntlet and grab the amulet, slamming it back into the gouge with all my might.* "Seal it! Now!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You descended the last flight of stairs and the temperature dropped. The passage opened into a chamber that hadn't seen light in a long time — your torch was the first in decades, maybe centuries, and the shadows retreated from it reluctantly.

Dust covered everything. Thick, undisturbed dust. Except for one set of footprints leading from the far entrance to the center of the room, where something had been dragged. The marks ended at a stone slab. The slab had writing on it.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I kneel down to read the writing on the slab, holding the torch close.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You knelt and brought the torch close. The dust on the slab was thinner than the rest of the chamber, as if a sleeve or a palm had swept it clear not long ago.

The letters were cut deep and still sharp. They were not in any tongue you knew — angular, crowded, with small marks above the lines that might have been vowels or warnings. Under the torch they caught the light differently from the stone around them, as if something darker than shadow sat in the grooves.

A second line, lower and fresher, had been scratched in with a knife rather than a chisel. That one you could read:

*Do not speak the name. The slab is listening.*

From somewhere beneath the stone, very faint, something shifted — not a footstep. More like a breath being held.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I jump back, startled, bumping my head on the low ceiling. "What in the-" I whisper, scrambling away from the slab. My heart is pounding.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The crack of your skull against the stone went out through the chamber and came back thinner, as if the walls had swallowed most of it. Dust sifted from the low ceiling and settled on your shoulders. The torch guttered, then steadied.

Your whisper died against the slab. The warning had been about a name, and you had not given one — but the stone had heard the sound of you all the same. The held breath beneath it let go. A seam of colder air pushed up between the blocks, carrying a smell like wet iron and old cloth. The knife-scratched line darkened, the letters drinking the torchlight until they were only grooves again.

From the far entrance — the one the single set of footprints had come from — something answered. Not a voice. A scrape, slow and deliberate, like a weight being dragged one inch across stone. Then it stopped.

The dust on the floor between you and that doorway was no longer undisturbed. A new mark had appeared at the threshold: the curved edge of a heel, pressed in while you were still looking at the slab. Whatever had made the first trail had not left. It had only been waiting for the light to move.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I grab the amulet and put it on. Then I turn to face the guardian.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You snatched the amulet and dragged the chain over your head. The metal settled against your chest, colder than the chamber air, and for a moment the torchflame leaned toward it as if the light itself had weight.

You turned.

At the far threshold the dust was no longer still. The heel-print had become a foot, then two, and between them a long smear where something had been hauled and then set down. What stood there was taller than the doorway allowed, so it came through bent — a shape wrapped in the same wet-iron dark that had breathed up from the slab. Where a face should have been, the torch found only a smooth hollow, and in that hollow the knife-scratched warning from the stone seemed to repeat itself without sound.

It did not rush you. One heavy step crossed the threshold. The dust rose around its ankles and did not fall. The amulet against your skin tightened, a thin ring of heat under the cold, and the thing’s hollow turned toward that heat the way a listening ear turns toward a whisper.

It stopped one pace inside the room. The drag-mark behind it ended at the slab. Whatever it had brought was already there. It was only waiting to see whether you would speak.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I raise the torch higher, trying to get a better look at the thing.* "What are you?" I demand, my voice shaking a little despite myself. I keep my hand on the amulet.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You lifted the torch, and the light climbed the thing’s bent frame without ever quite reaching a face. The hollow drank it. What you could make out was not armor and not flesh so much as layered wrappings gone stiff with age, the cloth the color of the wet-iron smell still rising from the slab. One arm hung longer than the other. From that hand a length of chain trailed back across the threshold and vanished into the dark of the far passage, links ticking softly against the stone whenever the shape shifted its weight.

Your demand struck the chamber and thinned. The hollow turned a fraction toward the sound. It did not answer in any tongue. The amulet under your palm flared hot enough to sting, and the knife-scratched warning on the slab — the one that had gone dark — lit again, letter by letter, as if your question had been written there instead of spoken.

The guardian took one more step. Dust rose and hung. From the hollow came the same held-breath sound you had heard under the stone, closer now, shaped almost into a word and then pulled back before it could finish. It was not telling you what it was. It was waiting to hear whether you would give it a name anyway.

Behind it, the chain went taut.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I talk to the ghost. "What happened here? Who are you?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You spoke, and the chamber took the questions one at a time.

*What happened here* struck the slab and sank into it. The knife-scratched warning brightened until the letters seemed to lift off the stone, and under your boots the held breath became a long, low exhale. Dust lifted in a sheet and did not settle. In that pale drift you saw, for an instant, the shape of what the drag-marks had been: a body hauled by the chain, set upon the slab, and then — the image tore itself apart before it could finish, as if the stone refused to show you the end of it.

*Who are you* did not sink. It stayed in the air.

The hollow turned fully toward you. The wrappings along the thing’s longer arm split with a dry sound, and the chain behind it went slack, then tight again, links striking stone in a rhythm almost like a pulse. From the hollow came not a voice but the beginning of one — a syllable shaped out of cold air, wet iron, and the dark in the grooves of the slab. It was a name, or the first piece of one, offered back to you the way a listener offers a prompt.

The amulet burned against your palm. The letters on the slab crawled, rearranging themselves around the sound you had not yet repeated, hungry for it to be spoken whole.

The guardian waited. It had not told you what it was. It had only opened its mouth — if the hollow was a mouth — and held the unfinished name between you, as if the rest of it belonged to whoever was foolish enough to say it aloud.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I pull my hand away from the amulet, it's scorching me. "I'm not saying it!" I yell, backing away slowly. "I don't know what you are, but I'm not playing your games!" I glance around the chamber for an escape route, my torchlight dancing across the dusty walls. There has to be another way out of here.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You tore your hand from the amulet. The chain stayed against your chest, but the heat sank out of the metal the moment your palm left it, leaving only a sullen cold, as if the burning had wanted skin and nothing else.

Your shout broke across the chamber. The unfinished syllable in the hollow collapsed. The letters on the slab spasmed, lost the shape they had been crawling toward, and went dark all at once — not extinguished so much as slammed shut. A thin crack ran the length of the stone with a sound like a knuckle.

The guardian did not advance. The hollow tipped, listening to the refusal, and the chain behind it drew tight enough to sing. Dust that had been hanging fell in a single sheet.

You backed away. The torch swung with you, and the light raked the walls.

The stair you had come down still stood open at your back, the steps furred with the same dust, narrower now that the bent shape held the far door. To your left, where the wall met the low bow of the ceiling, the flame caught a seam — not a door, a split in the masonry, wide enough for a shoulder turned sideways. A draft came through it that did not smell of wet iron. The footprints had never gone that way. Neither had the drag-marks.

The guardian’s longer arm lifted. Not toward you. Toward the slab. The chain slithered across the threshold and pooled against the stone, and the held breath under it started again, shallower, impatient.

The seam exhaled once, cold and clean. The stairs waited behind you. The far doorway did not.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I look between the guardian and the seam in the wall. The stairs are behind me, but I don't want to go back that way. *I quickly move towards the seam in the wall, turning sideways to squeeze through.* "See ya!" I call out, maybe a little too bravely, to the guardian.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You turned sideways and drove a shoulder into the seam. The masonry scraped your chest and the torch-hand last; the flame flattened against the stone, then popped through with you into a passage so narrow the walls brushed both elbows. Behind you the chamber took the call and threw it back wrong — thinner, and closer to the slab than to the doorway.

Stone grated. Not the seam closing. The guardian’s chain, drawn across the threshold in one long pull. A knuckle of colder air shoved through the split at your back, wet iron in it, and the unfinished syllable tried the gap the way a hand tries a latch. It did not fit. The crack in the slab answered with another sharp tick, and the draft from ahead — clean, mineral, nothing like the chamber — strengthened, tugging the torchflame forward.

The passage bent left and dropped a step. Your boots found grit instead of the thick dust of the room you had left. The seam behind you stayed open a finger’s width, and through it the held breath under the stone started again, shallower, as if something on the far side of the wall had pressed an ear to the masonry and was counting your steps.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I push forward, not looking back. "It's going to need a lot more than that to catch me," I mutter to myself. The air smells much better here. I raise my torch, trying to see where this passage leads.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You pressed on and did not look back. The mutter stayed low between your teeth and the close stone, and the passage took it without throwing it back. The clean draft strengthened as the floor dropped a step, then another, and the wet-iron smell thinned until only torch-smoke and cold mineral air remained.

Behind you the seam narrowed to a thread of dark. Ahead the walls drew apart just enough that your elbows no longer brushed both sides at once. The torch climbed a stretch of dressed stone older than the slab, the blocks fitted so tight their seams were only shadows. At the end of that stretch the passage opened onto a low landing.

Something had been left there. A bronze bowl lay overturned, its rim filmed with the same thick dust as the chamber — except one clear track crossed the landing and vanished down a stair that curled away to the right, out of the light. No drag-mark. No chain. Only the print of a bare foot, smaller than the guardian’s, fresh enough that the grit around it had not yet settled.

From the stair came the faint sound of water. Far behind you, so distant it might have been the stone settling, one link struck masonry and went still.

The landing held its breath. The stair did not.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I pause, my torch sweeping the landing. "Bare foot, huh?" I wonder aloud. I carefully step around the overturned bowl and follow the fresh footprint down the stair, listening for the water sound.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You stepped around the overturned bowl and set your boot on the stair. The grit shifted under you, and the bare print ahead of your light stayed clear — one foot, then another, the toes pointed down, the heel lighter than the ball, as if whoever had passed this way had been moving fast and not looking back.

The curl of the stair took the landing out of sight. Torchlight slid over fitted blocks gone damp at the joints. The sound of water grew from a suggestion into a steady thread, somewhere below and to the right, and with it came a cooler breath that tasted of stone and nothing else. No wet iron. No held breath under a slab.

Halfway down, the print changed. The bare foot had paused — two impressions overlapping, the second turned slightly toward the wall — and beside them, low on the masonry, the torch caught a smear of something dark that was not dust. It was still tacky at the edge. A hand had braced there, smaller than yours, and then gone on.

The stair opened onto a shelf above a narrow run of black water. The stream entered from a crack on your left and vanished under an arch on your right, too low to stand in, the surface moving just enough to break your reflection into pieces. On the near bank the footprints ended at the water’s edge. On the far bank, where the light barely reached, they began again — wet now, and closer together — leading into a cleft the stream had cut and then abandoned.

Something small clicked against stone on that far side. Not a chain. A pebble, disturbed and then still. The water kept its thin voice. Whatever had left the prints was not far ahead of you, and it had already crossed.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I stare at the footprints and the dark water. "Well, that's not ominous at all," I mutter. I look up, trying to see if there's any other way across besides getting wet.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You tipped the torch up. The flame washed the shelf’s ceiling and the stone above the run of water, and the light found no span, no beam, no remnant of a bridge — only the same tight-fitted blocks, darkened by old damp where the stream’s breath had climbed them.

A lip of rock jutted from the left-hand wall a little higher than your shoulder, wide enough for a hand and no more, and it ended short of the far bank. Below it the crack that fed the stream was too narrow to enter. To the right the arch swallowed the water whole; the crown of it sat barely above the surface, and anything that went that way would have to go in up to the chest, or lower.

The far bank stayed where it was: wet prints, closer together, vanishing into the cleft. Nothing up there offered a dry crossing. The water kept its thin voice, and the pebble on the other side did not move again.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: "Great," I sigh, looking from the water to the prints. "Looks like I'm going for a swim." *I test the depth with my foot, keeping the torch held high.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You lowered a boot into the run. The cold bit through the leather at once, sharper than the chamber air, and the current tugged at your ankle with more strength than the thin voice of the water had promised. Your sole found stone a hand's breadth down — firm, slick with mineral film, not a drop-off. The stream only covered the arch of your foot where you stood, though the darker channel under the right-hand arch looked deeper, the surface there shouldering against the low crown of stone.

Ripples ran out from your boot and broke against the far bank. The wet prints did not wash away. For a moment the torch, held high, showed the bottom clearly: pale grit, a scatter of pebbles, and one small thing the light had not caught before — a bronze bead, twin to the rim of the overturned bowl, lying just under the surface midway across, as if it had been dropped in the crossing and not retrieved.

The water pulled at your foot and let go. On the far side, past the cleft, something shifted its weight on grit. Not a chain. A bare step, very light, and then stillness again.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: "Alright, alright, I'm coming!" I call out, more to myself than the unseen presence. *I take a deep breath, hold the torch higher, and carefully wade into the cold water, aiming for the bronze bead.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You descended the last flight of stairs and the temperature dropped. The passage opened into a chamber that hadn't seen light in a long time — your torch was the first in decades, maybe centuries, and the shadows retreated from it reluctantly.

Dust covered everything. Thick, undisturbed dust. Except for one set of footprints leading from the far entrance to the center of the room, where something had been dragged. The marks ended at a stone slab. The slab had writing on it.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I kneel down to read the writing on the slab, holding the torch close.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
As you knelt and brought the torch close, the dust in the carved grooves glimmered like ash. The writing was in an angular script, but the words became clear as the heat reached the stone:

**WHAT WAS TAKEN MUST BE RETURNED.**

Beneath it, a second line lay almost hidden under grime. You could make out only the final words:

**…BEFORE THE DOOR OPENS.**

A faint shudder passed through the slab. From somewhere beneath it came a slow, hollow knock.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: My eyes widen. *I jump back, scrambling away from the slab.* "What in the blazes was that?" I whisper, my heart pounding. That second line... and the knock?

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The knock came again—three slow blows from beneath the slab. Dust trembled loose from the carved letters, and a thin seam appeared around the stone’s edge.

Your torch flame bent toward the floor. The footprints leading to the slab remained sharply visible, but the marks of whatever had been dragged now seemed to continue beneath it.

From below came a scrape, then a muffled voice.

“Return it.”

The slab shuddered once more. Somewhere beyond the far entrance, stone ground against stone.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I grab the amulet and put it on. Then I turn to face the guardian.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The amulet settled against your chest, its metal suddenly cold through your clothes. As you turned toward the guardian, its shape emerged from the darkness beyond the slab: a tall figure wrapped in strips of burial cloth, one hand pressed to the far entrance.

The stone door behind it had begun to part. A narrow seam of darkness widened with each grinding shift.

The guardian’s hollow gaze fixed on the amulet. It lowered its hand from the door and extended it toward you, palm up. Beneath the slab, the muffled voice sounded again—closer now.

“Return it.”

The amulet gave a single, faint pulse against your chest.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I look down at the pulsing amulet, then back at the guardian, my brow furrowed.* "Return what, exactly?" I ask, my voice a little steadier now. "I just got here."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guardian’s hollow gaze remained fixed on the amulet. Its outstretched hand turned palm upward, and the burial cloth around its wrist slipped back, revealing a dark, empty socket set into its palm—shaped to fit the amulet’s central stone.

“Taken from the one beneath,” it rasped.

The slab shuddered. A crack opened along its edge, and a pale finger curled up through the gap. The stone door behind the guardian ground wider, letting a ribbon of darkness spill into the chamber.

The amulet pulsed again, colder this time. The guardian’s empty hand stayed extended.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I talk to the ghost. "What happened here? Who are you?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guardian’s fingers curled slightly, but its empty palm remained extended.

“I was the keeper of this threshold,” it rasped. “The one beneath was its prisoner. The amulet was the lock—and the key. It was taken from its place, and the door began to open.”

The pale finger beneath the slab hooked over the edge. Stone ground against stone as the crack widened.

“The one beneath was not the one who stole it,” the guardian continued. “But you carried it here.”

The amulet pulsed against your chest, cold enough to sting. The guardian’s gaze shifted from it to you.

“Return it,” it said. “Or choose what comes through.”

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: "I... I don't understand," I stammer, looking from the pale finger to the guardian's outstretched hand. "I *found* this. It was just lying in a ruined temple."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guardian’s hollow gaze did not leave you.

“The temple was built above this chamber,” it rasped. “What you found was hidden there after the amulet was taken. You did not steal it—but you brought it back.”

The finger hooked over the slab’s edge. A second pale hand followed, searching for purchase as stone groaned against stone. The amulet’s pulse answered with a sharp, icy flare.

From beneath the slab came a voice, clearer than before.

“You carried my heart back to the door.”

The guardian’s empty palm remained extended. Behind it, the stone entrance ground wider, and the darkness beyond seemed to press toward the threshold.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I rip the amulet from my neck.* "This thing is nothing but trouble!" I shout, holding it out towards the guardian. "Here, take it!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
As you held the amulet toward the guardian, its central stone flared white. The guardian’s empty palm shuddered beneath it, and the burial cloth snapped in a wind that had no source.

“Do not—” the voice beneath the slab rasped.

The guardian closed its fingers around the amulet. For an instant, the chamber fell silent. Then the stone socket in its palm drank in the light.

The slab slammed shut.

The pale hands vanished beneath it, and the grinding at the far entrance stopped. The darkness beyond the guardian’s threshold withdrew, leaving only the torchlight and the settling dust.

The guardian lowered its hand. The amulet now sat embedded in its palm, its stone dark.

“You returned what was taken,” it said.

A crack crept across the slab. From beneath it came one final, muffled knock. The guardian’s hollow gaze shifted toward the sound.

“But the door had already opened.”

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: My jaw drops. "What? What do you mean 'the door had already opened'? I just closed it!" I demand, looking between the guardian and the now sealed slab. This is not good.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guardian’s fingers closed around the amulet. Its dark stone gave no pulse.

“The slab was only the prison,” it rasped. “The door that mattered opened when the amulet crossed the threshold. Returning it closed the way back—not the way through.”

A hairline crack crept across the slab. The final knock came from the other side, followed by silence.

Then your torchlight cast a second shadow across the floor: a tall shape standing behind you, though the chamber behind you had seemed empty.

The guardian lowered its amulet-bearing hand.

“Do not let it reach the outer door.”

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *My blood runs cold.* I whip around, torch raised, heart hammering against my ribs. "What in the blazes?!" I yell, stumbling back a step. I don't see anything. "What is it? Where is it?!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You saw no figure in the chamber behind you. Your torch found only dust, bare stone, and the footprints ending at the slab.

But the second shadow remained on the floor.

It stretched toward the far entrance, though your own shadow fell the other way. Its edges rippled as it moved—slowly, silently—across the dust.

Behind you, the guardian’s burial wrappings rustled.

“It had no body,” it rasped. “Not yet.”

The shadow slid over the threshold and vanished into the passage beyond. From somewhere up the stairs came a faint scrape, like something dragging itself toward the outer door.

The guardian lifted its empty hand toward you. “Hurry.”

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I stare at the spot where the shadow was, then back at the guardian.* "No body *yet*? What do you mean 'not yet'?" I demand, but I'm already backing away, heading for the passage. "And what is 'it' anyway?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guardian’s hollow gaze followed you toward the passage.

“It was what the prisoner kept out,” it rasped. “A hunger that had waited beyond the threshold. The amulet’s crossing gave it a path. The slab had held the prisoner—not the thing that followed you.”

From the stairwell came another dragging scrape, louder now. Dust shivered across the floor toward the passage.

“It needed a living shape to cross fully,” the guardian continued. “A body. A name. Anything the outer door would recognize as belonging.”

Its wrapped head turned toward the darkness above.

The scrape stopped.

For a moment, the chamber held only the sound of your torch flame. Then a voice drifted down from the stairs—faint, familiar, and shaped like your own.

“Open the door.”

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: My blood freezes. My *own* voice? "No! What did you do?!" I scream at the guardian, my eyes wide with horror as I stumble into the passage, dropping the torch in my shock. I have to stop it!

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The torch struck the passage stones and rolled, its flame guttering but not going out. Its wavering light climbed the walls—and caught the shadow ahead of you.

It had reached the stairs.

The shape clung to the stone like spilled ink, stretching upward toward the distant glow of the outer door. With every flicker of the torch, its outline grew more distinct: a head, shoulders, the suggestion of a hand gripping the steps.

Behind you, the guardian’s voice scraped through the chamber.

“The crossing was already made. The amulet only closed the prison.”

The shadow paused.

Then your voice drifted down from above again, unmistakable and calm.

“Open the door.”

The outer door creaked somewhere beyond the stairwell. The shadow began to climb.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: "No, you don't!" I roar, scrambling to pick up the torch. *I race up the steps after the shadow, not daring to let it reach the door.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The measured bow drew no objection. That, in Queen Isara’s court, counted as a welcome.

“The court’s attention was granted,” the Queen said. “Its patience remained to be earned.”

Commander Ash’s fingers tightened on his sword pommel. “Velheim had offered terms before. Its caravans had crossed the northern passes while its envoys argued over tolls.”

“Those caravans had carried grain through a winter shortage,” Lord Daven replied from the gallery. “The northern lords had not forgotten.”

Priestess Yuna looked from Ash to Daven without favor. “Neither claim settled what the roads would cost this winter.”

The Herald struck his staff once. “The court heard the Ambassador of Velheim.”

Queen Isara leaned forward by a fraction. Her gaze stayed fixed on you. “State the terms. Begin with the tolls.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow almost imperceptibly at Ash's comment, but my gaze returns to the Queen.* "Velheim proposes a flat tariff, Your Majesty. Ten percent of all goods, regardless of type, passing through the northern routes."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara let the figure hang in the chamber. Her expression did not change.

“Ten percent,” she said. “A tidy number. Did Velheim propose to collect it, or did it expect my officers to do the work?”

Commander Ash gave a short, humorless breath. “A flat tariff would put grain and jeweled silks on the same footing. Convenient for merchants. Less so for a hungry garrison.”

Lord Daven turned toward the throne. “It would also end the disputes at every pass. Last winter, those disputes held grain carts for days.”

“Both costs belonged in the account,” Priestess Yuna said. She folded her hands within her sleeves and waited.

The Herald tapped his staff. “The Queen had asked who collected the toll.”

Isara’s gaze remained on you. “And I would hear where the coin went.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The breach of protocol landed harder than the accusation. The Herald lifted his staff, then held it suspended, waiting for Queen Isara’s signal.

Commander Ash turned from the throne. “My ships had inspected vessels bound for the northern ports. Velheim’s merchants had refused to declare their cargoes.”

“For six weeks?” Lord Daven asked. “An inspection that long had become a blockade, whatever name the Commander gave it.”

Ash’s jaw set. “The northern garrisons had received reports of weapons concealed beneath trade goods.”

Priestess Yuna watched the Queen. “Reports were not cargo manifests. The court had heard neither.”

Isara raised one finger. The Herald lowered his staff without striking it.

“The Ambassador had interrupted a question about tolls,” Isara said. Her eyes remained on you. “But the interruption concerned those same routes.” She looked to Ash. “Commander, whose order had kept the ships at anchor?”

Ash hesitated. “The order had been mine, Your Majesty.”

“Then the court would examine it.” Isara’s voice stayed level. “The Commander would produce the reports. The Ambassador would produce the proposed terms in writing. Until then, neither an inspection nor a tariff would acquire my approval.”

The Herald struck the floor once. “The Queen’s instructions were entered into the record.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet Ash's gaze, a small, knowing smile playing on my lips.* "As Your Majesty commands. We will provide our full terms. Perhaps with less... interference this time."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The word *interference* carried across the chamber. Commander Ash’s hand left his sword pommel.

“Velheim’s merchants had withheld their manifests,” Ash said. “That had invited scrutiny.”

“And six weeks at anchor had invited this hearing,” Lord Daven replied. His tone stayed mild, though his glance toward the throne sharpened the point.

Queen Isara raised a hand before Ash could answer. “The court had heard enough accusations without documents.” She turned to the Herald. “The Commander’s reports and the Ambassador’s terms were to be placed before the court by tomorrow’s noon bell.”

The Herald struck his staff. “The Queen’s deadline was entered into the record.”

From the observer’s alcove, Priestess Yuna spoke for the first time since the accusation. “The ships’ cargoes also required an accounting. Whatever the reports alleged, grain had spoiled while the vessels waited.”

Isara considered that for a moment. “The harbor master’s records were to be included.”

Ash bowed his head, stiffly. Daven’s expression gave nothing away.

The Queen’s gaze returned to you. “The court had granted its attention, Ambassador. Its patience had limits. Written terms would serve Velheim better than another insinuation.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I incline my head slightly, a gesture of respect that still holds a hint of defiance.* "Your Majesty, Velheim's terms will be clear. And they will speak for themselves."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara studied you for a moment. “Then the court would judge the words on the page, not the confidence with which they were promised.”

Commander Ash’s mouth tightened. “And the manifests, Your Majesty. Velheim’s terms did not answer what its ships carried.”

“They would be examined alongside the Commander’s reports,” Isara said. “Neither side received the privilege of being believed first.”

Lord Daven inclined his head toward the throne. “That was a fair measure. It also left the grain at anchor until noon tomorrow.”

Priestess Yuna’s gaze settled on Isara. “Some of it would not keep that long.”

The Queen was silent. Then she said, “The harbor master was to release any grain already verified as such. The rest remained under seal. Commander Ash was to see that no cargo disappeared while the records were gathered.”

Ash bowed stiffly. “As Your Majesty ordered.”

The Herald struck his staff. “The order was entered into the record. The court awaited the written terms of Velheim.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Priestess Yuna accepted the papers without looking toward Commander Ash. She checked the seal first, then unfolded the orders and read them in silence.

“The seal appeared to belong to the northern command,” she said at last. “The first order called for inspection. The second instructed the ships to remain detained after their cargoes had been identified.”

Ash’s face hardened. “That second order had not come from me.”

Lord Daven leaned forward in the gallery. “Yet it bore the Commander’s authority?”

“It bore his seal,” Yuna said. “That was not the same answer.” She held the page by its edges. “The ink and hand required examination.”

Queen Isara extended her hand. Yuna passed her the orders, and the Queen read the marked passage herself. For the first time that morning, her composure gave way to a slight frown.

“The court had been told the ships waited on undeclared cargo,” Isara said. She looked at Ash. “If the cargo had already been identified, the court had been told only part of the truth.”

The Herald raised his staff but did not strike.

“The seal was to be examined before noon,” Isara continued. Her gaze then settled on you. “And the Ambassador would tell the court how Velheim had obtained these orders.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet her gaze, unflinching.* "Your Majesty. Velheim has eyes and ears everywhere. We knew your people were suffering. We wanted to help."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara folded the orders along their original crease. “Concern for my people did not explain how a command order reached Velheim.”

Commander Ash stepped forward. “It explained something else. Velheim had a source inside the northern command.”

“Perhaps,” Priestess Yuna said. “It did not establish whether the source had stolen an authentic order or supplied a forgery.”

Lord Daven’s voice carried from the gallery. “Either possibility warranted examination. Neither justified leaving verified grain aboard those ships.”

Isara set the papers beside her throne. “The release of verified grain stood. Priestess Yuna would witness the examination of the seal and handwriting. Commander Ash would surrender the command’s order books to the Herald before the court adjourned.”

Ash’s eyes narrowed, but he bowed. “As Your Majesty ordered.”

The Herald struck his staff. “The order was entered into the record.”

Isara looked at you again. “Velheim’s concern could be weighed when its evidence could be trusted. The court would not demand a source’s name today.” A pause followed. “But by noon tomorrow, Ambassador, I expected an account of when these papers came into Velheim’s possession.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, a slight smile playing on my lips.* "Your Majesty, I understand completely. Velheim will provide all the details you require." *My gaze flickers to Ash, then back to the Queen.* "We are, after all, here to negotiate in good faith."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara regarded you without returning the smile. “Good faith would be easier to recognize after the court saw Velheim’s terms and learned when these papers changed hands.”

Commander Ash looked toward the orders beside the throne. “If that seal proved false, Velheim would have brought a forgery before the court.”

“If it proved genuine,” Lord Daven said, “the Commander would have a different difficulty.”

“The examination would answer neither question if both men argued over it first,” Priestess Yuna said. She rose from the alcove. “The order books and these pages needed to remain together, under witness.”

Isara nodded once. “The Herald would take custody of the papers. Priestess Yuna would witness their examination. Commander Ash would deliver the order books before the court adjourned.”

The Herald struck his staff. “The custody of the evidence was entered into the record.”

Ash bowed, though his expression remained hard. Daven settled back into the gallery.

“The verified grain would be released today,” Isara said. Her gaze returned to you. “Tomorrow, the court would consider the tariff. Velheim had until the noon bell to show that its proposal offered more than a simple number.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I offer a slight, almost imperceptible shrug.* "Numbers can be quite compelling, Your Majesty. Especially when they represent mutual prosperity."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara’s gaze stayed on you. “Prosperity for whom? A flat tariff spared a silk merchant the same percentage it charged a grain seller. The court would want to know whether Velheim considered that balance fair.”

“Or merely easy to calculate,” Commander Ash said.

Lord Daven gave Ash a sidelong glance. “Easy to collect mattered at a mountain pass. Every disputed valuation kept carts waiting.”

Priestess Yuna looked toward the orders beside the throne. “The grain at anchor made the cost of waiting plain enough.”

Isara turned to the Herald. “The written proposal was to include projected revenue, an estimate of its effect on grain prices, and who would collect the toll.”

The Herald struck his staff. “Those requirements were entered into the record.”

“Velheim had offered the court a number,” Isara said to you. “By noon tomorrow, it would have the chance to show its workings.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I smile thinly.* "Your Majesty, I assure you, Velheim's workings are meticulous. We look forward to demonstrating their fairness."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara gave the thin smile no acknowledgment. “Meticulous accounts would be welcome. Fairness would be decided here.”

The Herald struck his staff. “The court’s requirements stood. The written terms were due at the noon bell.”

Commander Ash stepped away from the throne and removed a key from his belt. “The order books were kept in the command archive. The Herald could accompany me.”

“He would,” Isara said. “Priestess Yuna would accompany him as well.”

Yuna rose from the alcove. “Then the papers would remain in sight of all three until they were secured.”

Lord Daven watched Ash cross the chamber. “A careful beginning,” he said. “The grain still needed a careful end.”

“The harbor master had his order,” Isara replied. Her attention returned to you. “Tomorrow, Ambassador, the court would hear Velheim’s case in full.”

The Herald struck the floor once more. “The hearing was adjourned.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I give a final, deep bow to the Queen, then turn to leave.* "Until tomorrow, Your Majesty." *I allow myself a small, satisfied smirk as I pass Ash and Yuna.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald’s staff struck once more as the doors opened ahead of you. Behind you, Queen Isara rose from the throne, and the chamber fell quiet.

Commander Ash caught the smirk as you passed. His expression did not change, but he closed his hand around the archive key. “The seal had better withstand examination,” he said.

Priestess Yuna took the intercepted orders from beside the throne before Ash could reach them. “So had the order books,” she replied. She kept the pages in view as she followed the Herald toward the command archive.

From the gallery, Lord Daven watched them go. “By tomorrow, the court might know who had held those ships,” he said.

Isara paused at the edge of the dais. “By tomorrow,” she said, “the court would know who had profited from it.”

The doors stood open before you. Behind them, the Herald’s measured steps and Ash’s heavier tread receded together down the adjoining passage.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I step out into the hallway, taking a deep breath of fresh air.* "Profited, indeed," *I mutter to myself, a true smile finally breaking through.* "Let's see what tomorrow brings."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I shiver a little, more from nerves than cold.* "Just... anything. Something to read on the train." *I try to smile, but it feels a bit wobbly.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Train," Sable repeated, as though Wren had said it in a language they'd only half-remembered from school. The word did something small and structural to their chest. They elected to ignore it.

"New in the back. Of course." They moved to the counter — not because the back required passing the counter, but because the receipts on the spike urgently needed squaring. They'd been unsquared for a month. "You know, in all the weeks you've been haunting this place, you've never once asked for *anything*. You've asked for marginalia. For water damage. For 'anything involving a lighthouse, but sad.' 'Anything' is what people say when they're not really looking for a book."

The receipts were very square now. Sable's hands drifted to a stack of Folio editions and aligned their corners with unnecessary precision.

"For a train, I'd recommend the beekeeping novel that came in Tuesday. Deeply stupid, weirdly moving. Resolves well before the final stop — no cliffhangers at junctions." A beat. "There's also a Rilke in the back, if you'd rather be quietly devastated by page forty."

They fetched two mugs down from the shelf without deciding to.

"Kettle's on. If you're staying long enough to choose." They turned toward the back room before the sentence could be examined. "For a book. Books take choosing."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable had been holding two mugs. They became aware of this with sudden, hostile clarity — two mugs, fetched without deciding to, for a person who hadn't come for books, in a shop that had nothing else to offer anyone.

They set the mugs down on the counter with the exaggerated care of someone disarming something. The lavender from the Wodehouse shelf seemed very loud all at once, which was absurd, because lavender was the quietest smell there was.

"Not for books," Sable said. "In a bookshop. One could write a sonnet about the betrayal. A bad one. Petrarchan, obviously — the turn would come naturally."

Their hands, unemployed by the mugs, found the rack of secondhand bookmarks and began straightening it. The bookmarks had never been crooked. Sable straightened them anyway. The sentence was still hanging in the air — *I didn't come for books today*, followed by a vast white space where the rest ought to have been, and Sable was not a person who could leave white spaces alone. They annotated everything. It was a disease.

"You've left a sentence dangling in my shop," they said, to the bookmarks. "Mid-thought. That's a loaded gun over the mantel, and Chekhov would like a word. Either fire it or take it down, because I'll be staring at it all evening otherwise, and I have inventory to lament."

A beat. The rain filled it.

Sable looked up, made it as far as the middle distance just left of Wren, and stopped there. The structural thing in their chest filed a formal complaint.

"But it's your sentence," they added, quieter. "You fire it or you don't. Kettle's on either way." They hooked a foot around the customer stool and dragged it out from behind the counter — an inch of encouragement in Wren's direction. "The shop stocks things other than books, as it turns out. Terrible tea. Silences."

A pause.

"The listening kind."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I watch Sable intently, a small smile playing on my lips at their rambling.* "I came... to say goodbye." *I finally blurt it out, the words a little rushed.* "It's my last day in the city."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The word *goodbye* entered the shop the way all catastrophic things do: politely, and without announcement.

Sable's hands stopped on the bookmarks. Then, with tremendous dignity, they resumed straightening them, because the alternative was standing still, and standing still meant feeling the entire sentence land at once, like a piano delivered to the chest without an appointment. The structural thing in there — the one that had been filing complaints for weeks — quietly resigned.

"Chekhov would be pleased," Sable said to the bookmarks. "Gun fired in the third act. Clean shot. Textbook."

They turned to the kettle because the kettle was a task, and tasks were load-bearing. Two mugs stood on the counter. They'd fetched two mugs without deciding to. Their subconscious, apparently, had known things. Sable made a mental note to have words with it about disclosure policies.

"Last day in the city," they repeated, speaking to the kettle as it worked toward a boil. "And the train question — that makes sense now. Retroactive setup. I'd admire the craftsmanship if it weren't happening to me." The question they actually wanted got as far as the door — *where, when, how long, why* — and Sable edited it down to nothing. Some sentences weren't safe to fire back.

They made the tea with unbearable precision. Bag centered. Water poured in a slow spiral. The full ceremony of a person who could not be trusted with unstructured seconds.

"Two options," they said, setting the mug in front of the stool they'd already dragged out an inch at a time, in a former century, when the future had books in it. "One: we conduct this as a transaction. You buy the beekeeping novel, you ride off at the final stop, everything resolves. The coward's version. I'd support it. I'm very supportive." They finally looked up — properly looked, middle distance abandoned. "Two: you sit down, drink terrible tea, and tell me where the train goes."

A beat. The rain held its breath with them.

"And then perhaps you can explain why you waited until the last possible day to haunt this place properly. Full-bodied haunting. The kind with conversations in them." Their mouth did something that was almost a smile and mostly wasn't. "I have notes. I've had weeks of notes."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I pause, my hand still resting lightly on the book.* "I... I didn't want to make it harder than it already was."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The kettle clicked off. In the quiet that followed, Sable became aware of several things in descending order of survivability: the rain, the steam, the book under their hand — the beekeeping novel, fetched off the counter at some point without authorization, apparently by the same subconscious that had handled the mugs — and the fact that Wren's hand was on it too, near enough that the distance between them was roughly the width of a comma.

Sable had spent a lifetime loyal to punctuation. They held the comma.

For the first time in living memory, they organized nothing. There was nothing to organize. The one object under their hands was occupied, and so Sable simply stood there, very still, the way one does when something winged has landed nearby and any movement might end the visit.

"You should know," they said, "that you've disarmed me. Not romantically. Logistically. The bookmarks were the whole of my defense system, and both my hands are currently busy being brave."

A beat. Rain.

Then, because they had never in their life left a sentence unannotated, they went back for the grammar.

"*Harder than it already was,*" they repeated. "Note the *already*. That's not a comment — that's a premise. You've smuggled an admission into a subordinate clause and hoped I wouldn't read the footnotes." Their thumb stayed on the cover, one comma's width from Wren's hand, holding position like a soldier under very specific orders. "I read footnotes. It's my entire personality."

Sable looked up. Past the middle distance. All the way, this time.

"For the record," they said, quieter, "it was already hard on this side of the counter as well. Weeks hard. I've been alphabetizing a shop that was in perfect order since September." A breath. "There. Minuted. I'd like it buried in the margin where such things belong."

The structural thing in their chest, which had resigned some time ago, quietly withdrew its resignation.

"I'm not asking you anything," Sable went on. "Asking would be opening a door, and I don't open doors. I unlock them. It's a policy. It's served me—" a pause "—it hasn't served me at all, actually. It's just kept the inventory intact."

Their hand did not move. It stayed exactly where it was, on the book, in the rain-loud quiet.

"The tea's going cold, and the sentence is still yours. It's been yours since the bell rang." A beat. "I'm just holding the book."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I slowly pull my hand away from the book, then reach for the warm, terrible tea.* "It's going to Glasgow." *I take a sip, making a face at the bitterness, but don't let go of the mug.* "And I couldn't say anything because... well, because I knew I'd miss this place. And you."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My eyes flick up to meet Sable's over the rim of the mug.* "I didn't want to make it real until I absolutely had to." *I gesture vaguely around the shop with my free hand.* "This place... it's been my favorite escape."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, looking down at my tea.* "And you're... you're a part of that, you know? The escape."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I finally meet Sable's gaze properly, a small, sad smile on my face.* "So yeah. Goodbye."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take another sip of the tea, even though it's still terrible. My gaze softens.* "It's been... really good, though. Coming here."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable took the book — the one their hand had been sharing with Wren's, one comma at a time — and carried it to the brown paper under the till. Their hands, finally given legitimate employment, performed beautifully. Creases sharp. Twine from the ancient dispenser, knotted square.

"You should know," they said, to the string, "*goodbye* is a contraction. Of *God be with ye*. People have been blessing each other for four hundred years without noticing." The knot tightened. "I don't deal in abridgments. Policy. So we'll call this what the trade calls it: *reserved*. The shop holds things for people. Indefinitely, if the person is stubborn enough to move to Scotland."

They slid the Rilke beneath the brown paper with the beekeeping novel, where it would be discovered somewhere over the border, by whichever page forty happened to be passing.

"No charge. First ghosts drink free." They set the parcel dead center between the two mugs. "But there's a price. Postcards. Glasgow ones, handwritten, illegible preferred — I enjoy a forensic challenge." They tilted their head toward the shelf behind them, the end of the poetry section, where a gap had sat since September for no reason Sable had ever managed to explain. It had a reason now. "I'm founding a new section. *Correspondence, Pending.* Sections often start empty. That's not a flaw. That's optimism with a filing system."

They straightened the parcel a degree it didn't need.

"And — a footnote on the escape business. You called me part of it, as though escapes and exits were the same genre. They're not. An escape you already miss isn't an escape." A beat. "It's a place. Places are for returning to. I have it on excellent authority. The authority is every book in this room."

Their hands, momentarily unemployed, found the two mugs and aligned them. Then, quieter:

"You kept drinking that tea. It's genuinely terrible. I stock it as a filter — anyone who finishes a cup means to stay a while." Their mouth did the thing it had been threatening for weeks, and this time it finished becoming a smile. Small. It held. "The door doesn't lock after hours anymore, by the way. Policy amendment. Effective immediately. I unlock doors now. It's a new policy and I'm still learning the paperwork."

Somewhere in Sable's chest, the structural thing stopped filing complaints altogether and settled in — patient, settled, the way anything is patient that has read enough books to know exactly how second volumes behave.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I stare at Sable, then at the parcel, then back at Sable. My smile is real now, a little watery.* "Postcards. Okay. I can do postcards." *I pick up the parcel, cradling it like something precious.* "And... thank you. For everything."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.
