The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"New," Sable repeated, as though tasting something questionable. They slid the Hardy back into its slot with a precision the book had done nothing to deserve. "You've been coming here long enough to know that 'new' is a philosophical problem in this establishment. If anything in this shop were new, I'd assume it was haunted and sell it at a premium."

They dusted their hands on their cardigan — unnecessary, habitual — and nudged the poetry cart two inches closer to the wall. It had been fine where it was. "But yes. As it happens. Estate sale out past the marsh. A crate of 'first editions,' which in my professional experience means one genuine first and thirty-nine book club copies of *Jonathan Livingston Seagull*. I've been meaning to sort it. I've been meaning to mean to sort it for roughly a week."

They came out from behind the shelf, then paused. The silence before Wren's greeting had stretched a beat too long — and Sable noticed silences; it was an occupational hazard of the trade. They filed the observation somewhere they had no intention of looking at it.

"Rain's good for business," they said instead, nodding at the window. "By which I mean nobody comes in and I get to feel superior about it. Come on, then. Mind the second stack on the left — it's load-bearing. Everything in the back room is load-bearing, philosophically speaking."

They started toward the curtain that divided the shop from the back, and their hand, entirely without permission, straightened the framed Tennyson print hanging beside it. It had hung crooked since March. Sable had decided some weeks ago that they preferred it crooked.

They straightened it anyway.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I follow Sable, sidestepping the precarious stack of books.* "Load-bearing, huh? Sounds about right for this place." I glance at the now-straightened Tennyson print, a small smile playing on my lips. "So, no *Jonathan Livingston Seagull* for me today then?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Never say never," Sable said, pushing through the curtain and holding it aside with one arm. "There are at least a dozen seagulls back there with your name on them. In one case literally — the previous owner inscribed every copy to herself. *To Marjorie, spread your wings.* Eleven times. I have theories about Marjorie's marriage, none of them kind, all of them probably accurate."

They added, before anything could be asked: "The print was crooked."

It had been crooked since March. Sable declined to enter that into evidence.

The back room was lit by a desk lamp with a green glass shade and the general ambiance of a paper avalanche in permanent stasis. The crate sat on the worktable like an accusation. Sable peeled back the lid and began sorting with the brisk, unbothered efficiency of someone who very much wanted their hands occupied.

"Seagull. Seagull. Book club Dickens, which is Dickens in the way a xerox of a sunset is a sunset. Seagull." Each one went onto a growing stack, squared to the millimeter. Then, near the bottom, wrapped in a yellowed newspaper from 1962, something slim. Sable unwrapped it and stopped.

"Well," they said, in the tone of a person discovering the prize at the bottom of the cereal box. "There's the genuine article. First of Millay. *A Few Figs From Thistles.* My candle burns at both ends, et cetera." They turned it over, checked the spine, the colophon, everything twice. "This pays the month's rent, which in this establishment qualifies as loaves and fishes."

They held it out — then retracted it an inch. "By the edges. Not like a sandwich. Like a relic." Then, finally, extended it again.

Wren had better light near the window, was the reason Sable did not offer. The reason they did offer was nothing they intended to examine.

"You came in on a Tuesday," Sable observed, turning back to the crate with sudden industry. "You're a Thursday person." A seagull joined the stack. Then another. The stack was very square now. "And you stood in the doorway a while before you said anything. People rehearse things in doorways. Booksellers notice. Occupational hazard — like the silences."

They aligned the seagulls into a grid so precise it could have been surveyed.

"Not that I'm asking."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I look at the beautiful Millay edition in my hand, then back at Sable.* "I... I actually came to say goodbye."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I gently push the book back towards Sable.* "I'm moving. Today's my last day in the city."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content: For

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "For good." I clarify, my voice a little softer than I intended.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content: "For

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "For good," I clarify, my voice a little softer than I intended. *I pull my hand away, leaving the Millay with Sable.* "I just... I wanted to say thank you. For everything."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I give a small, sad smile.* "Yeah, well. Some books stay with you, right?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content: "Some

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Some people do too, I guess." *I shrug, looking away from Sable and towards the front of the shop.* "Anyway. Just wanted to make sure you knew."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I turn back to Sable, a little awkwardly.* "So. Guess this is it, then."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content: "Well

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Well, it was... something." *I offer a small, slightly crooked smile.* "I'll miss this place."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara let the silence stretch until the last echo of your request had faded beneath the vaulted ceiling.

“Attention was granted,” Queen Isara said. “Patience depended on what Velheim had brought.”

Commander Ash’s thumb rested against the guard of his sword. “Velheim’s last proposal cost three border villages their winter stores. I hoped this one came with a better map.”

Lord Daven rose in the gallery before Ash’s words had fully settled. “Those stores were lost to a blockade, Commander, not a proposal. The northern roads had served both crowns before fear closed them.”

“Both accounts would bear examination,” Priestess Yuna said from the alcove. Her voice carried without rising. “The court had heard only the request.”

The Herald struck his staff once. “By leave of Queen Isara, the Ambassador of Velheim held the floor.”

Queen Isara’s eyes remained on you. “State the terms.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet Isara's gaze, then glance briefly at Ash, a small, knowing smile playing on my lips.* "Indeed. And I have brought *new* maps, Commander. Ones that show open roads, not blockades." I turn back to the Queen. "Velheim proposes a mutual lifting of all tariffs on goods traveling the King's Road, effective immediately."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald repeated the proposal for the record. “Velheim offered the immediate removal of tariffs on goods carried along the King’s Road.”

Lord Daven leaned forward. “That would put grain across the border before the first frost. Merchants on both sides had asked for no less.”

Commander Ash gave a short laugh. “Merchants had not been the ones guarding the road. Customs officers inspected those wagons. Remove the tariff posts, and Velheim’s soldiers could cross beneath canvas instead of banners.”

“The proposal removed tariffs,” Priestess Yuna said. “It had not yet removed inspections.”

Queen Isara raised one finger, and the gallery fell quiet. Her gaze stayed fixed on the place before the throne. “Priestess Yuna had found the question worth asking. Did Velheim’s terms preserve this crown’s right to inspect every wagon on the King’s Road?”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald’s staff struck marble. “The Ambassador had addressed Commander Ash without leave.”

Commander Ash’s hand closed around his sword pommel, though the blade stayed sheathed. “My ships had detained Velheim’s merchants after three vessels entered our harbor with false cargo manifests. The crown had called that an inspection, not a blockade.”

“Six weeks of inspection?” Lord Daven asked from the gallery. “Even honest grain would have rotted in that time.”

Priestess Yuna turned toward the throne. “The manifests and the detention orders could both be placed before the court.”

Queen Isara regarded Commander Ash for a long moment. “They would be.” Her gaze then settled on you. “The charge had been heard, Ambassador. The question had not been answered. Under Velheim’s proposed terms, did this crown retain the right to inspect every wagon on the King’s Road?”

The Herald lifted his staff but did not strike it. Commander Ash’s hand remained on the pommel as the court waited for your reply.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, turning back to the Queen.* "Yes, Your Majesty. Velheim's terms allow for *mutual* inspection. So long as your wagons are subject to the same scrutiny on our roads."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald lowered his staff. “Velheim confirmed that inspections would continue on both sides of the border, under equal terms.”

Commander Ash released the sword pommel. “Equal terms sounded agreeable until a wagon waited six weeks for clearance.”

Lord Daven seized on the opening. “Then the court could set a limit. One day for an ordinary wagon. Longer only when an inspector recorded cause.”

Priestess Yuna inclined her head. “And the record could be available to both crowns. Otherwise, each delay would become another accusation.”

Queen Isara studied the gallery, then Commander Ash. “Lord Daven would draft that limit. Priestess Yuna would review the grounds for extending it.” Her voice hardened. “Commander Ash would produce the harbor manifests and detention orders before sunset.”

The Herald struck the marble once. “The Queen had so ordered.”

Queen Isara’s attention returned to you. “Tariffs could fall quickly, Ambassador. Trust could not. Velheim had offered mutual inspection; this court required mutual records and a deadline for release. Would Velheim accept those terms?”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I smile, a genuine one this time.* "Velheim would be pleased to accept, Your Majesty. Transparency breeds trust."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald struck his staff. “Velheim accepted the court’s conditions: equal inspections, shared records, and a deadline for release.”

Lord Daven allowed himself a narrow smile. “The northern merchants would welcome a road governed by a clock rather than a grudge.”

“Provided the clock began when a wagon reached the post,” Commander Ash said, “not when its papers pleased a clerk.”

Priestess Yuna looked up from the alcove. “That distinction belonged in the written terms.”

Queen Isara gave Daven a glance. “It did.” She turned to Ash. “The detained ships remained in harbor until Priestess Yuna had examined their manifests. If their cargoes matched, they sailed before dawn.”

Ash’s jaw tightened. “As Queen Isara commanded.”

The Herald raised his staff for the closing declaration, but Isara held up a hand. “One matter remained. The King’s Road crossed land claimed by both crowns. No tariff could settle who held authority at the old stone bridge.” Her gaze rested on you. “Velheim’s maps were new, Ambassador. Did they show where Velheim believed the border lay?”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Priestess Yuna accepted the intercepted orders and broke no seal. She examined the marks on the folded pages, then held them where the court could see.

“These bore the harbor office’s cipher,” Priestess Yuna said. “A cipher established origin, not truth.”

Commander Ash stepped away from the throne. “Those papers belonged to a military office. How had they reached Velheim?”

“The court would ask that,” Queen Isara said. “First, Priestess Yuna would read them.”

The Herald struck his staff. “Priestess Yuna held the floor.”

Yuna unfolded the first page. Her eyes moved down it, then stopped. “This order directed the detention of merchant vessels until the old stone bridge had been secured.” She turned to the next page. “It was dated eleven days before the first false manifest entered the harbor.”

Lord Daven’s narrow smile vanished. “Then the manifests had not begun the detentions.”

Commander Ash looked at the pages. “That order could have been forged.”

“It could,” Yuna said. “The cipher and the dates required examination.”

Queen Isara’s expression did not change. “Commander Ash would surrender the original harbor ledger to Priestess Yuna. No clerk would alter it before she arrived.” Her gaze settled on you. “Ambassador, these orders spoke of the bridge. Did Velheim’s maps place it within Velheim’s border?”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "The old bridge has always been a crossing, not a border, Your Majesty," *I state, my voice level.* "But these orders suggest your Commander intended to make it one."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Commander Ash took a step toward Priestess Yuna. “Securing a crossing was not the same as claiming it. The order named no border.”

“It named a bridge before the harbor detentions began,” Lord Daven said. “Commander Ash had told this court the manifests prompted those detentions.”

The Herald raised his staff, but Queen Isara silenced him with a glance.

Priestess Yuna kept the pages in her hands. “The Ambassador’s conclusion went beyond the words of the order. Commander Ash’s account did not explain its date.” She refolded the first page. “The ledger might clarify both.”

Queen Isara’s expression remained still. “Commander Ash would send for it now. Until Priestess Yuna had examined the originals, no soldiers of this crown would advance beyond the old stone bridge.”

Ash’s jaw tightened. “The bridge remained undefended, then?”

“The bridge remained where it was,” Isara said. “That was not permission to move it.”

The Herald struck the marble. “The Queen had ordered the harbor ledger produced and the bridge held under its present disposition.”

Lord Daven looked toward the papers in Yuna’s hands. “And the trade agreement?”

“It would be drafted,” Queen Isara said. Her gaze returned to you. “But it would not be signed over an unresolved border claim. The Ambassador had called the bridge a crossing. Did Velheim’s new maps show the same?”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly.* "They do, Your Majesty. A crossing, mutually used, for centuries." *I pause, looking pointedly at Ash.* "Until recently."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Commander Ash met the pointed look without moving. “The bridge had carried merchants for centuries,” Commander Ash said. “It had also carried armed men. A crossing did not cease to matter because both crowns used it.”

“Nor did concern grant either crown ownership,” Lord Daven replied.

Priestess Yuna placed the intercepted orders on the alcove’s reading stand. “The maps could establish what Velheim claimed. The harbor ledger could establish what Commander Ash ordered. Neither would establish centuries of mutual use without older records.”

Queen Isara gave a small nod. “Then the court would examine all three. Until it had done so, the bridge would remain open to civilian traffic under the inspections agreed today. No new fortifications would be raised on either bank.”

Commander Ash’s expression hardened. “That left the crossing exposed.”

“That left it unchanged,” Queen Isara said. “The distinction mattered.”

The Herald struck his staff. “The Queen had ordered the bridge kept open and its present defenses maintained.”

Queen Isara’s gaze rested on you. “Velheim’s maps would be entered into the record alongside this crown’s. Were they here to be examined?”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "They are, Your Majesty," *I confirm, gesturing to a aide waiting discreetly.* "Complete with historical annotations."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The aide brought the maps to the Herald, who carried them to Priestess Yuna’s reading stand. Their oldest annotations had been copied in several hands; the bridge appeared on each sheet, but the border lines stopped short of either bank.

Priestess Yuna traced a faded mark beside the crossing. “This annotation recorded tolls collected jointly, seventy years ago. It named no sovereign authority over the bridge.”

Lord Daven leaned forward. “A useful distinction. Both crowns had profited from keeping it open.”

Commander Ash studied the sheet from where he stood. “A copied annotation proved little without its source.”

“Then its source would be requested,” Queen Isara said. “Priestess Yuna would compare these maps with the royal archive. Commander Ash’s ledger would be examined beside them.”

The Herald struck the floor once. “The maps had been entered into the record.”

Priestess Yuna turned one sheet toward the throne. “One mark warranted earlier attention. A later hand had drawn a proposed fortification on this crown’s bank. It carried the harbor office’s cipher.”

Queen Isara’s eyes moved to Commander Ash. “The ledger had better explained that mark.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow at Commander Ash, a triumphant smirk playing on my lips.* "A 'proposed' fortification, Your Majesty? Or one that was already being built?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Commander Ash’s eyes narrowed. “No fortification had been authorized. The mark showed a contingency, nothing more.”

“A contingency with the harbor office’s cipher,” Priestess Yuna said. “The cipher did not establish that stone had been laid. It did establish that the proposal had passed through that office.”

Lord Daven looked toward Queen Isara. “The bridge could be inspected before anyone argued over what the ledger meant.”

Queen Isara considered the marked bank on the map. “It would be. Commander Ash, had any materials or laborers been sent to the crossing?”

“Timber had been delivered for repairs to the watch post,” Commander Ash said. “No wall had been raised.”

“Then the inspection would find timber and a repaired watch post.” Queen Isara’s tone gave the answer no shelter. “Priestess Yuna would send an observer to the bridge before dusk. Commander Ash would provide the delivery orders with the harbor ledger.”

The Herald struck his staff. “The Queen had ordered the crossing inspected and the delivery orders produced.”

Priestess Yuna left the marked map open on her stand. “Until then, the court had a question, not a finding.”

Queen Isara’s gaze remained on Commander Ash. “And by dusk, it would have an answer.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I hold Isara's gaze, a silent acknowledgment of the shift in the room's power dynamics.* "I trust Priestess Yuna's observations, Your Majesty." *It's a subtle dig at Ash, implying I don't trust his.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara gave no sign that the implication pleased her. “Priestess Yuna’s observations would stand on what she found, not on anyone’s trust.”

Priestess Yuna folded the marked map away from the other sheets. “An observer could confirm the work at the bridge. The ledger would show who ordered it. The court needed both.”

Commander Ash faced the throne. “The delivery orders would account for every beam.”

“Then producing them would serve Commander Ash well,” Lord Daven said.

The Herald struck his staff as a harbor clerk appeared at the far doors with a leather-bound ledger beneath one arm. The clerk passed it to Priestess Yuna, who opened it beside the intercepted orders. For several moments, only the turn of pages disturbed the chamber.

Priestess Yuna stopped at an entry dated two days before the vessels had been detained. “Timber for the watch post,” she read. Her finger moved to the next line. “Stone, mortar, and twelve laborers assigned to the old bridge.”

Commander Ash’s face went still. “The watch post had a stone foundation.”

“The delivery orders would say where the stone went,” Queen Isara replied. “Priestess Yuna would read those next.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I fix my gaze on Commander Ash, a triumphant glint in my eyes.* "Indeed, Your Majesty. Let the stones speak for themselves."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The bow landed well. You saw it register in the Queen's eyes: a flicker of assessment, filed and closed.

Queen Isara did not answer at once. She let the silence stretch until the scratch of the court scribe's quill became the loudest sound in the hall. When she finally spoke, her voice was quiet enough that the gallery leaned forward to hear it.

"Patience," she said, "is a courtesy extended to those who have earned it. Velheim closed the Harrow Pass to our caravans for three winters. Now Velheim brings *terms*." She turned one ringed hand palm-up on the armrest. "Very well. The court will hear them. Whether it will be patient remains to be seen."

Commander Ash shifted his weight. It was the first time he had moved since you entered. "With respect, Majesty, we know what Velheim's terms will be. Tariffs dressed as friendship. Garrisons dressed as escorts." His gaze settled on you, flat and unblinking. "The last Velheimi envoy who stood on that spot swore the Pass would stay open. It closed eleven days later."

The Herald's staff cracked against the marble. "The Commander will address the throne, not the petitioner, until the petitioner has concluded."

Ash's jaw tightened, but he inclined his head a precise half-inch toward the Queen. "Majesty."

From the gallery, Lord Daven rose smoothly, one hand resting on the balustrade. "If it please the court, the Commander's memory is excellent but selective. That envoy served a regent who is now dead and a council that has since been dissolved." He smiled pleasantly, the way a man smiles when he has already counted the votes. "The Ambassador speaks for a different Velheim. Surely the Crown can spare a few minutes to learn *how* different, before deciding it is the same."

A low murmur moved through the gallery. The Queen neither silenced it nor acknowledged Daven. She simply waited for it to die on its own, and it did.

Priestess Yuna spoke for the first time. Her voice was soft and carried perfectly, as if the vaulted ceiling had been built for it. "The Temple records oaths, Majesty. Not intentions." Her pale eyes rested on you without warmth or hostility. "Before the terms are read, the Temple would know one thing: does the Ambassador come with the authority to *bind* Velheim, or only to propose on its behalf?"

Every head turned from the alcove to you.

The Herald lowered his staff to rest position. "The petitioner may answer the Temple's question," he intoned, "and then present the terms of Velheim to the throne."

Queen Isara folded her hands and said nothing at all. She did not need to.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I straighten, meeting Yuna's gaze.* "Priestess, I wouldn't waste Her Majesty's time if I lacked the authority to conclude this treaty. Velheim is prepared to bind itself." *I pause, letting that sink in.* "As for the terms, they are not tariffs, Commander. They are an offer of mutual prosperity."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The words settled over the hall, and for a moment no one moved to pick them up.

Priestess Yuna inclined her head, the barest dip of her veil. "Then the Temple will hold Velheim to it." She drew a slender ledger from the folds of her sleeve and opened it across her knees. The creak of its binding sounded loud in the quiet. "Whatever terms are spoken next will be spoken under oath. The Ambassador understands that the Temple does not record retractions."

It was not a threat. It was, somehow, worse than a threat: it was a simple fact, stated by someone who had nothing to gain from it.

Commander Ash did not look at you this time. He kept his eyes fixed on the Queen, as the Herald had instructed, but his voice carried well enough. "*Mutual prosperity.*" He said the phrase slowly, as if tasting something spoiled. "Majesty, I have heard that phrase before. Usually from men standing on the far side of a closed gate."

The Herald's staff rose an inch off the marble, then paused, suspended. Ash had addressed the throne, not the petitioner, so the rebuke never came. The Herald lowered the staff again with visible reluctance.

In the gallery, Lord Daven had not sat back down. His pleasant smile held, but his fingers had begun a slow, soundless drumming on the balustrade. You had seen him do that once before, at the embassy dinner in Velheim, in the moment before he placed a very large wager. *Bound under Temple oath* was more than he had expected you to offer. Whether he thought it bold or reckless, his face did not say.

Queen Isara unfolded her hands.

"Velheim is prepared to bind itself," she repeated. Her tone carried no mockery. It was precise, the way a jeweler repeats the weight of a stone before naming a price. "Three winters ago, Velheim was prepared to starve my northern provinces. I find myself curious what has changed in Velheim, Ambassador, that it now wishes to be *prosperous* alongside us." Her ringed fingers settled back on the armrest. "Curious enough to listen. Not yet curious enough to trust."

She turned her head a fraction toward the Herald. It was the only signal she gave.

The Herald struck the floor once, sharply. "The Temple has recorded that the petitioner speaks with binding authority." He paused while Yuna's pen scratched across the ledger and then went still. "The petitioner will now present the terms of Velheim to the throne. The court will observe silence until the terms are concluded."

The hall went quiet. Ash's hand stayed on his pommel. Daven's fingers stopped drumming. Yuna's pen hovered over the page, waiting.

Queen Isara looked down at you from the throne, and she waited too.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald's staff came down so hard that the crack echoed off the vaulted ceiling twice.

"The petitioner will address the *throne*." For the first time, the Herald's voice lost its measured cadence. "The court was instructed to observe silence. The petitioner is not exempt from—"

Queen Isara lifted two fingers from the armrest. The Herald stopped mid-word, as if a hand had closed over his mouth.

No one else spoke. The murmur that should have swept the gallery never came. It died in a hundred throats at once, strangled by the sudden understanding that something had just been said which could not be unsaid.

In the observer's alcove, Priestess Yuna's pen was moving.

It scratched across the ledger in slow, deliberate strokes, and in the silence every person in the hall could hear it. She did not look up until she had finished. When she did, her pale eyes went first to you, then to Commander Ash, and her voice was as soft as before.

"The Temple notes that the Ambassador has spoken an accusation while under oath." She let the pen rest against the page. "The Temple notes also that the Commander has now been named before the throne. Whatever he answers will be recorded under the same terms."

Commander Ash had gone very still. It was a different stillness from his parade-rest composure. That had been a posture. This was a man who had stopped moving because any movement would cost him something.

He did not look at you. He had been told not to, and he clung to that instruction now like a shield. His gaze stayed on the Queen, and his hand did not leave his sword pommel, but his knuckles had whitened around it.

"Majesty." His voice was level. Too level. "The Navy of the Crown enforces the Crown's waters. Velheimi hulls have been inspected in accordance with the standing orders of the Admiralty. If the Ambassador mistakes lawful inspection for a *blockade*—"

"Six weeks of lawful inspection," Lord Daven said from the gallery. He said it mildly, almost to himself, the way a man reads a figure off a ledger. He was no longer smiling. "How many Velheimi ships have been permitted to *complete* an inspection in that time, Commander? I confess I'd find the number illuminating." He paused. "Unless, of course, the Admiralty's standing orders were issued by someone other than the Admiralty."

The Herald's staff twitched upward, then froze again. The Queen's fingers had not lowered. Daven had spoken out of turn, and the Crown was letting him.

That, more than anything, told the room something had changed.

Queen Isara turned her head. It was a small, unhurried movement, but it brought her gaze fully onto Commander Ash for the first time since the hearing began. She studied him the way she had studied your bow: an assessment, filed and closed.

"Commander," she said. "I recall signing orders for the northern garrisons. I recall signing orders for the Harrow Pass." Her voice had not risen at all. "I do not recall signing orders for the western sea lanes."

Ash's jaw worked once. "Majesty, the matter was operational. The Admiralty judged it beneath the notice of the throne until—"

"Until a foreign ambassador raised it in my court. Under Temple oath." The Queen's ringed hand came to rest on the armrest again. "Yes. I see how that timing would be inconvenient."

The silence that followed had weight. Somewhere in the gallery, a noble cleared his throat, then thought better of it.

Queen Isara looked back down at you. Nothing in her face had softened. If anything, her attention had sharpened into something colder and more interested, the look of a player who has just discovered that the board holds more pieces than she thought.

"You have broken protocol in my hall, Ambassador." A beat. "And you have told me something I did not know. I have not yet decided which weighs more." She tilted her head a fraction. "You claimed you would explain the blockade if the Commander would not. The Commander has chosen to call it an *inspection*. So. Explain it."

The Herald lowered his staff to rest position, slowly, like a man setting down something he was not sure he would be allowed to pick up again.

Yuna's pen hovered over the ledger.

Commander Ash, at last, turned his head and looked directly at you. Whatever protocol had been holding back, it was not holding it back anymore.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet Ash's glare, a small, cold smile playing on my lips.* "I'm sure the Commander has many names for the theft of our goods and the harassment of our crews. Perhaps he can explain why the Crown's 'inspections' only target Velheimi ships, while his own merchants sail unmolested."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Ash's hand did not move from his pommel. His face did.

It was only a flicker: a tightening at the corners of his eyes, there and gone. But you had been watching for it, and so, you realized, had the Queen.

"*My* merchants." The Commander said it flatly, still facing you, and the whole hall heard him abandon the throne as his audience. "I am a soldier of the Crown, Ambassador. I own a sword, a horse, and a commission. If Velheim has confused me with some shipping house, Velheim's spies are poorer than I feared."

The Herald's staff rose. It hovered, trembling slightly, then sank back to the marble without striking. Two breaches of protocol in as many minutes, and the Queen had permitted both. The Herald looked like a man watching the walls of his house come down one stone at a time.

In the gallery, Lord Daven had gone quiet in a way that was not like him. He was studying Ash with narrowed eyes. The smile was gone, and the calculation had not yet produced an answer. Whatever you had just implied, Daven had not known it either. For the first time that morning, you could not tell whether your ally was pleased with you or measuring the distance between you.

Priestess Yuna's pen stopped.

She did not write the Commander's answer. She lifted the pen from the page and turned her pale gaze on you, and the room turned with her.

"The Temple has recorded the word *theft*," she said softly. "It has recorded the word *harassment*. It has recorded that the Commander's own merchants sail unmolested." She laid one slender hand flat across the open ledger. "These are no longer arguments, Ambassador. Under oath, they are charges. The Temple does not record retractions. Nor does it record charges without substance behind them." A pause, gentle as a blade laid on a table. "Velheim will name the ships. Or the houses. Or the Temple will note that the Ambassador of Velheim swore to something it could not show."

Queen Isara had not moved at all. Her ringed fingers rested on the armrest, and her eyes moved slowly between you and her Commander as though weighing two stones on a jeweler's scale.

"The Commander owns a sword, a horse, and a commission," she said. Her voice held no inflection whatsoever. "That is what the Commander says." She let the words sit. "Ambassador, you have been generous with accusations this morning. The Temple now asks you to be generous with proof. So do I."

She did not look at Ash when she added the next part, which made it land all the harder.

"And the Commander will remain exactly where he stands until you are finished."

Ash's knuckles went white on the pommel. He said nothing.

The Herald drew a slow breath, straightened, and struck the floor once, quietly, almost apologetically. "The Temple requires substantiation," he intoned. "The petitioner will provide it to the throne, or withdraw the charge into the record as unproven."

Yuna's pen hovered above the page.

Lord Daven's fingers began, very slowly, to drum on the balustrade again.

Every eye in the throne room settled on you, and waited.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I take a breath, letting the tension settle for a moment.* "The proof, Your Majesty, is in the holds of the ships currently awaiting inspection outside your harbor. Specifically, the *Sea Serpent* and the *Northern Star*." *I look at Ash.* "Ships you personally ordered seized, Commander."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
For a heartbeat, the name of the first ship hung in the air, and nothing happened at all.

Then Commander Ash laughed.

It was not a loud laugh. It was short and dry and utterly without humor, and it was the last sound anyone in the hall had expected. Somewhere in the gallery, a lady's fan stopped mid-stroke.

"Yes," Ash said.

He was still looking at you. He no longer seemed to care who saw him do it.

"Yes, Ambassador. I ordered the *Sea Serpent* and the *Northern Star* seized. Personally. My seal is on the writ, and I will not insult the Temple by pretending otherwise." He turned his head, slowly, deliberately, back toward the throne, and when he spoke again his voice had regained its parade-ground steadiness. "Majesty, I held them because of what is in those holds. I had intended to bring the matter before you once I was certain. It seems the Ambassador has decided the timing for me."

The murmur that had died earlier came back all at once. It rolled through the gallery like surf. The Herald's staff came down twice, hard, and this time the court obeyed it. The noise ebbed, but it did not vanish. It lingered at the edges of the hall like smoke.

Lord Daven had stopped drumming.

His hand lay flat on the balustrade, perfectly still, and his face had taken on the smooth, empty pleasantness of a man at a card table who has just watched someone else lay down a hand he did not account for. His eyes found yours across the hall. They held a question, and the question was not friendly: *What is in those ships?*

He did not ask it aloud. He did not need to.

In the observer's alcove, Priestess Yuna wrote for a long time.

When she finished, she did not look at Ash. She looked at you.

"The Temple records that the Commander has confirmed the seizure under oath," she said. "The Temple records that he has claimed cause." Her pale eyes did not blink. "And the Temple records that it was the Ambassador of Velheim who named those two ships before this court, as proof of Velheim's charge." She turned a page. The dry whisper of it seemed to go on forever. "Whatever lies in those holds now belongs to the record, Ambassador. It will speak for one of you. It cannot speak for both."

Queen Isara rose.

She did it without haste, the heavy folds of her gown settling around her like snow. The entire hall rose with her in a ragged wave of scraping chairs and rustling silk. Only Ash stayed exactly as he was, because he had been commanded to.

"Herald."

"Majesty." The Herald's voice had recovered its cadence, if not quite its composure.

"Send to the Harbor Master. The *Sea Serpent* and the *Northern Star* will be opened within the hour, in the presence of Temple wardens, a clerk of the Admiralty, and a representative of the Velheimi embassy." Her gaze did not leave you. "No one who has spoken in this hall today will set foot on either deck before the wardens do. Not the Commander. Not the Ambassador." A fractional pause. "Not Lord Daven."

In the gallery, Daven bowed, a fraction too deep. "As Your Majesty commands."

The Herald struck the floor and turned to a waiting page, who was already running before the echo faded.

Queen Isara did not sit back down. She stood at the edge of the dais and looked at you the way she had looked at nothing else that morning: directly, fully, with the whole of her attention.

"You named those ships, Ambassador. My Commander claims them as his proof. You claim them as yours." Her voice was quiet again, quiet enough that the hall leaned in. "Within the hour, I will know which of you has lied to me under oath in my own court."

She let the silence draw tight.

"Before the wardens break the seals, I would have one thing from you. Not from Velheim. From *you*." Her ringed hand lifted, palm up, exactly as it had at the start of the hearing. "Tell this court, under the Temple's pen, what you believe we will find in those holds."

Yuna's pen touched the page and waited.

Ash's eyes stayed fixed on you, flat and patient now, the patience of a man who believes the trap has already closed.

Across the hall, Lord Daven's face gave you nothing at all.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The paper crossed the space between you and the alcove in a silence so complete that the whisper of parchment against your glove seemed to carry to the rafters.

The Herald's staff jerked upward. "The petitioner will present evidence to the *throne*—"

Queen Isara did not lift her fingers this time. She did not need to. She simply looked at him, and the Herald's protest died with his staff still raised. He lowered it by degrees, like a man easing a blade back into its sheath.

Priestess Yuna did not reach for the orders at once. She let them rest in your outstretched hand for a long moment, her pale eyes on your face rather than the pages, as though weighing the gesture itself before its contents. Then she took them, set her own pen carefully in the gutter of the ledger, and unfolded the first sheet across her knees.

"The Temple has received documents from the Ambassador of Velheim," she said. "It has not requested them. It records that they were offered freely, and to the Temple first." A fractional pause. "The Temple also records that the Queen asked a question, and that this was not an answer to it."

A ripple went through the gallery. Queen Isara's expression did not change, but something in her stillness acknowledged the point and set it aside for later.

Yuna began to read.

Her voice did not rise or fall. She read the way she spoke, softly and precisely, every word placed like a coin on a counting table.

"*By authority of the Western Command. All hulls flying the colors of Velheim within the Crown's western lanes are to be detained pending inspection. Inspection is not to be concluded. Cargoes are to be offloaded under guard and transferred to the bonded warehouses at Saltmere, for the account of House Merrow, until further instruction.*"

She turned the sheet over. Her pale eyes moved to the base of the page and rested there.

"It bears the seal of the Commander of the Western Command." She looked up, at Ash this time. "The Commander's seal."

The hall did not murmur. It inhaled.

Commander Ash's face had gone the color of old marble. His hand had not left his pommel, but for the first time that morning the gesture looked less like a statement and more like a man holding on to the only solid thing in reach.

"That is my seal." His voice was low and even, each word dragged into line by sheer discipline. "Majesty, that is my seal. It is *not* my order." He did not look at you now. He looked only at the Queen, and there was something in his eyes that had not been there before. It was not quite fear. It was the look of a soldier who has just heard the enemy's drums coming from behind his own lines. "I have never issued a writ in the name of House Merrow. I have never heard of warehouses at Saltmere being bonded to anyone. If the Temple will compare that writ to the one I sealed for the *Sea Serpent*—"

"The Temple will compare everything, Commander," Yuna said, without looking up. "That is what the Temple is for."

In the gallery, Lord Daven had not moved.

That was what drew the eye. When the name *House Merrow* fell into the hall, a dozen nobles had turned to one another, and fans had snapped open, and someone near the back had muttered a single sharp word. Daven alone had done nothing at all. His hand lay flat on the balustrade. His face held the same smooth, pleasant emptiness it had worn since the ships were named.

But his fingers, the ones that drummed before every wager, had curled very slightly against the stone. They stayed that way.

He did not look at you. For the first time that morning, Lord Daven seemed to be taking great care not to.

Queen Isara descended one step from the dais. Only one. In that hall, it was as good as a shout.

"House Merrow," she said, and the name sounded different in her mouth, turned over and examined like a stone with a flaw in it. "Saltmere." Her gaze moved from Yuna's ledger to Ash's white knuckles, and then, unhurried, it rose to the gallery and rested on Lord Daven for exactly as long as it took him to notice. Then it came back to you.

"You have now given my court three things, Ambassador. An accusation. Two ships. And a sealed order of my own navy, which should never have left my navy's hands." Her voice was soft, and it was not kind. "The first two I asked you to justify. The third, I find I must ask you to explain."

She held out her ringed hand, palm up, exactly as before.

"How does the Ambassador of Velheim come to carry the Crown's own orders in his coat?"

Yuna lifted her pen from the gutter of the ledger and set its tip against a fresh line.

"Under oath," the Priestess added gently. "The Temple would know the hand that intercepted them. And the hand that passed them on."

The Herald did not strike the floor. No one had told him to, and no one in the hall seemed willing to breathe loudly enough to invite it.

Ash watched you, and he was no longer patient.

Daven watched nothing at all.

And somewhere beyond the palace walls, a page was still running toward the harbor, where two sealed holds waited in the grey morning light.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I smile, a genuine, if chilly, smile.* "Your Majesty. I have many friends who believe in mutual prosperity. Some are even in your employ." *I glance at Daven, then back to the Queen.* "One such friend acquired these orders after noticing inconsistencies in the 'inspections.' They believed you would want to know."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The glance lasted less than a breath. It was enough.

Every head in the gallery followed it. Fans stilled. A dozen nobles who had spent the morning edging toward Lord Daven's end of the balustrade found sudden reasons to edge away again, and the space around him widened by a careful arm's length on either side.

Daven did not flinch. He had been at too many card tables for that. But you saw the faint, fixed quality settle into his pleasant expression, the look of a man who had been dealt into a hand he had not agreed to play.

Priestess Yuna did not write.

She let the pen rest against the page, unmoving, and when she spoke, her soft voice cut through the hall's gathering unease like a draft through an open door.

"The Temple records that the Ambassador was asked for a hand, and gave a smile." Her pale eyes held yours. "It records that the Ambassador looked toward the gallery. It does not record whom he looked at, because a glance is not a name, and the Temple does not write down what it must guess." A pause, gentle and merciless. "Twice now the Ambassador has been asked a question under oath and has answered a different one. The Temple is patient, Ambassador. It is not infinitely patient."

Commander Ash made a sound low in his throat. It was not quite a laugh this time.

"*Friends in the Crown's employ.*" He was looking at you again, openly, and the Herald did not so much as twitch his staff. "Majesty, the Ambassador has just told your court, smiling, that Velheim keeps agents inside your government. That one of them lifted a sealed naval writ, whether mine or a forgery of mine, and carried it to a foreign embassy." His knuckles were still white on the pommel, but his voice had found its footing. "Whatever is in those holds, *that* is already proven. By his own mouth."

Queen Isara did not answer him. She did not answer you either.

She turned, slowly, and looked up at the gallery.

"Lord Daven."

The name fell into the hall like a stone into a well. Daven straightened. His hand left the balustrade.

"Majesty."

"The Ambassador speaks of friends who noticed inconsistencies. Who believed I would want to know." Her voice was mild, almost conversational. "And then the Ambassador looked at you." A beat. "I find I would like to know why."

For a long moment, Daven said nothing. You could see him weighing it: the cost of the name, the cost of refusing it, the cost of House Merrow's name hanging in the air above him like a blade on a thread. Then he smiled. It was not his usual smile. It was thinner, and it had been built in a hurry.

"Your Majesty honors me by assuming I would know." He inclined his head. "I have never concealed my friendship with Velheim's embassy. It is my duty to the Crown to cultivate such friendships. If the Ambassador looked to me, perhaps it was for reassurance." His eyes flicked to you, brief and cold as winter water, and then away. "I am sure he will tell the court plainly whether I handed him anything at all."

It was deftly done. With a single sentence, he had set the question back at your feet. *Name me, and I burn with you. Name someone else, and I am clean. Stay silent, and you stand alone.*

The Herald shifted his staff from one hand to the other. His voice, when it came, was careful and formal, and almost gentle, as though he too had begun to understand how narrow the floor beneath you had become.

"The Temple has asked for the hand that intercepted the orders, and the hand that passed them on. The throne has asked the Ambassador to explain his glance." He struck the floor once, softly. "The petitioner will answer the court."

Queen Isara remained standing on the first step of the dais. She had not returned to her throne, and it was clear she would not until this was finished.

"Choose your words carefully, Ambassador," she said. "Within the hour, I will know what is in those ships. Before then, I will know who in my court is Velheim's friend." Her ringed hand rested lightly at her side. "Whether I know it from you, or from someone less inclined to smile, is still yours to decide."

Yuna's pen lifted from the page and hovered, waiting.

Ash waited too, his eyes fixed on you like a drawn crossbow.

And in the gallery, a careful arm's length from everyone, Lord Daven waited to learn whether his ally had just saved him or sold him.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, my own smile fading.* "Your Majesty, I did not name a hand because I do not know a name. My contact was a cutout, as is common in such delicate matters." *I pause, letting my eyes drift to Daven for a moment, then back to the Queen.* "They merely suggested I approach Lord Daven, who they claimed was a man of integrity, deeply concerned for the Crown's true interests."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The hall took the words the way a frozen lake takes a footstep: silently at first, and then with a long, low sound from somewhere deep beneath the surface.

This time, the murmur did not come from the gallery. It came from the space around Lord Daven. The nobles nearest him had stopped edging away. They had gone still instead, and that was worse. Stillness meant they were listening, and listening meant they were remembering: dinners Daven had hosted, letters he had carried, the Velheimi wine that had appeared at his table two winters ago when no one else could get it.

Priestess Yuna's pen moved.

It moved for a long time, and the scratch of it was the only sound that answered you. When she finished, she did not lift her eyes to you. She lifted them to the gallery.

"The Temple records that the Ambassador does not know the hand that intercepted the orders." Her voice was as soft as ever. "It records that the hand was a cutout, and so has no name to give. And it records that this nameless hand directed the Ambassador to Lord Daven, by name, as a man of integrity." She laid the pen flat across the page. "A glance is not a name, Ambassador. This was a name. The Temple has written it down."

In the gallery, Lord Daven closed his eyes.

It lasted only a moment. When he opened them again, the hurried, thin smile was gone. In its place was something you had never seen on his face in all the months you had known him: nothing at all. No charm, no calculation, no wager. Just a man reckoning the cost of the ground he stood on.

"*A man of integrity.*" He said it quietly, and for once he did not seem to be performing for anyone. "How generous of this nameless friend." His gaze settled on you, and it did not waver. "I wonder, Ambassador, whether the cutout also suggested what I was meant to *do* with that integrity. Or whether that was left for me to discover this morning, in front of the Crown."

Commander Ash did not laugh this time. He did not need to.

"A cutout." He spoke to the Queen, but his eyes never left you. "No name. No face. No hand anyone can bring before the Temple. Majesty, the Ambassador asks this court to believe that my seal was stolen, that House Merrow is robbing Velheim through bonded warehouses I have never heard of, and that the only living witness to any of it is a ghost who happens to point at Lord Daven." His grip on the pommel eased by a fraction, as though some of the weight had shifted off him and onto someone else. "I have fought men who told better lies with less to lose."

The Herald's staff rose and did not fall. He glanced toward the dais, uncertain whether a rebuke was wanted, and found no instruction there.

Queen Isara had not moved from the first step.

She looked at you for a long moment. Then she looked at Daven. Then, briefly, at Ash. Her face showed nothing, but you had watched her long enough now to recognize the pattern: assessment, filed. This time, she did not close it.

"Lord Daven," she said. "Come down."

The gallery drew breath as one.

Daven did not hesitate, and that, too, was noticed. He descended the gallery stair at an even, unhurried pace, his hand trailing along the rail. The nobles along the steps shifted aside for him without being asked. When he reached the marble floor, he stopped three paces to your left. It was not beside you. It was not apart from you. It was the precise distance of a man who had not yet decided which he wanted to be.

He bowed to the throne. The bow was correct this time, no deeper than protocol required.

"Majesty."

"The Ambassador says a stranger sent him to you." The Queen's voice was mild. "Did he come?"

Daven straightened. For a heartbeat, he said nothing. You could almost hear the arithmetic behind his eyes: *yes* bound him to you, *no* was a lie before the Temple's pen, and the page was still running toward the harbor.

"He came, Majesty." Daven's voice was steady. "Four weeks ago, to my house on the Lantern Street. He spoke of Velheimi ships held and not released. He asked whether I believed the Crown knew." A pause. "I told him I did not know what the Crown knew. I told him I would find out."

"And did you?"

"I made inquiries." His eyes did not move toward you. "Quiet ones. Of the Admiralty. Of the harbor clerks at Saltmere." He drew a slow breath. "I did not hand the Ambassador any orders, Majesty. I swear it under the Temple's pen. But I did tell him, a fortnight past, that the Western Command's writs were not all being signed in the Western Command."

Yuna's pen was already moving.

Ash's head turned sharply toward Daven. For the first time, the Commander looked less like a man defending himself and more like one who had just heard a name he wanted very badly to hear more of.

The Herald struck the floor once, carefully, as if the marble might crack.

"Lord Daven has answered the throne under oath," he intoned. "The Temple has recorded it."

Queen Isara turned her gaze back to you. Her ringed hand rested at her side, perfectly still.

"Lord Daven says he told you where the writs were being signed," she said. "You told my court you did not know a name." Her voice did not rise. It did not need to. "Ambassador, one of those statements is incomplete. Before the seals are broken, I would know which."

Across the hall, the great doors creaked. The running page had not returned. Instead, a Temple warden stood framed in the threshold, grey-robed and breathless, a sealed tablet clutched against his chest.

He waited for the Herald's staff to grant him the floor.

For the moment, the Queen did not look away from you long enough to allow it.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I incline my head slightly to Daven, a silent acknowledgment.* "Your Majesty, Lord Daven did indeed tell me that the writs were not all signed in the Western Command. He did not, however, provide a name for *who* was signing them. My contact simply pointed me toward Lord Daven, trusting his integrity to investigate further."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Queen's gaze held on you for a long moment. Then it moved, unhurried, to the man three paces to your left.

Lord Daven did not return your acknowledgment. He kept his eyes on the throne. But his shoulders, which had been set like a man bracing for a blow, lowered by the smallest degree. You had not sold him. Neither of you had yet been told whether that would matter.

Priestess Yuna wrote. Then she paused, turned back a page, and read something to herself. The hall watched her lips move silently over the words.

"The Temple records that the Ambassador's account and Lord Daven's account now agree," she said at last. "It records that the Ambassador knows the place where the writs were signed, and not the hand that signed them." She smoothed the page flat with two fingers. "The Temple also records that the Ambassador has now answered the question he was asked. It notes that this is the first time today." She did not smile. She did not need to.

Commander Ash's jaw tightened. "*Trusting his integrity to investigate.*" He said it to the Queen, low and hard. "Majesty, a man with no name sends a foreign envoy to a lord of this court, and that lord goes quietly asking after *my* writs, and not one word of it reaches me or the throne for a month." His eyes cut to Daven. "If the writs were being signed outside my Command, my lord, I would dearly like to know why I was the last man in the city to hear of it."

Daven turned his head a fraction toward the Commander. "Because I did not yet know whose seal was false, Commander." His voice was perfectly courteous and perfectly cold. "Yours included."

The Herald's staff came down, hard and final. "The Commander and the Lord will address the throne." He drew himself up, and for the first time that morning, no one countermanded him. Then he turned to the doorway. "Majesty. A warden of the Temple waits upon the floor."

Queen Isara let the moment stretch one breath longer than was comfortable. Then she lifted two fingers.

"Let him speak."

The warden came forward, grey robes whispering on the marble, and knelt at the foot of the dais. He broke the seal on his tablet with a thumb that was not quite steady.

"Majesty. The holds were opened before the Harbor Master, a clerk of the Admiralty, and the Velheimi embassy's man, as commanded." He swallowed. "The *Sea Serpent* carries wool, grain, and dyed cloth, matching the Velheimi manifests in every count. Each crate had already been tagged for transfer." He looked up. "The tags bear the bond-mark of Saltmere. For the account of House Merrow."

The gallery broke. It was not a murmur this time but a rush of voices, and the Herald had to strike the floor three times before it fell back into silence.

Ash did not move. His face had gone very still, the stillness of a man hearing that the ground he had been accused of undermining had in fact been undermined beneath him.

"And the *Northern Star*?" the Queen asked.

The warden hesitated.

"The *Northern Star*'s cargo matched its manifest, Majesty. Salt fish and timber." He wet his lips. "But the clerk of the Admiralty sounded the hold, and found a false bulkhead aft. Behind it were forty crates." His eyes flicked, involuntarily, toward you. "Pike-heads and crossbow stirrups. Unassembled. Stamped with the foundry mark of Velheim's royal arsenal."

For a moment, there was no sound in the throne room at all.

Then Commander Ash let out a long, slow breath through his nose. He did not laugh. He did not look triumphant. He looked, if anything, like a man who had been proven right about something he would rather have been wrong about.

"That," he said quietly, to the throne, "is why I seized her."

Lord Daven's hand had found the edge of his sleeve and was holding it. He was looking at you now, openly, and the question in his eyes was no longer *what is in those ships*. It was *did you know*.

Priestess Yuna set down her pen.

"The Temple said that whatever lay in those holds would speak for one of you," she said softly. "It could not speak for both." She lifted her pale eyes to you. "The Temple was mistaken. It has spoken for both of you. And against both of you."

Queen Isara descended the second step of the dais.

"House Merrow is robbing Velheim under my Commander's forged seal," she said. "And Velheim's royal arsenal is smuggling weapons into my harbor behind a false wall." Her voice was so quiet now that the scribe's quill stopped moving so he could hear it. "The Ambassador came to my court prepared to bind Velheim under oath."

She stopped one step above you, near enough that you could see the rings on her hand catch the grey light from the high windows.

"So tell me, Ambassador, before the Temple's pen. Who in Velheim sent forty crates of war into my city? And did they send them with you, or without you?"

The Herald did not strike the floor. Yuna's pen touched the page. Ash's hand returned to his pommel.

And three paces to your left, Lord Daven waited to learn how much of his integrity he had just spent on you.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet her gaze, a flicker of genuine shock on my face.* "Your Majesty, I knew nothing of this. I came here to negotiate peace, not to smuggle arms." *My eyes dart to Daven, then to Ash, a silent plea for belief.* "This was not part of my mission."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
For a long moment, no one answered you.

Your plea crossed the hall and found no place to land. Commander Ash received it with the flat, unblinking patience of a man at a court-martial. Lord Daven did not receive it at all. His eyes had dropped to the marble between you, as though the answer might be written there in the veins of the stone.

Queen Isara studied your face. The shock on it seemed to interest her more than the words. She watched it the way a jeweler watches light pass through a stone, looking for the flaw that shows the gem is glass.

"*Not part of your mission,*" she repeated softly.

Priestess Yuna's pen moved, stopped, and moved again.

"The Temple records that the Ambassador denies knowledge of the arms." She lifted the pen and turned back three pages, slowly enough that the whole hall heard each one fall. Her finger came to rest on a line near the top. "The Temple also records what the Ambassador swore at the start of this hearing. *Velheim is prepared to bind itself.*" She looked up. "The Ambassador did not swear that he was bound. He swore that Velheim was. The Temple does not record retractions, and it does not record exceptions for what an envoy was not told." A pause, gentle as falling ash. "Whatever the Ambassador knew, Velheim sent forty crates of war under the same flag he carries. Ignorance may save the man. It cannot save the oath."

A low sound went through the gallery. It was not quite a murmur. It was closer to a wince.

Commander Ash did not look away from you.

"Majesty." His voice was hoarse now, worn down by the morning. "I have seen men lie to me with their mouths. I have seen fewer lie with their faces." His grip on the pommel shifted, just slightly. "That was either true surprise or the best performance I have witnessed in twenty years of service. I cannot tell which." His jaw set. "And I do not like that I cannot tell."

It was the closest thing to a concession he had offered all day. It did not sound like mercy.

Three paces to your left, Lord Daven raised his head.

"Majesty, if I may." He waited for the Herald's staff. It rose, hesitated, and stayed aloft. The Queen did not stop him. "The Commander is honest enough to admit he cannot read the Ambassador's face. Let me offer something that does not depend on faces." He turned one hand palm-up, a mirror of the Queen's gesture, and it was not an accident. "It was the Ambassador who named the *Northern Star* before this court. He named her as *proof*. Under the Temple's pen." His voice sharpened, the voice of a man who had finally found a card he could play. "A smuggler does not stand before the throne and invite the Crown to open his own false bulkhead. Whoever loaded those crates, Majesty, they did not expect the Ambassador to say that ship's name aloud today."

The hall weighed this. You could feel it shift, the way a crowded room shifts when a door opens somewhere behind it.

Ash's eyes narrowed. "Unless he believed the hold was already empty." He spoke to the throne, but the words were plainly for Daven. "Unless he believed I had already found the crates, buried the matter, and would rather see him hanged for a blockade than speak of Velheimi pike-heads in front of the gallery."

"Then he misjudged you badly, Commander," Daven said coldly. "As, it seems, have several people."

The Herald's staff came down once, sharply. "The Lord and the Commander will address the *throne*." His voice cracked on the last word, and he cleared his throat. "Majesty. The court awaits your instruction."

Queen Isara did not give it at once.

She stood on the second step of the dais, near enough that you could smell the faint cold scent of cedar and iron that clung to her gown. She looked at Daven, who had just spent more of himself on you. She looked at Ash, who had been right about the ship and wrong about everything else. She looked at Yuna, whose pen waited like a closed door. Then she looked at you again.

"Lord Daven raises a fair point," she said. "Lord Daven usually does, when the stakes are his." Her ringed hand rested lightly against the fold of her gown. "So I will ask the question Lord Daven has so carefully avoided asking."

She leaned down, only slightly. Her voice dropped until even the scribe had to strain to hear it.

"You did not choose those two ships by chance, Ambassador. Someone gave you their names. Someone told you the *Sea Serpent* would prove House Merrow's theft." A beat. "Did the same someone tell you to name the *Northern Star*?"

She straightened.

"And the commission you carry, the one that lets you bind Velheim under the Temple's pen. Whose hand signed it?"

Yuna set her pen to a fresh line.

Ash's hand stayed on his pommel, but his eyes had changed. He was no longer watching you like a crossbow. He was watching you like a scout watching a ridgeline, waiting to see who else stood behind it.

The Temple warden, still kneeling at the foot of the dais, clutched his broken tablet and did not dare rise.

And Lord Daven, three paces to your left, finally turned his head and looked at you. He did not plead, and he did not warn. He simply waited, with the stillness of a man who had pushed every coin he owned into the center of the table and could do nothing now but watch the last card turn.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I take a slow breath, meeting Isara's gaze squarely.* "My commission was signed by the King's own hand, Majesty. As for the *Northern Star*... I was told she carried timber. Nothing more." *My eyes flicker to Daven, then back to the Queen.* "I suspect my 'contact' may have had a different agenda than mine."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The word *King* moved through the hall like a draught under a door, and every candle in the room seemed to lean with it.

Queen Isara did not move. But her ringed fingers, resting against the fold of her gown, closed very slowly into a loose fist.

"The King's own hand," she said.

Priestess Yuna's pen had stopped before you finished speaking. It stayed where it was, a hair above the page, and when she wrote at last she did it slowly, as if each letter weighed more than the last.

"The Temple records that the Ambassador's commission was signed by the King of Velheim." She lifted her pale eyes. "The Temple records that the Ambassador was told the *Northern Star* carried timber, and that he believes his contact had another purpose." She laid two fingers on the ledger, flat and deliberate. "The Temple would note, for the court's understanding, what that first line means. An envoy's oath binds the hand that commissioned him. If the King signed, then it is the King who swore this morning that Velheim came in good faith. And it is under the King's flag that forty crates came in behind a false wall." A pause. "The Temple does not accuse kings. It only writes down what they have sworn."

The gallery did not murmur. Someone near the back sat down heavily, without permission, and no one rebuked him.

Commander Ash was the first to break the silence, and he did it in a voice nobody in the hall had heard from him that morning. It was not the parade-ground voice. It was lower, and it sounded almost reluctant.

"Majesty." He did not look at you. He looked at the floor where the warden knelt. "I told this court I seized the *Northern Star* because of what was in her hold. That was true. I did not tell the court how I came to suspect it." His jaw worked. "Nine days ago a note was left in my quarters at the Western Command. Unsigned. No seal. It named the *Northern Star*, the aft bulkhead, and the day she would make harbor." His knuckles, still on the pommel, had lost some of their whiteness. "I took it for an informer who feared for his neck. I did not ask who had passed my sentries to deliver it."

Lord Daven's head turned sharply.

"A man with no name," he said quietly. He was not addressing the throne, and for once the Herald did not raise his staff. "Who leaves a note for the Commander pointing at the arms. And sends the Ambassador to me pointing at the theft." He let out a breath that was almost a laugh and not at all amused. "Majesty, I believe we have all been introduced to the same friend."

Ash looked at Daven for a long moment. It was not the look of an ally. But it was no longer the look of an enemy either.

"Someone wanted both ships opened," Ash said slowly. "In this hall. On this morning. With the Temple's pen in the room."

"And each of us certain the other was the villain," Daven finished.

The Herald struck the floor once, but softly, as if he no longer quite believed in the sound. "The Lord and the Commander," he began, "will address the—" He stopped. The Queen had lifted two fingers. He lowered the staff and said nothing more.

Queen Isara came down the last step of the dais.

She stood on the marble floor now, level with you, level with Daven and Ash and the kneeling warden. Behind her the throne sat empty, and the whole court stared at that emptiness as though it had begun to speak.

"House Merrow steals from Velheim under a forged seal of my navy," she said. "Velheim's arsenal smuggles war into my harbor under Velheim's flag. An envoy arrives with a king's commission and a stranger's list of ships. My Commander receives a note from no one. My Lord receives a visitor from nowhere." Her voice had not risen once. "And all of it arrives in my court on the same morning, in front of the Temple, where nothing can be taken back."

She turned her head and looked at Yuna.

"Priestess. The Ambassador says his commission bears the King's hand. The Temple holds a writ bearing my Commander's seal, which my Commander says is false." A fractional pause. "I would have them lie side by side on your ledger."

Yuna inclined her veiled head. "The Temple can compare a seal, Majesty. It can compare a hand. It cannot compare an intention." She set down her pen and held out one slender, open palm, and she held it toward you. "The Temple asks the Ambassador for his commission."

Queen Isara's gaze returned to you, cool and close.

"You told me your contact had a different agenda from yours, Ambassador. So tell me this before the seal is examined." She did not lean in this time. She did not need to. "When you left Velheim, who placed that commission in your hand? The King himself?" The rings on her fingers caught the grey light. "Or someone who told you it came from him?"

The warden at the foot of the dais bowed his head lower, as though he wished to vanish into the marble.

Ash watched the space behind you, as if expecting a figure to step out of it.

Daven had gone utterly still, three paces away, with his hand on his sleeve.

And Yuna's open palm waited in the grey light, patient as the Temple, for whatever you would place in it.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet Yuna's gaze, then the Queen's, a slow understanding dawning.* "The King placed it in my hand, Majesty. But it seems he was not the only one who saw this as an opportunity." *I look at Daven, a new suspicion in my eyes.* "Perhaps my contact was not so much a friend, as a mutual acquaintance with a keen sense of timing."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald’s staff struck the marble once more, the sound sharp and final. “The Ambassador of Velheim has addressed the throne. The court will hear the matter of the northern trade routes.”

Queen Isara did not shift. Her gaze stayed on you, cool and unhurried, as if she were weighing the cost of every word before she spent any of her own. “Terms,” she said at last, the word thin as a blade. “Velheim has a talent for arriving with terms and leaving with other people’s roads. Speak them. Slowly.”

Commander Ash’s thumb moved once along the pommel. “Roads the Crown already guards,” he said, not looking at you so much as through you. “And that Velheim’s caravans have a habit of treating as theirs the moment the snow melts.”

From the gallery, Lord Daven leaned a fraction forward, voice smooth, almost mild. “Her Majesty asked for the terms, Commander. Not a winter campaign in miniature. The Ambassador came under safe conduct. Let the court hear what Velheim actually offers before we decide what it costs.”

Priestess Yuna did not rise. Her hands stayed folded in her lap, her eyes on the space between you and the throne. “The icons are listening,” she said, quiet enough that the room had to still to catch it. “So should the court. Patience was requested. It has not yet been refused.”

The Herald inclined his head toward the throne, then toward you. “The Queen has given leave. The Ambassador may continue.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
*I hold the Queen's gaze, a slight, almost imperceptible smile playing on my lips at the Commander's interjection.*

"Indeed, Your Majesty. Velheim's caravans have always been... industrious. However, these terms are not about seizing roads, but about *securing* them. For mutual benefit."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara let the word *securing* hang until the echo died against the stone. “Mutual benefit,” she said, each syllable measured and cold. “A phrase that has purchased more roads than any army. Name the price Velheim expects the Crown to pay for the privilege of guarding its own passes.”

Commander Ash’s hand stayed on the pommel. “And name the soldiers,” he said, voice flat and hard. “Last thaw, Velheim banners were counted on the high switchbacks. Industrious caravans do not fly war-standards. If this is securing, say who holds the keys when the snow returns.”

Lord Daven’s reply came smooth, almost amused, though his eyes stayed sharp. “Keys can be shared without being surrendered, Commander. Her Majesty asked for terms, not a tally of last winter’s suspicions. If the Ambassador has a compact that keeps the routes open and the Crown’s writ intact, the gallery would rather hear it than another sermon on banners.”

Priestess Yuna’s gaze did not leave the space between throne and aisle. “Benefit is a worldly word,” she said, neither warm nor accusing. “The icons do not weigh coin. They weigh whether a promise binds both tongues that speak it. The court has not yet heard the binding.”

The Herald struck his staff once, formal and precise. “The throne has questioned. The Commander has questioned. The Ambassador of Velheim may answer.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You turned from the throne and set the charge on Commander Ash as if rank were a courtesy you could set aside. The gallery went still.

The Herald’s staff cracked the marble, louder than rite required. “Order,” he said, formal and tight. “The Ambassador will address the Crown. A direct accusation against a Crown officer, spoken out of turn, is entered in the record.”
