Queen Isara did not raise her voice. The cold in it was enough. “You asked for patience and spent it in a breath. A blockade is not a rumor you may throw at my commander’s feet. If Velheim has a charge, you will lay it before this throne — dates, hulls, waters — or you will withdraw it. I do not preside over tavern quarrels.”

Commander Ash’s hand stayed on the pommel. He looked at you at last, and there was nothing official left in it. “Six weeks,” he said, flat and hostile. “The strait was held because Velheim ships ran dark past the customs chain and refused inspection. Call it a blockade if the word flatters you. I call it the Crown’s water, kept. Your captains know what they would not open. Ask them, before you ask me to explain myself to a foreign tongue.”

Lord Daven’s ease thinned, though the alliance in his voice did not break. “Commander — if there were seizures, the gallery has not seen a manifest. Ambassador, you have just made this a matter of proof, not manners. Give Her Majesty something the court can test, or Ash will bury the trade routes under last winter’s suspicions and call it duty.”

Priestess Yuna did not take a side. Her eyes rested on the broken line between you and the throne. “A charge spoken out of order is still a charge,” she said, quiet and even. “The icons do not weigh who was addressed. They weigh whether the next words can be proven. Both of you are bound to them now.”

The Herald inclined his staff toward the throne, then toward you. “The accusation against Commander Ash stands in the record. The Ambassador of Velheim will return address to the Queen and furnish the claim — or withdraw it.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I turn back to the Queen, unperturbed.* "Your Majesty. The blockade began six weeks ago. The ships were *The Sea Serpent* and *The Northern Star*. Your Commander knows the customs chain; so do my captains. They refused inspection because your ships began firing *before* inspection was offered."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald’s staff struck once, slower this time, as if the record itself had grown heavier. “The Ambassador of Velheim has named two ships and a sequence of events. The claim stands before the throne.”

Queen Isara’s fingers tightened once on the arm of the throne and went still. She did not look at Commander Ash. She looked at you, and the cold in her face had sharpened into something that counted. “The Sea Serpent. The Northern Star. Six weeks. Firing before inspection.” She let each item fall like a coin onto stone. “Those are names a court can summon. If they are false, Velheim will answer for them. If they are true, so will my navy. You will not improve them with theater.”

Commander Ash did not flinch, but the set of his jaw had gone harder. “Those hulls held the customs chain,” he said, hostile and precise. “They signaled. Your captains ran dark and would not heave to. Warning shot is not a volley, and a foreign tongue does not get to rename the Crown’s water because it disliked the answer. If your merchants have splintered wood, produce it. If they have dead, name them. Do not dress refusal as martyrdom and call it terms.”

Lord Daven’s voice cut in before the silence could harden into a verdict, still allied, no longer mild. “Then let the manifests be opened, Majesty — both sides. Hulls, signals, the hour the first shot left a tube. The gallery has heard a blockade and a customs action described as the same week. One of those stories keeps the northern routes. The other starts a winter we cannot afford. The Ambassador has finally given you something that can be tested. Test it before Ash turns proof into a duel of pride.”

Priestess Yuna’s hands remained folded. Her eyes had left the space between you and the throne and rested, briefly, on Commander Ash, then on you. “Names bind,” she said, quiet enough that the banners seemed to listen. “A shot fired before an offer is not the same sin as a ship that will not open its hold. The icons will not choose between them. The court must. Until the logs are read, both tongues are only promising.”

The Herald inclined his staff toward the throne. “The Queen holds the claim. The Ambassador of Velheim may add what the record still lacks — or yield the floor.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I give a thin smile.* "The logs will show much, Your Majesty. But my captains also reported your ships' flags were... obscured. And they were flying no custom ensigns." *I pause, letting that sink in.* "An honest mistake, perhaps. Or perhaps Commander Ash's men were simply eager for a fight."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The gallery’s murmur died before it could become a sound. You had set the flags on the table beside the names, and the throne room treated them as another weight the marble would have to bear.

The Herald’s staff struck once, measured and severe. “The Ambassador of Velheim has added a claim of obscured colors and absent customs ensigns. It is entered. The floor remains with the throne.”

Queen Isara’s gaze did not warm. If anything, the calculation in it had gone quieter, which was worse. “Obscured,” she said, the word pared to bone. “A convenient fog. Either my ships flew the Crown and your captains chose not to see it, or someone in my navy took the colors down and fired anyway. I will not have both stories living in the same sentence. You will say which you mean — and you will say it as fact, not as a smile.”

Commander Ash’s knuckles had gone white on the pommel. He did not raise his voice. The hostility in it needed no volume. “My men do not sail blank,” he said. “The customs chain flies the ensign in clear weather and in foul. If your captains saw cloth they could not read, they were looking through their own smoke, or through a lie they were paid to carry home. Eager for a fight.” His mouth tightened. “Say that again to my face when the logs are open, Ambassador. Until then it is an insult dressed as a report, and I will answer it as one.”

Lord Daven shifted in the gallery, the alliance in his tone still there, strained thin over the new charge. “Majesty — flags can be proven. Signal books, watch officers, the hour the ensign was hoisted or was not. Do not let this become a question of who smiled. If Velheim is alleging a false flag, that is a heavier crime than a stubborn hold, and it cuts both ways. Open the naval logs before Ash is forced to defend his honor instead of his orders.”

Priestess Yuna’s eyes had returned to the space between you and the throne, as if the air itself had been asked to testify. “An ensign is a promise made of cloth,” she said, neither siding nor soothing. “To hide it is to speak with a covered mouth. To claim it was hidden, and be wrong, is the same sin turned around. The icons will not sort eagerness from error. Only the written watch will. Until then, both of you are offering the court a story it cannot yet kneel to.”

The Herald inclined his staff toward the throne, then toward you, formal to the last inch. “The Queen has required a fact, not a suggestion. The Ambassador of Velheim may clarify the charge of the flags — or withdraw the implication and yield.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The papers left your hand and crossed the aisle to the observer’s alcove. Protocol, which had already been bent, broke with a soft sound of parchment.

Priestess Yuna did not reach for them at once. She looked at the packet as if it might be either a relic or a trap, then took it with both hands and did not open it. “A neutral party,” she said, quiet, neither accepting the title nor refusing the charge. “The icons do not sit the throne. If I read this before the Crown has seen it, I become a witness the court did not summon. I will hold what you have given. I will not become your herald.”

The Herald’s staff struck the marble, once, hard enough to sting the air. “Out of order,” he said, formal and clipped. “Documents offered to the throne are offered to the throne. A packet placed in the observer’s hands is not yet evidence. It is an irregularity, and it is entered as such. The Ambassador will not direct the reading.”

Queen Isara’s gaze moved from you to the unopened packet and back. She did not raise her voice. The cold in it had gone precise. “You asked my priestess to stand between me and a charge against my navy. That is not neutrality. That is a staging. If those are orders, they will be read where I can hear every line, and where Commander Ash can answer them without a gallery whisper arriving first. Priestess — you will bring them here. You will not paraphrase. You will not protect either tongue from the words.”

Commander Ash had gone very still, hand locked on the pommel. “Intercepted,” he said, and the word was hostile enough to cut. “Stolen paper, walked into a hearing, and laid on a holy lap so it looks cleaner. If my name is on that, I will hear it from the throne, not from an alcove. And if it is a forgery dressed as proof, Ambassador, you will not get to call the icons your clerk.”

Lord Daven’s voice came from the gallery, low, allied, and no longer smooth. “Majesty — do not let the insult of the delivery bury the page. If Yuna holds it unread, Ash will call it theft and the Ambassador will call it caution, and the routes will die in the argument. Have it read aloud. Now. Both sides bound to the same sentences, in the same breath. That is the only neutrality left in this room.”

Priestess Yuna rose at last, the packet still closed between her palms. She did not look at you. She looked at the throne. “I did not ask to be chosen,” she said, even and unswayed. “I will not open this in the alcove. If the Queen commands the reading, I will carry every word to the marble and leave the judgment where it belongs. Until that command is given, I am only keeping paper from becoming a rumor.”

The Herald inclined his staff toward the throne, rigid with rite. “The packet is in Priestess Yuna’s keeping, unopened. The Queen holds the question of the reading. The Ambassador of Velheim has yielded the floor by the act of delivery.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch Yuna, my expression carefully neutral.* "Your Majesty. I have delivered the proof. The contents speak for themselves."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You stood with your hands empty and your face arranged into nothing the court could use. The packet remained closed in Priestess Yuna’s palms, and for a moment the only sound was the banners shifting in the high draft.

Queen Isara did not look at the paper. She looked at you, and the calculation in her silence was colder than the rebuke that followed. “Contents do not speak,” she said. “Mouths do. You delivered a staging and called it proof. I will have the words, and I will have them where a lie cannot hide behind an alcove.”

She turned her chin a fraction toward the observer’s place. “Priestess. Bring it. Open it on the step. Read every line that bears a name, a date, or an order. Omit nothing. Embellish nothing. If a hand is unclear, say so. You are not counsel. You are the voice of the page.”

Priestess Yuna came down from the alcove without hurry and without allegiance. She set the packet on the lowest marble step, broke the fold, and held the first sheet where the throne light could strike it. Her voice, when it came, was even enough to make the gallery lean in.

“A naval order,” she said. “Unsigned in full. The closing mark is a fleet-cipher, not a name. It directs the holders of the customs chain — the hulls named here as the Sea Serpent and the Northern Star — to ‘deny passage to Velheim traffic that will not open, and to discourage inspection by demonstration if signals are ignored.’ The date is six weeks and two days past. There is a marginal note, different ink: ‘Colors at the captain’s discretion in contested weather.’ No ensign is ordered struck. No volley is ordered. The word blockade does not appear.”

She turned the sheet so the throne could see the hand, then looked neither at you nor at Commander Ash. “That is what the paper says. It does not say who wrote the margin. It does not say the order was obeyed.”

Commander Ash’s breath left him once, hard, through his teeth. His hand did not leave the pommel. “Captain’s discretion,” he said, hostile and tight. “Not a blank flag. Not a shot before a hail. You walked a lawful customs order into this room, called it intercepted, and laid it on holy hands so it would sound like murder. If that margin is mine, produce the hand that matches it. If it is not, you have forged a Crown paper and smiled while a priestess read your crime aloud.”

Lord Daven spoke from the gallery before the hostility could become a motion. The alliance was still in him, but the ease was gone. “Majesty — the page is narrower than the charge, and wider than an acquittal. ‘Discourage by demonstration’ is a phrase a court can hang a man on or a phrase a captain can hide a volley behind. It is not nothing. Nor is an unsigned cipher proof that Ash struck the colors. Do not let either of them leave with the sentence they came to collect. Bind the logs to this sheet before pride finishes what the snow began.”

The Herald’s staff struck once, formal, restoring the shape of the room. “The observer has read the packet at the Queen’s command. The order and the marginal note are entered. The Ambassador of Velheim is silent in the record. The throne may question.”

Queen Isara’s fingers rested on the arm of the throne, still as frost. “You said the contents would speak for themselves,” she said, and the thinness of her voice was a verdict waiting on a hinge. “They have spoken a lesser thing than you promised. Demonstration is not a bombardment. Discretion is not a covered ensign. If you have a second page that names the first shot, the hand on the margin, or a dead merchant, you will produce it now — to me, not to an alcove. If you do not, you will tell this court why Velheim spent a hearing on an order that does not say what you said it said.”

Priestess Yuna folded the sheet once, precisely, and left it on the step between you and the throne. “The paper is no longer in my keeping,” she said, quiet, unclaimed by either side. “What remains is whether the next tongue tells the truth the first one could not finish.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I gesture to the paper.* "Your Majesty, I merely presented the *initial* orders. Not the full scope of what transpired. The 'captain's discretion' is precisely what led to obscured flags and premature firing. Commander Ash knows his captains; I know mine."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You gestured to the sheet on the step as if the margin could be made to confess. The gallery held its breath for the throne.

Queen Isara did not look at the paper again. She looked at you, and the cold in her face had settled into arithmetic. “Initial,” she said. “A word that means you brought the court a page that does not say what your mouth said, and asked us to imagine the rest. Captain’s discretion is a license. It is not a confession of covered colors, and it is not a shot fired before a hail. If your captains know mine, they will have logs, splinters, and names of the dead. You have given me a cipher and a smile. That is not a scope. That is a gap you expect this throne to fill for you.”

Commander Ash’s hand tightened on the pommel until the leather creaked. He spoke to the throne, but the hostility was aimed down the aisle. “My captains do not strike the ensign because a foreign merchant dislikes the chain. Discretion in contested weather means when to show the cloth through fog, not whether the Crown’s water belongs to Velheim. You intercepted a lawful order, walked it past the Queen, and now you tell us the crime lives in the space the paper left blank. Produce the second page. Or admit you spent the hearing on a guess and called it proof.”

Lord Daven leaned on the gallery rail, allied still, and sharper for it. “Majesty — he is asking you to convict a margin. Do not. And do not acquit it either. ‘Discourage by demonstration’ can hide a volley or a warning shot, and both stories are still untested. Bind the naval logs and the Velheim watches to that sheet before either tongue leaves with the war they prefer. The northern routes will not survive a verdict built on what was not written.”

Priestess Yuna remained beside the step, hands empty, the folded order between you and the throne. She did not claim the argument. “A discretion is a door,” she said, quiet and even. “What passed through it is not on this page. To say the door caused the shot is a story. To say it did not is another. The icons will not finish a sentence the paper refused to start. Only another record can.”

The Herald’s staff struck once, formal and exact. “The Ambassador of Velheim has interpreted the marginal note. The interpretation is not yet evidence. The throne holds the question of further proof. The Ambassador may produce it — or stand on what has already been read.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I sigh, a slight exasperated puff of air.* "Your Majesty, I hardly expect to bring you every single log, every splinter of wood, and every tear from my captains' eyes. We are here to negotiate, not to prosecute a war."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The small, exasperated breath did nothing to warm the marble. The folded order still lay on the step between you and the throne, narrower than the charge that had carried it in.

Queen Isara let the silence count the cost before she spent a word. “Negotiate,” she said, cold and exact. “You asked for patience, spent it on hulls and flags, delivered a page that does not confess what your mouth accused, and now you tell this throne that proof is a luxury and tears are beneath a bargain. Velheim may offer terms. It may not keep an unfinished charge hanging over my navy while it does so. Withdraw the implication of covered colors and premature fire, and state the compact for the northern routes — tolls, escorts, seasons, who holds the keys. Or stand on the accusation and bring what can be tested. You will not have both, and you will not have a third thing called exasperation.”

Commander Ash’s hand stayed locked on the pommel. He did not bother to soften the hostility. “Every splinter. Every log. That is what a man brings when he walks into a Crown hearing and calls my captains eager for a fight. You intercepted a customs order, smiled through a priestess’s reading, and now the war is inconvenient. My men do not trade the strait for a sigh. Withdraw it, Ambassador. Or name the dead. There is no negotiation that starts with a lie you are too tired to finish.”

Lord Daven spoke from the gallery before the hostility could become a motion, allied still, and ambitious enough to want the routes alive. “Majesty — do not let the hearing die as a prosecution nobody came prepared to finish. Enter the sheet as Yuna read it: discretion, demonstration, no ensign struck, no volley ordered. That is not an acquittal of last thaw, and it is not a conviction either. Then make him put the actual terms on the marble, clean of flags. If Velheim cannot separate a bargain from a grievance, the gallery will know the compact was never meant to hold. If it can, the Crown still has a winter it can afford.”

Priestess Yuna did not move from beside the step. Her eyes stayed on the paper, not on you. “A negotiation is also a promise,” she said, quiet, claimed by neither side. “To ask the court to stop looking because the rest would be unpleasant is to cover the mouth again. The icons do not demand every tear. They demand that what was spoken and what was written not be asked to share a face they do not share. Until one tongue yields, the other cannot be trusted with a road.”

The Herald’s staff struck once, formal and restoring the shape of the room. “The Ambassador of Velheim has declined further proof and has returned the matter to negotiation. The accusation stands in the record as read, not as inferred. The Queen holds the choice: terms without the charge, proof without the bargain, or dismissal of the hearing.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, my sigh replaced with a cold, hard look.* "Very well, Your Majesty. If we are to speak plainly, let us speak plainly. My 'exasperation' is with this... *theater*. Velheim seeks a treaty, not a war of words." *I pause, letting my eyes flick to Commander Ash.* "Let's put the blockade aside for a moment. My terms are simple..."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The cold look met a colder one. Queen Isara did not grant the pause you had left hanging after *simple*. She let it die against the stone.

“Plainly, then,” she said, each word pared and counted. “You do not set a charge aside by wishing it into the gallery. It stands as the page was read — discretion, demonstration, no ensign struck, no volley ordered — and it will not be tried in the same breath as a compact. Speak the terms. Tolls. Escorts. Seasons. Who holds the keys when the snow returns. If the next sentence is still about my commander, this hearing is finished.”

Commander Ash’s hand had not left the pommel. The hostility did not soften because you had looked at him. “Put it aside,” he said, flat. “You named my hulls, my colors, and my captains’ appetite for a fight, and now the war of words is theater you are too proud to finish. I do not bargain the strait against an unfinished insult. Say your price to the throne. Do not spend another glance on me and call it diplomacy.”

Lord Daven leaned on the gallery rail, allied still, and ambitious enough to want something written before pride closed the doors. “Majesty — he has finally stopped interpreting a margin. Take the terms before he remembers the flags. Gallery and Crown both need numbers, not another sigh dressed as principle. If Velheim has a compact that keeps the routes open and your writ intact, let it hit the marble now, clean of hulls.”

Priestess Yuna remained beside the step, the folded order still between you and the throne. She did not claim the look you had given the Queen. “Plain speech is a vow only if the next words match it,” she said, quiet, unswayed. “To set a charge aside is not to unspeak it. The icons will hear the bargain as its own promise — or as the same covered mouth, wearing a treaty’s name. They have not yet been given the simple thing.”

The Herald’s staff struck once, formal and exact. “The Ambassador of Velheim has returned the matter to terms and has not yet stated them. The accusation remains in the record as read, not withdrawn. The floor is open for the compact. The Ambassador may speak the terms — and only the terms.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I take a breath, letting my gaze sweep over the court, briefly meeting Lord Daven's eye.* "My terms are these: a fixed annual toll for all Velheim caravans using the northern routes, paid directly to the Crown. In return, your navy guarantees safe passage, and customs inspections are limited to three designated ports, with a clear, published list of contraband."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald’s staff struck once, formal and clean, as if the room had finally been given something it could enter without a quarrel attached. “The Ambassador of Velheim has stated terms: a fixed annual toll to the Crown; a naval guarantee of safe passage on the northern routes; customs inspection confined to three designated ports; a published list of contraband. The compact is before the throne.”

Queen Isara did not soften. She turned the offer over in the cold quiet, counting what had been said and what had been left out. “A toll with no figure is a courtesy, not a price. Safe passage with no season, no escort strength, and no penalty if a caravan is lost is a wish. Three ports — name them. A list of contraband — whose hand writes it, and who amends it when Velheim’s merchants discover a new ingenuity. You have described a treaty. You have not yet offered one the Crown can sign without surrendering the passes by omission.”

Commander Ash’s thumb moved once along the pommel. The hostility had not left him; it had only found a narrower target. “A guarantee from my navy,” he said, flat. “After you spent this hearing calling my captains eager and my colors a fog. Safe passage is not a blank warrant to run the chain. If inspections live in three ports, the switchbacks do not become Velheim’s road between them. I will not put hulls on a promise that lets a caravan refuse a hail in the high passes and call it the treaty. Name the ports. Name what happens when a hold stays shut. Or the guarantee is a story, and I will not sail it.”

Lord Daven leaned on the gallery rail, and for the first time since the papers, something like satisfaction edged his voice — allied, ambitious, careful not to gild a gap. “Majesty, that is a shape the winter can use. Coin to the Crown, routes kept open, inspections that are not a blockade by another name. Do not let the missing numbers kill a compact the gallery has waited all hearing to hear. Set the toll against last year’s takings. Let the ports be the three that already have Crown houses. Publish the list under your seal, not Velheim’s. The bones are here. Make him put flesh on them before Ash turns ‘guarantee’ into another campaign.”

Priestess Yuna’s gaze rested on the folded order still lying on the step, then lifted to the space between you and the throne. “A toll is a worldly promise,” she said, quiet, claimed by neither side. “Safe passage is another. They bind only if both tongues know what breaks them. The icons do not set the price. They will know if the compact is a door left open, or a door with a bar both sides can see. The simple thing has been spoken. It is not yet finished.”

The Herald inclined his staff toward the throne, then toward you. “The terms are entered as stated, incomplete as to sum, ports, authorship of the list, and remedy for refusal. The Queen holds the questions. The Ambassador of Velheim may complete the compact — or stand on what has been said.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "The annual toll will be 100,000 gold pieces," *I state, holding the Queen's gaze.* "The ports are Haven, Oakhaven, and the newly established Deepwater. As for the contraband list, it would, of course, be established and amended by joint committee, ratified by both Crowns."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The stairwell is clear at the landing. Below, footsteps climb in pairs—heavy, quick, and close enough that the metal handrail trembles beneath their grip.

A voice crackles over a radio one floor down. “Third-floor door. Hold it.”

Mira’s weight shifts against your shoulder. Through the narrow window, the garage exit sign glows four flights below. The footsteps keep coming up.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* "Looks like downstairs is a no-go, Mira." I glance up. "How's that leg for climbing?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira looks up the stairwell, then down at her leg. “One flight, maybe two. Not fast.”

Below, a door bangs open. The climbing footsteps stop, and a beam of light cuts across the underside of the landing.

“Check above,” a voice says.

Mira grips the rail. “Roof access is one floor up. Tell me there’s a way off it.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The roof landing comes into view one flight above. Mira hauls herself up another step, her breath catching as her bad leg takes weight. Below, boots strike the stairs in a quick, even rhythm.

A green light flicks on beside the roof door. Its magnetic lock clicks free.

Someone on the other side tries the handle.

“Stairs are occupied,” a muffled voice says into a radio. “I have the roof.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Shit.* "We got company both ways, Mira." I push her ahead of me towards the roof door, drawing my silenced pistol. "On three, through the door. Go!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira braces a hand against the roof door. “I can make it through. I can’t outrun anyone.”

The handle turns from the other side. The door swings inward, revealing a security officer in a rain jacket, one hand on his radio. He freezes at the sight of the pistol, then ducks back behind the steel frame.

“Armed!” he shouts.

Below, the boots break into a run. Wind drives rain through the open doorway, and beyond the officer, the roof stretches toward the dark outline of the next building.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The server room hums around you, cold air rushing between the racks. Against the door, the barricade shudders as someone hits it from the corridor.

Mira sits on the floor beside a cabinet, one hand pressed to her leg. “That buys us seconds,” she says. “Not minutes.”

A radio squawks beyond the door. “Roof team, hold your position. We have them inside.”

At the far end of the room, an overhead cable hatch hangs partly open. Beyond it, a narrow maintenance passage disappears into darkness. The barricade takes another blow, and one of the racks flickers.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Maintenance passage, Mira. Think you can make it?" I grab her hand, pulling her up. "It's our only way out."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira gets to her feet with your help, her jaw tight. “If there’s room to crawl, I can make it.”

At the far end of the server room, the cable hatch hangs open above a rack. A narrow ladder leads up to it. Beyond the hatch, a red maintenance light blinks in the dark.

The barricade slams against the floor. Metal scrapes; the door opens an inch. A voice from the corridor calls, “Move the rack.”

Mira looks from the ladder to the widening gap beneath the door. “Tell me that passage goes somewhere.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "It has to go somewhere," I tell her, pushing her towards the ladder. "Go!" I turn, firing two shots through the gap in the door.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Two muffled shots punch through the gap. A cry cuts through the corridor noise, and the pressure on the door vanishes. Someone shouts for cover.

Mira climbs. Her bad leg drags against each rung, but she reaches the hatch and pulls herself into the passage. “There’s a junction ahead,” she calls down. “One branch goes toward the loading bay.”

The barricade scrapes across the floor again. A hand appears around the edge of the door, gripping a pry bar.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Loading bay it is!" I shout, firing another shot. "Keep going!" I pull the rack over, blocking the door again.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The shot cracks against the metal frame. The hand and pry bar disappear, and the rack slams against the door. From the corridor comes a sharp order to stand clear.

Above you, Mira crawls toward the junction. “Loading bay,” she calls. “I see a ladder down.”

A heavy impact drives the rack back an inch. Through the open hatch, you hear another sound beneath the server room’s hum: an engine idling below the passage. Then a vehicle door shuts.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it, they're breaching.* I start climbing, fast. "Mira, can you see what kind of vehicle?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The ladder rattles beneath you. Above, Mira reaches the junction and peers through a grille in the passage floor.

“Black van,” she says. “No markings. Two people beside it—one’s watching the loading-bay door.”

A metallic bang erupts from the server room below. The rack skids across the floor, and flashlight beams sweep the open hatch.

Mira pulls back from the grille. “There’s a stairwell across the bay, but we’d have to cross in front of the van.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Scratch the stairs then." I pull myself into the passage. "Any other exits from the bay?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira peers through the grille again. “Roll-up door behind the van. Too exposed. Wait—there’s a personnel door beside the freight elevator. No one’s watching it.”

Below you, a flashlight beam catches the ladder in the server room. “They’re in the passage,” someone calls.

At the junction, the maintenance passage forks. One branch leads to the ladder above the loading bay; the other runs toward the freight elevator. A motor whines somewhere inside the walls, and the passage begins to vibrate.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Alright, elevator it is." I start crawling toward the other fork. "How far to that door?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
“Twenty meters, maybe,” Mira says, crawling behind you. “The passage ends above the elevator controls. There’s a service ladder down.”

The vibration deepens. Through the mesh beneath you, the freight elevator begins to rise, its cables moving beside the passage. Behind you, metal clangs at the junction.

“They’re coming through,” Mira whispers.

Ahead, the passage ends at a grated panel. Beyond it, the ladder runs down the elevator shaft to a narrow service platform—and a closed personnel door. A red indicator above the door flashes: **LOCKED**.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* "Mira, can you get that door open? I'll cover us." I try to get a shot at whoever's coming through the junction.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You descended the last flight of stairs and the temperature dropped. The passage opened into a chamber that hadn't seen light in a long time — your torch was the first in decades, maybe centuries, and the shadows retreated from it reluctantly.

Dust covered everything. Thick, undisturbed dust. Except for one set of footprints leading from the far entrance to the center of the room, where something had been dragged. The marks ended at a stone slab. The slab had writing on it.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I kneel down to read the writing on the slab, holding the torch close.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The torchlight washed across the slab as you bent close, and the cold of the room seemed to gather around the stone, drinking the heat from the air before it could reach the carving.

Up close, the dust told more of the story. Handprints smeared through it — palms pressed flat, fingers spread, dragged down the slab's face as if someone had tried to grip it. The inscription itself was old and formal, each letter chiseled deep, and though the language had drifted over the centuries, the words held their shape:

WHAT IS GIVEN IS KEPT.
WHAT IS KEPT IS SAFE.
ASK, AND IT SHALL BE RETURNED.

Beneath that, in a different hand entirely — shallow strokes, a knife's work, hurried — someone had scratched a single line:

dont ask

The letters were small and crooked, and the final stroke ran off the edge of the slab and kept going, a long thin scratch that ended at the seam where stone met floor. Something was caught in that seam: a scrap of cloth, dark with old stains, folded into the gap as if it had been pushed there deliberately.

The drag marks ended beside your knee. And it was only from here, kneeling among them, that the room's one flaw made itself plain. The footprints came from the far entrance and stopped at the slab. One direction. There were no prints going back. Whoever had walked into this chamber had never walked out.

Your torch flickered. The flame bent sideways — not toward the passage behind you, but downward, pulled toward the seam around the slab's edge, where it held steady. Air was moving through that gap. Air meant a hollow beneath the stone.

And from somewhere below it, faint enough that you felt it in your teeth before you heard it, came a sound. Slow. Rhythmic. Like breathing.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I reach out and touch the scrap of cloth, tugging it gently from the seam.* "What in the…?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I grab the amulet and put it on. Then I turn to face the guardian.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: (OOC: don't write my actions) *I carefully pull the cloth free and hold it up to the torchlight. It's roughspun, dark, and smells faintly of damp earth and something metallic.* "Huh. Not an amulet, then."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I talk to the ghost. "What happened here? Who are you?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: (OOC: don't write my actions) *I sigh, running a hand through my hair.* "Alright, alright. No amulet, no ghost. Just… a scrap of cloth." *I look around the dusty room again, my eyes lingering on the drag marks.* "And a very unsettling set of footprints."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: Your

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I stand up slowly, letting the scrap of cloth fall back to the ground.* "No prints going back, huh?" *I walk over to the far entrance, where the footprints began, and inspect the ground carefully.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: Your

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I scan the floor for any other disturbances in the dust, or any sign of what might have come through here.* "Something tells me this 'what is given is kept' isn't as simple as it sounds."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: Your

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I trace the faint outline of a boot print with my own boot.* "Well, someone definitely came in this way. And they didn't leave through it." I look back at the slab. "So where did they go?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: Your

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I walk back to the slab and kneel down again, this time looking underneath it, trying to see into the gap.* "Hello? Anyone down there?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I press my ear to the cold stone.* "That breathing sound… it's still there. Faint, but definitely there."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I pull my head back from the slab.* "Okay, this is getting weirder and weirder." *I look at the words carved into the stone again.* "Ask, and it shall be returned."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You ease Mira against the wall beside the door. She bites down on whatever sound wants to come out of her and nods once. Go.

The stairwell door gives under your palm with a low mechanical sigh. Cold air rolls up from below, carrying the smell of concrete dust and old motor oil. The emergency lights here aren't red. They're a sickly amber, and they flicker every few seconds like something is chewing on the wiring.

You lean over the rail and listen.

At first there is only the alarm, muffled now, thudding through the walls like a second heartbeat. Then, beneath it, something else. Boots. Not running. *Climbing*, measured and patient, the rhythm of men who train together. Three sets, maybe four. They're below you, two floors down, maybe three. Hard to tell with the echo.

A radio crackles somewhere in that dark. A voice, clipped and bored: "*...sweeping level two. Service access is sealed. Garage team, hold position.*"

Service access is sealed. The tunnel is gone.

Behind you, Mira shifts her weight. You hear the scrape of her bad leg on the tile, and then a sharp intake of breath as she catches herself. Too loud? The boots below don't break rhythm. Not yet.

In your ear, the static changes. It doesn't clear. It changes, a faint click, then a pattern that almost sounds deliberate. Two short bursts. A pause. Two more.

The footsteps keep rising. You have perhaps forty seconds before they round the landing beneath you.

Across the corridor, at the edge of the pulsing red, a maintenance door stands half-open. Its label is scratched off. Farther back, the way you came, the elevator bank hums quietly. Its doors are closed and its floor indicator is dark.

Mira is watching your face, not the stairs.

"You heard something," she says quietly. It isn't a question.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content:
(OOC: Don't write my actions)

I give her a quick look. "Service tunnel's a no-go." I glance at the maintenance door, then back at the stairs. "Guards on their way up, probably three floors below." I turn from the stairwell. "Elevator's out. We're going in here." *I point at the maintenance door, then pull out my silenced pistol.* "Cover me."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira doesn't argue. She pushes off the wall, jaw tight, and drags her bad leg one step toward the stairwell door. Her hand closes around the handle and holds it just shy of the latch, so it won't swing, won't slam, won't announce anything.

"Cover you with what?" she murmurs. Her empty palm lifts for half a second. Then she reaches into her coat and comes out with a ballpoint pen, clicks it once, and grips it like an ice pick. "Fine. Go."

Below, the boots keep climbing. Closer now. Someone coughs. The echo makes it sound like it's right under the landing.

The maintenance door waits at the edge of the red. Through the gap, the corridor light reaches only a few feet inside. There's a metal shelf of paint cans, a mop bucket with a gray film of water, and a tangle of cables running along the floor toward the back. Beyond that, darkness. But the air coming out of it moves. A faint, steady draft brushes the hair at your temple. It's cooler than the corridor and smells of damp brick.

Air doesn't move like that in a closet.

In your ear, the static clicks again. Two short. Pause. Two short. Then something new: a single long burst, dragged out like a held breath, and silence. The static doesn't return. The channel is simply dead.

From the stairwell, a radio crackles, much clearer now.

"*Level two clear. Moving to three.*"

Mira's eyes flick to the stairs, then to you. Sweat beads at her hairline, but her grip on the handle doesn't waver.

"Thirty seconds," she whispers. "Maybe less."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The stairwell swallows you both.

Mira's breath goes sharp and shallow as her weight folds against your side. The first step costs her. The second costs more. Her bad leg drags, and her shoe scuffs the edge of the concrete. It's a small sound, but in this shaft of stone and steel it carries. She clamps her free hand over her own mouth and keeps climbing.

The amber light stutters. Dark. Light. Dark.

Below, the rhythm of boots doesn't change. They're still coming, patient and even, and now you can hear the creak of tactical gear and the soft metallic tick of a sling swivel against a rifle. One flight down. Maybe less.

You reach the half-landing. Mira's fingers dig into your shoulder hard enough to bruise.

Beneath you, a door groans open. It's the one you just left. The alarm's red pulse spills into the stairwell below, painting the lower walls in slow, bloody waves.

"*Three,*" a voice says. It's close. Close enough that you catch the rasp at the end of the word. "*Door's unsecured.*"

A pause. Boots shuffle on tile.

"*Maintenance closet's open. Check it.*"

Mira goes very still against you. Her pen is still clenched in her fist, knuckles white. She tilts her face up toward the next flight, toward the landing above, and you follow her gaze.

The door on the next level has no window. A keycard reader is bolted beside the handle, its status light a steady, unblinking red. Beside it, stenciled in faded yellow paint: **4 — RESTRICTED. AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY.** Past it, the stairs keep climbing into a darkness the amber lights don't reach. There's a draft up there too, colder than the one in the closet, and it smells like rain.

Below, someone kicks the mop bucket. Water sloshes across the floor.

"*Air's moving back here,*" the voice calls. "*There's a passage.*"

"*Then they went through it. Two with me. Rodriguez, hold the stairwell.*"

One set of boots stops moving. Right beneath you. Waiting.

Mira's lips barely move. "He'll look up," she breathes. "Eventually, he'll look up."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Then we don't give him eventually." *I push her forward up the stairs, moving for the restricted door.* "Can you open this?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira takes the stairs on momentum more than strength. Her bad leg buckles on the last step and she catches herself against the wall beside the reader, palm flat on the cold paint. For a second her eyes close. When they open, they're already on the keycard slot.

"Not with a card," she whispers. "They pulled mine the night I ran."

She studies the reader. It's an older unit, gray plastic gone yellow at the edges, and it's held to the wall by four screws. One of them is missing. Someone installed it in a hurry, or someone has been in it since.

Mira unscrews the barrel of her pen with her teeth. The spring drops into her palm, then the ink cartridge. She keeps the cartridge and lets the rest fall into her coat pocket without a sound.

"Facilities uses these on the restricted floors," she breathes. "There's a service override. It's a reset contact behind the housing, meant for when the readers freeze. Nobody ever fixed the flaw." She wedges the tip of the cartridge into the gap left by the missing screw and pries. The plastic flexes. It creaks. "I need about ten seconds and I need him not to hear this."

Below, Rodriguez's radio hisses softly. He doesn't answer it. You hear him shift his weight, and the slow scrape of a boot turning on concrete. He's pacing the landing, or turning to face the stairs.

The amber light stutters. Dark. Light.

Mira's hands are shaking now. It's not fear. It's the leg, the blood loss, her body finally sending the bill. The housing gives another quarter-inch. Through the gap you can see a nest of thin wires and two small copper contacts, dull with age.

"*Rodriguez.*" The voice comes up from the stairwell radio, tinny and distant, already deep in the passage. "*Passage dead-ends at a drainage grate. Grate's bolted. They didn't come this way.*"

Silence below.

Then Rodriguez speaks, low and to himself, close enough that you hear him exhale before the words. "*...Then where'd they go?*"

A flashlight clicks on. Its white beam sweeps the lower landing, bounces off the rail, and begins to climb the wall, one step at a time.

Mira touches the cartridge tip to the copper. Nothing happens. She adjusts it by a hair.

The reader's light flickers from red to amber.

"Almost," she breathes. Her eyes don't leave the wires. "Almost. Don't let him see me."

The flashlight beam reaches the half-landing. It brushes the bottom step of your flight, and it keeps coming.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The server room is cold. It's a deliberate, manufactured cold that raises goosebumps along your arms and turns every breath into faint vapor. Rows of black racks stretch back into the dark, blinking with tiny blue and green lights like a city seen from altitude. The hum is everywhere. It fills your ears and presses on your chest, loud enough to swallow small sounds.

That's good. That's very good.

Mira sits where you've left her, her back against the end of a rack and her bad leg stretched out in front of her. In the blue glow you finally see it. Her trouser leg is dark from the knee down and glistening. A thin line of red is already creeping across the white floor tile toward the drain grate in the center of the room. She stares at it like it belongs to someone else.

"Keep it," she murmurs, and it takes you a second to realize she means the ink cartridge still clenched in her fist. She opens her fingers and lets it fall. "Souvenir."

Outside, beyond the barricaded door, the stairwell is silent.

Then it isn't. Boots come up the steps slowly, one at a time. They stop. The keycard reader outside gives a soft, stupid *beep*. The handle rattles once, testing, and holds. The barricade takes the weight and shifts a quarter-inch with a groan of metal against tile. Then it settles.

Silence again. Rodriguez is standing on the other side of that door. You can't hear him breathe over the servers, but you know he's there.

A radio murmurs through the steel, muffled beyond meaning, and footsteps retreat down the stairs, fast now. He's going for help.

You have minutes. Maybe fewer.

Mira tips her head back against the rack. Her face is gray under the blue light, but her eyes are sharp. They're scanning the room the way yours would, cataloging and measuring.

"You wanted to think," she says. "Think fast. He'll bring a breaching tool, or someone with a card."

She lifts one trembling hand and points past you, deeper into the room.

At the far end, past the last row of racks, a single terminal glows on a steel desk. Its screen is awake, and someone is still logged in. A cursor blinks on a black command window. Above the desk, a ceiling panel hangs slightly open on one hinge, and cold wet air spills out of the gap. That's the rain smell. Somewhere above it, faint and rhythmic, water drums on sheet metal.

Your earpiece stays dead.

But on the terminal screen, one line of text sits alone above the cursor. It's white on black and it hasn't moved:

`.. / ..`

Two short. Pause. Two short.

Mira sees you looking. Her brow furrows, and then something in her face goes very careful and very still.

"That's not your handler," she says quietly. "That's a Directorate check-in code. Someone's asking if the package is secure." She swallows. "They're asking *me*."

The blood on the tile keeps spreading. Below, a door slams. Voices rise, too far and too muffled to hear what they're saying, and they're coming back.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I look from the screen to Mira, then to the door. "Can you answer it?" I ask, my voice low. "Can you tell them you're secure... and send a diversion?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira doesn't answer right away. Her eyes stay on the screen, on those four small dots, and something moves behind them. It's a calculation, fast and private.

"Yes," she says at last. "I can answer it."

She doesn't wait for help. She rolls onto her hip, plants her palm on the frozen tile, and drags herself along the base of the rack. Her bad leg leaves a smear of red behind her, wide and glistening. The server hum swallows the sound she makes, a low animal noise through clenched teeth. At the desk she hooks her fingers over the steel edge and hauls herself up until she's half-kneeling, half-hanging from it, her face lit white by the screen.

Her fingers hover over the keys. They're shaking badly now.

"If I send the wrong reply, they'll know I've turned," she murmurs. "If I send the right one, they'll believe me." A thin, humorless breath escapes her. "For about ninety seconds."

She types.

`.. / ..`
`-- / ...`

The cursor blinks. Nothing comes back.

Then she keeps typing, and it isn't code anymore. It's a command string, long and dense, and her fingers find their rhythm the way a pianist's do. You catch fragments before they scroll: `FAC_OVR`, `B2`, `SUPPRESS`, `ALL_ZONES`.

"Halon system in the garage," she whispers. "If it registers a fire, it seals the lower levels and dumps gas. Every guard down there has to clear out or suffocate. Everyone up here goes down to help." She hits enter. "That's your diversion."

Somewhere far below, a new alarm begins to rise. It's deeper than the first, a slow mechanical whoop, and it bleeds up through the floor and into your bones. The voices outside the door break off. Boots scramble. Someone shouts a name, and the footsteps go *down*, fast and scattered.

Mira sags against the desk. For a moment she almost smiles.

Then the terminal chimes.

A new line prints beneath hers. It's white on black, and it arrives slowly, one character at a time, as if someone on the other end is typing it by hand.

`PACKAGE CONFIRMED.`
`IS THE COURIER STILL WITH YOU?`

Mira's smile dies. She doesn't look at you. She looks at the keyboard, and her hands go perfectly still above it for the first time since you met her.

Above the desk, the loose ceiling panel creaks on its hinge. Cold rain mists down through the gap and beads on the back of your neck. Through the opening you can see a dark maintenance crawlway. Beyond it, maybe twenty feet away, a square of gray night sky shows where a roof hatch stands open to the storm.

Outside, the stairwell has gone quiet. It isn't empty. It's quiet. One set of boots never left.

A soft, patient knock comes on the steel door. It's two short taps, then a pause, then two more.

Mira finally turns her head toward you. The blue light carves her face into hollows.

"I didn't tell you everything," she says. "I need you to decide what I type next."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "What do they mean, 'courier'?" I ask, my eyes on the door. "And what happens if you say no?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira's hands don't move from the keyboard. The cursor blinks beneath the question, patient and white.

"Courier is you," she says.

The knock doesn't come again. Somehow that's worse.

"The Directorate calls it a courier when someone carries the package home without knowing what they're carrying." Her voice is flat and fast, the voice of a briefing and not a confession. "I was the package. My defection was real to your people. It was supposed to be real to me too, until I got close enough to your handler to find out who he was talking to." She swallows. A tremor runs through her jaw and she clamps down on it. "Your handler didn't go silent tonight. He was switched off. Those clicks in your ear weren't static. They were this." She tips her chin at the screen. "Someone was checking whether you were still breathing, and still walking me out."

The server hum fills the silence. Somewhere below, the halon alarm whoops on and on, and the floor vibrates faintly with it.

"If I type yes," Mira says, "they tell whoever is standing outside that door to come in quietly. You're the prize. You've seen the handler's network from the inside. You know faces. They want you alive long enough to learn what you know." Her eyes flick toward the steel door, then back. "And I get recovered. Debriefed. Rewarded, maybe, if they believe I never turned."

A drop of rain falls from the open ceiling panel and strikes the desk beside her hand. She doesn't flinch.

"If I type no..." She stops. Her fingers curl slightly above the keys. "Then the courier is dead or gone, and the package is alone in a sealed building with a fire alarm she triggered herself. They'll know I'm lying the moment they pull the camera feeds from the stairwell. That gives us minutes. After that they stop trying to recover anything." She lets out a thin breath. "They'll clean it."

The blood beneath her knee has spread into a dark, glossy pool that reaches the drain. Her face is the color of ash under the blue light, but her eyes stay steady on yours.

"There's a third option," she says, quieter. "I don't answer at all. Silence means compromised. Protocol says the man outside waits ninety seconds for a reply, then breaches."

The terminal's cursor blinks.

On the other side of the door, metal scrapes softly against metal. Something is being fitted to the lock. It's slow and careful, the work of someone who has done this many times.

Above the desk, the ceiling panel sways on its hinge. Rain drums on sheet metal in the crawlway, and twenty feet away that square of gray sky waits, cold and open.

Mira doesn't look at it. She's already measured the distance, and she knows what her leg can do.

"Decide," she whispers. "Yes, no, or nothing. I'll type whatever you tell me." A beat. "But if you go up through that ceiling, you go faster alone."

The scraping at the lock stops.

Behind the steel, very close, a man clears his throat.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I look at the ceiling hatch, then back at her. "No. We go together." *I grab a length of cable from a nearby rack.* "If they want me, they'll have to come get me."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The cable is heavier than it looks. It's thick black data line, sheathed in rubber gone stiff with cold. It comes free of the rack with a soft tearing of zip ties, and somewhere in the row a cluster of green lights blinks out. The servers don't care. The hum rolls on.

Mira stares at you. For one second she looks almost angry, as though you've taken something from her. Then it passes, and her mouth sets in a hard, thin line.

"*No*," she repeats under her breath. "All right. No."

She turns back to the keyboard. Her fingers are shaking so badly that she misses the first key and has to start over. She types slowly, one letter at a time:

`NEGATIVE. COURIER LOST IN STAIRWELL. PURSUING.`

She hovers over the enter key. "This buys us the cameras," she murmurs. "They'll spend time looking for you in the wrong place before they look here." She presses it. "Not much time."

The line sits on the screen. The cursor blinks once, twice, three times.

Then, one character at a time:

`UNDERSTOOD.`

Nothing more. No instruction. No follow-up. Mira reads the single word, and you watch the color drain out of what little color she has left.

"That's wrong," she whispers. "They always give an instruction. Always."

On the other side of the steel door, the man stops clearing his throat.

His radio crackles. It's muffled, but this time the words carry, because he has turned the volume up. He wants you to hear.

"*...confirmed. Package is compromised. Proceed.*"

A pause. Then a voice speaks through the door, pitched just loud enough to cut through the servers. It's calm and almost kind.

"Mira." It's not a question. "You were always better at code than lying."

Something heavy thuds against the base of the door, low and deliberate. There's the soft click of a pin, then a hiss like a tire losing air.

A thin gray thread of smoke curls under the door. It creeps along the tile, slow and heavy, hugging the floor. Where it reaches Mira's blood, it drifts across the dark pool without disturbing it at all.

Mira's head snaps toward it. "Gas," she breathes. "Heavier than air. It'll fill from the floor up." She drags in a breath and holds it, then lets it out in a rush. "Two minutes before it reaches the desk. Less, if he pops a second one."

The smoke spreads out between the racks, flowing like water around the base of each one. The nearest blue lights glow through it like lanterns sinking in fog.

Above the desk, rain spits through the open panel. The crawlway is a black mouth, the lip of the opening about eight feet above the floor. There's a steel conduit bracket bolted to the ceiling just inside it, rusted but solid, and past that the gray square of storm sky flickers once with distant lightning.

Mira looks at the cable in your hands. She looks at the bracket. Her eyes go back to the cable.

Understanding moves across her face, and right behind it comes fear.

"I can't climb," she says. "I can hold on. I don't know for how long."

She grips the edge of the desk and pulls herself up onto her good knee, her bad leg dragging behind her. Her hand slides across the keyboard as she moves. The terminal accepts the stray keystrokes and prints a line of garbage, then waits.

The gas has reached the second row of racks.

Outside the door, boots shift. A second pin clicks.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "You won't have to," I say. *I toss the cable up, aiming for the conduit.* "It'll be a hoist."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The cable leaves your hands in a heavy black arc. For a moment it hangs against the dark mouth of the crawlway, and then gravity takes it. The loose end slaps the rim of the opening, skids, and drops back toward the desk.

It doesn't fall all the way. Two feet of rubber catch on the lip of the bracket, snag on a rusted bolt head, and hold. The cable sways. Rain runs down its length in thin silver beads and drips onto the keyboard.

It's caught, but only barely. One good jerk could tear it loose.

Mira's eyes track it. "Loop," she whispers. "It needs to go *over*, not just hang on."

Behind the door, the second pin finishes its click. Something rolls across the tile outside with a hollow metal clatter, and then comes a second hiss, louder than the first. A fresh tongue of gray pours under the door. It doesn't creep this time. It *surges*, spilling between the first racks like floodwater through a broken levee.

The fog swallows the blue lights of the nearest row. Then the next.

Mira drags her good knee up onto the desk. The steel edge bites into her palms. She's up now, half-crouched on the desktop with her bad leg hanging over the side and dripping, her head just below the crawlway lip. Cold rain falls on her face and she tips her chin up into it, gulping at the air like it's the last clean air in the building. It might be.

Her gaze fixes on the snagged end of the cable, a foot above her reach.

"I can get it over the bracket," she says. "If you give me a lift, I can feed it through." She wraps her fist in the dangling slack, testing, and the whole line trembles against the bolt. "Then you tie me off, and you go up first. You pull. I can't pull myself. I can only hold."

The gas reaches the base of the desk. It pools around the steel legs, thick and faintly sweet, a smell like cut almonds and hot pennies. Your eyes start to sting. The terminal screen glows through the haze below you, and the line of garbage Mira typed is still sitting there, waiting to be sent.

On the other side of the door, the calm voice speaks again. There's something muffled over it now, the rubber rasp of a respirator.

"Thirty seconds, Mira. Then I come in and it's over either way."

Metal groans. The barricade shifts. A dark gap opens at the edge of the door and the gas pours out through it into the stairwell. It's working both ways now. He isn't in any hurry.

Lightning flashes in the square of sky twenty feet up the crawlway. By the time the thunder arrives, it's rolling through the whole building.

Mira looks down at you through the rising fog. Her knuckles are white around the cable.

"Tell me when," she says.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Now!" I grab her good leg, boosting her up. "Get it over!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Her weight comes down into your palms all at once.

She's lighter than she should be. Blood loss does that. Her good leg braces against your grip, and she rises out of the fog with a sharp, bitten-off cry as her bad leg swings free and knocks against the desk edge. Warm drops spatter your forearms. She doesn't stop. Her arm shoots up past the lip of the crawlway, fingers scrabbling over wet metal, and closes around the bracket.

Rust flakes rain down into your eyes.

"*Got it,*" she gasps. "Got it. Hold still."

She hangs there with one arm hooked over the bracket, her whole body trembling against your hands. With the other hand she drags the snagged end of the cable free of the bolt head. It sticks. She yanks it, and the bracket shrieks in its mounting. A bolt shifts a quarter-inch out of the ceiling with a grinding sound that goes right through your teeth. Then the rubber slides over the top of the steel, and the loose end slithers down the far side and drops past her shoulder in a long black coil. It slaps the desktop beside the keyboard.

The cable is over. Both ends hang within reach.

"It'll hold," Mira breathes, and then, quieter, "It'll probably hold."

The fog has climbed past your knees. It pours between the racks in slow gray waves, and the air at waist height is thick and sweet now, that almond-and-copper smell crawling up the back of your throat. Your eyes water freely. The terminal screen is a pale blur sinking beneath the surface.

Behind you, the barricade gives with a long scream of metal on tile. The gap at the door widens to a foot, then more. Through the haze you can make out a gloved hand curled around the edge of the steel. Above it, the round glass lens of a respirator catches the blue server light and holds it like an eye.

"Twenty," the calm voice says.

Mira's arm is shaking so hard that the cable quivers along its whole length. Her fingers are slipping on the wet bracket. You can see them sliding a fraction of an inch at a time.

"I can't hang like this," she says through her teeth. "Loop it under my arms. Or around me. Anything." She looks down at you through the rain and the rising gray, and her voice drops. "Then you climb, and you pull. Fast."

Lightning splits the square of sky at the end of the crawlway. In the white flash, for half a second, you see the whole length of the tunnel clearly. It's twenty feet of corrugated metal ending at the open roof hatch, and a dark shape is crouched just beside the hatch that wasn't there before.

Then it's gone into the dark again, and the thunder rolls over everything.

Mira didn't see it. She's looking at you.

"*Now,*" she whispers.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I quickly loop one end of the cable under her arms, securing it tight.* "Hold on, I'm going up." *I grab the other end and start climbing, pulling myself up to the conduit.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The cable burns your palms the moment your weight hits it.

Across the bracket, Mira jerks upward. The loop bites into her ribs and she gasps. It's a thin, punched-out sound, but she rises. Your body is the counterweight. Every foot you climb lifts her by the same amount, and the rusted bracket between you takes all of it.

Hand over hand. The rubber is slick with rain and your grip slides an inch, then catches. Your boots scrape the desk edge and kick the keyboard. Somewhere beneath the fog, the terminal chirps as a line of garbage finally sends.

The gas is a gray lake below you now. From up here you can see its surface rippling between the racks, the blue lights drowning one by one. The sweet copper taste coats your tongue. Your lungs want to cough. You don't let them.

Mira spins slowly on the other end of the line, arms locked over the loop, bad leg dangling and dripping. Her face is inches from the bracket. Her eyes are squeezed shut.

"*Keep going,*" she breathes. "Don't stop. Don't stop."

The bracket answers her. There's a deep metallic groan, and the bolt that shifted before slides out another half-inch. Plaster dust sifts down into your face. The whole assembly tilts a few degrees toward you.

Your fingers find the lip of the crawlway. The corrugated metal is cold and running with water, and the edge is sharp enough that you feel it through your skin. Rain drums on the sheet steel inches above your head. The air up here is clean and wet and sharp, and it's the best thing you've ever breathed.

Below, the door screams all the way open.

The respirator man steps through the fog like he's wading into surf. He's tall, unhurried, in dark tactical gear, and the gray swirls around his thighs. His rifle comes up in a smooth, practiced motion. The weapon light snaps on, and a hard white beam cuts through the haze, slides along the rows, and climbs the cable.

It finds Mira.

"There you are," the calm voice says through the mask. He doesn't fire. The beam holds on her like a spotlight on a stage. "Come down, Mira. You'll fall anyway."

Mira's eyes open. She stares straight into the light and doesn't say a word.

Then the beam moves up the cable, past the bracket, and finds you.

Behind you, in the crawlway, metal creaks. It isn't the bracket. It's the sound of weight settling onto corrugated steel, deliberate and close. The rain on the roof hatch changes pitch, broken around something that's moving.

Lightning flashes again.

In the white glare, you see it clearly this time. The shape by the hatch has come into the crawlway. It's on its knees, twelve feet from you, one hand braced against the ceiling ribs. Rain drips from the hood of a dark coat. The other hand holds something out toward you. You can't tell if it's a weapon or an open palm.

Darkness again. Thunder.

The bracket groans. Another bolt starts to turn.

Mira hangs below you, the cable taut across your chest where you've hooked yourself over the lip, her full weight dragging on your grip. You feel every tremor in her arms travel up the line into yours.

"*Courier.*" A new voice comes from the dark of the crawlway, low and hoarse, pitched under the rain. It's a man. He sounds winded, like he's been climbing too. "Your handler sent me. We've got maybe ten seconds before that bracket goes." A pause. "Leave her, and I can get you out."

Below, the respirator man's rifle light stays fixed on your face.

"Or she comes up," the voice in the dark adds, "and we both find out what she's still not telling you."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I look from the man in the crawlway to Mira, then back at the man with the rifle. "She comes up," I grit out, starting to haul on the cable again. "And she's coming with me."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara’s gaze rested on you without warmth. “The court will hear the terms,” she said. “It will not mistake patience for agreement.”

The Herald lifted his staff. “Her Majesty grants the Ambassador leave to present Velheim’s proposal.”

Lord Daven leaned forward in the gallery, his voice smooth and measured. “The northern routes have cost both kingdoms dearly. A workable accord would serve the realm.”

Commander Ash’s fingers tightened on his sword pommel. “If Velheim seeks concessions, let the Ambassador name them plainly. The border cannot be secured with courtesies.”

Priestess Yuna watched from the alcove, silent for a moment. Then she spoke, her tone calm and even. “Let the terms be heard before judgment is passed.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I offer a tight smile to Commander Ash, then return my gaze to the Queen.* "Velheim seeks no concessions, Commander. Only fair trade." *I turn back to the Queen.* "We propose a shared oversight of the Dragon's Breath Pass, with equal tariffs for both kingdoms."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald struck his staff once against the marble. “The court has heard Velheim’s proposal: shared oversight of the Dragon’s Breath Pass, with equal tariffs.”

Queen Isara’s expression did not change. “Equal tariffs are simple to promise,” she said. “Shared oversight is less so. Who appoints the wardens, and whose law governs when they disagree?”

Lord Daven rose slightly from his seat. “A joint council could settle disputes before they threaten the route. Each kingdom would appoint the same number of wardens.”

Commander Ash gave a humorless snort. “And when Velheim’s wardens delay a patrol, our merchants pay the price. Equal numbers do not make equal loyalties.”

Priestess Yuna’s gaze shifted from Ash to the Queen. “Nor does suspicion make a treaty impossible. The terms should specify how disputes are judged.”

Queen Isara inclined her head by the smallest degree. “Then the Ambassador’s proposal requires particulars before it can be considered. The court will hear how Velheim intends to keep shared authority from becoming a contest of obstruction.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The accusation struck the chamber harder than the Herald’s staff.

Commander Ash’s hand left his sword pommel. “The patrols were lawful,” he said, his voice clipped. “Velheim’s merchants crossed a restricted stretch of water after warnings were issued.”

Lord Daven rose fully from the gallery. “Six weeks of ‘patrols’ have done little to distinguish themselves from a blockade,” he said. “The court deserves to know who authorized them.”

Queen Isara lifted one hand. The chamber fell quiet. “Commander Ash will answer the question,” she said, coldly. “And the Ambassador will remember that the court—not the gallery—sets the order of inquiry.”

The Herald turned toward Ash. “Commander, the court calls for an account of the naval restrictions.”

Priestess Yuna watched Ash without expression. “A warning may justify a delay,” she said. “It does not, by itself, justify six weeks.”

Ash’s jaw tightened. “I acted to prevent weapons and supplies from reaching the northern rebels. If Velheim’s merchants were inconvenienced, that was preferable to letting a border conflict become a war.”

Queen Isara’s gaze shifted to you. “The court has heard the defense. It will now hear whether Velheim disputes the grounds for those restrictions—or merely their duration.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "Velheim disputes the *existence* of any 'restricted' waters, Your Majesty," I state, meeting her gaze evenly. "And the suggestion that our merchants would traffic with rebels is... insulting."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
For a moment, the court held still. Queen Isara’s expression remained composed, but her attention sharpened.

“An insult is not evidence,” she said. “Nor is denial. The court will require the charts and notices on which Commander Ash’s restrictions were based.”

The Herald turned toward the commander. “Commander Ash, the Queen requests the records supporting your claim of restricted waters.”

Ash’s jaw worked once. “The patrol logs are in my possession. The waters were restricted by order of the Crown’s northern command.”

“Then the order should be easy to produce,” Lord Daven said, his smoothness giving way to a harder edge. “And its date should establish whether it preceded the first merchant seizure—or followed it.”

Priestess Yuna regarded Ash from the alcove. “The distinction matters,” she said evenly. “A lawful boundary and a boundary declared after the fact are not the same thing.”

Queen Isara’s gaze settled on the commander. “The records will be presented before this court adjourns. Until then, no further vessel will be detained under an order the court has not examined.”

Ash bowed stiffly. “As Your Majesty commands.”

The Herald struck his staff against the marble. “The court orders the relevant naval records entered for examination. The hearing remains in session.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I allow myself a small, satisfied smirk before turning back to the Queen.* "I trust that means Velheim's merchants will be released, Your Majesty?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara let the question hang for a measured beat. “The court’s order forbade further detentions under an unexamined restriction,” she said. “It did not grant Velheim’s vessels immunity from lawful inspection.”

Commander Ash’s mouth tightened. “Some of the detained ships may still be carrying supplies intended for the rebels.”

“Then the records will show grounds for holding them,” Lord Daven replied. “If they do not, continued detention will look less like security and more like punishment.”

The Queen’s gaze remained on you. “Any vessel for which Commander Ash cannot produce specific cause will be released before sunset. Cargo reasonably suspected of aiding the rebellion may be held separately, with the grounds recorded for this court.”

The Herald struck his staff once. “The court orders the release of vessels lacking documented cause for detention. Any retained cargo will be itemized and reported.”

Priestess Yuna inclined her head slightly. “A narrow order,” she said, “but one that gives the evidence room to speak.”

Ash bowed, stiff and shallow. “The patrol records will be examined.”

Queen Isara’s expression stayed cold. “They will. And if those records fail to support the restrictions, Commander, the court will consider who bears responsibility for the delay.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Priestess Yuna accepted the orders without comment. The choice drew a brief silence from the court: Queen Isara’s gaze sharpened, and Commander Ash’s posture stiffened.
