Yuna examined the papers, first their seals, then the dates and signatures. “These appear to be directives to detain Velheim merchant vessels,” she said evenly. “The date precedes the first reported seizure. The wording makes no distinction between suspected cargo and ordinary trade.”

Commander Ash took a step forward. “Those papers could have been altered. The patrol logs will establish what orders I received.”

Lord Daven’s voice cut in, smooth but firm. “Then the logs can be compared against the document the priestess holds. That is precisely why the court needed evidence.”

Queen Isara lifted her hand before Ash could answer. “Priestess Yuna, can the court rely on the seals?”

“I can describe what I see,” Yuna replied. “I cannot certify their origin from appearance alone. The court should compare them with the Crown’s records.”

The Herald raised his staff. “The intercepted orders will be entered as evidence, pending verification of their seals and provenance.”

Queen Isara’s attention returned to you. “The document’s date and wording matter. So does its chain of custody. The court will examine all three before it reaches judgment.”

Ash’s jaw tightened. “And until then, the patrol logs will speak for themselves.”

“They will be heard beside the orders,” the Queen said coldly. “Not in their place.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I assure Your Majesty, these orders are authentic," I say, my voice steady. "They came directly from a high-ranking officer in Commander Ash's fleet."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara’s gaze stayed on you. “Assurance is not verification, Ambassador. The officer’s name, the original order, and the means by which it reached Velheim will all matter.”

The Herald raised his staff. “The court requests the identity of the officer and an account of the document’s custody.”

Commander Ash’s expression hardened. “A claim that the order came from my fleet is not proof that my command issued it. Until its seal and provenance are verified, the paper proves nothing.”

Lord Daven rose from the gallery. “It proves enough to warrant an inquiry. The patrol logs should reveal whether the order was obeyed—and whether Ash’s account matches the record.”

Priestess Yuna kept the document in her hands, her voice calm. “I can preserve it for comparison with the Crown’s records. I cannot establish its origin without them.”

Queen Isara gave a small, precise nod. “So ordered. The document will remain in Priestess Yuna’s custody until the seals are compared. Commander Ash will produce the patrol logs and the Crown’s copy of the restriction order.”

Ash bowed stiffly. “The records will be brought.”

“They will be examined before the court adjourns,” the Queen said. Her attention returned to you. “If the officer’s identity can be established, the court will hear it. If not, the claim will remain an allegation.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "The officer's name is Captain Valerius," I state, looking directly at Ash. "He was displeased with your conduct, Commander."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Commander Ash’s composure faltered for the first time. “Captain Valerius served under my command,” he said, each word clipped. “His displeasure does not establish that he issued this order.”

Lord Daven’s gaze stayed fixed on Ash. “Nor does denying it establish that he did not. The captain’s testimony could settle the question.”

Priestess Yuna held the document steady. “The name gives the court a person to question. The seal and the Crown’s copy must still be compared.”

Queen Isara considered the matter in silence, then turned her attention to Ash. “Captain Valerius will be summoned to testify. Commander, the court will also hear whether he had authority to issue these directives.”

Ash bowed stiffly. “As Your Majesty commands.”

The Herald struck his staff against the marble. “The court orders Captain Valerius summoned to give testimony. The patrol logs and Crown records remain due for examination.”

Queen Isara’s gaze returned to you. “The court will determine whether Captain Valerius acted on his own, under Commander Ash’s authority, or under an order from the Crown. Until then, the name is a lead—not a verdict.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "Indeed, Your Majesty. A lead is all we ask for, at this juncture." *I offer a slight, deferential nod.* "Perhaps we can now return to the matter of the trade treaty?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara held your gaze for a moment. “The treaty may return to the court’s attention,” she said. “But the trade routes cannot be separated from the restrictions placed upon them. Any accord must account for both.”

The Herald struck his staff. “The court resumes consideration of Velheim’s proposal for shared oversight of the Dragon’s Breath Pass and equal tariffs.”

Lord Daven rose. “A joint council, with equal appointments and a defined procedure for disputes, would answer the Queen’s concern without giving either kingdom sole control.”

Commander Ash’s expression remained hard. “And while that council argues, who commands the patrols? A treaty that leaves security undefined is an invitation to test the border.”

Priestess Yuna regarded the Queen. “The terms could distinguish routine trade oversight from emergency security measures,” she said evenly. “Each would need limits, records, and a way to challenge misuse.”

Queen Isara inclined her head slightly. “A useful distinction. The court will consider a joint council, but Velheim must specify how disputes are resolved and how emergency measures are reviewed. The question of the patrols will remain before the court until the records are examined.”

The Herald lifted his staff toward you. “The court invites the Ambassador to clarify Velheim’s proposed procedures for disputes and emergency measures.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "Velheim proposes a neutral third party mediate all disputes," I suggest, "and that emergency measures be ratified by both kingdoms' representatives *within 24 hours* or be nullified."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara considered the proposal in silence. “A neutral mediator would be acceptable only if both kingdoms agreed to the appointment,” she said. “Otherwise, neutrality would become another matter of dispute.”

Lord Daven inclined his head. “Each kingdom could submit a short list of candidates. The parties would choose from the names appearing on both lists.” His gaze shifted to the Queen. “That would prevent either side from choosing its own judge.”

Commander Ash’s expression hardened. “And a commander facing an immediate threat would be expected to wait for representatives to convene before securing the border?”

Priestess Yuna answered evenly. “The proposal allowed emergency measures to take effect at once. It required review within a day. If neither kingdom ratified them, they would lapse.”

“Unless the danger persisted,” Ash said. “A deadline does not make a threat disappear.”

Queen Isara’s gaze moved to the commander. “Nor does invoking danger make every restriction lawful. The measure could lapse unless both representatives approved an extension, supported by recorded grounds.”

The Herald raised his staff. “The court records Velheim’s proposal: disputes would go to a mutually selected neutral mediator; emergency measures would require ratification by both kingdoms’ representatives within twenty-four hours, or they would lapse.”

Queen Isara’s attention returned to you. “The court will consider those terms. The mediator’s selection and any procedure for extending emergency measures remain to be specified.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "Indeed, Your Majesty. Perhaps the selection could be made from a pre-approved list of scholars, chosen annually?" *I offer, trying to appear reasonable.* "And extensions... perhaps a review every three days?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara considered the proposal, her expression unchanged. “A list chosen jointly and renewed each year would be workable,” she said. “Provided no scholar with a direct interest in either kingdom’s trade or security could serve.”

Lord Daven gave a measured nod. “Each kingdom could nominate the same number of candidates. The final list would require approval from both courts. That would make the mediator’s authority clear before any dispute arose.”

Commander Ash’s mouth tightened. “And a commander would still be bound by scholars’ opinions while the border burned.”

Priestess Yuna regarded him calmly. “The mediator would judge disputes under the treaty. Emergency measures would remain in force during the initial review period. The question is whether they remain justified afterward.”

“Every three days,” Queen Isara said, “the measures would be reviewed by both kingdoms’ representatives. Any extension would require recorded grounds and approval from both. Without that approval, the measures would lapse.”

Ash’s gaze stayed fixed on the Queen. “That leaves security dependent on Velheim’s willingness to cooperate.”

“It leaves extraordinary powers dependent on evidence,” Isara replied. “That is not the same thing.”

The Herald lifted his staff. “The court records the proposed terms: a jointly approved list of neutral scholars, renewed annually; disputes referred to a mutually accepted mediator; and emergency measures reviewed every three days, with extensions requiring approval from both kingdoms’ representatives.”

Lord Daven glanced toward the throne. “A framework with safeguards for both trade and security.”

Queen Isara inclined her head by the smallest degree. “The framework is fit for negotiation. The court will reserve judgment on the treaty until the naval records have been examined and the wording has been drafted.”

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I bow my head slightly.* "Velheim looks forward to a swift resolution, Your Majesty. Perhaps we can return to the naval records, then?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Beyond the stairwell door, footsteps strike concrete two floors below. Three people, moving fast. Their voices blur beneath the alarm, but the sharp click of a radio carries through.

A second sound comes from above: one set of boots, descending slowly.

Mira’s grip tightens on your shoulder. “They know about the garage,” she whispers. “The service tunnel might still be open.”

The boots overhead stop. A shadow cuts across the narrow window in the door.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* "No time for the tunnel." I push Mira gently behind me, pulling my sidearm. "We're going up."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The shadow pulls away from the stairwell window. Above, a radio clicks.

“Fourth-floor door,” a man says. “Two targets. Hold your fire. We need the woman alive.”

Mira goes still behind you. “That isn’t security.”

The footsteps below quicken. A key turns in the lock on the other side of the door, and the narrow pane fills with the silhouette of a rifle.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The stairs rise into a tight concrete shaft. Mira’s breath catches beside you; her injured leg scrapes each step.

Below, the fourth-floor door slams open. “Upstairs,” a voice calls. Three sets of boots hammer onto the stairs.

The lone figure above stops at the fifth-floor landing. A flashlight snaps on, its beam cutting through the railing toward you. Mira flinches.

“Don’t shoot,” the figure says into a radio. “They’re coming to me.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Shit.* "Stay behind me." I push Mira harder, trying to shield her from the light. We need to move. "Keep going!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The flashlight beam holds on the stairwell. At the fifth-floor landing, the figure lowers it just enough to reveal a dark jacket and a rifle held across his chest.

Mira presses close behind you. “That’s Voss,” she whispers. “He’s not with them.”

Voss glances down the stairwell, toward the boots closing from below. “Mira. The fifth-floor door is open. Move.”

A radio crackles beneath you. “Visual on the landing. Take the armed one.”

Voss’s expression tightens. His rifle shifts toward the stairs below, but he doesn’t fire. The fifth-floor door stands ajar behind him; beyond it, the corridor is dark.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The server room hums around you. Blue status lights blink across the racks, and cold air pours from vents beneath the floor. The barricade holds against the door, but the first impact makes its metal frame shudder.

Mira sits against a cabinet, her face pale. “Voss knows another way out,” she says. “If he’s still out there.”

A burst of gunfire cracks through the corridor. Then silence.

Your radio hisses. Voss’s voice breaks through, low and urgent. “The service shaft connects to that room. Back wall, behind the last rack. You have maybe thirty seconds.”

Something heavy strikes the door again. This time, the barricade shifts.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Thirty seconds.* I scan the back wall, then look at Mira. "Can you move?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
“I can crawl,” Mira says. She plants a hand against the cabinet and tries to stand. Her injured leg buckles, but she stays upright against the rack. “Not fast.”

Behind the last row of servers, you can see a square maintenance panel set low in the back wall. Two latches hold it shut. A narrow strip of darkness shows along its bottom edge.

The door takes another hit. The barricade skids across the floor, and a rifle barrel appears through the widening gap. “Mira,” a voice calls. “Come out.”

Your radio crackles once. “Shaft drops to the tunnel,” Voss says. “Don’t take the ladder. Slide.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Here." I push my sidearm into her hand. "You first. Go." I shove the barricade back against the door, buying us a few more precious seconds.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira grips the sidearm, then catches herself against the last rack. The two latches on the maintenance panel snap open under her fingers. She pulls it aside, exposing a shaft barely wide enough for her shoulders. Cold air rises from the dark.

The barricade groans. A rifle fires through the gap; a server screen bursts, scattering glass across the floor.

Mira drops into the shaft and vanishes from sight. A moment later, her voice echoes up. “I’m down. It’s clear.”

Metal tears at the doorframe. The barricade shifts again, leaving room for someone to squeeze through.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I fire a burst at the gap, trying to keep them pinned. "Cover me!" I yell, then dive into the shaft.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Gunfire rips through the widening gap. Someone curses and drops out of sight. Mira fires once from the tunnel below; the shot rings up the shaft, and the rifle at the server-room door falls silent.

The shaft angles steeply through darkness. Cold metal flashes beneath you, then the tunnel floor rushes into view. Above, a man shouts, “They’re in the shaft!”

Mira braces herself against the opposite wall, sidearm trained on the opening overhead. A strip of light cuts across the tunnel behind her.

“Voss says east,” she says. “But there’s someone at the far end.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* I hit the floor hard, wincing. "How far east?" I peer down the tunnel.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
“Maybe sixty meters,” Mira says. “There’s a junction halfway.”

The strip of light at the far end sweeps across wet concrete. A silhouette stands beside a steel door, too distant to identify. Above, the shaft rattles as someone forces the panel wider.

Your radio crackles. “East junction,” Voss says. His voice strains beneath a burst of static. “Turn right. Whoever’s at the door isn’t with me.”

Mira keeps the sidearm aimed down the tunnel. The distant light snaps off.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Right," I grunt. "Let's go." I start moving, staying low, keeping an eye on the ceiling for anyone dropping down.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The tunnel narrows toward the junction. Water drips through a seam overhead, but nothing moves in the shaft behind you yet. Mira limps alongside the wall, one hand dragging against the concrete for balance, the sidearm pointed toward the far door.

A metallic thud sounds above. Then another. Someone is coming down.

Halfway east, a red EXIT sign marks the junction. The passage to the right slopes into darkness. At the far end, the steel door swings inward, and a flashlight beam sweeps low across the tunnel floor.

Mira catches the light on her sleeve and flattens against the wall. “They see us,” she whispers.

Voss’s voice breaks through the radio. “The right-hand passage has a gate. I can open it from here. Keep them away from the junction.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Gate?" I hiss. I glance at Mira, then at the approaching light. "Okay, Mira, cover the junction. Let's see if we can buy Voss some time."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira braces against the wall beside the junction and aims down the east tunnel. The flashlight beam jerks toward her. A shot cracks from the far door, punching dust from the concrete above the EXIT sign.

“Gate’s moving,” Voss says over the radio.

From the right-hand passage comes a grinding motor—and then a hard metallic clunk. The gate stops. In the dark beyond it, a small green indicator turns red.

Mira fires once. The flashlight vanishes, but footsteps keep coming.

“Voss,” she says, “tell me that isn’t locked.”

“It’s jammed,” he answers. “There’s a manual release on your side. Yellow box, beside the frame.”

The shaft behind you rings with the impact of boots on metal. Ahead, a flashlight clicks back on, closer now.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Damn it!" I grab Mira, pulling her back. "Behind the junction! Give me covering fire!" I need to get to that box.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The stairwell gives back only the alarm’s distant pulse and the low hum of ventilation. Then, from below: a metallic clank, followed by measured footsteps climbing.

Mira goes still against your shoulder. The steps pause one landing down. A radio crackles, muffled by concrete.

“Upper levels first,” a voice says. “Check the stairs.”

The footsteps start again. They’re coming up.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* "New plan." I push Mira gently behind me, pulling out my silenced pistol. "Stay quiet."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira presses herself against the wall behind you, jaw tight, one hand clamped over her mouth. The footsteps climb into the red wash of the alarm, slow and deliberate.

A shadow stretches across the landing below. Then a flashlight beam sweeps the stairwell, cutting up the concrete steps toward you.

“Hold,” the voice calls. The footsteps stop. “You hear that?”

Mira’s breath catches. The beam climbs another step. A weapon’s muzzle appears beneath it.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The flashlight snaps upward as the guards hear movement above. “They’re going up!” one shouts. Boots hammer the steps below, closing fast.

Above, the stairwell door stands ajar. A strip of emergency light cuts across the landing, and beyond it, something scrapes against the floor—then goes quiet. Mira’s grip tightens on your shoulder. The alarm keeps pulsing red around you.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Quiet," I hiss, pushing Mira through the door. I glance back down the stairwell, then follow her, pulling the door shut behind us. *Hope this isn't a dead end.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The door shuts with a soft, reluctant click. The stairwell noise dulls—but the boots keep climbing on the other side.

Ahead, the corridor runs beneath flickering emergency strips. A service lift waits at the far end, its indicator dark. To your right, the scraping sound comes again: a rolling cart shifts behind a half-open utility-room door.

Mira leans against the wall, breath tight but silent. Her eyes flick to the lift, then to the utility room.

“Don’t take the lift,” she whispers. “They’ll have it locked down.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The server room seals you in with a wash of cold air and the steady whine of the racks. The barricade holds across the door, but the handle shifts once from the corridor side.

Mira lowers herself beside a cabinet, face pale beneath the emergency lights. She keeps pressure on her injured leg and listens.

Bootsteps pass outside. A pause. Then the scrape of the cart rolls nearer.

Mira leans close, voice barely audible. “There’s a maintenance hatch behind the central rack. It leads to the cable run—but I don’t know where it comes out.”

The door handle turns again. This time, it doesn’t stop.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Alright, show me." I grab her arm, pulling her up. "Now."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira winces as you haul her upright, then points toward the central rack. “There.”

The barricade jolts. Metal scrapes across the floor outside, followed by a sharp knock against the door.

Mira limps to the rack and drops to one knee beside its base. She hooks her fingers beneath a narrow floor panel and pulls. It lifts with a muted click, revealing a dark cable run barely wide enough to crawl through. Cold air rises from below, carrying the smell of dust and hot insulation.

The door shudders again. A voice comes through the gap: “Cut the hinges.”

Mira looks into the opening, then back at you. “It’s the only way out.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* "Go!" I push her toward the opening. "I'll cover you."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira drops into the cable run, biting back a cry as her injured leg catches on the hatch rim. She twists and pulls herself forward into the dark, then looks back up at you.

The barricade shrieks across the floor. A blade bites into the door near its hinges.

“Keep moving,” Mira whispers. “The run narrows ahead.”

A second strike lands. The door bows inward, and a wedge of flashlight beam cuts across the server room floor.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Go! I'm right behind you." I fire a quick shot through the door, hoping to buy us a few more seconds, then drop into the hatch myself.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The silenced shot snaps through the room. On the other side of the door, someone grunts; the blade clatters against the floor. The flashlight beam jerks away.

You drop through the hatch. The cable run is tight and hot, cables brushing your shoulders as you crawl after Mira. Above, the door crashes open. Boots pound across the server room.

“Keep moving,” Mira whispers from ahead. The passage slopes sharply downward, then forks around a thick bundle of conduit. A red status light blinks beyond the left branch. From the right comes a faint rush of air—and, underneath it, the distant clatter of machinery.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Which way?" I hiss, trying to see past her in the cramped space. *This is going to be tight.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira peers past the conduit bundle. The red blink on the left branch catches the cables in brief, uneven flashes.

“Right,” she whispers. “That airflow means it connects to something.”

Behind you, the hatch rattles. A voice echoes down the cable run, closer now: “They went below.”

Mira edges toward the right-hand passage, keeping one hand against the wall. The machinery’s clatter grows louder ahead. Somewhere in the dark, metal grinds against metal.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Let's go then." I push her forward gently, trying to ignore the noise behind us. *This better not be a dead end.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira crawls into the right-hand passage, one elbow dragging against the narrow wall. The airflow strengthens, carrying a sharp smell of oil and hot metal. Behind you, voices spill into the cable run, followed by the scrape of someone forcing the hatch wider.

The passage opens onto a grated maintenance ledge above a machinery bay. Far below, a conveyor belt rattles between heavy rollers. A ladder descends along the wall to a narrow catwalk, and a yellow service door sits across the bay beneath a green exit sign.

Mira pauses at the opening and scans the drop. “That door might lead to the service tunnel,” she whispers. “But we’ll have to cross the catwalk.”

A metallic bang echoes behind you. Flashlight beams begin to jitter through the cable run.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Looks like we're going down." I grab her arm, helping her onto the ledge. "Can you make it?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira catches the ledge with both hands, her injured leg hanging stiffly behind her. “I can,” she whispers, though pain tightens her face. “Just don’t let me rush.”

The ladder shivers under her weight as she starts down, rung by careful rung. Below, the conveyor groans and carries a stream of metal crates beneath the catwalk. Across the bay, the yellow service door remains shut.

Behind you, a flashlight beam cuts through the cable-run opening. A guard’s voice follows it. “There—on the ledge!”

Mira reaches the ladder’s bottom and clings to the side rail, looking toward the catwalk. A loose section of grating hangs near its midpoint, swaying above the moving belt. She glances back up at you, waiting.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* "Go, I'm right behind you!" I pull my pistol, firing a quick shot into the cable run opening to keep their heads down. Then I start down the ladder after Mira.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You ease the stairwell door open a crack and hold your breath. Cold air rises from below, carrying the smell of concrete and old oil. For a second there is nothing — just the alarm hammering somewhere behind you and Mira's weight against your side.

Then you hear them. Not running. Walking. Two sets of boots, maybe three, one floor down, moving slow and careful. A radio clicks. Someone says something you can't make out, low and clipped. The footsteps stop.

Mira's fingers tighten on your jacket. She doesn't speak. Neither do you.

Above you, a door bangs open two flights up. More boots. Faster this time. They're coming down.

The stairwell isn't clear. Not above. Not below. The door at your back is still half-open, and the red light from the corridor spills across the landing at your feet. You have seconds before someone sees it.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* "They're coming from both ends," I whisper. *Think. What's nearby?* I glance around the landing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You sweep the landing in one quick look. Bare concrete. A dripping pipe along the ceiling. To your left, a narrow utility door sits half-hidden behind folded tarps, latch only, no lock. The red light from the corridor pulses across the floor at your feet.

Below, the boots start again. Closer. Above, the faster set hits the next landing and keeps coming down.

Mira’s grip tightens. She doesn’t speak. The half-open door at your back still spills light onto the landing. Seconds left before someone sees it.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: You haul Mira up the stairs. Her bad leg drags and catches on the step. Boots pound harder from below. A shout cuts through the alarm. Above, the other set of footsteps hits the landing you just left and keeps coming. Red light vanishes behind you as the door swings shut. Cold concrete meets your boots. Mira’s breath rasps against your shoulder. The radio stays dead.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Almost there," I lie, pushing us faster. *Another floor. Gotta be another way out.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hit the next landing and the stairwell narrows. A service door stands half-ajar on the right, marked with a faded yellow stripe and a broken keypad. Cold air leaks through the gap. Somewhere beyond it, machinery hums — low, steady, close.

Below, the boots take the turn you just left. A flashlight beam snaps up the shaft and skims the wall a step behind Mira’s heel. Above, the faster set slows. Someone calls a floor number. The voice is near.

Mira’s weight shifts hard against you. Her bad leg buckles on the last step. She catches herself on the rail and doesn’t make a sound. The radio in your ear pops once — a burst of static, then nothing.

The service door drifts an inch wider on its hinge. Through the crack you see a dim utility corridor, a rolling cart, and a second door at the far end with a green exit sign that flickers and dies. The stairwell behind you is no longer empty. Footsteps hit the landing below. A hand finds the rail.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You drag a rolling server rack against the door. It scrapes loud across the raised floor. Mira slides down the wall between two humming cabinets, bad leg stuck out, breath coming short and hot. The room is narrow and cold. Rows of machines blink green and amber. A cable tray runs overhead. The only other way out is a vent grate low on the far wall, screws rusted, and a maintenance hatch in the ceiling you can't reach without standing on something.

Outside, boots hit the corridor. Someone tries the door. The rack holds. A voice calls for a breaching tool. The radio in your ear stays dead.

Mira watches the door, not you. Her hands are empty. The alarm still pulses somewhere beyond the walls, muffled now by steel and fans. You have a minute, maybe less, before they force their way in.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "This isn't good," I mutter, checking the vent. *Too small. Too rusty.* I look up at the hatch. "Can you stand on your own for a second?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You glance at the vent again. The grate is barely wider than your shoulders, screws bled orange, and the duct beyond looks choked with dust. No way both of you go through it. Not fast. Not quiet.

Mira braces one palm on the cabinet and pushes. She gets halfway up before her bad leg folds. She catches the edge of the rack and stays there, half-standing, jaw tight, eyes on you.

"I can hold," she says. Her voice doesn't shake. "Not for long."

Above you the maintenance hatch sits in a square of stained ceiling tile, latch dark with grime, just out of reach unless you climb. The rolling rack you shoved against the door is the only thing tall enough. Moving it means the door is open again.

Outside, metal clinks. Someone sets a tool down. A low voice counts — one, two — and stops. The fans keep humming. The radio in your ear gives you nothing but the soft rush of dead air.

Mira shifts her weight onto her good leg and nods at the ceiling.

"Whatever you're doing," she says, "do it now."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Right." *I need to move that rack.* "Can you brace yourself against the wall, just for a second?" I move towards the door, ready to pull the rack away.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You yank the rack clear. It shrieks across the raised floor. The door swings inward an inch before Mira throws her shoulder into it and braces, good leg planted, bad leg dragging useless behind her. Metal bites the frame. Something heavy thuds against the other side.

“Go,” she says through her teeth.

You climb. The rack wobbles under your boots. Your fingers find the hatch latch, slick with grime, and it sticks. You wrench it. The panel drops on its hinge and cold dark spills down over your face — a maintenance shaft, rungs, a faint draft from somewhere above.

Below you, the door bucks. Mira’s boots skid. A pry bar jams through the gap and scrapes paint. Voices crowd the corridor, close enough now that you hear the click of a safety.

The shaft swallows the light from the server room. The first rung is cold in your hand. Mira is still holding the door, and she is not going to hold it long.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Come on!" I shout down, already pulling myself into the shaft. *It's a tight squeeze.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: You wedge your shoulders into the shaft and the metal closes around you. Cold bites through your jacket. The rung under your left hand is greasy and your boot slips once before it catches. Below, the door gives. Mira’s brace breaks with a sharp crack of metal on tile. She doesn’t make it to the rack. Flashlight beams jump across the server cabinets and one of them swings up, white and hard, pinning the open hatch. A voice shouts your height, your jacket, the woman with the bad leg. The radio in your ear spits static and dies again. The shaft above you stays dark, the next rung just within reach, and the draft pulling at your face smells like rain and exhaust.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Mira! Get up here!" I yell, reaching down a hand even as I scrabble for the next rung. *They're right behind us.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You stretch your hand down into the white glare. Fingers brush nothing but cold air. Mira is on the floor between the cabinets, one arm thrown up against the light, the other pinned under her as boots pour through the door. A gloved hand grabs her collar and hauls her half-upright. She twists once, hard, and her eyes find the hatch.

“Go,” she says. Not a shout. Flat. Final.

Someone fires a round into the ceiling tile beside the shaft. The crack slams through the metal and your ears ring. Sparks spit off the rung above your head. A second flashlight locks onto your reaching arm. A voice below barks for a hook, for cuffs, for the woman alive and the one in the shaft not.

Mira’s mouth moves again. You can’t hear it over the fans and the shouting. The draft from above pulls harder now, rain-smell and exhaust, and the next rung waits in the dark just past your shoulder. Below, they drag her toward the door. Her bad leg leaves a dark smear on the raised floor. The hatch is still open. The light is still on you. They are already looking for a way up.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *No.* "Damn it!" I ignore the bullet hole and dive back down, kicking out at the hands on Mira.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You drop back through the hatch. Your boot drives into the wrist clamped on Mira’s collar. Bone jars under the impact. The grip breaks. She twists free and claws for the rack as bodies surge in around her.

A second pair of hands snatches at your ankle. You kick again. The shaft rings with the strike. Flashlights whip upward. Someone yells to hold fire—she’s too close. A pry bar swings and misses your leg by inches, sparking off the rung.

Mira gets one hand on the rack frame. Her bad leg folds under her. They drag at her jacket. The open hatch floods with white light and shouting. Cold air still pulls from above, but the rungs are behind you now and the floor is right there, crowded and closing.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *They're trying to take her.* "Get off her!" I shout, pulling myself the rest of the way out, grabbing for anything I can use as a weapon.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hit the floor hard between the cabinets. Your hand snatches a loose power cable from the rack—thick, heavy, sparking where it tore free. The nearest man reels from your kick, wrist bent wrong, but two more close in fast. One swings the pry bar at your head. You duck under it and the cable lashes across his face. He stumbles back into the doorframe, blood bright under the flashlight glare.

Mira claws halfway up the rack. A gloved fist catches her hair and yanks her down again. She hits the raised floor with a choked sound. Boots stamp around her. Someone shouts to cuff her now, forget the one in the shaft. The open hatch still spills cold air and rain-smell down over all of you. The radio in your ear crackles once—your handler’s voice, broken, saying a word you almost catch—then dies under the alarm and the shouting. The cable is slick in your fist. They are three steps away and closing.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I swing the cable, aiming for the man with the pry bar again. "Get back!" I yell. *They want her alive, that's something.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s jaw tightened. He took the coal bucket’s handle and eased its weight onto the floor, then set himself between Apprentice and the front door.

“Stay by forge. Grum will hear him.”

He crossed the shop, pulled the door open, and looked out at the visitor without bowing.

“Grum is master smith. State your need. If it must be done soon, it will cost more.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I watch Grum go, then turn to the forge. It *is* hungry. I start carefully shoveling coal in, trying not to make too much dust. "Urgent commission," I mutter. "Always urgent."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
The noble stood beneath the shop sign with a cloth-wrapped bundle in his arms. His cloak was fine, but one cuff bore a dark stain. At the sound of coal settling in the forge, Grum shifted farther into the doorway.

“I need this repaired by dawn,” the noble said. He drew back the cloth to show a sword snapped just above the hilt. “And I need you to remove the maker’s mark.”

Grum studied the break. Its edges were fresh. The mark stamped near the guard belonged to a smith Grum knew—and that smith’s blades did not snap easily.

“Grum can mend steel,” he said. “Grum will not hide mark.”

“I’ll pay twice your rate.”

“Then Grum will turn down twice your coin.” Grum kept his hand on the door. “Tell Grum how blade broke.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
The noble’s demand shifted from the broken blade to a ceremonial sword, finished by morning. Grum’s gaze flicked from the fresh break to the stain on the man’s cuff. He kept his broad frame in the doorway.

“Fine show sword by dawn? No. Grum will not rush steel for your pride. And Grum will not hide that mark.”

The noble’s face reddened. “Do you know who I am?”

“Grum knows whose work you broke.” Grum nodded toward the wrapped hilt. “Tell Grum how it broke. Then Grum will tell you what can be done.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I hear the raised voices. *Ugh, another difficult customer.* I keep tending the forge, making sure the fire is just right. I wonder if Grum will let me try hammering something later.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum heard the steady crackle of the forge behind him. Good heat, held well. He kept his eyes on the noble.

“Blade broke at guard,” Grum said. “That takes force. What did you strike?”

The noble drew the cloth tight around the hilt. “That is none of your concern. I asked for a new sword.”

“By dawn. For show.” Grum glanced at the stained cuff. “Yet you brought this one here first.”

For a moment, the noble said nothing. Then he lowered his voice. “There will be a ceremony tomorrow. I need a sword at my side.”

“Grum has sound blades on rack. You may buy one.” Grum did not move from the doorway. “This one stays as it is. Mark stays too.”

The noble’s grip tightened around the bundle. Grum waited, giving him room to leave—or to tell the truth.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I watch from the forge, pretending to be busy. *Grum is really sticking to his guns on this one.* I wonder if the noble will actually buy a sword off the rack. Probably not.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
The noble looked past Grum toward the rack of finished blades. His grip on the bundle loosened.

“The ceremony is for my brother,” he said. “He died tonight.”

Grum’s eyes returned to the dark stain on the cuff. He did not ask whose blood it was.

“Grum is sorry for your loss,” he said. “But grief will not mend steel by dawn.”

“My father expects me to carry his sword.”

“Then carry it as it is.” Grum nodded at the wrapped hilt. “Break is part of its tale. Mark is too.”

The noble stared at the bundle for a long moment. When he spoke again, the anger had left his voice. “Will you at least make it safe to carry?”

Grum stepped aside just enough to let the man bring the sword in.

“Grum can bind edge. No false mend. No lost mark.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum turned at the cry. He left the noble and crossed the shop in three strides, his eyes going straight to Apprentice’s hand.

“Step back from forge. Show Grum burn.”

He pulled a clean cloth from a shelf and cleared space beside the wash basin. The noble and his sword could wait.

“Cool water, now. Keep hand in it. No ice, no salve.” Grum’s voice stayed low, though his jaw had gone tight. “Grum will tend forge. If burn is deep, Grum will fetch healer.”

He glanced over his shoulder at the noble. “Set sword down or go. Grum has work here.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *My hand stings like crazy.* I pull it back from the forge, whimpering a bit. "It's just a little burn," I say, though it feels like more than that. I put it under the cool water right away. "I'm fine, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum crouched beside the basin. Apprentice’s claim did little to ease his worry, but he kept his voice steady.

“Maybe so. Keep hand in cool water for twenty minutes. Then let Grum see.”

He glanced at the noble, who still stood near the door with the wrapped sword.

“Your blade can wait. Sit, or come back at dawn.”

Grum turned back to the basin and set a clean, dry cloth within reach. He left the forge untended for now; the fire could be built up again.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I keep my hand in the water, wincing. "Sorry, Grum. I wasn't paying attention." I feel really stupid for burning myself.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum shook his head. He remembered enough burns of his own to know how quickly hot iron punished a lapse.

“Do not say sorry. Burns come fast. Keep hand in cool water. Grum will fetch healer.”

He looked toward the noble. “Go for healer. Now. Your sword can wait.”

Grum stayed beside the basin, his hand resting on its rim.

“Grum should have watched forge. We will see to your hand first.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "No, Grum, don't get the healer!" *I pull my hand out of the water for a second, then quickly put it back in.* "It's really not that bad, just stings a lot. I can keep working."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum watched the hand go back beneath the water. He moved the coal shovel away from the basin, out of reach for now.

“Coal can wait. Keep hand in cool water. Grum needs you with both hands fit to work.”

He stayed beside the basin, giving Apprentice room while keeping an eye on the burn.

“When time is up, Grum will look. If skin is pale, numb, or has blisters, Grum will fetch healer. No forge work till then.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "Okay, Grum," I say, trying to sound brave, but my voice still wavers a bit. *It really does sting.* I keep my hand submerged, watching the water.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum drew a stool close to the basin, then checked the forge. Its fire had sunk low, but it would hold. The noble still stood by the door, sword in his arms.

“Set sword on bench. Grum will see to it when hand is safe.”

Grum returned to the basin and sat nearby. He had burns of his own beneath the soot on his knuckles.

“Pain can be loud,” he said. “Grum knows. You did right to speak up.”

He glanced at the small clock above the tool rack. “Keep hand cool. Grum will watch time.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, trying to focus on Grum's words instead of the throbbing in my hand.* "Thanks, Grum," I mumble. I really hope it's not a bad burn. I don't want to be out of commission.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum gave a short nod. He checked the clock, then dipped two fingers into the basin to test the water. It was still cool.

“Grum knows you want to work. But forge will be here when hand heals.”

He drew the clean cloth nearer and looked at the wrapped sword on the bench. The noble could wait; the broken blade was going nowhere.

“Keep hand in water. When time is up, Grum will look at burn. If it needs care, we will get help.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I keep my hand in the water, trying to ignore the tingling. "How long is 'when time is up'?" I ask, my voice a bit shaky. I just want this to be over.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's hands went still on the rag. For a long moment the only sound in the smithy was the forge, breathing its low orange breath against the stone. Then he took the coal bucket by its handle and lifted it one-handed, the way another man might lift a cup, and tipped a heap of black lumps into the firepot. Sparks rose and died.*

"Noble." *He said the word the way some men spat.* "Nobles always say urgent. Urgent for them means Grum drops good work for bad money. Then Grum waits three months to be paid. Then Grum waits more."

*He set the empty bucket down and looked, finally, at the curved blade cooling on the anvil. The steel was a dull, honest gray, and the curve was nearly right. Nearly. He had spent four days on nearly.*

"Stay here. Keep bellows going. Slow and even, not fast." *He jabbed a thick finger toward the blade.* "Grum puts that back in fire. You watch color. When edge goes straw, like old wheat, you pull it out. Not blue. Blue is ruined. Blue means Grum starts over, and Grum is not happy."

*He wiped his palms once more on his apron. It did nothing. He didn't bother with his face, either. Soot in the creases of his knuckles, a burn scar across one tusk-heavy jaw. Let the man see it. Let him see exactly who he was asking.*

*At the doorway to the front room he paused, one hand on the frame, and spoke without turning.*

"And you do not come out front. Not for shouting, not for coin, not if he says your name. Nobles look at young smith and see cheap hands. Grum knows this game."

*Then he ducked under the low lintel and pulled open the front door. Cold morning air rushed in over the threshold. He planted himself square in the gap, arms folded, filling the frame so completely that no one would be stepping past him.*

"Grum is master smith." *His voice was flat as a quenched bar.* "You talk from there. Noble boots do not cross Grum's floor. So. What is so urgent?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I nod, watching Grum go. He's right about nobles. I grab the bellows, pumping them slowly and evenly, just like he said. The fire brightens.*

"Straw, not blue," *I mumble to myself, focusing on the blade. Hopefully, this noble won't cause too much trouble.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The noble was younger than Grum had expected. Twenty, maybe. Fur at his collar, rings on three fingers, and two hired men behind him in matching blue cloaks, standing the way men stood when they'd been told to look dangerous. The young lord's boots were very clean. He stopped a pace short of the threshold. He had clearly meant to walk straight in, and had just as clearly reconsidered.*

"Lord Cassian Venner," *the young man said, as though the name should open doors. When it didn't, he cleared his throat.* "I require a sword. A dueling blade. I need it by dusk tomorrow."

*Grum did not move from the doorframe.*

"Tomorrow." *He let the word sit there.* "Good sword takes weeks. Fast sword breaks. You want sword that breaks, go to market square. Plenty there. Cheap, too."

*Venner's jaw tightened. He reached into his coat, drew out a purse fat enough to strain its drawstring, and set it on the stone step between them. It landed with the heavy, particular clink that only gold made.*

"Payment in full. In advance."

*Grum looked at the purse. He did not bend for it.*

"Gold on step is still noble gold. Noble gold comes with hooks." *He tilted his head.* "City has other smiths. Human smiths. Smiths who bow. Why come to Grum?"

*For the first time, something cracked in the young lord's composure. His eyes flicked down, then back up.*

"Because Edric Harrow's champion carries a blade you made. Two years ago. I've watched him fight with it." *He swallowed.* "It has never lost. And the duel is to first blood, officially. But Harrow's men have been told to aim for the throat."

*Behind Grum, faint through the wall, the bellows wheezed. In, out. Slow and even. Good.*

*He remembered the sword. Long blade, plain guard, a hilt wrapped in dark leather because the buyer had wanted silver wire and Grum had told him silver wire slips when hands sweat. The buyer had grumbled. Then he had paid. Grum had been proud of that one.*

"So." *Grum's voice dropped low.* "You want Grum to make sword to beat Grum's sword."

"I want to live past tomorrow, smith."

*Grum studied him. The rings. The clean boots. The hired men who would not bleed for him when it came to it. And under all that, a boy who was plainly afraid and trying very hard not to show it. Grum hated that he could see it.*

"No new sword by tomorrow. Nobody can do this. Not Grum, not king's smith, not god of forge." *He unfolded his arms, slowly.* "But Grum has blade in back. Old work. Not for sale. Maybe Grum shows it. Maybe."

*He jerked his chin at the purse.*

"Pick that up. Grum does not want it on his step. We talk price after you hold steel, not before. Wait there. Boots stay outside."

*Then the smell reached him, drifting through the smithy door behind him: hot iron, sharp and close. Grum's head turned, fast, his whole body angling toward the back room without leaving the door.*

"Apprentice!" *His voice carried over the forge-roar.* "What color?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*No answer came from the back. Or if one did, Grum could not hear it, because Lord Cassian Venner had found his voice again, and it was louder now.*

"I don't *need* your old work, smith. I need a ceremonial blade. Gilded hilt, my house crest on the guard, ready by tomorrow morning. It's a simple request. Every smith in this city says the same thing, *weeks*, *time*, as though I'm asking you to raise the dead. Name your price and do your job!"

*One of the blue-cloaked men shifted his weight. The other glanced at his employer the way a man glances at a dog that has started barking at a bear.*

*Grum did not raise his voice. He had found, over many years, that he rarely needed to.*

"Before, you said dueling sword. Dusk. Now you say sword for show. Morning." *He held up two thick fingers, then folded one down.* "Story changes, price changes. Grum does not trust man whose story moves like smoke."

*Venner opened his mouth. Grum kept going, low and even, each word set down like a stone.*

"You want to know why no new sword. So. Grum tells you. Steel does not care whose son you are. Steel needs heat. Steel needs time. Steel needs rest, same as men. Rush it, and steel lies to you. Looks good. Shines good. Then it meets real blade and it snaps like dry stick."

*He leaned forward. Only slightly, but his shadow fell across the young lord's clean boots.*

"Pretty sword for show still gets swung, yes? Harrow's man swings at your throat. Your gold hilt, your house crest, all very nice. Blade breaks. Then crest is on floor next to you."

*A long pause. The forge-roar filled it.*

"Shout more if you want. Shouting does not make iron cool faster. Shouting does not make Grum bow."

*But the whole time he spoke, some other part of him was listening past the noble, past the street noise, back through the wall to the forge. The bellows. Was that still the bellows? The smell of hot iron was stronger now, and Grum knew that smell the way he knew his own hands. Close. Very close to the turn.*

*His knuckles whitened on the doorframe. He did not take his eyes off Venner, but he turned his head a fraction and pitched his voice to carry, hard and sharp as a struck bell.*

"Apprentice! Color! Say it loud. Grum needs to hear."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*My eyes are glued to the blade, trying to judge the color. I hear Grum's voice, sharper now.*

"Straw! It's straw, Grum! Just like you said!" *I yell, hoping he can hear me over the noble's complaining.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Relief went through Grum like cold water, though nothing of it reached his face. He did not turn from the door.*

"Good! Pull it now. Tongs, not hands. Set it on bricks by wall. No water. Let it cool slow, like Grum showed you."

*A beat. Then, quieter, almost to himself:*

"Good eyes."

*He looked back at Lord Cassian Venner, who had gone red in the face and seemed unsure whether he had been insulted or ignored. Both, Grum thought. Mostly ignored.*

"Now. Truth." *Grum folded his arms again.* "Which is it? Duel, or show?"

*The young lord's jaw worked. For a moment Grum thought he would turn on his heel and take his gold and his blue-cloaked men to some smith who bowed. Then the shoulders under the fur collar sagged, just slightly.*

"Both," *Venner said.* "The duel is at dusk. But my father insists I carry a blade bearing our crest. Gilded. Every Venner who has ever fought for the family's honor has carried one. If I show up with anything else, he'll disown me, win or lose." *His mouth twisted.* "Assuming I live to be disowned."

*Grum was quiet for a long moment. He had heard many stupid things from nobles over the years. This one was not the stupidest. But it was close.*

"So. Father wants pretty. Harrow wants blood. You want to live." *He shook his head slowly.* "Only one of these matters. Father does not bleed tomorrow. You do."

*He scratched at the burn scar on his jaw, thinking. The forge-roar behind him had eased. Iron cooling. Good.*

"Grum makes you deal. Grum has old blade. Good steel. Tested steel. Blade stays as it is. Nobody touches edge." *He held up one finger.* "Gold on hilt, Grum can do. Thin leaf, over old guard. Not heavy. Not fine work. But it shines. Father sees gold, father is happy."

*A second finger.*

"Crest, Grum cuts into guard. Not deep. Not pretty like court smith. But it is there. Any fool looking will see it."

*Venner's eyes had gone sharp and bright. Hope, Grum thought sourly. He did not like being the cause of noble hope.*

"Price is old blade, plus one night of Grum's work. Grum does not sleep tonight. You pay for that." *A third finger, and his voice hardened.* "And two more things. Your men wait in street. Not at Grum's door. They look at Grum's shop like they own it."

*The nearer blue cloak had the grace to look at his feet.*

"And Grum's name stays out of your mouth. Harrow asks who made your sword, you say you found it. Nobles fight nobles. Smith does not stand in middle. Smith gets crushed in middle."

*He stepped back half a pace, just enough that the doorway was no longer entirely filled with him, and gestured with his chin toward the street.*

"Think. Then say yes or no. But say it fast. Grum has blade on bricks and merchant's curve still not right, and day is getting old."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I hear Grum's side of the conversation, mostly the raised voices, and then his low, steady tone. I'm proud I got the color right. I carefully use the tongs to set the blade on the bricks, watching the metal cool.*

"Straw, not blue," *I say again, quieter this time. Grum's right, the day is getting old. I hope this noble hurry's up.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Lord Cassian Venner looked at the purse on the step. Then at his men. Then, for a long time, at Grum. The street noise washed around them: a cart wheel, a dog, someone selling onions badly.*

"Yes," *he said at last.* "All of it. Your terms."

*He bent and scooped up the purse. It was the first honest labor Grum had seen him do.*

"Keep gold till noon tomorrow." *Grum did not unfold his arms.* "You come back, you hold blade, you swing it. If it sits right in your hand, then we talk price. If not, you walk and Grum keeps nothing but lost sleep." *He jerked his chin at the blue cloaks.* "Men wait at corner. Not here. Send drawing of crest by boy, within hour. Clean lines. Grum cuts what Grum sees. Bad drawing, bad crest."

*Venner nodded, stiff, and turned. His men followed him down the street, and the taller one glanced back once, not at the lord but at the smithy door, with something like respect. Grum shut the door on all of them.*

*He stood a moment in the dim front room, breathing out slow. Then he ducked back under the lintel into the heat.*

*The curved blade lay on the bricks where it belonged. Grum crouched beside it, not touching, only looking. He turned his head this way and that, catching the forge-light along the steel. The color ran even from tip to heel: pale straw, old wheat, no bruise of blue creeping in at the thin edge where it always wanted to start. He looked at it longer than he needed to.*

"Straw," *he said.* "Tip to heel. Even."

*He stood, knees cracking.*

"Grum knows men with ten years at forge who still pull blue. They get scared, they wait too long, they think one more breath of fire makes it better. Fire does not make better. Fire only makes more." *He tapped his temple with one blackened finger.* "You pulled when steel said pull. That is whole trade, right there. Rest is just sweat."

*Then his face settled back into its usual heavy lines, and he crossed to the far corner of the smithy, where an old iron-banded chest sat under a pile of spare aprons and broken tongs no one had thrown out. He shoved the pile aside with his boot. The lid groaned when he lifted it.*

*Inside, wrapped in oilcloth gone dark and stiff with age, lay something long.*

*Grum did not unwrap it right away. He only rested his hand on it.*

*Eight years. Eight years since a quiet man with a soldier's shoulders had stood at that same front door, paid half in copper and half in promises, and said he would be back for it after the spring campaign. Grum had made him the best blade he knew how to make. The spring campaign had ended. The quiet man had not come back. Grum had never asked anyone why. He had not needed to.*

"Blade Grum made long time back," *he said, not looking up.* "Man who asked for it did not come for it. Grum kept it. Oiled it every winter." *His thumb moved once over the cloth.* "Steel should be used. Hung on wall, steel is sad. Grum thinks... better noble boy lives with it than it sits in box one more year."

*His mouth twisted around the word noble, as if it tasted of ash. But he lifted the bundle out and laid it across the workbench, gentle as a man setting down a sleeping child.*

"Now. Bad news." *He turned, fists on his hips.* "We do not sleep tonight. Curve blade waits. Merchant waits. Merchant can wait. He has waited this long, he can learn more of it."

*He pulled open a narrow drawer beneath the bench and began setting things out: a pot of glue that smelled like boiled hooves, a soft brush, a little book of gold leaf thin as moth wings, a row of small steel chisels.*

"Gold leaf wants no fire. Wants clean hands, slow breath, and no wind. Sneeze once, gold is gone. Crest wants sharp chisel and patience." *He glanced over at his apprentice, one brow lifting over a heavy-lidded eye.* "Boy comes with drawing soon. While we wait, you go wash. Hands, arms, face. All soot off. Then eat something. Bread, cheese, whatever is there."

*A pause. Then, gruffer:*

"You hold light for Grum tonight. Maybe, if hands stay steady, Grum lets you lay first leaf." *He picked up the smallest chisel and squinted down its edge.* "Or maybe you want only bellows and sleep. Say now. Grum does not ask twice."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The chisel hit the floor before the cry had finished leaving the apprentice's throat.*

*Grum crossed the smithy in three strides. He did not remember taking them. One moment he stood at the bench, and the next he had the apprentice's wrist in his hand, firm but careful, turning it toward the forge-light. The skin across the palm and the heel of the thumb had gone an angry, shining red, already tightening.*

*His stomach dropped. His voice did not.*

"Show Grum. Hold still."

*He looked fast and close: the edges, the color, whether any patch had gone white or waxy. It had not. Red and raw, and it would blister badly, but it had not gone past that. Something in his chest unclenched a single notch.*

"Not slack tub." *He steered them away from the quench barrel with its black, scale-flecked water.* "Slack tub is dirty. Burn plus dirt is worse burn."

*He hauled the drinking bucket off its hook by the back door, the clean one, and set it on the bench, then guided the burned hand down into it without letting go of the wrist.*

"In water. Keep it there. Long time. Grum means long. Count to hundred, then count again, then again. Burn keeps cooking under skin even after fire is gone. Water stops it cooking."

*He stayed close, a broad wall of heat and soot at the apprentice's shoulder, one hand still resting on their forearm to keep the palm under.*

"It hurts more in water first. Then less. Breathe slow. Like bellows. Slow and even. You know how."

*While the hand soaked, he reached across with his free arm and dragged the clean linen off the shelf, the good linen he kept for polishing finished work, and tore a long strip from it without a second thought.*

"When hand comes out, no butter. No grease. Old women say butter. Old women are wrong. Butter keeps heat in." *He shook out the linen strip.* "Grum wraps it loose. Clean cloth, loose, so skin can breathe. Blisters come tonight. Big ones. You do not pop them. Blister is skin making its own bandage. Leave it be."

*He was quiet a moment. Then he turned his own left hand over and held it beside the bucket, palm up. Old shiny scars crossed it like a map of rivers.*

"First one. Grum was younger than you. Grabbed bar at wrong end. Cried like baby goat." *A grunt that was almost a laugh.* "Old smith who taught Grum said, now you know fire is real. Every smith learns it once in hand. After that, head never forgets."

*His eyes went back to the burn, sharp and watching.*

"But listen. If skin goes white. If it goes hard like old leather. If fever comes, or red lines run up arm. You tell Grum. No brave face. Then Grum takes you to healer, and Grum does not care what healer costs."

*Behind them the forge muttered on, and on the bench the gold leaf lay forgotten in its little book. Grum glanced at it once, then away, as if it had said something foolish.*

"Tonight you do not hold light. You sit. On stool, there, where you see bench. You watch Grum work. Watching is learning too." *His voice went gruff.* "Noble boy's sword can wait one hour. Your hand cannot."

*He tightened his grip on the wrist just slightly, keeping the palm under the water, and did not move from the apprentice's side.*

"Now. Count out loud. Grum wants to hear it. One."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*The cold water stings, making me gasp. I try to pull my hand back, but Grum's grip is firm. I wince, tears pricking my eyes, and start to count, my voice shaky.*

"One... two... three..."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's grip did not loosen. Not when the apprentice's arm jerked against him, not when the breath hitched. He had held hot iron steady through worse, and this mattered more than any iron.*

"Four," *he said, low, counting with them.* "Five. Good. Pulling back is body being stupid. Body thinks water is enemy. Body is wrong. Grum holds, so you do not have to fight it. Just count."

*He saw the tears. He pretended, with great care, that he did not.*

"Six. Seven." *A pause.* "Tears are fine. Tears are only water. Put them in bucket too. Grum does not mind. More water, better."

*It was a bad joke. He knew it was a bad joke. He said it anyway, because the old smith had said something just as bad to him once, thirty years ago, over a bucket much like this one, and Grum had laughed through snot and forgotten for one breath that his hand was on fire.*

*Under the counting, something heavier sat in him. He had been at the door. Talking to noble boy, listening for straw and blue, and then back at the bench, fussing over glue and gold, telling the apprentice to wash and eat and sit while the forge was still roaring. He had not said, "Mind the fire." He always said it. Today he had not. His jaw tightened around the thought, and he set it aside the way he set aside a cracked blank. Later. Look at it later.*

"Nine. Ten. Say numbers, Grum says them with you. Eleven."

*From the front of the shop came a sharp rapping at the door. Small knuckles, quick and impatient. Noble's boy, with the drawing.*

*Grum did not turn his head.*

"Wait!" *he bellowed at the wall, loud enough that dust sifted from the rafters.* "Stand there! Grum comes when Grum comes!"

*The rapping stopped.*

"Twelve." *His voice dropped back to its low, even rumble, as if nothing had happened.* "Door can wait. Drawing can wait. Noble can wait. Whole city can wait. Thirteen."

*He dipped his free hand into the bucket beside the apprentice's, testing. Already the water had gone from cold to cool, the burn giving its heat away. Without letting go of the wrist, he hooked a tin cup off the shelf, reached behind him to the rain barrel by the back door, and poured fresh cold in slow, at the far side of the bucket so it would not slap the raw skin.*

"Fourteen. Water gets warm, Grum makes it cold again. You only count. That is your whole job now. Easy job. Best job in smithy." *A grunt.* "Grum's job is harder. Grum has to listen to you count badly."

*He watched the hand under the surface, the red shining up through the water. Still red. Not white. Not waxy. He let himself breathe.*

"Fifteen. Keep going. Grum is right here."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*The water is still cold, but the stinging is easing a little. Grum's firm grip is actually a comfort. I take a deep breath, trying to steady my voice as I continue counting.*

"Sixteen... seventeen... eighteen..." *I can't help but glance at the door when the rapping stops. Grum's yell was impressive.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum saw the glance toward the door. His mouth moved at one corner, not quite a smile.*

"Yes. Grum yells good." *He poured another slow cup of cold into the far side of the bucket.* "Grum yells at goats. At nobles. At rain. Rain never listens. Boy listened. Boy is smart."

*He raised his voice again, not a bellow this time, just enough to carry through the wall.*

"Boy! Slide drawing under door. Then go home. Tell lord Grum has it."

*A pause. Then the faint scrape of parchment on stone, and quick feet going away down the street. Grum grunted, satisfied, and forgot the door as if it had never been there.*

"Nineteen. Twenty." *He watched the red skin under the water, still angry, still shining, but no worse.* "Keep numbers going. If voice gets tired, Grum counts, you breathe. Either way works."

*He was quiet for a stretch, counting under his breath. Twenty-one. Twenty-two. The forge muttered, low and sulky, having been ignored too long. Then he spoke again, and his voice was lower still, rough at the edges.*

"Grum did not say mind fire today. Every day Grum says it. Mind fire, mind fire, like old crow. You roll eyes. Today, head was at door, with noble and gold and crest. Grum forgot." *His thumb moved once, gently, against the apprentice's forearm where he held it.* "So. That is on Grum. Not on you. Hear this, and keep it. Burn is not you being stupid. Burn is fire being fire, and Grum not watching."

*He did not look up from the bucket while he said it. It was easier to say to water.*

"Twenty-three. Twenty-four. Twenty-five."

*He let one number pass unspoken, the one with too many sounds in it, and went on as if he hadn't.*

"Twenty-eight. Twenty-nine. Thirty." *A grunt.* "Grum skips some. Do not tell old smith. Old smith is dead, but he would find out."

*He reached behind him again without letting go and dragged the stool over with his boot, scraping it across the stone until it sat right behind the apprentice's knees.*

"Sit. Hand stays in. Grum stays here. We do whole hundred, then more. Then Grum looks. Then wrap." *He jerked his chin at the bench, at the forgotten gold leaf and the long bundle in its oilcloth.* "Old blade waited eight years. It waits one more hour. Blade has good manners. Better than noble."

*He dipped the cup again. Cold water, slow, at the far edge.*

"Thirty-one. Keep going. Grum is not going nowhere."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I try to shift my weight on the stool, wincing a little. Grum's words about the burn not being my fault make my throat tighten. I just nod, trying to focus on the counting.*

"Thirty-two... thirty-three... thirty-four..." *My voice is still a bit shaky, but the sting is definitely less now. I'm grateful for the cold water.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Thirty-four. Thirty-five. Grum listened to the numbers the way he listened to steel under the hammer, hearing past the sound for what lay under it. The shake was still there, but thinner now, and the breath between numbers came slower.*

"Better," *he rumbled.* "Voice is steadier. Grum hears it. Sting goes down, yes? That is water doing its work. Thirty-six."

*He dipped the cup and poured again, slow, at the far side of the bucket. The skin under the surface was still that furious shining red, but the edges had stopped creeping outward. He watched it the way he watched straw color, patient and suspicious, waiting for it to lie to him.*

*It did not.*

"Thirty-seven. Thirty-eight." *A pause, then, because the silence between numbers was long and the apprentice's shoulders were still tight as a drawn bowstring:* "Old smith. Grum never says her name to you. Horga. Big woman. Bigger than Grum. Arms like tree roots, voice like rockfall." *He snorted.* "She burned bread every morning. Every single one. Master of forge, and could not bake one loaf. Forty."

*He had, in fact, skipped thirty-nine. He did not correct it.*

"Horga said, fire is honest. Fire never pretends to be cold. Only people pretend." *His thumb moved once more on the apprentice's forearm, slow.* "So we do not pretend. Hurts, you say hurts. Grum does not think less of you. Grum thinks more."

*They counted on. Fifty. Sixty. The forge settled into a low, sulking glow, and outside the street noise thinned as the day wore toward afternoon. Twice more Grum poured cold from the rain barrel. Once his knee cracked loud as a snapped stick when he shifted his weight, and he muttered something in orcish that was probably not polite.*

*At one hundred he did not let go right away. He made them count to twenty past it, just to be sure. Then, carefully, he lifted the wrist and brought the hand up out of the water, into the forge-light, turning it slow.*

*Red. Swollen along the heel of the thumb, already puffing where the blisters meant to come. But no white. No waxy patch. No gray. He looked at it for a long moment, longer than he needed to, the same way he had looked at the curved blade on the bricks.*

"Good." *The word came out rougher than he meant.* "Bad burn. Not deep burn. Skin will heal. Hand will work. Few weeks, you swing hammer again. Maybe leave scar." *He glanced at his own river-mapped palm, then back.* "Scar is fine. Scar means you are real smith now. Horga would say so."

*He took up the strip of good linen and wrapped it loosely, never tugging, laying each turn flat so nothing pressed on the raw heel. His big soot-black fingers were slow and exact, as careful as they would be with gold leaf. He tucked the end in and did not tie it.*

"Loose, see? No knot. Knot pulls." *He guided the wrapped hand up and rested it against the apprentice's other shoulder.* "Keep hand high. Up by heart, not down on knee. Down, blood rushes, hand throbs like drum. Up is better. And tonight, if it throbs, you wet cloth again. Cold. Grum puts bucket by your stool."

*He hooked the bucket with one finger, emptied it out the back door, refilled it from the rain barrel, and set it on the floor beside the stool. Then he stood a moment, looking down, fists loose at his sides.*

"Hungry? Grum brings bread. Cheese. You eat with one hand. Good practice. Smiths need two hands, but must know how to live with one."

*Only then did he turn toward the front room. He ducked under the lintel and came back a moment later with the folded parchment the noble's boy had slid beneath the door. He opened it by the forge-light, frowning.*

*It was a heron. Or it was meant to be a heron. It stood on one leg inside a shield, and its neck bent in a way no bird's neck had ever bent, and there was a small blot where the drawer had clearly sneezed.*

*Grum stared at it for a long time.*

"Noble house. Old blood. Gold and rings and hired men." *He turned the parchment sideways, then back.* "And this is their bird."

*He held it out where the apprentice could see it from the stool, one heavy brow climbing.*

"Tell Grum true. Is that heron, or is that goose that fell off roof?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I look at the drawing, then at Grum, then back at the drawing. My hand still throbs a little, but the cool linen feels good. I can't help but crack a small smile.*

"It's... definitely a bird, Grum. A very... unique bird." *I pause, then add,* "Looks like a goose that had a bad day, if you ask me."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's laugh came up out of him like a bellows-breath, short and rough, and it surprised him as much as anyone. It rattled around the smithy and set the forge muttering.*

"Goose that had bad day." *He shook his head slowly, still looking at the parchment.* "Yes. Goose fell off roof, landed on shield, and some old Venner looked at it and said, good. That is us. Paint it on everything."

*He laid the drawing flat on the bench beside the oilcloth bundle and pinned its corners with two spare chisels. Then he stood over it, arms folded, the humor fading into the heavy, frowning look he gave any piece of work that had gone wrong before it ever reached him.*

"Grum told lord, Grum cuts what Grum sees." *He grunted.* "But Grum's hands will not cut this. Hands have pride, even when mouth does not."

*He plucked a stub of charcoal from the clutter on the shelf and bent close. His strokes were quick and sure, nothing like his slow, blunt speech. The neck came first, drawn fresh beside the old one: a long S-curve, folding back on itself the way a real heron's did when it stood still in the reeds. Then the leg, one straight and thin, the other tucked up high under the body instead of jutting out sideways like a broken chair leg. A sharp bill. A narrow head. He did not bother with feathers. Steel could not hold feathers at that size, not in one night.*
