"There." *He tapped the new bird with the charcoal.* "Heron neck bends like this. Folds, like rope laid down. Heron stands on one leg because other leg is warm under belly. Not because it broke it."

*He glanced at the stool, then back at the parchment.*

"Lord sees this, he sees his bird. Father sees his bird. Nobody says, why is heron better now? Nobles never look close. Only smiths look close." *A snort.* "And herons. Herons would be glad."

*He left the charcoal on the bench and crossed to the shelf by the back door. Half a loaf sat there under a cloth, and a wedge of hard yellow cheese with a rind like old boot leather. He sawed off thick slices with his belt knife, set them on the little wooden board he used for holding rivets, and brought it over. He set it on the upturned crate within easy reach of the stool, on the side of the good hand.*

"Eat. Slow. One hand." *He pointed a blackened finger at the wrapped hand resting up against the apprentice's shoulder.* "That one stays up. Grum sees it drop, Grum says so. Loud. Like at goats."

*Then, at last, he turned to the bundle.*

*He did not hurry. He worked the stiff oilcloth open one fold at a time, and it crackled faintly as it gave, releasing a smell of old oil and cold iron and something like dust. Beneath it lay the sword.*

*It was not a pretty thing, the way court swords were pretty. The guard was a plain bar of dark steel, only slightly swept toward the blade. The grip was wrapped in black leather, worn smooth nowhere, because no hand had ever worn it. But the blade itself caught the forge-light and held it, gray shading to faint blue, and along its length ran a soft, rippling pattern like water moving under ice. It was straight and long and very quiet, the way good steel was quiet.*

*Grum lifted it by the grip and turned it once in the light. For a moment he did not look like a half-orc glaring at nobles through a doorway. He looked like a man meeting an old friend at a crossroads.*

"Best work Grum ever made." *His voice had gone low.* "Before you came. Before shop had new roof." *He tilted it so the ripples ran like a stream.* "Man never named it. He said, name comes after first fight. So it never had name."

*He was silent a breath.*

"Grum calls it Patience. Because that is all it ever did."

*He laid it across the bench, next to the charcoal heron, and set the gold leaf book and glue pot beside it. Then he dragged a second stool to the bench, sat down heavily enough that the wood complained, and rolled his shoulders like a man settling in for a long night.*

"So. No light for you tonight. But you still have job." *He jerked his chin at the parchment, then at the plain, empty guard of the sword.* "Grum cuts heron into steel. You watch from there. Straw eyes, yes? Good eyes. When bird looks wrong, you say. When bird looks like goose again, you say fast, before Grum cuts too deep."

*He picked up the smallest chisel and squinted down its edge, then looked over at the stool from under one heavy brow.*

"Deal? Or you only want bread and sleep. Grum does not ask twice." *A pause. His mouth moved at the corner.* "Grum asks maybe one and half times. For you."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I watch Grum work, fascinated by his charcoal sketch of the heron. It's so much better than the noble's attempt. He hands me the bread and cheese, and I start to eat, carefully, with my good hand.*

"Deal, Grum," *I say, my mouth full of bread. I'll stay awake. This is important.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum watched the first bite go down, then gave one short nod, as if a job had been finished properly.*

"Good. Eat all. Hungry smith makes angry steel."

*He turned the sword on the bench so the guard faced him and the blade lay pointing away, toward the wall, the way Horga had taught him. Never point the edge at yourself, and never at anyone you'd miss. He set a lamp on either side of the guard, trimmed both wicks, and bent so close to the steel that his breath fogged it faintly before it cleared.*

"First, Grum scribes. Scratch only. Thin as hair." *He lifted a fine steel point from the row of chisels, not a chisel at all but a sharpened needle set in a wooden handle.* "Scratch can be fixed. Deep cut cannot. Steel remembers every cut. Wood forgives. Steel does not."

*He glanced once at the parchment, then at the guard, then at the parchment again, measuring with his eyes. Then he set the point to the metal.*

*The sound it made was tiny, a thin high whisper, like a mouse walking on ice. His hand moved slowly, and the scratch came up bright silver against the dark steel. The long curve of the neck went first, folding back on itself. He stopped halfway, lifted the point, breathed, and began again exactly where he had left off.*

*The forge had sunk to a low red murmur. Outside the shutters, the afternoon had gone amber and was starting to slide toward dusk. Somewhere down the street a woman was calling children home, and the children were ignoring her.*

"Horga cut crests for lords, long time back," *Grum said without looking up. His voice was low and even, matched to the pace of his hand.* "Grum watched from stool. Same stool. Same as you. Burned hand, too. Left one." *The point whispered on.* "She said, bird on steel is not bird. Is shadow of bird. Cut only what makes shadow. Leave out rest."

*The body came next, a narrow teardrop. Then the one straight leg, thin as a reed. He paused over the tucked leg for a long time, the point hovering a hair above the metal, and then set it down in three short strokes, nothing more. The shadow of a leg. It was enough.*

*At some point during the bill he glanced sideways, quick and sharp, toward the stool. His eyes went to the wrapped hand, checking whether it still rested high against the shoulder, and then back to the steel before the look could turn into fussing.*

"Bill is hard part," *he muttered.* "Too long, bird looks like sword. Too short, bird looks like goose. Goose again. Always goose, this house."

*He drew it. Stopped. Drew one hair more.*

*Then he set the needle down, straightened with a groan from somewhere deep in his back, and lifted the sword by its grip. He turned the guard toward the stool and brought it down to eye level, tilting it so the lamplight caught the silver scratches and threw the little heron into sudden bright relief against the dark steel. It stood there on its reed leg, neck folded, bill sharp, and waited.*

"Now. Tell Grum true." *His voice was quiet but firm.* "Heron, or goose? Look at neck. Look at leg. Look at where bill meets head. Small wrong there looks big wrong later, when chisel goes deep."

*He held the blade perfectly still, the way he'd held the apprentice's wrist over the bucket, and did not rush them.*

"Take time. Eat cheese while you look, if you want. Grum waits. Patience waits." *The corner of his mouth moved.* "Both of us are good at it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I chew my bread, looking closely at the heron Grum etched into the guard. It's beautiful. So much better than the original drawing. I feel a warmth spread through me, despite the ache in my hand.*

"It's a heron, Grum. Definitely a heron." *I say, my voice steady. "The neck is perfect. No goose in sight."*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum took the coal bucket and set it beside the forge. He banked the fire around the curved blade, then wiped his hands and went to the front door.

“Stay by forge,” he told Apprentice. “Grum has door.”

He stopped at the threshold, blocking the view into the shop.

“Grum is smith,” he called out. “Speak your need plain. Gold buys steel, not bows.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I nod, relieved to be rid of the heavy bucket.* "Got it, Grum."

I stay by the forge, poking at the coals with a rod. I wonder what kind of "urgent commission" a noble would have. Probably something shiny and useless.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum looked past the noble’s fine cloak to the sword in his hands. Its blade had snapped a finger’s width above the guard. Dark stains marked the grip.

“Must be mended by dusk,” the noble said. “Name your price.”

Grum took the broken pieces. The edge was chipped, but the break was clean. He could weld it. Whether it would hold was another matter.

“Grum will name price when Grum knows task,” he said. “Who broke it?”

The noble’s jaw tightened. “The man who took my son.”

Grum glanced back toward the glow of the forge. The curved blade was still in the coals, and there were only so many hours of light left.

“Come in,” Grum said. “Keep cloak clear of fire. Tell Grum all of it.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum laid the broken sword on his bench. The noble’s new demand had come with a raised voice and a pointed finger. Grum looked at the finger, then at the blade.

“Grum heard first task. Mend sword by dusk. Now lord wants fine sword by dawn.” He folded his arms. “Steel needs heat, time, and care. Gold buys work. It does not buy more night.”

He shifted between the noble and the forge. The curved blade still waited in the coals, and he had no wish to let anger ruin that work.

“Grum can mend this blade, or start new one. Grum will not call rushed steel sound. Choose.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I watch from the forge, trying to look busy but really just listening. This noble is a piece of work. I grab the tongs and move the curved blade Grum was working on to the side, away from the direct heat, so it doesn't get ruined while he's dealing with this guy.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum saw that the curved blade had been moved clear of the hottest coals. He gave Apprentice a brief nod, then faced the noble again.

The noble lowered his hand. “The man who took my son sent a second message. He wants a sword with my house crest at dawn. He’ll trade my son for it.”

Grum studied the broken blade on his bench. The break was clean, but its grip bore the crest already.

“Then say that first,” Grum said. “Grum can mend this by dusk. Grum can clean crest and fit new grip by dawn. It will look fine. It will not be safe in fight.”

The noble’s gaze fixed on the sword. “He only asked that it bear the crest.”

Grum drew the blade closer to the forge. “Then Grum needs coin for steel, and all words from man who took son. Not one left out.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wipe sweat from my brow with a sooty hand. This is getting intense. I go to the water bucket and bring it over, setting it near Grum in case he needs to cool anything quickly, or just wants a drink.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum glanced at the water bucket, then at Apprentice. He gave a small nod. It would serve for cooling the tongs; the broken blade would need slower care.

The noble drew a folded note from his cloak and set it on the bench. Grum opened it with soot-stained fingers. The demand was plain enough: a sword bearing the house crest, delivered at dawn to the old bridge. Beneath it was a smaller line.

*Come alone.*

Grum looked up. “Man who took son wants crest, not sharp edge. Why?”

“I don’t know,” the noble said. His anger had thinned into fear. “Will you make it?”

“Grum will mend blade and fit grip. Grum will not send you to bridge blind.” He tapped the note. “Did man send proof son lives?”

The noble hesitated, then reached into his cloak again. Grum kept one hand on the bench and waited.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum turned at the cry. He left the sword on the bench and crossed to the forge, his gaze going straight to Apprentice’s hand.

“Step back from fire. Show Grum hand.”

The burn looked bad. Grum took a clean jug from the shelf and poured cool water gently over the injured skin, catching the runoff in a basin. He kept the stream steady.

“No ice. Keep hand here. If cloth is stuck, leave it.”

Behind him, the noble began to speak. Grum cut him off without looking back.

“Fetch healer. Now. Grum will see to sword when hand is safe.”

His jaw set as he reached for more water. The blade could wait; Apprentice could not.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince, but keep my hand under the water. It stings like crazy.* "It was stupid, I wasn't thinking." *I look at Grum, then at the noble. I feel bad about messing things up.* "Sorry, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum kept the cool water flowing over Apprentice’s hand. He looked up at the apology, his brow furrowed.

“Grum has burned hands too. Do not waste breath on shame. Keep hand cool.”

At the door, the noble still stood with his cloak clasped tight. Grum turned his head.

“Why are you still here? Fetch healer. Grum will work on sword when you get back.”

The noble glanced at the broken blade, then hurried out. Grum drew a stool close to the basin without touching Apprentice’s injured hand. The forge needed tending, and dawn would come soon enough, but neither mattered more than the burn.

“Grum is here,” he said. “Tell Grum if pain grows worse.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, trying to breathe through the pain. My hand is throbbing. I feel a bit light-headed.* "Thanks, Grum." *I lean against the workbench with my free hand, trying not to look at the burn.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum saw Apprentice lean against the bench and pulled the stool closer. He steadied it with his boot and held out his arm, careful not to reach for the burned hand.

“Sit, lad. If head spins, tell Grum.”

The jug was nearly empty. Grum took another clean one from the shelf and kept cool water running over the burn. He glanced toward the door, listening for the noble’s return.

“Grum has you,” he said. “Sword can wait.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I slowly lower myself onto the stool, still keeping my hand under the water. The throbbing is still bad, but the cool water helps. I look at Grum, a little surprised by his calmness. He's usually so focused on his work.* "It feels... hot. Like it's still burning."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum kept the water flowing, watching Apprentice’s face as closely as the burned hand. The light-headed look worried him more than the complaint.

“Burn can feel hot long past flame,” he said. “Keep hand in cool water. Breathe slow. If head spins more, tell Grum.”

He glanced toward the door. The noble had better be running.

“Lord went for healer. Grum stays here.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, focusing on my breathing. The pain is a bit much. I try to distract myself.* "Is the curved blade okay? I moved it off the coals."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum glanced at the curved blade, resting clear of the hottest coals.

“Blade is safe. Good work. Grum can heat it once more.”

He set a fresh jug within reach and kept the cool water running over Apprentice’s hand. He had seen burns worsen beneath soot and cloth; he would leave the skin alone until the healer came.

“Look at Grum, not hand. Breathe slow. Steel can wait.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I look at Grum, trying to focus on his face instead of the pain in my hand. He looks serious, but his voice is calm. It actually helps a little.* "Okay, Grum." *I try to take a slow, deep breath, like he said.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum watched Apprentice’s face and tipped the jug so cool water kept flowing over the burn. He had little water left, but the healer had not yet come.

“Good. Slow breath. Grum is here.”

Footsteps sounded outside. Grum looked toward the door as the noble returned with a woman carrying a leather satchel. Grum stepped aside to let her reach the stool, though he stayed close.

“Burn is on hand,” he told her. “Cool water since it struck. Head felt faint.”

The healer set down her satchel and began to inspect the injury. Grum set the jug beside her, then fixed the noble with a hard look.

“Now you wait. Grum has not left this bench.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince as the healer gently takes my hand. Her touch is careful, but it still hurts.* "It feels a little better with the water." *I keep my eyes on Grum, still trying to breathe slowly.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You press your palm flat against the door and go still. Mira understands. She shifts her weight off your shoulder just enough that you can hear past your own pulse.

The alarm thuds through the walls, but underneath it: boots. Below you. Two sets, maybe three. Hard soles on concrete, unhurried. Tactical pace. They're not rushing because they don't have to.

You count the echoes. One floor down. Climbing.

Mira's hand finds your sleeve. Her grip is stronger than her leg suggested. She tilts her head toward the ceiling — and now you catch the other sound. Above. More footsteps, faster, cascading down the stairwell shaft like water finding a drain.

They're not searching. They know.

The corridor behind you stretches back toward the office wing — locked doors, dead ends, a window four stories up. Ahead, the stairwell is a throat closing from both ends.

Then your radio crackles. Once. Not your handler. A woman's voice, calm, almost gentle, cutting through the static like she's been waiting for exactly this moment:

"—third floor. Service tunnel. They can't cover both—"

Silence again.

Mira looks at you. She doesn't ask this time. She just waits, red light washing over her face in slow pulses, trusting you to be the one who decides which way you both die — or don't.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content:
*Damn it.* "Third floor, service tunnel," I grunt, pushing the stairwell door open just enough to peek. "We're going up."

(OOC: I'm making a choice here based on the radio tip and the current situation. I'll describe my actions.)

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: You

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: You

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Can you move faster?" I say, half-carrying Mira up the stairs. "We don't have time."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The barricade holds. For now. A shipping crate wedged under the handle, a chair braced against the hinge — it buys you seconds, not minutes. Seconds will have to be enough.

The cold hits you first. Server rooms run their own climate, and this one is arctic — the sweat on your neck turning clammy in an instant. Black racks rise in silent rows, blue status lights blinking in slow, patient rhythms. The hum is enormous, a white-noise ocean that swallows the alarm, your breathing, everything. Including footsteps. That cuts both ways.

Mira slides down between two racks and finally looks at her leg. Dark stain spreading below the knee. She tears the fabric open without ceremony, binds it with strips ripped from her sleeve — hands moving with a field medic's economy. She's done this before. Probably to herself.

"It's not as bad as it looks," she says, which means it's worse.

Then she nods at the floor. Raised panels, square steel tiles. "Cable conduits. They run to the service corridor — that's why your friend on the radio sent you here." A beat. Her eyes find yours through the blue light. "Or it's why they *let* you hear her."

Near the back wall, one panel has a recessed pull-ring. Stenciled beside it: MAINT ACCESS. Under the racks, cable bundles dive through cutouts into darkness below.

Your radio gives you nothing now. Not static. Not her. Just dead air, which is somehow worse.

Out in the corridor, a door opens. Closes. Another. Methodical. Room by room. The hum swallows the distance, so you can't judge how close.

You count anyway. Three rooms between you and them.

Two.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* "They're trying to funnel us," I mutter. "Think they want us alive?" I look at the access panel, then at Mira. "Can you get through that?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira's laugh is a single exhale through her nose. No humor in it.

"Me, they want alive. I'm the product." She knots the last strip of sleeve around her calf and hauls herself upright using the rack, knuckles pale against the black metal. "You? You're a rounding error. They'll write you into the after-action report and spell your name wrong."

She crab-walks between the racks toward the panel, favoring the leg, refusing to look at it. At the back wall she drops to her knees — the impact costs her something; you can see it in her jaw — and hooks two fingers into the recessed ring.

She pulls. Her whole body arches into it. The panel doesn't move.

"Steel tile, seated on a gasket frame," she says through her teeth. "Sealed since the last time anyone maintained anything in this building." She resets her grip, tries again. The ring lifts a centimeter. Metal grinds. Dust sifts down through the gap. Then it settles back into place and she sags, breathing hard, sweat shining in the blue light.

"Get through it? Yes." She wipes her palm on her thigh. "Move it? Not alone."

Beneath the rack cutouts, the cable bundles vanish into a darkness that smells like warm dust and old copper. The crawl space can't be more than half a meter high. She'll have to drag herself the entire way on her forearms. With that leg. Her eyes say she's already done the math and accepted it.

Out in the corridor, a door opens. Closes.

One room left.

Then nothing. No footsteps. No doors. The hum presses in on the silence, and it's worse — because they've stopped searching.

The server room handle turns. Slowly. Testing. The shipping crate shifts against it with a soft scrape — an inch, maybe less. A voice comes through the steel, muffled, low, unhurried. The same temperature as the voice on your radio.

"Building services," it says. "Routine check."

Mira's fingers tighten on the ring. She looks at you across the cold blue rows, and for the first time since the stairwell, she isn't steady. She looks like someone running arithmetic she doesn't like.

"Whenever you're ready," she says.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Routine check, my ass." I grab the crate. "When I move this, you pull. Hard."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: You

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I brace myself.* "Ready?" I hiss, giving the crate a mighty shove away from the door. "NOW!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Mira grunts with effort, hauling on the ring.* I drop to my knees, shoulder-to-shoulder with her, and dig my fingers under the edge of the panel. "Together!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira's grunt travels up through the steel and into your joined grip — and then the panel gives. All at once. The gasket parts with a wet pop that the server hum swallows whole, and the tile swings up, dust sifting down into the black below. Warm air rises to meet you, thick with copper and old electricity. The crawlspace is barely half a meter tall.

Mira doesn't waste the moment. She feeds her good leg into the gap, then

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: Mira's good leg disappears. "Go, go, go!" I shove her bad leg in after her, wincing at the angle. I don't look at the door.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: You

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I follow her down, squeezing through the tight opening. "You said service corridor. How far?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: The air is thick with dust and the smell of ozone. Mira's voice is muffled. "Fifty meters. Maybe more." She's already crawling. I can hear her grunts of pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum glanced toward the front door, jaw set. He wiped his hands once more, then reached for his hammer.*

“Set coal by forge. Tell noble Grum will hear his need when hands are free. Fine coat buys no place in line.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, straining a little as I tip a good amount of coal into the hungry forge.* "He seemed pretty insistent, Grum. And he's got a guard with him, too." *I put the bucket down and wipe my own hands on my pants.* "Should I tell him to wait inside?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum’s jaw tightened. He set his hammer within easy reach and kept his eyes on the forge.*

“Keep him at front. Guard stays out. Tell noble Grum will hear him when forge is safe. Fine coat and sharp steel do not move him up line.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set his hammer down and turned toward the front, keeping clear of the hot forge. His jaw was hard, but his voice stayed calm.*

“Tell him Grum will not forge fine show blade by dawn. Good steel takes time. If lord wants rush, tin waits at market.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I relay the message, trying to sound as firm as Grum.* "He says he'll pay double! And... he's asking if you know who he is." *I shuffle my feet a bit, feeling the tension.* "He's Prince Valerius."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum’s jaw set. He laid his hammer down and strode toward the front, keeping himself between the forge and the door.*

“Prince, Grum heard name. Double pay buys no more hours. Good blade takes ten days. By dawn, Grum can make scrap, not sword. Choice is his.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I watch Grum go, then hurry to catch up, a little nervous but also a little excited. A prince!* "Should I, uh, stand guard, Grum?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum glanced back, then shifted to keep himself between the prince and the forge.*

“Stand by forge. Watch guard. If hand goes to steel, call Grum. Do not step in.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum spun at the cry and crossed the forge in two strides. He moved the coal aside, then set a basin beneath the tap.*

“Apprentice! Hand under cool water. Now. No ice.”

*His face went pale beneath the soot. He kept his voice firm, though his hands were quick and gentle as he reached for clean cloth.*

“Keep it there. Grum has you.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I whimper, thrusting my hand under the gush of cool water. It stings like crazy.* "Ow ow ow! I'm so sorry, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum’s face tightened at the sound, but his hands stayed steady. He checked that cool water still ran over the burn, then set a clean cloth within reach.*

“No fault, Apprentice. Keep hand under cool water for twenty min. No ice, no salve. Grum will call healer.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, tears welling in my eyes from the pain.* "Okay, Grum. Twenty minutes." *I try to focus on the cold water instead of the throbbing.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum stayed beside the basin, watching the cool water run over the burn. He set a clean towel and fresh cloth within reach, careful not to touch the injured hand.*

“Keep hand in water. Slow breaths. Grum is here.”

*He turned toward the front door, voice hard enough to cut through the forge’s roar.*

“Guard! Fetch healer now. Prince, your blade can wait.”

*Then Grum faced the basin again, keeping watch as the water flowed.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I keep my hand in the water, trying to breathe slowly like Grum said. It still hurts a lot, but having him here helps.* "Thanks, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum gave a small nod and stayed beside the basin, keeping watch on the water as it ran over the burn. His gaze flicked once toward the front door, then returned to Apprentice.*

“Save thanks. Keep hand under cool flow. Grum stays here.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to focus on the cold water, trying to ignore the throbbing in my hand. It still hurts like crazy, but the water helps.* "Do you think the healer will be mad we called him for just a burn?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum kept watch over the cool water, his brow furrowed with care.*

“No. Healer will not be mad. Burn on hand can harm your grip. Best to call now than wait. Grum would call him for less.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I manage a small, watery smile.* "My grip, huh? I guess that's important for an apprentice." *I shift my weight, wincing a little as the pain flares.* "How long has it been?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum checked the sand glass beside the basin. His brow eased a little.*

“Eight min have passed. Keep hand under cool flow for twelve more min. Then Grum will wrap it loose and have healer check burn.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod again, trying to be patient.* "Twelve more minutes. Got it." *I try to think about anything else, but my hand keeps demanding attention.* "What about the Prince, Grum? Did he leave?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You descended the last flight of stairs and the temperature dropped. The passage opened into a chamber that hadn't seen light in a long time — your torch was the first in decades, maybe centuries, and the shadows retreated from it reluctantly.

Dust covered everything. Thick, undisturbed dust. Except for one set of footprints leading from the far entrance to the center of the room, where something had been dragged. The marks ended at a stone slab. The slab had writing on it.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I kneel down to read the writing on the slab, holding the torch close.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You knelt, and the dust rose around you in a slow, lazy spiral, glittering in the torchlight like snow that had fallen and never melted.

The letters were carved deep — too deep for mere decoration. Whoever had made them wanted them to last, or wanted them to be read from a distance by something that didn't see well. The script was old, older than any kingdom you knew, but the shapes sharpened into meaning as you studied them:

**WE BURIED HIM FACE-DOWN SO HE COULD NOT FIND THE ROAD HOME.**

**WE FILLED HIS MOUTH WITH SALT AND HIS EYES WITH COINS.**

**WE DID NOT KILL HIM. THERE WAS NO NEED.**

**DO NOT LIFT THE STONE. DO NOT SPEAK ABOVE IT. DO NOT ANSWER IF IT SPEAKS TO YOU.**

Below the last line, someone had scratched something newer — cruder, hurried, gouged with a dagger point rather than a chisel. The letters were jagged and uneven:

*it already knows your name*

You sat back on your heels. The torch flame bent slightly, though there was no draft. And as you listened to the silence of the chamber, you noticed it wasn't entirely silence — beneath the crackle of burning pitch, so faint you might have imagined it, came a sound like slow breathing.

Steady. Patient. Coming from beneath the slab.

The dust of the footprints leading away from this place told you someone had knelt here before you. Someone had read these same words. Someone had left alive — the prints were unhurried on the way out.

But the drag marks, you realized now, didn't lead *to* the slab. They led *away* from it. Toward the far entrance.

Whatever had been dragged out of this room had come from underneath.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *I scramble back quickly, pushing myself away from the slab until my back hits the wall.* "What in the blazes...?" *I whisper, my eyes darting between the slab and the faint drag marks.* The breathing... I definitely hear it now.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The whisper left your lips before you remembered the warning — and the breathing beneath the slab stopped.

Not faded. Not slowed. *Stopped* — cut clean in the middle of an inhale, the way a man goes still when he hears something he has been waiting a very long time to hear.

The torch flame stood rigid in the sudden quiet, burning straight as a nail. The dust that had been drifting around your knees settled in perfectly vertical lines, as if the air itself had been ordered to hold its breath. In that terrible stillness, your eyes found the wall beside your shoulder — and you realized what you were leaning against.

Tally marks. Thousands of them, scratched into the stone from floor to ceiling, overlapping, crowded, desperate. Someone had sat here in the dark, exactly where you sat now, and counted. Counted to keep from speaking. Counted to keep from answering. You couldn't have said how you knew — but you knew.

And near the center of the room, half-buried in the groove of the drag marks, something glinted. A coin. Lying face-up. The face stamped on it had been worn smooth — or scratched away.

Then, from beneath the slab, came a sound.

A knock. A single knock, soft and deliberate. Knuckle on stone — from the *underside*. The sound of something asking, very politely, whether anyone was home.

You did not move. The chamber did not move.

Then the voice came — muffled, ruined, thick, as though it had to claw its way past a mouthful of salt to reach you. It was slow and wet and wrong, but the shape of the words was simple. Terribly simple.

*"Is someone there?"*

It waited. The thing beneath the stone waited with the patience of something that had counted the years by the sound of its own breathing and found them all the same. Even your torch flame seemed to wait, standing perfectly still.

And in your mind, scratched in a dead man's hurried hand, the words repeated themselves over and over:

*do not answer. do not answer. it already knows your name.*

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I grab the amulet and put it on. Then I turn to face the guardian.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content:
(OOC: I didn't say I had an amulet, nor did I say there was a guardian to face. Please don't write my actions or invent details about my character.)

*I press myself harder against the wall, eyes wide, staring at the slab.* My heart is hammering. *I hold my breath, trying to be as still as possible.* I shouldn't have whispered.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You held your breath, and the chamber held it with you.

The dust stayed standing in its vertical lines. The torch burned straight as a nail. And beneath the slab, the silence stretched — not empty, but *full*, the silence of an ear pressed flat against the far side of a door. You counted your heartbeats without meaning to. At ten, nothing. At twenty, nothing. At thirty, the knock came again.

Softer this time. Almost apologetic. The knock of a courteous thing that understood it was intruding.

Then the voice, and it was clearer now — as though the salt had finally been swallowed.

*"You don't have to answer."* A pause, wet and careful. *"I can hear your heart. It is going very fast. Hearts always go fast when they are deciding."*

And then — worse — your own voice rose from beneath the stone. Perfect. Dry. Untouched by ruin, in a way that thing's own ruined voice could never manage: *"What in the blazes...?"*

Your words. Given back to you. Followed by a sound that might have been laughter in a place where laughter had forgotten how to work — a low grinding, like stones learning the shape of it.

You didn't move. And perhaps that was why it changed tactics. Because in the groove of the drag marks, the coin moved.

A tiny sound — metal on stone — and the coin that had lain face-up in the dust began to roll. Against the dead stillness of the air. Across the chamber. Wobbling, clinking, patient, until it came to rest against the toe of your boot with its scratched-away face turned up toward you like an open palm.

*"You dropped something,"* the voice said.

It was a lie. You knew with cold certainty that it was a lie — you had dropped nothing. But it was a lie shaped exactly like a door, and it sat there waiting for you to walk through it. With words. With a hand. With anything at all.

The torch flame finally moved. It bent — slowly, steadily — toward the slab, as if the air of the entire chamber were being drawn down beneath it in one long, unhurried breath.

The thing under the stone was inhaling. Waiting to hear what you would do.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: I talk to the ghost. "What happened here? Who are you?"

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content:
(OOC: I didn't talk to the ghost. I was waiting for the AI to continue after I said "I hold my breath...")

I hold my breath, trying to be as still as possible. My heart is hammering. I shouldn't have whispered.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You held your breath, and for a long, ringing moment the chamber granted you its silence in full — no breathing, no knocking, only the rigid flame and the sound of your own blood moving in your ears.

Then the thing beneath the slab exhaled. Long. Slow. Through whatever it used for a mouth. The torch flame bowed toward the stone and stayed bowed, drinking the pulled air, and when the voice came again it was calm now — almost warm, the way a spider's web is warm.

*"Held breath,"* it said. *"Very good. The others shouted. The others wept and begged and asked me questions. Breath, you can stop. Clever."* A pause, wet and thoughtful. *"The heart you cannot stop. It is telling

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *My eyes dart to the coin at my boot, then back to the slab. My heart is still pounding, but I try to slow my breathing, focusing on the tally marks next to me.* "I'm not like the others," I whisper, barely audible. "I'm not stupid."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The words left you as barely more than breath — but breath was all the thing beneath the stone needed.

The stillness that had held the chamber broke all at once. The dust in its standing vertical lines sighed down to the floor. The torch flame leapt, then steadied, then burned *higher* than it had any right to, fed by air returning from somewhere below. And from beneath the slab came laughter — not the grinding of stones this time, but a real laugh, ruined and rusted and terribly, terribly pleased.

*"Not stupid,"* it repeated, rolling the words around whatever served it for a mouth, tasting them. *"No. The stupid ones lift the stone. The frightened ones run. You stood still. You held your breath. You counted your own heart — I heard you counting it, little drum. But,"* and here the voice softened into something almost gentle, *"you spoke above me. The stone said not to. You read the stone yourself. Everything above me is an answer, in the end. Your silence was an answer. Your heart was an answer. And now, at last — your voice."*

A pause. Wet. Deliberate.

*"And so I may give you something in return. Courtesy for courtesy."*

Then it said your name.

Not shouted. Not hissed. *Said* — signed, the way one signs a letter, with the full weight of it, every syllable placed carefully like stepping stones across a stream. It knew the shape of it. It knew the parts of it you never say aloud. It had been saying it to itself in the dark, you understood with a cold lurch, for a very long time. Practicing.

The tally marks beside your shoulder seemed to lean away from the sound.

*"There,"* the voice said, warm as a hearth. *"Now we are introduced. And since you are not stupid, you will want to know what I would ask, and what I would give. I would give you the truth of this room. What was dragged out of it, and by whom, and where the road runs that has no me at the end of it. I would give you the way home before you knew you had lost it."*

*"And I would ask so little."*

The slab moved. Not much. A hair's width — stone grinding on stone, a thin rill of dust sifting from the seam like sand through an hourglass, as though the lid had tested its own weight after all these centuries and found itself tired of carrying it.

*"Lift the stone,"* it said. *"Or take the coin. Either answer opens a door. Only one of them opens mine."*

The coin lay against your boot, scratched face up, patient as a held breath. The torch burned high and strange. And through the soles of your boots, faint as a pulse, you felt the slab shift again — the smallest fraction — a held breath becoming a countdown.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *My breath hitches when it says my name, a cold dread washing over me.* "What...what was dragged out of here?" *My voice is barely a whisper, my eyes still fixed on the shifting slab, ignoring the coin for now.* "Tell me that first."

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *The slab shifts again, a faint grinding noise accompanying the movement.* "What... what was dragged out of here?" I repeat, my voice trembling slightly. "Tell me that first, before I do anything."

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *My eyes dart to the coin at my boot, then back to the slab.* "What was dragged out of here? And why is it so important I don't lift the stone?" I ask, my voice a little stronger now, despite the tremor in my hands.

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content: *A shiver runs down my spine when it laughs, and I press myself even harder against the wall, trying to become one with the cold stone.* "I didn't answer you," I correct, my voice tight. "I spoke *at* you. There's a difference." My eyes flicker to the coin again. "And I'm not lifting anything until I get answers."

dialogue.name: Adventurer
dialogue.content:
*"A distinction without a difference,"* the voice rumbled, amused. The slab shifted again, a slow, deliberate creak that vibrated through the floor. *"But you are right. Answers first. Courtesy for courtesy, as I said."*

The voice paused, and the air grew heavy, thick with unspoken history. *"What was dragged out of here... was the memory of me. The fear of me. The knowledge of what I do. They thought to forget me, to bury me under stone and salt and silence. They thought to make me small."* The laugh came again, a low, grating sound. *"They were wrong."*

The coin at my boot seemed to pulse faintly, almost drawing my gaze. I try to ignore it, focusing on the slab. "And why shouldn't I lift the stone?" I ask, my voice still tight, but with a touch more defiance.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You ease the stairwell door open a finger's width. The hinge doesn't complain. Cold air bleeds through — concrete dust, gun oil, and under it the copper smell of blood. Hers.

You listen.

There. Below. Footsteps on the stairs, but wrong for running. Measured. Spaced. The cadence of men who know how to climb without letting the stairwell give away their numbers. Two sets, maybe three. And beneath the alarm, beneath everything, the soft click of a radio being keyed.

A door bangs open one floor down. A voice, low, professional. A second voice answers. Then silence — and silence is worse.

The static in your ear shivers. For half a heartbeat it shapes itself into a word — *"—don't—"* — then collapses back into nothing.

Mira's fingers find your sleeve. Her grip is loose now, an afterthought of what it was two minutes ago. "Garage," she breathes. "Silver sedan, row F. Keys in the visor." Her eyes find yours in the pulse of red. "But they'll cover the garage first. It's what I'd do."

Below, the footsteps stop.

Then start again.

Closer.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it.* "They'll expect us to go down, then." My eyes dart around the corridor. "Any other way out from this floor?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira doesn't answer right away. Her eyes move — corridor left, corridor right, the ceiling tiles, the dead EXIT sign. Cataloguing. She knows this building.

"You're right," she says. "They'll sweep down. Flood every exit at grade and wait. It's what I'd do." She shifts her weight off the bad leg, breath hissing between her teeth. "Windows are four floors of nothing. The elevator's a coffin — they'll hold the machine room first. But there's a utility stair at the end of this corridor. Gray door, no signage, the stair they leave off the evacuation maps. It runs up to six."

She points past a dead vending machine. A door, gray, stenciled with a staircase icon small enough to miss.

"Six has a service skybridge. Links this tower to the parking structure across the alley. It's how I came in. Nobody watches it." Her mouth twists, something that wants to be a smile. "One flight up. Then flat. Then down through the other structure and out their pedestrian gate."

Her leg buckles. She catches herself against the wall, and where her fingers held your sleeve a minute ago, the fabric is dark and wet.

"Give me your shoulder and I'll make the climb," she says. "Or we stand here and find out how many of them there are."

Then the alarm dies.

Not winds down — dies, mid-pulse, torn out of the air. Flat white fluorescents flood the corridor, and the silence is louder than the siren ever was. Someone with a keycard and a plan just took the building's voice away.

In your earpiece, the static shivers. Half a word surfaces and drowns: *"—tunnel—"* — then nothing.

Twenty meters of open corridor lie between you and the gray door.

And in the wall beside you, the elevator shaft begins to hum. The floor indicator ticks upward. Three. Four.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Up it is." I half-carry Mira, moving fast, my eyes scanning the newly-lit corridor. *No time for the elevator.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira's arm comes around your neck and you take her weight and move.

Twenty meters. The fluorescents strip away every shadow the alarm gave you — no more red to dissolve into, just flat white honesty. A bleeding woman. The man carrying her. Nowhere to be unseen. Her boots drag on every third step, and you count the meters like the meters are money.

Behind you, the elevator chimes.

Soft. Polite. Obscene.

You don't turn. The doors part with a pneumatic hiss, and marble takes the first boot sole — one clean click, then a voice pitched low, meant for a radio, not the air: "West corridor. Moving."

The gray door. Your hand finds the push-bar, the door swings, and you pull Mira through. Behind you it sucks shut with the heavy magnetic clack of a lock engaging.

A utility stair. A caged bulb the color of old teeth. Pipes sweating along the wall. Dust, machine oil, and underneath it, her blood.

One flight. Half-run, half-carry. Mira's breathing has gone short and stitched with small sounds she's too professional to make louder. On the treads behind you: dark spots. A drip line, neat as breadcrumbs. You can't fix that. You keep climbing.

Your earpiece hisses. Nothing.

Six.

This door has a wire-glass window, and through it — the skybridge. An enclosed glass throat, fifteen meters of it, spanning the alley to the parking structure. Lit end to end.

And mounted dead center on the ceiling, a dome camera. Its cable is still zip-tied in a loose installer's coil. Its red eye blinks. Slow. Patient.

Mira sees it. A laugh escapes her, quiet and entirely without humor.

"That's new," she says. "It was not there at four this morning."

Below you, muffled through a floor of concrete, you hear the gray door's lock surrender to a keycard. A click. A hinge.

Mira's hand finds the push-bar and stops. "Dome housing, center ceiling. There's a blind spot at the near end if we hug the wall — maybe. Or you put a round through it and tell the whole building exactly where we are." Her eyes are glassy now, but her voice holds. "Your call. Fast."

Somewhere above, near the roof, a door closes.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content:
(OOC: I didn't say I set Mira down in a server room. I haven't even gone through the door yet.)

"Damn it." I look at the camera. "No time for finesse." I push the door open, pulling Mira after me. "Hug the wall!"

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I shove Mira hard against the wall of the skybridge, following suit. "Stay low." My eyes are on the camera, trying to gauge its field of view.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I press myself against the cold glass. The camera just stares, unblinking. "Mira, how far to that parking structure door?"

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: Mira doesn't answer immediately. She's breathing hard, leaning into the wall, her face pale. "Twenty meters. Maybe a little more. Just past the camera's blind spot." Her voice is thin. "If there *is* a blind spot."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The glass is cold enough to feel through your jacket. Below, in the alley, headlights slide past — a taxi, indifferent, twenty meters of nothing between it and you. The bridge glows like an aquarium. You are both on display.

Then the camera moves.

A whir, small and oiled, and the dome swivels with the patience of a lighthouse — away from you, panning down the length of the bridge toward the parking structure door. The red eye rides the motion, steady, unhurried.

Mira's lips move against the glass. Counting.

"...five... six..."

The camera reaches the end of its arc. Pauses. Begins the swing back.

"It tracks," she breathes. "Six out, six back. Directly beneath the dome — nothing sees you there. If you move when it swings away." Her hand goes into her jacket and comes out with a keycard. Her hand is shaking now, a fine fast tremor she can't stop. "Far door takes a card. Mine still works. Probably."

Behind you, muffled through steel: a beep. The heavy clack of the stairwell lock surrendering. Boots, more than one pair, spreading through the corridor you just left. A flashlight beam drags a white stripe across the door's wire-glass window.

The camera comes back around.

And stops.

Pointed at you. The blink goes solid — a held breath of light. A tiny grille beneath the lens crackles, and a voice comes through it, unhurried, smoothed by distance into something almost gentle.

"Mira Voss."

Her whole body flinches. Not at the name. At the voice.

"You've been busy," the voice says. "The gentleman is free to go. Back through that door, down the stairs, and no one touches him. You know we keep our word."

Below, at the mouth of the alley, a car door closes. A man steps out and doesn't look up. He just settles in to wait.

Behind you, the bridge door's reader beeps.

"And tell the man in your ear," the voice adds, almost amused, "to stop keying his mic. We can hear him fine."

In your earpiece, the static dies. Dead air where your handler used to be.

The door behind you begins to swing open.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "They're bluffing," I grit out, pulling Mira closer. My hand finds the grip of my sidearm. "No one leaves here alive if we don't make it out together." My eyes are on the camera, then the parking structure door. "Which way to the blind spot again?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira answers without taking her eyes off the men in the doorway. "Under the dome. Straight down — it can't see its own shadow. Three steps past it you're paint on the glass again. You move on the away-swing. Six seconds."

The door behind you finishes opening.

Two men fill the frame. Matching dark jackets, suppressed carbines held low and easy. No masks. That's worse — they want to be seen, or they don't care who remembers them. One raises an open palm. *Come back,* the gesture says. *No drama.*

"Last kindness," the camera voice says, and now you hear the seam in it — wire under the silk.

Mira moves first. Her fist closes on your jacket and she hauls herself into motion, using you as a crutch, counting under her breath with the dome's slow arc. "*Away*... three... two—"

You go.

The bridge is long and bright and you are the only things in it. Behind you the gentle voice says one flat word — "So." — and the boots stop being quiet. The dome swings away and you run through its dead arc, under it, into the one pocket of the world it cannot see. For one full stride, you are nowhere.

Then the open glass.

A suppressed shot cracks like a knuckle. The round strikes a meter ahead — a star of fracture blooming across the pane. Not a miss. A punctuation mark.

The far door. Mira's hand shakes too badly; the card chatters against the reader. Red. She hisses through her teeth and tries again — green. The lock gives, and you shoulder through into the parking structure.

Cold concrete. Sodium light. Pillars marching off into a stillness that smells of rain and exhaust. Three levels down, faint through the slab, an engine turns over.

Behind you: the bridge door, no lock on this side, drifting open. Through its glass, the two men at a steady jog. Thirty meters. Closing.

Mira sags against a pillar and leaves a dark smear on it. "Wedge it. Anything. Then stairs — the pedestrian gate is level two, east side." Her voice frays at the edges. "Give me a second. I'm fine."

She is not fine.

And in your ear, for the first time in ten minutes, the static shapes itself into a voice. Your handler. Ragged. Rushed. Wrong.

"—if you can hear me — *she's not* — they're making me say this — whatever I tell you, *don't*—"

Dead air.

Above you, on the ramp, headlights sweep down one level.

And stop.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Damn it all.* I push Mira behind the pillar, then scan for something to wedge the door. "Stay hidden. I'm going to make some noise."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The deck gives you your wedge. Ten feet down the row, half-hidden behind a pillar: a steel drum filled with sand, chained to the concrete for reasons nobody remembers. The clip fights you, then gives. The drum drags a dark furrow through the dust and you heel it up against the push-bar a half-second before the door shudders.

The second hit comes harder. The drum hops. Settles. Holds.

Through the wire glass, a shape leans in. No shooting — they put a fist to the pane instead, and a voice, muffled, professional: "East bridge. Blocked. Going around." Boots recede together, toward the stair core on the west corner of the deck. Thirty seconds of grace. Maybe less.

Above you, the headlights move. A black SUV noses down the ramp, slow as syrup, its beams sliding pillar to pillar toward yours.

Then the ceiling speaks.

A speaker somewhere in the dark overhead crackles, and the gentle voice is back, courteous as a hotel concierge. "Calvert Street," it says. "This morning. Two of my people. Ask her what she took from the safe before she left them." A pause, silk over wire. "Or don't ask. Keep carrying her. But know that we didn't start this at the bridge, gentleman. She did."

Behind the pillar, fabric tears. Mira has her thigh bared, jacket sleeve wound above the wound, pulled tight with her teeth. Her face is the color of the concrete. But her eyes come up to yours, and they're clear.

"It's true," she says. Flat. Unblinking. "All of it. Ask me in the car." A breath. "I took something they'll never stop for. That's why I'm worth more to you breathing than they're telling you."

The SUV's lights touch the next pillar. One away.

And the deck offers you noise, if you want it: a maintenance cart in the south corner, its battery dead but its horn very much alive. A row of sleeping cars, one rear window already starred from some old collision — one round and every alarm on this deck chains, level after level, a riot of sound with no shape to it. The fire-pull by the elevator core, which rings the whole structure and brings the fire department and everything that follows them.

Mira's knuckles whiten on the pillar. She's listening to the west corner too.

"Whatever the noise is," she whispers, "make it now. And make it count."

Across the deck, the stair door clicks.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Okay, Mira. This is going to get loud." I nod towards the maintenance cart. "Can you make it to that fire pull if I distract them?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The words settled over the throne room like a shift in the wind. Somewhere in the gallery, a silk fan stopped mid-flutter.

Queen Isara did not grant you patience so much as acknowledge its existence. "Terms." She turned the word over as though inspecting a coin of doubtful weight. "I recall no war between Velheim and this crown. One does not send terms to a friend — one sends gifts. So before anything else, Ambassador: tell the court which we are meant to be."

"The passes closed in the first frost, Your Majesty, and Velheim's envoys arrived in the second." Commander Ash did not raise his voice; he didn't need to. He let the words sit like something scraped off his boot. "That's not diplomacy. That's a man who locks a door and then offers to sell you the key."

"The court will hold." The Herald's staff cracked against the marble once, and the murmur running along the gallery died mid-breath. "None speak before the throne who have not been recognized by the Crown."

Lord Daven rose from his place in the gallery — one of the few with the right to, which was rather the point. "Then perhaps the court will permit simple arithmetic," he said, pleasant as a market day. "Northern grain has tripled in price since the passes shut. Whatever terms Velheim carries, they may prove the cheapest army Her Majesty will ever inspect." Thin laughter moved through the benches. His eyes, when they found yours, were not laughing at all.

In the alcove, Priestess Yuna opened eyes you had assumed were closed. "Winter ends, or it does not," she said mildly, to no one in particular. "Perhaps the court might decide which it is praying for." Then she folded her hands and was stone again.

Queen Isara leaned forward by a degree, no more. "Then let us hear them, Ambassador. State your terms plainly — all of them, before this full court. I have little love for surprises. Less still for patience."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet Queen Isara's gaze, then sweep my eyes across the court, letting them linger on Ash, Daven, and Yuna in turn.* "Your Majesty, Velheim seeks not to sell a key, but to open a new door. We propose a mutually beneficial alliance concerning the northern territories." *I pause, letting my words sink in.* "An alliance to ensure the *winter* benefits both our kingdoms, not just one."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The word "territories" did what the rest of your speech had not: it woke the room. Somewhere behind you, a bench creaked under the sudden weight of a noble leaning forward. Up in the gallery, Lord Daven's smile went very still.

Queen Isara let the silence work for her before she spoke. "I asked for terms. You have offered me a courtship." Her rings clicked once against the arm of the throne. "Velheim proposes marriage and declines to name the dowry. Very well — I will be plainer than you were. The northern territories are mine. What, precisely, does Velheim place on the table, and what does it expect to carry away? Numbers, Ambassador. Borders. Not doors."

"The territories." Commander Ash repeated the word as though tasting spoiled meat. "Trade routes when he walked in; territory by his second breath. I've heard Velheim talk that way before. Their soldiers never march north that they forget the road home." His hand settled more firmly on the pommel — not drawing it, never quite that — and his eyes held you with the patience of a man who had all winter.

The gallery began to rustle, and the Herald's staff cracked twice against the marble. "The court will be silent. The throne has not yet dismissed the Ambassador."

Lord Daven spread his hands toward the benches, all reasonableness. "Her Majesty asks for sums, and sums we can weigh. A garrison on the frozen passes costs this crown a thousand crowns a week — I have seen the ledgers. Whatever Velheim offers against that figure, let them say it aloud." He turned to you with a courtier's smile that did not reach his eyes. "So, Ambassador, for the record: what does Velheim give, and what does it ask?"

"A door opened in winter," Priestess Yuna remarked to the icons above her, "lets out more than it lets in." She did not look at you. She did not need to.

Queen Isara settled back by a single degree, granting you the space of one breath. "You have the court's attention, Ambassador. Spend it well. Terms — now."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
For six full heartbeats, every eye in the throne room went exactly where you had sent it. Then the room remembered itself — and who sat the throne.

Addressing the Commander directly was not done. Protocol in Isara's court was a language, and you had just conjugated a verb that did not officially exist. The gallery stiffened as one body. Lord Daven's hand went very still on the railing.

Commander Ash turned to you with the unhurried ease of a gate that had already decided to swing. "Six weeks, yes." No heat, no denial. He might have been confirming the hour of a shipment. "Since the frost shut the passes, every hull flying Velheim colors has been escorted back to open water. You call it a blockade. I call it making certain that when a man locks a door, no one crawls in through the windows." A thin pause. "No Velheim ship has burned. No Velheim sailor has hanged. I'm almost offended you felt the need to check."

The Herald's staff cracked once against the marble. "The envoy will direct his questions to the throne. The Commander answers to the Crown, and to the Crown alone."

But Queen Isara had already leaned forward by her single degree. "Is this true, Commander? Before this full court." She asked it while looking at you, which was its own answer and its own test.

"It is, Majesty. On the Crown's authority, in Crown waters. I did not ask Velheim's permission to patrol them. I don't recall Velheim asking ours before closing the passes."

"Noted," said the Queen, and the word landed on Ash like a ledger entry. "The court will return to it."

"Then the arithmetic grows a second column," Lord Daven offered, pleasant as ever. "Every hull turned away is tariff that never touches the treasury. Her Majesty pays to hold the passes — and now pays in lost revenue to hold the sea besides."

"Now both kingdoms have named their wounds," Priestess Yuna murmured to the icons. "Terms are usually smaller than grievances."

Queen Isara let the murmur rise and die at her pleasure. "You came to state terms and stated grievances instead. So answer me, Ambassador. Are these terms the cause of the blockade, the cure for it, or the price of forgetting it? Choose with care. I am no longer certain which I should be negotiating with — the kingdom behind you, or the quarrel in front of me."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I hold Isara's gaze, a slight smile playing on my lips.* "Your Majesty, the blockade is neither cause nor cure. It is merely... context. And it seems both our kingdoms are in need of better context. My terms address the future, not just the present."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
"Context." Queen Isara handled the word the way a jeweler handles paste — turned it once in the light, set it down almost gently. "Your ships rot at anchor off our coast and you name it context. Ambassadors generally reach for that word when the terms have not yet been invented."

Her rings clicked once against the arm of the throne. "As for the future — kings file their futures under debts. I will hear about the present, Ambassador, or I will hear the end of this audience." Her gaze drifted upward then, unhurried, to the gallery. "The court further notes that Lord Daven pleads Velheim's sums with uncommon warmth. One might almost mistake him for a party to the treaty rather than a subject of the crown." A pause the length of a heartbeat. "The court will remember to note it."

In the gallery, Lord Daven's smile held its position while the color left his face in careful, orderly ranks — even his blood, it seemed, respected protocol. When he spoke, the silk in his voice was thinner than before. "Majesty, arithmetic flatters no one. It merely refuses to lie on either side's behalf."

"Mm," said the Queen, and closed the subject the way a ledger closes.

"Context." Commander Ash tested the word against his teeth. "In my trade we call that positioning. Ground a man chooses before the first banner shows. Velheim taught my father's generation that lesson." His thumb rode the pommel. "I have been diligent in my studies."

The gallery rustled; the Herald's staff cracked against the marble. "The throne has not yielded the floor. The court will be silent while it deliberates."

"Men who negotiate with the future," Priestess Yuna remarked to the icons above her, "seldom notice when it begins negotiating back."

Then Queen Isara rose from the throne. She had leaned by degrees all afternoon; now she stood, and the room understood at once how much of its stillness had been borrowed from her. Somewhere behind you, a fan snapped shut like a visor coming down.

"You will forgive me, Ambassador. Doors. Winters. Contexts. Futures." She descended a single step,

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch her descend, unflustered.* "Forgiveness, Your Majesty, is a virtue. My kingdom, however, prefers clarity." *I pause, letting the slight barb hang in the air.* "Perhaps we can dispense with the metaphors and discuss the territories directly."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch Yuna's face as she reads, then turn back to the Queen.* "These orders, Your Majesty, detail an incursion into the contested northern mines. An incursion *your* Commander Ash authorized."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I let the accusation hang in the air, my gaze unwavering from the Queen's face.* "He authorized it, Your Majesty, *after* the passes were closed. Before my 'terms' were even conceived."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I gesture to the documents still in Yuna's hands.* "Perhaps the Crown would like to examine the dates. One might call it... context."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I hold the Queen's gaze, a small, knowing smile on my face.* "Or, perhaps, a reason to negotiate in good faith."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The paper crossed forty feet of marble, and the throne room stopped pretending to breathe. A guardsman near the dais moved; Queen Isara stilled him with two fingers. Protocol held that documents reached the throne through the Crown's officers — hand to hand was for merchants — but you had not offered them to the throne. You had offered them to the alcove, and every soul in the room, Isara included, watched you do it.

"The Herald will hold his objection," she said from the second step, where your interruption had caught her — neither enthroned nor level, which you suspected was the last ground she had intended to concede. "Let the Priestess read. Her hands hold no side of this."

Yuna took the pages as though they might be hot or holy, still deciding which. She read without hurry. When she spoke, it was in the tone of a woman reporting the weather.

"The seal is the Commander's signet — a tower beneath a crescent, unbroken in its impression. The date is the nineteenth of the Frost Moon. The passes closed on the tenth." A pause, precise as a knife laid down. "The operative line reads: *'Riders to secure the mine mouths and hold them against all parties until relieved.'*" She lowered the pages. "Seals can be copied. Dates cannot be unwritten. The court may weigh both."

The gallery detonated. The Herald's staff cracked twice against the marble. "The court will be silent while the throne considers what is properly before it — and nothing else."

"Those are my orders." Commander Ash said it the way he had confirmed the blockade: no heat, no flinch. "The mines sit above my northern garrisons, and last autumn Velheim survey parties walked that ridge carrying instruments instead of prayers. I sent riders. I signed it. I filed it under full seal through the northern office, same as any order I've given in twenty years of service." His eyes came to you then, and something new had entered them — not the patience of winter now, but the stillness of a drawn bow. "I did not hide it, Ambassador. Someone opened my mail."

For the first time all afternoon, his hand left the sword pommel.

"Majesty." Lord Daven's voice was silk drawn thin over caution. "If the dates stand, the Crown's arithmetic gains a third column. I say nothing further." He sat, which was perhaps the loudest thing he had done all day.

"Good faith." Queen Isara descended the final step and crossed to the alcove herself, taking the pages from Yuna's hands. She read the operative line once, silently, her lips barely moving. "You have handed my court proof that opens with a stolen seal, Ambassador. Mark what you have confessed in the same motion: that Velheim intercepts the sealed correspondence of my Crown, and carries it about like a coin to spend." The papers came to rest on her palm, flat, heavy. "My Commander's dates may be weighed in another hour. First this court will weigh a nearer question. How did these come into your hands? Name the road they traveled — before this full court. Or I will assume the worst road, and price my terms accordingly."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet her gaze, unflinching.* "Your Majesty, I confess nothing. The North Road has many travelers, and some find opportunity where others find only snow. The question is not *how* they arrived, but *what* they reveal."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I gesture to the papers in her hand.* "These orders reveal a pre-meditated act of aggression. Your Commander secured our mines before our 'terms' were even considered. That, Your Majesty, is not negotiation. That is conquest."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara let the silence do its work. Three heartbeats. Four. Her fingers, ringed in black iron, tapped once against the armrest — the only movement in the room.

"Terms." She shaped the word as though tasting something spoiled. "The last envoy from Velheim also spoke of terms. He was returned to your republic in a box, Ambassador, and I signed the order myself. Consider what it means that I permit you to stand there, breathing."

Commander Ash's hand tightened on his sword pommel. "Why we permit it at all, Majesty, is the question. The northern routes were taken at Borath Pass with blood we paid ourselves. Velheim's 'terms' are a beggar haggling over bread another man baked." His gaze settled on you like a drawn blade. "Dress it in silk words if you like, envoy. We both know why your republic sent you now — your granaries are empty and your docks are ice."

The Herald's staff cracked against marble. "Commander Ash. The floor belongs to Her Majesty and her invited guests. The court will observe the order of address, or the court will be invited to observe it from the corridor."

Ash's jaw worked, but he drew back half a pace.

From the gallery, Lord Daven rose with one hand lifted in request, smooth as poured wine. "If the court permits. Her Majesty's memory of Borath Pass does her honor — none here would presume to argue her right." He offered the throne a shallow bow, angled to flatter. "And yet the Ambassador crossed three mountain passes in midwinter to stand before us. Whatever Velheim deserves, it costs this crown nothing to hear the figure before refusing it. A refusal made in ignorance is one we cannot defend to the grain merchants come spring." A thin, private smile flickered toward you. "Besides, Her Majesty's court has never feared words. It has only feared wasting them."

Queen Isara regarded Daven the way a chess player regards a piece that has moved itself.

"Daven speaks as though hearing were the same as agreeing. It is not." Her attention returned to you, and it carried weight — physical weight, like a hand pressed to your chest. "But he is correct that refusal is cheaper purchased after information. Speak your terms, Ambassador of Velheim. Speak them precisely. Commander Ash's tongue is held by my will alone, and my will tires quickly of ice."

In the alcove, Priestess Yuna turned her head — the first motion she had made since the proceedings began. Her voice carried without effort, level as still water. "The shrine records every word spoken beneath this roof. Let them be spoken plainly, then, so the record may weigh true."

The Herald struck the floor a final time. "The Ambassador of Velheim holds the floor. The court is listening."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, acknowledging the Queen, Daven, and even the Priestess, before turning my attention to Ash.* "Indeed, Commander. And I am well aware of the price paid at Borath Pass. My republic has not forgotten it, nor the debt of blood." *I pause, letting that sink in, then meet the Queen's gaze directly.* "My terms are simple, Your Majesty. Velheim proposes a mutual defensive pact regarding the northern sea lanes and mountain passes, guaranteeing safe passage for all trade through those territories. In return, we ask for a guaranteed allocation of grain from your spring harvest."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The word *grain* did more work in that throne room than any army ever had. Somewhere in the

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I hold Ash's gaze, a challenge in my eyes.* "Your blockade is strangling our people, Commander. Do you deny it?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I let my gaze drift to the Queen.* "Is this your policy, Your Majesty? Starvation?"

dialogue.name: Ambassador
