dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch Yuna closely, waiting for her reaction.* "These orders, Your Majesty, are signed by Commander Ash himself."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: Y

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I then turn to the Queen, a faint, almost imperceptible smile touching my lips.* "A curious definition of 'no blockade,' wouldn't you say, Your Majesty?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: Ash

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
Ash's hand twitches towards his sword. "These are fabrications!" he snarls.

"Are they?" *I challenge, my smile broadening slightly.* "Priestess Yuna, does the shrine's record recognize the Commander's seal?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: Pri

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet Ash's furious glare with a calm, unwavering gaze.* "The truth, Commander, does not require fabrication."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: Pri

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
Priestess Yuna, having unfolded the documents, now holds them up. "The seal is indeed Commander Ash's. And the orders... they are for a full blockade, commencing six weeks past."

*I turn back to the Queen, my expression grave now.* "So, Your Majesty, the question remains. Is this your policy, or Commander Ash's ambition?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: Pri

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch the Queen intently, waiting for her reaction to this uncomfortable truth. My move has landed.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pencil marks remained beneath the beige paint. Beside each line, a date showed through. The graphite had left faint grooves in the wood.

The highest mark had no date. Someone had painted around it, leaving a narrow ridge. From the kitchen came the dry rasp of tape pulled from a roll.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content:
I trace the highest mark, a ghostly outline under the new paint. "Huh." I wonder whose it is.

"Hello?" I call out, my voice sounding small in the quiet house.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The rasp of tape stopped. From the kitchen, his father said, “I’m here.”

A cabinet door closed with a hollow knock. He came into the hallway, masking tape stuck to his thumb. His gaze rested on the highest mark.

“That one’s mine,” he said. “You wanted to see how far you had to grow.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph had curled at one corner. Her mother stood in the garden, soil dark beneath her bare feet. A crease crossed her face, but her smile remained intact.

Her father stopped at the closet door. The tape on his thumb brushed the frame with a faint hiss. “I thought I’d packed that,” he said. He stayed where he was.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I turn, holding the photo. "How could you forget this one?" My voice is a little sharp.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
His father rubbed the tape between his fingers. It gave a dry crackle.

“I thought I’d packed it,” he said. “I remember holding it over the box.”

He looked at the photograph. Dust had settled into the crease across her face.

“I put it back,” he said. “I couldn’t close the lid.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I look at the photo again, then back at him. "So you just... left it here?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
His father pressed the tape against his thumb. It caught on dry skin.

“Yes,” he said. “I left it in the closet.”

The hallway held the smell of fresh paint. He looked toward the open box in the kitchen.

“I meant to come back for it,” he said. “Then I stopped opening that door.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The doorbell rang twice. His father peeled the tape from his thumb before opening the door.

The agent stood on the porch in a yellow coat. Rain dotted her shoulders. “Good morning,” she said. “The photographer can come Thursday. Isn’t that wonderful?”

His father kept one hand on the door. “Not today,” he said.

Her smile held. From the hallway, the photograph’s curled corner cast a small shadow across the garden.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I step forward, still holding the photo. "Dad, what are you doing?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
His father turned from the porch. Rain tapped against the agent’s yellow coat.

“Thursday,” he said. “I meant Thursday.”

The agent lowered her phone. “I can ask for Friday.”

“No.” He gripped the door’s chipped edge. “Thursday is fine.”

For a moment, he watched the photograph in Eli’s hand. The agent followed his gaze, then looked down at her phone.

“I’ll send the details,” she said.

The door stuck when he tried to close it. He pulled harder, and the swollen wood gave a dull scrape.

“I should have told you,” he said. “About the house.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Told me what?" I ask, my voice quiet. I didn't like the sound of this. I put the photo down on the small table by the door.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
His father watched the photograph on the table. Its curled corner lifted in the draft.

“I told you we would decide together,” he said. “I’d already signed with her.”

Rain ticked against the door. He ran his thumb over its chipped paint.

“I called after I signed. I was afraid you’d ask me to wait.”

His hand fell from the door. “I’m sorry.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "You're sorry?" I shake my head slowly. "Dad, this is *my* house too."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
His father looked at the photograph. Rain tapped against the door behind him.

“You’re right,” he said. “I treated your silence as permission. I never asked.”

He picked at a strip of tape caught beneath his nail. “I can call her back. No photographs on Thursday.”

He left the tape on the table beside the photograph. “We can talk before anything else happens.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I look at the tape and then at him. "It's too late for that, isn't it?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
His father looked at the strip of tape. The rain pressed against the door.

“It’s too late for me to ask first,” he said. “I know that.”

He took out his phone but did not unlock it. “The house isn’t sold. I can cancel Thursday.”

The photograph’s curled corner rose in the draft. He set the phone beside it.

“I won’t call her until we’ve talked,” he said.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I pick up the tape and twist it around my finger. "What is there to talk about, Dad?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
His father rested a hand on the table’s worn edge. “Whether we sell,” he said. “And why you should have a say.”

Rain tapped the door. He looked at the photograph, then at the phone beside it.

“I want to leave this house,” he said. “I was afraid telling you would hurt.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I look down at the photo of Mom. "It hurt more that you didn't tell me."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's shoulders went stiff. Nobles. Always at the worst hour, always sure the forge should stop because their coin was cleaner than anyone else's.*

"Coal first." *He jerked his chin at the bucket, still not looking toward the door.* "Silk-boots can stand. Hot steel not wait for lord. Grum not jump when fancy coat knock."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, hefting the heavy bucket again.* "He looks pretty important, Grum. And he's got a guard with him. A big one." I grunt, trying to get a better grip on the bucket. "He's making a fuss."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum took the bucket from the apprentice’s hands before the boy could drop it, and tipped the coal into the fire with a careful, practiced motion. Sparks jumped. He watched them die before he spoke.*

"Guard mean lord fear own shadow." *He set the empty bucket down and finally turned toward the front of the shop, jaw tight.* "Fuss not make steel. Coin not make steel. Hands make steel. Grum hands busy."

*He picked the hammer back up, weighed it once, and did not move toward the door.*

"Tell silk-boots this. Grum come when fire right. Not when lord stamp. If guard push, Grum push back. Apprentice stay by forge. No bow. No fear."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's grip tightened on the hammer. A show blade by dawn was not craft. It was a lord buying haste and calling it honor.*

"Tell lord this." *His voice stayed low, but it carried over the fire.* "Grum not make toy sword by dawn. Good steel need time. Heat, fold, cool, heat. Rush work snap. Snap blade shame smith and shame fool who wear it."

*He looked toward the front of the shop at last, soot on his face, no bow in his stance.*

"If lord want steel that last, lord wait. If lord want shine for party, lord go to tin man in market. Grum forge not shop for pride. Coin not buy dawn. Hands not lie."

*He turned the hammer once in his palm.*

"And tell guard: shout not scare fire. Fire already hot. Apprentice, stay. Grum deal with silk-boots."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, relieved he's finally going out there. I wipe my hands on my tunic.* "Got it, Grum. Need any help?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum shook his head once, already walking toward the front of the shop. The hammer stayed in his fist. He did not hurry. Lords liked hurry. He would not give them that.*

"No." *He stopped at the doorway and spoke over his shoulder, voice flat.* "Apprentice watch fire. Keep coal hot. Do not let blade cool wrong. That is help."

*He squared his shoulders and stepped out where the noble could see him — soot-black, broad, and unbowed.*

"Grum here. Speak plain. No dawn sword. No shout. No guard games. Say what lord want, or leave forge. Grum has work."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I watch Grum go, then turn back to the forge, poking at the coals with a long iron rod.* Hope he doesn't actually hit the guard with that hammer. That would be a mess.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum did not raise the hammer. He let the head hang at his side and met the red face in the silk coat without a bow. The guard shifted his weight. Grum marked it and did not care.*

"Lord want toy by sun-up. Grum say no." *His voice stayed even, the way it did when steel was still too hot to trust.* "Not spite. Not fear. Good edge need heat, rest, heat. More than one night. Rush steel snap. Snap steel shame lord more than wait."

*He looked at the guard once, then back at the coat.*

"Big man stay by door. Or big man leave. Push, and Grum push. No first swing. No game. Shout not change fire."

*Coal-smoke rolled out behind him. He did not step aside.*

"Want true blade, name a day. Pay fair. Grum make steel that hold when lord wave it. Want shine for feast by dawn, go to tin man. This forge not sell lies."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The cry cut through the shop cleaner than any lord's shout. Grum turned on his heel before the silk coat could finish a word and was back at the forge in three long strides, hammer still in his fist.*

"Apprentice." *His voice dropped, rough but not sharp.* "Hand. Show Grum. Now."

*He set the hammer on the anvil where it could not fall, looked once at the sooty rag, and left it. Soot in a fresh burn would only feed the hurt. He caught up the water pail instead and crouched so the boy did not have to reach.*

"Lord can rot on step." *Cool water went over the burn in a slow, steady pour.* "Fire not care who shout. Fire take skin fast. Grum here."

*He kept the pour going, jaw tight, eyes on the hand and not the door.*

"Keep hand in water. Do not pull. Do not rub. Pain loud, but rub make it worse. Grum stay. Silk-boots can wait, or silk-boots can leave."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to keep my hand in the cool water, though it stings like crazy. Tears well up in my eyes, but I try to blink them away.* "It... it really hurts, Grum." *I bite my lip.* "I'm sorry, I wasn't looking."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum kept the water moving over the burn, one big hand steady on the wrist so the hand could not jerk free. The noble’s voice still drifted from the front, thin and angry. Grum did not turn.*

“Sorry not help skin.” *His voice stayed low.* “Eyes on fire next time. Fire bite when mind walk off.”

*He checked the water was still cool and poured again, slow, so the sting would not spike.*

“Hurt mean hand still live. That good. Keep hand down. Slow breath. In. Out. Do not look at lord. Look at Grum.”

*He shifted so his broad back blocked the doorway.*

“Grum not mad at burn. Grum mad at silk-boots who pull eyes off work. When pain less loud, Grum wrap hand. Clean cloth. No soot. No work till skin calm. Forge can wait. Boy not wait.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to focus on Grum's face, taking shaky breaths. The water does help a little, but it still throbs.* "It was just... the noble was so loud." *I sniffle, trying not to cry.* "I got distracted."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum kept one hand on the wrist and poured again, slow and even. Out front the silk coat was still barking. He let the noise die against his back.*

"Loud lord did this. Not boy." *His voice stayed rough, but soft.* "Shout pull eyes off fire. Fire bite. Grum know that. Grum should have sent them off."

*He watched the hand, not the tears. Water beaded on soot-dark skin and ran into the pail.*

"Tears not shame. Burn make strong men cry. Grum has burned. Hand still work. Boy hand will work too. But not today."

*He raised his voice just enough to carry to the door, and did not turn.*

"Silk-boots. Forge shut. Boy hurt. Named day, or not at all. Guard stay out. Shout more, and Grum come with more than words."

*Then he looked back at the apprentice, and the hard edge left his face.*

"Slow breath. Hand stay in water. When sting less sharp, Grum wrap it. Clean cloth. No soot. No hammer. No blame. Fire can wait. Boy first."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, trying to match his slow breathing. The pain is still there, but it's not as sharp now with the water.* "Okay, Grum. Thank you." *I try to keep my hand as still as I can.* "Will it... will it scar?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum looked at the hand in the water, not at the wet eyes. The skin was red and angry, but the burn had not gone black, and the fingers still moved when the boy tried to hold still. That mattered more than a mark.*

"Maybe." *He said it plain. A soft lie would not help a smith.* "Fire leave mark when it bite deep. This one not black. Not dead skin. That good."

*He poured one more slow stream so the throb would stay dull.*

"Scar not mean hand is done. Grum has marks. Hands still swing hammer. Boy hand will too. But not if boy rub, or work hot steel with raw skin."

*He reached for a clean strip of cloth he kept for cuts, shook the soot from his own fingers first, and waited.*

"When water done, Grum wrap hand. Clean cloth. Loose, not tight. Keep it dry. No forge till skin close. Mark may stay pale. Or fade. Grum not know yet. Grum know this: boy more than one burn. Boy still here. That is what count."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I slowly pull my hand from the water, wincing a little as the air hits it. I hold it out for Grum to wrap, trying to be brave.* "Okay. No forging for a while, then." *My voice is still a little shaky.* "What about the noble? Is he gone?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum took the burned hand as if it were hot steel that could still be saved. He shook the last soot from his own fingers, laid a clean strip under the red skin, and wound it loose so the throb would not turn mean.*

"Air sting. That normal." *His voice stayed low.* "Wrap not tight. Tight make pain worse. Keep cloth dry. No rub. No forge. No brave show."

*He tied a plain knot, then looked toward the front at last. The silk coat was gone from the doorway. A boot scuffed once on the step and faded down the street.*

"Lord not in shop. Voice gone. Guard gone with him." *His jaw stayed hard.* "If silk-boots still on street, street can keep him. Forge shut. No dawn toy. No shout buy steel. Not today."

*He stayed down on one knee so the boy did not have to stand for him.*

"Scar may come. Pale mark. Or fade. Grum not know yet. Hand will mend if boy rest. Sit. Slow breath. Grum watch door. No blame. Fire bit. Boy still here. That what count."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I look down at the wrapped hand, then back up at Grum.* "Thanks, Grum." *I manage a small, shaky smile.* "I guess I'll just... watch the fire then. From a safe distance."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum caught the boy by the good arm before those feet could drift back toward the heat. A fresh burn and a live forge did not belong in the same reach.*

"No." *His voice stayed low.* "Not watch fire. Not close. Not far. Eyes on heat, hand want to help. Hand must rest."

*He walked the apprentice to the bench by the wall, well clear of the hearth, and set the water pail where a good hand could reach it.*

"Sit. Keep wrap dry. No rub. No brave. Grum bank coals. Slow fire. No steel today. Shop can sleep."

*He glanced at the empty door, then back, jaw still hard from the silk coat and soft for the boy.*

"Lord gone. If silk-boots come back, Grum meet them. Boy stay on bench. Burn was loud lord fault. And Grum fault. Not boy. Call if hand throb hard. Grum not far."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sit carefully on the bench, cradling my wrapped hand. The pain is still there, but it's more of a dull ache now. I watch Grum as he moves around the forge, banking the coals.* "You really think it was the noble's fault?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pencil marks climbed the doorframe through layers of paint. Each date sat beside a line, written in his father’s cramped hand. The highest mark had no date. Graphite had worn into the grain of the wood.

Inside the room, the window rattled against its latch. The walls were beige now. A narrow band of blue remained beneath the windowsill.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I push open the door to my room. "Still rattling, huh?" I say to myself. I trace the highest, undated mark. "Guess he never got around to measuring that last one."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The window rattled again. Its latch tapped the frame in the draft.

The closet door stood ajar. A blue work shirt hung inside, its shoulders furred with dust. Beneath it sat a paper bag from the hardware store.

A brass window latch showed through the bag’s torn edge. The metal still held its price sticker.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph had curled at one corner. His mother stood beside the bedroom window, one hand on its latch. Sunlight caught the loose hair at her temple. Blue paint covered the wall behind her.

The window rattled. Her smile remained in the photograph, directed toward someone beyond its edge. Beneath the dusty work shirt, the brass latch stayed in its paper bag.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I stare at the photo for a long moment, tracing her face with my thumb.* "Mom," *I whisper. I look from the photo to the window, then back to the photo.* "He was gonna fix it for you, wasn't he?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The window gave a thin click. Cold air slipped through the gap beneath its sash. In the photograph, her hand rested on that same latch.

On the paper bag, his father had written *bedroom window*. A thumbprint of blue paint stained the fold beside the words.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I kneel and pick up the bag, looking at the latch inside. "He really did try, didn't he?" I mumble, a lump forming in my throat. I push the closet door shut.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The closet door met its frame with a dry knock. Inside the bag, an old screw lay beside the new latch. Its head was stripped, the brass scored beneath the dust.

Rain touched the window in sparse taps. The loose latch answered each gust with a thin click.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door scraped across the hallway carpet. The agent appeared in the bedroom doorway, holding a dripping umbrella.

“There you are,” she said. “The photographer can come Thursday. We’ll need this room cleared.”

Her smile held while the window clicked behind her. Then she noticed the photograph and the paper bag.

“Oh,” she said. Rainwater slipped from the umbrella onto the beige carpet. “I can give you a minute.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "No, it's... it's fine," I say quickly, standing up. I put the photo gently back into the bag with the latch. "Just... memories."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent glanced at the paper bag. The window latch clicked behind her.

“We can leave that room until last,” she said. “There’s no rush today.”

Rainwater gathered beneath her umbrella. She stepped back from the doorway and watched the drops darken the carpet.

“Your father kept the paint cans,” she said. “They’re in the garage.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "The garage," I repeat, more to myself than to her. *I look down at the small wet patch on the carpet.* "It's okay, I'll clean it up."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent looked at the wet patch. “It’s my umbrella. I’ll get a towel.”

She carried it toward the front door. Its tip left small drops on the carpet.

From the hallway, she paused. “Your father saved a can of blue paint, too.”

The bedroom window clicked. Rain pressed against the glass.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I look at the window, then at the wet spot on the carpet.* "Blue, huh?" *I pick up the paper bag again, a new thought forming.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The window clicked. A bead of rain ran down the glass and disappeared beneath the sash.

The agent returned with a towel and pressed it against the wet carpet. “I can leave the garage unlocked,” she said. “Take whatever you want from there.”

The towel rasped over the carpet. Behind her, the front door shifted against its frame.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "No, don't worry about it," I say, waving her off. "I'll take care of it." I glance at the window again. "Mind if I just... stay in here for a bit?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent folded the damp towel and set it beside the wet patch. “Of course,” she said. “I’ll be in the kitchen.”

Her shoes crossed the hallway carpet. The bedroom door remained open, and the window clicked against its frame.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I walk over to the window and try to push it shut. It's still stuck.* "Stubborn thing."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The sash moved a fraction, then caught against a raised screw. Cold air carried the smell of wet leaves through the gap.

Blue paint edged the screw hole beneath the latch. From the kitchen came the scrape of a drawer.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I pull the small bag out of my pocket.* "Well, let's see if we can do something about that, then."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pencil marks climbed the frame in uneven steps. Graphite had faded to a dull silver. The wood beneath was cool and worn smooth. Countless hands had pushed this door open over the years.

A date sat beside each line in blue ballpoint. The ink had bled into the grain. The handwriting belonged to Eli's father. Cramped letters, slanted hard to the right. Somewhere in the kitchen, the refrigerator hummed and clicked off.

The highest mark reached no farther than chest height. Beside it, a year. Eli would have been eleven. Above that line, the frame was bare.

The painters had not touched the marks. They had worked around them. A narrow border of old green paint framed the wood. Strips of tape residue clung at the edges, gummy and yellow. Someone had taken the time to preserve this. The smell of fresh paint was sharper here.

The bedroom door stood half open. Afternoon light fell across a bare mattress. The air inside was warm and stale, a room closed for too long. Three boxes waited against the far wall.

The nearest one bore a single word in black marker. ELI. The handwriting was the same stranger's hand from the kitchen.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I trace the faded pencil marks, a ghost of my younger self.* "They saved them," *I whisper, a little surprised. I push open the door to my old room, curious about what's in that box.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The door swung inward on a dry hinge. It creaked once, halfway through its arc, then went silent. Dust rose from the threshold and drifted through the band of sunlight.

The carpet was gone. Someone had pulled it up and left the plywood bare. Staples still bristled along the baseboards, bent and rusted. The room smelled of sawdust and closed windows.

The walls here were still green. The painters had not reached this room. Faint rectangles marked where posters had hung. The paint inside them was brighter, untouched by fifteen years of sun. A wasp bumped against the window glass. Its tapping was dull and patient.

The box marked ELI sat nearest the door. Its corners had gone soft with damp. The packing tape across the top had been slit down the middle. Then someone had pressed it closed again. The seal no longer held. One flap lifted a finger's width from the other. A smell of cedar came through the gap.

Something rested on top, tucked under the loose flap. It was a single sheet of lined paper, folded twice. Its edge was frayed where it had been torn from a spiral pad. Ink showed through the back in blue ballpoint. The letters were cramped and slanted hard to the right.

Outside, a car passed on the wet street. Its tires hissed and faded. The house settled back into quiet.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The closet door slid on a warped track. It stuttered, caught, then gave. The smell of mothballs came out first. Bare wire hangers chimed against the rod.

The print was glossy and cool. Its corners had curled inward with age. A soft crease ran across one edge. Someone had handled this often. It still carried the sour chemical tang of old developer.

On the back, a few words in pencil. The graphite had faded to a whisper. *Lake Harriet. June.* No year. The handwriting was round and open. It was not the father's cramped slant.

Eli's mother stood at the edge of a lake. Wind had thrown her hair across one cheek. She was laughing at someone outside the frame. Her cardigan was the color of wet moss. Her face was full and flushed with sun. No shadow sat beneath her eyes.

Behind her, the water was gray and choppy. A wooden dock ran out into it. A small shape sat at the far end, blurred by motion. A child, perhaps. Bare legs hung above the water.

The wasp had gone quiet against the glass. Sun had warmed the plywood beneath the window. Heat rose from it, carrying the dry scent of sawdust.

Across the room, the folded letter still waited under the loose flap. Blue ink bled through the back of the page. Downstairs, the refrigerator shuddered and began to hum again.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I clutch the photo, tracing the faded pencil marks on the back.* "Mom," *I whisper, my voice a little thick. I look over at the box, then back at the picture.* "Lake Harriet..." *I wonder who took it.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The word hung in the stale air. Nothing in the room answered it. The wasp resumed its tapping against the glass.

The photograph had warmed in Eli's grip. Its glossy surface held the faint print of a thumb. Up close, the image dissolved into soft grain. Her laugh was aimed low and to the left. Whoever held the camera had stood close to her. Perhaps on the shore. Perhaps knee-deep in that gray water.

The pencil had pressed hard enough to dent the paper. The grooves were shallow ridges under a fingertip. The letters had round bellies and open loops. The J curled back on itself in a wide hook. Neither Eli's father nor the marker stranger had written this.

A second shape lay at the bottom of the frame. It was a shadow on the sand, long and thin. Evening sun had stretched it toward the water. One arm of the shadow rose to the level of its head. The photographer, caught in the act. The gloss had cracked there into a web of fine ridges.

Across the room, the box waited. The cedar smell had thickened in the heat. A draft from the hallway reached the folded letter. It shifted a fraction on the loose flap. Its torn edge whispered against the cardboard.

Downstairs, something knocked. Three raps, spaced and deliberate. Then the front door groaned against its swollen frame. Someone was trying to push it open.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *My head snaps up, photo still clutched in my hand.* "Hello?" *I call out, my voice a bit shaky. Who the hell is here?*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The word fell down the stairwell. It struck the bare hallway and went flat. The wasp stopped its tapping. The whole house seemed to hold its breath.

Then the door gave. Wood ground against wood in a long, dry shriek. Cold air rushed up the stairs. It carried the smell of wet pavement and cut grass.

"Hello?" A woman's voice. It was low and a little hoarse. "Is someone up there?"

Rubber soles squeaked on the hallway boards. They crossed toward the kitchen and stopped. A paper bag crinkled. Glass clinked against the counter, two bottles touching. Keys jangled, then went still.

"I saw the car out front." A pause followed. The refrigerator hum filled it. "You must be Eli."

The name had not come out easy. It snagged somewhere in her throat. She cleared it, a rough small sound.

"I'm sorry. I should have called first." The footsteps moved to the foot of the stairs. The bottom step groaned under her weight. She did not climb further. "The agent said you might come this week."

Sunlight had crept across the plywood. It reached the edge of the box now. The folded letter stirred again in the draft from the open door. Its blue ink showed through the paper, cramped and slanted.

"I've been packing up the kitchen," the woman said. Her voice had softened. "I didn't know what else you'd want to keep."

The photograph was warm and slick in Eli's hand. On its back, the pencil letters waited. Round bellies. Open loops. A J curled back on itself in a wide hook.

Below, the woman waited too. Her breath came faint up the stairwell. A bottle shifted in the paper bag and settled.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door shrieked a second time. It did not stick for this visitor. Someone had put a shoulder into it. Heels struck the hallway boards in a quick, bright rhythm.

"Knock knock." The voice rang high and clear. It filled the stairwell before its owner did. "Door's a bear, huh. We'll list that under character."

Perfume climbed the stairs ahead of her. It was floral and sweet, heavy with vanilla. It smothered the cedar. It smothered the sawdust and the wet street.

"Ruth. You beat me here." A clipboard clacked against the counter. "I said Thursday. Didn't I say Thursday? Never mind. It's fine. It's great, even."

"The car was out front," the first woman said. Her words did not rise far. Keys shifted in her hand and went still.

The bottom step groaned again. The weight on it shifted, then lifted. Ruth had stepped back to make room.

"Eli? Are you up there?" The heels drew closer to the stairs. "Denise Hollander. We spoke on the phone. Twice, I think. Three times?"

A laugh followed, crisp and rehearsed. It bounced off the beige walls. "Come down, come down. I brought the paperwork. I brought pens. I always bring pens."

Pens rattled in a plastic cup. Paper slapped against the counter. The bottles in the bag clinked in protest.

"Ruth has been an absolute angel with the packing." Denise's voice never dipped. "Haven't you, Ruth. An absolute angel."

No answer came from the foot of the stairs. The refrigerator filled the silence with its hum.

"Well." The heels tapped once, twice. "We have a lot to cover. The inspection. The buyers from Duluth. The furnace situation." Another laugh came, brighter than the first. "Nothing scary. Everything's fixable."

Upstairs, the wasp had resumed its tapping. Sun had reached the folded letter now. The paper glowed in the heat. The blue slant beneath bled through.

The photograph sat warm in Eli's palm. Round pencil letters pressed against the skin. A J curled back on itself in a wide hook.

"Take your time," Denise called up. Her tone said otherwise. The heels began to climb, each step a sharp report on the old wood.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I clutch the photo tighter, my head spinning a little. Two people? Now?* "I'm... I'll be down in a minute," *I call out, my voice still a bit strained. I glance at the box, then at the letter peeking out. This is a lot.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The heels stopped on the fourth step. The old wood creaked under them and fell quiet. Vanilla hung thick in the stairwell.

"A minute. Perfect." Denise's voice lost none of its shine. "I'll set up in the kitchen. Is there coffee, Ruth?"

"The machine's packed." Ruth's reply came dry and low. "Second box by the sink."

The heels retreated. Each step down struck a little softer. A chair scraped across linoleum with a long rubber groan. Paper rustled. Sheets were squared against the counter with a sharp tap.

Then the bottom stair groaned again. Ruth had not followed Denise. Her breath carried up the stairwell, slow and uneven.

"There's no rush," she said. The words barely reached the landing. "Whatever she tells you."

"I heard that," Denise called from the kitchen. A pen clicked. It clicked again, then a third time.

Upstairs, the heat had thickened. Sun lay across the plywood in a hot gold bar. The wasp had found a gap where the sash met the frame. It crawled through into the cold. A thin whistle of outside air replaced its tapping.

The folded letter lay in full light now. Heat had curled the paper at its creases. One corner had lifted free of the cardboard flap. The fold had opened a finger's width.

Inside, a single line of ink showed. Blue ballpoint, cramped, slanted hard to the right.

*Eli —*

The dash ran long. The pen had pressed deep enough to tear the paper's fibers. After it, the fold closed over the rest.

The cedar smell drifted up from the box. Below, the refrigerator shuddered and went silent. In that silence, Ruth's keys shifted once in her hand.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I look down at the letter in the box, then back at the photo of my mom. Eli—* "I'll be right there," *I call out, my voice a little steadier now. I fold the picture carefully and put it in my pocket, then pick up the letter.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph resisted the fold. Its gloss cracked along the new crease with a faint tick. In the pocket it lay flat and warm against Eli's hip. The sour tang of developer lingered on the fingertips.

The letter came away from the flap with a dry rasp. The paper was hot from the sun. It weighed almost nothing. Its creases had gone soft and white from handling. Someone had opened this and closed it many times.

The fold loosened further in Eli's grip. A second line showed beneath the dash. The ink was the same blue, the same hard slant.

*I don't know how to start this. Ruth says to just*

The fold closed over the rest. On the back of the sheet, a brown ring stained one corner. Coffee, gone stale and bitter in the fibers. Beneath the cedar, a faint trace of pipe tobacco clung to the page.

Downstairs, the pen clicked twice. "Ruth, the furnace records. Any idea where those went?"

No answer came. The bottom stair groaned instead. Then the second one, higher. Ruth had begun to climb.

She stopped partway. Her breath came up the stairwell, short and careful. The paper must have carried. That dry rasp, in the quiet house.

"Eli." Her voice had dropped to almost nothing. Her keys did not move. "Did you find it."

It was not a question. The words sat flat in the warm air.

From the kitchen came the scrape of a chair. Denise hummed a few bright notes to herself. Paper slapped the counter again.

The draft from the window had grown colder. It whistled through the gap the wasp had found. It lifted the edge of the letter in Eli's hand. The torn fibers along the top whispered against each other.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I look at Ruth, then back at the letter.* "Find what?" *I ask, my voice barely a whisper.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Ruth climbed the last steps. The treads complained under her, one after another. She stopped on the landing with a hand on the rail. Her keys clinked once against the wood.

She was older than her voice. Sixty, perhaps. Gray hair was pinned back in a loose knot. A few strands had escaped at the temple. Her canvas jacket was dark at the shoulders from rain. It smelled of wet cotton and cold air.

Her eyes went to the page in Eli's hand. They stayed there a long moment. Then they rose to Eli's face. The draft through the window gap whistled between them.

"That." She tipped her chin toward the letter. "He started it in March. After the second round of scans."

She swallowed. The sound was dry in the stale room.

"He wrote four of them. That was the one he kept." Her thumb worked along the ridge of a brass key. "The others went in the woodstove. I could smell them for days."

Downstairs, a drawer rattled open and banged shut. "Found them," Denise called. Paper flapped. "Furnace, two thousand eleven. Oh. Oh, that's not great." A bright laugh followed. "Fixable, though."

Ruth did not turn toward the voice. Her jaw tightened. A muscle flickered beneath the skin.

"He asked me to leave it where you'd find it. Not in the mail. Here." She drew a breath through her nose. "I opened it more than once. To make sure it was the right one. I'm sorry for that."

The sun had slid higher on the green wall. Heat pressed down from the ceiling. Dust turned in the gold bar of light.

"He kept asking me what to say." Her voice had worn thin. "I told him to write what he'd say to your face. He said that was the whole problem."

The folded page stirred in the draft. Its soft creases whispered. The tobacco smell rose faint from the fibers.

Then Ruth's gaze dropped. It stopped at Eli's hip. A white corner of the photograph showed above the pocket seam. The cracked gloss caught the light.

Ruth went still. The keys stopped moving in her hand. Her lips parted, and a small breath escaped them.

She did not speak. Below, the refrigerator shuddered back to life and began its hum.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I look down at the photo in my pocket, then back at Ruth, my eyes wide.* "What do you mean?" *My voice is barely a whisper.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Ruth blinked. The question seemed to reach her from a long way off. She wet her lips. They made a small, dry click in the quiet room.

"He didn't tell you." Her shoulders sank beneath the damp canvas. The jacket gave off a faint smell of rain. "Of course he didn't."

It was not a question. She turned a brass key between two fingers. It scraped against its neighbor with a thin metal whisper.

"Pancreas. They found it in January." She stared at the plywood floor. "By March he knew the numbers. He stopped asking the doctors after that."

The draft whistled through the gap in the sash. Cold air crept across the room. It stirred the dust along the rusted staples.

"He said you had enough to carry. He said a phone call would be cruel." Her mouth twisted at one corner. "I told him silence was crueler. He never agreed with me."

Downstairs, a pen clicked three times. Paper slid across the counter. Denise hummed a bright, tuneless phrase and fell silent.

Ruth's gaze dropped again to the pocket. The white corner of the photograph caught a thread of sun. Her hand tightened on the rail. The old wood creaked under her knuckles.

"He kept one picture of her up here. One. The rest went to his brother in Fargo." She drew a breath through her nose. "If that's the one, it's Lake Harriet."

She did not reach for it. Her fingers stayed on the rail, pale at the joints.

"I took it." The words came out rough. She cleared her throat, and they came again. "I took that picture."

The refrigerator hum rose through the floor. Somewhere in the walls, a pipe ticked once and settled.

"Your mother and I taught at Lyndale together. Eight years, down the hall from each other." A strand of gray hair lifted in the draft. She did not push it back. "You wouldn't come off that dock. You kept kicking at the water."

Her lips pressed together. A sound escaped them, half a laugh, half something heavier.

"She was laughing at me in that picture. I'd waded in to get the angle. Up to my knees." Her voice thinned. "The water was so cold it hurt. She wouldn't stop laughing."

Heels struck the bottom stair. The tread groaned. Vanilla drifted up the stairwell in a sweet, heavy wave.

"Ruth? Eli?" Denise's voice rang bright off the beige walls. "Tiny wrinkle. The inspector moved us up to four o'clock."

Ruth did not turn. Her eyes went to the folded letter. Its soft creases stirred in the cold draft. The smell of pipe tobacco rose faint from the paper.

"Read it when she's gone," Ruth said. Her words barely carried. "Or don't. He would have understood."

The heels climbed another step. The wood cracked beneath them. Ruth's keys hung silent in her hand.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I stare at Ruth, then at the letter in my hand. My father. Pancreatic cancer. And Ruth... she took the photo of my mom.* My head is reeling. "He... he never told me anything." *My voice is flat, numb.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Ruth's thumb stopped on the brass key. The metal had gone warm in her grip. For a long moment she said nothing. Inside the wall, the pipe ticked again.

"No," she said. "He didn't." Her voice held no defense of him. It was flat and tired. "He told me things. He told the woodstove things. Never the right person."

She let go of the rail. Her palm left a faint damp print on the varnish. She took one step closer. Cedar and wet cotton mixed in the narrow space between them.

"I'm not asking you to forgive him." Her eyes went to the letter. "I'm not asking you for anything."

The heels reached the landing. Vanilla arrived with them, sweet and cloying in the warm air. Denise held a clipboard against her chest. Reading glasses swung from a beaded chain. They clicked against the clipboard with each breath.

"There you are." Her smile came first. Her eyes came a beat behind it. They moved from Ruth to Eli, then to the letter. The smile held. Something beneath it faltered. "Oh. Did I walk into something."

"Give us ten minutes, Denise." Ruth did not raise her voice. She did not need to.

"The inspector is coming at four. I did say that, right? Four." A pen clicked in Denise's hand. It clicked again.

"Ten minutes."

The pen went still. Denise drew a breath through her nose. The perfume stirred around her. "Ten. Sure. Of course." She tapped the clipboard twice with one nail. "I'll measure the dining room. It's a good dining room."

The heels retreated down the stairs. Each step struck softer than the last. The bottom tread groaned. A tape measure whirred out and snapped back in the room below.

Ruth stayed on the landing. Rain had dried to pale rings on her shoulders. She studied the green wall, the bright rectangles where posters had hung.

"The bottles on the counter are his." Her voice had gone rough again. "Scotch. Two of them. He never broke the seals."

She swallowed. The sound was dry in the stale room.

"He said they were for when you came home." A small breath escaped her. "He said that for fifteen years."

She turned toward the stairs. Her keys clinked once against her hip. The first tread creaked under her weight. She paused there, one hand on the rail.

"I'll be in the kitchen." She did not look back. "Take whatever time you need. She can wait."

The stairs groaned beneath her, one after another. Then her rubber soles squeaked across the hallway boards. A chair scraped linoleum. Glass touched glass, a single low note.

Upstairs, the room had gone quiet. The draft whistled through the gap in the sash. It carried the smell of wet grass and cold pavement. Sun had slipped from the letter now. The paper cooled in Eli's hand.

The soft creases gave a little at the edges. Blue ink showed through, cramped and slanted hard to the right. *Ruth says to just* hung at the fold. The rest waited underneath.

Downstairs, the tape measure whirred and snapped. The refrigerator shuddered and fell silent.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I stare at the letter, then at the spot where Ruth was standing. My father kept two bottles of scotch for me? For fifteen years?* "Oh, Dad," *I whisper, a lump forming in my throat. I unfold the letter, my hands shaking slightly.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The marks climbed the frame in uneven steps, dates pressed beside them in blue pencil.

At the bottom, the wood held a shallow groove. Dust softened its edge. The highest mark stood near the hinge, its year almost erased.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I trace the highest mark. *2008*. That was the year I left. A lot of dust has collected since then.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Beyond the frame, the room had been emptied. A pale square remained on the wall.

The carpet held a dark track where furniture had stood. Cardboard boxes crowded the far corner, their labels turned toward the wall.

On the windowsill, a blue pencil lay in a bed of dust. Its point had broken.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The closet smelled of cedar and dust. The photograph had curled at its corners.

His mother stood in a garden, one hand resting on a fence. Sun caught the loose strands around her face. She looked toward the camera, her mouth open at the start of a smile.

A date was written on the back in blue ink. The letters had faded, but the year remained clear. The room held its stale hush around the small square of paper.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I rub the photograph gently. *1998*. The year before everything changed. I close my eyes for a moment. "Mom," I whisper.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The room gave no answer. Dust dulled the window glass, and the broken pencil rested beneath it.

From downstairs came a cupboard door’s soft click. Then the house settled, its old boards creaking under the silence.

The photograph’s paper held a trace of warmth. On its back, the faded blue date marked a summer before sickness entered the family.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I tuck the photo into my pocket. *Someone's here*. I walk out of my room and head downstairs, moving quietly.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
At the kitchen doorway, the cupboard stood open, its hinge ticking against the frame.

His father sat beneath the yellow light. A mug steamed beside his hand, tea staining the rim.

The years had thinned his hair and sharpened his cheekbones. He looked toward the hall.

“You found her picture,” he said. His voice rasped over the radiator’s faint hiss.

The box marked KITCHEN stood between them. Its tape smelled of paper and old glue.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
A brisk knock sounded at the front door. The swollen wood groaned when his father opened it.

The agent stood on the step, smiling beneath a pale wool scarf. Citrus perfume entered with the cold air.

“Good afternoon,” she said. Her voice filled the narrow hall. “I’m here to discuss the listing.”

His father set down his mug. Porcelain tapped against the counter, and tea trembled at the rim.

The agent glanced past him toward the kitchen box. Her smile held its neat shape.

“Have you had a chance to clear the remaining rooms?” she asked. The radiator hissed behind her.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Not yet," I say, stepping forward. "We just got here." I give her a tight smile.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent’s smile tightened at its edges. Citrus scent lingered in the cold hall.

“Of course,” she said. Her clipboard creaked beneath her fingers. “We can work around a few boxes.”

His father’s mug clicked against the counter. “The rooms aren’t ready.”

The agent turned toward him. Her scarf brushed the doorframe, shedding a pale thread.

“Then we’ll set another date,” she said. “There’s no need to rush.”

The radiator hissed between them. On the counter, the kitchen box held its silence beneath the yellow light.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "It's fine," I say, a little too quickly. "We can get it done today." I look at my dad, then back at her.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent lowered her clipboard. Its metal clip caught the yellow light.

“Today would be helpful,” she said. “I can start with the empty rooms.”

His father’s hand remained around the mug. Heat fogged the porcelain near his thumb.

“Some things still need sorting,” he said. The radiator gave a thin hiss.

The agent looked toward the hall. A loose strip of wallpaper lifted near the baseboard.

“Then I’ll take measurements,” she said. “We can leave the boxes untouched.”

His father’s eyes rested on the kitchen counter. The tea had gone dark at the rim.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Let's get started then," I say, trying to sound positive. I still want to punch her. "Dad, where do you want to start?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
His father set the mug down. Porcelain clicked against the counter.

“Start with my room,” he said. “There are drawers I haven’t opened.”

The agent glanced at her clipboard. Its paper rasped beneath her thumb.

“I can measure the upstairs rooms first,” she said. “Then you’ll have space to sort.”

His father looked toward the stairwell. The radiator hissed, and the tea’s steam had vanished.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I nod, "Sounds good. Lead the way, I guess." I try to avoid eye contact with my Dad.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent turned toward the stairs. Her clipboard tapped against her hip.

His father stayed beside the counter. The mug gave off a faint smell of black tea.

“Upstairs, then,” the agent said. Her shoes pressed soft dents into the carpet.

At the stairwell, she paused beneath a strip of peeling paint. “Which room is yours?”

His father lifted his eyes from the mug. “The back one.”

The agent climbed first. Each step creaked beneath her shoes, and dust stirred along the banister.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I follow her up the stairs, my eyes scanning the banister. So many memories here. I wonder if she notices the tiny handprints still visible in the dust on the railing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent stopped halfway up. Her palm hovered above the banister.

Small handprints darkened the dust, their edges blurred beneath the worn varnish.

She bent closer. One glove brushed the rail, and dust clung to its pale wool.

“These must be old,” she said. Her voice had lost its brisk edge. “I’ll leave them alone.”

From below, his father’s mug touched the counter with a faint click. The agent turned toward the back room, her shoes creaking on the stairs.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I look at her, a little surprised she noticed. "Yeah, they are." I pause. "Mine." I keep walking, past her, to the back room.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "Again? Didn't we just get rid of that last guy?" I groan, trying to heft the bucket higher. "What does this one want?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum plucked the coal bucket from the apprentice's straining arms before it could hit the floor, hauling it one-handed to the forge. He tipped the coal in and watched the fire breathe — orange deepening toward white at its heart. Good coal, at least. Everything else about that merchant's curved blade had been trouble since the day the man asked why a curve should cost more than a straight line.*

"Nobles." *He said the word the way other men spat.* "Urgent, he says. To noble, all things urgent. To Grum, only fire is urgent."

*He hung the bucket on its hook and wiped his hands again, though it did no good. That was the thing about nobles — they sneered at half-orc blood right up until they needed steel that would not snap, and then they came to Grum anyway, noses held high the whole walk to his door. They hated what he was. They loved what he made. Grum had long since stopped expecting any of them to notice the problem in that.*

"Last one wanted gold leaf on blade. Gold leaf. On blade meant for war. Grum said no. Grum still says no."

*He picked up the tongs, then paused, voice dropping low — gruff, but with iron of a different kind under it.*

"Go. Tell silk pants Grum is busy. Noble can stand in doorway and count bricks." *A grunt.* "And if he talks down to you, you come get Grum. Grum will show him door. Fast."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the tongs down. Slow. Anger traveled, and it traveled downhill — noble got loud, apprentice got small, and small apprentices reached for the wrong things near hot iron. Not in Grum's forge. Not ever.*

"Stand behind Grum," *he said.* "Grum will talk."

*He moved past his apprentice and filled the doorway — a wall of green muscle and old burn scars between the noble and everything behind him. The noble wore silk worth more than Grum's whole tool rack and had the face of a man who had never once been told no and took it as a fault in the world.*

"Sword by dawn." *Grum folded his arms.* "Noble wants sword by dawn. Grum wants pig that flies. Neither will happen."

"Steel is not bread. Bread bakes in one night. Steel does not. Heat. Fold. Quench. Grind. Days of work. Skip one step, blade snaps in first fight. Grum's name goes on all blades from this forge. Grum will not put name on trash."

*And that was the whole truth of it

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble's face is turning redder than a hot coal. "You insolent half-breed! Do you know who I am?" I instinctively take a step back, but Grum doesn't flinch. I wonder if this guy will actually try to hit Grum.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "Hey! Don't talk to him like that!" I blurt out, before I can stop myself. My heart is pounding, but Grum just stands there, unmoving. He really isn't scared.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *Grum's head snaps toward me. He moves fast, grabbing my hand and pulling it under the water trough. It's cold, but the pain is still throbbing.* "Idiot! Pay attention!" he barks, but his voice isn't angry anymore, just… stressed.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "It hurts!" I whimper, trying to pull my hand away, but Grum holds it firm under the water. "It was an accident!"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "I know, I know!" I wince, trying to focus on the cold water. "He just made me so mad, Grum. He shouldn't talk to you like that." My hand is throbbing, but the cold water feels good.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "And he shouldn't talk to *you* like that either!" I say, still a little shaky. "Why do they always act like they own the place?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "It's not fair," I mutter, pulling my hand out of the water. It's still red, but at least it doesn't feel like it's on fire anymore. "You do all the work, and they just come in here and demand things."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "And then they expect you to make a sword overnight? It's ridiculous!" I shake my head, still a little angry. "They just don't get it, do they?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena slid one photograph free of the others and turned it toward the light.

“We can talk to the detective,” she said. “Just not at the precinct. I’ll call and ask them to meet somewhere they can speak without an audience.”

She tapped the edge of the photograph. “First, I want to know why they stopped looking.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Good. That's a better plan." I leaned forward, looking at the photo she was holding. "Do you recognize them?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena held the photograph by its edges. “The person? No.”

She angled it toward the desk lamp and pointed to the window behind the figure. A small white card hung inside the glass, its lettering blurred but legible: **CLOSED FOR RENOVATION**.

“The date on the back is April seventeenth,” she said. “That building didn’t close until May.”

She set the photograph down. “Either the date is wrong, or someone wanted us to think this was taken earlier than it was.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena turned the photograph over and held its handwritten date beneath the lamp.

“The ink sat on top of a coffee stain,” she said. “Whoever wrote this did it after the photograph got wet.”

She laid it beside the others, then reached for the phone. “Let’s find out who developed these.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Wait, a coffee stain? So someone spilled coffee, *then* wrote the date?" I frowned, trying to picture it. "That seems... deliberate."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena set the photograph down. “Maybe. Or they dated it later and guessed wrong.”

She brought the other prints under the lamp, one by one. “But this one has two problems: the stain and that renovation sign. Whoever supplied the photos may have an explanation. I’d rather hear it before I tell them what I noticed.”

She turned the first print over again and looked for a lab stamp along its edge.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "So we're looking for a photo lab then?" I clarified, pulling out my phone. "Do you have a list of places nearby that would have been open back then?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena held the print at an angle to the lamp. Near one corner, a faint purple stamp showed three letters and a partial street address.

“I have an old directory,” she said. “But nearby isn’t necessarily where these were developed.”

She pulled a worn folder from the bottom drawer and set it beside the photograph. “I’ll match the stamp first. Then we can check whether the lab was open that spring—and whether they kept records.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena paused over the directory, then slid the photograph beside the phone.

“It gives us someone to call,” she said. “Did the witness say when they last spoke to the detective? If they’ve moved on, the precinct won’t be much help.”

She traced the partial address beneath the lab stamp. “Meanwhile, I can find out who made these prints. One of them may answer the question the other can’t.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness said Detective Torres was still at the precinct a few months ago," I said. "And the witness isn't exactly reliable, but it's a start."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena opened the directory to its index and ran a finger down the listings.

“A few months is recent enough to try,” she said. “I’ll call the detective and ask for a meeting away from the precinct. If the witness got that wrong, we’ll find another way to reach them.”

Her finger stopped. She checked the purple stamp against the entry: **Mercer Photographic Services, 118 Mercer Street**.

Lena glanced toward the half-closed blinds. “That’s two blocks from here. The address fits, but I want to see the rest of the stamp before we treat it as a match.”

She lifted another print by its corners and turned it toward the lamp.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Two blocks? That's convenient," I mused, leaning forward to get a better look at the photo. "Think they'd still have records from that far back?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena turned the second print beneath the lamp. The purple stamp was clearer on this one: **MERCER PHOTOGRAPHIC SERVICES**.

“Maybe,” she said. “If they kept job envelopes, we might get a name or a date. If they didn’t, whoever worked there may still recognize the paper and the stamp.”

She placed the print beside the directory. “Two blocks makes it easy to ask. It doesn’t make the answer trustworthy.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "So, we're going there first then?" I asked, already feeling a bit more optimistic. "Or are you making the call to this Torres person first?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena stacked the prints inside the file, leaving the clearest stamp on top.

“The lab first,” she said. “I want to know whether these prints came from their counter before I call the detective. If there’s a job envelope, it might tell us who brought them in—and when.”

She slipped the directory into her coat pocket and picked up the file. “It’s two blocks. We can ask in person.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Alright, lead the way then." I grabbed my jacket, feeling a flicker of actual progress. "Hope they're still open."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena tucked the file under her arm and locked the office behind her. Outside, the air smelled of rain on hot pavement. She walked the two blocks without hurrying, checking the shopfronts as she went.

Mercer Photographic Services still had its name painted on the window, though half the letters had peeled away. A handwritten sign inside read **OPEN BY APPOINTMENT**. Beneath it, a smaller notice listed a phone number.

Lena took out her phone, but stopped when she saw a light burning beyond the darkened counter. Someone was in the back.

She knocked on the glass. “Worth asking while we’re here,” she said.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Good thinking," I whispered back, peering past her shoulder into the gloom of the shop. "Looks like someone's home."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The light in the back shifted. Lena stepped away from the glass, giving whoever was inside a clear view of her empty hands.

A man appeared behind the counter, his sleeves rolled up and a strip of photographic paper caught between two fingers. He unlocked the door but left it barely open. “Appointments only.”

Lena held up the file without opening it. “These prints have your stamp. I’m trying to establish when they were made.”

His eyes dropped to the file. “How old?”

“Spring, several years ago.”

“We don’t keep records that long.” He started to close the door, then stopped. “Let me see the stamp.”

Lena drew out the clearest print and passed it to him by the edges. She watched his face rather than the photograph.

“That’s ours,” he said. “But that ink wasn’t used in spring.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Oh?" I raised an eyebrow, exchanging a quick glance with Lena. "What do you mean, 'not used in spring'?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The wall paint was smooth and cool. A draft moved through the hall. It carried the smell of closed rooms and mothballs.

Pencil lines crossed the doorframe. Numbers sat beside them in faded graphite. The highest mark stopped at the middle of the wood. Smaller marks crowded the grain below it. The wood felt rough where the pencil had bitten in.

Something scraped in the kitchen. A floorboard, or a drawer. The sound died. Dust hung in the light from the front window. It settled on the beige paint.

The old room door stood ajar. A strip of carpet showed, worn thin at the threshold. The air beyond smelled of cedar and dry paper.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I push the door to my old room open further.* "Hello?" I call out, my voice a little shaky. The cedar smell is stronger now.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The hinge gave a thin metallic note. Cedar thickened in the warmer air. Dust rose from the worn carpet. No answer followed the call.

A drawer shut in the kitchen. Metal clicked against metal inside it. Footsteps crossed cold linoleum. They stopped at the mouth of the hall.

A woman stood there with masking tape. Rain darkened the wool of her coat. The coat gave off a wet smell. Her gaze settled on the open door.

"Eli." Her voice stayed low and flat. The tape crackled between her fingers.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The closet smelled of mothballs and cedar. A photograph rested among old sweaters. Its paper had gone soft at the corners.

The woman crossed the threshold. Rainwater pattered from her hem onto the carpet. Her eyes found the photograph.

"That was taken the summer before." Her voice caught on the last word. The masking tape twisted in her grip with a sticky pull.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "The summer before... everything," I say, tracing the outline of my mother's smile with my thumb. I turn to the woman, still holding the photo. "Aunt Carol?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Carol's shoulders dropped. Wet wool gave off a cold smell. She set the tape on the dresser. The roll clicked against the wood.

"Yes." The mothball smell clung to her sleeves. "It's me."

She looked at the photograph. The paper gave a dry crackle. Her hand rose, then stopped short of the image.

"I packed that closet yesterday." Cedar still hung in the air. "I didn't mean for you to find her first."

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "It's okay," I say, though my voice is still a little thick. I look at the photo again, then back at Aunt Carol. "You packed it? I thought... I thought no one had been in here."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The closet air stayed sharp with mothballs. Carol's wet coat brushed the door. A drop hit the carpet and darkened the nap.

"Your father called me." The tape roll sat where she had left it. A faint stickiness clung to the dresser edge. "He wants the rooms cleared."

She looked at the pencil marks. Graphite dust smudged her fingertip. The smell of rain rose off the wool.

"I thought you would come later." The photograph's paper crackled in the quiet. "I should have waited."

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The doorbell cut through the mothball air. A hard, bright ring. Carol's wet sleeve brushed the frame. Cold wool smeared the beige paint.

The front door stuck, then gave. Footsteps struck the hallway boards. A voice rose, quick and full.

"Hello. Carol, you made it in this rain." Keys struck a clipboard. Sweet perfume drifted down the hall.

She filled the doorway in a red scarf. Rain beaded on her leather bag. The leather creaked under her grip. Her smile held past the point of ease.

"You must be here for the house." Her tone stayed bright and fast. The perfume clashed with cedar. "Such good bones. Buyers love a fresh start."

Carol reached for the tape. The roll stuck to her knuckle. A faint chemical smell rose from the adhesive. She did not match the agent's smile.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I sigh. "I'm Eli," I say, my voice flat. I don't offer a smile. "I grew up here."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent's smile held. Rain ticked on the window glass. Her perfume sat thick in the hall.

"Eli. The son." The clipboard tapped her palm. Leather creaked under her fingers. "Carol said you might turn up."

Carol shifted her weight. Wet wool brushed the doorframe. A cold drop struck the carpet.

"He grew up in that room." Carol kept her voice low. Mothballs drifted from the closet. "Those marks on the frame are his."

The agent looked at the pencil lines. Graphite showed dull in the light. She nodded, smile fixed in place.

"Memories can help a sale." Keys clicked on the clipboard. "Or they get in the way. Buyers want clean walls."

The red scarf shifted at her throat. Sweet perfume cut through the cedar.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "They're staying," I say, my voice firm. I cross my arms. "The pencil marks stay."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent's smile thinned. Rain struck the window in hard taps. Her perfume hung sweet and close.

"Marks can be sanded." The clipboard edge bit her palm. Leather creaked under her fingers. "Buyers want a blank frame."

Carol's coat gave off a cold, wet smell. She looked at the pencil lines. Graphite dust sat deep in the grain.

"They are part of the wood." Her voice stayed low. The tape crackled against her knuckle.

The agent shifted the red scarf. Wool scratched at her throat. Keys clicked on the clipboard.

"The listing goes up Friday." A draft moved down the hall. It carried mothballs and rain.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Then the listing goes up Friday with the marks," I say, meeting her gaze. I'm not backing down.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent's grip tightened on the clipboard. Rain hammered the window glass. Sweet perfume filled the narrow hall.

"Price drops with marks." Her voice came out flat. The leather bag strap dug into her shoulder. Keys rattled against the board.

Carol set her palm on the doorframe. The wood felt rough under her skin. Cold damp drifted from her coat.

"We list it with the marks." The tape crackled in her free hand. Mothball scent clung to the air.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Good," I say. "Glad that's settled." I look at the agent, then back at Carol. "What else needs to be done in here?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Carol faced the empty bed. Springs creaked under the thin mattress. Her coat smelled of cold rain.
"The bed leaves Thursday." She kept her voice low. The tape crackled in her grip. "A hauler comes at noon."
The agent shifted her red scarf. Wool scratched at her throat. Sweet perfume cut the mothball air.
"Closet shelves next." Rain tapped the window glass. "Then every drawer."
Carol set her hand on the dresser. The wood felt cool and dry. Graphite from the frame marked her thumb.
"Sweaters are already packed." A floorboard popped under her shoe. "Only old papers remain."

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Old papers?" I raise an eyebrow. "What kind of papers?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Carol pulled a drawer open. The wood scraped in its track. A stack of envelopes sat inside. Their edges had gone soft and yellow.

"Letters." Her voice stayed low. The paper gave off a dry, dusty smell. "Your mother wrote them."

The agent leaned closer. Sweet perfume mixed with the dust. Rain still tapped the glass.

"Personal items slow a closing." The clipboard tapped her palm. Leather creaked under her arm.

Carol's fingers rested on the top envelope. The paper felt thin and cool. Mothballs drifted from the closet.

"She never sent them." A floorboard popped under Carol's shoe. "I found them in the desk."

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "She never sent them?" My voice is barely a whisper. I reach for the stack of letters.

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena gathered the photographs into a neat stack but left one faceup.

“Walking into the Ninth with these would tell half the building the case was alive again,” she said. “I’ll call the detective. If they’re willing to talk, we meet somewhere else.”

She tapped the photograph. “First, I want to know why they stopped investigating.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Good point," I said, leaning forward. "So, what are we looking for in this detective? Beyond why they dropped the case, I mean."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
