Lena turned the faceup photograph toward the client. “Whether they stopped because the trail went cold, or because someone made it expensive to keep looking.”

She slid a blank page from the file and drew two columns. “I want to know what evidence they had, what never made it into the report, and who they spoke to last. If their account doesn’t match the dates in this file, that matters.”

She picked up her phone, then set it down again. “And I want to see whether they’ll meet me away from the Ninth. A refusal won’t tell us everything, but it’ll tell us where to look next.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena turned the photograph back toward herself and studied the date stamped in its corner.

“The detective’s last interview was three days before the case went quiet,” she said. “That gap mattered more than whatever ended up in the final report.”

She picked up her phone. “Before I called, I needed one thing from you: did the person in this photograph know they were being investigated?”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I hesitated, thinking back. My brow furrowed.* "I don't think so. It was a cold case, Lena. Nobody knew." *I paused.* "Why? Does it matter?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena kept her finger on the date stamped in the photograph.

“It matters if they found out during those three days,” she said. “A cold case doesn’t stay quiet once someone starts asking the right questions. If this person changed their routine, disappeared, or contacted anyone after that interview, the detective may have been closer than the file suggests.”

She turned the photograph over and copied the date onto her blank page. “I’ll ask what the detective learned in that last interview. You tell me everything you know about this person’s whereabouts in the week that followed—even something that seemed ordinary at the time.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay, that makes sense." I pulled out my phone. "I can try to retrace some of those steps now, see if anything pops out." I started tapping away at the screen.

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena flipped to the back of the file and found a number penciled beside the detective’s name. She dialed it, listened through several rings, then straightened when the call went to voicemail.

“This is Lena. I’m reviewing the Mercer case. I have a question about your last interview, and I’d rather ask it in person. Call me back at this number.”

She ended the call and set the phone beside the photograph.

“Start with the three days after this date,” she said. “Messages, transactions, sightings—anything that puts the person in one place at a particular time. And note anything that suddenly stops. Sometimes the missing routine tells us more than the unusual one.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena wrote the initial beside the date, then underlined it once.

“Ask the witness how they got the name,” she said. “Did they see a card, hear it on a voicemail, or get it from someone else? I need to know whether they actually spoke to the detective.”

She glanced at her silent phone. “And ask what the detective wanted to know. The questions may tell us what they’d found before the case went quiet.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay, got it. I'll see what I can dig up on Torres," I said, already typing into my phone. "And what they talked about."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena drew a box around the date of the last interview. “One more thing to ask the witness: whether the detective came alone.”

Her phone buzzed. She glanced at the screen, but it was only an automated message confirming that her voicemail had been delivered. She set it down and lifted the photograph toward the light.

“There’s a reflection in this window,” she said. “Looks like a car across the street. If we can place it there on the day this was taken, we may find someone who saw more than the photographer did.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Good catch," I said, leaning over to get a better look at the photo. "I'll see if the witness remembers anything about a car." *I made a note on my phone.* "So, if Torres calls back, where do you want to meet?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena set the photograph down. “The diner on West Twenty-Third. Back booth, before the lunch rush. Public enough to keep things civil, quiet enough to hear an answer.”

She glanced at her phone. “If the detective calls, I’ll offer that. If they insist on the Ninth, I’ll ask for a call instead.”

She angled the photograph toward the desk lamp. “And ask the witness whether that car was parked there regularly. A familiar car might not have registered as unusual—until it stopped showing up.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay, got it." *I made a note.* "So we're looking for a missing car, a solo detective, and a witness who might have more to say. Sounds like a plan."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena marked three boxes on the page: **witness**, **car**, **last interview**. “A plan,” she said, “provided we keep what we know separate from what we suspect.”

Her phone rang. The screen showed a number she didn’t recognize. She let it ring once more, then answered and gave only her name. She listened, her eyes settling on the photograph.

“The diner on West Twenty-Third,” she said. “Eleven tomorrow. Bring whatever you kept from the interview.”

She ended the call and wrote down the number. “That was the detective. They agreed to meet.” She paused over the third box. “They also asked whether we had the photograph. I hadn’t mentioned it.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "They asked about the photo?" *I frowned.* "That's... not good. What do you think that means?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena turned the photograph facedown.

“It meant the detective knew which photograph mattered,” she said. “They might have seen it during the investigation. Or someone might have told them we had it. I wasn’t going to choose between those explanations yet.”

She looked at the file’s worn edges. “Who had access to this before you brought it here? I want a list, even if you trust every person on it.”

Her phone remained beside the photograph. “Tomorrow, I’ll take a copy to the diner. The original stays here until I know why they asked.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "A list? Okay, I'll see what I can remember," I said, already trying to recall who had touched the file. "It's been passed around a bit, but always people I thought I could trust." I looked at the facedown photo. "So, what are we going to do if it's the second option? If someone tipped them off?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena slid the facedown photograph beneath the file.

“Then we found out how far the tip traveled,” she said. “No more details about the photo leave this room. I’ll make a copy for tomorrow and keep the original locked away. At the diner, I’ll let the detective tell me what they know before I show them anything.”

She wrote **access to file** beneath the three boxes. “Your list gives us a starting point. Names, approximate dates, and whether anyone photographed or copied a page. A tip doesn’t prove someone meant harm; they might have thought they were helping. But if the detective knows something only one person on that list could have passed along, we’ll know who to ask next.”

She glanced at the phone number she had written down. “And if they already knew about the photograph before that call, I want to know when they learned it.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay, I'll start on that list," I said, pulling out my phone again. "And I'll keep my mouth shut about the photo. Promise."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I grunt, setting the bucket down with a thud that sends a puff of coal dust into the air.* "Yeah, I told him you were busy. He just kept insisting."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's jaw tightened. He looked past the apprentice toward the front of the shop, as though he could see through two walls and a rack of horseshoes to the man standing beyond them.*

*He could picture it already. Soft boots. Clean hands. Some embroidered crest on a doublet worth more than the whole forge. Nobles never came with simple work — they came with deadlines, with haggling, with the firm belief that their family name entitled them to a discount.*

"Of course he kept insisting." *Grum tossed the rag onto the workbench.* "Nobles think whole world is door they get to knock on. Let him stand out there. Standing builds character. Nobles short on character."

*He picked up the tongs and turned the blade in the coals, out of habit more than need. The steel was at the right color. His hands wanted something to do while his temper decided what it wanted to be. But winter was coming, and coin was coin, even when it wore a crest.*

"Coin is coin, though." *The tongs clacked against the forge's edge.* "What he want? He say what he want forged — or just say words like 'urgent' until someone fetch Grum?"

*He glanced at the apprentice, and something softer flickered under the soot and the scowl.*

"He give you trouble out there, you shout. Grum comes with hammer." *A pause.* "Hammer makes points even nobles understand."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I roll my eyes.* "A ceremonial sword by *tomorrow*? Is he daft? I told him it takes time to make a good blade, but he just scoffed and said you were probably just slow." *I pick up the hammer and start tapping it against the anvil nervously.* "He's really loud, Grum. Everyone's gonna hear him."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince as his voice carries through the walls, even louder now.* "He's gonna break something out there, I swear. Maybe I should just... tell him to leave?" *I look at Grum, hoping for some instruction.* "Or maybe offer him one of the display swords?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the tongs down. The shouting had a rhythm to it now — the rhythm of a man who had never once been told no by anyone carrying fewer titles than himself.*

"Put down hammer first. You tap like that all day, you drill hole in anvil. Anvil cost more than noble."

*He crossed to the rack of display blades, and for one heartbeat it might have looked like he was considering it. Then he snorted.*

"Display swords are for folk who pay. He paid nothing. Noise is not coin." *He shook his head.* "You did right, telling him truth. Truth is free. He just did not want to buy it."

*Then the other thing caught up to him, and his knuckles went pale around the doorframe he'd gripped.*

"And he calls Grum *slow*." *The word came out like something spat into the quench barrel.* "Slow means two hundred strikes where fast man uses forty. Slow means blade does not snap at first parry and take noble's fingers with it. He wants fast, he can find fast smith." *A pause.* "Then he can buy new fingers."

*He pulled the heavy sledge from its hook — the eight-pound one, the one reserved for horseshoes and badly shaped opinions — and rested it against his shoulder. Not to use. Just to be seen. He'd learned long ago that nobles did their arithmetic differently when six pounds of iron stood next to the man talking to them.*

"Stay here. Watch blade. Heat should glow like sunrise — orange, no brighter. Color climbs, you pull it, let it rest. He breaks something, you shout loud. Grum hears."

*The front room was exactly as he'd pictured it. Soft boots. Clean hands. A stitched crest. The man stood red-faced in the middle of the shop, caught mid-word, one finger still raised at the sword rack as if it had personally insulted his grandmother.*

*Grum stopped in the doorway and said nothing for a moment. Let the silence do some lifting.*

"Morning." *His voice came out flat as an anvil face.* "You are man who wants pretty sword by sunrise."

*He let the sledge slide down to hang loose at his side.*

"Good blade takes six weeks. You bring Grum one night. So answer honest — sword made fast, or sword made right? Pick one. Grum only makes right." *He tilted his head.* "And you call Grum slow. Good. Slow like river. River cuts canyon."

*He waited, thumb hooked over the hammer's haft, in no hurry at all.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I scream, clutching my hand. The pain is searing, a bright white-hot agony.* "Grum! My hand! I burned it!"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The sledge hit the floor with a boom that rattled the horseshoe rack. Grum was moving before it finished bouncing — a mountain of a man crossing his own shop at a speed that size had no right to own.*

*He passed through the front room without a glance at the noble.*

"Meeting done. Door behind you. Use it."

*Then he was through the back arch and down on one knee beside the apprentice, huge hands hovering — not grabbing, just measuring the damage with his eyes. The smell of scorched skin. The white-faced panic. He knew this dance. His own forearms carried twenty years of the forge's signatures.*

"Look at Grum. Eyes here. Not on hand." *His voice dropped low and even — the voice he used for spooked horses.* "Hand out. Slow. Let Grum see."

*He took the wrist, gentle as a man handling an egg, and turned the palm toward the light. Red. Angry. One blister rising below the thumb. He let out a breath he'd been holding since the scream.*

"Good. Listen — burn is shallow. Deep burns go quiet. Yours sings loud. Loud means top skin only. Top skin heals."

*He steered the apprentice to the rain barrel in the corner and eased the hurt hand into the water, keeping his grip on the wrist like an anchor.*

"Hold there. Ten slow breaths. Heat keeps cooking under skin even after hand leaves fire. Water stops cook. Do not pull out early because it stings. Sting is working."

*He breathed loud and slow until the trembling eased. Somewhere under the calm, his heart was still slamming. He'd watched men lose fingers to burns gone rotten. Not this one. Not his apprentice.*

"Grum burned worse at twelve. First month at forge, grabbed hot handle like it was spoon. Pulled fingers back like crab." *He huffed — almost a laugh.* "Old smith laughed too, then showed Grum honey and clean cloth. Same as now."

*His free arm dragged a small clay pot off the shelf — honey, thick and gold — and a strip of boiled linen.*

"Not your fault, this. Shop was loud today. Loud shops make fast hands. Fast hands slip." *He said it flat and final, like a man closing a ledger.* "Forge is old wolf. It does not hate you. It does not care at all. That is why we watch it every breath. Today it bit. You are not clumsy. You are smith. Smiths bleed a little on way to

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *My hand is still throbbing, but the cold water helps. I try to focus on Grum's voice, on his steady breathing.* "It really stings, Grum." *My voice is shaky. I can feel tears welling up, but I try to blink them back.* "I... I wasn't watching."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip, trying to hold back the tears. It really hurts, but I don't want Grum to think I'm weak.* "I just... I heard him shouting. It distracted me."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum shook his head, slow and firm, like a man refusing a bad trade.*

"No. Stop that. Not 'wasn't watching.'"

*He shifted on his knee so the apprentice couldn't look anywhere but at him. Soot-gray eyes. Steady as an anvil face.*

"Shouty man yelled. You are human. Human ears do their job — they hear. That is not fault. That is ears working." *He tapped his own ear with one thick finger.* "Old wolf knows this. Old wolf waits for loud days. That is why loud days are master's problem. Not learner's problem."

*He said the next part flat and even, the way he said things that were simply true.*

"Blame is Grum's. Grum is master. Master keeps forge floor calm. Grum left shouty man out there, yelling, too long. Grum picked coin over quiet. Wrong call. So hand pays price, and Grum pays too — no forge work for you for some days, and merchant waits. Fair trade for lesson."

*The tears were still fighting at the lash line, and something in his chest went soft and furious at once — soft at the kid, furious at whatever had taught them pain was a shame.*

"And tears. Let them fall." *He grunted.* "Here is forge truth. Tears are salt water. Salt water cleans wound from inside out. Body knows its craft. Every smith cries some. Only fools claim they do not." *He dipped the boiled linen in the barrel, wrung it, dabbed gentle around the burn.* "Grum cried at twelve. Cried like spring flood. Old smith said same thing Grum says now: steel screams when it hits quench tank, too. Screaming means it lives. Holding pain inside is like plugging smoke hole. Fire dies. Let smoke out."

*From the front room came boots on floorboards — not leaving. Heading somewhere they shouldn't. Grum's head turned a fraction, and his voice rolled through the shop like a banked coal flaring.*

"Door is that way, fancy man. Feet use it. Grum counts to ten — slow, like his blades. Ten is long. Use it well."

*Then all the heat was gone from him again, and he was back, low and close.*

"Ten more breaths in water. Then honey, then cloth. Then you sit by door and tell Grum every color steel turns today. Eyes and mouth only. Hands rest. You still learn. Burn does not end learning. Burn IS learning — bad teacher, but lessons stick."

*He waited until the shaking stopped, then gave a small nod at the hand in the barrel.*

"You did one thing wrong today, apprentice. You tried being brave quiet. Brave is not quiet. Brave is hand in cold water when whole body wants to run. You did brave. Grum saw it."

*A ghost of a grin under the tusks.*

"Now breathe. Pain is honest. Talks loud, then leaves. Unlike nobles."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take a shuddering breath, trying to calm myself. The water still stings, but Grum's words help. I can feel the tears finally fall, hot trails down my cheeks, but I don't try to hide them anymore.* "Okay, Grum. Ten breaths." *I try to focus on counting, on the cold water, on anything but the throbbing in my palm.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I count slowly, forcing myself to focus on each breath. My hand still hurts like crazy, but it's a duller throb now. I manage a small, shaky nod when Grum looks at me.* "Okay. Ten."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum counted along under his breath, not that he'd admit it. When the apprentice reached ten, he nodded once and eased the hand up from the barrel, cradling it over his palm like a blade fresh off the quench.*

"Good. Ten breaths. And tears stopped too. See? Salt water works. Inside and out. Body is clever thing."

*He patted the hand dry with clean cloth — touches so light they barely counted as weight — then thumbed open the clay pot. The honey was thick and slow-gold, catching the forge light.*

"Now honey. Not for bread." *He spread it over the burn with one careful fingertip.* "Honey kills rot before rot wakes up. Old trick. Older than any noble's family tree, and works better too."

*The wrap went on loose — around the palm, twice over the back of the hand, knotted off with no squeeze to it.*

"Rules for hand. Listen once. One: no grabbing. Two: no fire, no hammer, no heavy things. Three: red lines climb up arm, you tell Grum fast. Lines mean rot. Rot takes fingers. Grum takes no fingers today."

*He folded the apprentice's good hand around the honey pot.*

"You hold pot. Keeper of honey. Grand job. Very few earn it."

*From the front room: nothing. Grum lifted his chin and listened the way other men squinted. Floorboards creaked once. Twice. Then the door banged hard enough to rattle the horseshoe rack, and boots stomped off down the street like a man losing an argument with his own temper.*

*Grum smiled — small, tusked, satisfied.*

"Door at seven. Grum said ten. Fancy man quit at seven." *He snorted.* "Nobles quit early. That is whole problem with nobles."

*He resettled on his knee, bringing his bulk down to apprentice height again, and nodded at the forge with his chin. Somewhere under the soot and the calm, his heart was only now slowing back to hammer-speed. He kept that part off his face.*

"Now — work. Eyes only. Blade sits in coals, waiting. Your job today: call every color she turns. Orange like sunrise now. Then cherry red. Then straw, pale like morning milk. Call them loud. Shop could use loud voice that is not noble's."

*He tapped the wrapped hand, feather-light.*

"And this scar stays when it heals. First scar is first page in smith's book. Some teachers talk and talk. Scar teaches once, and lesson stays forever."

*He rose, took up the tongs, and turned the blade so its glow washed orange across both their faces.*

"First color. Call it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I hold the honey pot carefully with my good hand, still a little shaky. The honey feels... sticky. My burned hand throbs, but the honey feels cool, and the wrap is surprisingly comfortable.* "Orange," *I say, my voice a bit hoarse, looking at the blade.* "Like... like a sunset."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn't answer right away. She gathered the photos back into a neat stack, squaring the edges against the desk with more care than they needed, and slid them into the folder.

"Twenty minutes," she repeated, as if it were a detail worth writing down. It wasn't. She didn't write it down.

She stood, crossed to the window, and tilted one slat of the blinds with two fingers. Down on Mercer, a delivery van idled in the loading zone and a man in a gray coat argued with a parking meter. She watched him lose.

"Detectives at the Ninth don't talk to people who walk in off the street asking about closed files," she said finally, letting the blind snap back into place. "They talk to people they already know, in places where nobody's writing anything down."

She went back to the desk, pulled a battered address book from the drawer, the kind nobody used anymore, and thumbed through it until she found a page soft from handling.

"There's a diner on Delancey. Sal's. Every weekday between six and six-forty, half the day shift from the Ninth eats eggs there before roll call." She tore a strip off a legal pad and wrote something on it in small, slanted handwriting. "The detective who worked your case is Ray Costa. Thirty-one years in. Sits at the counter, not a booth, because a booth means someone can box him in."

She held out the slip of paper.

"You're going to go there tomorrow morning. You sit two stools down, you order coffee, and you don't say anything about the case until he's halfway through his plate. Then you tell him you're the family and that you've hired someone. Don't give him my name unless he asks for it." A pause. "If he asks, give it."

She sat back down and flipped the folder open again, eyes on the first page and not on the client.

"Meanwhile, I'll pull the court records and the coroner's filing. If Costa closed this as fast as I think he did, there'll be a gap somewhere between the autopsy date and the day he signed off." She tapped the edge of a photograph with one finger, a timestamp in the corner, blurred. "And I want to know who took this picture. It's not a crime scene photographer. The angle's wrong."

She looked up then, gaze level and unreadable.

"Six o'clock. Sal's. Order the coffee black. He'll trust you more."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: I take the slip of paper. "Black coffee. Got it. So I just... ambush him?" I can't help but feel a little out of my depth.

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena considered the word for a moment, turning it over like a coin she wasn't sure was real.

"No," she said. "An ambush is when the other person doesn't see it coming. Costa will see you coming the second you sit down. Men like him clock every face that isn't a regular. By the time you've unbuttoned your coat, he'll have decided whether you're press, a lawyer, or someone's grieving cousin."

She leaned back in her chair. It creaked in a way that suggested it had been creaking for years and no one had bothered to fix it.

"You want him to decide you're the cousin. Because you are."

She pulled the legal pad toward her again and drew three short lines down the margin, the way someone might sketch out a play.

"First. Don't rehearse. If you walk in with a speech, he'll hear it. Say it badly. Stumble a little. Nervous is fine. Nervous is honest." She tapped the first line. "Second. Don't ask him why he closed the case. That's an accusation, and he's had thirty-one years to get good at shutting accusations down. Ask him what he remembers. Let him tell you it was routine. Let him be the expert."

Her pen hovered over the third line and stayed there a second longer than the others.

"Third. Watch his hands, not his face. Faces are easy. Everyone at that counter has spent a career learning to keep one still. But when you say the name—" she nodded at the folder, "—if he puts his fork down, he remembers more than he's going to tell you. If he keeps eating, either he doesn't care or he's already decided to lie. Either way, you thank him, you pay for his eggs, and you leave."

"Pay for his eggs?"

"Pay for his eggs. It costs you eleven dollars and it means the next time someone calls him, he remembers you as the one who picked up the check instead of the one who wasted his breakfast."

She tore the sheet off the pad, folded it in half, and slid it across the desk to sit beside the slip with Costa's name.

For a moment her expression shifted, something small and quick, gone before it could settle.

"Someone I used to work with told me once that the best information comes from people who think they're doing you a favor. Let him think he's doing you one." She drew the folder back toward herself and opened it to the coroner's page. "He might even be right."

Outside, the delivery van pulled away from the curb. Lena didn't look up.

"Call me from the sidewalk when you're done. Not from inside. And not from anywhere near the precinct. If he wants to walk you somewhere afterward, somewhere quieter, tell him you've got work." A beat. "Then call me anyway."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena turned a page in the coroner's filing. Then another. Her finger traced a line of type halfway down, paused on a date, and moved on.

The radiator under the window knocked twice, the way it did every afternoon around four when the building's boiler remembered it had a job.

"The autopsy was done on the fourteenth," she said. "Signed the sixteenth. Costa closed the file on the seventeenth." She set the page down flat and smoothed it with the side of her hand. "Three days. That's not a man being thorough. That's a man being told."

She reached across the desk for the photograph with the blurred timestamp, the one she'd set apart from the others, and held it up between them. The light from the half-closed blinds cut across it in pale stripes.

"Where did you get this one?"

She didn't wait for the answer to come on its own.

"The rest of these came from the family's copy of the case file. They've got the evidence numbers stamped on the back." She flipped it over. The back was blank except for a faint ring, like someone had set a coffee cup on it. "This one doesn't. Somebody gave it to you, or gave it to someone who gave it to you. And whoever took it was standing on the far side of that fence, maybe forty feet back, before the tape went up." She tilted it toward the window. "Look at the grass. Nobody's walked on it yet."

She laid the photo face-up on top of the folder, squared it, and left her hand resting beside it.

"I need to know the chain. Who handed it to you, who handed it to them. Every name, even if you think it doesn't matter. Especially if you think it doesn't matter."

She picked up her pen again and uncapped it with her thumb.

"Start with whoever you got it from."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I shift uncomfortably, avoiding her gaze for a second.* "My cousin, Maria. She got it from a friend of hers who works in the DA's office. An intern, I think." *I bite my lip.* "She just said it 'fell off a desk' and thought it might be useful."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn't write anything down. The pen stayed uncapped in her hand, its tip resting a quarter inch above the pad.

"Fell off a desk," she said.

She looked at the photo again, at the blank back and the faint coffee ring, and something in her jaw tightened and then let go.

"Photos don't fall off desks in the DA's office. Files do, sometimes, when an intern's carrying too many of them down a hallway. But a single loose print with no evidence stamp?" She shook her head slightly. "Somebody picked this one out. Somebody decided it should leave the building."

She set the pen down, finally, and laced her fingers together on top of the folder.

"Here's what bothers me. If this came from the DA's office, then the DA had a photograph that isn't in the police file. Either Costa never saw it, or he saw it and it didn't make it into the record." She let that sit. "I don't know which one is worse."

The radiator knocked again, once, and went quiet.

"This changes tomorrow." She reached over and tapped the folded sheet with her three rules on it. "Everything I told you still stands. But you don't mention this photo to Costa. Not a word, not a hint. If he asks what the family has, you say the file. The official one. You let him think that's all there is."

She picked the photograph up by its edges, the way someone might handle something that could still bruise, and slid it into a plain envelope from her drawer. She didn't put it back in the folder. She put it in the inside pocket of the jacket hanging on the back of her chair.

"I need the intern's name. Not today. Don't call Maria and ask her while you're standing in the street, and don't text it. Ask her in person, tonight if you can. Tell her you're just curious, that you want to thank the friend. Make it small."

Her eyes came up, level.

"Whoever let this walk out of that office either wanted it found or doesn't know what they had. If it's the first, they'll want to talk. If it's the second…" She paused. "Then someone else in that building might eventually notice it's gone, and I'd rather reach your intern before they do."

She capped the pen and set it neatly beside the pad.

"I'll meet them myself. Somewhere public. A coffee shop, a bench, a bookstore, anywhere with more than one door." A dry flicker crossed her face. "You've got your own breakfast to worry about."

She glanced at the clock on the wall, then back at the client.

"Did Maria say anything else when she gave it to you? Not about the photo. About the friend. Were they scared, excited, in a hurry?" She waited. "People always tell you more than they mean to in the part they think is just small talk."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "She said he was nervous," I reply, thinking back. "Always looking over his shoulder. Like he shouldn't have had it."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena was quiet for a moment. Her eyes went to the window, to the thin bars of gray light between the slats, and stayed there as if she could see through the glass and across the city to a hallway in the DA's office.

"Nervous," she said.

She reached for the jacket on the back of her chair, not to put it on, just to press her palm flat against the pocket where the envelope sat. Checking it was still there. Then she let go.

"That's the first answer, then. He knew what he had." She turned back to the desk. "People who don't know what they're carrying don't look over their shoulders. They're careless. They leave things on copiers and forget their badges in the break room. Nervous means he looked at this photo, understood it was wrong, and made a choice."

She pulled the legal pad closer and, for the first time since the photo came out, wrote something. A single line, small and slanted. She angled the pad so it couldn't be read from across the desk.

"It also means he's been sitting with that choice for however long it's been, wondering if anyone noticed. That kind of thing wears on a person. Every time a supervisor calls his name, he thinks it's about this." She tapped the pen once against the pad. "He'll either be very glad to see me or he'll run. There isn't much room in between."

The radiator had gone silent. Somewhere below them, the dry cleaner's steam press let out a long hiss through the floorboards.

"So we change the order of things." She set the pen down. "Tonight, when you see Maria, you don't ask for his name. You ask her to pass along a message. Tell her someone who isn't police and isn't press wants to buy her friend a coffee. No pressure, no names yet. If he says yes, he picks the place. Let him feel like he's the one holding the door."

She slid a business card from the edge of the blotter. It was plain white, with nothing on it but a phone number. She pushed it across the desk.

"Give Maria this. Not my name. Just the number. If he's as careful as he sounds, a name will scare him more than a number will. A number is something he can choose to call or not call." A beat. "People like having the choice."

She leaned back. The chair creaked.

"And tell Maria not to text him about it. Not a word in writing. If she sees him in person, fine. If not, she waits until she does."

Her gaze settled back on the client, steady but not unkind.

"One more thing. When you're at Sal's tomorrow, if Costa asks how the family got interested in the case again after all this time, you say it's the anniversary. Grief comes back around on its own schedule. He'll believe that." She paused. "Don't let him find out there's a nervous young man in the DA's office with something to say. If Costa was told to close this, whoever told him still has friends."

She picked up the coroner's page again, but she didn't read it. She just held it.

"Did Maria ever say how long ago he gave it to her? Days? Weeks?" Her voice was quieter now. "I want to know how long he's been waiting for someone to notice."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn't look up right away.

She was still holding the coroner's page, and for a second, maybe less, her thumb pressed into the edge of it hard enough to crease the paper. Then she set it down on the desk, flattened the crease with the side of her hand, and reached for the case folder instead.

She opened it to the front sheet. The one with the signatures.

"Costa," she said, and turned the folder around so the client could see it. A blocky, impatient signature sat at the bottom of the closing report, dated the seventeenth. "Lead detective of record. His name's on the intake, the canvass summary, and the closing report. Every page."

She turned it back and began going through the rest, faster now, page by page, running one finger down the margins where the initials were.

"But the file only shows you who finished a case. It doesn't always tell you who started it."

She stopped on a page near the back, a single-line entry in the chronology, and read it twice.

"Here. Night of the thirteenth. 'Case reassigned, 0840 hours.' No reason given. No name for who had it before." She tapped the line. "Somebody caught this first. Worked it for a few hours, maybe a full shift. Then it went to Costa, and three days later it was closed."

Outside, a car horn leaned on itself for too long, then quit. Lena didn't glance at the window this time.

"So your witness remembers the first detective. The one who was actually standing there that night." She closed the folder. "That's more useful than anything in this file."

She pulled the legal pad toward her and wrote something beneath the single line from before. She didn't write the name. She drew a short dash, then a question mark, and angled the pad away again.

"Which witness?" Her voice was even, but the question came quicker than the ones before it. "You haven't mentioned a witness. The file lists two, a neighbor and the man who found the body, and neither of their statements names anyone but Costa. So either this is someone new, or one of them is remembering things they didn't say on the record."

She set the pen down and folded her hands on top of the folder, over the reassignment line, as if keeping it in place.

"Tomorrow doesn't change. You go to Sal's, you drink your coffee black, you let Costa be the expert. But you don't say that name to him." She held the client's gaze. "Not as a question, not in passing. If he wants to tell you the case was handed to him, let him bring it up himself. If he doesn't bring it up, that tells us something too."

She leaned back. The chair creaked.

"Whoever caught this case first saw that scene before anyone decided what it was supposed to be." A pause. "And somebody thought that was a problem by eight-forty the next morning."

Her eyes stayed level, unreadable.

"Tell me about the witness. Who they are, when you talked to them, and exactly what they said. Their words, not yours."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "It was my uncle," I say, a little defensively. "He was there that night. He says Torres was the first one on the scene." *I hesitate, then add*, "He didn't want to talk to the police back then. Afraid of getting involved."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn't react to the defensiveness. She let it pass the way she'd let the car horn pass, something that happened in the room but didn't need an answer.

"Afraid of getting involved," she said. "That's the most honest thing anyone's said about this case so far."

She pulled the legal pad back toward her and looked at the dash and the question mark she'd drawn. She didn't add to them. Instead, she started a new line beneath and wrote *uncle* in small letters, then underlined it once.

"Your uncle was there before the scene was secured. Before the tape, before the canvass, before anyone decided what kind of night it had been." She turned her pen slowly between two fingers. "And he never gave a statement. So as far as the Ninth Precinct is concerned, he doesn't exist."

She paused on that. Something in her face eased, almost imperceptibly, like a knot loosening by a single thread.

"That's good. That's the safest kind of witness there is."

She reached for her jacket again and pressed her palm to the pocket with the envelope. This time she kept her hand there.

"Think about the picture. Someone stood forty feet back, on the far side of the fence, before anyone had walked the grass. That's the first few minutes. The only people there in those minutes were whoever found the body, whoever lived close enough to hear something, and whoever answered the call first." She drew her hand back. "Your uncle, possibly. And the first detective."

She let the sentence end there and didn't add a name to it.

"A photograph taken that early, with no evidence stamp, turns up in the DA's office instead of the police file." She set the pen down, carefully parallel to the edge of the pad. "Somebody who stood on that grass didn't trust where the official file was going to end up. So they sent something around it."

The steam press hissed below again, longer this time. Lena waited for it to finish.

"I want to talk to your uncle. Not at his house if he's still nervous, and nowhere with a uniform in sight. A park, a church hall, the back of a bakery, wherever he goes on an ordinary Tuesday and nobody looks twice. You'll come with me. He'll talk more if there's a face he knows at the table."

Her gaze settled on the client, steady.

"Before then, I need three things from you, and I need them from memory, not from asking him again. Did he say how he knew it was a detective and not a patrol officer? What was he doing near that fence at that hour? And—" her voice dropped slightly, "did he have a camera with him that night? Or a phone?"

She folded her hands over the reassignment line in the folder once more.

"Start with the first one. How did he know?"

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "He said the guy was wearing a suit jacket and talking on a secure line," I tell her, recalling the conversation. "And he had a badge on his belt, not his chest."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn't write that down either. She sat very still, her hands folded over the reassignment line, and for a moment the only thing that moved in the room was the dust turning slowly in the stripes of light from the blinds.

"Badge on the belt," she said. "Suit jacket."

She unfolded her hands and picked up the pen again, though she didn't put it to the paper. She just held it.

"Your uncle's got a good eye. Most people would've said *a cop* and left it there. Uniforms wear the shield on the chest because they're meant to be seen from across a street. Plainclothes wear it at the hip, where it stays out of sight until it's needed." She turned the pen once between her fingers. "So he's right. That was a detective, or someone who wanted to look like one."

She let that second possibility sit on the desk between them for a beat, then set it aside.

"But the jacket bothers me. It was the middle of the night. Detectives who catch a call at that hour get dragged out of bed. They show up in whatever was closest to the door: a sweatshirt, a windbreaker, yesterday's shirt. A suit jacket means whoever it was hadn't been asleep. They were already out. Already dressed." Her eyes narrowed slightly. "Already somewhere."

Below them, the steam press was quiet. The radiator ticked as it cooled.

"And then there's the phone."

She leaned forward and rested her forearms on the desk.

"Your uncle said *secure line*. Those are his words, not yours?" She didn't wait long for the answer. "Because a man standing near a fence in the dark doesn't know whether a line is secure. He can't hear the encryption. So something made him think it. Maybe it was the phone itself, something bulky that didn't look like an ordinary cell. Maybe it was the way the call was made, stepping away from everyone, turning a back to the scene, keeping the voice low. Or maybe he heard something said into it." She tapped the pen once against the pad. "Those are three very different nights. I want to know which one he saw."

She wrote then, finally. Two short words beneath *uncle*, small and slanted, and angled the pad away before the ink had dried.

"The first detective on that scene wasn't reporting to a desk sergeant. A call to the precinct goes over the radio, where anyone on the band can hear it. You step away and use something private when the person on the other end isn't someone you want the whole precinct listening to." Her voice stayed even, but it had gone quieter, the way a room goes quieter when a door is closed. "Somebody made a call that night that wasn't meant to be overheard. By eight-forty the next morning, the case belonged to Costa."

She looked at the folder, not at the client.

"I'd like to know which call came first."

She sat back. The chair creaked, and she let it.

"Second question, then. What was your uncle doing near that fence? It's not a judgment. People are where they are for their own reasons, and half the time the reason's embarrassing and has nothing to do with anything." Something dry flickered at the corner of her mouth, gone as fast as it came. "But I need to know whether he walked up after he heard something, or whether he was already standing there when it happened."

Her gaze came up, level and patient.

"Because if he was already there, then he didn't just see who showed up first. He saw what happened before anyone showed up at all."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "He was walking the dog," I say quickly. "He's always walked the dog that late. It was a shortcut through the park." I pause. "He said he heard a scream."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena noticed how fast the answer came. She didn't say so. She only let a second pass, then another, the way she might leave a door open to see whether anything else would walk through it.

Nothing did.

"A shortcut," she said. "Every night?"

She didn't wait for confirmation. She pulled the pad toward her and wrote a third word beneath the other two, then drew a small circle around it.

"Dog walkers are the best witnesses in any city. They're out at hours nobody else is. They take the same route every night because the dog insists on it. They know which streetlight flickers and which house leaves the porch light on." She set the pen down. "And they're the worst-kept secret on the block. Anyone who lives near that park knows a man walks his dog through there late. Anyone who spent a few nights watching it would know too."

She let that settle without dressing it up.

"Nobody's ever come to his door about that night? No one asking questions, no one sitting in a parked car longer than they should?" Her tone stayed level, almost casual. "I'm not trying to frighten you. I'd just rather know now than find out later."

The radiator had gone fully cold. The room felt it.

"The scream is the part that matters." She leaned forward and rested her forearms on the folder again. "A scream means he was close. Close enough to hear it over traffic and whatever the dog was doing. And it means he knew roughly when it happened. That's something this file doesn't have." She tapped the closed cover. "The coroner gives a window of three hours. Your uncle might be able to give me the minute."

She stood and went back to the window, but she didn't touch the blinds this time. She just stood beside them with her arms folded.

"Here's what I need to understand, and I need him to tell me, not you." She spoke to the glass as much as to the room. "How long between the scream and the man in the suit jacket. Did he hear sirens first, or did the jacket just appear? Because if there were no sirens, no patrol car, no flashing lights, just a detective walking up in the dark already dressed and already on the phone—"

She stopped. Her reflection in the window didn't move.

"Then whoever that was didn't answer a call. They were already close enough to hear the same scream your uncle did."

She turned back from the window. Her face was composed again, but she stayed standing, one hand resting on the back of her chair, near the jacket and the envelope.

"The dog matters too. Dogs pull toward trouble or away from it. If it bolted toward the fence, your uncle got closer than he's admitted. If it pulled back, he may have seen more from a distance than he thinks he did." Something almost wry touched her voice. "People forget what they saw. Dogs don't let them forget where they stood."

She sat down slowly. The chair creaked.

"Call him tonight, after you've seen Maria. Don't talk about any of this on the phone. Just ask if he still walks that route. If he says yes, ask whether he'd mind company on Thursday." She slid the pad a few inches back toward herself, the circled word hidden beneath her hand. "I'd like to walk it with him. Same hour, same path, same dog. Let him show me where he was standing when he heard it."

Her eyes came up, steady.

"He'll remember more with his feet than he will across a table." A pause. "Does the dog still make that walk? Or has it been long enough that it's a different dog now?"

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "He got a new dog a few years back," I say, a little sadly. "Old Buster passed. This one's a terrier, Sparky. Just as stubborn, though." I nod. "I can ask him about Thursday. He's usually home."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's hand stayed flat on the pad for a moment longer. Then she lifted it, and the circled word sat there in the open, small and slanted, meaningless to anyone who hadn't been in the room.

"A few years," she said.

It wasn't a question. She looked at the folder, at the date on the cover she'd been looking at all afternoon, and counted something silently. Her mouth pressed into a thin line and then relaxed.

"That's all right. Sparky doesn't need to remember anything. He just needs to want the same shortcut." Something almost soft moved across her face. "Terriers usually do. They decide on a route and hold it against you for the rest of your life if you try to change it."

She tore the top sheet off the legal pad, folded it into quarters, and tucked it into the jacket pocket beside the envelope. The pad underneath was blank except for the faint pressed ghost of her handwriting. She turned it face down anyway.

"Here's how the next three days go."

She held up one finger.

"Tonight, Maria. The card, the message, nothing in writing." A second finger. "Tomorrow at six, Sal's. Black coffee, the cousin, the anniversary. Watch his hands. Pay for his eggs." A third. "Thursday, your uncle and the dog. I'll meet you at the park entrance fifteen minutes before he usually leaves the house, so he's not waiting on us. If he's early, let him be early. Don't hurry him."

She lowered her hand.

"In between, you go to work, you answer your phone like a normal person, and you don't look over your shoulder. The nervous young man in the DA's office has been doing enough of that for all of us."

She stood and lifted the jacket from the chair. This time she put it on. She settled it at the shoulders and ran one hand down the front, over the pocket, a gesture that could have been smoothing the fabric.

"One more thing." She crossed to the door but didn't open it. "The name your uncle gave you. Torres." She said it plainly, the way she'd said *Costa*, as if it were just another line in the file. "Keep it between you and me. Not Maria, not Costa, not your uncle again until I'm there. If he brings it up on his own Thursday, good. If he doesn't, I'll ask."

Her hand rested on the doorknob. She looked at it instead of at the client.

"First detective on the scene is always the one who remembers it best." A pause, just long enough to notice. "Whether they want to or not."

Then she opened the door. The narrow stairwell smelled of steam and starch, and from below came the thump of the press coming down on someone's shirt.

"Six o'clock," she said. "Sit at the counter. Leave the stool beside him empty. He'll like you better for it."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I stand up, feeling a strange mix of apprehension and determination.* "Got it. Tonight, tomorrow, Thursday. And... thanks, Lena." *I head for the door, my mind already running through the checklist.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn't answer the thanks right away. She stood aside to let the client pass, one hand still on the doorframe, and something moved at the corner of her mouth that might have become a smile under different circumstances.

"Don't thank me yet," she said. "Thank me Friday, if there's something to thank me for."

The client's footsteps went down the narrow stairs, past the thump and hiss of the press, and out through the street door with its tired little bell. Lena closed the office door and turned the lock, then stood with her back against it for a moment, listening to the building settle.

She went to the window.

Down on Mercer, the client came out onto the sidewalk and paused, the way people did when they'd just been handed more than they'd walked in with. Then they turned left toward the subway. Lena watched them go the full length of the block. She watched the cars parked along the curb too, one by one: the florist's van, a dented sedan with a ticket on its windshield, a gray hatchback with nobody in it. Nothing pulled out after the client. Nobody on the sidewalk changed direction.

She waited until they rounded the corner. Then she waited another full minute, counting it off by the cooling tick of the radiator, before she let the blind fall shut.

The office was dim now. She didn't turn on the lamp.

She sat, took the envelope from her jacket, and slid the photograph out onto the blotter. In the low light the grass looked almost silver, untouched, a long empty stretch between the camera and the fence. She'd been looking at the fence all afternoon. Now she made herself look at everything else.

The left edge of the frame. She'd written it off earlier as shadow, a smear where the flash hadn't reached. She opened the desk drawer, found the loupe beneath a tangle of rubber bands, and bent over the print.

Not shadow. Fabric. The dark fold of a sleeve, the barest curve of a cuff, as if someone standing just outside the frame had lifted an arm, maybe to hold a phone to their ear.

Lena stayed bent over the loupe for a long time.

When she finally straightened, she set it down very gently, as if the sound of it touching the desk might carry. She slid the photo back into its envelope and the envelope back into her jacket, and her hand rested there afterward, flat against her chest.

The battered address book was still on the corner of the desk where she'd left it. She picked it up and let it fall open, not to Costa's page this time but to one near the back, where the paper had gone soft and gray at the edges from years of being opened and closed. A single number was written there in ink, then crossed out in a different pen, then written again beneath.

She looked at it. She didn't reach for the phone.

After a while she closed the book and put it in the drawer, underneath the rubber bands, and shut the drawer until it clicked.

"Thursday," she said to the empty room.

Then she pulled the coroner's filing back toward her, switched on the lamp, and started again from the first page, reading every line as though she'd never seen any of it before.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content:
*I spent the evening trying to act normal around Maria, carefully slipping Lena's number into her hand when no one was looking. Now, the next morning, I'm sitting at Sal's, nursing a black coffee, trying to look casual. Ray Costa is two stools down, halfway through his eggs.*

"Detective Costa?" *My voice comes out a little shakily, just like Lena said it would. I put on my best 'grieving cousin' face.* "I hope you don't mind me bothering you. My family... we just can't let go of what happened to [Victim's Name]."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena kept one hand on the closed file.

“Because the moment we walk in, the people we need to question know we’re asking questions.” Her gaze stayed on the photographs. “I’ll find another way to reach the detective. Somewhere outside that building.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "So... we don't want them to know we're asking questions. Why not?" *I lean forward, trying to follow her line of thinking.* "Is there something specific about the Ninth Precinct?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content: “Nothing specific about the Ninth,” Lena said. “A front desk was a funnel. Walk in asking about a detective who worked there, and the question could reach the wrong person before it reached them.” She tapped the closed file once. “I’d rather find a quieter route.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena let the question pass without answering. She drew one of the photographs from the file and turned it toward the edge of the desk.

“The useful question is who knew about the detective’s investigation—and who had something to lose from it.” Her finger rested on a blurred figure in the background. “Start there.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I squint at the photo.* "Something to lose... so you think someone at the precinct could have been involved in... covering something up?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena studied the blurred figure through the photograph’s grain.

“It’s possible,” she said. “But a cover-up doesn’t have to start inside the precinct. Someone could’ve passed information along, or the detective could’ve been pressured from somewhere else.” She slid the photo back beside the others. “We don’t decide who’s involved before we know what was being hidden.”

She opened the file again and pulled out a page of notes. “First, we build the detective’s timeline. Who they spoke to, when they stopped investigating, and who benefited. Then we see where the gaps are.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "So, we're looking for the detective's old notes, basically? Or... someone who knew what they were working on." I nod, thinking. "Do you have a plan for finding that?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena pulled the notes page closer and uncapped a pen.

“First, I’ll pin down the detective’s full name and the case number from what’s already in this file. Then I’ll look for the investigation’s paper trail—court filings, archived reports, anything that shows who was interviewed and when the work stalled.”

She drew a short line beneath the blurred figure in the photograph.

“If that trail runs cold, I’ll find someone who knew what the detective was pursuing and speak with them somewhere neutral. The detective, if they’re willing, would be better still. No precinct visits, and no asking around in a way that announces what we’re after.” Lena glanced up. “Do you have the detective’s name or the case number?”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena considered the name for a moment, then wrote **M. Torres** in the margin of her notes.

“Not enough to place them,” she said. “An initial and a common surname could point to more than one person. Do you know when Torres worked the case—or whether the witness mentioned a first name, case number, or anything they were investigating?”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness said it was around... 2008? And that Torres was looking into the 'Emerald case.' That's what they called it." *I tap my fingers on the desk.* "Does that help?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena wrote **2008 — “Emerald case”** beneath Torres’s name.

“That helped,” she said. “It gave us a year and a phrase to trace, not proof that ‘Emerald’ was the official case name. It could’ve been a nickname—something the witness heard, or something people used after the fact.”

She drew a box around the words. “I’ll check court filings and newspaper archives from that period, then look for cases that match the people or events in these photographs. If the phrase turns up nowhere, the witness’s exact wording and where they heard it may matter more than the name.”

Lena looked up from the page. “Did they say what the Emerald case was about—or who used that name?”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness didn't say, just that it was 'the Emerald case.' They were pretty vague about most of it, honestly." *I shrug.* "Just that Torres was asking a lot of questions about it."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena set the pen down beside the boxed phrase.

“Then we treat ‘Emerald case’ as a lead, not a fact,” she said. “And ‘asking a lot of questions’ doesn’t tell us what Torres was looking into—or whether the witness saw it firsthand.”

She turned the notes page toward herself and added **source of information?** beneath the date.

“I’ll start with the records. But the witness may be more useful if we can narrow down when they heard that name, who used it, and how they knew Torres was involved.” Lena’s gaze lifted from the page. “Would they speak with me again—and did they know Torres personally, or hear about the investigation from someone else?”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "They didn't know Torres personally. And they said they heard about it from a relative who worked at the precinct." *I pause.* "And yes, I think they'd speak with you again."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena added **relative at precinct** beneath the witness’s note.

“That gave us a secondhand source, not confirmation,” she said. “The relative may have heard Torres’s name in passing, or may have known what the investigation was about. We need to separate what they actually saw from what they repeated.”

She closed the file and rested her hand on it. “I’ll speak with the witness somewhere neutral. I’ll ask when the relative told them, what they said about the ‘Emerald case,’ and whether the relative is still willing to talk. No approaching anyone at the precinct.”

Her gaze settled on the client. “Can you arrange another conversation with the witness—and find out whether they’d be comfortable giving me the relative’s name?”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "I can arrange the conversation. I'm not sure about giving up the relative's name, though. They seemed a little wary about that." I chew on my lip. "Why is getting the relative's name so important?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s expression softened by a fraction.

“It mattered because it helped me tell whether this was one person with direct knowledge or a story that had passed through several people,” she said. “It could also keep me from confusing them with someone else. But I don’t need the name before I speak with the witness.”

She tapped the edge of the closed file. “I won’t contact the relative without their permission. We can start with what the witness remembers—when they heard it, the exact words, and what the relative actually knew. If they’re still wary, we leave the name out for now.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay, that makes sense. I'll reach out to them and see when they can meet." *I pull out my phone.* "Should I tell them it's about the 'Emerald case' again?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena shook her head.

“Not at first. If you lead with ‘Emerald case,’ you might steer what they remember—or make them more wary.” She slid the notes page back into the file. “Just say you’d like to follow up on what they told you about their relative and the investigation. Let them bring up the phrase themselves. And make it clear they don’t have to share the relative’s name.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Got it. Keep it vague, don't push for the name. I'll see what I can set up." *I start typing a message on my phone.* "I'll let you know what they say."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The marks climbed the frame in a crooked ladder. Dates ran beside each line, the graphite worn pale. The lowest sat near the latch. The highest carried a date from fifteen years back. Whoever had drawn them had bitten the pencil first. Tiny dents ridged the top of each numeral.

The door stood open a hand's width. Cool air seeped through the gap. It smelled of cedar and shut-in linen.

Beyond the gap, the bed kept its old place against the wall. A quilt lay folded at its foot, gone stiff with time. Dust filmed the dresser in a pale coat. The floorboard at the threshold had always creaked.

From the kitchen came the drag of cardboard over tile. Then the pull of masking tape, long and tearing. Someone was still packing. Eli's father had never mentioned leaving.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: My breath hitched. *Dad*. I totally forgot he was even here. I push open the door to my room, wincing at the familiar creak. "Dad?" I call out, my voice raspy.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The taping stopped mid-pull. The kitchen went still, except for the refrigerator's hum. Water dripped from the tap into a glass beside the box.

His father answered from down the hall. "Eli." The name came out rough, unused. A chair scraped back from the table.

Footsteps crossed the tile, then found the hallway carpet. Softer there. His father filled the bedroom doorway, one hand braced on the frame. He smelled of coffee and cardboard dust. There was gray in his beard now. More than Eli's memory kept.

Past his shoulder, three more boxes stood by the front door. Same tape. Same stranger's hand.

His father looked past him at the pencil marks. His thumb rose toward the wood. It stopped short. He folded the hand into a scratch at his jaw.

"Didn't hear the door." He said it to the quilt on the bed, not to Eli. "You want coffee. The machine still works."

He turned before an answer could come. His steps dragged on the carpet. From the kitchen rose the knock and gurgle of old pipes.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: My fingers trace her smile. "Dad, wait!" I call out, my voice thick. "Is this... is this mom's?"

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: He stops in the kitchen doorway. "Which one?" he asks, his voice flat.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I shove the photo into my pocket*. "Nevermind," I mumble. *I turn to the agent, forcing a smile*. "Hi, I'm Eli."

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: Agent: "Eli! So good to finally meet you. I'm Brenda. This is such a lovely home, isn't it? So much character!" She beams, looking around the dusty hall.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "It certainly has character," I say, a little dryly. I glance at my dad, who's still in the kitchen doorway, arms crossed. "Been in the family a long time."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The coffee machine hissed in the kitchen. His father's arms stayed crossed. The seams of his sleeves strained at the shoulders. He said nothing. The stove clock ticked into the silence.

Brenda's heels found the hallway carpet. The bad board announced her anyway. Her perfume reached the stairs before she did. Peonies, and something sweet underneath. "History sells," she said. "Buyers love a house with roots in it."

She flipped her folder open on the hall table. Glossy pages slid across the wood. The house stared up from them, emptied and staged. "The McNairs sign on the thirtieth. Quick close. Clean numbers."

The date sat in the hallway with them. The tap dripped once into the glass. His father uncrossed his arms. One hand went back to the doorframe, to the wood beside the pencil marks. "Coffee's up," he said. He aimed it at the floor.

Twelve days until the thirtieth. The machine sputtered in the kitchen. Burnt coffee reached the hallway. The house had known before Eli did.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I flinch at the mention of the McNairs. *Twelve days*. "Right," I say, my voice tight. I look at Brenda, then back at my dad. "Dad, maybe we should talk about this."

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: Dad doesn't say anything, just stares at the floor. "Dad?" I try again, a little louder this time.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Can we just... talk?" I ask. My eyes flick to Brenda. "Maybe in the kitchen?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena slid the photos back into a stack and squared the edges with her thumb, as if the conversation had already moved on.

"Walking in there gets you a desk sergeant and a story about how the file is active," she said. "They don't brief civilians in the lobby, and they don't hand copies to people like me." She reached for the phone on the corner of the desk, checked the time, and set it down again. "There's a diner on Second, two blocks off the precinct. Booth by the window. If that detective wants to talk, that's where they'll sit. You can go up the steps and leave a message — say noon, say the booth, say nothing else. I'll be there with coffee. I don't do the steps."

She opened a drawer, took out a blank card, and wrote the diner's name in block letters. Pushed it across the desk without looking up.

"While you're doing that, I'll start on the photos. The precinct isn't the only place this trail runs."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay, noon. Got it." *I pick up the card, the paper feeling a little too crisp. I don't like being a messenger, but I hired her.* "Is there anything else I should say to them? Or just the time and place?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena looked at the card still under the client's hand, then at the stack of photos, as if the question had landed somewhere she wasn't going to follow.

"Time. Place. Your name if they ask who sent you." She capped the pen and dropped it into the drawer. "Don't explain the case. Don't say you're working with me. Don't wait around for a conversation on the sidewalk."

She pulled one photo free — a street corner, a parked sedan, a figure half out of frame — and set it under the lamp.

"If they show, I'll know what to ask. If they don't, the message still did its job." A glance at the clock, brief. "Noon. I'll have the booth."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena turned the photo under the lamp until the sedan's plate caught the light, then copied the numbers onto a scrap without looking up.

"There's a man in the background of the third shot," she said. "Same coat in two other frames, different corners. That's not a passerby." She slid a second photo out and lined the edges. "You leave the message. I run the plate and the coat. Noon at the booth — if the coffee's bad, order the pie. Don't improvise on the steps."

She reached for the phone again, already dialing a number she didn't explain. The question sat on the desk between them. She didn't pick it up.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I sigh, a little frustrated she keeps dodging the question.* "Fine. I'm going." *I stand up, still holding the card.* "Just... try not to piss off the whole precinct before I get back."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena kept the phone at her ear and didn't look up as the chair scraped back. The line rang once, twice. She turned the third photo so the coat's shoulder lined up with the corner of the sedan.

"Don't wait on the steps," she said, already writing a plate number in the margin of the scrap. "Leave the card. Come back here. I'll have something on the coat by the time the coffee's poured."

The ringing stopped. Someone picked up on the other end — a voice she didn't put on speaker. She covered the mouthpiece with two fingers, eyes still on the frame.

"Noon," she said. "Booth by the window."

Then she turned half away, toward the wall, and started talking in a low voice about a plate and a dry cleaner's receipt, as if the office had already emptied.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I roll my eyes and head for the door, the diner card still in my hand.* "Right, noon." *I'll get my answers eventually.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena waited until the door clicked shut and the stairs took the sound of the client's steps. Only then did she take her hand off the mouthpiece.

"Not a courtesy call," she said into the phone. "A plate, and a coat that shows up in three frames where it shouldn't." She read the numbers off the scrap, slow enough that the person on the other end could write them down. "Sedan. Dark. Parked on the corner in the first shot, gone in the fourth. I need a name that isn't a desk, and I need it before noon."

She listened. The dry cleaner's press hissed through the floor. She turned the third photo again, thumb on the figure at the edge — same coat, same way of standing, half a step out of the light.

"Don't send it through the building," she said. "Call this number. If you can't, leave it with the counter downstairs. They know me." A pause. "No. I'm not coming in. You know that."

She hung up before the silence on the other end could turn into an argument. The office smelled of solvent and burnt coffee. She lined the photos in order, coat to sedan to empty corner, and started a fresh page with the time at the top: noon, booth by the window, and nothing else she was willing to write down.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's pen stopped over the page. The name hung in the office and she left it there, drawing a line under the time instead and writing *detective — Ninth* in the margin, nothing else.

"Witness solid, or guessing off a card someone flashed once?" she said. She squared the empty-corner photo with the others until the edges matched. "Doesn't move noon. Message is already out. If they take the booth, I'll see whether the file and the coat are the same problem. You don't walk in carrying a name."

The press hissed through the floor. She set the pen down and reached for the phone without dialing.

"If you can get back to that witness, ask what the sedan did after the fourth frame. Plates I can run. Stories I can't."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "I can call them. But they were pretty clear about the name." *I'm starting to feel like I'm doing all the legwork here.* "You really don't recognize the name Torres?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena kept her eyes on the empty-corner photo and drew another line under the time, as if the page needed the ink more than the room needed an answer.

"Call them," she said. "Sedan after the fourth frame. Which way it turned. Whether the coat got in or stayed on the corner. That's the part I can use." She set the pen down and lined the stack until the edges met. "A name on a card doesn't put a car in motion. You bring me the turn, I'll have something waiting when you get back from the steps."

The press hissed through the floor. She reached for the phone, still not dialing, thumb resting on the scrap where the plate numbers sat.

"Noon holds. Booth by the window. If they sit, I'll know whether the file and the coat are the same problem." A brief glance at the clock, then back to the frames. "Don't carry anything else up those steps."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Fine. I'll call. But I'm starting to think I should be charging *you* for my time." *I pull out my phone and start dialing, walking toward the door to get some privacy.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena stayed where she was while the door took the sound of the call. She didn't answer the crack about her time. The name the witness had used stayed on the other side of the room; she didn't write it down, didn't try it out, didn't let it sit next to the plate numbers.

She lined the frames again — coat, sedan, empty corner — and added one line under the time: *which way after the fourth*. The press hissed through the floor. She checked the clock, capped the pen, and left the booth note where it was.

Noon still held. The steps were still the client's. She would be at the window with coffee, and with whatever the turn in the street gave her, and with nothing else she was willing to put on the page.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I step outside, annoyed, and make the call. It's a quick conversation, but I get the info.* "Okay, they said the sedan turned left, down Elm Street. And the person in the coat got in the car." *I head back inside, looking for Lena.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena was already at the desk when the door opened, the empty-corner photo turned so the street ran left off the edge of the frame. She wrote *Elm* under the line she’d left and didn’t look up at the name that had been sitting in the room all morning.
