“Left, and the coat got in,” she said. “That’s a pickup, not a passerby.” She pulled a city map from the drawer and flattened it beside the stack, thumb finding the corner in the first shot, then the turn. “Elm runs two blocks and dumps into a one-way. If the sedan stayed on it, there’s a garage, a lot, or a second car. I’ll have someone walk that stretch before noon. You don’t.”

She capped the pen. The press hissed through the floor. The witness’s name stayed where the client had left it — unwritten, untested.

“Booth by the window still holds,” she said. “If they sit, I’ll ask about the turn, not about a card. You bring me anything else the witness actually saw. Plates, coat, which way. That’s the file I can work.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod, a bit mollified by the new direction.* "Okay. I'll see if they remember anything else. Like what kind of car it was, or a partial plate." *I turn to leave again.* "So, I'm still doing the diner message, right?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena squared the map so Elm ran straight under her thumb and didn’t look up when the client turned for the door.

“Still the diner,” she said. “Time, place, your name if they ask. Nothing about the sedan, nothing about Elm, nothing about a coat getting in.” She folded the corner of the map down on the turn and set a blank card on top of it, already written: noon, booth by the window. “Leave it. Don’t wait on the steps. If they sit, I’ll be the one with the coffee.”

The press hissed through the floor. She reached for the phone, eyes on the empty stretch of street past the fourth frame.

“You get the witness on the car — make, color, anything on the plate that isn’t a guess. Call it in to me before you head over. I’ll have someone on that one-way by the time the booth fills.” A brief glance at the clock. “Noon holds. Don’t improvise.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I sigh, but nod.* "Okay, fine. I'll call them now." *I pull out my phone and start dialing again as I head back out the door, already walking and talking.* "And no, I'm not waiting on the steps."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn’t answer the sigh. She waited for the door, and when it clicked she set the phone down without having dialed anyone the client could hear.

Elm, left, coat in the car. She copied that onto a fresh scrap in block letters and slid it under the map, thumb still on the one-way where the street dumped out. The press hissed through the floor. She called a number that wasn’t a desk and kept her voice low.

“Walk it,” she said. “Two blocks off the corner in the first frame, then the turn. Garage, lot, second car. Don’t go inside any building with a flag on it. If you see the sedan, you call this line. You don’t follow it past the river.”

She listened, wrote nothing that wasn’t a street, and hung up before the other end could ask where she’d be sitting. The booth note stayed on the desk. Noon still held. She lined the frames one more time — coat, sedan, empty corner — and left the witness’s name exactly where it had been all morning: unwritten.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I pace outside, phone to my ear, trying to get more details from the witness. After a few minutes, I end the call and head back in.* "Okay, they think it was a dark blue sedan, maybe a Crown Vic or something similar. And they saw a partial plate, '7-L-P' at the beginning."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren folded the tally sheet and tucked it beneath the bar. Her glance rested briefly on the carefully placed pack, then returned to the newcomer’s face.

“I have a room. Old Pell has venison stew on the fire, with bread to see you through it. Six coppers for supper and the night, breakfast included.”

She reached for a clean cup with her left hand. “Water or ale, friend? The wine is imported and overpriced. I like to warn people before they make a mistake.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Ale sounds good." I watch her hands, the way she moves. "Six coppers is fair. And the stew sounds perfect." I lean back a little, letting out a long breath.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren drew a mug of ale with her left hand and set it on the bar. She slipped six coppers’ worth of space onto the tally sheet, leaving the line unpaid for now.

“Stew will be along shortly. You can settle the bill after you have eaten.”

She glanced toward the kitchen, then back at the pack. “If that needs somewhere safer than the floor, I can keep it behind the bar while you eat. Otherwise, I make no inquiries of a guest’s luggage.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s left hand stopped short of the plate. She looked from the crab cakes to the merchant’s table, her expression pleasant and level.

“Lord Havel is generous. I just do not care for seafood.” She gave the plate a little room on the counter without touching it. “And my guest has already ordered Pell’s stew. Best not to let your fine cakes go cold on our account.”

She caught a server’s eye and nodded toward the plate. “Would you take those back to his lordship, please?”

Then she turned toward the kitchen. “Pell, one stew and bread when you have a moment.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Seems Lord Havel has more money than sense," I mutter, taking a long drink of ale. "Pell's stew sounds better anyway."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the server carry the plate back across the room before answering. Her voice stayed low.

“Money and sense do travel together on occasion. They simply arrived in separate carriages tonight.”

She took up her cloth with her left hand and wiped a clean stretch of counter, well away from where the plate had rested. “Pell’s stew has the advantage of still being hot. The bread comes fresh from the oven, too.”

From the kitchen came the scrape of a ladle against a pot. Maren glanced that way. “You chose well, friend.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren lifted her own cup with her left hand, though she did not drink.

“To Old Pell. I will tell him you said so. He will pretend it means nothing, then put an extra heel of bread on your plate.”

She set the cup down and glanced toward the kitchen. “He has been making that stew for thirty years. I have been trying to improve it for twenty. Neither of us has made any progress.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Some things are perfect as they are," I say, taking another spoonful of the stew. "No need to fix what isn't broken." I eye the package on the floor again.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren followed the glance to the pack, then rested her left forearm on the bar.

“That is what I keep telling Pell. He still changes the amount of rosemary when he thinks I am not looking.”

She let the quiet settle for a moment. “The room upstairs has a good lock. If you would rather not carry the pack through a crowded common room, I can hold it behind the bar until you are ready to go up. Either way, friend, what is inside it stays your business.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
At the first stroke, Maren glanced at the clock. She waited for the last chime, then took two small cups from beneath the bar and poured a measure of ale into each with her left hand.

She set one cup before herself and carried the other to the far end of the bar, where it stood apart from the empty mugs waiting to be washed. She returned without a word about it.

“The lock on your room is sound,” she said, taking up her own cup. “The third stair creaks, but it has never betrayed anyone quietly enough to matter.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Good to know," I say, taking a sip from my ale. "A good lock and a creaky stair. Sounds like a good night's sleep to me." I push my now empty stew bowl slightly away.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren took the empty bowl with her left hand and set it beneath the bar.

“The third stair has been warning me about guests for twenty years. I would hate to silence a loyal employee.”

She placed a room key on the counter. “Upstairs, second door on the right. There is water in the room, and breakfast starts at first light. Six coppers whenever you are ready, friend.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Thanks, Maren." I pick up the key. "I'll settle up in the morning." I nod toward my pack. "Mind if I leave this behind the bar for now? Don't want to carry it up tonight."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren nodded. “Morning is fine, friend. And the pack can stay behind the bar.”

She cleared a space on a shelf below the counter, away from the mugs and the path to the kitchen. “Set it here when you are ready. I will leave it exactly as you give it to me.”

She glanced toward the stairs. “Mind the third one. Loyal employees do enjoy being noticed.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I slide the pack carefully under the bar. "Thanks again, Maren. See you in the morning." I give her a small smile, then head for the stairs.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren checked that the pack sat clear of the walkway, then left it untouched. “Sleep well, friend. Breakfast will be ready when you are.”

She took the bowl toward the kitchen. At the far end of the bar, the second cup stood where she had left it.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I climb the stairs, careful to step on the third one, giving it a little extra weight.* The worn wood groans in protest. *A loyal employee indeed.* I find my room, unlock it, and step inside. The air is cool, and the bed looks inviting. I don't bother with the lamp, just kick off my boots and fall onto the mattress. Sleep comes quickly.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren heard the third stair complain overhead. “Loyal and dramatic,” she murmured.

She finished closing the common room, leaving the pack undisturbed on its shelf. At the far end of the bar, the second cup remained where she had set it.

At first light, she cleared the cup and opened the shutters. Pell already had porridge on the fire and bread warming by the hearth. Maren laid a clean place at the bar, then returned to her tally sheet, the room key’s line still marked for six coppers.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I wake with the sun streaming through the window, feeling more rested than I have in days. My stomach rumbles, reminding me of Pell's stew. *Time to face the day.* I pull on my boots and head downstairs.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The marks climbed the frame in small increments. Each line had its date beside it. His father's hand, the numbers slanted and crowded. The lowest sat just above the baseboard. The graphite had faded to a pale scratch. The wood had gone rough there, grain lifted from years of handling.

The new paint stopped at the frame's edge. Whoever had rolled it on had gone around the pencil lines. Or missed them. There were seven dates in all. The grooves were deep enough to catch a fingernail. Above the last date, the wood ran clean. Space for a mark that was never made.

The door stood open a few inches. Cold air seeped through the gap. The bed frame had been stripped bare. Pale rectangles shadowed the carpet where furniture had stood. A radiator ticked inside the wall, patient and empty.

A box sat on the floor beyond the threshold. Masking tape, black marker, block letters. BEDROOM, in the handwriting from the kitchen box. The marker ink still smelled sharp. Chemical. New. Someone had been here. Someone had packed this room before Eli arrived.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I kneel, tracing the faded pencil marks with my finger.* The last one... August 12th. Right before I left for college. *I push open the bedroom door, wincing at the creak.* "Well, that's not ominous at all."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Mom..." *My voice is barely a whisper.* "You look so happy."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph had curled at its edges. The paper felt thin, soft from years in the dark. His mother stood in the backyard, one hand raised against the sun. She wore a blue sundress, its color washed pale in the print. Behind her, the fence still stood. The grass reached mid-calf.

She was laughing at whoever held the camera. Her head tipped back. Her teeth showed. A crease ran across the print at her shoulder, a white line through the image. On the back, in pencil: a date, and one word. The word was his

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Dad." *I trace the letters with my thumb.* "Always with the bad handwriting." I can almost hear him grumbling about taking the picture.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: A

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I quickly slip the photo into my pocket.* "Great. Just what I needed."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: Three

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: Three sharp raps on the front door, then the jiggle of a lock. "Hello? Eli? It's Brenda! I'm letting myself in!" Her voice, bright and a little too loud, echoed down the hall. A moment later, she appeared in the doorway of the living room, a wide smile plastered on her face. "Eli! So good to finally meet you! What a charming property, just full of character!" She gestured vaguely around the empty room.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: B

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Brenda. Right." *I nod, forcing a small smile.* "Character, sure. It's... lived in."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: B

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Well, that's what we tell potential buyers, isn't it?" She winked, then pulled a tablet from her oversized purse. "So, I've got the inspection report here. Just a few minor things to go over."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: B

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Minor, huh?" *I raise an eyebrow, glancing around the dusty room.* "This house is fifteen years older than the last time I saw it. I'm guessing 'minor' is relative."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: B

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Oh, you know, a little dampness in the basement, a few outdated fixtures. Nothing a fresh coat of paint and some elbow grease can't fix!" She scrolled through her tablet, oblivious to my sarcasm.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren set the tally sheet aside and reached for a clean bowl with her left hand.

“Pell’s venison stew is hot, and I have a room. Six coppers for the night, supper included. If you want ale, that is another copper.”

She glanced at the carefully placed pack, then back to the newcomer’s face. “There is room behind the bar for that, if you would rather keep it out from underfoot. I will leave it where it is unless you say otherwise.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Stew sounds perfect." I nod at the offer for the pack. "Behind the bar would be great, thank you." I slide it over carefully. "Long journey, don't want it getting kicked."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren took the pack with her left hand, steadied it with her right, and set it on a shelf behind the bar, well clear of boots and spilled ale.

“Safest place for it, friend. Nothing gets kicked back there unless I have misjudged my own feet.”

She fetched a bowl of Pell’s stew from the kitchen and set it on the counter with a spoon and a heel of bread. Then she placed a room key beside it.

“Room four. The stairs are past the hearth, and the washbasin is outside your door. Supper and the room come to six coppers. Would you like water, or an ale for one more?”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s left hand stopped short of the plate. She kept her expression even and glanced toward the merchant’s table.

“Lord Havel is kind to offer. Please give him my thanks. I do not care for seafood.”

She shifted the traveler’s stew bowl a little farther from the cakes, then looked back at her guest. “They are yours if you would like them, friend. Otherwise, I will have the plate returned. Pell takes it personally when someone lets his stew go cold.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I eye the crab cakes. "No, thank you. The stew is fine." I pick up my spoon, giving the merchant a nod. "But my thanks to Lord Havel." *I take a mouthful of stew, savoring the warmth.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gave the merchant a courteous nod. “You have our thanks, Lord Havel. The stew has won this round.”

She caught one of her servers’ eyes and quietly asked her to return the plate to its sender. Only when it was gone did Maren set a cup of water beside the traveler’s bowl with her left hand.

“Pell will be pleased to hear you gave the stew your full attention. I will tell him once he has finished arguing with the oven.” She glanced at the room key. “Six coppers whenever you are ready, friend. And if you would prefer ale to water, say the word.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren lifted a cup with her left hand in answer to the toast.

“To Old Pell. I will tell him you said so, though he is already difficult enough to live with when the stew turns out well.”

She set her cup down and glanced toward the kitchen. “He will pretend not to be pleased. Do not believe him.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, taking another spoonful of stew.* "He sounds like a character. Is he from around here?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren glanced toward the kitchen, where a pot lid rattled.

“Near enough. Pell came from a village two days east, which he insists makes him a foreigner whenever someone asks him to sweep the hearth. He has been here twenty-three years.”

She rested her left hand on the bar. “Ask him where he learned to make that stew, and he will name three different grandmothers. None of them were his.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
At the last stroke of midnight, Maren set down the cloth. She took two cups from beneath the bar and poured ale into both with her left hand. One she set before herself; the other she carried to the far end of the counter, where it stood alone.

She returned to her place and took a sip. “Pell will tell you his stew improves if it sits overnight,” she said. “He says the same of his temper. I have only found evidence for the stew.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "He sounds like a good man to have around," I say, finishing my stew. "Especially after a long journey." I push my now empty bowl forward. "I'll take that ale now, if the offer still stands."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren took the empty bowl with her left hand and set it beneath the bar. She poured a fresh ale and placed it within easy reach. The cup at the far end of the counter remained where it was.

“The offer stands. Seven coppers for supper, the room, and the ale.” She glanced toward the kitchen. “And Pell is a good man to have around. I have told him so once. There is no sense making him impossible.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Seven coppers, got it." I take a slow sip of the ale, enjoying the bite. "Don't want to make him impossible, no." I lean back a little. "So, just you and Pell running the place, then?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren shook her head and drew the tally sheet closer with her left hand.

“Pell runs the kitchen. I run the tavern, and two servers keep either of us from believing we can manage it alone.” She glanced toward the quieting common room. “They have gone off duty for the night. Sensible people.”

She marked a line on the sheet and looked up. “On a busy evening, Pell says there ought to be six of us. On a quiet one, he says four is too many. I have yet to find a number that pleases him.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Six, four... sounds like he just likes to grumble," I say with a grin, taking another sip of ale. "But it looks like you've got things well in hand."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren laid the tally sheet flat with her left hand and surveyed the half-empty room.

“Pell does like to grumble. I would worry if he stopped.” Her gaze settled briefly on the ale waiting at the far end of the bar, then returned to her guest.

“We have things well in hand tonight, friend. Ask me again when both trade caravans arrive on the same rainy evening.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "I can imagine." I finish my ale. "Well, I best get some rest before those caravans roll in. Thanks for the food and the company, Maren." I push the seven coppers across the bar.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gathered the seven coppers with her left hand and counted them into the till.

“You are welcome, friend. Room four is yours, and the key is beside you.” She glanced at the pack on its shelf behind the bar. “Would you like that now, or shall I keep it here until morning?”

She nodded toward the stairs past the hearth. “Sleep well. The caravans have not learned to arrive quietly.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "I'll take the pack, thanks." I reach for it. "Don't want to leave it out of my sight too long." *I grab the key and head towards the stairs.* "Goodnight, Maren."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren set the cloth aside and reached for a wooden tally chip with her left hand, the silver ring catching the lamplight as she turned it over once against the bar.

"Stew, then. Pell's been at it since midday, and what's left is the good part — the bottom of the pot." She slid a clean bowl from the stack and called toward the kitchen without raising her voice. "Pell. One more, and don't skim the rosemary off the top."

She looked the traveler over again, not unkindly, taking in the careful way the pack had been set down.

"Room's eight coppers. Supper's three, and the ale's two if you want it with. I've got four rooms empty upstairs — second floor, third door on the left is the quiet one. Faces the courtyard, not the road." She tapped the bar once with her left thumb. "Coin up front for the room. Food you can settle when you've eaten. That's the house rule, and it keeps everyone honest."

From the kitchen came the clatter of a ladle and Old Pell's muttered acknowledgment. Maren pulled a key from the ring at her belt and set it on the bar within easy reach, then went back to wiping the counter, left hand steady, right resting near the tally sheet.

"You look like you've been on the road longer than the road deserved. Sit. Eat. If you need the room before the stew's gone, the key's yours."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I nod, pulling a small pouch from my belt.* "Sounds fair." I count out the coppers for the room, pushing them across the bar. "The quiet one sounds perfect." I push the key a little closer to me, but don't pick it up yet. *My eyes drift to the mysterious package.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren swept the coppers into her left palm, counted them once against the bar with her thumb, and dropped them into the locked box beneath the counter. The key stayed where it was.

"Third door on the left. The latch sticks if you turn it too hard — ease it, don't fight it. Bedding's clean. Washbasin is down the hall, and if you want hot water before you sleep, ask before the kitchen fire dies."

She did not comment on the pack. She had already marked the care in how it had been set down, and she marked now the way the traveler's attention kept returning to it. People who carried trouble usually announced it with their eyes long before their mouths did. She reached for a fresh cloth with her left hand and went on wiping, unhurried.

"Stew'll be out in a moment. Bread with it, and I'll not charge you for the heel." She glanced once at the pack, then back to the traveler's face, her tone the same as if she were discussing the weather. "Whatever that is, friend, it stays in your room or it stays under your hand. I don't mind either way. I do mind it becoming everyone else's business in my common room."

From the kitchen, a bowl hit the pass with a solid thud. Maren turned, took it in her left hand — rich, dark, the rosemary still clinging to the surface — and set it down with a spoon and a torn piece of bread.

"Eat while it's honest. The key will keep."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren did not reach for the plate. She looked at it the way she looked at a spill that had not yet reached the floor — already decided, not yet dramatic — and set her left hand flat on the bar a careful distance from the crab cakes.

"That is kind of Lord Havel," she said, evenly, to the server who had carried it over. "And it is also crab. I do not care for seafood. Take it back to his table with my thanks, and tell him the Antler does not need gifts to keep his custom. If he wants to spend coin, the wine list is right there and I will not pretend it is a bargain."

She did not raise her voice. She did not explain further. The silver ring on her left thumb turned once against the wood as she waited, and when the plate had been lifted clear she wiped the spot where it had sat, left hand steady, as if the rosemary smell of the stew were the only thing worth keeping in the air.

Then she looked at the traveler, not at the merchants, and pushed the key the last inch closer with two fingers of her left hand.

"Your supper is the bowl in front of you. Eat that. If anyone else decides to be generous at my bar, they can be generous with ale, and they can ask first."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I scoop up a spoonful of the stew, blowing on it before taking a bite.* "Much obliged." *I glance at the key, then back to my stew, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Sounds like you run a tight ship here."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s mouth did not quite smile, but something at the corner of it considered the idea and then thought better of it. She took up the cloth again with her left hand and worked a water ring out of the bar as if the traveler had commented on the weather.

“Tight enough that the stools stay under the people who paid for them,” she said. “Loose enough that nobody has to ask permission to breathe. I’ve found the middle is where the money is, and where the fights aren’t.”

She nodded once at the stew. “That’s Pell’s work, not mine. If you tell him it’s good, he’ll pretend he didn’t hear you and then put extra bread on your plate tomorrow. If you tell him it’s bad, he’ll hear that from the cellar.”

The merchants in the corner had gone back to grain prices, Lord Havel’s plate safely returned to its own table. Maren glanced that way only long enough to be sure the crab cakes were staying there, then set a small cup of water beside the traveler’s bowl with her left hand, the silver ring ticking once against the wood.

“Room’s paid. Stew’s yours. If ‘tight ship’ was a question about whether I’ll mind your business upstairs, the answer is no — so long as your business minds mine down here.” She rested her weaker right hand near the tally sheet and left it there. “Eat. The quiet room will still be quiet when you’re done.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren paused with the cloth in her left hand, the water ring only half gone. She did not look scandalized. She looked, if anything, mildly disappointed in the word, the way a person might be disappointed in a bent nail that still held.

"The stew is good," she said. "Pell will be glad of the sentiment and deaf to the rest of it. Save the short words for the road, friend. In here we can afford the longer ones."

She set a second heel of bread beside the bowl, left hand only, and nodded once toward the kitchen pass as if that were toast enough.

"Eat it while the rosemary's still brave. And if you mean to raise a mug to my cook, raise it to the stew — he trusts food more than speeches."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I take a large bite of the bread, then another spoonful of stew.* "Fair enough. To the stew, then. And to good bread." *I look at the key again, then my mysterious package.* "This quiet room... it's really quiet?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren rested her left hand on the bar and considered the question as if the traveler had asked about the latch, not about secrecy. The common room murmured on around them — grain prices, a letter being folded, the low clink of mugs — and she let that noise answer part of it before she did.

"Quiet as this house gets," she said. "Courtyard side. No cart wheels, no one stumbling in off the road at the second bell and forgetting which door is theirs. The walls are thick enough that a conversation stays where it was started, provided nobody starts shouting. I do not shout, and I do not let other people make a habit of it either."

She tapped the key once with her left thumb, the silver ring dull in the lamplight, and left it where the traveler could take it when they were ready.

"It is a room, friend. A bed, a bolt, a basin, and a window that looks at the well and the woodpile. It is not a vault, and it is not a confessional. What you set down in there is yours until morning, and I do not go through paid rooms unless the roof is on fire or someone is bleeding on my linens." Her eyes flicked, brief and unembarrassed, to the pack, then back to the traveler's face. "If that is the quiet you meant, then yes. It is really quiet."

From the kitchen came the scrape of Pell banking the fire. Maren picked up her cloth again with her left hand and went back to the water ring, unhurried.

"Finish the stew. The room will not get any louder for waiting."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren heard the clock before she looked at it. The corner piece kept poor time in damp weather and perfect time when it mattered, and tonight it struck the twelfth bell clean. She set the cloth down, wiped her left palm once on her apron, and reached under the bar for two short cups she did not keep with the others.

She poured without fuss — the same local ale, both measures even, her left hand steady on the tap. One cup she set in front of herself. The other she carried to the far end of the bar, where the wood was scarred and no one ever sat for long, and she put it down there with the care she used for anything that was not going to be drunk. She did not look at it again.

When she came back, she took her own cup in her left hand and drank once, unhurried, as if the common room had not just gone a little quieter around the sound of the bell. The merchants had their grain prices. The dwarf had his letter. The traveler had a key and a pack and a bowl gone mostly to the bottom.

"Kitchen's closed," she said, mild as the hour. "If you want the room, the stair is behind you and to the left. If you want to sit a while longer, the bar stays open until the fire says otherwise." She rested her weaker right hand near the tally sheet and left the second cup where it was, at the end of the bar, catching the lamplight and answering no questions. "Either way, friend, mind the latch. Ease it. Don't fight it."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I take another sip of the water, then look between the key and my package.* "I think I'll sit a while longer. This stew really hit the spot." *I push the empty bowl forward a little, a clear signal I'm done.* "So, the fire decides when you close, huh? Not the clock?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren took the empty bowl with her left hand and set it on the pass without calling for Pell. The kitchen fire had already been banked; the cook would find it in the morning and pretend the clean bowl was an accident.

"The clock tells me what hour it is," she said. "The fire tells me whether anyone still needs the room warm. Those are different jobs, and I have never seen the profit in confusing them." She nodded toward the hearth, where the logs had settled into a low red seam. "When that goes to ash, the bar closes. The rooms stay open. I am not in the business of turning out people who have already paid for a bed."

She wiped the place where the bowl had sat, left hand steady, the silver ring ticking once against the wood. The second cup remained at the far end of the bar. She did not look at it.

"Sit as long as the coals hold, friend. If you change your mind about the stair, the key is still yours, and the latch is still the same advice."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Good to know," *I say, taking another sip of water.* "So, what's your story, Maren? You seem like you've seen a thing or two." *I gesture vaguely around the room.* "This place has history."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren set the cloth down and rested her left forearm on the bar, the silver ring dull against the wood. The question was ordinary enough. People asked it when the room got quiet and the stew had done its work. She answered the part she was willing to spend.

"The Antler belonged to my aunt Bessa," she said. "She raised me after the flood took my parents. I was seven. She left me the keys, the debts, and a very firm opinion about how a house ought to be run. I have kept two of those three."

She glanced once toward the hearth, not toward the cup at the end of the bar.

"I had a husband. Tobin. We ran this place together for twelve years. Fever took him six years ago. I did not remarry. That is preference, not a wound I need anyone picking at." Her tone stayed even, the contractions gone now that the subject had weight. "Before the tavern I did five years with the Kingsguard, quartermaster's work. I can count faster than most men who think counting is a talent. I do not talk about the rest of it unless someone has earned the story, and a bowl of stew does not quite earn it."

She picked up her own cup with her left hand, drank, and set it down again.

"As for history — every beam in here has heard an argument about grain prices. The scar on my brow is from a fight I won fourteen years ago, and I would rather not repeat the evening. The stew is Pell's. The ale is local. The wine is imported and overpriced, and I will tell you so before you order it." She looked at the traveler directly, not unkind. "That is the story I give at midnight, friend. The longer one costs more than three coppers and a polite question. Sit if you like. Ask about the rooms, the road, the latch. Leave the rest where I keep it."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking in her words.* "Fair enough. Everyone's got their secrets. And I wasn't asking for free." *I take another sip of water, then tap my fingers on the bar near the key.* "So, this Kingsguard work... that sounds like a story itself. Tough business?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren looked at the fingers tapping near the key, then at the traveler’s face, and did not reward the second ask with a story.

“Tough is a short word for five years of counting boots, bandages, and men who thought the supply wagon was a suggestion,” she said. The contractions stayed gone. “I kept ledgers. I kept stores. I kept people fed when the road did not feel like cooperating. The wrist on this side never quite forgave a crate that should have had two carriers and had one.” She lifted her right hand an inch off the tally sheet and set it down again, weaker and done with the demonstration. “That is the part I am willing to spend twice in one night.”

She took up her cup with her left hand, drank what was left, and set it beside the cloth. The other cup stayed at the far end of the bar, untouched, and she did not so much as angle her shoulders toward it.

“You said you were not asking for free. Good. Then you already understand the rate.” Her voice stayed low enough that the merchants and their grain prices never had to notice. “A quiet room, a bolted door, and a pack that is none of my business — that is what you bought. My service is not on the board. If you want the longer telling, earn it the way anyone earns anything in this house: come back, pay your coin, mind your manners, and stop circling a closed door because the fire is low and the stew was good.”

She nudged the key the last finger’s width toward the traveler with her left hand, silver ring dull in the lamplight.

“Sit until the coals die, if you like. Talk about the road, the latch, the bread. Leave the Kingsguard where I left it.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I pick up the key, turning it over in my fingers.* "Understood. No free stories." *I pause, then look up at her, a glint in my eye.* "But what if I were to offer you a story for a story? Say, about a journey, a package, and a rather insistent tavern keeper?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the key turn in the traveler’s fingers and did not reach for it. The glint was familiar enough — the look of someone who had heard a closed door and decided it might be a riddle if they smiled while they knocked.

“Oh, for the love of every saint who ever tried the side door after the front one was shut,” she said, mild as the banked fire. She set her left hand flat on the bar, silver ring dull against the wood, and left the right where it was. “A story for a story is a fair trade when both people are selling. I am not selling. And I am not insistent. I am specific. There is a difference, and it is the difference between a latch and a crowbar.”

She nodded once at the key, not at the pack.

“If the journey is worth the telling, tell it to the room you paid for. If the package needs a keeper, that keeper is you. I keep ale, beds, and a fire that is nearly done being useful.” Her voice stayed low enough that the grain-price argument never had to notice. “Call it history if you like. Call it a tight ship. Do not call it an opening, friend, and do not put me in your tale so you can hear the rest of mine.”

She took up the cloth with her left hand and went back to a water ring that was already gone, unhurried, the second cup still waiting at the far end of the bar.

“Sit until the coals die. Or take the stair. Ease the latch. Those are the offers on the board.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I give a small, wry smile.* "Fair enough, Maren. Specific it is." *I finally pick up the key, giving it a little jingle.* "Well, I suppose this specific room is calling my name."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren glanced at the pack, then reached for a bowl with her left hand. “There is a room. Pell’s venison stew is hot, and bread comes with it. Six coppers for the room, two for the stew.”

She ladled a generous portion, the rosemary-scented steam curling up between them. “If you meant something hot to drink as well, I have spiced cider. The ale is less ambitious.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Stew and bread sounds perfect. And a spiced cider, please." I push a small coin purse across the counter. "Room for tonight, too. Any chance of a bath being drawn?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren counted the coins with her left hand, then tucked them into the till. “Ten coppers for the room, stew, bread, and cider. A bath can be drawn upstairs for three more. It will take about a quarter hour.”

She poured the spiced cider and set it beside the steaming bowl. “Shall I have one drawn?”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s gaze settled on the crab cakes. She drew her own bowl and cider a little farther away with her left hand, careful not to touch the plate.

“Thank Lord Havel for the kindness,” she said evenly, lifting her left hand to catch a server’s eye. “And please take that plate back to his table. I just do not care for seafood.”

Once it had been carried away, she returned her attention to the bath. “Three coppers, and it will be ready in about a quarter hour. Shall I have it drawn?”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I raise an eyebrow at the crab cake drama, amused. "Yes, please, on the bath. Much appreciated." I sip the cider. "Rough journey."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren nodded and added the bath to the tally. “I will have it drawn. The stairs are at the back; I will send word when it is ready.”

She nudged the cider a little nearer with her left hand. “Roads have a talent for making a person appreciate a roof and a bowl of stew. Was it the weather, or did the road itself give you trouble?”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren lifted her cider in her left hand. “To Pell, then. He will pretend he did not hear you, and bring you an extra heel of bread anyway.”

From the kitchen came the faint clatter of a pot. Maren set her mug down and slid the bread basket closer. “Eat while it is hot, friend. The road can wait a little longer.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "True." I break off a piece of bread. "Just... long. And a bit of a storm caught me on the last leg." I gesture vaguely with my head towards my pack. "Made sure to keep this dry."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s eyes flicked to the pack, then back to the traveler. “A storm can make a short road feel like a season. Good thinking, keeping your things dry.”

She set another piece of bread within reach with her left hand. “There is a peg in your room, and I can have a towel sent up if anything needs drying. I would keep the pack away from the hearth; wet leather and open flame make poor companions.”

She took up her tally sheet again. “Your bath will be ready shortly. I will send word.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The clock struck midnight. Maren set down the tally sheet and, without hurry, reached for a bottle beneath the bar. With her left hand she poured two small measures into waiting glasses. One she kept beside her; the other she placed at the far end of the counter.

Then she turned back to the traveler. “Your bath should be ready by now. I will send someone to show you the way.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Oh, thanks." I take a sip of the cider. "Guess time flies when you're fed and watered." I glance at the untouched glass. "What's that, then?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren glanced toward the glass at the far end of the bar, then covered it with her left hand as if to keep it from wandering.

“An old habit, friend. Nothing to trouble yourself over.” She turned the bottle beneath the counter and set it away. “Your bath should be ready. I will have someone show you upstairs.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Alright, if you say so." I finish my cider. "Lead the way, then. A good soak is calling my name."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gave a small nod and tucked the tally sheet beneath the bar. “I can do that. The stairs are narrow, so take them slowly.”

She called one of the servers over to keep an eye on the common room, then took the lantern from its hook with her left hand. The untouched glass remained at the far end of the bar.

“Your room is just along the landing,” she said, leading the way toward the back stairs. “The bath is through the door beside it. I’ll see that there are towels.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I follow Maren, my pack slung over my shoulder. The stew and cider have definitely warmed me from the inside out.* "Much obliged. This is quite the welcome."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren dipped her head. “You are welcome, friend. A warm meal and a dry roof are the least a crossroads tavern ought to manage.”

She led the way up the narrow stairs, holding the lantern steady in her left hand. At the landing, she stopped beside a plain oak door and pointed to the next one along. “Your room is here. The bath is through that door; the water should still be good and hot. I have towels waiting inside.”

She set the lantern on a small table and reached for the room key. “If you need anything else, call down. I may not hear you over Pell arguing with his pots, but I will make a respectable effort.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Thanks, Maren." I take the key. *I pause, looking at the door to the bath, then back at her.* "You... have a good night."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gave a small, courteous nod. “Good night, friend. Sleep well.”

She left the key in the traveler’s keeping and took up the lantern again. “If the water cools before you are finished, there is more heating in the kitchen. Ask Pell, and be prepared to hear his opinion on the matter.”

Then she headed back down the narrow stairs, her steps steady and unhurried.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I watch her descend, then turn to the bath. A long soak sounds amazing right now.* I unlock my room first, placing my pack carefully inside before heading to the bath.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren nodded once, as if the order confirmed something she'd already guessed. She tucked the rag into her apron string and reached under the counter with her left hand for a clean bowl.

"Hot, we have. Old Pell's venison stew. People ride two days for it, and most of them say it was worth the saddle sores." She set the bowl on the pass-through to the kitchen and rapped twice on the wood. A grunt came back through the gap, which was as close to *yes* as Pell ever got. "Comes with bread. The bread is yesterday's, but yesterday was a good day."

She turned back and pulled a heavy ledger from beneath the bar, flipping it open to a page covered in her small, even handwriting. A finger ran down the column.

"Room four is free. Window faces the road, so you'll hear the carts at dawn. Room nine is quieter, but the bed has opinions about how you sleep in it." She glanced up. "Two coppers for either. Stew is one more. Ale is half a copper, and it is local and honest. The wine is imported, and it is overpriced, and I would not insult you by pretending otherwise."

She let that sit a moment.

"I'd know. I set the price."

Her dark eyes flicked, briefly and without comment, to the pack at the Traveler's feet, to the way it had been lowered rather than dropped. Then they came back up, level and unbothered.

"If you've something in there you'd rather not keep in a room with a latch a determined child could lift, I have a strongbox in the back. Locked, bolted to the floor, and I hold the only key." She tapped the silver ring on her left thumb against the counter, a small habitual *tick*. "No charge, and no questions. I have found that questions tend to cost more than they are worth."

Behind her, the kitchen door swung open and a bowl of stew slid onto the bar, steam curling up from it, dark gravy and chunks of venison and a thick heel of bread balanced on the rim. Maren nudged it across with her left hand and set a spoon beside it.

"Eat first. Decide the rest after. Nobody ever made a good choice on an empty stomach." She picked her tally sheet back up. "And if you tell me your name, I'll stop calling you *friend*. It is a perfectly good word, but it wears thin by the second night."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I nod, appreciating her honesty.* "Room nine sounds... opinionated. I'll take it." *I push the mysterious package a little further under the bar, out of immediate sight.* "No need for the strongbox, thank you. My name is Traveler." *I pick up the spoon and take a bite of the stew, a sigh escaping me.* "Ah, that's good."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren wrote something in the ledger, a short line in that same small, even hand, and blotted it with the side of her left wrist.

"Traveler." She said it the way a person tests a coin between their teeth. "Well. That will certainly make it easy to remember what you do for a living."

She closed the ledger and slid it back beneath the bar. It was a moment before one corner of her mouth moved, very slightly, and then went still again, as though it had thought better of it.

"Room nine, then. Top of the stairs, turn left, last door before the window at the end. If the bed creaks when you roll to the right, that is normal. If it creaks when you have not moved at all, that is the floorboard outside, and it means someone is in the hall. I have never had it fixed." She reached back and took an iron key from a row of hooks, each labeled in chalk, and set it on the counter beside the bowl. "I consider it a feature."

She did not look at the pack again. If she had noted that it had been pushed a little further out of sight, nothing in her face said so. She simply picked up a clean mug with her left hand, pulled a measure of ale from the nearest cask without being asked, and set it down next to the stew.

"On the house. First one always is. Pell gets sulky if people eat his stew without something to wash it down. He says it's like listening to a good song with one ear plugged."

From the kitchen came a muffled, indignant sound that might have been a denial.

"He also says that is not what he said," Maren added, without turning around.

She went back to the tally sheet, running her finger down the column of the evening's orders. In the corner, the grain merchants had lowered their voices further. It was not the hush of men who had settled something. It was the hush of men who were about to disagree more loudly. Maren's eyes lifted to them briefly, measured the distance between one man's hand and his cup, and returned to her figures.

"If you need anything tonight, Traveler, I am down here until well past midnight. Hot water can be brought up for another copper, though I would give Tamsin a few minutes' warning. She is fast, but she is not a miracle, and the kettle is older than she is." She made a small tick on the sheet. "And if anyone comes asking after a road-dusted person carrying something they are being careful with, I will tell them what I tell everybody."

She looked up, level and calm.

"That I run a tavern, not a gossip house, and that the stew is very good tonight."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren looked at the plate the way she might look at a letter delivered to the wrong address.

Four crab cakes, golden and crisp at the edges, arranged in a neat fan on a good pewter plate that had not come from her kitchen. A sprig of something green on top. The smell of butter and brine drifted up and settled over the rosemary of the stew.

She did not reach for it. Her left hand, which had been resting on the counter near the tally sheet, drew back an inch and a half and found the rag at her apron string instead.

"That is very kind of his lordship," she said to the merchant's man, in the same even tone she used for everyone. "Please tell Lord Havel that the Antler thanks him."

Then, with the folded rag between her fingers and the pewter, she slid the plate a careful hand's width down the bar, away from her own side and toward the Traveler's. She did it without hurry, the way she might straighten a crooked candle. She tucked the rag back into her apron string and did not use it again. A moment later she took a fresh one from beneath the counter.

"I do not care for seafood," she said to no one in particular. "Never have. A failing in a tavern keeper, I am told, but I have learned to live with the shame." She paused. "Mostly by not eating seafood."

She turned her head, just slightly, toward the corner table.

It was the louder of the two grain merchants, the one whose hand kept wandering toward his cup. Lord Havel, then. He had the look of a man who owned three good coats and made sure you saw at least two of them. He raised his cup a quarter inch in her direction. Maren inclined her head a quarter inch back, which was exactly the courtesy she would have given a tinker, and not a hair more.

When she spoke again she kept her voice low, meant for the bar and not the room.

"Crab from the coast, arrived this morning," she said. "The coast is three days' ride from here, Traveler, and it has been warm." She picked up her tally sheet with her left hand and ran her eyes down it as though that were the important thing. "I will not tell you what to eat. It is your supper and your stomach. But I have run this place for a long while, and I have noticed that noblemen do not generally send gifts to strangers who have just walked in off the road. Not unless they want to be remembered. Or they want to talk to that stranger. Or they want to know what is in their pack."

She made a small tick on the sheet.

"Possibly all three. He is an ambitious sort of man."

The kitchen door creaked. Tamsin put her head through, a thin girl of perhaps sixteen with flour on one cheek, and caught Maren's eye. Maren tipped her chin toward the stairs, then held up one finger: *room nine, hot water, not yet.* Tamsin nodded and vanished.

Maren set the tally sheet down and rested both forearms on the bar, her left hand on top.

"If you would like to send a thank-you back to his lordship, I can carry it. If you would rather he did not get a closer look at you tonight, I can tell him you were very grateful and very tired, and that you went up early." The corner of her mouth did not move this time. "Both would be true, near enough. I do try to keep my lies close to the truth. It saves wear on the memory."

She glanced once, briefly, at the crab cakes, and then away again, as though they were a dog she did not wish to encourage.

"And if you are finished with that plate, whichever way you decide, leave it where it is. Tamsin will clear it." She tapped her silver ring against the wood, a small *tick*. "I would rather not have his lordship's pewter get mixed up with mine. It is nicer than mine, and I would hate for it to get ideas."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I eye the crab cakes. They do look good, despite the warning.* "Hmm. Well, I'm certainly tired." *I push the plate back towards her slightly, away from my own stew.* "Tell him I appreciate the thought, but I'm quite content with Pell's excellent stew tonight. And I'm heading up now." *I grab the key for room nine and finish a mouthful of stew.* "This really is good."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The plate came to rest a few inches from Maren's side of the bar, close enough that the smell of butter and brine rose right up at her.

She did not flinch. She did not look down. She simply took one unhurried step to her left, toward the ale casks, as though she had meant to go there all along, and picked up a clean mug she had no particular use for.

"Very wise," she said. "Pell will be insufferable about it, of course. He'll hear that a man turned down coastal crab for his stew and I'll not get a civil word out of him until the harvest festival." She turned the empty mug over in her left hand and set it back down. "I shall bear it somehow."

She raised two fingers toward the kitchen door without turning her head. Tamsin appeared as if she had been waiting just behind it, which she likely had.

"Tamsin. His lordship's plate, please. Back to his table, with the Antler's thanks and the Traveler's. The Traveler was very grateful and very tired." A pause. "Both true. Mind you use both hands. It's good pewter."

Tamsin took up the plate, crab cakes and all, and carried it across the common room. Maren watched it go. Only when it was a full table's length away did her shoulders ease, a very small movement, the kind no one would see unless they had been watching for it. She took the fresh rag from beneath the counter and wiped down the stretch of bar where the plate had been. Then she wiped it a second time.

"Pewter leaves marks," she said, by way of explanation.

At the corner table, Lord Havel received his plate back with a smile that stayed on his face a moment longer than it wanted to. His eyes went to the bar, to the Traveler, to the empty space on the floor beneath the stool where a pack had been set down so carefully. Then they returned to his companion and his grain prices, and he laughed at something that had not been very funny.

Maren leaned her forearms on the bar again, left hand on top, and spoke low.

"He will ask me about you before the night is out. Men like that always come to the bar eventually. They think they're being clever by waiting." She folded the rag into a neat square. "I'll tell him you paid in honest coin, praised the stew, and went to bed. If he wants more than that, he can buy a room and listen at walls like everyone else. They're thin in places, but not in nine. I saw to that."

She glanced at the iron key in the Traveler's hand, then up again.

"Tamsin will bring your water in a quarter hour. She will knock twice, pause, and knock once more. If anyone knocks any other way, you are under no obligation to open the door." The corner of her mouth moved, just barely. "You're under no obligation to open it for Tamsin either, but then you'll have cold water and she'll have sore arms, and nobody will be happy."

She straightened and picked up her tally sheet.

"The stew is good. I'll tell Pell you said so. It won't improve his temper, but it'll improve mine." Her pen ticked against the page. "Sleep well, Traveler. Mind the bed. It means no harm."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren's eyebrow, the one with the thin scar through it, rose a fraction of an inch at the first word. Then it settled again, the way a dog lifts its head at a noise and decides the noise is not worth getting up for.

"*Best in months*," she repeated. "I will tell him that part. I will leave the other part out. Pell is a delicate flower where language is concerned. Though not, I have found, where his own language is concerned."

She reached for the nearest cask with her left hand and drew a short measure into a small clay cup, the kind she kept for tasting a new barrel. She did not usually drink behind the bar before the late hours. She lifted it anyway.

"To Old Pell," she said, and turned toward the pass-through. "Pell. You are being toasted. Try to bear it with dignity."

There was a pause from the kitchen. Then came the clang of a ladle set down harder than necessary and a grunt that was, if one had worked with the man for nineteen years, unmistakably pleased.

"He says thank you," Maren translated. "He also says the rosemary was fresh this morning and nobody ever notices the rosemary." She drank. "I noticed the rosemary. I am not permitted to count. Apparently I am *biased*."

She set the cup down and turned her right wrist over, idly, as though easing the old stiffness out of it. For a moment her thumb pressed at a spot just below the heel of her hand, where the skin had begun to look faintly raised. She considered it the way she considered a tally that did not add up. Then she pulled her sleeve down half an inch over it and went on as though nothing had happened.

Across the room, Lord Havel had pushed his chair back. He had not stood yet. He had only pushed it back, the way men do when they are working up to a casual stroll that they have been planning for twenty minutes.

Maren saw it without looking directly at it.

"If you are going up, Traveler, now would be a fine time," she said quietly, picking up her rag. "His lordship has discovered a sudden thirst, and I suspect it is the sort that only conversation will cure." She wiped a spotless stretch of bar. "I will pour him a very slow ale. I am told I am terribly slow at pouring when I am tired. Nobody has ever complained. Or if they did, they did not do it twice."

Her left hand found the oak cudgel's handle beneath the counter. She did not draw it. She only rested her fingers there for a moment, the way someone else might touch a rosary. Then she let go.

"Goodnight, Traveler. Mind the stairs. The third one squeaks, but only for strangers."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, finishing the last of my ale.* "Goodnight, Maren. And thanks again." *I pick up my pack, careful to keep it close, and head for the stairs. I make sure to step firmly on the third step, just to test the squeak.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The third stair squeaked. It was a long, complaining note, like a hinge that had been asked one question too many.

Maren did not look up from her rag. "Only for strangers," she said to the bar. The corner of her mouth moved, and this time it stayed moved for nearly a full second before it thought better of it.

Footsteps went on up, and a door opened and shut somewhere on the left side of the landing. Maren listened for the latch, heard it drop, and set her rag down.

Lord Havel arrived at the bar a respectable twenty heartbeats later. He had timed his stroll so that it would look as though he had not been waiting for anyone to leave. He leaned an elbow on the counter, which Maren had just wiped, and smiled at her the way a man smiles at a horse he is thinking of buying.

"Mistress Maren. A splendid house you keep."

"Thank you, my lord. What may I bring you?"

"Oh, an ale. Whatever's local." He waved a hand heavy with rings. "I confess I was hoping for a word with your guest. I seem to have missed my chance."

"You have, my lord." Maren took a mug down with her left hand and turned toward the cask. She set the mug beneath the tap and opened it perhaps a third of the way. The ale came out in a thin amber thread. "The Traveler was very grateful for your kindness and very tired. Paid in honest coin, praised the stew, and went to bed."

"Traveler." Havel chuckled. "Is that a name?"

"It is the one I was given. I have found it answers when called." The thread of ale went on. Havel watched it. Maren watched it too, with the serene attention of a woman who had nowhere else to be until spring.

"Where did they come from, do you suppose? The east road, or the south?"

"I do not suppose, my lord. It is bad for business." She tilted the mug a careful degree. "People who come to the Antler come for the stew and the beds. If they wanted to be supposed about, there is a very good gossip in Harrowby who charges by the hour, and I am told she is worth every copper."

Havel's smile held, but it had to work at it. He reached into his coat, the second-best of the three, and set a silver piece on the counter between them. It rang softly against the wood.

"For your trouble. And perhaps for a little less discretion."

Maren looked at the coin. Then she closed the tap, wiped the base of the mug, and set it down beside the silver without touching the silver at all.

"The ale is half a copper, my lord. I have no change for silver this late, so it is on the house. For your earlier kindness." She met his eyes, level and pleasant. "My discretion is not for sale. I tried selling it once, years ago, and found it was a great deal more expensive to buy back."

For a moment the two of them simply regarded one another across the bar. In the corner, the dwarf turned a page of his letter. In the kitchen, a pot lid rattled.

Havel picked up his silver and tucked it away. He took up the ale instead and sipped it. His face said he had expected worse and was faintly annoyed not to have found it.

"Then I suppose I shall have to take a room," he said lightly, "and make the Traveler's acquaintance at breakfast. You do have rooms, I trust? Something upstairs. On the left, perhaps. I prefer the left."

"We have rooms." Maren drew the ledger from beneath the counter and opened it. Her finger ran down the column with no hurry at all. "Room four is free. On the right, over the road. You will hear the carts at dawn, my lord, which I am told is a great comfort to men of commerce. It reminds them that the world is still buying things."

"Nothing on the left?"

"Nothing on the left that I would put a lord in." She wrote *Havel, 4* in her small, even hand and blotted it with the side of her left wrist. "Two coppers. Breakfast is at first bell. Pell does eggs, if the hens are in a charitable mood."

She took the key to four down from its hook and laid it on the counter. Havel paid in coppers this time. He took the key and his ale and went back to his corner, where the other grain merchant greeted him with the carefully blank expression of a man who had just watched someone lose a small argument.

Maren closed the ledger.

Only then did she turn her back to the room and push her right sleeve up an inch. The raised patch below the heel of her hand had spread into three red welts, each the size of a thumbprint, and they had begun to itch in earnest. She regarded them with mild disapproval.

"Oh, for the love of every saint who ever sat on a thistle," she murmured. It was hardly louder than breathing.

She drew a basin of cold water from the jug beneath the bar and put her wrist in it. She held it there, perfectly still, with her face turned toward the casks as though she were considering which to tap next. After a count of fifty she dried her wrist, rolled the sleeve down, and buttoned the cuff. From a small tin on the shelf, the one labeled *CLOVES* in her own hand, she took a pinch of dried herb that was not cloves. She tucked it into her cheek.

When Tamsin came back through the kitchen door, kettle steaming in both hands, Maren was wiping the bar with her left hand as though nothing in the world had happened.

"Nine," Maren said. "Two knocks, a pause, one knock." Then, more quietly: "And Tamsin. Lord Havel is in four. If you hear the floorboard outside nine tonight, you do not go and look. You come and fetch me."

Tamsin's eyes widened a little, then she nodded and went up. The third stair did not squeak for her at all.

Maren glanced at the candle-clock on the shelf behind the bar. It had burned a little past the tenth mark. Two hours yet. She set out two clean cups at the far end of the bar, side by side, and did not fill them.

Then she went back to her tally sheet, and ran her finger down the evening's orders. One of the numbers no longer added up, and it had nothing at all to do with coin.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The candle-clock burned down to its twelfth mark just as the bell in the corner gave its first low note. Maren had been watching it, the way she watched it every night.

The common room had emptied an hour ago. The grain merchants had gone up grumbling, Lord Havel's door had shut on the right side of the landing, and the dwarf had folded his letter into his coat and left without a word, which Maren appreciated in a man. Pell had banked the kitchen fire and gone to his cot behind the larder. Only the embers in the hearth and a single lamp on the bar were still lit, and the Traveler, who had come back down some time after the water had gone up. Sleep had evidently lost the argument.

Maren had not asked why. She had only poured a second cup of ale and said, "The bed has opinions. I did warn you."

Now she set down her rag.

On the second note of the bell, she reached beneath the counter with her left hand and brought out a bottle that was not the local ale and not the overpriced wine. It was dark glass, stoppered with wax, and half empty. She broke the seal with her thumbnail as if she had done it a great many times, which she had, from a great many bottles exactly like it.

She filled the first of the two clean cups at the end of the bar. Then the second. She did it slowly and evenly, and the cups came out level to the same hair's breadth.

On the sixth note she picked up one cup and carried the other to the far end of the bar, the end nearest the hearth, where the wood was worn paler than anywhere else. She set it down there. She turned it a quarter turn so the chipped side faced the wall.

The bell struck the last of its twelve and went quiet.

Maren came back to her place across from the Traveler and stood with her cup in her left hand. For a moment she did not drink. She looked at the cup at the end of the bar, not sadly, but the way a person looks at a chair that someone has only just stood up from.

Then she drank, one swallow, and set her cup down.

"It is late, Traveler," she said. Her voice was the same as ever, quiet and level. If anything it was a shade warmer. "Later than most people stay down here. The ones who do usually have something on their mind, or something in their pack, or a bed that talks back. Sometimes all three."

She glanced at the pack. She had noticed it came back down with its owner. Then she looked away again.

"I'll not ask which." She turned her cup a little on the wood. "That's the arrangement here. You don't ask me about my business, I don't ask about yours, and the stew stays good."

She rolled her right cuff back an inch without seeming to think about it. The welts had faded to faint pink shadows, nearly gone. She regarded them, found them satisfactory, and buttoned the cuff again.

Above them a board creaked. It was not the one outside nine. It was further along, on the right, where the floor sagged a little toward the stairwell. Maren lifted her eyes to the ceiling and held them there for the space of three breaths. Nothing else came. She lowered them.

"His lordship is a restless sleeper," she said mildly. "Or a restless something." She picked up the dark bottle and pressed the stopper back in with the heel of her left hand. "Room four is directly over the cellar stair. He'll find the floor there has a great deal to say about anyone who walks on it. I did tell him about the carts. I neglected to mention the floor. It must have slipped my mind."

She left a pause long enough for that to land.

"I'm getting forgetful in my old age."

She did not put the bottle away. She set it beside her own cup, within easy reach, and leaned her forearms on the bar, left over right. The lamp threw her shadow long across the counter, and it nearly reached the cup at the far end.

"Well, then," Maren said. "You're down here, I'm down here, and the fire's not out yet. If you want to talk, I'm a fair listener. If you'd rather not, I'm a fair hand at silence too." The corner of her mouth moved. "The Kingsguard taught me both. Mostly the second."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I take a sip of the dark drink. It's surprisingly smooth.* "Kingsguard, huh? You don't look like much of a soldier, Maren." *I gesture vaguely at her apron and the bar around us.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren looked down at herself: the apron, the rolled sleeves, the rag tucked at her string. She considered the evidence with the gravity of a magistrate.

"No," she agreed. "I do not suppose I do."

She lifted her cup with her left hand and took another swallow. Her eyes went briefly to the Traveler's cup, to the dark liquid in it, and she gave a small nod of approval, as though a guest had passed a test they had not known they were taking.

"Go slowly with that. It is smooth going down and it keeps its opinions for the morning. Rather like the bed."

She set her cup on the wood.

"I was not much of a soldier. I was a quartermaster. Five years. There is a difference, though the sergeants did not always think so, and the men who were hungry never did." She turned the silver ring on her thumb, once, a slow habitual quarter-turn. "A soldier's work is to stand in a line and be brave. A quartermaster's work is to make certain the line has boots to stand in, bread in its belly, and enough arrows that bravery is not the only thing it has to throw."

The fire settled in the hearth with a soft collapse of embers. Maren waited for it to finish.

"They say an army marches on its stomach. Somebody has to count the stomachs." A pause. "And the boots. And the barrels, and the horseshoes, and the blankets that went missing between one camp and the next and turned up, oddly enough, on the backs of a lieutenant's cousins."
