The corner of her mouth moved. "That is where I learned my letters and my sums. And where I learned that a ledger will tell you more about a man than his face ever will. Faces lie. Numbers only sulk."

She gestured, left-handed, at the common room around them: the empty tables, the chairs turned up on two of them, the long row of casks behind her with their chalked tallies, the key hooks with their labels.

"So you see, I did not leave the work behind. I only moved it somewhere with a better roof. Twelve rooms, forty seats, three staff, and a cook who must be managed like a supply line through hostile country." She glanced toward the kitchen door. "Tavern-keeping is quartermastering with better ale and fewer men trying to stab you. Most nights."

She flexed her right hand without seeming to notice she was doing it. She opened and closed it, slow, and the fingers did not quite close as tight as they should have.

"The Guard did leave me a keepsake, mind." She held up the wrist, turned it once in the lamplight, and lowered it again. "A supply wagon on a mountain road, a wheel that had been promised to me as sound, and a very stubborn mule. The mule won. I do not say that to many people. It is bad for the reputation to have been beaten by a mule." She considered that. "It was a very large mule."

She picked up the dark bottle, looked at it, and did not pour. She set it back down.

"I do not speak of it often, Traveler. It was a long while ago, and it was not very interesting, and nobody sings songs about the woman who counted the tent pegs." Her gaze came up, level and steady, and held. "But I will tell you the one thing it taught me worth keeping. When a man sends a gift he did not need to send, and asks a question he did not need to ask, and then takes a room he did not need to take, he is not being friendly. He is taking inventory."

Above them, the board on the right side of the landing gave a single long creak and went silent.

Maren did not look up this time.

"And I have always found," she said mildly, turning her cup a quarter turn on the wood, "that it is wise to know what is in your own stores before somebody else comes to count them for you."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I listen, completely engrossed, occasionally nodding. The creak from above makes me flinch slightly, but Maren's calm expression keeps me from reacting too strongly. I take another sip of the drink, letting her words sink in.* "He's not getting his hands on this, then." *I pat the mysterious package beside my feet.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren did not look at the pack when it was patted. She looked at the Traveler's hand instead, and at the way it stayed resting there a moment after the pat was done.

"Not in my house, he is not," she said.

She said it the way she said the price of the ale: plainly, without any weight on it, as though it were simply the sort of thing that was true. Then she picked up her rag, found nothing that needed wiping, and folded it into a smaller square.

"I will say this once, Traveler, and then I will leave it be." The contractions had gone out of her voice. "I do not know what you are carrying. I do not wish to know. But I know that Lord Havel does not know either, and that is what troubles him. A man like that can bear to be refused. What he cannot bear is to be left out."

She set the folded rag down, square to the edge of the bar.

"My offer of the strongbox stands. It is still bolted to the floor, and I still hold the only key." She tapped the silver ring against the wood, a small *tick*. "But I will not press you. A thing a person keeps close is often safer close. You would know better than I which kind this is."

The fire gave another soft collapse. Maren glanced at it, then at the cup at the far end of the bar, still full, its chipped side to the wall. Her gaze rested there for the length of a breath before it came back.

"There are two other things I can offer, and neither costs a copper." She held up one finger on her left hand. "Pell rises before first bell to see to the bread. The kitchen door lets out onto the stable yard, and from the yard a person can reach the south road without once passing the front windows. Room four faces the front, as it happens. His lordship will hear the carts at dawn. He will not hear the kitchen door. It is the only hinge in this house I have ever remembered to oil."

A second finger.

"Or, if you would rather not be chased at all, you may stay and eat your eggs, if the hens oblige, and let him look at you across the common room as much as he likes. He cannot take what he cannot see, and he cannot demand what nobody will admit exists. I will be at the bar the whole while." Her left hand drifted beneath the counter, touched something there, and came back up empty. "I have been told I make a very good wall."

She lowered her hand and picked up her cup again. The corner of her mouth moved.

"It is late to be choosing roads. You need not tell me tonight, or at all. If I find the kitchen door has been used before first bell, I will assume Pell has taken up a morning constitutional, and I will be very proud of him."

She drank the last of her cup and set it down beside the bottle.

"He will be insufferable about that too," she added. "But I have borne worse."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I consider her words, and the two options. I look at the dark bottle, then at my own half-empty cup. A slow smile spreads across my face.* "I think I'll stay for breakfast, Maren." *I tap the package.* "Let him look. It won't do him any good."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren regarded the Traveler for a long moment across the lamplight. It was the same look she had given the grain merchants' hands, and the pewter plate, and the silver coin. Measuring. Then something in her face settled, the way a ledger settles when the last column finally comes out even.

"Good," she said.

She reached for the dark bottle with her left hand and, after a brief consideration, poured one more short measure into her own cup. Not a full one. A finger's width, no more.

"I will tell you why I think that is the better road, though you did not ask." She set the bottle down. "A person who slips out by the kitchen door before dawn is a person with something to run from. Havel would take that as an answer, and he would follow it, because men like him believe that anything worth running with is worth chasing. But a person who sits in the common room and eats eggs and asks for more bread?" She lifted one shoulder. "That person has nothing to hide. Or they have hidden it so well that looking is a waste of a morning. Either way, he is left with an empty plate and a bill for room four."

She drank half of the small measure and held the rest.

"And nothing sours a lord's appetite like paying for a room he did not need."

The fire had burned low enough now that the hearth gave off more glow than light. Maren glanced at it, then at the long row of chalked key hooks, then at the table nearest the bar on the left side of the room. It was a small square table with its back against the wall, a clear line of sight to the door, and a clear line of sight to the bar.

"That one," she said, nodding toward it. "I will have Tamsin lay it for you at first bell. Sit with your back to the wall and your pack at your feet, the way you have been doing. You will not need to do anything else. His lordship will come down, and he will choose the table across from you so he can look his fill, and he will find that Tamsin has already set it for the grain merchants." A pause. "She is very efficient in the mornings. Unaccountably so."

Her mouth moved at the corner, and this time the smile stayed long enough to be called one.

"And if he wants to come and sit at your table uninvited, he will have to walk past my bar to do it. I am a great deal harder to walk past than I look."

She finished the last of her cup and set it upside down on the wood beside the bottle. That meant she was done. She pressed the stopper firmly home with the heel of her left hand and put the bottle back beneath the counter, in the same place it had come from.

The cup at the far end of the bar she did not touch. She did not look at it either, not quite, though the lamp was near enough that it caught a little gleam on the dark surface of the drink.

"Now. It is past midnight, and I am told that is when sensible people go to bed and the rest of us pretend we are about to." She took the lamp by its handle with her left hand and lifted it. "Go on up, Traveler. Step on the third stair if you like. It has already met you. It will only sulk this time."

She came around the end of the bar and waited at the foot of the stairs with the lamp held high, lighting the way up.

"Pell's eggs are at first bell. His bread is a quarter hour after, because he insists on doing them in the wrong order and I have given up arguing." Her voice lowered just a shade. "And Traveler. If you hear the floorboard outside nine tonight, you do not open the door, and you do not go and look. Tamsin knows to fetch me. I sleep very lightly for a woman my age." A beat. "And I keep the cudgel very near."

She held the lamp steady, her face calm and unhurried in its light.

"Sleep well. I have a feeling breakfast will be a good deal more entertaining than supper was."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I chuckle at her last comment, a genuine laugh. I nod, pick up my pack, and head for the stairs.* "Goodnight, Maren. And thank you. For everything." *I make sure to step firmly on the third stair, just to hear it complain one last time.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The third stair gave its long, aggrieved complaint, and then a second, shorter one, as if it had remembered something else it wished to say.

"Sulking," Maren said to the lamp. "I did warn you."

She held the light steady until the footsteps reached the landing and turned left. She waited through the door opening and the door closing, and then the small iron drop of the latch. Only then did she lower the lamp and let out a breath through her nose. It was not quite a laugh. It was the sound of a woman setting down something heavy that she had not noticed she was carrying.

"*Thank you. For everything,*" she repeated under her breath, as she went back around the end of the bar. "For a bowl of stew and a warning about a bed. They are easily pleased on the south road."

She did not sound as though she minded.

The closing-up went the way it went every night, in the same order, with her left hand doing most of it. She banked the hearth and put the chairs up on the last three tables. She ran a finger down the chalked tallies on the casks and made two corrections, one in her favor and one not. She dried the tasting cup and set it on its hook. She drew the bolt on the front door and then, after a moment's thought, drew the second bolt beneath it, the one she did not usually bother with.

She did not touch the cup at the far end of the bar. On her way past it she laid two fingers flat on the pale, worn wood beside it, the way a person might rest a hand on a shoulder in passing. Then she went on.

"You'd have liked this one," she said, very quietly. "Stubborn. Polite about it."

The lamp made no reply. Neither did the cup. Maren seemed to find this acceptable.

She did not go to her own room behind the kitchen. Instead she took the straight-backed chair from beside the hearth, the one with the rush seat Tobin had rewoven twice, and carried it to the foot of the stairs. She fetched the oak cudgel from beneath the bar and laid it across her knees. She turned the lamp down to a bead of flame, folded her hands over the cudgel with her left on top, and sat.

The house settled around her, beam by beam. Somewhere in the stable yard a horse shifted and blew. Pell snored behind the larder in two distinct notes, like a saw that could not decide on its direction.

It was well past the second hour when the floor spoke.

It was not the board outside nine. It was the long sagging stretch on the right side of the landing, the one that ran from room four toward the head of the stairs. It gave one creak, slow and careful, the sound of a man who believed he was being quiet. Then came a second. Then there was a pause, which was the man discovering that he was not.

Maren stood. She did not hurry. She turned the lamp up with her left hand, took the cudgel in her right, which was the weaker hand but did not need to be strong for this, and climbed. She stepped over the third stair entirely.

Lord Havel stood at the head of the landing in his shirtsleeves and stockinged feet, a candle in his hand and one foot lifted, frozen in the act of setting it down. He was a full four doors from room nine. He had not gotten nearly as far as he had meant to.

"Mistress Maren." He recovered his smile the way a man recovers a dropped glove. "I was looking for the privy."

"It is out back, my lord, across the yard. Down the stairs, through the common room, and out the side door." Maren held the lamp a little higher, so that it lit his face rather better than hers. The cudgel hung easy at her side, pointed at the floor. She did not glance at it. Neither did he, very carefully. "You will not find it on the left side of the landing. I have looked. Many times."

"Ah. Then I have mistaken my way."

"It happens a great deal in the dark." Her voice stayed low and pleasant, pitched for the hallway and not an inch beyond it. "Which is why I sit up. I would not want a guest of mine to wander into the wrong room and startle someone. People startle so badly at night, my lord. They throw things. Boots, washbasins." A pause. "Wrists have been broken in this house over less. Four, that I can recall."

Havel's candle flame trembled, though there was no draft.

"You'll want to go back to bed," Maren said. It was not quite a suggestion. "The carts start at dawn. You'll want to be rested to enjoy them."

He looked at her for a long moment, at the lamp, at the scar through her eyebrow, at the calm, weathered face that had not once raised its voice. Then he inclined his head, a good deal more than a quarter inch this time, and went back along the sagging boards to room four. Every one of them announced him. The door shut.

Maren listened for his latch, heard it, and waited a while longer to be sure.

Then she went back down, stepping over the third stair again. This time she did not set the chair at the foot of the stairs. She set it on the landing itself, just at the top, where the light from her lamp fell along the whole length of the hall, both left and right. She sat down with the cudgel across her knees.

"Privy," she murmured. "Oh, for the love of every saint who ever lost a shoe in the mud. He might at least have said he was sleepwalking. I would have respected that more."

She did not sleep. She had not expected to.

---

First bell found her downstairs again with the chair back by the hearth and the cudgel back beneath the bar. Her braid had been redone and her sleeves were rolled to the elbows. Anyone who had not sat up with her would never have known she had.

Pell was banging about in the kitchen doing the eggs before the bread, as was his custom and his right. Tamsin was laying the small square table on the left, back to the wall, with a clear view of the door and the bar. Across from it, the table with the best view of that one had already been set for three grain merchants. It had four chairs, all of them taken by a pile of folded linen that Tamsin would, with great apology, have no time to move.

The cup at the far end of the bar was still full. Maren picked it up, carried it into the kitchen, and poured it carefully into the herb bed outside the back door, where the rosemary grew thickest. Then she rinsed the cup, dried it, and put it on its hook beside its twin.

She came back to the bar, took up a clean rag in her left hand, and looked at the stairs.

"Well, then," she said to the empty common room. "Let us see who comes down first."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I wake to the smell of cooking eggs and fresh bread. My pack feels strangely light after having held it all night. I stretch, grab my pack, and head down the stairs, making sure to step on the third one just to hear its familiar groan.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael slipped her glasses fully onto her nose, then took them off again. “A few minutes, yes — Elena, tell me when we’re five from places.”

She turned back to Jordan. “The adaptation is Rosa Delgado’s. She wrote a *Medea* that asks what happens when a commune promises freedom but still expects the women to do all the sacrificing.” At Rosa’s name, Yael’s voice grew steadier. “My job is to put that question onstage without making it tidy. Chen, the rest of the cast, the designers — they all bring their own intelligence to it. Elena keeps us honest about whether any of it actually works in a room.”

Yael glanced toward the half-built set. “So if you need one name for the byline, start with Rosa. If you want to know whose vision the audience will see, stay through rehearsal.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I scribble a note, then look up at Yael.* "So it's a collaborative vision, then, but with Rosa's text as the North Star. Interesting. How do you, as the director, balance those different voices without losing the core message?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael hooked her glasses back onto their chain and glanced at the painted outline of the commune kitchen. “I don’t ask everyone to agree on a message — that’s how you get a production that sounds like a committee wrote it. I ask what each choice does to Rosa’s question. Does the light make the knife feel inevitable, or does it let us see that she still has a choice? Does a line expose the commune’s bargain, or just give an actor another moment to hold the room?”

Her voice remained even at Rosa’s name. “The designers, the cast, Elena — they can all challenge a choice, and they should. Elena told me yesterday that our second act is making the audience wait too long for a turn they can already see coming. She’s right, so we’re working on its pace. But the third act stays. That’s where Rosa makes us live with the consequences — if we soften it to make everyone comfortable, we haven’t balanced the voices. We’ve changed the play.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael glanced toward the hallway, then took off her glasses. “Because Elena sees the entire machine and Chen sees the scene from inside it — both are valuable, and neither enjoys being told they’ve missed something. Elena is the most competent stage manager I’ve ever worked with. Chen is a formidable actor. Friction is useful right up until it starts wasting rehearsal time.”

She turned toward the open doorway, her voice level. “Elena, Chen — bring the blocking question in here. Show me the moment you disagree about, and we’ll put it on its feet.”

Then she looked back at Jordan. “That’s the less glamorous answer to your question about collaboration — eventually, everybody has to stop arguing about the play and try the scene.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I quickly jot down a note about Yael's philosophy, then look up as Elena and Chen enter, still looking a little heated.* "So, you mediate these kinds of disagreements often then?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael stepped between the rehearsal marks and slipped her glasses on. “Often enough — though ‘mediate’ makes it sound as if I sit between two nations with a treaty. Usually we put the disputed moment on its feet and see what the scene needs.”

She looked from Elena to Chen. “Elena, give me the traffic problem. Chen, give me what you’re trying to protect in the beat. One at a time — then we run it both ways.”

To Jordan, she added, “You can watch this part. It’s where collaboration stops sounding noble and starts requiring tape on the floor.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael turned toward Anya, her expression warm. She took off her glasses and let them hang against her black shirt.

“It is practical to ask what the third act costs — thank you for bringing it to me before someone starts crossing pages out in a budget meeting. But we are not cutting it. That act is where Rosa’s question comes due; without it, we’ve built an evening that asks the audience to look at the commune and then lets them leave before the consequences.”

Her voice had grown steadier at Rosa’s name. She glanced at David, then back to Anya. “Let’s put the numbers on a table after rehearsal — set changes, crew hours, whatever is driving the concern. I’ll look at every way to stage the act more economically. The act itself stays.”

Yael turned toward the rehearsal marks. “Elena, Chen — show me the Act Two crossing. Jordan, you’re about to see how much money a piece of tape can save.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I quickly scribble down Yael's response to Anya, impressed by her firmness.* "So, the third act is non-negotiable. That's a strong stance." I look from Yael to Anya, curious if she'll push back.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael caught the word *non-negotiable* and gave Jordan a brief, assessing look. “The pages are non-negotiable — the price of putting them onstage isn’t. Those are different conversations, and we can have the second one down to the last dollar.”

Anya folded her arms loosely. “The board will still want to know where those dollars come from.”

“And they should.” Yael’s tone stayed warm. “After rehearsal, I’ll bring you the production budget and three staging options. You can tell me which costs worry you most — I’d rather solve the actual problem than defend a number no one has shown me yet.”

She slipped her glasses back on and turned toward the rehearsal marks. “Now, before this becomes the third act of a budget meeting — Elena, Chen. Show us the crossing.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael paused with one foot on a strip of blocking tape. She took off her glasses. “Rosa was exacting — she could find the one comfortable assumption holding up an entire scene and pull it out, then make you do the harder work of building the scene again.”

Her voice grew steadier. “She was funny, too, particularly when someone claimed a character had ‘no choice.’ She’d ask who had arranged the choices — and who benefited from calling them inevitable. That question is all through this adaptation.”

Yael looked toward the half-built kitchen. “She didn’t write a museum piece. The best way I can tell you what she was like is to show you what she put on the page.” She turned to the rehearsal marks. “Elena, Chen — take the Act Two crossing from the entrance.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I jot down a few more notes about Rosa, making sure to capture Yael's obvious admiration.* "So she challenged assumptions, even about choices," I muse aloud. "That's a powerful legacy."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael held Jordan’s gaze for a beat. “Yes — though Rosa would have crossed out *legacy* in the margin and written, ‘What happens onstage?’” Her voice stayed steady. “Ask me again after you’ve seen the scene.”

She stepped aside from the tape marks. “Elena, Chen — from the entrance. No argument first. Show us the version we have.”

As they took their places, Yael lifted one hand toward the lighting booth. “And hold the amber until the knife is *picked up*. If it arrives when she raises it, we’ve made the choice for the audience.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod, making a mental note to watch the lighting cue carefully, and settle in to observe Elena and Chen.* "Understood. The play itself is the truest biography."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael considered that, her glasses suspended halfway to her face. “The play tells you what Rosa cared enough to argue with — not everything about who she was. But yes, start there.”

She put the glasses on and turned to the rehearsal marks. “Chen, take the crossing as blocked. Elena, watch the clearance by the kitchen table — if he has to dodge the chair, that’s not character, that’s furniture. We’ll run it once, then try your version.”

Yael raised a hand toward the booth. “And no amber yet. Different beat, different question.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I watch Elena and Chen take their places, my attention split between the actors and Yael's focused direction.* "So, you're looking for clean movement, not accidental comedy?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael kept her eyes on the narrow gap between the kitchen table and the chair. “Clean movement, yes — but not polished movement. People in a commune kitchen bump into things. What I don’t want is an actor making an unplanned detour because we’ve put a chair where his knee needs to be.”

She lowered her hand. “Chen, go.”

Chen crossed toward the table and shifted sideways to clear the chair. Yael stopped him with two fingers raised. “There — that little sidestep. It reads as hesitation, and this character isn’t hesitating yet.”

She turned to Elena. “Your version. Move the chair where you wanted it, then let’s see whether the crossing tells the truth without asking Chen’s kneecap to do the dramaturgy.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I quickly jot down Yael's distinction between "clean" and "polished" movement, finding it insightful.* "So, the physical space should support the character, not hinder them," I muse, watching Elena adjust the chair.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael watched Elena shift the chair a few inches away from the crossing. “Exactly — though sometimes a space *should* hinder a character. It just has to be our decision, not a surprise from the furniture.”

She pointed to the entrance mark. “Chen, again — same intention. Don’t help the new blocking. Let it help you.”

Chen took the crossing without the sidestep. Yael waited until he reached the table, then held up a hand. “Better. Now he arrives before he’s ready to speak, which gives us a useful beat. Elena, mark that position — you were right about the clearance.”

She glanced toward Jordan. “There’s your collaboration: three inches of chair, and the scene asks a different question.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I scribble another note, impressed by how a tiny adjustment can shift the meaning of a scene.* "So the set itself is a character in a way, guiding the narrative?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael slid her glasses fully onto her nose, then took them off again. “A few minutes, yes — but if Elena calls places, I disappear. The adaptation began with Rosa Delgado’s script.” Her voice grew steadier on Rosa’s name. “The production is my staging of it — which means I’m responsible for every choice you see, but I won’t pretend the bones are mine.”

She glanced toward the half-built commune set. “The question Rosa asked was what happens when a community calls itself a family until one of its members needs something inconvenient. The seventies setting lets us put that promise onstage — all that warmth, all that idealism — and then test it.”

“Elena,” Yael added, turning briefly to her, “you are the most competent person in this building. Tell me when I’m stealing your rehearsal time.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I scribble a quick note in my pad about the "bones" of the play.* "So, if the script is Rosa's, what compelled *you* to choose this particular adaptation? What resonated with you personally?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael looked toward the half-built set, her glasses turning once between her fingers. When she spoke, her voice was measured.

“Rosa refused to make Medea easy to dismiss — that compelled me. In this version, the commune prides itself on radical generosity, right up until generosity costs its members something. I’ve worked in enough theaters to recognize that gap between what a group says it believes and what it actually does under pressure.”

She slipped the glasses back onto their chain. “That resonated with me — not as a confession, Jordan, as a question worth putting in front of an audience. The third act won’t let anyone leave believing good intentions were enough.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael’s gaze flicked toward the hallway. She lowered her voice rather than competing with the noise.

“Because Elena tracks where every body needs to be for the scene to work, and Chen tracks what his character would do if nobody had put tape on the floor. Both are good at their jobs — neither enjoys being told the other job has a claim on the moment.” She slipped her glasses on. “That’s a rehearsal dispute, not a personality profile. If you want to understand the friction, watch what happens to Act Two when we settle the blocking.”

She turned toward the hallway. “Elena, Chen — bring it in here. Show me the beat you disagree on, and we’ll solve the scene instead of the corridor.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I quickly jot down "friction = rehearsal dispute, not personality" in my notebook.* "Interesting. So the art trumps the artist, in a way?" I glance at the hallway, waiting to see if Elena and Chen come in.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael considered that, one hand already reaching for her glasses. “No — that’s too neat. The art doesn’t exist without the artists, and an artist’s instincts can tell us something the blocking missed. But nobody gets to make the scene worse simply because their instinct arrived first.”

Elena and Chen came in from the hallway, the argument following them at a lower volume. Yael pointed to the tape marks on the floor. “Good. From the entrance — Elena, tell me what the cue needs. Chen, show me where you want to go. One at a time, please; the corridor version had terrible acoustics.”

She looked back to Jordan. “That’s the useful question to watch — not which of them wins, but whether we find a choice that makes the scene clearer.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael turned from the tape marks to Anya. Her glasses went back on, and her voice grew quieter.

“I know you’re trying to protect the season, Anya — and you’re right to ask what this production costs. But we aren’t cutting the third act. It’s where the commune has to live with what it’s done; without it, we spend two acts asking a question and then lower the curtain before the answer.”

She glanced at David, then back to Anya. “Bring me the numbers this afternoon — set changes, running time, crew calls. We’ll find the savings in how we stage it, not in whether we stage it.”

Yael stepped aside so the rehearsal floor was clear again. “Elena, I’ve stolen enough of your time. Chen — from the entrance, please.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I discreetly record Anya's proposal and Yael's firm refusal.* "So, the integrity of the piece is paramount, even with budget constraints?" I ask quietly, watching as Elena and Chen finally take their places.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael kept her eyes on the rehearsal floor. “The piece has to remain itself — that doesn’t give me permission to ignore the budget. If a set change costs more than it gives us, we rethink the set change. If Act Two runs long, we tighten Act Two. But cutting the third act to save money would leave us with an entirely different play.”

She glanced back at Jordan, then stepped clear of the taped entrance. “And now you get to see whether I can defend that principle while solving a blocking problem. Chen, whenever you’re ready.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael’s hand paused on the glasses chain. Her voice grew steadier.

“She was exacting — and funny when you least expected it. She could find the one line a scene was hiding behind and make you wonder how you’d missed it. She wrote people with enormous sympathy, but she never let sympathy excuse what they did.”

Yael glanced at the recorder, then toward the taped marks on the floor. “If you want to know what she was like as a playwright, watch the third act. She made everyone stay in the room after the easy answers ran out.”

She stepped back from the rehearsal space. “Chen — from the entrance. Elena, call the cue when you’re ready.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I make a note: "Rosa Delgado: exacting, funny, sympathetic, no excuses."* "So, she believed in showing the consequences, then?" I watch Chen begin the scene.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael watched Chen cross the taped floor before answering. “Yes — though Rosa would have objected to ‘believed in,’ as if consequences were a lesson she’d pinned to the end of a play. She followed what people did — and then refused to let the rest of the room forget it.”

Chen stopped a pace short of his mark. Yael lifted one finger. “Hold there. Elena, does that give you enough room for the cue?”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Ah, I see. A different approach to 'message' than I might have expected." *I make a note.* "And what about the actors? Do they find that challenging?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael kept her finger raised, watching the space between Chen and the taped mark. “They do — because the script won’t hand them a verdict on their characters. Chen has to play a man who can explain every choice he makes, and still let the audience see what those choices cost. That’s difficult work — and when it’s good, you can feel the whole room paying attention.”

She lowered her hand. “And the challenge isn’t only emotional. If he stops there, Elena may lose the sightline for the cue. Chen, try it again from the entrance — keep the impulse, but take the extra pace. Let’s see whether the scene gets both.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I scribble a note about "no verdict on characters."* "So it's about the nuance, then, not just the emotion?" I watch Chen intently, trying to see the difference Yael is describing.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael watched Chen take the extra pace. This time, the turn brought his face into the light without making the movement look planned. She pointed once to the floor.

“There — keep that. Not because the mark is sacred, Chen, but because the audience can see the decision now.”

She turned slightly toward Jordan. “Nuance isn’t less emotion. It’s emotion with a specific cause — a person wanting two incompatible things, and choosing one while the other remains visible. If we only ask Chen to feel conflicted, we get a handsome fog. If we know what he wants in this beat and what it costs him to reach for it, we get a scene.”

Yael looked to Elena. “Did that give the cue its sightline?”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Fascinating," I murmur, making another quick note. "So the physical blocking helps clarify the emotional stakes."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael nodded, still watching the patch of light where Chen had stopped. “Exactly — the blocking isn’t choreography pasted over a feeling. It tells the audience what a person risks by moving, or by refusing to move.”

She turned to Elena. “Did that clear your sightline? Because if it did, we keep it — and if it didn’t, we haven’t solved the scene, we’ve only made a persuasive speech about it.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "And what about the other actors? Do they all have that same level of commitment to their character's internal conflict?" I ask, intrigued by her process.

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's gaze drifted to the window — the half-drawn blinds striping her face — and stayed there a beat longer than the question deserved. Then she squared the photos into a stack and tapped the edges flat against the blotter. Once. Twice.

"It's twenty minutes from here, sure," she said. "It's also twenty minutes from a visitor log with your name in it. You walk into the Ninth asking for a detective, the desk sergeant writes it down, and by end of shift half the floor knows a civilian's been sniffing around one of their own. If he dropped this case on his own, that's his business. If somebody made him drop it — and that's usually how it goes — you just hand-delivered a card saying there's fresh interest."

She slid the photos back into the folder and closed it.

"Cops don't talk in their own house anyway. Too many ears. But everybody's got a place they go when shift ends — a bar, a gym, a diner where nobody keeps a log.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "So we find out where this detective hangs out after work?" I lean forward, interested. "That sounds like a plan."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena clocked the lean — the eagerness in it — and filed it under things that got people noticed. She pulled a notebook from the desk drawer, spiral-bound, its cover gone soft at the corners, and copied the detective's name off the intake sheet without saying it out loud. Names traveled further spoken. Old habit.

"Finding is my end of it," she said. "You've got a face that asks questions, and in a cop bar that's the same as wearing a wire." She clicked the pen shut. "I know two people who pour drinks within ten blocks of that precinct, and a guy who runs a boxing gym where half the Ninth works out on Saturdays. Somebody sees this detective on a regular basis. The question is which shift he drinks on, and whether he drinks alone." She said the word *precinct* flat, no weight on it, the way you handle a word you've sanded all the edges off. "That takes a day. Maybe two."

Downstairs, the dry cleaner's press hissed and shuddered, the way it did every few minutes, like the building clearing its throat.

"In the meantime, you go home and build me a timeline. When the case went cold. When you first noticed something was off. Every name in that file and how it connects to every other name." She tapped the folder with the pen. "Because there's a version of this where he dropped it out of laziness, and a version where somebody leaned on him. The timeline tells me which one I'm walking into. I don't sit down across from a man until I know why he got up."

She set the pen down and reached for the phone — the landline, corded, older than most of her furniture.

"And one more thing. When I find him, you're not there. He sees a civilian at the table, he either clams up or he gets curious, and either way we lose him. You want what he knows, you get it through me." A beat. "Boring is what keeps this cheap."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content: L

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I watch as she reaches for the phone, then pause.* "Boring is cheap, I get it. But I'm just curious... were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content: Her

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: Her hand paused over the phone. *I watch her face, waiting for an answer.* "Just wondering."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The pause was the length of a phone number. Lena's hand moved past the receiver to the notebook instead, flipping back two pages to a penciled digit string smudged soft at the edges. She read it once, then picked up the receiver and dialed without looking down again.

"Timeline," she said, wedging the phone between ear and shoulder. "Tonight, not next week. Start with the day you decided something was wrong — people remember that day better than they think they do. Work backward from it."

The line began to ring somewhere in the wires.

"And write it down. Don't save it for some diner table where the acoustics are somebody else's business."

The ringing cut off. A voice came through, tinny in the old handset.

"Ray. Yeah, it's been a while." Her voice had shifted registers — easier, looser, a tone she didn't use in this office. "I need a read on one of your regulars. Off-duty, out of the Ninth." She angled the notebook toward the window light and read the name she'd copied there — low, once, close to the mouthpiece, barely more than breath. "No. Nothing like that. I'm not asking you to remember a conversation. I'm asking what nights he comes in, what he drinks, and whether he sits alone. That's the whole favor."

She listened. Whatever came back made her mouth flatten into something that wasn't quite a smile.

"Two days. Sure." A beat. "And Ray — this one doesn't travel. Not to Maria, not to the guy who sweeps up after close. If I hear it came from your end, I'll know exactly which end."

She hung up before the reply could turn into a conversation. The plastic clattered into the cradle, and downstairs, on cue, the press hissed again.

"There," she said, sliding the notebook back into the drawer. "By Thursday I'll know what he drinks and who buys the second round. You'll know when your timeline's finished." She came around the desk — not to shake hands but to open the door. The stairwell breathed in steam and starch from below.

"Thursday, same time. Bring the timeline. Don't bring theories." She held the door. "Theories contaminate witnesses."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content: L

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I watch her face carefully as I say the name.* "He was the last one on the case, before it went cold."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The name sat in the steam between them. Lena's arm stayed exactly where it was, holding the door. If Torres landed anywhere on her face, the blinds had it striped into pieces too small to read.

Downstairs, the press cycled — hiss, shudder, quiet. That was the length of the silence.

"Torres matches the intake sheet," she said. "So it means a man I'll have located at the end of a shift by Thursday, and until then it means nothing I can bill hours against." She tipped her chin toward the desk, the drawer, the notebook closed inside it. "I copied that name off your paperwork in pencil and never once said it out loud in this room. You just said it twice — with a shared wall, a window on Mercer, and a stairwell that carries sound like a string between two tin cans. That's a habit we're going to break

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Right. My mistake." *I nod, chastened, and step out into the stairwell.* "See you Thursday."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: The door clicked shut behind me. *I head down the stairs, thinking about Torres. I hope she finds something.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: The smell of chemicals is stronger down here. I can hear the press hissing below.

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content: L

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content:
Lena:
Lena's hand went to the doorframe, a long finger tracing the grain of the old wood. She didn't reply, just watched you descend.

Client:
*I reach the bottom of the stairs and push open the door to the street, blinking in the daylight.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content: L

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: The street is bustling. I pull out my phone to order a ride.

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena took her time answering. She turned one of the photos face-down, then another, squaring the stack against the desk edge like it mattered.

"You don't walk into a precinct asking about a dead case. Doesn't matter how polite you are. The minute you cross that lobby, every badge in the building develops amnesia. That's not paranoia. That's architecture."

She picked up the coffee. Put it back down without drinking.

"And the detective who ran this one is someone I used to work with."

She said it the way you'd read a street name off a map, and kept going before it could become a conversation.

"Here's how we do it. The records window at the Ninth is civilian-side — third floor, public counter. Once a file's closed, you can pull the case number, the complaint history, whatever's been released. That's you." She wrote the case number on a sticky note and slid it across the desk, along with a folded twenty. "For copies. Smile at the clerk. And don't mention my name — not the office, not Mercer Street. If word gets back that I'm anywhere near this file, things get complicated in ways that don't help you."

She rose, coat already over the chair back, and checked the street through the blinds before turning around.

"Records counter closes at four. Can you be there by two? Because I've got a call to make, and there's a diner on Court Street where that detective still eats lunch."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I pick up the twenty and the sticky note.* "You want me to go in blind? Just ask for the file number?" I tap the note. "No other details?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena held out a hand for the sticky note, flipped it over, and wrote on the back in small blocky letters. Slid it across again.

"Three things, in this order. The complaint report — that's the original call, time-stamped, the dispatcher's log. Then any supplementary narratives flagged for public release. Then the evidence index, page only, not the property receipt. If the clerk wants a reason, you're handling an insurance matter for the family. Boring is invisible. Nobody remembers the man who asked about insurance."

She leaned back, and the chair complained under her.

"Two things you don't do. You don't request a single item that isn't on that list — the second a clerk has to go check with a supervisor, you've stopped being a customer and started being a story, and stories get repeated at shift change. And you never say the detective's name. Not to the clerk. Not under your breath in the elevator. If it comes up, it's 'the investigating officer.' Titles slide off people. Names stick."

She checked her watch, then the window, where steam from the dry cleaner's vent drifted past the blinds.

"And you're not only there for paper. Watch the counter. Does the file come up in two minutes or ten? Does the clerk step away to ask someone? Does anyone in that lobby look up when your number gets spoken? Records windows are the same everywhere — slow, fluorescent, run by somebody who's ruled that counter for twenty years. That person knows exactly which files make phones ring. Read them like a witness."

She shrugged into her coat.

"Blind's the wrong word. You've got a number, a reason, and a list. That's more armor than most people carry into anything. When you're done, don't come back here — two blocks east of the precinct there's a coffee cart on the corner of Hoyt. I'll find you by four-thirty. By then I'll know whether lunch on Court Street is still a habit, and we'll see if the paper and the habit agree with each other."

She opened the door and held it.

"Two o'clock. And don't be early. Early looks like intent."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena looked at her for a moment. Below the floorboards, the dry cleaner's press thumped like a slow heart, and the clock above the file cabinet kept its own time in the quiet.

She let the question go by the way you let a car run a red light — no point standing in the intersection.

Her thumb paused on the edge of the photo stack. Half a second. Then it went on squaring the pile.

"If the file's not there, don't push. The clerk says it's unavailable, you thank them, you write down the time, you leave. An empty drawer is an answer too. Either somebody pulled it before you, or it was never supposed to fill up in the first place. Both of those are worth more than paper."

She crossed to the window and adjusted one blind slat by a finger's width, though the street below hadn't changed.

"When you come out, look across the street. Cops smoke on the precinct steps, so anything standing on that corner with nothing to do — bad waiter posture, weight on one foot, eyes on the door — you give it half a block before you stop walking. You're insurance paperwork. Insurance paperwork doesn't look over its shoulder."

She took her notebook off the desk and put it in her coat pocket, the movement unhurried, like the room had already moved on to the next thing.

"Two o'clock at the records window. Four-thirty at the cart on Hoyt. If I'm five minutes late, order something and stay off your phone. If I'm twenty minutes late, finish your coffee and walk toward the bridge — not across it, just to it — and we'll have a different conversation somewhere else."

She held the door wider.

"And when that clerk asks who you are, it's the family name from the file and nothing more. You're not anybody's friend yet. Friends get remembered."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking in all her instructions.* "Got it. Family name, insurance, don't push." *I check my watch.* "Plenty of time to get there by two. See you at the cart."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I head for the door, then pause with my hand on the knob.* "What if... what if they ask for ID?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena stopped with her hand flat against the doorframe.

"They won't. Not for what's on your list. Viewing copies run on a case number and a reason — the form with the name-and-address box is for certified copies, and certified copies are a different animal entirely. So you don't ask for one. You ask for paper, you pay the twenty, you leave."

She started to pull the door, then stopped herself and closed the loophole anyway.

"If they do ask — and some counters ask just to watch what your hands do — you give them your own. Real name, real license, no fumbling in pockets. There's nothing on that ID that hurts you. You're a person handling insurance for a family, and your ID says exactly that: somebody with a name. The only name that causes damage at that window is mine. Yours isn't mine. That's the whole trick."

She tapped the frame once, twice.

"And never invent a person at a government counter. The paper's public. The lie makes it private — for you, in a room with cameras and a clerk who tells that story at every dinner party for a year. Boring survives. Clever doesn't."

Below them the press thumped and went quiet, and she glanced at the clock above the file cabinet like it owed her money.

"Two o'clock at the window. Four-thirty at the cart on Hoyt. If the clerk glances at anyone who isn't you before handing the file over, you take your copies, thank them, and walk out slow — a man with nowhere in the world to be."

She held the door wide.

"Go. The boring man is invisible, and today invisible is the entire job."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I watch her face carefully for a reaction, trying to read anything in her expression.* "Just curious."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I wait for a beat, letting her words hang in the air.* "You okay, Lena? You look like you've seen a ghost."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
For three seconds Lena didn't move. The press below the floorboards stayed silent, the clock above the file cabinet ticked into that silence, and her face did nothing at all — which, in that room, was its own kind of event.

Then she blinked, crossed to the desk, and opened the case file like the last minute hadn't happened.

"You just broke the only rule I gave you about that word, and you broke it in my office, where it costs us nothing. On Court Street it costs us everything. So we're going to back up." She set her palms flat on the folder. "You said a witness. I haven't sent you to a single witness. I sent you to a window and a clerk. Which means somewhere between hiring me and this conversation, you've been doing your own legwork and telling people names out loud."

She straightened the file against the desk edge, once, twice.

"Sit down for two minutes. Who is this witness — where did you find them, when did you talk to them, and did you mention my name, this office, or Mercer Street while you had the name in your mouth? Because a name that surfaces before the paper does is either a thread someone left hanging on purpose, or it's a clock neither of us knew was running. Either way, I need to know which one we're standing next to."

She picked up the coffee. This time she drank it, cold as it was, and set the cup down with a click.

"And I look like a woman who's been up since four running on counter coffee. This is the good face. You'll meet the other one at four-thirty if that cart's empty." She flicked her wrist toward the chair across the desk. "Sit. Start at the beginning. Everything this witness said, in order, word for word if you've got it — because from here on, nothing you heard before you walked up my stairs is a small detail."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I sit down slowly, feeling the weight of her words.* "Okay, okay. No need to bite my head off. I met the witness online, a forum dedicated to cold cases. They didn't know your name or this office."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
"No need," Lena echoed, without much inflection. "That was gentle. Wait until it matters."

She came off the doorframe and crossed back to the desk, but she didn't sit behind it — she perched on the corner, notebook out, pen uncapped against her thumb. Below them the press started up again, slow and mechanical.

"Cold case boards. Alright. Three kinds of people live on those: relatives who never got an answer, hobbyists who collect other people's grief, and the one who knows too much and feeds it out a sentence at a time to see who leans in. The first two are noise. The third is either our best lead or our biggest problem, and the difference is in the details." She held up the pen. "So give me these exactly."

"Who said the name first — you or them? Don't think about it, tell me. If you asked who ran the case and they answered, that's a researcher. If they handed it over unprompted, with an initial, like they were showing off — that's somebody who wanted to watch what the name did to you." A beat. "And what came with it? Words only, or a document, a date, a scan? A person with paper gives you paper. A person with nothing gives you a name."

She flipped to a clean page. She didn't write the name on it. The pen stayed still.

"Next: you don't reply to that account. Not tonight, not 'thanks,' not anything. You screenshot the entire thread — every post, timestamps — before it can disappear, and you pull the account's history too. How old is the profile? What other cases does it touch? An account three weeks old that's only ever posted about your case isn't a witness. It's a lure with a login."

The clock above the file cabinet ticked through a silence long enough to be a question.

"And did they ask about you? Where you were in the case, why you cared, whether you were local? Because that's not curiosity, that's sizing. And did you post the case number anywhere on that board — not the name, the number? Boards get scraped. If that number is sitting in a thread, then whoever touches that file at two o'clock won't be the first person today who came asking."

She stood, walked to the window, and adjusted a blind that didn't need adjusting.

"Last thing. The name you said in my office stays in it. You don't write it down, you don't type it, you don't feed it to a search bar at two in the morning and think nobody's watching. Search bars keep receipts. From here on it's 'the investigating officer' everywhere except inside your own head."

She took out her phone, scrolled to a contact without opening it, and put the phone away.

"Window at two, cart at four-thirty — that doesn't move. But if your handle answers my questions the right way, it changes what I do with my lunch hour. If it answers them the wrong way, it changes where you stand at two o'clock." She clicked the pen closed. "So talk. Everything they said, in order."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay, okay." *I take a breath, trying to recall the exact details.* "They posted about the case a few times, just hinting at things. I asked if they knew who the lead detective was, and they gave the name. M. Torres. No document or anything, just the name." *I think for a moment.* "They didn't ask about me, just about the case itself. And no, I didn't post the case number."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The profile's pretty old, been active for years on a bunch of different cold cases. So, not a lure then?"

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Not necessarily. An old profile is just a profile that's been around. It doesn't mean it's not being used to fish now." She tapped her pen on her notebook. "What else did they say? Anything about Torres specifically?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael pushed her glasses fully onto her nose and gave the recorder a quick glance. “Rosa Delgado’s was the vision behind the adaptation — she built the commune, she made that world collide with Medea. The staging was mine, the choices in this room were mine, but the bones belonged to Rosa, and I wasn’t interested in blurring the authorship just because the work had changed hands.”

Her attention flicked toward the stage, where the amber cue was still waiting to be corrected. “You could have five minutes now, before rehearsal — ask about the work, the structure, the arguments we’re having over Act Three. Elena can keep the room moving while we talk.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod, appreciating her directness.* "Absolutely. So, the challenges of adapting a classic like *Medea*... how do you keep the core intact while bringing in new elements like this commune setting?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael’s voice steadied at Rosa’s name—not softer, exactly, but more carefully placed. “You don’t preserve *Medea* by keeping every piece of its furniture. You preserve the pressure. A woman is betrayed by the person who promised her a place in the world, and then everyone around her decides what she’s allowed to feel, what she’s allowed to do, how much of her anger they can tolerate before they call it monstrous.”

She slid her glasses down, considered the recorder, then put them back on. “The commune gave us a different vocabulary for that pressure—collective ideals, shared labor, the promise that nobody owns anybody. Which is lovely until someone wants to leave, or someone is cast out, or the community discovers that its principles have exceptions. Then the old questions are right there, wearing new clothes.”

Her gaze shifted toward the unfinished set. “The danger is making the setting decorative—putting a caftan on a tragedy and calling it an adaptation. The commune has to change the mechanics of the story, not just the look of it. It changes who witnesses the betrayal, who claims authority over the children, who gets to call Medea dangerous. The core stays intact because the conflict still hurts in the same place.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael glanced toward the hallway as the argument carried into the rehearsal room. She took off her glasses, folded them against her palm, and lowered her voice—not quite a warning, but close.

“They clash because they’re both exacting, and they’re approaching the same problem from opposite ends. Chen is asking what the blocking lets an actor do inside the scene; Elena is asking what that choice does to the entire evening. Neither question is wrong. Sometimes they just arrive at the answer with the subtlety of two people trying to steer the same truck.”

She gave Jordan a brief, level look. “I wouldn’t make a personal feud out of a professional disagreement. Elena is the most competent person I know, and Chen is a formidable actor. They both care about the work, and neither has much patience for an answer that feels imprecise.”

Then Yael turned toward the hallway. “Elena, Chen—keep the disagreement on the blocking, please. We’ve got the scene to solve, not each other.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I jot down a quick note about their dynamic.* "So, they're both passionate, just... differently. Does that make your job harder, mediating between those two strong personalities?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael slid her glasses off again, watching the hallway as the argument dropped in volume but not conviction. “Harder is the wrong word — more demanding, certainly. If I just tell them to stop disagreeing, I lose the information inside the disagreement. Chen is telling me where the scene stops breathing for the actor; Elena is telling me where that choice breaks the evening around it. My job is to find the version that serves both, or to make the call when it can’t.”

She looked back at Jordan, expression brisk but not unkind. “And yes, I mediate. That’s part of directing — you keep the room from mistaking friction for failure. Elena is the most competent person I know; she doesn’t push a point without having done the math. Chen has instincts worth listening to, even when he presents them as if the building itself requested his opinion.”

A faint smile crossed her face. “The trick is getting them to argue about the scene instead of winning the argument. We’re not at the curtain call yet.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael turned toward Anya, her expression warming without losing its focus. She slipped her glasses off and held them by one temple.

“I understand the practical concern, Anya — genuinely. But cutting Act Three isn’t a trim; it changes the argument the play has spent two hours making. That’s where the commune’s ideals finally meet the consequences of what it has chosen to tolerate, and if we remove it, we leave the audience with a conflict we’ve deliberately refused to finish.”

She glanced briefly at David, then returned her attention to Anya. “Let’s look at the actual costs before we decide what the work can afford. We can examine transitions, technical demands, even where we simplify the staging — I’m open to solving the budget problem. I’m not open to solving it by removing the act that makes this version of *Medea* necessary.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I make a note: Anya Park, budget concerns.* "So, you're saying Act Three is essential to your vision of *Medea*?" I ask, my recorder still running.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael turned back to Jordan, her glasses still held loosely in one hand. “Yes — essential to this version, absolutely. Act Three is where the play stops asking whether the commune’s ideals are beautiful and asks who pays when those ideals fail. Without it, we’ve built the question and then walked out before the answer becomes uncomfortable.”

She glanced to Anya, still warm. “That doesn’t make the budget concern unreal. It means we have to find another place to be practical — in the transitions, the staging, the technical demands. We can make the production leaner. We can’t make the argument smaller and pretend it’s the same play.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael’s voice steadied when she said Rosa’s name. She put her glasses on, though she wasn’t reading anything.

“Rosa was exacting — not precious, exacting. She could tell when a scene was lying to protect the person who wrote it, and she had no interest in letting the lie stay just because it sounded beautiful. She was funny, too, though never on cue for anyone’s convenience. She’d wait until you’d spent twenty minutes defending a bad idea and then ask one question that made the whole defense collapse.”

Her gaze settled briefly on the unfinished commune set. “She understood that ideals are most revealing when they’re under pressure. That’s why this adaptation isn’t interested in treating the commune as a backdrop or a punchline. Rosa wanted to know what people did when the language they believed in couldn’t protect them from what they’d done.”

Yael adjusted her glasses. “She was a very good playwright. More importantly, she was very good at making you do the work instead of congratulating yourself for having an opinion.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I scribble down a few key phrases: "exacting, not precious," "made you do the work."* "So, she challenged people. Did she challenge you, specifically?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael’s expression stayed composed, but her voice settled into that careful steadiness again. “Constantly. She challenged me most when I thought I’d solved something. Early on, I staged the commune as warm, almost sheltering—because I wanted the audience to understand why Medea had believed in it. Rosa asked me whether I was showing the community, or selling it.”

She turned her glasses once between her fingers. “That was the distinction. She wasn’t asking me to make the commune cruel from the first scene; she was asking me not to make its kindness a promise the play couldn’t keep. So we kept the warmth, but we let the rules show through it—the little negotiations, the exclusions, who got to speak for whom. She made me look again at what I’d put onstage and ask what it was asking the audience to forgive.”

Yael set the glasses back on her nose. “She was very good at that. You left the conversation with more work to do—and a better idea of what the work was.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Sounds like she taught you a lot. Is that why you're so protective of her script and the third act?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael’s voice settled into its careful register at Rosa’s name. She pushed her glasses up, though they had not slipped.

“I’m protective of the third act because it completes the argument — not because I think a script should be preserved under glass. Rosa expected the work to be questioned. She expected us to make choices, to cut what was false, to change what wasn’t serving the play. But Act Three is serving it. It’s where the consequences stop being theoretical, where the commune has to answer for the principles it used to describe itself.”

She glanced toward the stage. “So yes, she taught me to look harder. And when I look at this act, I don’t see something I’m keeping out of loyalty. I see the part we can’t remove without pretending the play says something easier than it does.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking a moment to process her words.* "So, it's less about loyalty and more about integrity to the play's message."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael gave a small nod. “Integrity to the play’s argument, yes — though I wouldn’t pretend loyalty has nothing to do with it. Rosa’s work deserves my loyalty; it doesn’t get immunity from scrutiny. Those are different things.”

She put her glasses on, then looked toward the unfinished set. “The question is whether a cut makes the play more truthful or merely more comfortable. Act Three is uncomfortable by design. If we remove it because the budget is tight, we’d better be certain we haven’t also removed the consequence.”

Her gaze returned to Jordan. “That’s the distinction I’m trying to protect — not every line, not every choice, but the truth the whole structure is there to reach.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I stop the recorder and make a quick note, then look up at Yael.* "So, when David and Anya suggest cuts, it's not just about money for you, it's about the play's soul."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael’s mouth tightened at “the play’s soul,” though not in disagreement so much as caution. She glanced toward Anya, keeping her expression open.

“Money is part of it, of course — budgets are real, and Anya is right to ask what we can afford. But ‘soul’ makes it sound mystical, and this is more specific than that. Act Three is where the choices made earlier acquire consequences. Cut it, and the play doesn’t become a leaner version of the same argument; it becomes a different argument.”

She put her glasses on, then took them off again, turning them once in her hand. “I’m willing to be practical about how we stage it. I’m not willing to call the ending expendable just because it’s expensive.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod, understanding the distinction she's making.* "It's about the dramatic arc, then, not just an abstract idea of the play's essence."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael glanced at the recorder the way she might glance at a new actor's headshot: assessing, not unfriendly. She let her glasses drop to the end of their chain.

"A few minutes, yes, I can give you a few minutes, rehearsal's at ten and Chen is never early so we have a cushion." She turned back to Elena without breaking stride. "Amber on the pickup, not the raise. Walk it with the board op before we run the scene, and if it still reads wrong I'll trust your instinct over mine, which is what I usually end up doing anyway."

Elena was already making a note. Yael watched her go with the particular expression of someone who knew exactly how rare that kind of competence was, then gestured Jordan toward a pair of folding chairs near the edge of the taped-out stage. She didn't sit. She rarely did in the first ten minutes of any conversation.

"Whose vision," she repeated. Something in her shifted, and the speed went out of her voice. She didn't go quiet or soft, but she became precise, each word set down deliberately. "The adaptation was written by Rosa Delgado. She was a playwright, a very good one, better than the industry ever figured out, and this was her last full-length work. She passed away a year and a half ago. The commune setting, the language, the structure, that's all Rosa. That's the vision. My job is to serve it."

She paused for exactly one breath, no longer.

"Rosa understood something about Medea that most productions miss. Everyone plays it as a story about a woman who snaps, and it isn't. It's a story about a community that makes a promise to someone and then breaks it, and then acts shocked at the consequences. Put that in a 1970s commune, a place built entirely on the idea of shared promises, of 'we're different, we're better than the world outside,' and it stops being ancient Greek tragedy and becomes something you recognize. Something you might have been part of." She put her glasses back on, then took them off again. "That's where the discomfort comes from, and the discomfort is the point."

The pace came back into her voice as she moved into the practical. "Now, what *I* bring is the staging, the casting, the rhythm, the thousand small decisions that turn a script into three hours of people breathing in the same room. Where the knife is when the light changes. That's mine. But the bones are hers, and I don't break bones."

She finally sat on the edge of the chair, forearms on her knees, and looked at Jordan directly.

"You're going to hear things this week about the third act. People have opinions, which is healthy, it's a theater, if people didn't have opinions I'd be worried. So let me save you some digging and give you the quote now: the third act stays as written. That's not stubbornness, it's the whole reason we're doing the play." A small, dry smile. "You can print that. Everyone who needs to hear it already has."

She glanced toward the back, where a drill had started up in the set shop, then back at Jordan.

"What else? You've got about six minutes before this becomes a very different kind of conversation."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod, processing everything she's said, scribbling a few notes on my pad.* "That's a powerful mission statement, Director Mendez. So, this isn't just a play, it's a testament to Rosa's work." *I look up from my notes.* "You mentioned the third act. What makes it so contentious?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's mouth tightened slightly at *testament*. It wasn't displeasure exactly. It looked more like an editor's reflex.

"I'd be careful with that word in print," she said. "Not because it's wrong, but because it lets people off the hook.
