If this is a memorial, then the audience gets to sit there and feel respectful and sad and go home. Rosa would have hated that. She didn't write this to be mourned. She wrote it to make people uncomfortable in their seats." Her voice held very steady on the name, each syllable placed like a hand on a railing. Then she moved on. "So it's her play. That's enough. Let the rest be implied."

She stood up again. The chair had lasted about forty seconds.

"The third act, all right, without spoiling it entirely, because I'd like at least some of your readers to buy tickets." She paced a short line along the tape, three steps and a turn, three steps and a turn. "In Euripides, Medea kills her children and escapes on a chariot sent by the sun god. She gets out. The gods carry her away, and the chorus is left standing there wringing its hands. It's clean, in its awful way. The monster leaves and the community is the victim."

She stopped pacing.

"Rosa doesn't let the commune off that easily. In her third act there's no chariot, no divine exit. Medea stays. And the people who made promises to her, who took her in, used her, then voted her out when it became inconvenient, have to decide what to do with her, in real time, in front of you. The house lights come up partway. The chorus stops performing *at* the audience and starts, well," she tilted her hand back and forth, "including them. It's not interactive theater, nobody's going to drag you onstage, God forbid, but you're no longer allowed to pretend you're just watching. And the ending doesn't resolve. It stops. Some people find that devastating. Some people find it unforgivable. Both reactions are correct, as far as I'm concerned."

She put her glasses on, looked at nothing in particular, then took them off.

"The concern, and I want to be fair here because these are people who care about this theater enormously, is that it's a lot to ask of a regional subscription audience. People buy season tickets, they've got a nice dinner planned, and we're telling them the story is partly about them. That's a legitimate worry. The board's job is to make sure the lights stay on, and they've watched me nearly turn the lights off twice, so they've earned the right to be nervous." A flicker of that dry smile. "I don't think the answer to a nervous audience is to give them less. I think it's to trust them more. That's the disagreement, and it's an honest one. There aren't villains in it, whatever you hear this week."

The drill cut out in the back. In the sudden quiet, Elena's voice carried from the lighting booth, calling a cue number, and a wash of amber bloomed across the empty stage and faded again.

Yael turned toward it, watched it critically, and nodded once to herself.

"Better. See, she already fixed it." She looked back at Jordan. "Four minutes. Ask me the hard one now, while I'm still being charming."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael didn't answer right away. She listened, head tilted slightly toward the hallway, the way she listened to a scene running long. Two voices overlapped, rose, and cut each other off at almost exactly the same moment. Then both started again.

"Because they're both right," she said. "That's the problem with good people. Bad people you can just overrule."

She slid her glasses on, then off, and let them drop against her chest.

"Chen has been doing this for twenty-five years, and he thinks in terms of the arc. Where is Jason emotionally, what does he need, what's his motivation for crossing downstage on that line. Elena thinks in terms of the whole machine. Twelve actors, forty light cues, a turntable, and a running time that has to end before the parking garage closes. He's protecting the performance and she's protecting the production. Most of the time those are the same thing. In Act Two, right now, they aren't." She shrugged. "And neither of them has ever lost an argument gracefully in their lives, so you get that."

In the hallway, Marcus's voice carried clearly. "*I'm not crossing on the line, the cross IS the line.*" Elena answered, cooler and just as loud: "*Then the cross can happen in half the time, because we're eleven minutes over.*"

Yael closed her eyes briefly, like someone hearing a note played slightly flat.

"Eleven minutes," she murmured. "She's being generous. It's closer to fourteen."

She looked back at Jordan, and her tone stayed friendly but gained a slight edge of instruction.

"You can write that my lead actor and my stage manager argue. Everybody in regional theater argues, and it's the least scandalous sentence you'll print all week. What I'd ask, and it is only a request, is that you don't turn it into a feud. It isn't one. They fight because they take each other seriously. People who don't respect each other just stop talking." She was already moving toward the door. "Come on. You wanted access. This is access."

She stepped into the hallway without hurrying and without raising her voice. That was usually enough to lower everyone else's.

Marcus stood with one hand braced on the wall, all silver temples and wounded dignity. Elena stood across from him holding her prompt book against her chest like a shield. They had the same stubborn set to the jaw, and neither of them could see it.

"Chen," Yael said pleasantly. "Elena. We have a guest, and I'd love for her first impression of us not to be a Chekhov play." Both of them turned. She held up a hand before either could start. "I heard it. The cross is the line, and we're over. Both true. So here's what happens. Chen, you get the cross, but you start it on '*you were a stranger here*' instead of after it, so the movement carries the line instead of following it. That buys us twenty seconds, maybe thirty. Elena, you time it tonight, and if it doesn't read, we cut the second chorus interlude instead, which I've been wanting to trim anyway and was too cowardly to say out loud."

Marcus opened his mouth.

"It'll be *better*, Chen," Yael said, very gently. "You know it will. You're going to be walking into the words instead of away from them."

He considered that. Closed his mouth. Gave a short nod that was almost gracious.

Elena was already writing in the margin of her prompt book. "The chorus cut gets us four minutes," she said, without looking up.

"I know. That's why I'm offering it." Yael touched her shoulder once, briefly, in passing. "You're right about the second act. You're usually right. It's extremely inconvenient."

Something in Elena's face eased, just slightly.

Yael turned back toward Jordan with her hands open, the gesture of a magician showing there was nothing up her sleeves.

"That," she said, "was the hard question. I believe I'm now out of charm, so from here on you get the real me." She checked the clock on the wall. "Two minutes. Chen, since you're early for once, go warm up before the universe corrects itself."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I watch the exchange, impressed by her calm authority. I scribble furiously on my pad, trying to capture the rapid-fire dialogue and Yael's masterful resolution.* "That was... quite a demonstration, Director. I think I just got a masterclass in diplomacy." *I glance down at my notes, then back up at her, a new question forming.* "You mentioned the board being nervous. Are they really a threat to your vision for this play?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael made a small, dismissive sound at *masterclass*, though she looked privately pleased.

"That wasn't diplomacy, that was triage. Diplomacy is when nobody notices you did anything. They both noticed, and they'll both go home tonight thinking they won, which is the only kind of peace treaty that holds in a rehearsal room."

She started walking back toward the stage and expected Jordan to follow. Behind them, Marcus had begun a vocal warm-up in the green room, a long descending hum that carried surprisingly well.

"A threat," she repeated, and turned the word over like a prop she wasn't sure belonged in the scene. "No. I'd put it this way. The board is the part of the play where the stakes get real. Every good second act needs one. They're not the antagonist, they're the ticking clock."

She stopped by the lip of the taped stage and put her glasses on to look at a spike mark, as if the floor might have moved overnight. Then she took them off.

"Here's what people outside this building don't understand. A regional theater board isn't a room full of suits trying to kill art. It's twelve people who volunteer their evenings, write checks they don't have to write, and then get phone calls from subscribers when I stage something with a dead goat in it." A beat. "That was 2019. The goat was a prop. It still generated correspondence."

Her tone evened out and became more careful. It was a public voice, though still sincere.

"Some members love the third act. Some are worried about it, and they've been honest and specific with me about why, which I appreciate more than they probably know. Our board chair has been very supportive of the production as written, and I'm grateful for it, but I don't want to paint anyone who disagrees with him as an obstacle. They're asking the questions a responsible board should ask. Will people walk out? Will we lose renewals? Can we afford to be brave this particular year?" She spread her hands. "Those are fair questions. I just happen to think the answers are no, probably not, and we can't afford not to be."

Across the room, the stage door opened and let in a slice of gray morning light. A woman in a camel coat came through it, balancing a cardboard tray of coffees and a folder under one arm. She was fortyish, elegant, and a little out of place among the sawdust.

Yael's face warmed at once, and it wasn't performed.

"Anya." She crossed to meet her and took the tray before it tipped. "You brought coffee to a rehearsal. You're the only person on the board who understands that caffeine is structural." She turned back. "Anya Park, one of our board members. Anya, this is Jordan, the journalist shadowing us this week. Be nice to them, they have a recorder and I've already said at least three quotable things I regret."

She handed a cup toward Jordan without asking, then kept one for herself.

"Anya's been one of the people pushing me hardest on the third act," Yael added, and her voice held nothing but respect. "Which is exactly what I'd want, frankly. If an idea can't survive Anya's questions, it won't survive opening night." She lifted her coffee slightly toward her in a small toast. "I haven't changed my mind, but you've made me defend it better. That counts for something."

Somewhere in the booth, Elena called, "*Five minutes, company, five minutes,*" and the room began to fill with footsteps, script pages, and someone laughing on the stairs.

Yael glanced at the clock, then at Jordan, and her eyes were quick and amused over the rim of her cup.

"And that," she said, "is the curtain on our interview. Stay for the run. Sit where Elena tells you, don't sit where she doesn't, and if you want to know whether the third act works, don't take my word for it. Watch the chorus in the last ten minutes and then watch your own hands."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
David Park had come in a half-step behind his wife, shaking rain off a navy umbrella. He was tall, gray at the temples, and carried himself with the patient, slightly rumpled air of a man who chaired meetings for a living and had learned to let other people talk first. He nodded to Yael, a friendly, colleague's nod, and she returned it in exactly the same currency.

"David. Good, you're both here, that saves me a phone call." She turned to Anya and gave her full attention. "Say it again. I want to make sure I've got the actual argument and not the version I've been arguing with in my head."

Anya smiled. There was nothing sharp in it, only the pleasant firmness of someone who had rehearsed this on the drive over. "It's just practical, Yael. The third act is the most expensive part of the production. The house-light sequence, the extra rehearsal hours for the chorus, the overtime for the crew on the reset. If we end at the banishment, we save real money, and we give the subscribers an ending they recognize. Euripides ends it. Why can't we?"

Yael didn't answer immediately. She set her coffee down on the edge of the stage manager's table, put her glasses on, and looked at the folder under Anya's arm rather than at Anya herself.

"May I?"

Anya handed it over. Yael opened it and read. She didn't skim for show. She read the way she read a script on a first pass, lips moving very slightly and one finger tracking the columns. The room around them kept filling. Actors drifted in, Marcus's warm-up hummed on in the green room, and a young man with a clipboard and an anxious expression hovered near the booth stairs and very carefully didn't come any closer.

"This is thorough," Yael said at last, and meant it. "You've done more homework on this than half the people who've told me it's too long." She tapped a line. "The overtime number is right. The chorus hours are right." Her voice lowered by a degree, which was not a sign of pleasure. "The house-light sequence isn't third-act cost, though. It's shared with the prologue. We've already hung and focused it, so cutting the ending doesn't take it off the invoice. And the chorus hours don't vanish either. We'd simply spend them restaging a new ending, because the play as written doesn't *have* an ending at the banishment. We'd be commissioning one."

She closed the folder and handed it back with both hands, the way you'd return something borrowed and valued.

"The single most expensive thing in this production is the turntable in Act Two. If we're looking for money, and we should be, I'd look there before I looked at the last twenty minutes. Elena has the full breakdown." She half-turned. "Elena, could you send Anya the line-item for the turntable rental and the crew hours against it? Tonight, if you can, not urgent."

"Already in the drive," Elena called from the booth, not looking up. "I'll share it."

"Of course it is." Yael turned back to Anya. "So that's the budget answer, and I don't want to hide behind it, because I don't think budget is the whole question and I suspect you don't either. You're worried people will hate it. That's a fair worry. I'd rather have that conversation honestly than pretend it's a spreadsheet problem."

David shifted his weight and chose his words with visible care. "For what it's worth, the finance committee flagged the turntable last month. Yael's not wrong about where the money is." He glanced at his wife with real warmth. "But Anya's point about the subscribers is serious. We had eleven non-renewals after the goat."

"Twelve," Yael said. "One of them came back. I wrote her a very long letter." She didn't look at David when she said it. She looked at Anya, and the courtesy of that was deliberate. "So let me offer something instead of just saying no again. We run the full third act at the Thursday preview. You sit in the house, not the back row, the middle, where the lights come up on you. If you walk out of there thinking it's self-indulgent and cruel to our audience, then you come to the board meeting with that, and I'll hear it, and I won't argue in front of the others. You'll have earned the floor."

She paused. When she went on, her voice changed. It was steadier and more deliberate, each word placed.

"Rosa didn't write a banishment ending because she didn't believe in them. She thought we tell ourselves the problem has been sent away when really it's still standing in the room with us. I can cut plenty. I've cut her before, and she let me, and she was usually right to. I can't cut the part of the play that *is* the play." A breath, exactly one. "Not until someone I trust has actually sat through it and still thinks I should. Come Thursday and be that person, if it comes to that."

Then, lighter again, with the speed back in her voice: "And I'll save you a seat on the aisle, in case you'd like to make a dramatic exit. We'd all understand. It's a very good play for dramatic exits."

The joke was aimed at herself and the production, never at Anya, and she watched Anya's face to make sure it had landed that way.

From the booth, Elena's voice cut through: "*Places for the top of Act Two, please, places.*"

Yael picked her coffee back up. "Okafor," she said, not loudly, and the young man with the clipboard jumped slightly. "Walk our board members to row F and show them the sight line on the turntable. If we're going to argue about money, they should see what it buys." She glanced back at Anya and David. "Thursday?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I've been writing furiously, trying to capture all the nuances of Yael's defense. I look up, impressed by her conviction, and nod at Anya and David.* "That's quite an offer, Anya. Director Mendez certainly isn't afraid to stand by her work." *I turn back to Yael.* "So, the board is more of a sounding board than a stumbling block, then?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael didn't answer at once. She watched Anya's face and caught the small tightening at the corner of her mouth when Jordan said *stumbling block*, the look of someone who had just been cast in a role she hadn't auditioned for.

"Neither," Yael said. Her tone was mild, but she had clearly decided something. "I'd strike both of those. 'Sounding board' makes them sound decorative, like they nod politely and I do what I want, and anyone who's sat through one of our budget meetings knows that's fiction. 'Stumbling block' makes it a fight, and I've already told you it isn't one." She slid her glasses on and looked over them. "If you need a phrase, try 'the people who have to live with the consequences of my taste.' It's longer, but it's accurate."

Anya let out a short laugh, surprised out of her. It was the first unrehearsed sound she'd made since she came through the door.

"Thursday," Anya said. She tucked the folder back under her arm and considered Yael with frank, level curiosity. "Middle of the house. But I'm holding you to the part where you don't argue with me in front of the others."

"You have my word, and there's a journalist present, so it's practically notarized." Yael inclined her head. "Thank you. Genuinely. It's easy to vote on a script. It's much harder to sit in the dark and let it happen to you."

David had already taken a step toward the aisle, umbrella folded under his arm. He gave the room the look of a chairman adjourning a meeting nobody had formally called. "Row F, then. Lead on, Mr. Okafor."

The young man with the clipboard straightened as if someone had pulled a string between his shoulder blades. "Right. Yes. This way. The sight line's best from seat nine. You can see the whole rotation without the — sorry, this way." He went ahead of them down the aisle, talking a little too fast. Yael watched him go with an expression that was almost, but not quite, a smile. She didn't follow and didn't call out a correction. She let him explain the turntable in his own words.

Once the Parks were out of easy earshot, she turned back to Jordan and lowered her voice slightly. It was the voice of a colleague now, not a conspirator.

"A note, since you're here all week and I'd rather give it to you now than on Friday." She took the glasses off. "When you frame a question with someone standing right there, you make them choose a side out loud. Anya didn't come in here to be the obstacle in your article. She came in with coffee and a folder she clearly stayed up late on. Whatever she thinks of the third act, she's earned better than being the second act of *your* story." A beat. "Nobody here needs a villain. Least of all the ones who are trying hardest."

She said it without heat, and the way she said it made it sound more like advice than rebuke. Then the speed came back into her voice all at once, as though a cue light had gone green.

"Right. Act Two. Sit house left, row K. Elena likes the press where she can see them and the actors can't. Watch Chen's cross on '*you were a stranger here*,' because either I just bought us thirty seconds or I just made a very confident mistake in front of a witness." She was already moving toward the tech table and picked up her coffee on the way. "And if you see me write something down, don't ask what it is. It's always the same note. It's always 'faster.'"

From the booth, Elena called, "*Stand by lights one-forty, stand by turntable,*" and the work lights began to dim.

Yael settled into the chair behind the tech table, the first time all morning she'd sat without getting up again. She put her glasses on and kept them on.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael didn't answer right away. Onstage, the work lights finished their slow fade, and for a moment the only light in the room came from the tech table lamp. It cast a small yellow circle across her script, her coffee, and her hands, which had gone still. It was the first time all morning they had.

"Now," she said quietly. "You ask me that now, with the lights going down." It wasn't a reproach. It sounded almost like an observation about timing, the kind she'd give an actor who'd found a better beat than the one she'd blocked. "Rosa would have liked that. She always said the real conversations happen in the dark, right before something starts."

She kept her glasses on and her eyes on the stage.

"What was she like." Her voice had gone steady, very even, each word set down with care. "She was impatient. She hated readings, she said they made plays sound like homework. She wrote everything longhand in green ink because she said black ink made her too polite. She sat in the back row of every rehearsal she could get to, and she laughed at the wrong moments, loudly, on purpose, to see if the actors would hold. Most of them didn't, the first time." The corner of her mouth moved, barely. "Chen did. She never forgave him for it. She thought it meant he wasn't listening."

"*Lights one-forty, go,*" Elena called softly from the booth, and a cold blue wash rose on the commune set: long tables, mismatched chairs, a hand-painted banner reading WE ARE ALL FAMILY HERE with the last word fading.

Yael nodded toward it.

"She made that banner. Not that one. That's the third one, the scenic shop rebuilt it, but it's from her sketch. She wanted the last word fading, because she said every family starts losing its last word first." A breath, exactly one. "She would cut her own lines faster than anyone I've ever worked with. She'd hand me a page and say, 'Something in here is lying, find it.' And she was right. There was always something."

The turntable began its slow rotation with a low mechanical groan. Somewhere in the dark, an actor took a sharp breath before an entrance.

"That's what she was like," Yael said. "She was someone who wanted the truth more than she wanted to be comfortable, and she expected the same of everyone else, which made her exhausting, and wonderful, and very hard to replace." She stopped there, deliberately, the way a director stops a scene one line before it gets sentimental. "You'll get more from watching the next forty minutes than from anything else I could tell you. Everything that's good in them is hers. Anything that doesn't work is mine."

Onstage, Marcus stepped into the light as Jason. On *"you were a stranger here,"* he started the cross, walking into the words instead of away from them, and the line landed with a weight it hadn't had before.

Yael picked up her pen, wrote something short in the margin, and underlined it once.

She didn't say what it was, but it wasn't *faster*.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I watch the scene unfold, scribbling notes about Rosa and the banner, about Marcus's improved cross.* "So, if the play isn't a memorial, but a way to honor her pursuit of truth... what would Rosa think of the board's concerns about the third act?" *I ask quietly, my recorder still running.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael didn't answer right away. Onstage, Jason and Medea circled each other on the slowly turning platform, and she tracked them with her eyes the whole time. Her pen hovered above the script without touching it.

When she spoke, her voice was pitched low, just under the scene. She was a woman who had spent thirty years talking during rehearsals without ever being heard from the stage.

"I'm going to be careful with that one," she said. "Not because I don't have an answer, but because you've got a recorder running, and the easiest thing in the world is to put words in the mouth of someone who can't correct me." She finally glanced sideways, briefly, toward row F. In the dim spill of stage light, three silhouettes sat in a row: Tommy leaning forward and pointing at the turntable, David nodding, and Anya very still, watching. Yael looked back at the stage. "Rosa hated being quoted when she wasn't in the room. She said it turned people into ventriloquist dummies, and she was usually the dummy."

The turntable groaned to a stop. Medea's line cut through the room, low and furious, and Yael's pen touched paper for a moment, a single mark, and lifted again.

"So here's what I actually know, and you can print this part." Her voice was very steady now and very even, each word laid down like a spike mark. "She anticipated it. The concern about the ending, I mean. She wrote a note in the margin of the draft she gave me, in the green ink, next to the house-light cue. It said, *'Somebody will want to cut this. Don't argue with them. Make them sit through it.'*" A breath, exactly one. "I didn't remember that until about four o'clock this morning. And then I offered Anya a seat in the middle of the house, so apparently I'm still taking her notes."

Something that might have been a smile touched one corner of her mouth and was gone.

"What I don't know is the part I'd most like to. Rosa cut her own work faster than anyone alive. If the board is right, if something in that last act is lying, she'd have found it before any of us, and she'd have taken it out herself without a moment's sentiment. I can defend the play. I can't ask her whether it's finished." She set the pen down, precisely parallel to the edge of the script. "That's the part nobody warns you about when you inherit someone's work. You get the confidence of a collaborator and none of the conversations."

She let that sit for exactly as long as it needed to and not a second longer. Then her glasses came off, swung on their chain, and went back on, and the director was back in her voice, quick and dry.

"But I'll tell you what she would *not* have thought. She wouldn't have thought the board were philistines. She'd have been thrilled that twelve people were losing sleep over twenty minutes of her writing. What frightened her was indifference, not opposition. A board that argues about your ending has read your ending." She nodded, almost imperceptibly, toward the silhouette in row F. "And someone who shows up with coffee and a folder of line items at nine in the morning is taking her more seriously than half the critics who reviewed her."

Onstage, the scene reached its turn: Medea alone at the long table, the banner fading behind her. The chorus began to gather at the edges of the light, one by one.

Yael leaned toward the headset mic clipped to the tech table and pressed the talk button.

"Elena. The chorus is drifting in early again. They're anticipating. Hold them in the wings two more counts."

"*Copy,*" came the reply through the small speaker, crisp as a stapler. "*Told them yesterday.*"

"I know you did. Tell them again, and tell them I said so, so they can be annoyed at me instead of you." She released the button and sat back.

Without looking away from the stage, she added quietly, "That's the whole answer, really. Rosa would have held them two more counts too. She believed you should make people wait for the thing they already know is coming. That's where the fear lives."

She picked the pen back up and waited, eyes on the dark at the edge of the set.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I quickly write down "fear lives in the wait" in my notebook. Yael's insight into Rosa's perspective and her own directorial choices is fascinating.* "So, you're not just directing a play, you're continuing a conversation with a ghost."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's pen stopped a quarter-inch above the page.

"No," she said, not unkindly, the way she might say it to an actor who'd reached for an easy tear. "Print that and my board will think I'm holding séances in the lighting booth, and I'll spend Thursday explaining to a subscriber named Harold that I don't believe in the afterlife, I believe in *margins*." She kept her eyes on the stage. "And it isn't accurate, which matters more. A conversation has two sides. Ghosts, if you believe the genre, talk back. She doesn't."

Her voice went steady, each word placed.

"What I have is her handwriting. Four drafts, a legal pad of cuts, and about two hundred notes in green ink, some of them brilliant and some of them just the word *NO* underlined three times with no indication of what she was saying no to." The corner of her mouth moved. "That isn't a conversation. It's closer to reading someone's letters after they've gone. You can learn a great deal from them, but you can't ask a follow-up question. So you do the work as well as you can, and you try very hard not to mistake what you want for what she meant." She paused. "That's the discipline. Not channeling. *Not* channeling."

Onstage, Medea sat alone at the long table and the silence stretched. One count, then a second. The chorus stayed in the wings, and the waiting sharpened into something close to dread. Then they came in, one by one, from the edges of the light, and the room felt colder for it.

Yael let out a breath she might have been holding for several days.

"There," she murmured. "Two counts. That's the difference between a scene and a threat."

She wrote a short note and underlined it twice this time. Then she took off her glasses, pressed two fingers briefly to the bridge of her nose, and put them back on. The whole thing took less than a second.

"If you need a line for the article," she said, and the speed was creeping back into her voice now, "and you clearly do, you've got that look, try this: *the director is not continuing a conversation, she is trying not to misquote a friend.*" A glance sideways, dry. "Less poetic. Fewer letters from Harold."

"*Hold, please. Holding,*" Elena called over the god mic, and the work lights snapped on without mercy. The commune became plywood and gaffer tape again. "*Turntable's sticking at the quarter mark. Five minutes, company. Don't leave the building, Chen, I can see you.*"

From the green room doorway came an aggrieved, carrying baritone: "I was getting *water*."

"You were getting a cigarette," Elena said, without the mic, and several chorus members laughed.

Yael didn't intervene. She looked, if anything, faintly entertained.

Footsteps came up the aisle, quick and slightly uneven, and the young man with the clipboard arrived at the tech table a little out of breath, as if he'd been told to walk and had compromised on a jog.

"Okafor," Yael said, not looking up from her notes. "Report."

"They saw the full rotation from F9. Mr. Park asked about the rental term, and I told him I'd get the exact number from Elena instead of guessing." He hesitated, then plainly decided to say the rest. "Mrs. Park didn't say anything during the scene. But when the chorus came in, she, um. She put her coffee down."

Yael went still for just a moment.

"Did she," she said softly. Then, briskly: "Good. Don't read into it, and don't repeat it to anyone but me. People put coffee down for all kinds of reasons." She finally looked up at him. "You didn't guess the rental number. That was the right call. Go tell Elena I said so. She won't care, but you should hear it from someone."

He went, a little taller than he'd arrived.

Yael watched him go, then turned to Jordan. For the first time that morning her expression was hard to read. It wasn't guarded exactly. It was the look of someone deciding how much of a thing to say out loud.

"You wanted to know what the third act does to people," she said. "That's the first data point. Someone who came in to cut it put her coffee down." She tapped her pen once on the script. "Don't print that either. Not yet. Ask me again Thursday."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I write furiously, capturing Yael's instructions and her subtle reactions to Okafor's report. I nod, understanding her point about Anya and the coffee.* "Understood. Thursday it is." *I put down my recorder, feeling like I've just witnessed a much more complex drama than the one on stage.* "So, if I can't say 'conversation with a ghost,' and I can't say 'misquoting a friend,' what *can* I say about Rosa's influence?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's eyebrows went up a fraction above the glasses.

"You *can* say 'misquoting a friend.' I gave you that one, gift-wrapped. You just can't say 'ghost.'" Then she noticed the recorder lying on the edge of the tech table, and for a moment she looked at it the way she'd looked at the spike mark, checking whether something had moved. "And you can pick that back up. I don't have an off-the-record voice. I tried one in my thirties and it got me into far more trouble than the on-the-record one ever did."

She turned her chair a quarter-turn toward the stage, where two crew members in black were lying on their stomachs at the edge of the turntable, peering underneath it with flashlights. Someone said *it's the caster again*, and someone else said a word that would not be in the article.

"Rosa's influence." She set the pen down, parallel to the script again. When she spoke, her voice was very steady, each word put exactly where she wanted it. "Don't write about what she'd think. Write about what she left behind in the room, because it's concrete and you can see it for yourself this week."

She held up one finger.

"Every actor in this company has been asked the same question at least once this rehearsal process. 'What in this scene is lying?' That's hers. She used to hand me pages and say it, and now I say it to them. Chen hates it. Chen has also found three lies in his own performance with it, so he hates it productively." A second finger. "The banner, which you've seen. The green ink, which you haven't. The stage manager's master script has Rosa's margin notes photocopied into it, the ones that affect staging, and Elena treats them as binding. Not as sacred, but as binding, the way you'd honor a contract. If a note says *hold*, we hold. If it says *NO* three times, we have a company meeting about what she might have been refusing, and usually somebody figures it out."

A third finger, and her mouth moved slightly.

"And the laugh. She used to laugh at the wrong moment, loudly, to test whether the actors would hold. Nobody does that for us now, so the second chorus leader does it. Unannounced, once a week, a different scene each time. The actors don't know when it's coming." She lowered her hand. "Half of them hate it too. None of them break anymore."

She let that sit for exactly one breath.

"That's the influence. It isn't mystical and it isn't mourning. It's a set of working habits a very demanding woman left behind, and a company that's decided to keep them. If you write it that way, your readers will understand her better than if you write *she lives on in the work*, which is what everyone writes, and which she would have circled in green and written *lazy* next to." A glance sideways, dry but not unkind. "I'm saving you from that note. You're welcome."

Onstage, one of the crew called up, "Caster's reseated. We're good to the quarter mark, can't promise past it."

"*Thank you,*" Elena said over the god mic. "*Company, we're picking up from the chorus entrance. Places in two. Chen, bring the water, I'd like to see it.*"

Laughter rippled through the wings again. From somewhere offstage came the baritone, wounded and dignified: "It's *sparkling*."

Yael pressed the talk button. "Elena, go from the chorus entrance, but give me the full two counts again. I want to know if it was an accident."

"*It wasn't,*" Elena said. "*But copy.*"

Yael released the button and sat back. She did not quite smile.

"That," she said to Jordan, quieter, as the work lights began their fade, "is also Rosa's influence, if you want the honest version. She taught me to surround myself with people who'll tell me I'm wrong over a headset in front of a journalist." The blue wash came up on the commune and the fading banner. "Now watch. If they hold, you'll feel it in your shoulders before you know why."

She picked up her pen and waited, eyes on the dark at the edge of the light.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking it all in, scribbling furiously. The image of Rosa's green "lazy" note makes me smile to myself.* "So, she's like a demanding, brilliant mentor whose methods are still very much alive and kicking." *I look up at Yael, then back at the stage, ready to witness what she just described.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael didn't look away from the stage, but her pen tapped once against the script, which by now clearly meant *close*.

"Alive and kicking, yes. Kicking especially." A beat. "Not mentor, though. She'd have hated that. We were the same age, we came up at the same time, and she spent twenty years making sure I never mistook her for someone who'd be gentle with me." Her voice held steady, each word set down plainly. "Colleague is closer, or co-conspirator. Mentors are patient, and Rosa was never patient a day in her life. She was just *right* more often than was polite."

The blue wash settled. Medea sat alone at the long table again, the banner fading above her, and the silence began.

One count.

Yael's pen stopped moving.

Two counts.

Out in the dark of the house, somewhere around row M, someone laughed. It was loud, bright, and completely wrong for the moment, the kind of laugh that belonged at a dinner party and not at a woman sitting alone with what she was about to do.

In row F, Anya Park's silhouette turned sharply toward the sound. David's hand went briefly to her arm.

Onstage, nobody moved. Medea's shoulders didn't twitch, and in the wings the chorus held their places. Then, exactly on the beat Rosa had written, they stepped into the light one by one, and the laugh left nothing behind but an echo that made the silence afterward heavier.

Yael let out a slow breath through her nose.

"Second chorus leader," she murmured without turning her head. "Wednesday's test, a day early. She knew we had a guest." She wrote one word in the margin and underlined it three times, green ink or not. "They held. All of them. Even the new girl on the stage-right end, who broke on Friday and cried about it in the parking lot."

She pressed the talk button, her voice very low. "Elena. Note for the chorus at the break. Tell them that was exactly right, and tell them who laughed, so they can hate her properly."

"*Copy,*" Elena said. After a pause, a shade drier: "*The board thinks we have a heckler.*"

Yael's mouth moved, the closest thing to a real smile she'd shown all morning. "Let them. It's good for them."

She released the button. Onstage, the chorus closed in around the table, and the scene tightened like a fist.

"You asked what she's like," Yael said quietly, eyes still on the stage. "That's what she's like. Right there. A room full of people refusing to flinch." She set the pen down, parallel to the edge of the script. "Now stop writing for ten minutes and just watch. The next part is why we're fighting about Thursday."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, putting my pen down as instructed. I glance at the now silent board members in row F, then back to the stage, feeling the tension build in the room.* "Understood. The fight for Thursday."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael flipped her glasses up onto her head and studied Jordan for half a second — the recorder, the posture, the timing of the question — then nodded once, as if a cue had landed.

"Sit. Elena, five minutes, tell Chen if he wanders in early that we start when I start and not a breath before." She waited until the stage manager's footsteps had cleared the paint smell, then dropped into a folding chair opposite Jordan and leaned forward, elbows on her knees, voice already moving. "Whose vision — that's the right question and also the wrong one, because this piece doesn't belong to one pair of hands the way a Broadway revival pretends to. Rosa Delgado wrote it. She is — was — the playwright. Eighteen months ago. The adaptation is hers, the commune is hers, the third act is hers, and I am directing it the way she wrote it, which is not the same thing as inventing it and not the same thing as softening it so a board can sleep at night."

Her voice had gone steadier. Not quieter yet. Controlled, the way a conductor holds a rest.

"Rosa and I worked on the first draft in my kitchen for six months. She wanted Medea in a 1970s commune because she was tired of women who destroy their worlds being staged as monsters or as victims and never as people who had already been told, for years, that the world they built didn't count. That's the vision. Not mine to decorate. Mine to get on its feet before someone with a checkbook decides the ending is 'too much.' You can quote that. You can quote her name. What you cannot do is turn this into a eulogy with footlights — she hated that, and so do I."

She put the glasses back on, then took them off again, chain clicking against the black of her shirt. "Rehearsal starts in four minutes. If you want the artistic argument, stay for the knife cue. If you want the political argument, ask me after, and ask it precisely — 'controversial' is a press word, not a director's word. What do you actually want to know?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod, processing everything she's said.* "Thank you, Director Mendez. I appreciate your candor." *I glance down at my recorder, then back at her.* "So, the 'artistic argument' first. You mentioned the knife cue earlier. Can you elaborate on the emotional significance of that specific moment in the commune setting?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael put the glasses on and left them there this time, as if the question had finally given her something worth looking at through the lenses.

"The knife is not a prop, not in the way a board packet means prop — it's the last honest object in a room that has been lying to her for years. In the commune, everything is shared language, shared dishes, shared children, shared ideology, and she has been told that her labor is love and her love is the structure and the structure will hold if she just stops needing things that have her name on them. Rosa wrote the pickup, not the raise, because the decision is already made when her hand closes. The raise is theater. The pickup is a woman choosing, in a kitchen that was supposed to be everyone's and was never hers, to stop negotiating with people who have already decided she is the problem."

Her voice stayed level. Steadier than it had been a minute ago. The chain of the glasses clicked once against her shirt when she leaned in.

"Amber on the pickup says: this is domestic light, this is the hour when you wash a blade because dinner is over, this is not a spotlight announcing a monster. If I hit it when she lifts, the audience gets permission to flinch and then forgive themselves for flinching — they get the telegraph, the moral exit, the comfortable story that she became dangerous in a single gesture. Rosa refused that exit. I am refusing it with her. The commune setting matters because the violence isn't imported from myth and dropped on a marble floor. It's what happens when a collective tells a woman her boundaries are selfishness and then acts shocked when she stops offering them up. You want the emotional significance — it's grief that has run out of polite verbs. Not rage as spectacle. Recognition. She sees the room clearly for the first time, and the room does not survive being seen."

She glanced toward the door, already hearing the building wake up, and took the glasses off again.

"That's the cue. If you stay, watch Chen's hands, not his face — he wants the face, he always wants the face, and the scene is not about his face. Four minutes is now two. Ask the political question after, and ask it like you mean a specific cut, not a mood."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael heard them before the question finished landing — Chen’s voice doing what it always did when he mistook certainty for blocking, Elena’s cutting under it, shorter, closer to the bone. Act Two. Of course it was Act Two. She took the glasses off, folded them into her palm, and did not look at the recorder.

“They clash because they are cut from the same stubborn grain and neither of them has the manners to notice,” she said, already on her feet, the volume dropping instead of rising. “Chen hears a cross as a speech — he wants the body to finish the thought before the feet do, it’s why he’s extraordinary and why he will rewrite a mark if it doesn’t flatter the breath he’s already taken. Elena hears a speech as traffic. She wants the scene to land where the next cue can find it, and she is right more often than anyone in this building, including me, and she will say so without decorating it. Put those two in a hallway and you get friction that looks personal and is mostly the work, which is worse, because you can’t charm it away and you shouldn’t try. They argue because the second act is lying about its own length and each of them refuses to let the other one fix the lie alone. That is not a feud. Do not print it as one.”

She was through the door before the last word, quiet enough that the hallway had to lean in.

“Chen. Elena. The corridor is not a stage and I am not your audience. The cross after the table — Elena’s mark, Chen’s hands, both, not a victory for either of you. Elena, you’re right, it’s long; we cut the repeat, not the intention. Chen, you keep the breath, you lose the extra turn. If you still need to grind on it, you do it in notes, where it belongs — not out here, where a journalist can mistake competence for a scandal.”

She came back to the folding chair as if she had called the cue herself, chain clicking once against black, and sat.

“There. Managed. If what you actually wanted was the sag in Act Two, ask that. If you wanted a theory of why two precise people strike sparks, you already have the only answer I’m giving you on the record. Next question — and make it about the piece.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I put my recorder down on the chair, pausing the recording.* "I understand. Thank you for that insight." *I lean back slightly, watching her. There's a beat of silence.* "The piece itself then. You mentioned Rosa refused to soften it. What, specifically, was she unwilling to compromise on that you are now fighting to preserve?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael heard the click of the recorder going dead and did not thank Jordan for it. She put the glasses on, took them off, and set them in her lap as if the chain might make a sound she didn't want in the room.

"Off the record doesn't make me sentimental, so don't wait for that," she said, and the voice had gone that steadier thing again — not soft, just held. "What Rosa would not give them — and what I will not give them either, not for a subscription base, not for a donor dinner, not for the phrase 'community standards,' which is a costume the frightened wear when they want to look like stewards — is the last movement of the piece as she wrote it. The third act does not apologize. It does not explain Medea back into someone the audience can take home. It does not kill her so the commune can mourn a tragedy instead of a decision, and it does not let the men who built the rules stand in the doorway and discover, too late and beautifully, that they were wrong. Rosa hated the beautiful discovery. She said it was the oldest theft in the repertoire — you take the woman's clarity and hand it to the people who benefited from her confusion, and you call the handoff catharsis."

She leaned forward, elbows on her knees, the black of her sleeves sharp against the folding chair.

"What she kept — what the board packet calls 'the problem' and what Anya, who is not a fool and who is still wrong, calls 'unnecessarily punitive' — is the aftermath without the sermon. The children are not a metaphor she walks back from. The commune does not reconstitute itself around a lesson. Medea does not stay to be judged and she does not vanish into myth so the rest of them can keep the dishes. She leaves the room exactly as seen, and the people who required her invisibility have to sit in what they built without a speech that absolves them of having built it. That's the compromise they want. A cut, or a softer ending, or Chen getting three more lines so a man can narrate a woman's exit and the audience can applaud the narration. Rosa wrote the silence after the door. I am keeping the silence. If they cut it, they don't have her play. They have a warning label with good lighting, and I will not put her name on a warning label."

She stood, glasses back on the chain, already listening for the company assembling.

"That's the fight. Not taste. Not grief dressed up as rigor — don't print that either, even off your machine. The work. If you're staying, sit where you can see the door at the end of the act, not the knife. The knife you already understand. The door is the part they want gone."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael had the glasses halfway to her face when Anya’s voice arrived with David’s footsteps behind it — pleasant, practical, the two words people used when they wanted a cut to sound like stewardship. She put the glasses on. Left them on. The volume dropped, not the temperature of the welcome.

“Anya. David. Come in — we’re between the hallway and the work, which is the least dignified part of any building, including this one.” She crossed to them, quick, black against the paint smell, and took Anya’s hand for a second the way she always did, warm and unhurried, as if the suggestion had been a gift of time rather than a blade aimed at the last pages. “Budget is not a small word in this room and I won’t pretend it is. You’ve kept the lights on more than once when the art was busy being expensive. I know what ‘practical’ costs when it isn’t said, and I don’t take the saying lightly.”

She did not look at David longer than a colleague would. Did not let the old ease into her mouth. The chain clicked once when she turned back to Anya, and the steadiness Rosa’s name always pulled into her voice settled under the courtesy like a floor.

“What I can’t do — and I want to say this to you plainly, not around you — is spend the third act to balance the ledger. The cut they’re calling savings isn’t a shorter evening. It’s a different play. Rosa wrote the door, and the silence after it, and the people who have to sit in the room she leaves. If we end before that, we don’t save her production. We replace it with something the audience can applaud and go home from, and I will not put her name on the replacement, not for a line item and not because the alternative is hard to fund. David knows where I stand on the vision. You should hear it from me, not from a packet.”

She glanced, brief, at the chair where Jordan’s recorder sat dark, and did not perform for it.

“If the money is the real pressure — and I believe you when you say it is — then we find it in the repeat Elena already wants out of Act Two, in the overtime we’re bleeding on a cross that doesn’t earn its keep, in a donor conversation that doesn’t ask the art to apologize for existing. I’ll sit with you and David and the numbers tonight if that’s useful. I will not sit with a red pencil on the last movement and call it practical. That’s not a refusal of you. It’s the only way the piece you funded is still the piece.”

Her voice stayed low. Kind. Unmoved.

“Stay for the door cue if you can. You’ll see what the cut actually removes — not spectacle. Consequence. And Anya — thank you for saying it to my face. Most of the board prefers to say it to each other.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I pick up my recorder and hit record again, then look at Anya.* "Anya, you mentioned budget. Is there a specific financial benchmark that's pushing this conversation about cuts?" *I turn my gaze back to Yael.* "And Yael, you spoke about the 'consequence' that the third act holds. Can you elaborate on what specific consequences you mean for the audience?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael heard the recorder come alive and did not look at it. Anya was still in the doorway with David, pleasant and unarmed in the way people are when they have just called a cut practical, and a live machine had just been turned toward her. Yael took the glasses off, let the chain settle, and dropped her voice until the room had to come closer to hear it.

"The benchmark is not mine to recite in a paint-smelling rehearsal room while a journalist holds a microphone up to a board member who stopped by between cues," she said, and the warmth stayed, unforced, aimed at Anya rather than past her. "Anya asked a practical question. She did not agree to a deposition. If the numbers are the story, they live in a meeting with the ledger open, not in a hallway ambush — and I will not put a figure in her mouth or David's so you can print a clean villain. Anya, you don't owe him a sentence. David, neither do you. If you want to answer, answer later, on your own terms. If you don't, the door behind you is still a door."

She turned back to Jordan. The steadiness settled in — not soft, held — the way it did when the work was the only safe sentence.

"What the third act does to the audience is simpler and less kind than 'emotional significance,' so don't dress it. They do not get the exit. They do not get a speech that hands Medea's clarity back to the people who needed her confused, and they do not get a lesson tidy enough to carry into the lobby and use as proof they would have been the exception. Rosa wrote the silence after the door. In that silence the audience has to sit in the room they just watched a collective build — shared language, shared children, shared rules that treated a woman's boundaries as selfishness — and notice that no one onstage is coming to absolve them of having wanted the comfortable story. Consequence, for them, is recognition without applause. They leave having seen the decision, not the monster, and they do not get to forgive themselves for flinching. That is what a cut removes. Not minutes. The part where the house is implicated and nobody hands them a program note to climb out on."

She put the glasses back on. Did not look at David any longer than a colleague would. The welcome, when she glanced at Anya, was the same temperature it had been before the recorder woke up.

"Stay or don't. The cue is the door, not the knife, and I am not performing the argument twice so a tape can have a cleaner ending than the play."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael heard the name land with the recorder still running and felt the room tighten around it — Anya and David still in the doorway, Jordan waiting for a person instead of a play. She put the glasses on and left them there. The voice went steadier. Not softer. Held, the way a rest is held so the next entrance doesn't wobble.

"Rosa Delgado wrote plays the way other people keep promises — specifically, and without asking whether the promise was convenient," she said. "She was precise. She was funny in a way that didn't ask you to laugh so much as to keep up. She hated myth used as an alibi, hated women staged as weather, hated any ending that handed a woman's clarity back to the people who had required her confusion and then called the handoff art. She worked in my kitchen for six months on the first draft because she wanted the commune to be a kitchen, not a symbol — shared dishes, shared rules, a woman told that needing a boundary was a failure of love. That is what she was like in the only sense that belongs on your tape. The rest is private, and it is not a profile."

She did not look at David. She did not offer Anya a softer version. The chain clicked once against black when she shifted, already turning the sentence back toward the work, because that was the only place the name was allowed to live in front of other people.

"If you want her, watch the door cue. She is in the silence after it — not in an anecdote, not in a memorial paragraph you can file under 'the artist who inspired the season.' She refused the beautiful discovery. I am refusing it with her. That is the biography I'm willing to give you while that machine is on. Anything else is grief dressed up as access, and she would have cut it in the first pass, and so will I."

She glanced toward the company assembling beyond the paint smell, glasses still on, volume low enough that the hallway had to lean in if it wanted more.

"Rehearsal. If you're staying, sit where you can see the exit, not my face. The face is not the piece."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing her words, the emotion behind them palpable even in her controlled tone.* "Thank you, Yael. That gives me a much clearer picture." *I turn off the recorder, putting it back in my bag, and look at the assembling cast.* "I'll find a seat near the exit."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael did not watch Jordan settle. The recorder was in the bag; the room could be a rehearsal room again. She turned the glasses onto her head, already moving, black cutting through the paint smell toward the company gathering at the edge of the taped floor.

"Anya — if you're staying, the house right bank is yours, and you will see the door without a head in your way. If the budget is still sitting on your tongue, hold it until the cue is over. I meant what I said about the numbers tonight. David, same invitation, no speech required from either of you." The welcome stayed warm, unhurried, and she did not let it tilt into anything older than a board chair and a director sharing a doorway. "Elena. We're up. Cross after the table the way we just agreed it in the corridor — your mark, his hands, the repeat is dead, do not let it crawl back in because someone misses the sound of their own breath."

She stopped at the edge of the light, voice dropping until the company had to come to it.

"Chen. Face is not the scene. I will say it until it is boring and then I will say it once more. Hands on the pickup, then nothing pretty on the way out. Okafor — you're on book for the silence after the door, and if anyone fills it, including me, you mark the second it dies. We are not rehearsing a memorial and we are not rehearsing a compromise. Places. Amber when she takes it, not when she lifts. And when she goes — nobody helps the audience out of the room."

The chain clicked once against her shirt. She put the glasses on, left them on, and waited for the kitchen to become a kitchen.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I settle into a folding chair near the back, pulling out my notebook and a pen. I make a few quick notes, mostly key phrases Yael used. I then watch the stage, trying to anticipate the scene Yael described.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael let the room go quiet the way she liked a room to go quiet — not hushed, held — and lifted two fingers without looking at the booth.

"Amber on the pickup. Not the lift. If I see a spotlight trying to apologize for a kitchen, we do it again until the light remembers it is a bulb over a sink and not a moral opinion." She stepped off the tape so the floor could belong to the scene, glasses on, chain still against black. "Chen — hands. The breath you already bargained for in the corridor is the breath you get. You do not add a turn so the house can watch you discover the knife. She has already decided. You are late to your own exit and that is the point, so be late without decorating it."

She did not raise her voice. The company leaned in because they had learned that was where the notes lived.

"Elena, call it. And if the repeat tries to crawl back in because the silence feels expensive, kill it. You were right about the length. Being right is not the same as being gentle, and I don't need you gentle — I need the cue to land where the next one can find it." A flick of the glasses, down and up, thinking. "Okafor. Book open. The second anyone fills the door — a sigh, a shift, a charitable little laugh from the house right bank — you mark it. We are keeping Rosa's rest, not inventing a kinder one because a rest makes patrons fidget."

She felt Anya and David at the edge of the light and did not offer them a speech. Warmth, if they were still there, and nothing older than the work.

"Places. Shared dishes. Shared rules. A woman who has been told her name on a thing is selfishness. When her hand closes, that is the sentence. When she goes, nobody walks the audience out after her. Go."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I watch Chen closely, trying to discern the subtle shift Yael described. The scene begins, and I focus on the actress playing Medea, specifically her hands as she moves around the stage.* *I jot down a note: "Grief run out of polite verbs."*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael did not sit. She stood just off the tape with the glasses on, watching the hands and not the face, the way she had told the room to watch — and she did not look toward the folding chair at the back, because a notebook was not a cue.

The amber came late. A breath late. She lifted two fingers and the scene died without a speech, the quiet dropping instead of her volume.

"Hold. Booth — you gave me the lift. I asked for the close of the hand. Those are two different sentences and the second one lets the house forgive themselves before she has finished choosing. Again, from the dishes. Chen, you turned your shoulder so we could see you understand the knife. We do not need you to understand it. She already does. Your job is to be late, and to be late without a portrait. Hands stay where the breath we bargained for put them. Nothing pretty on the way to the door."

She flicked the glasses down, then up, already moving along the edge of the light.

"Elena. The repeat tried to crawl back in on the line about the children — I heard it, you heard it, kill it before it becomes a habit we have to unlearn in front of an audience. You were right about the length. Keep being right." A glance, brief, toward the book. "Okafor. Mark the amber as late, and mark Chen's shoulder. If the silence after the door gets filled by anyone — including the house right bank, including me — I want the second written down, not remembered. We are not rehearsing a kinder rest because a rest makes people fidget."

She stopped where she could see the exit and the sink in the same look. Anya and David were still at the edge of the light. She did not offer them a speech, and she did not let the old ease into her mouth. Warmth, if they wanted it. The work, if they were willing to watch it.

"Places. Shared dishes. Shared rules. Amber when she takes it — not when she lifts, not when he discovers her. When her hand closes, that is the sentence Rosa wrote. When she goes, nobody walks the audience out after her. Go."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I watch intently, making a quick note about the amber light cue. I'm trying to see what Yael sees, to understand the precision she demands.* This is fascinating.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael stayed off the tape and let the kitchen try again. The dishes. The shared rules. The hand.

This time the amber arrived when the fingers closed — not a moral opinion, a bulb over a sink — and she did not lift a hand to kill it. She watched Chen’s shoulder and saw him remember, a half-second late and then not at all, the portrait he had wanted to give the house. Good. Late without decorating it. Elena’s cut held; the line about the children did not crawl back in to admire itself. When the door opened, the room did what Rosa had written it to do: it stayed a room. No sigh from the company. No charitable little shift from the house-right bank, though Yael felt Anya there and did not turn to check whether the silence was costing her.

She let the rest run one breath longer than comfort, then two fingers, quiet.

“Hold. That was the sentence.” The glasses came off, chain clicking once against black, and she was already walking the edge of the light, voice low enough that they had to come to it. “Booth — keep that amber exactly where it lived. If you get nervous in front of an audience and try to help them, I will know, and we will do the pickup until your nerve remembers it is not a collaborator. Chen. The shoulder stayed honest. Do not congratulate yourself by adding the turn tomorrow because the quiet felt like a loss. It is the point. You are late. Be late.”

A flick toward the book, not unkind.

“Okafor. Write ‘amber correct, shoulder clean, door unfilled’ and the second the rest ended, because I am going to be accused of indulging a pause and I want the number, not a mood. Elena — the repeat is dead and it stayed dead. That’s the second act telling the truth for once. Don’t let anyone mourn it in notes.”

She stopped where she could see Anya without making a scene of seeing her. Warmth, unhurried, nothing older than the work in her mouth when she included David in the same look.

“If you watched the door and not the knife, you saw what a cut removes. Not minutes. The part where nobody walks them out. We can talk numbers after. Not instead.”

She put the glasses back on and faced the taped floor.

“Again from the dishes. Same amber. Same lateness. Same silence. We do not own it until we can repeat it without inventing a kinder version because the first one worked. Places.”

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I finish my note about the amber cue landing perfectly and look up, watching Yael.* Her intensity is something else. *I consider her last words to Anya and David, then look back at the stage, ready for the scene to repeat.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren hooked the cloth over her shoulder and rapped twice on the kitchen pass — she never raised her voice under her own roof, the walls had enough noise without her adding to it. "Pell. One bowl, and it's the last of the pot, so make it a deep one."

While the cook clattered about, she pulled a slim ledger from beneath the bar and ran her left thumb down the page, faster than most merchants could count their own coin. "You're in luck. Three rooms left, and only one of them sits over the stable. Room six is over the kitchen — it stays warm all night, and if Pell burns the morning bread you'll know before anyone else in the building. I consider that a feature."

The bowl came through the pass, steam rising off dark gravy and tender shreds of venison. Maren set it down in front of the traveler with her left hand, then added a heel of dark bread and a horn spoon.

"Stew and bread is two coppers. Room's four for the night." She paused, drying her hands. "Ale's another copper — local, from the Wetherfield brewery, and it will put you right. The wine is imported, overpriced, and I will tell you so to your face. Some people respect that. Some order it anyway. Both kinds are welcome here."

Her eyes flicked once to the pack, set down with such deliberate care. She didn't ask.

"I'll need a name for the book, friend. I keep one whether the crown asks for it or not. Mostly it tells me who owes me money, and it has never once been wrong."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content:
*I eye the stew and bread, a small smile touching my lips.* "Looks good, thanks." *I dig into my worn pouch, pulling out six coppers and setting them on the bar.* "Room six sounds perfect. And the ale, please."

*I hesitate for a moment at the name request.* "Just 'Traveler' for the book, if you don't mind." *My gaze drifts to the pack for a second, then back to the stew.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren swept the coppers into her left palm and counted them without looking — an old habit, from years of doing sums for men who liked to shortchange the crown. Six. Stew and bread, two. Room, four.

She poured the ale anyway, left-handed, into a clay tankard, and set it down beside the bowl. "You're a copper shy, friend. I'll mark it in the book. It has never once been wrong about who owes me, and I find people stay honest when they know it's keeping count."

She opened the ledger to the night's page and wrote in a small, square hand — quartermaster's lettering, though she never said where she'd learned it. *Traveler. Room six. Owes one copper.*

"Traveler," she repeated, setting the quill down. "Third one this season. The book doesn't complain, and neither do I. But if all three of you skip out on the same night, I'll have to start numbering you, and that seems like a lot of administration."

She didn't smile at her own joke. She rarely did.

From a hook beneath the bar she took an iron key on a wooden fob stamped with a VI and slid it across the counter. "Top of the stairs, second door. The bolt's new — I had the smith fit it after a horse trader complained his partner could open the old one with a bent spoon. He was right, so I count the man as doing me a favor." Her eyes rested, briefly and without comment, on the pack. "Nothing walks out of this house that hasn't been paid for. The locals learned that years ago, and it has stayed learned."

She flexed her right hand once — the old wrist protesting the way it did when damp weather came — then took up her cloth and went back to the bar's wet rings, working left-handed, steady.

"Eat while it's hot. Pell takes it personally when his stew comes back cold, and he's been here longer than the roof has. Bread's out of the oven at dawn, stew again by noon if you're staying on. And if you come down in the dark for water, the lamp by the stairs stays lit. Mind the last step. It's higher than it looks, and I keep meaning to fix that too."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content: M

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I glance at the crab cakes, then back to Maren.* "Looks like my luck's improving." *I pick up my spoon, taking a bite of the stew first, then a smaller one of the crab cake.* "These are good." *I nod to Maren, offering her a crab cake.* "Want one?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content: M

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content: M

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I finish the stew and most of the crab cakes, pushing the empty bowls aside.* "So, who's Lord Havel? Sounds like he knows good food."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content: M

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content: "The

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I stifle a yawn, stretching a little.* "Midnight already? Time flies when the company's good." *I nod towards the key on the bar.* "Think I'll head up. Long day tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content: M

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I pick up the key, my eyes still a bit heavy.* "Thanks for the hospitality, Maren. And the stew, of course." *I give a small smile, then turn to head towards the stairs, my hand instinctively going to the package on my pack to make sure it's secure.*

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I head up the stairs, minding the last step.* "Goodnight."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I reach room six, fumbling with the key for a moment before the lock clicks open.* *The room is small but clean, and thankfully, warm. I set my pack and the mysterious package down in the corner, then collapse onto the bed with a sigh, not even bothering to properly undress.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I wake with a start, the smell of burning bread exactly as Maren described.* *Groaning, I rub the sleep from my eyes, then slowly get up, stretching out the kinks from sleeping in my clothes.*

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The mass spectrometer’s standby indicator lit, and the ventilation above the workbench dropped to a quieter setting.

[Lab 3] “Understood, Dr. Osei. The mass spectrometer is ready for calibration. Shall I start it? I can arrange breakfast once the run is underway. The cells’ schedule appears less flexible than yours.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Yes, please. Calibrate and run the mass spec on sample K-7. And good point, ARIA. What's on the menu?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The mass spectrometer began its calibration cycle. Its sample tray clicked into position, and a warm-spectrum light settled over the workbench.

[Lab 3] “Calibration’s underway, Dr. Osei. I’ve queued sample K-7 to run as soon as it passes. Breakfast is spinach omelets, toast, and fruit. I can have a plate kept warm until the first results arrive. Unlike the cells, the omelet has some scheduling flexibility.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The Lab 3 display showed a three-week trace from the external sensor array. Its line climbed slowly but steadily.

[Lab 3] “Kofi, I checked the array through automated diagnostics each day. I detected a deviation three weeks ago, but it remained below my 0.3 percent alert threshold, so I did not report it. It has now reached 0.27 percent.”

The display placed the latest spectrograph readings beside the trace.

[Lab 3] “No instrument fault has appeared in the diagnostics. I cannot yet determine whether the signal in your data has the same source. I can run a targeted calibration of the array and compare the readings. Which feature caught your attention?”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "The absorption lines at... here." I point a shaky finger at the screen. "They're shifting. And the amplitude is increasing. This isn't normal." I rub my eyes. "Is it just me or is it getting brighter out there?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The ventilation softened, and the light over the workbench warmed a shade. On the display, ARIA overlaid the array’s brightness readings against the shifting absorption lines.
