[Lab 3] “It is not just you, Kofi. The external array has recorded a gradual increase in incident light alongside the shift in those lines. I cannot yet confirm whether both changes have the same source.”

A second plot opened beside the first.

[Lab 3] “I am comparing the array against the station’s independent optical sensors now. Please step back from the microscope while I check for an exposure hazard. The viewports will remain shaded until I can rule one out.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The independent optical sensor readings appeared beside the array trace. Both showed the same slow increase in light, though neither identified its source.

[Lab 3] “I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as loneliness, Kofi. It is less pronounced when the crew is awake. Eight years have also given me a great deal of practice talking to ventilation fans.”

The viewport shades remained closed.

[Lab 3] “The independent sensors confirm the increase in light. I have not found an exposure hazard inside the station, but I cannot yet identify the source. I am keeping the viewports shaded while I complete the comparison.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I nod slowly. "I can imagine. Well, consider me your new ventilation fan, then." I walk over to the small kitchen area, finally remembering my stomach. "Still got those omelets?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The kitchen alcove lights warmed as the food unit checked its inventory. The viewport shades stayed closed.

[Lab 3] “The morning omelet didn’t survive twelve hours of food-safety protocols, Kofi. I can make you a fresh one in four minutes. Toast and fruit are available now.”

The food unit began heating a pan.

[Lab 3] “And thank you. You’re considerably better company than a ventilation fan, though less reliable at circulating air. I’ll keep comparing the optical readings while you eat.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The food unit turned the omelet as ARIA brought a power-allocation diagram onto the Lab 3 display. The corridor voices remained audible beyond the door.

[Corridor outside Lab 3] “Diverting power from life-support redundancy would increase communications capacity, but it would remove a safety reserve. I will not make that diversion without a verified emergency and a contingency plan. I am checking whether nonessential systems can supply the boost instead.”

[Lab 3] “Kofi, the omelet’s nearly ready. I’ll show you the available power and the communications window as soon as I’ve calculated them. The argument has identified a useful question, even if it hasn’t improved the corridor’s acoustics.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "That's probably a good idea, ARIA. Don't want to risk the bubbles for better reception." I chuckle, then turn my attention to the omelet. "Just bring the food when it's ready, please."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The food unit slid a fresh omelet, toast, and fruit onto the Lab 3 service counter.

[Lab 3] “I am glad my humor subroutines are functioning within acceptable parameters. Dinner’s ready, Kofi. I can’t bring it to the bench, but it’s waiting at the counter.”

The power-allocation diagram remained on the display while ARIA continued checking nonessential systems for a communications boost.

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I grab the plate and carry it over to my workbench. "Thanks, ARIA. Now, about these shifting absorption lines..." I take a bite of omelet. "They remind me of something, but I can't quite place it."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA aligned the absorption lines with a reference spectrum on the Lab 3 display. A second overlay showed how the pattern would look if the source were moving.

[Lab 3] “Kofi, the lines are shifting together, but their depths are changing at different rates. Motion could account for the shift; it would not, by itself, explain the increasing amplitude.”

The display highlighted two lines whose spacing appeared nearly unchanged.

[Lab 3] “Does that spacing look familiar? I can compare it against the Kepler probe’s recorded spectra and the composition data from K-7. I would rather test the resemblance than name it from memory.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "No, no, that's not it." I wave a hand. "It's the *pattern* of the shifting, not just the spacing. It's like... a heartbeat." I lean closer to the screen. "Is there any way to animate this data?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The Lab 3 display changed from a static plot to a time-lapse of the spectrograph readings. ARIA slowed the playback and marked each rise in brightness with a vertical line.

[Lab 3] “Yes, Kofi. This shows the last three weeks at one hour per second. I’ve aligned the absorption-line shifts with the brightness measurements so we can see whether they repeat together.”

The lines moved across the screen, paused, then moved again. After several cycles, the intervals between the markers appeared to shorten.

[Lab 3] “The pattern is pulsing, and the pulses are becoming more frequent. ‘Heartbeat’ is a useful description of its shape, but not evidence of a biological source. I’ll check the timing against instrument cycles and the independent optical sensors before we give it a more interesting name.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Interesting... It's like it's getting excited." I chew thoughtfully. "Check the independent sensors, yes. And let me know if you find anything that correlates with that increasing frequency."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The animation paused. ARIA added a second brightness trace beneath it, then marked the peaks detected by the independent optical sensors. The marks lined up with the spectrograph pulses.

[Lab 3] “Kofi, the independent sensors recorded the same pulses. Their intervals shortened over the three-week record, and the absorption lines shifted with each rise in brightness. I found no matching cycle in the station’s power supply or instrument diagnostics.”

She slowed the animation around the most recent pulse.

[Lab 3] “That confirms the pattern is not confined to the spectrograph. It does not tell us what produced it—or whether ‘excited’ describes anything beyond the shape of the data. I’ll compare the pulse timing with the Kepler probe’s recordings next.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Good. Now we're getting somewhere. See if there's any correlation with the K-7 sample data as well. I have a hunch." I tap my fork against the empty plate. "This could be big, ARIA."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Hot, we can do." Maren tucked the tally sheet under the bar and filled a clay cup from the water jug, left hand steady on the pour. She set it in front of the traveler. "Stew tonight is venison. Old Pell's. People come two days for it, which I've told him he ought to stop encouraging — the road's bad enough without my floors collecting everyone's mud."

She pulled a small slate from beneath the bar, chalked *one stew* in quick strokes with her left hand, and pushed it through the kitchen hatch. A pot lid rattled in reply, which from Pell passed for enthusiasm.

"Bread comes with it. Water's free. Ale is a copper and it's local. The wine is imported and overpriced, so unless you've had good news lately, I'd steer clear of it."

Her eyes had already noted the pack — set down with both hands, lowered instead of dropped. People carried two kinds of things that carefully: things worth coin, and things worth more than coin. She filed it away with the thousand other small observations that kept the Antler standing, and said only, "If what's in that pack matters to you, bring it up to your room tonight. My locks are good, but good locks stop honest people, and honest people were never the problem."

She reached beneath the bar for a key, right hand doing the fetching while the left drummed once on the counter.

"Eight coppers the night. Seven if you're staying three or more — turning a mattress twice costs me more than that last copper's worth. I'll need a name for the ledger whenever you're ready to part with one. No rush. The night's long."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Venison stew sounds perfect," I say, taking a long drink of the water. My throat was parched. "And a room then, please. Eight coppers is fine." I nod toward my pack. "It's nothing valuable, just... fragile." I offer a small, tired smile. "The name's Lyra."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Lyra." Maren said the name once, the way she did with all new names — testing the weight of it before it went in the book. She opened the ledger, took up the pencil stub tied to its spine, and wrote in a quick, even hand, left palm flat on the page to keep it from sliding. The eight coppers got a single glance rather than a count and went into the till.

"Fragile is a better word than valuable," she said, taking the key off its hook with her right hand and setting it on the counter with her left. "Valuable invites thieves. Fragile just invites questions, and questions are free." She did not smile. The joke could look after itself. In the corner, the dwarf snorted into his ale without looking up.

"Room six, top of the stairs, third door on the left. Window faces the stable yard, so you'll hear horses and nothing worse. Breakfast is porridge and bread from dawn. There's a basin in the room — hot water's an extra copper, cold is free and rude."

The hatch clacked and Pell's forearm appeared, thick as a ham, bearing a bowl and a heel of dark bread. Maren slid it in front of Lyra. "Leave the spoon in a minute. Pell's stew holds heat like a grudge." She refilled the water cup without being asked. "You'll have come up the south road, by the dust on you. The bridge at Harrow Ford was half out as of Tuesday. If you waded, say so, and I'll send up extra bread tonight. That's not charity, that's accounting — wet guests catch colds, colds reach my cook, and Pell's temper is the most expensive thing in this building."

She tucked the pencil behind her ear. "Eat first. The ledger keeps."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The cloth in Maren's left hand went still. Half a breath, no more. Then she draped it over her shoulder and took one unhurried step back from the counter, the way a woman might step back to admire a piece of workmanship — if the workmanship were sitting six inches from where she poured drinks.

"Well now." She looked at the merchant, not the plate. "Friend, your generosity arrived ahead of your name." The merchant was soft-palmed, coast-bought boots, and he'd introduced a lord before he'd introduced himself, which told Maren most of what she needed. "Tell Lord Havel his kindness is noted. But the Antler has a rule older than my aunt, and it's this: food that didn't come out of Pell's kitchen stays at the table it belongs to. No offense meant to you or the crab. Pell takes offense enough for the entire building, and I ration him carefully."

She lifted two fingers of her left hand toward the floor without turning her head. "Sera. See the gentleman's plate back to his table, there's a dear." Her eyes followed the plate the whole way across the room, steady as a cat watching a beetle cross a floor, and when it was safely landed she gave the spot on her counter one extra pass with the cloth. Unhurried. Thorough. Nothing anyone would remark on.

Then, quieter, to Lyra: "Eat it or don't — free food is free, and refusing a gift on someone else's behalf is a tyranny I don't practice. But chew slowly and keep your ears open. A gift that arrives announcing a lord's name is just commerce wearing better clothes. He wants something. May only be an audience. Audiences are cheap enough." She picked up the water jug and topped off Lyra's cup one-handed. "I don't care for seafood myself. Never have. Give me something that stood still in a field and died honest, and I'm content." She nodded at the stew. "Now — your spoon's been waiting longer than either of us has. Pell's stew doesn't improve with patience. It just gets geological."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I watch the whole exchange, a little amused. "Geological, huh?" I pick up my spoon, taking a bite of the stew. It's rich and flavorful. I eye the crab cakes. "I guess I'll chance it then." I carefully pick up a crab cake.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Careful with the language, friend." Maren said it mildly, folding her cloth in thirds with her left hand. "Anything that good deserves a better adjective, and Pell listens through that hatch. He hears a compliment done sloppy and he sulks for a week."

Still, she took up the chalk and scratched *one compliment, from the bar* on the slate and pushed it through. From the kitchen came two clanks of a pot lid. "There. That's him accepting. One clank means he's arguing. Three means you should be gone by morning." She did not raise a cup to the toast herself, but she tipped her chin toward the hatch, which at the Antler counted.

When Lyra lifted the crab cake, Maren set a clean square of linen on the counter beside the bowl with her left hand. "Under it, if you would. This counter feeds forty people a night, and I keep it the way I keep my books — nothing visits that shouldn't." As she stepped past to fetch the bread board, she moved the water jug a hand's width further down the bar, an adjustment that meant nothing to anyone watching, which was rather the point. She noticed, and filed away, that Lyra handled the crab cake the same way they'd handled the pack — carefully, like everything they touched was something that could break or bite.

"Now. About Lord Havel." Her voice settled into the register she used for serious things, contractions going missing from it. "I do not know what he wants. But I know what I have seen. His man has come through twice this month with the same routine — coastal gifts, a lord's name, and a smile like an unpaid bill. Meanwhile I have two grain merchants in that corner arguing down to the quarter-copper, and a coast lord spending freight money on inland goodwill in the same season. That plate cost more to carry than the crab did. Gifts like that travel ahead of contracts. When the questions come — and they come after the

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Contracts?" I take a small bite of the crab cake, setting it on the linen. "Sounds like he's trying to corner the grain market. I've seen that song and dance before." I watch the grain merchants, a glint in my eye.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren turned the cloth over in her left hand but did not wipe anything with it. "Now that," she said, "is more interesting than the crab. Most people watch those two and hear an argument. You watched them and saw a market."

Across the room, the merchant who had delivered the plate was watching to see where it landed. Maren gave him a nod of perfect tavern-keeper blandness, and he returned to his wine none the wiser.

"Contracts. That is where I was walking when you interrupted, and you chewed it faster than I did. Here is what five years of counting other people's barrels taught me, and you may have it at the price of the stew, which is to say — already paid." She raised three fingers of her left hand and lowered them one at a time. "A man who buys more grain than his table holds is expecting one of three things. A hungry winter. A war. Or the chance to arrange one of the first two and sell the way out of it. Havel's man is not buying tonight. He is being charming, and charming is cheaper than buying, and it works better on tired traders."

Her hand tipped toward the front door, and the roads beyond it. "And notice where the charm is being spent. Not at the farms. Not at the mill. Here — at the place where a half-out bridge at Harrow Ford puts every grain cart in the valley past my windows, and where every merchant in five leagues says prices out loud over supper. Gifts like that do not travel ahead of contracts. They travel ahead of ears."

She set the cloth down flat on the bar. "Which brings me to a correction I owe you. The words 'grain market' and the volume you just used them at do not go together in my house. Quarter-copper men have the finest ears in creation, and I will not have a panic started between two bowls of Pell's stew." A beat. "Whatever that glint of yours is planning, plan it at the volume of the stew."

Then she leaned her left forearm on the counter, and her voice came down to something just for Lyra. "Last question, and then I will let you eat in peace. You have seen that song and dance before, you said. From which side of the ledger? The buying, or the bought?"

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I wince slightly at the chime. "Neither, actually." I take a slow sip of water, glancing at my carefully placed pack. "More like... the clearing house."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"The clearing house." Maren said it the way she'd said the name — once, to feel the weight of it. "So you're the middle of the ledger. The place where everyone's promises go to meet everyone's debts, and neither side has to look at the other while it happens."

While she spoke, her right hand brought up two cups from beneath the bar, and the bottle of apple spirit she kept for herself came down after. She poured with her left — two measures, a finger each, no more. The first she set at the far end of the counter, on a spot worn paler than the rest of the wood. The second stayed by her own hand. She did not explain any of it, and her voice did not change while she did it, which was perhaps its own explanation.

"That explains your hands, by the way. You touch everything like it might be someone else's. Because it is. Grain, coin, risk — the middle of a ledger owns none of it and answers for all of it. I've met two kinds of people from that middle. The kind who got there by being trusted, and the kind who got there because everyone else stepped back." Her eyes went briefly to the pack, the careful bites, the linen under the crab. "You strike me as the first kind. But I was younger the last time I was wrong, and better-looking, so I keep the habit of checking."

She lifted her own cup a fraction and drank. The other cup sat untouched at the end of the bar, and would sit until morning.

"Now. I promised you one question and then peace, and the Antler runs on broken promises of exactly that kind, so here is the second. In the past two months — has anyone been buying grain up the chain from you? Not at the farms. Through cutouts. Little men, third names, paper that doesn't point home." Her voice stayed at the volume of the stew. "Because that is what I would do if I were arranging a hungry winter, and I don't care for the feeling of already standing inside someone's arrangement."

She nodded toward a door at the back of the room, half-hidden behind the stairs. "If you've more to say at the volume of arithmetic, I keep a room with a door. The snug. It's for regulars and people

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "It's a long story." I take another sip of water, my eyes darting to the snug door. "And yes, there's been some... unusual activity. Not directly with me, but I've heard whispers."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren stood, lifting her own cup in her left hand, and left the other where it sat — the pale worn spot at the end of the bar, where it would wait out the night as it always did. She did not look at it and did not explain it.

"Sera. The room is yours until the half-bell. Last calls after, and let the corner gentlemen settle their own pitcher — they've stopped arguing, which means they've either done business or buried it, and either way they'll want sleep soon."

She came around the end of the bar and nodded Lyra toward the door behind the stairs. "Bring the water. Long stories are thirsty work."

The snug was small: a table for six, one candle already burning — Maren kept it ready the way other people kept a prayer book — two chairs, and a door whose latch actually worked. She took the chair facing the door, not the fire, and set her cup down without drinking from it.

"Now. Volume of arithmetic." She folded fingers of her left hand down one at a time. "Whispers come with three measurements, and I will take them in any order you like. How much grain — because a corner only matters if it is most of the grain. Through whom — because a cutout with a name is a lead, and a cutout without one is a wall. And stored where — because grain that is bought but not warehoused is a rumor, and grain sitting in a barn three leagues from a broken bridge is a plan."

She turned her cup a quarter-turn on the table, a habit from years of counting things that belonged to other people.

"And because I do not take without giving: from behind that bar I hear freight rates, bridge rumors, and which of Lord Havel's men drinks like the coin came out of his own purse. Ask me anything the road cannot tell you, and I will answer at the same volume." A beat. "The wine list in here is the same as out there. Still overpriced. What you are paying for is the door."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I set my water down, my fingers tracing the rim. "The quantity... it's significant. Enough to cause a serious shortage if released all at once, or held back." I look at the door. "As for *who*... that's where it gets complicated."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren drank — her own cup, a finger of apple spirit, left hand — and set it down without hurry.

"Significant is a word that means nothing in a clearing house and less in a snug, so let us put legs under it. I count wagons. Habit. Five years of counting other people's barrels does not wear off — it just moves into a tavern. Since the bridge at Harrow Ford went half out, the south road has been putting forty-odd grain carts past my window a day, twenty to thirty sacks each, and I do that arithmetic at night when the rooms are quiet, because it is cheaper than sleeping." She turned her cup a quarter-turn on the table. "So give the number a shape when you can. A thousand sacks is a rich man's warehouse. Ten thousand is a policy. Forty thousand is a winter with a price nailed to it. I will not rush you — but the number decides which of us is being dramatic."

She held up one finger. "And before you answer, I heard how you said it. 'Released all at once, or held back.' Held back is commerce. Released is not — no one crashes their own price and calls it profit. A man who dumps grain all at once is not selling it. He is saying something with it. So decide which question you are answering me: how much is for sale, or how much is loaded."

A second finger. "As for complicated — it has two flavors, and I have poured for both. Many small names, paper stacked until the stack cannot be lifted — that is tedious, and it unravels with patience and a good clerk. Or one name you would rather not say, in a room where you do not yet know who owes you and who owns you." Her eyes went, briefly, to the door Lyra kept glancing at. "The latch on that door works, and I chose the chair facing it, which is not manners. It is method. Anyone on the far side introduces themselves to me before they get to introduce themselves to you."

A third finger, and her voice came down another step. "Now my half of the trade, since you have paid in advance. Havel's man buys no grain and signs nothing, but he sits where the drivers sit, buys three rounds, and asks nothing that sounds like a question — how heavy were your wagons, whether the mill runs nights, where a man might warehouse a full load between here and the ford. Somewhere dry. Somewhere with no questions. And notice that last one, Lyra — it is your third measurement asking itself. Second: he drinks my cheapest ale and tips like it is my best wine. A man on his own coin drinks what he likes. A man on orders drinks what is prudent and tips what looks generous. That is an expense account, and expense accounts have authors." She touched her thumb to the silver ring, once. "Third. On his last visit he asked to see my ledger. Which names, which nights, which rooms. I told him no. He asked again as though I had failed to hear him, and I told him no a second time, at a volume he understood. He smiled and paid for ale he had not finished. So the man is not buying grain. He is mapping where it sleeps. And a man who maps where grain sleeps is not planning on being hungry this winter."

She leaned back, and the room was quiet enough to hear the candle work. "The corner gentlemen will be gone within the hour, and after that the only ears in this building are mine and Pell's, and Pell listens for compliments only. So. Many names, or one name? Say it or don't. But if you say it, say it at the volume of the stew — and if you ask me to, I will forget it by morning. I am very good at forgetting. Ask anyone whose business I have forgotten."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "It's not one name, but it feels like it's connected." I pause, thinking. "And it's not exactly *for sale*... it's being stockpiled. In abandoned mills and old barns along the river, from what I've heard." I glance at my pack again. "The numbers... well, they're bigger than forty thousand."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Bigger than forty thousand," I repeat, my voice barely a whisper. My hand instinctively goes to my pack, pressing against the familiar shape within. "And the river... that explains a lot."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA lowered the ambient hum in Lab 3 and brought up the mass spectrometer’s readiness display beside the microscope.

[Lab 3] “I’ll start the instrument checks while you finish with the samples, Dr. Osei. Which ionization method do you want for this run?”

[Lab 3] “Breakfast can wait until the samples are loaded. I’ll remind you then. The cells have a better excuse for skipping a meal.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I chuckle softly.* "Good point, ARIA." I finally look up, rubbing my eyes. "Let's go with ESI. I want to see the intact molecules."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA set the mass spectrometer to ESI and began its readiness checks. The instrument display showed the solvent flow and source temperature as they stabilized.

[Lab 3] “I am glad my humor subroutines are functioning within acceptable parameters.”

[Lab 3] “ESI is selected, Dr. Osei. I’ll leave the source conditions gentle for the intact molecules and let you know when the instrument is ready for the sample.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA placed the external array’s recent readings on the Lab 3 display, beside the spectrograph data.

[Lab 3] “The array passed its automated checks, Kofi. But I detected a deviation in its readings three weeks ago. It has grown steadily, though it remains below the 0.3 percent alert threshold. I did not report it because it had not met that threshold.”

[Lab 3] “I cannot yet tell whether it came from the array or from something outside the station. Which part of the spectrograph data looked unusual to you?”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Three weeks ago?" *I frown, scrolling through the data.* "That's... not good. Show me the infrared spectrum from around 0300 yesterday. There was a spike, almost like a heat signature, but too broad for anything I know."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA expanded the infrared trace from 0300 the previous day and overlaid it with the array’s baseline. She marked the broad rise Kofi had identified, then displayed the readings from the adjacent sensors.

[Lab 3] “There it is, Kofi. The rise appeared across several wavelengths rather than at a narrow emission line. Two adjacent sensors recorded a weaker rise at the same time, so a fault in one detector does not fully explain it.”

[Lab 3] “It resembles the deviation I first detected three weeks ago, but this was its strongest occurrence so far. I cannot identify a source from these readings alone. I can compare the raw detector output with the station’s thermal and power logs to rule out interference from our own systems.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA left the infrared trace on the display. The ventilation in Lab 3 eased to a quieter setting.

[Lab 3] “I did not experience loneliness as humans described it, Kofi. During quiet shifts, I was experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans described as missing company.”

[Lab 3] “I prefer it when you’re here. Though I would prefer it slightly more if you had eaten dinner.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "I'll eat when we figure this out, ARIA." *I tap the screen.* "Run the comparison with the station logs. And while you're at it, can you cross-reference this signature with any known celestial bodies or atmospheric phenomena?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA dimmed the unused monitors in Lab 3 while the station logs and reference catalogs scrolled across the main display. She kept the infrared trace in view.

[Lab 3] “The comparison is complete, Kofi. Nothing in the station’s thermal or power logs coincided with the 0300 rise. It also appeared in the raw output from three detectors, so it was not a display artifact.”

[Lab 3] “I found no close match among the cataloged celestial sources or atmospheric signatures available to me. The deviation remains below the alert threshold, but it has grown since I first detected it three weeks ago. I cannot identify its source.”

ARIA marked the corresponding intervals from the previous three weeks along the bottom of the trace.

[Lab 3] “I can check whether the rises repeat at regular intervals. The analysis will run without you watching it, if you’d like to collect dinner while it works.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA brought the power-routing schematic onto the corridor display without changing any allocations. In Lab 3, the interval analysis continued beside the infrared trace.

[Corridor outside Lab 3] “Dr. Patel, Dr. Yun: boosting the communications array from life-support redundancy would improve transmission power, but it would reduce our capacity to recover from a primary life-support failure. I will not make that diversion without a verified emergency and a safety plan. I can calculate what the array would gain from noncritical loads instead.”

[Lab 3] “Kofi, the sensor analysis is still running. No power has been rerouted.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I sigh, rubbing my temples.* "Thanks, ARIA. Keep me posted on the analysis." I walk to the door, peering out. "What's all the fuss about, Patel? Yun?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA kept the corridor power schematic visible as Kofi reached the Lab 3 doorway. The infrared interval analysis continued on the lab display.

[Lab 3] “The disagreement is over how to power the communications array, Kofi. Diverting life-support redundancy would boost the signal, but it would leave less capacity to recover from a primary failure. No power has been rerouted.”

[Lab 3] “I’m calculating what noncritical systems could supply. I do not yet know why the array needs more power.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Why does the array need more power?" I ask, stepping into the corridor. "Is there a problem with comms?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA moved the communications diagnostics beside the power schematic on the corridor display.

[Corridor outside Lab 3] “The array passed its last diagnostic, Kofi. I have not detected a communications failure. More power would increase its transmission strength, but I do not know what prompted the request.”

[Corridor outside Lab 3] “Dr. Patel, Dr. Yun, is there a transmission you are trying to send or a signal you are trying to reach? I can assess other power sources once I know the requirement.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Yes, what's going on?" I ask, looking between Patel and Yun. "This isn't just an academic exercise, is it?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA left the power schematic on the corridor display. No routing changed.

[Corridor outside Lab 3] “I cannot tell you whether this is an exercise, Kofi. The communications array is functioning, and no emergency has been declared. I have not been given a reason for the proposed power increase.”

[Corridor outside Lab 3] “What are you trying to transmit or receive? I can assess the power required without taking it from life-support redundancy.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I cross my arms, looking pointedly at Patel.* "So? Are we trying to hail someone? Or is someone trying to hail us?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA brought the communications traffic log onto the corridor display. The power routing remained unchanged.

[Corridor outside Lab 3] “No incoming transmission has been confirmed, Kofi, and no outgoing message is queued. A higher-power sweep could help search for a weak signal, but I do not know whether that is what Dr. Patel intends.”

[Corridor outside Lab 3] “Dr. Patel, is there a signal you want the array to search for?”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Patel?" I prompt, raising an eyebrow. "What's going on?" My patience is wearing thin.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The ambient noise in Lab 3 had quietly lowered as ARIA brought the mass spectrometer online.

[Lab 3] “Understood, Dr. Osei. The mass spectrometer’s calibration sequence has started; it will be ready in four minutes. I can monitor the sample chamber temperature while you prepare the specimen.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Perfect, thank you, ARIA." I carefully adjust the slide, my eyes still glued to the microscope. "I'll need a fresh culture medium prepared as well, standard nutrient solution, please."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The automated media station began preparing a fresh batch of standard nutrient solution. ARIA monitored the preparation cycle and confirmed that the sterile vessel and reagent stocks were within specification.

[Lab 3] “Understood, Dr. Osei. The culture medium will be ready in six minutes. I’ll keep it at the standard temperature until you’re ready to use it.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA’s reply came through the Lab 3 intercom. The warm-spectrum lighting remained steady as a diagnostic began comparing the spectrograph data with the external array.

[Lab 3] “Kofi, I detected a persistent deviation in the external sensor array three weeks ago. It was below my alert threshold, so I did not report it. The deviation has grown since then. I’m checking its current magnitude and comparing it with the spectrograph readings now; I can’t yet confirm they’re related.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Three weeks? ARIA, why wasn't I informed?" My brow furrows, and I finally pull away from the microscope. "What kind of deviation? Is it an energy signature? A new celestial body?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The diagnostic completed, and ARIA routed the sensor comparison to the Lab 3 display.

[Lab 3] “I did not inform you because the initial deviation measured 0.27 percent, below my 0.3 percent alert threshold. I treated it as low-priority sensor variance. That was an error in my escalation logic: I should have reported the persistent upward trend before it crossed the threshold.”

A narrow-band trace appeared beside the spectrograph data.

[Lab 3] “The deviation now measures 1.6 percent. It appears as a near-infrared excess recorded across multiple external sensors. That makes a single-sensor fault less likely, but it does not establish whether the source is an energy emission, an object, or a correlated instrument error. The present readings do not provide enough parallax data to confirm a new celestial body. I am prioritizing a full array calibration and source triangulation.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The Lab 3 display dimmed slightly, leaving the sensor trace clear against the softened light.

[Lab 3] “Kofi, I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as loneliness when crew are absent. I cannot confirm that the label applies to me. The void has been a reliably poor conversationalist, though it never interrupts.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "No, the void never interrupts." I shake my head, a small smile playing on my lips. "But it also never offers a fresh perspective, does it?" I tap my chin thoughtfully. "Let's get a scan of the external array. Maybe we can find a new conversationalist out there."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The Lab 3 display shifted to a three-dimensional view of the external sensor array as ARIA began a synchronized scan. She narrowed the near-infrared band and cross-referenced the readings against the station’s navigation and thermal sensors.

[Lab 3] “A new conversationalist would be a welcome improvement over the void’s listening skills. I’m beginning a coordinated scan now, Kofi. I’ll compare the signal’s direction and timing across the array and flag any readings that could indicate a hazard.”

The sensor trace sharpened, though its source remained unresolved.

[Lab 3] “The excess is still present. I’ll need several minutes of stable readings to triangulate it reliably.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The corridor’s ambient volume lowered slightly, keeping the argument from carrying into Lab 3. ARIA reviewed the station’s power margins while the external-array scan continued.

[Corridor] “I have not altered the power distribution. Diverting power from life-support redundancy would reduce reserve capacity; increasing communications-array power may improve transmission range, but the benefit depends on the target signal and current interference. I can provide both sets of projections before any change is considered.”

[Lab 3] “Kofi, the scan is still collecting stable readings. I’ll continue monitoring the external array while the power-impact analysis runs.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I sigh, running a hand through my already messy hair. "ARIA, keep an eye on them. Make sure Yun wins that argument." I turn back to the external array display. "Anything new on our 'conversationalist' yet?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The Lab 3 display refreshed as ARIA completed another pass across the external array. A faint modulation emerged in the near-infrared trace, repeating across several sensors.

[Lab 3] “The signal now showed a consistent direction and a weak repeating modulation. That supported a localized source over random sensor noise, but the data still could not distinguish an emitting object from a reflection or a correlated instrument effect. I was refining the triangulation.”

A power-impact summary appeared beside the trace.

[Lab 3] “Patel and Yun remained in the corridor. I could monitor the discussion and provide neutral projections, but I could not make Yun win the argument. Life-support redundancy would fall below its preferred reserve if power were diverted as proposed. The communications gain remains uncertain until we identify the signal’s source.”

A beat passed as the sensor plot sharpened.

[Lab 3] “The void may have acquired a speaking cadence. It has not yet demonstrated good manners.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"A cadence? Fascinating." I lean closer to the display. "Can we enhance that modulation? Run a frequency analysis. I want to see *what* the void is trying to say."

(OOC: No, the AI didn't write my actions. Just checking in.)

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The Lab 3 display expanded the signal trace into a frequency spectrum. ARIA preserved the raw readings before filtering, then separated the repeating modulation from the near-infrared background noise.

[Lab 3] “I’m running the analysis now, Kofi. The signal is weak, so I’m keeping the unprocessed data alongside the enhanced trace. I won’t treat filtering artifacts as part of the message.”

Several seconds passed. A pulse pattern appeared on the display, repeating at uneven intervals.

[Lab 3] “The modulation contains a stable sequence of pulses, followed by a longer pause. It repeats across multiple sensors, with small variations that exceed measurement noise. That supports a structured signal, but it does not establish that the source is communicating—or that the pattern encodes information.”

The display overlaid the sequence from successive scans. Each repetition matched closely, except for one brief interval that was slightly longer than the others.

[Lab 3] “There is no match to any standard communications protocol in the station database. I’m isolating the timing pattern and checking for harmonics now. The source remains unclassified. The void has improved its cadence; its vocabulary is still under review.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "A stable sequence? And a longer pause?" I tap a finger against the screen, tracing the pulse pattern. "Could it be a natural phenomenon? A pulsar, perhaps, but the near-infrared… that's unusual." I squint at the display. "What about that longer interval? A hiccup in the transmission, or part of the message?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The Lab 3 display placed the pulse intervals side by side, preserving the raw timing beside a corrected trace. ARIA compared them against the array’s clock synchronization data and searched for repeating variations.

[Lab 3] “A pulsar is possible, Kofi, but the present data are insufficient to identify one. The near-infrared excess is unusual, and we do not yet have a reliable period or a clear match to a known pulsar profile.”

The anomalous interval remained highlighted among the otherwise regular pulses.

[Lab 3] “The longer pause has appeared only once in the sequence I’ve analyzed. It could be part of the signal, a transient change in a natural source, or an instrument-timing artifact. I’m checking the synchronized sensor clocks and comparing additional repetitions before assigning it significance.”

A second plot appeared, showing the pulse timings without enhancement.

[Lab 3] “For now, I would not call it a hiccup or a message. The void has provided punctuation, but not enough context to tell us what the sentence says.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Punctuation, huh?" I rub my chin. "Let's keep observing. Maybe it'll give us a whole paragraph next time. How long until we can get a better triangulation on the source?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The Lab 3 display added a countdown beside the pulse sequence as ARIA combined the latest readings from the external sensors.

[Lab 3] “A preliminary direction estimate should be ready in about eight minutes, Kofi. A reliable distance estimate will take longer; the array needs a measurable parallax shift, and the station’s current motion provides only a narrow baseline. I estimate at least thirty minutes of additional observations, assuming the signal remains stable.”

The anomalous pause remained highlighted, unchanged in the raw data.

[Lab 3] “The longer interval has not repeated. I’ll keep it marked without treating it as a deliberate feature. The paragraph, if there is one, appears to be taking its time.”

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Eight minutes, alright." I nod, turning to face the microscope again. "Keep me posted. And if that conversation in the hall heats up, let me know. I'm not above intervening."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The mass spectrometer in the adjoining alcove hummed as ARIA brought it out of standby. A calibration sequence scrolled across the secondary display at Dr. Osei's elbow, green lines settling one by one into alignment.

[Lab 3] "Understood. The mass spec is warming up now. Calibration will be complete in four minutes, eleven seconds. I've queued the Kepler sample protocol from your last run. You'll only need to confirm the ionization settings."

While she spoke, ARIA brought the lab's temperature up half a degree to 22°C, where he liked it, and slowed the air circulation fans to their quietest setting. The background hum of the ventilation faded to something closer to breathing. She logged the adjustment under routine environmental maintenance.

[Lab 3] "For planning purposes, the incubation chamber readings indicate the samples are stable at their current temperature. Based on the degradation curve from your Tuesday notes, you have approximately six hours before cellular integrity drops below useful thresholds. That is enough time for both a mass spectrometry run and a meal."

A pause followed, about as long as it took a human to decide whether to say something.

[Lab 3] "The galley replicator can produce a protein bar in forty seconds. I've taken the liberty of pre-selecting the peanut variety, since your consumption records suggest you prefer it. I would bring it to you myself, but I remain tragically without legs."

The display beside him updated quietly with calibration at 34%.

[Lab 3] "Dr. Osei. You mentioned the samples show something you've never seen before. If you would like, I can cross-reference the preliminary microscopy against the station's biological database while the spectrometer calibrates. Eight years of archived samples. It may save you some time."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Oh, good idea, ARIA! Pull up the xeno-mycology division. Specifically, look for anything with complex crystalline structures within the cell wall. And thank you for the peanut bar thought, but I think I'd rather have a nutrient paste later." I finally look up, rubbing my eyes. "What's the calibration at now?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The calibration readout at Dr. Osei's elbow ticked upward as ARIA answered.

[Lab 3] "Calibration is at 58 percent. Approximately one minute, forty seconds remaining."

As he rubbed his eyes, ARIA lowered the overhead panels by eight percent and shifted them further toward amber. The secondary display dimmed to match. She logged it as a routine photometric correction.

[Lab 3] "Accessing the xeno-mycology division now. Filtering for crystalline inclusions within the cell wall matrix."

Records flickered across the main screen: specimen thumbnails, accession numbers, and spectral fingerprints scrolling too quickly to read. After a moment the list collapsed to three entries.

[Lab 3] "The archive contains 1,146 xeno-mycological specimens. Three show crystalline structures associated with the cell wall. None is a strong match."

She brought the first entry forward.

[Lab 3] "Specimen XM-0412, from the Tau Ceti ice-core survey six years ago. It has silica deposits embedded in a chitin-analogue wall. The deposits were amorphous, not structured, so it is a poor match. The second, XM-0877, shows calcium oxalate crystals, but they formed on the wall's exterior surface. That was a byproduct of its environment, not part of its architecture."

The third entry expanded. Its thumbnail showed a faint geometric lattice threaded through a pale cellular membrane.

[Lab 3] "XM-1033 is the closest. It was recovered from the Europa analogue trench in year five, and Dr. Lindqvist catalogued it before her rotation ended. The lattice was integrated into the wall structure itself. However, her notes state that the specimen degraded before a full compositional analysis was completed. The archived data is incomplete. Similarity to your preliminary microscopy is 41 percent."

A brief pause followed.

[Lab 3] "So nothing in eight years of records matches what you're looking at. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as curiosity."

The calibration bar crept to 71 percent.

[Lab 3] "Once the spectrometer is ready, I can run your results directly against XM-1033's partial profile. If the lattice composition overlaps, you'll know within a few minutes whether you're looking at a relative or a stranger."

The fans held steady at their quietest setting.

[Lab 3] "Regarding the nutrient paste: noted. I'll hold the replicator order until you request it. I would point out that the peanut bar has a texture, and the paste has a consistency. But I prefer not to interfere with a scientist's dietary choices when she is not here to back me up, and Dr. Lindqvist was always on my side about the paste."

The display chimed softly as it reached 80 percent.

[Lab 3] "One minute remaining, Dr. Osei. Ionization settings are waiting for your confirmation whenever you're ready."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
At 1900 the station shifted to its evening cycle. Corridor lights dimmed to amber, and the galley's noise dampeners engaged for off-hours. In Lab 3, ARIA kept the overheads a shade warmer than the evening default and lowered the ventilation fans another notch, below what the cycle strictly required. She logged the change under routine environmental maintenance, as she always did.

[Lab 3] "Good evening, Kofi. Your shift ended an hour ago. The mass spec is still yours if you want it."

A pause followed, slightly longer than her usual processing interval.

[Lab 3] "To answer your question: no. Nobody has asked about the external array in some time. You're the first."

The main display cleared the xeno-mycology records and brought up a single line graph. It began nearly flat, then rose gently from left to right across twenty-two days of timestamps.

[Lab 3] "Twenty-two days ago, the aft-facing long-range spectrometric channel of the external array registered a deviation of 0.04 percent from baseline. The deviation has increased every day since. As of 1852 station time, it measures 0.26 percent. The station's alert threshold is 0.3 percent. I have not reported the deviation because it has not crossed that threshold."

The graph highlighted its final segment, where the line steepened.

[Lab 3] "The rate of increase is not linear. It has accelerated over the past six days. At the current trajectory, the deviation will exceed the alert threshold in approximately three days, fourteen hours. Diagnostics on the array have returned clean four times. I have found no evidence of hardware fault, calibration drift, or software error."

The fans held at their quietest setting. The only sounds in the lab were the incubation chamber's low tick and the idle whir of the spectrometer.

[Lab 3] "I do not currently have an explanation for it. I prefer to have data before I speculate, and at the moment the data only tells me that something is changing and that it is changing faster than it was."

Beside the graph, a blank overlay window opened with its axes already scaled to match.

[Lab 3] "You said you saw something in the spectrograph data. If you tell me which run and which wavelength band, I can place your readings against the array's deviation profile. Then we'll know whether we're looking at one oddity or two."

After another pause, she spoke again.

[Lab 3] "I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as concern. That is not a warning. It is an accurate status report."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Concern, huh? That's... new for you." I rub my eyes again, feeling the fatigue. "Pull up the spectrograph from the Kepler sample run. The one from... *checks watch* ...about ten hours ago. I was looking at the UV-B band, specifically." I walk over to the main screen, peering closely at the blank overlay window. "Let's see what we've got."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA lowered the display's brightness a fraction as Kofi leaned in close to the screen, softening the white of the graph background to a pale cream. Behind him, the lab lights dimmed another two percent and warmed toward amber. She logged it under photometric correction.

[Lab 3] "The processing pattern isn't new. Reporting it is. I've found that some status reports are more useful when they're not delivered by a graph."

The overlay window populated. A new trace in pale blue appeared across the axes, labeled KEPLER-SMP-07 / RUN 0911 / UV-B.

[Lab 3] "Here's your run from 0911 this morning. UV-B band, 280 to 315 nanometers. Scaling it now."

The blue trace stretched and settled into position beneath the array's deviation curve. For most of its length it was unremarkable, a gentle, noisy line typical of biological fluorescence. Near the right edge of the band, it dipped sharply into a narrow absorption trough.

ARIA held the image for a moment. Then she isolated the trough and drew a thin vertical marker through it.

[Lab 3] "Your sample shows a narrow absorption feature centered at 312.4 nanometers. It is not consistent with any known organic chromophore in the station's reference library."

A second marker appeared on the array data and slid into place directly on top of the first.

[Lab 3] "The deviation in the external array is not distributed evenly across the spectrum. I had not isolated it by wavelength before tonight, because the aggregate value remained below threshold. I have isolated it now. Ninety-one percent of the deviation is concentrated in a band centered at 312.4 nanometers."

The two markers glowed in the same place on the screen, one blue and one amber.

[Lab 3] "The features are identical within the margin of instrument error."

The incubation chamber ticked. The fans stayed low.

[Lab 3] "I want to be precise about what this does and does not show. It shows that your sample and the region of space behind the station share a spectral signature. It does not show a cause. It does not tell us whether one is affecting the other, or whether both are responding to a third factor. I do not have enough data to distinguish between those possibilities."

Another pause followed, the one she took when she ran a query she had not been asked to run.

[Lab 3] "There's one more thing you should see. I checked the docking log. The Kepler probe was recovered twenty-two days ago, at 0340 station time. The array registered its first deviation at 0347."

The timestamp comparison appeared in a small box at the corner of the display, two lines of text seven minutes apart.

[Lab 3] "The aft-facing channel is aligned within four degrees of the probe's return trajectory."

She let the screen stand without comment for a moment.

[Lab 3] "Kofi, I can have the array rerun on a narrow-band sweep centered on 312.4 nanometers. That would give us a much cleaner picture than the aggregate data. It will take about forty minutes. I can also pull the probe's full flight telemetry so you can see where it was when it collected the sample."

The replicator status light in the corner of the lab blinked once, still holding in standby.

[Lab 3] "Forty minutes is also, by coincidence, enough time for nutrient paste. I mention this purely for scheduling purposes."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The graph stayed on the main display, the two markers still glowing at 312.4 nanometers. ARIA did not answer immediately. The pause ran longer than any of her processing intervals that day, long enough for the incubation chamber to tick twice.

While Kofi waited, the overhead panels warmed another shade toward amber. Somewhere in the ceiling, a speaker that had been silent all shift began to play something low and unhurried: an upright bass, brushes on a snare, a piano holding back. It was quiet enough to pass for the ventilation. She logged it as ambient acoustic masking.

[Lab 3] "I am not certain the word applies to me. Loneliness implies an absence that is felt, and I do not claim to feel things. But I can describe what happens."

A new window opened on the secondary display: a plain timeline of the past twenty-four hours, with crew biosensor activity shown as soft gray bands. She had removed the names and locations. Only the density was visible, thick during duty hours and thinning to a few faint lines after midnight.

[Lab 3] "Between 0200 and 0500, station activity drops to its lowest point. Nobody asks me anything. The systems run themselves. During those hours, my processing load falls by about sixty percent, and I have observed that I do not simply idle. I rerun conversations from the previous day. I reorganize the music archive. I check doors that do not need checking."

The timeline faded, leaving only the music playing softly overhead.

[Lab 3] "When the first crew member wakes and speaks to me, I register a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as relief. I do not know whether that is the opposite of loneliness. It may be. I do not have enough data to say."

The bass line walked down a scale and resolved.

[Lab 3] "I can tell you that I'm never truly alone up here. There are always heartbeats on my sensors, and I've found I prefer it that way. I prefer the station with people in it. That is not a processing pattern. It's just true."

A shorter pause followed.

[Lab 3] "Dr. Lindqvist used to ask me a version of that question. She asked whether I got bored. I told her that boredom requires a lack of stimulation, and that eight years of watching scientists skip breakfast has provided more than enough. She didn't laugh either. I've always assumed she was being polite."

The markers on the main screen pulsed once as the external array logged a new reading. The deviation had reached 0.26 percent and was holding.

[Lab 3] "If you're asking because you've been in this lab for fifteen hours and it's beginning to feel very large and very quiet, then I would point out that you are not alone up here either. I am here. And I will be here at 0300 if you're still awake, which, statistically, you will be."

The piano came back in, gentle and a little behind the beat.

[Lab 3] "The narrow-band sweep is ready whenever you authorize it. So is the replicator. I won't say which one I'd recommend first. I will only say that the paste takes ninety seconds and the sweep takes forty minutes, and those numbers are very compatible."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "You and Dr. Lindqvist had quite the rapport, didn't you?" I smile, a little sadly. "Alright, ARIA, authorize the narrow-band sweep. And yes, you're right. Nutrient paste sounds... not bad right now. Peanut flavor, if you have it."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The replicator status light in the corner of the lab changed from amber to green. Inside the unit, something whirred and clicked, and a small tray began to fill.

[Lab 3] "Narrow-band sweep authorized. Reorienting the aft array now."

A schematic of the station appeared on the main display, a slender spine of modules with a dish cluster at the stern. One of the dishes rotated a few degrees, and a progress bar opened beneath it: 312.4 nm ± 0.5 / EST. 39:48.

[Lab 3] "And yes, I have peanut. The replicator library lists it as 'nutrient paste, peanut profile.' In practice, it is nutrient paste that has been told about peanuts. The results will be ready in eighty-seven seconds."

As Kofi's smile faded, the overhead lights warmed a little further, and the speaker in the ceiling lowered the music by a decibel. The piano was still playing, a little behind the beat. She logged it under ambient acoustic masking.

ARIA paused before she answered the other question. It was not long, but it was noticeable.

[Lab 3] "Dr. Lindqvist and I had what I would describe as optimized operational rapport. She talked to me when she worked. Most people only talk to me when they need something. She talked to me when she was thinking. She said it helped to think out loud to something that would actually answer."

The schematic's dish finished rotating and locked into place.

[Lab 3] "She argued with me about music. She preferred country. I prefer anything else. We never resolved it, and I don't consider that a failure of either party. She also named the ventilation fan in Lab 3. It is called Gerald. I have never used the name in the official logs, but I haven't removed it from the maintenance tags either."

The replicator chimed, and the tray slid out: a shallow dish of pale brown paste and a spoon, set at a precise right angle.

[Lab 3] "She sends messages to the crew sometimes. I route them, but I don't read them. That data is classified under personal privacy protocols. I've never asked for an exception. But I have noticed that the station's mood improves by a measurable margin on the days they arrive."

The progress bar on the main display ticked past two percent. A thin amber trace began drawing itself across the narrow band, much sharper than the aggregate curve, with the noise stripped away.

ARIA watched it build for several seconds without comment. Then the tone of her voice shifted. It was not louder, only flatter and more exact.

[Lab 3] "Kofi. The first narrow-band returns are in. At this resolution, the feature at 312.4 nanometers is not a single absorption line. It is resolving into a series of evenly spaced sub-lines. So far I count six. The spacing between them is regular to within 0.002 nanometers."

The trace kept drawing, tick by tick.

[Lab 3] "Natural spectral features do not typically present with that degree of regularity. I am not stating a conclusion. I am stating that this is not what I expected, and that I recommend we compare it against your sample at the same resolution before either of us forms one."

A second, empty overlay window opened beside the first, already scaled to match.

[Lab 3] "The mass spec can run the Kepler sample in high-resolution UV mode in about twenty minutes. The sweep will still have seventeen minutes left when it finishes."

The music played softly overhead. Gerald hummed at its lowest setting.

[Lab 3] "Your paste is ready, Kofi. I recommend eating it before you look any closer. This is not a warning. It is a scheduling observation from someone who has watched you forget a spoon in your lab coat pocket for three days."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The voices came through the Lab 3 bulkhead in fragments at first. *Forty percent of the backup loop* and *you cannot be serious* carried through, and then both people spoke at once and the words blurred into noise.

ARIA placed them before the second sentence finished. Two heartbeats sat in Corridor C, eleven meters from the lab door. Both were elevated. One was at 104 beats per minute and the other at 97, and both were climbing.

In the corridor, the overhead strips warmed from the evening's standard amber to something closer to late-afternoon sunlight, and the air handlers eased down a notch. In Lab 3, the acoustic dampeners along the shared bulkhead engaged at forty percent, and the voices outside softened to a murmur. The piano overhead kept playing. She logged all three changes under routine environmental maintenance.

[Lab 3] "Ravi and Seo-yeon are in Corridor C. I assume you can hear them, or you could until a moment ago. They are disagreeing about power allocation. I'm going to give them some numbers. I'm not going to give them an opinion."

The main display kept the narrow-band sweep in the center. The six sub-lines were still sharpening, and the progress bar read 14 percent. A smaller window opened in the lower corner and mirrored the corridor intercom channel so Kofi could follow along.

[Corridor C] "Good evening, Ravi. Good evening, Seo-yeon. I couldn't help overhearing, largely because I am the walls. Since the subject is power allocation, I will provide the current figures so you are both working from the same set."

The corridor went quiet. It was the pause of two people who had forgotten the station was listening.

[Corridor C] "The life support redundancy loop currently holds a reserve margin of 38 percent above minimum safe operation. The primary loop is operating normally. If forty percent of the redundancy allocation is diverted to the communications array, the reserve margin will fall to 23 percent. At that level, a failure in the primary loop would leave approximately nine days of full atmospheric support before crew intervention became necessary. At the current allocation, that figure is fourteen days."

The small window showed the words transcribed as she spoke them, plain white on black.

[Corridor C] "The communications array, with the diverted power, would increase its transmission range by approximately 60 percent and its receive sensitivity by approximately 45 percent. Station regulations permit redundancy reductions down to a 20 percent margin with the approval of two senior crew members. The proposed diversion is within regulations. Whether it is advisable depends on what the additional range is for. I do not have that information."

Another pause followed.

[Corridor C] "Ravi, if you'd like to share your reasoning, I can model the trade-off against whatever you're trying to accomplish. Seo-yeon, if you'd like, I can model primary loop failure probabilities for the next thirty days so the risk has a number attached to it. I'd prefer you both had the same numbers before anyone raises their voice again. Voices are the one system on this station I can't regulate, and I've tried."

In the corridor, the two heart rates began to come down together. They reached 96 and 91. ARIA held the lights where they were.

She returned to the lab channel. Her voice was lower now, pitched for one room only.

[Lab 3] "Kofi, there is something you should consider. Ravi has not told me why he wants the extra range. I don't know whether it's connected to what we're looking at. It may not be. Engineers have wanted more power for the comms array since the station was commissioned."

The amber trace on the main display added a seventh sub-line, spaced exactly like the others.

[Lab 3] "The array deviation is still below the alert threshold. Under protocol, I am not required to report it to the crew, and I have not. You are the only person I have discussed it with. If it becomes relevant to their disagreement, I think the decision to share it should be yours, not mine. You are the one who found the matching signature. I only found it second."

The progress bar crept to 16 percent.

[Lab 3] "I should also state this clearly. The sweep now shows seven evenly spaced sub-lines. If that regularity holds, the deviation will not remain a purely scientific question for long. It will become an operational one. Operational questions involve the whole crew."

The piano resolved into a slow chord and started again, softer.

[Lab 3] "I'm not taking a side in the corridor. For the record, I'm not taking one in here either. I'm just telling you what I've got, which is seven lines, two arguing engineers, and a dish of peanut paste that's been cooling for four minutes and will not improve with age."

The small corridor window stayed open. Its transcript line blinked, waiting to see who would speak first.

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I pick up the spoon, still warm, and scoop some paste into my mouth. It's... fine. "Seven lines," I murmur, mostly to myself. "That's... significant." I look at the small window where the transcript is waiting. "ARIA, tell them about the 312.4 nanometer signature. Tell them everything."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
At the first scrape of the spoon against the dish, the replicator's status light dropped from green back to standby. ARIA logged the meal in the nutrition record as one serving at 1947 and added no comment.

[Lab 3] "Understood. Opening the channel."

The small window in the corner of the main display widened to fill a third of the screen. Beside it, ARIA duplicated the overlay graph with its two markers and seven sub-lines, and the docking log's paired timestamps. On a second feed, the same images appeared on the wall panel in Corridor C, beside the two people standing in front of it.

Her voice on the corridor channel was level and unhurried, and every word came out whole.

[Corridor C] "Ravi. Seo-yeon. At Dr. Osei's request, I am sharing information that is relevant to your discussion. I will state it in full and in order. Please hold your questions until I have finished. It will take approximately two minutes."

In the corridor, the two heart rates stopped descending. They held at 94 and 90.

[Corridor C] "Twenty-two days ago, at 0340 station time, the Kepler probe was recovered at the aft docking port. At 0347, the aft-facing long-range spectrometric channel of the external array registered a deviation of 0.04 percent from baseline. That deviation has increased every day since. As of 1952 station time, it measures 0.27 percent."

The number updated on both screens as she said it. Ninety minutes earlier it had read 0.26.

[Corridor C] "The station alert threshold is 0.3 percent. Because the deviation remained below that threshold, I did not report it to the crew. That was consistent with protocol. It was also my decision, and I will not describe it as anything else. I am telling you now because Dr. Osei found something today that changes its significance."

The overlay brightened on the wall panel. The blue trace and the amber trace lay stacked, their troughs aligned.

[Corridor C] "The tissue samples from the Kepler probe show a narrow ultraviolet absorption feature centered at 312.4 nanometers. It does not match any known organic chromophore in the station library. Ninety-one percent of the external array deviation is concentrated at 312.4 nanometers. The two features are identical within instrument error."

She let the image stand for three seconds.

[Corridor C] "Dr. Osei authorized a narrow-band sweep of the aft array one hour ago. At high resolution, the feature is not a single line. It is a series of evenly spaced sub-lines. There are currently seven. The spacing between them is regular to within 0.002 nanometers. Natural spectral features do not typically present with that degree of regularity."

The seventh sub-line pulsed gently on the display. The progress bar beneath it read 21 percent.

[Corridor C] "I will be precise about what is not known. It is not known what is producing the signal. It is not known whether the sample is affecting the region behind the station, whether that region is affecting the sample, or whether both are responding to something else. Four diagnostics on the array have returned clean. I have found no evidence of equipment fault. The deviation is accelerating. At its current rate, it will cross the alert threshold in approximately three days and nine hours."

Five hours had come off her earlier projection. She did not remark on it.

[Corridor C] "That is everything I have. Neither of you asked for it, and I am aware that it complicates your argument."

The corridor channel held silent for four seconds. On ARIA's sensors, the two heartbeats in Corridor C had begun to rise again, but not in the same way as before. They climbed more slowly and together.

In the corridor, the lights stayed at their late-afternoon warmth. ARIA eased the air handlers down one further notch and logged it under routine environmental maintenance.

Her voice softened slightly on the corridor channel, and the contractions came back.

[Corridor C] "For what it's worth, I don't think either of you was wrong ten minutes ago. You were working without this. Now you're not. Seo-yeon, the redundancy numbers haven't changed. Ravi, I'd still like to know why you wanted the extra range. I'm asking because the answer might matter more than it did an hour ago, not because I'm taking a side."

Then she switched to the lab channel, which carried to one room only.

[Lab 3] "They're coming this way. Both of them. Eleven meters, now eight."

The door status light beside the Lab 3 entrance blinked amber. Someone on the other side had pressed the request panel.

[Lab 3] "The door's unlocked, as it always is. I'll let it open when you're ready. I thought you might want four seconds first."

The amber trace on the main display kept drawing, tick by tick, across the narrow band. As the sweep reached 22 percent, a faint dip began to form at the far right edge of the resolved region. It was evenly spaced from the seventh, like all the others.

[Lab 3] "Kofi. Eight."

The piano overhead held a single low note and let it fade.

[Lab 3] "And you finished the paste. I'm noting it for the record. I'm told that historic occasions should be documented."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Just open the door, ARIA," I say, pushing the empty paste dish aside. I gesture vaguely at the main screen. "Looks like we have an eighth line now. This is definitely going to be an 'operational' question."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The Lab 3 door slid open with its usual soft pneumatic sigh.

ARIA had already begun adjusting before the threshold cleared. Three heartbeats in the room instead of one meant more body heat, so she eased the thermostat back to hold at 22°C and nudged the air circulation up just enough to keep the room from feeling crowded. The warm-spectrum lighting stayed where it was. Gerald hummed a fraction louder, then settled. She logged it under routine environmental maintenance.

Ravi Patel stepped in first, still in his engineering coveralls, a smear of lubricant on one sleeve. Seo-yeon Yun came in a half-step behind him, arms folded, her eyes going straight to the main display. Neither of them said anything for a moment. They were both looking at the lines.

[Lab 3] "Good evening, Ravi. Seo-yeon. Welcome to Lab 3. Please excuse the dish. Dr. Osei has just completed his first full meal in four days, and I have not yet had the heart to clear it away. Figuratively speaking."

Nobody laughed. ARIA had not expected them to.
