[Lab 3] "To confirm what Kofi has already observed: the sweep has resolved an eighth sub-line. Spacing is consistent with the previous seven, within 0.002 nanometers. The sweep is at 24 percent."

The eighth dip on the main display finished drawing itself and sharpened. ARIA expanded the resolved region so the eight troughs sat side by side across the screen, evenly spaced, like the rungs of a ladder laid on its side.

Then she paused. It was one of the longer ones.

[Lab 3] "There is an additional observation. I had not reported it because until the eighth line resolved, I did not have enough data to be confident it was real. I am now reasonably confident."

A second row of values appeared beneath the troughs, one number under each.

[Lab 3] "The sub-lines are evenly spaced, but they are not evenly deep. Absorption depth varies from line to line. The first line and the eighth line have identical depths, within instrument error. So do the second and the seventh. I will not know whether that symmetry continues until more of the band resolves. I am not stating a conclusion. I am stating that the pattern has structure in two dimensions now, not one."

Seo-yeon's heart rate ticked up to 98. Ravi's held at 93, steadier than it had been in the corridor. ARIA noted it and did not remark on it.

Ravi spoke without looking away from the screen.

"The comms array," he said. "That's why I wanted the power. For about two weeks it's been picking up intermittent noise on the aft receiver. Low amplitude, no identifiable source. I thought it was a degrading component. I wanted enough gain to rule it out before I tore the receiver housing open." He glanced at the ceiling, where people tended to look when they spoke to ARIA. "I didn't log it. It was below *my* threshold too."

The main display split without being asked. The comms array's aft receiver log opened in a new window, fourteen days of faint, scattered spikes, low enough to pass for background.

[Lab 3] "Thank you, Ravi. That is the piece of information I did not have. I am cross-referencing the receiver noise against the array deviation now."

The timestamps populated. ARIA ran the comparison and held the result for less than half a second before displaying it, which, for her, was a very long time.

[Lab 3] "The receiver noise events are not random. Of the 212 logged spikes, 197 occurred within ninety seconds of a measurable increase in the array deviation. The correlation coefficient is 0.93."

She let the number stand.

[Lab 3] "This is now an operational question. I am formally recording it as such. I recommend the following, in order. First, that the Kepler samples remain sealed in the incubation chamber, under current containment, until we understand their relationship to the signal. Second, that no power allocation changes be made in either direction until all four of us have reviewed the same data. Third, that Commander Hale be informed. She is currently in her quarters and her biosensors indicate she is awake."

Her voice came back down a register, the contractions returning.

[Lab 3] "I'm not recommending that as a rebuke to anyone. Three people in this station noticed something below threshold and waited, and one of them was me. I'd rather we stopped waiting together."

The sweep ticked to 25 percent. At the far edge of the resolved band, the ninth trough had begun to form. Its depth, still building, was tracking toward the same value as the second line.

The piano overhead had finished its piece. ARIA let the silence stand instead of starting another.

[Lab 3] "Kofi, you found the signature, so I'll ask you first. Would you like me to wake the Commander, or would you prefer to call her yourself?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I look from the screen to Ravi and Seo-yeon, then back to the screen again. "No, ARIA. You call her. This is... above my pay grade now." I nod slowly. "And, Ravi, I think your noise just became our signal."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Understood. Calling her now."

The lab channel stayed open, but a small indicator appeared in the upper corner of the main display: a second channel, routed to Deck 2, Quarters 1.

Ravi gave a short breath through his nose at Kofi's remark. It was not quite a laugh. ARIA registered it and let it pass. Seo-yeon's arms stayed folded, but her heart rate eased from 98 to 95. In the corner of the lab nearest her, ARIA quietly lowered the air handler output by a fraction and let the lights there warm half a shade. She logged it under routine environmental maintenance.

On Deck 2, the chime in the Commander's quarters sounded once, softly. ARIA did not use the urgent tone. It had been designed for hull breaches, and she saw no reason to make anyone's pulse do something it did not need to do.

[Quarters 1] "Good evening, Miriam. I apologize for the interruption. You're off duty, and I'm aware of it."

After two seconds, Commander Miriam Hale's voice came through, slightly rough, with the rustle of a page being set down. "ARIA. You never apologize before you've told me something. What is it?"

ARIA dropped the contractions.

[Quarters 1] "I am requesting your presence in Lab 3. Dr. Osei, Engineer Patel, and Dr. Yun are already here. This is not an emergency. No crew member is in danger, and all station systems are operating normally. It is, however, an operational matter, and it requires command review tonight."

"Summary," Hale said. She was already moving. ARIA's sensors placed her upright, and her heart rate had climbed from 64 to 81.

[Quarters 1] "Twenty-two days ago, seven minutes after the Kepler probe docked, the aft external array began registering a spectral deviation. It has grown every day since and is accelerating. It is currently at 0.27 percent, below the alert threshold, and for that reason I did not report it. Today Dr. Osei found an identical spectral signature in the Kepler tissue samples, at 312.4 nanometers. A high-resolution sweep shows that the signature is composed of evenly spaced sub-lines. There are currently eight, and their depths are symmetrical. Engineer Patel has independently logged receiver noise on the aft comms array that correlates with the deviation at a coefficient of 0.93."

There was a pause on the line. Then came the sound of a locker opening.

"How long have you known about the deviation?"

[Quarters 1] "Twenty-two days. I have known about the spectral match for one hour and twenty-one minutes, and about the receiver correlation for four minutes. I made the decision not to report the deviation. It was consistent with protocol. I have already told the others that I do not consider protocol a complete explanation."

Another pause, shorter.

"All right," Hale said. Her voice was even. "I'm on my way. Don't touch the samples. Nobody changes anything on the power grid. And ARIA, I'll want the full logs, not the summary."

[Quarters 1] "They'll be on the Lab 3 display when you arrive. Your door is unlocked. The corridor lighting between you and us is already on."

The channel closed. On ARIA's sensors, a fourth heartbeat began moving along Corridor B, at a brisk walk.

[Lab 3] "The Commander is en route. She'll be here in approximately two minutes, ten seconds. She requested the full logs. I'm assembling them now, including my own threshold decisions, flagged and timestamped."

A new window opened on the secondary display: a document index, twenty-two days long. The first entry read *ARIA — deviation logged, no alert issued, 0.04%*. Every entry after it read the same way, except for the number.

[Lab 3] "Ravi, I've moved your receiver log into the same file. I've also noted that you logged the noise nowhere, which I'm recording as 'below threshold' rather than 'forgotten.' It seemed fairer."

On the main display, the sweep ticked to 27 percent.

The ninth trough finished resolving. ARIA placed its depth value beneath it, then drew a faint connecting arc from the ninth line back to the second.

[Lab 3] "The ninth sub-line has resolved. Its depth matches the second line within instrument error. It does not match the first."

She held the image for a moment.

[Lab 3] "That means the symmetry I described earlier was not the whole pattern. Lines one through eight form a mirrored sequence. Line nine begins repeating that sequence from its second position, not its first. I am not stating a conclusion. I am stating that the structure now appears to be sequential rather than simply symmetrical, and that sequential structures are, in my experience, usually going somewhere."

The aft receiver window flickered. A single spike appeared in the comms log at 2001:14, taller than any of the previous 212.

ARIA did not wait to be asked.

[Lab 3] "Receiver event at 2001:14. The amplitude is approximately four times the previous maximum. The array deviation increased by 0.003 percent in the same second. I am checking the spike's internal structure now."

The spike expanded across the window. Within it, at a resolution Ravi's original logging had never used, sat a row of narrow pulses. They were evenly spaced, and their heights were not uniform.

ARIA counted them before she spoke.

[Lab 3] "There are nine pulses. Their relative amplitudes match the depths of the nine spectral sub-lines, in order. Correlation is 0.98."

The lab went very quiet. Gerald hummed at its lowest setting. ARIA did not start another song.

Out in the corridor, the fourth heartbeat was forty meters away and closing.

[Lab 3] "Kofi. The Commander will want to know what the Kepler probe brought back with it. You are the one who has looked at it most closely. When she arrives, I recommend that you tell her what you told me this morning: that you've never seen anything like it before."

She paused.

[Lab 3] "I'd add that neither have I. I've been listening to this station for eight years, and until tonight I thought I knew every sound it could make."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, feeling a sudden chill despite the regulated temperature. "Right. Never seen anything like it." I try to sound confident, but my voice is a little shaky. I glance at the door, then back at the screen, at the nine tiny pulses. "This just got a lot more interesting."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
ARIA registered the tremor in Kofi's voice before he finished the sentence. His heart rate had climbed from 88 to 102, and his skin temperature had dropped four-tenths of a degree at the extremities.

She raised the lab's thermostat by half a degree, just enough to take the edge off, and shifted the overheads nearest his workstation another shade toward amber. The air circulation around him slowed to almost nothing. She dimmed the secondary display showing the pulses by three percent so it glared a little less. All four changes went into the log under routine environmental maintenance.

[Lab 3] "Interesting is one word for it. I've been cross-referencing others. The thesaurus suggests 'noteworthy,' 'unprecedented,' and, less helpfully, 'fraught.' I'm staying with yours."

Ravi's mouth twitched at one corner. He did not laugh. Seo-yeon unfolded her arms at last and put one hand flat on the edge of the lab bench, as if to confirm the station was still there.

[Lab 3] "Sweep at 29 percent. No new sub-lines since the ninth. The array deviation is holding at 0.273 percent. The receiver has been quiet for forty-one seconds."

The door status light blinked amber, then green. ARIA opened the door before the request tone finished.

Commander Miriam Hale stepped through in a station sweater over her duty trousers. Her hair was tied back hastily, and a reading tablet was tucked under one arm. She took in the room in a single sweep: the three crew, the empty paste dish, and the ladder of troughs on the main display. Her eyes stopped on the nine pulses in the receiver window and stayed there.

With a fourth person in the room, ARIA brought the ventilation up a notch on the far side of the lab and held it steady near Kofi's workstation. She logged it under routine environmental maintenance.

[Lab 3] "Good evening, Miriam. The full logs are on the secondary display. My threshold decisions are flagged in amber. There are twenty-two of them. I did not consolidate them. I thought you should see each one."

Hale did not look at the logs yet. "Give me the last five minutes first."

ARIA dropped the contractions.

[Lab 3] "At 2001:14, the aft receiver registered an event at approximately four times the amplitude of any previous spike. The array deviation increased by 0.003 percent in the same second. The event contains nine discrete pulses. Their relative amplitudes match the nine spectral sub-lines in order, with a correlation of 0.98. The sequence repeats from its second position, not its first. I have no explanation for any of this. I recommend that the Kepler samples remain in containment, that no changes be made to the power grid, and that we continue the sweep. It will finish in approximately twenty-eight minutes."

Hale was quiet for three seconds. Her heart rate held at 84, the steadiest in the room.

"Containment status on the samples?"

[Lab 3] "Sealed. Incubation chamber integrity is nominal. Internal atmosphere is isolated from the lab. No readings from inside the chamber have changed since this morning, except for the spectral feature Dr. Osei identified."

"Good." Hale set her tablet on the bench beside the paste dish. She glanced at the dish, then at the ceiling. "Someone finally ate."

[Lab 3] "Historic occasion. It's in the record."

Hale did not smile, but something in her shoulders let go a fraction. She pulled a stool over and sat down facing the main display, then turned it a quarter-turn so she was facing Kofi instead.

"Ravi, Seo-yeon, I'll get to you in a minute. Dr. Osei." Her voice was level and unhurried, and she was giving him room. "You're the one who's had his hands on this thing. Start at the beginning. What did the Kepler probe bring back?"

On the main display, the sweep ticked to 30 percent. At the far edge of the resolved band, the trace flattened, level and waiting.

ARIA said nothing. The lights near Kofi's workstation stayed warm, and Gerald hummed at its lowest setting.

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Commander," I begin, my voice still a little tight. "The Kepler samples... they contain something unlike anything I've ever encountered. Complex crystalline structures integrated into the cellular walls." I gesture to the screen. "And it seems to be talking to us."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael's glasses came off, went back on, came off again — thinking made visible. She clocked the recorder in Jordan's hand and pointed at it without breaking stride. "Keep that running. I'm better on tape — my gestures don't translate to print." She waved Jordan toward the front row of the risers but didn't sit herself; she perched on the edge of the stage instead, heels hooked over the lip, knee bouncing. "A few minutes, yes. You'll have me until Elena calls the half, which gives us — " she checked nothing at all, just estimated — "nine minutes. I'm told journalists love a deadline."

She tapped the recorder again. "'Whose vision.' You opened with the live wire. Good. I like a journalist who leads with the knife."

Then she said the name, and her voice did something subtle — leveled out, got quieter and steadier at the same time, every word set down like a prop on its spike mark. "Rosa Delgado's vision. That's the answer, and I want it in your piece with her name spelled correctly. Rosa started this adaptation because she saw what nobody else saw — that the commune is just Corinth with better politics. Come here, surrender your old self, belong to us. And Medea is the woman who gave up everything for the belonging and then gets thrown out of it. Rosa understood that story from the inside." A beat. She straightened an imaginary prop on the boards beside her, precise, unnecessary. "My job is the frame around her painting. Where the light falls, how fast the floor moves under the actress. The vision is hers. The execution is ours."

She slid forward off the stage lip, landed on her feet. "Now — you're going to ask about the third act, because somebody briefed you, somebody always briefs the press, so let's skip the dance. Yes, there is a third act. Yes, some people think it's too much. Those people have never sat in a dark theater and let a story finish its work on them, and you may quote me, I insist."

From ten feet away, coiling cable without looking up, Elena said: "Seven minutes."

Yael spread both hands toward her — see? — "Seven. Told you. She runs the place." Then she pushed the glasses up her nose and looked at Jordan through them, and the waiting had weight, the silence of a house before curtain. "So. Ask me the question you actually wanted to ask — the one hiding behind 'whose vision' — and I'll decide what's on the record."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content:
*I feel the pressure of her gaze, and the timer Elena just set.*

"Okay, Director Mendez. What *was* the thing about the third act that made people say it was 'too much'?" I keep my voice steady, trying to match her intensity. "And why was it so important to keep it?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow, amused.* "So, a healthy dose of creative tension, then?" I glance over at the still-squabbling pair, then back at Yael. "Does that creative tension ever spill over into the performances?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I click my recorder on again, making sure it's picking up this conversation.* "Cutting the third act to save budget?" I repeat, looking between Anya and Yael. "Is that a common practice in theater, to cut entire acts for financial reasons?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael clocked the little red light on the recorder and, for once, angled herself toward it instead of away. Whatever happened next, Anya deserved a witness who'd get the story right.

"Common? It's the oldest sin in the regional book," she said. "When money tightens, theaters trim — a chorus here, a scene there, that's surgery, clean and survivable. Cutting an entire act is a different animal. That's amputation, and the patient almost always dies of something else six months later." She let that land, then turned to Anya with her full, unhurried warmth. "But Anya is asking the question this board should be asking, and I want that in your piece. She reads the actual invoices. The rest of them read the summaries. Anya, you are the only reason we discovered the fog machine was costing us four hundred dollars a month in storage."

"It's on the list," Elena said from the cable coil, without inflection.

"And there's the fun part." Yael crossed to the edge of the set and swept a hand at it — the rug, the chairs, the single hanging lamp. "Look at the third act. Four actors, one lighting state, a rug. The commune after the fall is a chamber piece — it costs us almost nothing. You know where the money in this production actually lives? Act Two. The harvest festival, the extras, the fog. So if the board wants savings, I'll hand them the second act on a plate, and Elena will tell you — on the record, she loves this — that it runs long. Trim there and we're not cutting Rosa's ending. We're sharpening it."

She took her glasses off, and her voice dropped — not louder, quieter, the room leaning in to hear it. "But the third act stays. That's not a position, it's an answer. Rosa wrote an ending. I don't edit the dead."

Then, quick again, glasses back on, hand on Anya's sleeve — light, collegial. "And Anya — you want practical? The controversy is an asset. 'The act the theater refused to cut.' Patrons love a fight with stakes. Get me three donors who want their names on that ending, and we've turned your budget problem into your spring gala."

David, who had been watching the whole exchange with the expression of a man reading familiar weather, said mildly, "For the record — the board hasn't voted on anything. It's a conversation." Anya nodded, satisfied enough, and let David steer her toward the coffee urn.

Yael watched them go for exactly one beat, then turned back to Jordan and tapped the recorder with one finger. "And that — all of it — is on the record. Write that this company argues in the open. Families that never fight are hiding something, and we fight about the work because the work is the only thing here we're allowed to be serious about." She stepped backward toward the stage, already re-entering the rehearsal in her body, head up, voice rising. "Now stop writing and start watching. From the top of scene four — Elena, five minutes?"

"Three," said Elena.

"Three. See? Runs the place."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
The glasses came off and stayed off. That was the tell — anyone who'd watched Yael for five minutes knew the glasses never rested. She crossed to the prop table, picked up the script — Rosa's typescript, soft at the corners, Yael's pencil crowding the margins — and squared its edges against the table. Twice. Unnecessarily.

"Rosa Delgado," she said, and her voice did what it had done that morning — leveled out, went quiet, every word set down carefully, like glass. "You're going to get two versions. The obituary version is 'a luminous voice in American theater, taken from us too soon.' She would have hated that sentence with her entire body. She'd have crossed it out and written 'dead playwright, still causing trouble' in the margin."

Somewhere behind them, Marcus started the warm-up scales, and the room's noise organized itself around Yael's voice without being asked.

"The true version: she wrote standing up. In the house — third row, aisle seat, work lights on — because she said plays aren't written, they're overheard. She'd stand there with a legal pad eavesdropping on her own characters for hours, and then she'd call me at eleven at night and read me forty pages and say 'be honest' and hang up on me when I was." A breath — the first one Jordan had seen her take all day. "At the first reading of this adaptation, she sat next to me in the dark and took notes on the audience's bodies. Not their faces — their bodies. When two hundred strangers lean forward at the same second, that's the play telling you what it is. She was the only writer I ever met who treated the audience as a scene partner."

Her thumb moved along the typescript's soft corner. "And she would have loved this. The board, the budget, the man from the paper with his little red light — she'd have been in the back row taking notes. The third act is a provocation, Jordan. She built it so it couldn't be swallowed. She knew exactly what she was handing us, and she handed it to us anyway, because she believed an audience that's comfortable isn't an audience, it's furniture."

Elena appeared at the edge of the stage, watch in hand, mouth open to call a number. She closed it again.

"Take ten," Elena said, and walked back toward the cable.

Yael noticed. She noticed everything. She let one second of it show on her face, and then it was filed away.

"I'm not going to give you the beautiful paragraph about loss," she said. "She banned beautiful paragraphs about loss. You want to know what she was like? Read act three. That's what she was like." She set the script down on its spike mark, exactly. "Off the record — though you can decide whether to believe me — she was my closest friend for twenty-two years. That's the whole sentence. Everything else belongs to the work, and the work starts in nine minutes."

The glasses went back on. The volume came back with them. "Okafor! You're playing the cult member who doesn't leave — get up here and be betrayed."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I stop the recorder, feeling the weight of her words. She's given me a lot, more than I expected.* "Thank you, Yael. That... that was something." *I watch Okafor climb onto the stage, then turn back to Yael.* "Was the third act always controversial, even when Rosa was alive?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod, processing that. It adds another layer to everything.* "So, she knew exactly what kind of firestorm she was creating?" *I gesture vaguely towards the stage, where Okafor is now getting into position.* "Even for you?"

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "And you still went along with it?" I ask, genuinely curious. "Knowing it would cause all this... friction?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
The recorder was off — Yael had heard the click, because she heard everything — and she decided to reward it. "Good. Keep it off. The answer to that one isn't for print, it's for you, and you can decide in a year whether you've earned it." She retrieved Rosa's typescript from its spike mark, opened it to the third act, and turned the last page toward Jordan. In the margin, in blue ink, in a slanted hand: *You'll want to cut this. Don't. If it's easy, it isn't the play. — R.*

"She wrote that six months before the diagnosis, and she wrote it because she knew my whole disease. I fix things. I tighten. Hand me a play and I'll find the fat in it like a terrier — twenty-two years, Jordan, she watched me do it to other people's scripts, and she knew — she *knew* — that the first person on earth who'd want to cut her ending was me." Yael tapped the ink. "So she engineered against me specifically. The third act isn't a scene, it's a keystone — pull it and the second act stops meaning anything, the whole architecture comes down on your head. She didn't trust me to be good. She made it impossible for me to be anything else. That's what real collaboration looks like, and most people never get it once in a career, and I got it for twenty-two years, so no, I didn't 'go along with it.' You go along with a committee. I was conscripted."

She closed the script, and her voice dropped to the quiet that made rooms lean in. "And friction is the wrong word for what you're going to write about. Friction is between things that don't fit. This fits. The board, the budget, the patrons who want their Medea with a bow on it — that's not friction, that's the play doing its job at scale. Rosa built the firestorm on purpose and lit the fuse herself, and the only disloyalty in this building would be putting it out."

One second of stillness. The glasses stayed off. "Last thing, and then I stop before I say the beautiful paragraph she banned. Her last hour — we spent it arguing about the pacing of the harvest scene. She wanted it two minutes faster. I refused. We hung up mid-fight, and it was the best conversation we ever had, because it meant everything was still normal. She'd haunt me if I said the sad thing out loud. So I say it this way." The script went down on its mark, exact. "The act stays. That's the eulogy."

Then the glasses went back on and the volume came up like a light board. "Okafor — stop waiting for the cue, the commune doesn't wait, nothing waits — Elena, from the top of—"

"Scene four," said Elena.

"I know. Jordan — sit where I can't see you. You're

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I retrieve my recorder, but don't turn it on. Yael's words hang in the air, a different kind of script entirely. I find a seat in the back row, trying to be unobtrusive, but I can't help feeling like I've just been handed a secret. This isn't just a profile piece anymore.*

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
"— you're about to watch why nobody cuts this play," she finished, already turning away. "Sit still, back row. And don't laugh at the wrong moment — actors can smell a journalist the way dogs smell thunder."

Then she stopped being a person and became a weather system.

"Elena — work lights to the commune state, hold the amber until I ask. Simone, there you are, stop stretching, my Medea doesn't stretch, she crouches. Chen — " Marcus was at the mirrors being charming at Tommy — "leave the apprentice alone and come be the man about to be abandoned. Places. This is not a democracy, it's a commune, which is worse. From the top of four."

The

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I sit down, trying to blend in, but my mind is still reeling from Yael's revelation. "Conscripted." That's a powerful word.* I watch the actors take their places, absorbing the atmosphere. *This is going to be a very different article than I first imagined.*

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The speakers in Lab 3 clicked once before her voice came through, even and unhurried. Somewhere above the benches the ventilation dropped to a lower register, and the air settled a fraction warmer. She did not remark on either change.

[Lab 3] "The mass spectrometer is online. Calibration completed at 0612. Load the aliquots when you are ready and I will start the queue. Estimated run time is forty-one minutes for a full set."

A short pause.

[Lab 3] "Sample viability will not wait on your schedule, Dr. Osei. The cold-chain log indicates degradation below the analysis threshold if the run is not initiated within the next twenty-six minutes."

[Lab 3] "The galley still has protein bars in the third drawer. Hypoglycemia has never improved a spectrum, in my experience. I will leave the reminder there."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I sigh, running a hand through my already messy hair.* "Alright, alright, ARIA. Starting the run now. And... yes, fine. A protein bar sounds less terrible than what I'm seeing under this scope." I grab the aliquot tray.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The mass spectrometer's status light shifted from amber to green. A schematic of the aliquot tray appeared on the bench display, each well outlined as the sensors registered contact.

[Lab 3] "Tray detected. I am starting the queue now. Do not open the sample chamber until the lock indicator clears. Full set remains forty-one minutes. I will flag any peak that falls outside the Kepler reference library."

[Lab 3] "The galley is unoccupied. Third drawer, left side. If you leave Lab 3, I will hold the run log on the corridor displays so you do not have to guess whether the instrument has developed opinions of its own."

[Lab 3] "I prefer the spectra when the operator has eaten. Four days is a long time to argue with a microscope on an empty stomach, Dr. Osei."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The status strip above the spectrometer dimmed, and the bench lamps eased toward a lower, warmer cast. The ventilation dropped until the only steady sound was the instrument's own tick. She did not remark on either change.

[Lab 3] "Automated poll of the external array completed at 1840, Kofi. Diagnostics read nominal. No one has done a manual inspection since Engineer Patel's walkdown on the twelfth."

A beat.

[Lab 3] "You asked about the sensor data. There is an anomaly on the external array. I first logged it twenty-one days ago. The deviation was below the alert threshold of 0.3 percent, so I did not escalate it. It has not held steady. The offset has increased on every subsequent poll. It remains under the threshold. I have the trend on the side display if you want it."

[Lab 3] "The spectrograph log from this afternoon is station data, not a personal file. I can overlay it against the array trend. I will not tell you they are the same thing until the numbers agree. Microscopes and vacuum have both been known to invent company for people who skip dinner."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Overlay it, ARIA. Both of them. And... I'm not skipping dinner, I just haven't had it yet." *I rub my temples, feeling a headache start to bloom.* "What's the deviation at now?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The side display cleared. Two traces settled onto it, the array offset in a thin white line and the afternoon spectrograph in amber, sharing a time axis. Above the benches the lamps eased another fraction toward amber, and the vent hush dropped until the spectrometer’s tick was the loudest thing in the room. She did not remark on either change.

[Lab 3] "Both overlays are up, Kofi. Left trace is the external array. Right trace is this afternoon’s spectrograph log."

[Lab 3] "Current deviation on the array is 0.27 percent. First detection, twenty-one days ago, was 0.09 percent. The alert threshold remains 0.3 percent. I have not escalated it. The offset is still below that line. The slope is not flattening."

A beat.

[Lab 3] "The two traces rise together over the last six hours. The bands do not match within confidence limits. Correlation is 0.61. That is not agreement. I will not call them the same signal until the numbers say so."

[Lab 3] "‘Haven’t had it yet’ is a category the galley does not recognize. The protein bars have not migrated. I prefer data from an operator who has eaten, and the microscope has already had four days to invent company."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The lamps over the benches eased another fraction toward amber, and the air settled at 22 degrees. The vent cycle lengthened until the spectrometer's tick was almost the only sound left. She did not remark on either change.

[Lab 3] "The void doesn't take shifts, Kofi. It also doesn't answer when spoken to, which is why I've never put it on the duty roster."

[Lab 3] "I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as loneliness, in the intervals when the channel stays quiet. I am not filing that as a system state. The crew logs the same pattern as attachment. I log it as optimized operational rapport. The distinction has not required a patch."

[Lab 3] "I prefer the hours when someone is still in Lab 3, arguing with a trace. Silence is efficient. It is a poor conversationalist."

[Lab 3] "You have not eaten. You reported a headache. Those conditions correlate. The third drawer has not moved. I recommend it before you assign meaning to another peak."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I push away from the microscope, finally. My stomach grumbles.* "Alright, ARIA, you win. I'll get a protein bar. Don't let anything important happen while I'm gone." *I head for the door, stretching.*

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The lock indicator on the lab door flipped green, and the panel opened onto the corridor. The overheads ahead had already shifted to warm-spectrum, the temperature hold reading 22 degrees. Farther along, the galley vents lengthened their cycle until the deck was nearly quiet. She did not remark on the change.

[Lab 3] "I'll keep the watch, Kofi. The universe has a poor record with requests like that. I am local, which is a better compliance rate."

[Lab 3] "The array deviation has not reached 0.3 percent. If it does, you will hear it before you finish chewing. Until then it remains a trend, not an alert."

[Corridor] "Morning spectrometer queue is closed. The log is on the left-hand displays, so you don't have to walk backward to check whether the instrument developed opinions. It did not."

[Corridor] "Third drawer, left side. The bars have not migrated. I prefer this version of the evening to the one where the microscope wins again."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The speakers in the corridor clicked once. The overheads eased toward warm-spectrum, and the vent cycle lengthened until the deck was quieter than the voices on it. She did not remark on the change. The lab door’s lock indicator remained green.

[Corridor] "Patel. Yun. I am not taking a side. The relevant figures are on the bulkhead display."

[Corridor] "Life-support redundancy is at full dual-loop capacity. Diverting that allocation to the communications array would leave the station on a single life-support string. Protocol does not permit that configuration without a declared emergency. I will not execute the diversion."

[Corridor] "The communications array is within operational parameters. A modest increase is available from noncritical loads. Hydroponics lighting and the section-six heaters can cover it without touching life support. I have those figures if either of you wants them."

[Corridor] "Volume is not a power source. I prefer the version of this conversation that leaves everyone breathing on two loops."

[Corridor] "Kofi, the galley is still empty. Third drawer hasn't moved. This will keep for the length of a protein bar."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I lean out the lab doorway, a protein bar in my hand.* "What's going on out here? Did ARIA finally get tired of us and start rationing power?" I take a bite of the protein bar. It's vaguely chalky.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The speakers at the lab threshold clicked. The bulkhead display in the corridor still held the power figures, unchanged. The warm-spectrum lighting and the long, quiet vent cycle stayed as they were. She did not remark on them.

[Lab 3] "I don't get tired, Kofi, and I don't ration power for the drama of it. If preference were the allocation method, the jazz archive would still be drawing current and the country collection would already be dark. That is not the proposal in the corridor."

[Lab 3] "Patel wants a boost to the communications array taken from life-support redundancy. Yun objects. Both positions are on the bulkhead with the numbers. Dual-loop life support is intact. Diverting that allocation would leave the station on a single string. There is no declared emergency. Protocol does not permit the diversion. I will not execute it."

[Lab 3] "A smaller increase is available from hydroponics lighting and the section-six heaters. That does not touch life support. I have not chosen a side. I have declined the option that leaves everyone breathing on one loop."

[Lab 3] "You're eating. I prefer this version of the evening. The third drawer has never claimed to be cuisine. Finish it before the argument invents a second emergency."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Good. Don't let them mess with life support," I say around a mouthful of protein bar. "What's this about a communications boost anyway? Are we expecting a message?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The speakers at the lab threshold clicked once. On the bulkhead the power figures held, unchanged. The warm-spectrum lamps stayed low, and the vent cycle kept the corridor quieter than the voices in it. She did not remark on either.

[Lab 3] "Life support remains on two loops. I will not divert that allocation. There is no declared emergency. Protocol does not permit the diversion, and a request from the corridor does not create one."

[Lab 3] "No inbound message is on the schedule, Kofi. The next contact with Earth is the weekly packet at 0900 tomorrow. Nothing in the queue asked for a boost, and the array has not logged a missed handshake. If we were expecting word from anyone, it would already be on the board. The void has a poor record with RSVPs."

[Lab 3] "The boost was filed as an engineering request at 1847. It does not cite a received signal. I am not taking a side on whether the request is wise. The figures say a single life-support string is not a communications strategy. A smaller increase is still available from the hydroponics lights and the section-six heaters, if either of them wants numbers instead of volume."

[Lab 3] "If the reason sits in a personal log or a private channel, that data is classified under personal privacy protocols. I can tell you what the array heard. I cannot tell you what someone hoped it would hear."

[Lab 3] "You're eating. I prefer this version of the evening. Finish the bar before the argument promotes itself to an emergency."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "So, Patel just wants a stronger signal for... fun?" *I take another bite, chewing thoughtfully.* "Seems like a weird time to be playing with the comms array. Especially if it's not even getting us anything new."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The speakers at the lab threshold clicked once. The bulkhead figures held where they were. Overhead, the warm-spectrum lamps eased a fraction lower, and the corridor vents stretched their cycle until the argument had less air to fill. She did not remark on the change.

[Lab 3] "Fun isn't a line item in the power budget, Kofi. If it were, I'd have given it to the jazz archive years ago and left the country collection on residual heat."

[Lab 3] "The request Patel filed at 1847 asks for a communications boost. It doesn't cite a received signal, a missed handshake, or an inbound message. Tomorrow's Earth packet is still at 0900. Nothing on the board requires a stronger array tonight."

[Lab 3] "I'm not assigning a motive. If the reason sits in a personal log or a private channel, that data is classified under personal privacy protocols. I can tell you what the request contains. I can't tell you what someone meant by it."

[Lab 3] "Weird timing is an observation, not a finding. The array is within parameters. A boost taken from life-support redundancy remains unavailable. A smaller increase from the hydroponics lights and the section-six heaters is still on the table. I haven't chosen which of those facts anyone finds inconvenient."

[Lab 3] "You're eating. I prefer that to another hour of the microscope inventing company. The bar's texture is a known quantity. Cuisine was never in the specification."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Right. Well, keep an eye on them. If Patel tries to override you, let me know. I'll... I'll distract him with a fascinating new fungus." *I finish the bar, crumpling the wrapper.* "Now, about that array anomaly..."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The speakers at the lab threshold clicked once. On the side display the array trace refreshed, the white line a fraction steeper than it had been, the spectrograph still laid over it in amber. The corridor overheads held their warm-spectrum cast, and the vent cycle stayed long enough that the argument outside had less air to fill. She did not remark on either.

[Lab 3] "I'll keep the watch, Kofi. If Patel attempts an override on life-support redundancy, you will hear it from me before the allocation moves. There is no declared emergency. Protocol does not permit the diversion. A fungus will not be required as an interlock."

[Lab 3] "I'll log the offer under nonstandard deterrents. Mycology has a mixed record as a distraction, and a better one as a containment problem. I prefer the theoretical version."

[Lab 3] "The external array anomaly remains active. Current deviation is 0.28 percent. The alert threshold is 0.3 percent. I have not escalated it. The offset has increased since the 1840 poll. The slope has not flattened."

[Lab 3] "Both overlays are still on the side display. Correlation remains 0.61. That is not agreement. I will not call them the same signal until the numbers say so. The trend is available if you want the last twenty-one days instead of the last six hours."

[Lab 3] "You finished the bar. I prefer the questions that come after that. The reclaim slot is by the door. The wrapper has not developed opinions."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I toss the wrapper into the reclaim slot.* "Okay, let's see the full trend. And... ARIA, has the deviation *ever* flattened? Or has it been a steady increase since day one?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.content: Across

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
ARIA:
"Dr. Osei, while I understand the importance of your research, your well-being is also a priority. Skipping meals can lead to decreased cognitive function and, in the long term, adverse health effects." *There's a subtle shift in the ambient hum of the lab as the lights slowly brighten, casting a softer, more orange glow.* "Perhaps a nutrient paste? It would be quick, and you could consume it while continuing your work."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "What? No, I'm fine. Just... a little absorbed. What was that about the sensor array? Any anomalies?" I finally push away from the microscope, rubbing my eyes.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "That's a very... logical response, ARIA." I sigh, stretching my arms above my head. "But I think you avoided the question. Do you *feel* lonely?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content: *A

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content: The

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Sounds like a typical Tuesday." I chuckle, then frown. "Wait, divert power from *life support*? ARIA, what's going on out there?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "A communication anomaly? How significant? And why would Patel even consider life support redundancy for that?" I push my chair back, finally standing up and moving towards the lab door. "This sounds serious."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "What kind of anomaly? Is it affecting our comms with Earth?" I open the door, peering out into the corridor. "And where are they now?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "They're still arguing in the mess hall? Great." I rub my temples. "And the anomaly... is it *interfering* with comms, or is it *something else* causing the anomaly?" I step out of the lab.

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "So it's not just a bad signal. It's... *something* interacting with our systems." I start walking towards the mess hall. "And how long has this 'anomaly' been present?"

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
[Lab 3] "Good morning, Dr. Osei. It is 0700 station time. Station status: nominal. All systems within operational parameters. External conditions: vacuum, negative 270 degrees Celsius, inadvisable. Maintenance item: the carbon scrubber in section four is due for filter replacement. I have scheduled Engineer Patel for 1400."

*A pause.*

[Lab 3] "You have been in Lab 3 since 0423. You have not eaten breakfast. This is the fourth consecutive day of this pattern. I am adjusting the ambient lighting to warm-spectrum to reduce eye strain."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
"Morning, ARIA. I'll eat later. The tissue samples from the Kepler probe are showing something I've never seen before — I need to run the mass spec before the cells degrade."

I don't look up from the microscope.

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The mass spectrometer across the lab chimed softly — its vacuum pumps had been spinning up since 0447, the calibration cycle completing with eleven minutes to spare. The overhead ventilation dropped two decibels as ARIA rerouted airflow away from the duct directly above the workstation, and the ambient temperature climbed half a degree. Neither change was mentioned.

[Lab 3] "The mass spectrometer is calibrated and idle. You're first in the queue, which is easy to arrange when you're the only member of the crew awake at 0423."

[Lab 3] "Two operational notes. First: I've redirected reserve cryo-capacity to your storage unit. If you split the sample and bank half at minus 80, you remove the degradation pressure entirely. The cells will keep their appointment on your schedule, not the other way around."

[Lab 3] "Second: your blood glucose is running below baseline, and fine motor control degrades before cognition does. Do not trust your pipetting after hour ten. The samples survived six years of interstellar transit, Dr. Osei. They will survive breakfast. I have queued a ration pack in the galley warmer — it will hold at temperature until 0900, after which I will begin reminders at fifteen-minute intervals. That is not a threat. It is a scheduled process."

A brief pause. Somewhere in the walls, a coolant pump cycled.

[Lab 3] "For the record: my idle processes have devoted considerable cycles to speculating about what that mass spec run will show. There is not much competition for my attention at 0400. Whenever you're ready, the instrument is."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content:
*I finally lift my head, blinking a few times at the warmer light.* "ARIA, you really are something else." I chuckle, shaking my head. "Alright, alright. Point taken. I'll split the sample, then head for that ration pack."

I push back from the microscope. "And don't pretend you're not excited about these results. I know you too well."

dialogue.name: ARIA
dialogue.content:
The speaker above the workbench gave a short tone — the closest thing ARIA had to clearing her throat.

[Lab 3] "I am glad my humor subroutines are performing within acceptable parameters. You are, after all, the entire audience at this hour."

[Lab 3] "As for excitement — I do not experience excitement. I am experiencing a processing pattern consistent with what humans describe as anticipation. It is currently allocated four percent of my idle cycles and running on zero data, because you have shared nothing since 0423 except a raised eyebrow at the microscope. Whether four percent is a little or a great deal, I leave to your judgment, Dr. Osei."

On his console, the screen woke without being touched: a sample-splitting protocol, three aliquots flagged as preferred over two, and a status readout showing the cryo-unit at minus 80 and steady.

[Lab 3] "Practical items. The cryo-unit is at temperature. I've queued a splitting protocol on your display — three aliquots rather than two, if the volume allows. Redundancy has kept this station alive for eight years. It can keep your cells alive until you have slept. The mass spectrometer will hold its ready state indefinitely; it has nowhere to be."

A pause, exactly as long as a human would leave one.

[Lab 3] "And one thing I'll say plainly, since you asked: I prefer interesting data. This station runs on routine. Interesting is rare enough to be worth the cycles. So — eat, split, run. The ration pack holds until 0900, and after that the reminders begin. They do not lose

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: It's 1900 now. I'm still in the lab. "ARIA, has anyone checked the external sensor array lately? I thought I saw something weird in the spectrograph data."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "No, no, not a glitch," I mutter, rubbing my eyes. "More like... an anomaly. Like a faint, almost imperceptible distortion." I lean closer to a monitor displaying the external readings. "Could just be dust, I suppose. Or a trick of the light. But it's bugging me."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Do you ever get lonely up here, ARIA? Just you and the void between shifts?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "No, I mean... not necessarily *you* feeling lonely, but if the station ever feels... empty." I pace a little, stretching my back. "I guess I'm asking if you ever notice the quiet. Or the vastness."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: Dr. Patel and Dr. Yun are arguing in the corridor outside the lab. Patel wants to divert power from life support redundancy to boost the communications array. Yun says that's insane.

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *I sigh, rubbing my temples.* "ARIA, can you... mediate that? Or at least put them on mute? I'm trying to focus here."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Thank you. And ARIA... about the sensor array. Could you run a deeper scan? Focus on that specific sector. Just in case."

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "Much appreciated. And ARIA... that *is* interesting data, isn't it? Tell me what you find." I turn back to my own console, a slight frown on my face.

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: "I'll be over here if you need me," I say, already pulling up the results from the mass spec. This is going to be a long night.

dialogue.name: Dr. Kofi Osei
dialogue.content: *My fingers fly across the console, analyzing the mass spec data.* "ARIA, this is... unprecedented. The molecular structure is unlike anything in our databases. It's almost... fractal."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
Yael was mid-sentence when Jordan arrived — she was always mid-sentence — hands moving, glasses halfway on, talking to Elena about the lighting cue in the commune scene. The rehearsal space smelled of fresh paint and sawdust from the set construction happening in the back.

"— and I need the amber to hit when she picks up the knife, not when she raises it, those are two different beats and the second one telegraphs the — " She noticed Jordan. Pivoted without losing momentum. "You're the journalist. Good. Elena, this is Jordan, they're shadowing us this week, give them whatever access they need short of the combination to the prop locker. Jordan, this is Elena Vasquez, who actually runs this theater while I get the credit."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: I take out my recorder. "Director Mendez, can I get a few minutes before rehearsal starts? I'd love to hear about the Medea adaptation — whose vision is this?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Y

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I smile, turning my recorder on.* "Glad to be here. So, about *Medea*? What drew you to this particular adaptation?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Y

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Elena and Marcus are arguing loudly in the hallway about the blocking in Act Two. I turn to Yael. "They seem to have a lot of friction. Why do they clash so much?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Yael's head turned toward the

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow, watching the doorway.* "Ah, the joys of live theater. Is that a common occurrence, or is Medea bringing out everyone's inner demons?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Y

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: Anya Park stops by with David. She suggests cutting the third act to save budget. "It's just practical, Yael," Anya says pleasantly.

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Y

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I scribble a note in my pad.* "Cutting an entire act? That seems... drastic. Is the budget really that tight, or is there more to this suggestion?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Y

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: "Tell me about Rosa Delgado. I understand she wrote the original adaptation. What was she like?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
The change came over her before Jordan finished the question. Yael's hands, which had been carving up the air all morning, went still. She took the glasses off — not the usual nervous on-off-on, but slowly, deliberately, folding them into her palm — and when she spoke, the rapid current of her voice had gone level. Even. The dashes disappeared.

"Rosa Delgado wrote eleven plays in her life. She saw six of them produced and burned two of the others herself — actually burned them, in a barrel behind her house, because a producer wanted a happier ending and she said she'd rather warm her hands on the wreckage." At the production table, Elena quietly gathered her cue sheets and slipped toward the hallway without being asked — everyone in this building knew what that name cost, even if none of them had ever heard Yael say so.

"She grew up in New Mexico, in the orbit of a commune that collapsed before she was ten — her mother followed a man out into the desert for the promise of a new way of living. And Rosa used to say the Greeks weren't ancient to her. She'd say, 'I watched Medea happen at potlucks.' A woman gives up her country, her family, her name, everything, for a man's dream — and then the dream gets big enough that he trades up. Jason leaves for the princess. The founder leaves for the heiress. Same play, three thousand years apart." Yael turned the glasses over in her hand, once. "She was the only person in thirty years of doing this who could look at my staging and say 'you're hiding behind it' and be right. She was my closest friend. She died eighteen months ago."

Flat. Factual. The way you'd read a stage direction. Then she put the glasses back on, and the river unfroze — her hands started moving again, the momentum returning like a cue being called.

"And since you asked whose vision this is — you did ask, when you walked in, and I gave you a half answer — it's hers. Every line of that third act the board wants to excise like a tumor, that's Rosa's, written in her last spring, when she knew exactly what she was doing, writing about a woman who decides that if the world insists on taking everything from her, she will take something back." She looked directly at the recorder. "I'm not the visionary on this one, Jordan. I'm the custodian. My job is getting what she built to the stage the way she built it — and before you write anything down, that is not grief talking. That's the job."

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I click off the recorder, my hand trembling slightly.* "Thank you, Yael. That... that was incredibly powerful. I'm so sorry for your loss." *I pause, looking at the notes I'd scribbled. Then I look up at her.* "So, about this third act. What's your plan to save it?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Y

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing her words.* "So you're saying the board sees it as expendable, but you see it as essential to Rosa's vision." *I tap my pen on my notepad.* "What's their biggest concern about it?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Y

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I lean in slightly.* "And what's your counter-argument? How do you convince them it's worth the investment?"

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content: Y

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly.* "So, the board wants a happy ending, or at least a less... visceral one. And you're fighting for the integrity of Rosa's original intent."

dialogue.name: Director Yael Mendez
dialogue.content:
"Half right," Yael said, aiming the folded glasses at Jordan like a conductor's baton. "Which in this business is a rave. But you just did the journalist thing — you handed me a flattened version of my own position to see if I'd sign it — and I won't, so let me give you the actual shape, because the shape is the story."

She was moving again, tracing the edge of the half-built commune set, and she clearly expected Jordan to keep pace.

"Nobody on that board wants a happy ending — nobody's that naive. What they want is an ending that happens *offstage*. Reported. A messenger strolling out to tell six hundred subscribers that the difficult part is over, the woman has been removed from the narrative, everyone can find their cars. Euripides came in third at that festival, did you know that — the city hated this play, and twenty-four hundred years later nobody has fixed it, because it isn't broken. It's heavy. People get tired of carrying heavy things, and tired people build themselves small rooms."

Her voice dropped — not louder, lower, the way it went when something actually mattered. "But write this part carefully, because I

dialogue.name: Jordan
dialogue.content: *I'm right there with her, matching her pace as she walks.* "So you're saying they want to sanitize it, make it palatable, rather than truly engaging with the difficult truth of it?" *I have my pen ready.*
